First time reviewing a game on Steam, but I really want this game to be good so hopefully this will help out.
Pros
- Amazing world.  It is Lego, the possibilities here are endless.  They could theme each biome after different Lego sets, with cities and people.  I just think it would be amazing if they could have pirate ships patrolling the ocean and planes and spaceships from those sets as well, sprinkling in a city here and there or a Castle and village there.  Really excited about this.
- Building.  As expected, you can build with all of the basic lego shapes, with an addition of some more niche parts.  They also let you paste in existing builds such as a castle or a log cabin, which you can then expand on.  Overall, I like the idea of being able to build much more intricate worlds with this.
Cons
- The Camera needs a lot of work.  It is hard to navigate and it doesn't feel very tight.  It also makes it hard to build - you should never have to worry about the camera or think about what you have to do to see something.
- Because the pieces are much smaller than, say, Minecraft, it takes a very long time to build things.  I'd like to see some improvements and tool additions that would speed this up.  It might already be there, but a copy paste function would be really nice.
- For someone like me, there needs to be a story or objectives to optionally take part in.  Although building is a blast, I want it to be for something.  Some basic ideas are skeleton invasions, where you need to hunker down inside a base, with possibly cannons or other defenses.  Also I was thinking it would be cool if they had something like Dark Cloud, where you were asked to build up a city using a certain theme, and once you had it built with the required pieces and goals met, the village would populate and you interact with the people after.
I don't necessarily want another Minecraft, but one thing that I liked about that game, that I won't find in this, is the mindless mining.  When you just go digging for an hour or so, hollowing out a cave, and then using your rare resources to build the things that you needed.  There was something driving you.  So far, this is really just a Lego designer with skeletons and pre-rendered landscapes.  Don't get me wrong, it is fun (would be more fun with multiplayer for sure) but some people require goals and objectives and the ability to improve your character's position.  This game is pretty static.

If you are looking for a Minecraft-like experience, pass on by.  WHile the game is enjoyable, for a short while, the lack of goals of ANY type, plus no real survival difficulty leads to "exploring" by way walking/flying/driving through different biomes.   You don't even really build or craft, but make pre-selected items.

Game Dev Tycoon is an interesting and surprisingly deep video game development simulation.  In itself, it is a unique game that was an interesting take on the simulation genre.  It was deceptively simple; a few button clicks made a game but one mistake could cost you millions.  That being said, it did a fantastic job of providing numerous oportunities to try different combinations of genres that really gave the game a certain amount of depth that made it worthwhile to play for many hours.  It took a simple concept and continuously expanded on it throughout the duration of the game, to the point where you are developing much more than just video games.  However, it is not a God simulator.  You have to be smart with your money to be successful, which brings the game closer to reality.  All in all, the gameplay itself is intriguing with enough different layers to make you play for hours.
As for the developers, the small indie team did a fantastic job with development.  I have yet to experience a bug, and there is constant communication between the team and the fans.  It makes it seem like they really care about the fans, which they clearly do.  However, this game has been known to be easily pirated.  That being said, this game and the developers deserve every penny for making this game.  I strongly recommend the game, and any other games that Greenheart Games makes.
TLDR; I wholeheartedly recommend this game because it is unique and has a depth rare in many games these days, along with having a fantastic indie development team.

Stronghold Kingdoms offers an interesting combination of long-range and short-term tactical planning, strategic management of resources, and interaction with other players via a number of in-game and third party communication apps. The game mechanics allow players to choose from a variety of 'roles' within a faction and house, yet are flexible enough to allow a player to 'go it alone' and still have a reasonable chance of surviving. I particularly like how there are many layers to the game, and how the various aspects of those layers interact. As there are several 'roles' one can choose to play, there are also several ways to accomplish things in the game.
Research points, one of the basic elements of the game without which nothing could be done, can be obtained through either focusing on gaining honor in order to level up, by focusing on earning gold to buy them, or through a more balanced approach, combining both methods. Honor can be 'farmed' by manipulating food and ale rations and the tax rate. Honor is also earned through banqueting, attacking, defending, diplomacy, completing certain quests, and accomplishing achievements. Gold can also be 'farmed' like honor, and can be earned by selling excess materials, raiding enemies, and by completing quests.
Villages are where the player goes about transforming completed research into the material necessary to build a sronghold. In keeping with the freedom and variety theme, the food, ale, weapons, and building materials required by villagers can be produced in the villages, bought with merchants, pillaged from enemies, and yes, won as a reward for completing quests.
Not least of all, castles are used to defend the player's holdings. The appeal to this aspect of the game is that the player builds, maintains, and garrisons the castle himself (or herself). As with all the other elements in the game, castles can be improved through research.
An annoying but necessary feature of the game is the steady increase in time required to research and the increased cost and completion time of village buildings. However, this drawback is offset because as the player grows, the demands of logistics increase, requiring that less time be spent on the basics of village building and research, and more time be spent on scouting and attacking enemies, transferring, buying, and selling materials, and general maintenance of castles and villages. As the player interacts with other players, he or she may become involved in the politics of faction and house, which can be very time-consuming.
An extremely useful element of the game are cards, which are gained over time and by completing specific quests. Cards provide a wide range of enhancements and beneficial effects. Additionally, there are two other more advanced key elements to the game: monking, which bestows or inflicts many different parish and village bonuses and penalties, and stewardship, which entails the control and maintenance of parishes, counties, provinces, and countries.
Finally, the in-game tutorial is strongly recommended at the beginning of a game, as it provides many bonuses and extra resources with which to start a stronghold.
I do recommend this game to others.

I'll just say this really quick: Warhammer 40K: Space Marine is a fun game. It's only weaknesses aren't necessarily things it did wrong, but that it couldn't expand upon what it had leaving me with a sense "it could have been so much more!"
Rather than listing pros and cons I think it'd be better to discuss things in sections, no story spoilers!
[Gameplay]:
Shooting: Shooting in this game is just fine. Not ground breaking but mechanically sound. You have a pistol and asault rifle basicaly for all of the game which get upgraded. Your other two weapon slots are reserved for a variety of other weapons in the game, some of which can't be held in conjunction with others. You never feel under armed and there was plenty of tactical choise as well guns were usefull in the right circumstances (and looked damn cool). This game also isn't stingy with your ammo capacity, you only keep running to ammo crates because you keep expanding lots of ammo but yet never feel like you are purposesly being capped low.
The main weakness of shooting is that it felt like it needed  a cover system. Hiding behind certain objects without the ability to duck was annoying at times. The right stick for mostly unused for clicking except for one weapon to change the zoom level while using its scope. Otherwise it was free.
Melee: There are three weapons in the game and both felt mighty and powerful. The chainsword was, IMO, great for fast attacks with a good single target DPS. The axe was slower and IDK how well it did for single target damage, but many of its combos did broad sweeps hitting multipel enemies at once. Basically good soft AOE. The hammer hit the hardest, some attacks could hit multipel targets if times adn aimed right and it could stagger some enemies. Main weakness was that it was also slow and the game didn't let you use any guns other than your pistol and AR type weapon. Basically a situational thing.
Melee's main weakness was that it wasn't developed enough. Each weapon had five combo attacks. There was a basic attack button, a stun (which only worked when an enemy could be sent into the execution state), an execution to gain back base health (there was also a rechargable energy shield) and a dodge roll. The stun didn't do much unless it was part of a combo, and even then it was only effective if the enemy's health was low enough to be ready to be executed. There were painfully few executions; each weapon had effectively two animations for basic (AKA the weaker orcs you see throughout the game) and only one for stronger (AKA later game enemies that constitute all enemies eventually) enemies.
As amusing as it was to slam a hammer into an orc's balls and watch Titus reach into its mouth to rip its skull apart, it got old.
Dodge roll was servicable for shooting combat but felt slow and not swiftly responsive for melee use. It also didn't knock enemies out of your way despite Titus being heavy and strong enough to do so against most.
The lack of a counter/block/parry system really hurt melee combat. The game felt like such a thing belonged in it and some enemies charge you, can't get staggered normally and have lots of health so it takes a lot to get them ready for execute. Since I couldn't counter there attacks I often died if I tried to fight them head on so I kept running back to shoot at them. Melee really did not seem as strong as it should have been.
The Fury Mode: Fury mode had a bar that filled as you did damage. Once activated it made your melee attacks stronger or, if you aimed time slowed down to make you a better shot. Problem was that slow-mo didn't feel usefull except for a few times. Since melee combat wasn't strong I wasn't confident in using it.
Its main utility was to regenerate your base health. However, I am a rather silly person and managed to not notice this until I was almost done with the game. :(
[Level Design]:
Initially the levels were pretty neat, big epic spralling landscapes, huge buildings, etc. Except the game didn't really have much else. The environments got old and the set pieces for fights got reused over and over again. These areas weren't bad, but they just got old. It didn't help that there weren't enough enemy types. I got sick of fighting the orcs by the time another faction showed up and they got old by the last couple of levels as well.
There were also long stretches were the environment didn't change at all, no story bits happened or character quips, so fighting room after room of enemies got tedious. While the game actually has a large variety of things it gave you to do, it also had to pad itself too much.
There were a couple of boss fights but nothing of worth. Mechanics weren't really there, just bullet sponges who three mooks at you to keep things interesting. I'll forget their names by tomorrow, and within the next couple of days to a week I won't even remember what they looked like. It's not like there aesthetic design was bad, there just wasn't enough character there to remember.
[Story]:
The story was only okay. I've only read about WH40K before so some stuff at the beginning was nice because it was unfamiliar. Maybe some later stuff would have been more interesiting if I was knowledgable but for a series novice I just didn't see it. It did have a great premise and bullet point plot though so with some eleboration and added bits it could have been a fine story.
There were some collectable audio logs but as they were really just letting you know other people were getting killed besides you. Some side bits were interesting but I've already forgotten a bunch of them.
Length-wise I beat it in 10-11 hours on the hardest difficulty, though the game definately felt padded to get itself that long. Note that I didn't try too hard to find the collectable audio logs so I'm guessing this is close to average.
[Acting]:
Was only okay. Some characters didn't have good actors. Others felt like their actors could be decent if given better direction for tonal and emotional range.
[Most Dissappointing]:
During the early game you get a huge mech shown off in the background. I was looking forward to piloting it but the actual level it was involved in just had me help super charge its weapon by the time it left its hangar bay. Gross dissappointment but understandable as described in my silver lining.
[Silver Lining]:
This game was only Okay to Semi-Good because it didn't expand itself enough. IMO that's the best kind of an "Okay" game!
While there were lots of corners cut I felt like the devs tried there best to minimize those the best they could with their tiem and resources. The mech was huge, like if Godzilla monsters had a size scale it would be on the lower end of it.
In order to pilot it they would have needed a whole new environment for a level design, animations, as well enemies other than the orc gunship that could have been a threat. In order to introduce these enemies they also would have needed to tease them early on so they don't come out of nowhere.
Enemies felt varied believe it or not for this level of effort. As did the combat, weapon variety, mechanics and AI.
This game only needed a bigger budget and dev team, with maybe a better writer or at least the man or woman a chance to write a longer story.
When people this has aged well, they aren't kidding. And to reiterate, I liked it despite it's flaws.
It was, above all else, FUN!
[My Hopes]:
From what I've found this game didn't sell well originally, and since the dev also makes the Dawn of War RTS series they refocused on that.
However, my searches have shown that 4-5 WH40K games have released in the last 1-2 years and they've been either Okay, Mediocre or Terrible.
Since this game ends on a cliff hanger we may never know what happens to Titus. But given that it, and the first two Dawns of War, are the best selling and best reviewed games we may see them announce a sequel in the future. Definately worth a buy for the right price!

Skullgirls is an excellent fighting game, especially for newcomers. The game's tutorial is amazing, as it teaches you about all the techniques you will need to know to play basically any fighting game, along with teaching you the basics of each character in order to see which one you will use the most. Speaking of characters, one of the few problems with this game is that the character roster is very small. There are currently only 10 fighters (including the 2 DLC characters), but more are going to be added as DLC, which will be very nice. I also enjoy how this game covers both casual and competitive play. The Story and Arcade modes are very fun and challenging on the higher difficulties, and the Multiplayer isn't too shabby, either. Lag isn't that big of a problem when playing online, and it's always fun to go against other people, wether they're in the same room as you or across the country. The game also looks very nice. It has a movie-theater style theme to it, which may sound strange at first, but in-game you'll know what I mean. The stages are also very well-made, with exceptional musical accompaniment.
Overall, Skullgirls is a great fighting game to pick up if you're looking to get into fighting games, and also if you're a diehard fan of them. I give it a well-deserved 9/10.

Oh my gosh. I don't even know what to say. I just played through the whole game in one go (took my 4 hours) and it's just so sad. This game takes you through all the emtions - angry, sad, confused, dismayed, happy, and there are some hilarious moments. It's a beutifully written game and the music seals the deal. Buy it. Buy it.

As you can see from my total play hours, this story is VERY short. I'd recommend either getting it when there's a huge sale, or just go watch a let's play on YouTube. Whatever you choose to do, this is definetly worth experiencing in some way or another.
My only real issue is that navigating areas can be tedious and frustrating at times. As movement is limited to a square Up-Down-Left-Right grid, it is often difficult to tell where exactly you can stand. Some objects extend slightly into other blocks, which prevents you from going somewhere that would be perfectly open in a more free-moving game. This is most prevalent with bushes and trees. To the Moon would benefit greatly from being remade with a more powerful design tool that allows movement similar to a 2D Zelda game. Diagonal movement would also be appreciated.

I could sit here and just continue to harp about this all night and tell you more, but this is something that you have to see for yourself. You owe it to yourself for this wonderful experience.

It's okay for a game to be tongue and cheek about what it does, to lampshade tropes and poke fun at its subject matter. It's part of being self-aware, of understanding your medium and using it well.
This game is frustrating because it takes this to its illogical conclusion: EVERYTHING is lampshaded, the fourth wall is broken constantly, and you're never given even a second to immerse yourself without the game reminding you that THIS is what it is doing, and isn't it so clever that it's doing that and aware of it?
Coupled with bafflingly poor game design decisions (that you're perhaps supposed to appreciate for the irony?) like running across an entire established world several times for a quest, being all but required to adjust your date and time settings on your actual computer, and Twitter integration of all things, this game trips over itself to get in the way of your having fun.
The art is pretty, though. If they toned the smug faux-intellectualism down a notch and tried not intentionally designing the game poorly, it could've been a fun game.

Ah, finally I game I can speak well of... was my initial thought. In look and tone, Superbrothers embodies a lot of what I love about indie gaming - simple yet beautiful. Even on first impressions it wasn't perfect - not as deep as Undertale, not as complex as The Witcher, nowhere near as difficult as Binding of Isaac. I began to get annoyed at forced wait times for the moon cycles, but there are ways around it, inside the game and out. But I was enjoying myself... until near the end of the game.
Before that though, I have my own personal complaints. This game was originally designed for the iPad, and this especially shows in the game's combat. Fighting the handful of bosses/creatures relies on twitch reflexes, which is fine for touchscreens, but is abominable with mouse controls, especially for laptop mice. I can't move the cursor to switch between attack and defense quick enough unless I know in advance what attack they'll use and when - it's the same every time. I'd say the Trigon battles would be near impossible if they didn't follow a pattern AND that you can use your sword and shield with the Z and X buttons, respectively (I also don't recall that being explained at any point) Fortunately, you don't have to do this too much - once for each of the three trigons and maybe two or three other occasions. This brings me back to the atrocious wait times that would make freemium games facepalm. The lunar cycles can be manipulated easily enough through various means, but that isn't what I'm getting at. I'm talking about the Trigon boss fights. Due to the facts that you can only carry a few healing items, you can't leave the boss area once you enter it (not even dying will fix this), and the aforementioned terrible combat, you'll soon be stuck next to the boss with 1 star of health left, no mushrooms to heal yourself, and no way to leave to get more. I've been told that you can get health back between boss phases by holding the shield button. There's two problems with that. One, at no point in game is this explained until you actually say screw it and run headlong at the fight, and two, it only works for me when it feels like it. So, in my current position as of writing this, to beat the last Trigon I'll have to either have insane reflexes normally reserved for bullet hell shooters and not get hit once, find some way to make the shield heal thing work, or wait until the game resets me back in the real world to start the entire process over. Joy.
This game is, in my opinion, more about doing the most it can with very little. References are made to popular games like Zelda and Mario, and most of the speech uses modern colloquialisms, particularly social media lingo. Some might say that it's just trying to trigger nostalgia, spread the word about the game, and add to its supposed quirky, self-aware pretentiousness. I would have to half-agree there, however, I only casually use social media and nostalgia alone doesn't work with me. Personally, I think the soundtrack and personality of the game are good, but it's not for everyone. I'd still take this over bland AAA title du jour any day of the year.The combat is awful on PC (get the iPad version instead if you can), the wait times are up there with the mobile moneysuckers it desperately wants to rub elbows with, and there is little worth going back for once you beat the story. However, I've played much, much worse. Go for it if you want to support smaller indie devs, but if you do want this game, then maybe wait for a sale - given how short the game is, $8-9 is kind of a bit much.

If on the other you're looking for something you can enjoy over 3-4 nights, with the lights off and a good pair of headphones then it'll be a great experience. I've gotten stuck a few times not having a clue where to go that I required to look up a walkthrough just to get by that area, but for the most part, you just keep progressing all over the place and figuring out what to do or what you need as you go a long.

It is your typical Metroidvania platformer that you just get to locations that you have zero ability to get by yet, until later on you will eventually "upgrade" Ori so now he has the ability to go back and get by the area that was previously inaccessible.
Overall, I have 7.1hrs invested according to Steam and I believe it said I was around 59% complete with the game and for the most part I've tried to get everything possible although I know I'm probably missing a decent amount of hidden orbs that I've yet to go back for since I'm waiting on earning an ability to help on that. I am incredibly satisfied with this purchase and would urge anyone who is a fan of Total War to grab this ASAP - you will certainly not regret it. Solo/small groupers left in cold. To get anywhere this has become a clan game.
- It takes exorbitant amount of time invested daily to make progress in the game - gathering the materials for a ship is a group effort now. Time invested to make yourself useful to where a big clan would want to bring you to port battles so you eventually get the marks for a permit to be able to build one lineship (with all of those collected resources) - that can be lost in a single battle. Then back to square one.
- Pve server changes are not conducive to group play.  Missions by rank (level) are now locked by ship rate. Part of the fun was being able to bring a 2nd rate to a frigate fleet engagement with a buddy. Now you can't. Also the supporting AI fleet ships have been removed from the player's side in fleet missions, forcing you and your buddy to now fight an entire enemy fleet unsupported in same tier ships.
I think most people are ok with some grind - it's just gotten to the point it's much too steep and people who cant submit many consecutive daily hours will likely not see any ships of the line; they will be locked out of the good stuff (naval fleet combat) that this beautiful game offers.
For those spending 40 US it is a shame and I think i'd want to be warned myself. However, there is an arena game being released soon for those with limited time - however (until the next patch?) the open world alpha version is at the moment for the hardcore gamer.

Most of the negative reviews seem to be players frustrated with the reset and recent changes.  I like a lot of the changes to be honest.  Requiring PVP marks for ships of the line?  No problem with that, there should be something to prevent the game from eventually turning into everyone sailing around with giant ships of war.
The biggest issue right now is player numbers.  This game NEEDS more players and unfortunately all the negative reviews are going to kill that effort.  There is still plenty to do on your own but without other players the grind is real.  Don't get me wrong, there are still plenty of big port battles to take part in and plenty of players to join up with for some missions/convoy raiding but to truly hit the big battles you really need an entire evening to dedicated to it to organize.
There really isn't a decent other game like it out there.  Actual combat itself is a blast.  A very healthy mix between playability and arcade. You don't need to be a sailing expert but you will need to learn the basics to play the wind.  Crew control is pretty basic but involved enough to incorporate another level of strategy.
The only real negatives are 1) Player numbers and 2) To really get involved it takes a while.  Not a game you can just jump right into a fight unless you're just looking to do some PVE missions.
I highly recommend checking it out but the recent loss of numbers does have me concerned.

I think this game is great, it might be the nostalgia speaking, but I definitely recommend this games to my friends. 8/10

Good solid Indi god game - but waaayy too much focus on replayability.
I picked up this game on a sale, and I'm both glad to have picked it up, and to have done so whilst it was on sale.
The gameplay works on a sort of time line, where you (the planet & gods) 'wake up' and try to shape a world for humans to grow in, until you fall asleep and the session ends. The next time you 'wake up' you find the world has become barren again, and the cycle continues. The game focuses on repeatedly playing through, to unlock more upgrades, to help you achieve more each time.
It's kinda cool the first few times, but after a couple of games you get sick of what is essentially going through the same motions. You're supposed to play it diferently each time, and you have the scope to do that, but the variation and unlockables aren't enough to make it disimilar from previous plays, and it becomes less engaging.
That's my only real issue with it. But as it's a core game mechanic it's a pretty big one. Otherwise it feels balanced and it works really well if you're just a casual gamer. In spite of this I'd still reccomend it, I have enjoyed playing it and I can tell I will go back to it.

This game offers a charming presentation and approachable core mechanics, giving it the appearance of a marked improvement over other "god games".
Unfortunately, there are a few major factors holding it back-
1. Too much of the game experience is sacrificed for the sake of the whole "giant" fantasy. All of your commands feel unresponsive because you have to wait for your incredibly slow giants to move for each order, and then complete a painstakingly slow animation when they get there. This delay adds up and can account for literally 30-50% of your actual time "playing" in any given round. The animations are charming and immersive at first, but quickly become a source of frustration.
2. The game relies on "randomly generated math problems" to create the majority of its depth. Since you have control over the placement of absolutely everything, the only thing in the game that actually poses a "challenge" and offers a "reward" is the completion of your humans' randomly generated "projects". These projects require you to meet certain "productivity" targets, and doing so requires you to solve a complex math problem to determine which resource placements will grant you the correct symbiosis/specialization benefits to meet the target.
Because of the way the "Ambassador" system works for unlocking your giants' powers, you have very few options early to solve very easy problems. Then later on you have tons of choices, but usually ONLY ONE RIGHT ANSWER, or possibly no answer at all depending on how you slotted your Ambassadors.
Math problems are tolerable once in a while, but it's the hallmark of a "god game" that you get to make lots of "fun" choices that really tailor your world and your experience to match your own playstyle. Reus offers none of that.
3. The initial experience does a good job of guiding you through the basics, but then the game throws you at a wall of "achievements" that you have to complete to unlock additional "choices" (Possible solutions to the aforementioned math problems). Your initial set of choices is very limited, so naturally the goal is to complete these "achievements" ASAP.
These achievements are all very similar and can generally be completed at a rate of 6+ per game if you do your math well. But then you move on to the next set, and it's all the same challenges with bigger numbers. Get 600 Prosperity. Ok now 1200. Ok now 2400... It's really just completing longer and longer games and bigger math problems, and no other twists or challenges added in.
I would have much rather been presented with a series of carefully crafted and themed "challenges" with specific goals that all feel distinct from one another. If you ever played "Sim Earth" back in the day and did, for example, the Mars/Venus terraforming challenges, that's what I'm talking about.
--
ALSO: There's a major bug where your Forest Giant can get "stuck", and the only way to fix it is to Save/Load your game.
All in all, it's clear that the developers put a lot of effort into this game, and it was a very fun and polished experience until it started feeling repetitive about ~3 hours in. I would recommend spending a few hours with it if you can get it on sale, but I wouldn't consider it worth the full purchase price.

Meh. I'm into 40k. Right now I've got a nearly fully painted squad of Genestealer cultists, some 30k Marine sprues, a box of Deathwatch, a lone Necron Immortal, and a couple FW Deathguard torsos lying on my PC desk. I'm into 40k, and I've certainly warmed up to spess mehreens over the years, so I figured I'd give this game a shot.
It's just meh. It's fine. You play a Space Marine and you beat the crap out of things.
Pros:
- Solid 3rd person controls.
- Good, meaty hack and slash combat. I won't claim it to be very thoughtful or with any finesse, but if you just want to violently mulch the enemies of Man, it'll do you just fine.
-Graphics hold up well enough for being 6+ years old; the actual power armor designs are loving detailed and the faces still look good.
Cons:
- It's just bland, really. You can argue this is subjective: I won't deny it, it totally is. But hear me Out:  If you're new to 40k you'll probably have a good time, but if you've been into the franchise for over a decade like I've been, Ultramarines punching a nondescript Orc clan is like the plain cheese on white bread sandwich of Warhammer. The big selling point of 40k is that the setting is absolutely bugshit nuts, with all kinds of weird stuff happening that's so dumb it comes right back around to being awesome again in a way only it can pull off as a setting. You' not going to find any of that here, though. Just Smurfs being smurfs and Orks who are so boring they call people "humans" instead of "'UMIES" .
- The multiplayer at it's core is actually pretty entertaining because it cuts out the middleman that is the campaign and throws you right into the thick of battle with other Marines. Problem is it's pretty much dead. Should you manage to find a game, you're gonna be the bottom ♥♥♥♥♥ to a bunch of guys who are all max level and they'll turn your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ inside out . I can see how this was probably a lot of fun back in it's heyday, but if you're thinking of getting this for the multiplayer, you're gonna be dissapointed.
TL;DR: It's fine. Totally middle of the line. You'd be better off trying Eternal Crusade out at this point though; it's free and plays more or less the same and scratches all the same itches: customizing your guy, getting in massive brawls, and it actually has a living playerbase for the moment.

I've really dived into this game, and I understand that a lot of people are turned away by the learning curve, but holy heck this game has the best community I've ever seen. Everyone is extremely helpful, kind, and learning the ropes was amazingly easy. In its current state, the game feels rather clunky when you start playing in terms of the amount of buttons you don't know which what do, and the lack of a tutorial to offer a basic idea of where to start.
Nonetheless, I honestly believe in the devs and that this game has amazing potential. I love it already!
PRO TIPS:
STARTING:
If you decide to buy this game, when starting at your Capital city port, press the mission tab at the top left, and take 3 combat orders. These are your bread and butter combat missions against NPCs which allow for good money and XP for new players. No real need to go past midshipman difficulty, since it only increases XP per win, which isn't as important as money early on.
NAVIGATION:
Navigating in these ages was difficult. A storm when in the middle of the sea can get you lost, and I've found myself lost and circling an island 3 times in a heavy storm. Pretty funny when you think about it. Anyway, Press M to access your map, and press the protractor tool on the top left. Double click on your current location, and right click your destination. Then follow the red line which appears on your bottom right compass when not on map. You should be able to use this to sail to land marks, or in a straight line to your destinations. Combat order missions have white swords crossed, and say "Combat Order" when clicked. Otherwise, it is an event or another combat between either players or players and AI.
Lost? Press the trade button on the more tab when in map, and sort ports by distance. You can now see how far you are from the nearest port, or any port in the world. Use this to find which way you need to adjust to make it the rest of the way.
ATTACKED?:
Some players like to look for new players to attack in order to gain PVP marks, which are an important commodity in game. Always keep an eye out, and click nearby ships to check who they are- AI will not attack you, players will always have their name displayed. When close to an enemy, try to use the wind and your (usually) smaller/faster ship to escape. The white arrow on the bottom right shows you wind direction. In your basic cutter, you should be able to get a good speed at a roughly 20-40 degree angle from the wind. If you do lose your ship, you can re-buy a free Basic Cutter in the store of any port. All other ships are lost and must be rebought if they are sunk, whereas the basic cutter will always be free- Make use of this, don't worry about big ships until you're making big money!
TO TRADE OR NOT TO TRADE/MAKING MONEY:
Trading is usually risky, and should be avoided until you have a grasp on the game, and some friends to help you out. Combat missions are a great place to start- Don't forget that when you sink a ship, you can loot the cargo. Pull up next to it quickly before it sinks, and under 2knots you'll be able to press X and loot the cargo. Plenty of good stuff to sell!
Last thing to mention- Don't be afraid to ask for help in the Help chat. Also, Nation chat is a great place to make friends, join guilds, or group up for missions. Making money is easier with friends.

I've been playing this game since before Early Access on Steam, when the game was basically a lobby-based action game, and it has come quite a long way since then.  The developers have made improvements to basically every aspect of the game in the past year and a half, so I'm somewhat surprised and disappointed by the negative reviews that many people seem to be giving it.  Many of the negative reviews seem to have one or several complaints in common:
1. The developers don't listen to player feedback.  I find this claim almost silly.  Sure, the developers of this game change things a lot, but they try to get player input as to how the change is affecting the game.  If the changes don't work out, or don't make sense, they will change them back or find another solution.  For instance, in the early days of Early Access, there were finite numbers of repairs that could be used in battle, and once you used these, you were out for the rest of the battle.  The devs did what they called a "wacky patch" and removed the ability to repair ships altogether, much to the nay-saying and outright crying of many vocal players on the forums, but guess what?  It made the game more fun!  These same players that were complaining about losing their precious repair abilities are the same ones poo-pooing the game now for equally meaningless reasons.  Sure, they put repairs back into the game, but not in the same format as before, so as to make them more strategic now, but the fact that people complain about devs not listening to feedback is disappointing.  The devs might not agree with or implement every single little change you want to see in the game, but that doesn't mean they don't read what you have to say, especially if you say it in a polite and constructive way.  They can't make everyone happy all the time, but some people don't seem to realize that.
2. The grind is too hard/long.  In most MMOs, and most RPGs in general, the first few levels are usually designed to allow you to progress quickly and see noticeable progress from where you started in a short period of time.  In Naval Action, depending on what you do, you can spend a few hours sailing around, killing some NPC ships, collecting money to buy a new ship, getting a higher rank, and sailing your new ship that will feel eminently more powerful than the ship you started in.  Are cannons more expensive now?  They sure are!  Are ships more expensive now?  Absolutely!  There is a reason the devs changed the prices of things - to make things harder to get and be more precious to people.  Whereas before the latest wipe you could buy a ship with 5 durabilities complete with a full set of cannons for say 200k, now it might cost you that much for the same ship with a single durability, or even more.  But the cost means you'll be extra careful with that ship, instead of throwing it away like a disposable toy.  The problem most players that are complaing about the grind now have is that they are used to pre-wipe over-abundance of everything.  Money meant nothing to anyone because everyone had so much, and they all got used to being able to buy whatever they wanted at any time without a second thought.  Now, since everyone has had to start over, these spoiled players who were used to be rich are now poor again and they don't like it, so they'll come on here and bad-mouth the game.  I imagine if the devs gave them each 100 million gold, they would change their tune a bit.
3. The UI is poop.  Well, this is true, I guess.  It's extremely plain, but the devs have repeatedly said that the UI will be the last thing they work on before a full release, and that's fine by me.  The interface isn't pretty, but it's functional, and that's the key thing at this point.
4. Lower player population.  Sadly, this is the most true of the complaints about the game.  In a game would that can literally take hours of real time to sail from one side to the other, it can be almost depressing when you can't find anyone in the open world, even when you're looking for them.  The player base has seen an uptick since the wipe, with many players who stopped playing a while to wait for the wipe having returned to see what's new.  Granted, some don't like the changes and will stop playing, but plenty of people are still enthusiastic about the game.  If you find a group of people to play with, you can still have fun in this game, even if the sea isn't filled with scoundrel pirates or fat merchants to attack.
My own personal opinion of this product is that, while it is flawed in some ways, there is without a doubt the kernel of an amazing game here.  It is not a game that you can simply jump into and be a master at in two hours.  It will take time to learn the controls, how to handle your ship effectively, etc.  The learning curve can be steep, especially for someone who has not played a game like this before, but I find that games with the highest learning curves also usually offer the greatest reward once you overcome that curve.
You can get lost easily in this game if you aren't careful.  If you sail out of sight of land, you might not end up where you thought you would if you plot your course just a little bit off.  It kind of adds a little suspense to the game, but also relief and a bit of satisfaction when you plot a course across the open sea for 20 minutes and arrive precisely where you wanted to.  The graphics in the game are impressive for a development studio that doesn't have access to the big AAA dev studio budgets that other games have. They are certainly enough to give you the impression of sailing on a ship in the early 19th century, especially if you zoom in close all the way down to the deck level.

Total War: Warhammer 2, is perhaps the most enjoyable game I have ever had the pleasure of playing. I regret not being able to play it sooner, because it has taken over my life in so many aspects. It's just so hard to put down? Firstly, I did not play the first Total War: Warhammer, due to a lack of money. But, before this, I was obsessed with Shogun 2. That changed quickly. In almost every single aspect, Total War: Warhammer 2 is better than previous games under the same title, even going as far to nearly steal the top spot on my list of best games.
The graphics are incredible, the battles are beautiful and you really feel as though you're being pulled into the Warhammer universe, with all it's unforgiving greatness. Each faction plays to a different set of skills, which can be the key to victory if learnt and countered. The mechanics of the game, are both simple and hard, being that there are so many variables to take into play, yet they're simple to master when recognised.
If I were to pick one bad thing about the game, I'd chose the diplomacy. Sometimes, it just does not make sense, and I know it has been thundered into the ground a thousand times. The 'great power' negative is my worst criticism, seeing as a faction with greater power, thinks your feeble 12 strength can compare to their 2.
But, overall, Total War: Warhammer 2 is an impressive game, worth the time and money put into it. I look forward to the future of this game, as I know it has been put in good hands.

I got the gold edition on sale for $50 last December; having played as much as I have and enjoying it as much as I have, I would definitley have payed full price, even just for the base game.
End game turns into a real grind. However, it is a fun grind for me, no doubt: I really enjoy the different builds you can create and come up with. At times it drew me in a little too much, so be warry of that. The PVE aspect of the game is great and there is plenty of content to play. PVP is something that takes adjusting to, especially for me after exclusively playing short time-to-kill games like Battlefield and R6 Siege; things get a little wonky here and there, but its definitley fun; very thrilling at times. The overall 3rd person experience in this game is great: using cover is smooth and consistent, movement is quick and agile, and the shooter experience of it is fantastic. Though, things turn into bullet sponges at the higher levels, but it's an RPG, so I expected that.
I really haven't delved too deep into the DLC mostly because I enjoy what the base game has to offer; Underground is nice and will be better with the 1.8 update. I haven't actually played Survival (strangely enough, this DLC was part of the reason I bought the game in the first place). Last Stand was fun for the several times that I played it; I definitley want to go back and play more sometime.
The visuals in this game are amazing; it's just gorgeous.

What I can say about this game right now as of 11/13/2017 is that its ok. I got this game about a year ago when it went on sale. The game isn't what most wanted it to be, a Ghost Recon game but instead some Special Agent guys with cool tech in a gang war ridden NY. It is more of a Shooter MMO like Destiny, were the enemies have health bars and weapons are divided in differents roles like DPS, Spread, and etc. There are other reviews that can get more in depth with this game but I am here to give ya the quick gist of this game. So here it is:
-Dark Zone/PVP: With PVP its kinda meh, in my opinion, as everyone mostly uses the best DPS Assualt Rifle or SMG and just uses that. The Dark Zone is where most of the PvP happens and so it can get pretty nasty in there. The DZ does have NPC enemies that lurk there as well as bosses that offer (sometimes) better loot than those outside of the DZ. Now when you do obtain loot from the DZ you have to find a extraction point so a Helio can come in and recover them. However to extract the loot, you may have to go through players. Sometimes they may be like you and just want to kill the boss, get the loot, extract the loot, and get the hell out of dogde. But most of the time it will be players fighting it out with each other for DZ Points so they can get weapons off the vendors that stand next to the entrances to the Dark Zone. The vendors do offer some niffty stuff from time to time so it can be worth it to go around and gun down other players. The one upside right now though is the player count of this game is kinda low so extracting loot is more likely to go as plan.
PvE/Raids: Most of the PvE can be done solo as long as ya have the right equimpment and skills ready. There are a few Raids that are more vavorable to parties than solo players. As I mentioned in the above paragraph about players, getting into a raid party is a roll of the dice; sometimes it will be instant, other times it will be you twirling your guy or gal around for mintues on end. The Underground and Survival DLC adds more to the PvE player groups. The Survival DLC is basically Battlegrounds but with players randomly spawning in random safe houses across Manhatten. All player are infected with a disease that will kill them in a hour, no winter clothes, a pistol with a clip of ammo, enemy gangs roaming and with a blizzarad raging outside. The objective is to get to the DZ to get the cure and extract with the cure. There are two versions of this Survival mode, PvE and PvP. PvE is the most played as other players cannot kill each other directly. However you can quickly loot all the food, water, meds, and equipment before others can withc indriectly does kill them. Underground is basically build your own adventure but in the subways, sewers, and underground malls of NY. You can increase difficutly for better rewards but if you die during your run, you get sent back to the Underground HQ and have to start a whole new one that will be different from the preivous one.
All in all, its a fun game with a Dev team that is still around and willing to keep this game alive. I will say that you should wait until this game goes on sale, paying $50 or $90 is a bit of a waste. Its fun game but not at its current price tag. If you can, buy the season pass (as much as I hate typing that) as it will pay for its self with the DLC Underground and Survival. They do updates that are free and add a few changes here and there but sadly most of the good stuff is in the DLC. They do have microtransactions but its all cosmetic stuff so to me its fine.

I thought I'd write a review of this game since there seems to be a hell of alot of negative reviews about it, so I I'd try and share my experience of it so far.
I started pretty late on, and as such had no idea what was going on. I'd never played any MMO game before as my laptop specs are retro to say the least. I'm also puzzled at how people are giving negative reviews to a game that they spent two THOUSAND hours on. Some people spend less time with girl/boyfriends in their lifetime. I'm amazed at how it can take two thousand hours to find out you don't like a game.
To some extent the online the experience will be affected by more experienced players. For instance, when I started, the players were really helpful to new players, communicating lots of tips to level up, and advice about castle/village layout and build order. It's not a game for lone wolves, which may deter new players, and you have to play regularly to get to the attacking/defending stage. And although you do have an advantage if you pay to buy cards, it's not a single player game, and you can always ask a higher ranked player for help and advice. At worst, they won't message you back, but most active players seem to welcome newcomers to the game.
I'll continue to play as long as other people do.

The entire game seems to revolve around putting the right resources next to other resources, and if you can't figure out what order to put them in, you have nothing to do in this game. This game is probably the closest we've come to having a good Warhammer 40k title in a very long time, which is probably to be expected since this is a Relic title from the good days of Relic, before the "we must appeal to the wider audience!" nonsense made them ruin DoW3. While I don't have too many hours logged here on Steam, I have played this game extensively on console.
+Positives:
-The game without a doubt nails the feel of 40k. You're surrounded by Gothic architecture, people in British accents, explosions, and general carnage and death. The manufactorums blare constant messages to long dead workers, telling them to continue working for the glory of the Emperor and the Machine God. It's everything you would expect a 40k game's atmosphere to be.
-The weapons sound beautiful. Bolters sound like the automatic cannons that they are, chainswords rip and tear gloriously, Space Marines thud and shake the ground as they charge around like the walking tanks they are.
-Weapons feel right. They feel heavy and impactful. Bolter fire creates showers of blood and gore as .75 cal explosive rounds tear through bodies, each swing from your chainsword rips your enemies apart and absolutely drenches you in blood. Nothing feels like a nerf gun pretending to be a real gun.
-There is no health regen unless you're near death, and even then it's only about a quarter of your health bar. You want to heal? You heal by giving an Ork a chainsaw vasectomy. You want a health pack? Punch a Gretchin until it explodes. It only takes one punch. There's also a Fury mode which you can activate to gain health regen and increased melee damage after you rip and tear enough to please the Emperor.
-You're fairly durable. You're a Space Marine, wearing some of the best armor ever developed. You feel like a tank, but you aren't invincible. You can tear through hordes of smaller Orks without breaking stride, but fights between other Marines or large orks can go badly quickly if you get overconfidant. When you fight traitor marines, or other players in multiplayer, it feels like a clash between titans instead of a fight between mortals.
-The voice acting is on point. Mark Strong is fantastic as Captain Titus, and his squadmates voices were also well chosen. The voices for the enemy NPCs and the few other friendly NPCs are also fairly good.
-The story is decent. It's not going to win any awards, and if you know anything about 40k (or even if you don't) you'll probably be able to guess some of the plot points before they happen. That said, the story doesn't hurt the game and it's still possible to get interested and invested in the characters. You won't leave the game asking any deep, meaningful questions, but you also won't leave the game regreting your purchase. There are plenty of awesome moments, some cool dialogue, everything you'd expect to come out of 40k. The story fits the game. It's good, fairly simple, and pretty enjoyable.
-It controls well. The options menu isn't huge, but the controls are intelligent for the most part. It's not a game that you'll need an extra hand to play, and it works well on both keyboard and controller.
=Neutral:
-The multiplayer is pretty simple. Deathmatch, CTF, etc. The usual game modes. It's not as good as the single player, but it's a servicable time-sink if you want to shoot other players in a 40k game. Some single player mechanics are removed or changed to make them work in a multiplayer setting, but overall it's still decent.
-There is a co-op PVE mode, but it's very hard. It's a round-based game where you have to hold an arena against waves of Orks and eventually Chaos, with the waves going up in difficulty until you reach what is essentially an unbeatable last wave. I've only beaten it once, and we had a hacker playing with us who had unlimited ammo and was invincible. It's a fun mode, but it can get repetitive after a while.
-Negatives:
-The multiplayer is basically dead. The game is so old, and the actual multiplayer content is so basic and small that there aren't a whole lot of people still playing. The game also runs peer to peer instead of on a dedicated server, which can be seen as a blessing or a curse since, while you have to deal with all the problems that come from having the match running off of one of the players internet (so if he's far away or has bad internet you can have terrible ping), it also means that there are no servers to be shut down.
-The multiplayer modes can get boring quickly. There's a few maps, a few modes, and the co-op has even less in the way of options.
-There are hackers. Pretty much explains itself.
-You can't choose which faction you play as. You're randomly assigned to either Chaos or Loyalist when you join a match. While it doesn't effect the gameplay, since the wargear for both factions is stat identical save for flavor like chainaxes instead of power axes and daemon mauls instead of thunder hammers, you can't work towards cosmetics for one faction while playing the other. So if you really want a certain piece of armor for your Loyalist marine, but you keep getting put on the Chaos team, there's nothing you can do about it. You can't even switch teams once you're in the match.
-The campaign is very linear. While it's not entirely a bad thing, it does mean that there's not as much replayability as a more option game.
Overall, the game is good. It has a solid single player, and a decent multiplayer. Though you can easily tell it was made with the single player as top priority, the rest of the game can be enjoyable if you can find a community that still plays this game, or you have friends that do.

Welcome to Warhamer 40k, or as we'll call it w40k, it has six races, each with their own name classes, units, and heroes.  And then we have the.... <pause and slide that to the side.>
This is Warhammer 40k, but it's not.  Instead this is a third person hack and slash, with ranged weapons where you play a Space Marine (or an Ultramarine) and fight through 18 stages.  It is in the 40k universe, but it doesn't require the massive wealth of knowledge or fandom most of these games seem to expect.
And you know what?  It's the first Warhammer 40k game I really really enjoyed.   Dawn of War is a fine RTS if you really want to play an RTS, or really want to deal with that complexity, however Space Marine brings the user into the universe and creates a reasonable scope of the world for them to enjoy.
It avoid overly repetitive gameplay, it avoids the massively complex world of 40k which will overwhelm all but the few fans of sci fi with the ability to comprehend it all from a game, and focuses on just a single adventure in that universe.
And it works!   The gameplay is fantastic, where the main character has a decent amount of options.  You can choose from three weapons, and a number of ranged weapons (carrying up to 4 at a time, with I believe at least 7 different weapons, not counting full upgrades).   The enemies is a little similar, for a majority of the game you will fight the orks (one of the six races)  but there's enough variety in location, ability and configurations that it rarely feels like a slog, surprisingly so.
Even the graphics hold up well for a 6 year old (last gen) game.   The story is solid.  It's not going to win awards, but it at least has a driving force and while it does dig a bit into the lore (at least i think it does) isn't a distracting trip.  If you like the lore, I'm sure you'll get a lot out of it, but if you don't know the lore at a deep level (like me) you'll really enjoy the story.
Overall I like the game, I like the game a lot more than quite a few game.  It's definitely trying to be a bit like that "god of war" style that everyone was playing at the time, quite a bit of hack and slash is required, though this game finds a solid balance between third person shooting and melee fighting and it's pretty glorious when you have it right.    I recommend it, and considering it's often on sales, it's a great time to pick this up.

Overall its a good game, like any Total War with a nice Lord of the Rings feel to it.
A few notes to add that some might determine to be cons below:
Ocean:
The idea of a Power House Navy doesnt exist
No navy battles besides the auto sim
And theres a lot of treasure out in the ocean with no competition and no down side.
Basically the ocean is your treasure chest.
Campaign:
When you start the campaign theres really only one objective to "win", beat out the other 4 major factions in a race of collecting a specific resource. It creates a interesting twist to the original campaign of just conquer the world, due to when u hit a mile stone theres a random spawn of armies attacking you.
I enjoyed it in the beginning but realized towards the end I was at a point where i just had to sit and camp my cities for half the game waiting for them to spawn said enemy. To not only sustain my economy, but to win the game. So was fun but disheartening just waiting turn after turn instead of expannding.
Once you finish the big quest you have the choice to continue the campaign of taking over the world (normal Total War) but they give you a pretty strong buff which just makes it faceroll push to finish. But to be fair this was on Normal difficulty and I've done this with multiple Total War games. Reach a certain peak and then its faceroll.
Battles:
When you get about half way in the game your really involved with your actions. Not only from your General using his abilities but also your superior fire power minions. The flying power houses (dragons, etc) really make it a game changer. I personaly enjoyed this aspect of the game, it was a lot of fun learning the different abilities and how they effect the battle. But against the computer it might make it a little to easy for at least Normal difficulty.
As far as terrain goes it was very realistic and a nice touch to include in battles. Knowing how to properly use the terrain turned a basic battle into something beautiful.
Talent Tree for Generals:
Personally i liked the creativity this provided really enjoyed creating your own personal General only issue is you kind of build a very generic build with all of them. Especially in the later game, you realize the optimium output for your OP army and max it out. Almost identical for every General you have.
Expansions:
This part kind of left a poor taste. The game offers a free dlc thats basically the same game but offers a much larger variety of faction choices. Heres the issue, its only a free dlc if you bought the original Total War Warhammer. As far as thanking the community its a great idea, I definitly encourage it. But.. that game typcially runs $60 even though its the older version, thankfully i bought it during the christmas sell so easy $20 expansion right? Well kind of, theres some cool races you'd definitly want to play, but you had to buy those originally as well. So now you gota go buy those expansions from the original game too. Conclusion: That free dlc was actually just the original Warhammer game. Go figure.
So in other words TWW2 completely screws you over when offering multiple races to play. You get the core ones and thats all she wrote. As far as the actual expansion (egyptian) I didnt want to look into it after dealing with the free dlc, hopefully its much better than what I just explained.
Overall Conclusion:
When comparing it to a game like Total War Rome 2 which is a 2013 release, this game was missing some big factors. I would actually argue that this game is much more similar to the original Total War Rome.(2004 release date) But add some nifty ideas and different races and you have yourself a new game.
So sadly if I had to compare it to other older versions of Total War games i'd rate this game a 4/10 due to it being a 2017 release.
But just to give it a general rating i give it a 7/10 for its creativity and unique style of play in the battles.
If your a fan of midevil category, Lord of the Rings fan, etc. and also enjoy Total War games (tactical games) then you should definitely check this game out, its worth at least one good play through.
I absolutetly love this series, keep the content coming CA :D!

Honestly, I went into Scribblenauts Unlimited with high expectations when I bought it on 3DS, and I hated it. So when I bought this game on Steam, the game had a sour taste in my mouth. Boy did this game give me a good time when I got the RIGHT version. This game is amazing! The graphical style is very fresh while still nailing down that "Scribblenauts Style" to a tee! The story is excellent and I actually paid attention to it this time, because the 3DS' version was just so boring. It's very heartwarming and such a happy game deserves such a lighthearted story as well as a good moral in the end. And that's just the beginning to this amazing game.
Scribblenauts Unlimited also comes with an object creator, which I could just sit on for HOURS and make stuff on; and I would never get tired of all the strange monsters, celebrities and video game characters I make in the Object Creator that spring to life from Maxwell's notebook. While I admit I do miss the "Sandbox Mode" in Super Scribblenauts where Maxwell could destroy the terrain with bombs and whatnot and he was completely invincible; it doesn't matter to me that much really because Edwin's Farm still works in a similar fashion.
The game's story mode on the other hand, is also very good. The fact that Maxwell's sister gets frozen inside stone makes the game feel very urgent as if it was trying to say "Dude! Hurry up and help me!" and it kinda creates this feeling of being rushed to just get all the Starites so you can calm down and just mess around on Edwin's Farm.
To put it bluntly, Scribblenauts Unlimited is one of the best creativity-driven games I've ever seen, with it's charming graphics, music, story and endless possibilites for objects and creatures with an object creator; I'd say the Steam Version is miles better than the 3DS version. Even if you're not creative I think you could still get quite the kick out of this game. I recommend anybody who remotely considers themselves an 'artist' in some way shape or form. My compliments from me to you 5th Cell, this game is absolutely wonderful.
...Oh by the way if you're wondering why I didn't review Scribblenauts Unmasked instead; I'm not the biggest fan of superheroes so I decided to just stick with a 'pure' Scribblenauts game.

I still rate this positive experience and had plenty of fun hours, so no complaints - and yes can recommend this one.

Overall, Stronghold Kingdoms is a great game but there are few things that make it less popular than other stronghold games I own. For instance, Stronghold Kingdoms has various researchs which need to been done in order to advance further in the game, and various other advantages for paying users who buy crowns. But, ultimately the game becomes very time consuming taking days and months on end to advance very far. Which results in the fact that many people leave the game, because for example you leave for about a week with everything being fine but return to find a mess and half your castle destory. (Happened to me, and a few friends.) Lastly, the factions and glory race part of the game leaves something to be desired since, as the ages progress in the game all factions and houses are reset to help things over. But such is not the case since, more often then not I have found getting into a house is challenging and the members of the former winning all are top rank and join the same house over again to win the next age.
Ultimately, I would recommend the game, but would advise avoiding it unless you like a high degree of user-interaction and waiting around.

Once you get your head around the real-time play, Stronghold Kingdoms is an exciting, absorbing and really fun game for the dedicated player. You can choose to advance quickly or slowly (there are advantages and disadvantages to both) and you can build your empire to suit your own strategy. Once you join a faction, you can communicate and cooperate with other players in common goals. Or, you can play as a lone wolf, quietly inveigling yourself into positions of power (or weakness - be careful!)
The responsibility is yours to keep your peasants fed and housed, your fields producing, your businesses trading at a profit and your county free of villains. If warring strategy suits you best, you can battle against the wolves, the bandits or the Enemy for starters. Beyond that, there's the wicked marauders who will try to overcome your best plans and beat you down. Be ready for them or pay the price!
If your plans are successful and you grow in wealth and power, you can gain status as a sherrif or even a prince. You can muster multiple armies to defend your capital or extend your reach. During all this, you can chart a course of study and upgrades that will govern the way you earn victory. There's a lot to do in Stronghold Kingdoms and much to ponder on.

Minion Masters:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

Masters, are you ready? It’s time to choose your deck of cards. What tactics are you going to use? Would it be a defensive or an offensive strategy? What you really need to know is what your opponent’s plan is! Stop speculating, Master, you are about to enter the area. Good luck and I wish you well to lead our minions to victory, my Master!
Minion Masters is a PVP / multiplayer game where you compete with other players online to move up leagues!
As a newbie, you will be assigned to the Wood League to start. Each league has five divisions. Each time you are victorious, you will be given experience points which will go towards your ranking and therefore move you up divisions within the league.  In the Wood League, for example, you need to reach 100 points to move up a division.
You will be given one master as a default, and will have to access two other masters through the free weekly master rotation.
As soon as you are ready to battle against an online opponent, just press the play online button to enter the arena. It will not take too long for you to find an opponent. The longest I had to wait was around thirty seconds.
Your deck will consist of ten cards. All cards have a number on them. For example, an assassin card has a number four on it. What it means is that you can activate this unit when the mana gauge reaches the number four on its scale. Bear in mind, the highest number on the mana gauge is ten. So if you wait until the gauge reaches ten, you can activate two assassin units (if they are in your deck, of course) and a laser unit, which costs two mana points.
In terms of the battle map, you have two sides which are connected with two bridges. The trick is to capture and hold the bridges. If you do so, your mana gauge will rise faster than normal. Also, your master can access peaks faster if you hold the bridges. The goal is to destroy your opponent’s power tower where your opponent master stands to win the game. At the end of a game, you will receive experience points for rising within the league, and also levelling up your character. You might receive coins, shards or rubies.
How do you get new units or cards? With tokens! You can purchase tokens with your coins or rubies. Then you can use these token on your power tower to access a random draw; a bit like a roulette wheel. Each card has experience attached to it; it could be a regular, common, rare or supreme card.  The last one has the most experience as a unit.
Every twenty-four hours, you will earn a free token. The only difference is that instead of drawing a card, the draw will have coins, shard or rubies for the taking. Oh, by the way, you need shards and rubies to purchase new masters.
Graphically, Minion Masters is well done and very easy to understand and get into. The most important point is that you don’t have to wait too long to play a game online. However, I think we need more Masters and map designs.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Good selection of cards
-	Fun, addictive gameplay
-	Easy to access a game online
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	I would like to see more masters to choose from
-	It would be nice to have different maps
Minion Masters is seriously fun to play and is extremely addictive!
8/10

When the original Scribblenauts came out for the DS, it was one of my favorite games. While it did not have the option to customize objects or use adjectives, most levels were both fun and challenging, forcing you to push your creativity's limits in order to reach the starite. Scribblenauts Unlimited allows much more depth with creating items, but the levels/puzzles do not reach beyond simply creating a category of object when prompted. There are no action levels in Scribblenauts Unlimited and as a result none of the levels are really challenging and there is no satisfaction in completing them. The object editor also allows you to create overpowered objects as well, decreasing what little challenge there is. It is fun to fool around with the object editor, but Scribblenauts Unlimited does not offer much depth beyond customizing your own objects.
SUMMON ALL THE CTHULUS!

There is literally nothing bad that I can think of about Scribblenauts Unlimited. The custom content allows you to add in virtually anything to the game to complete the puzzles with. So if you're stuck for a solution, make your own!
Also, the inclusion of adjectives in this game is something I wanted since playing the first Scribblenauts game, and they did it in a BIG way. You can come up with all kinds of strange things. For example, I bet you've never been able to say you were flying around on a giant rainbow penguin with demonic wings that could breathe fire. With this game, now you can.
Your creativity is the only thing that limits what you can do in this game (aside from the profanity filter). If you haven't played it already by now, do it. You'll have an absolute blast.

It has become incredibly tedious to achieve anything in the game, especially for new players who do not get free redeemables like players from before the wipe have.
For a new player to earn money he has to grind the same mission over and over again for hours, just to get out of his basic ship or set up some basic resource building. And to make money with trading you have to sail for several real life hours.

Basically this game is geared more and more towards vocal no-lifers who can dump 10+ hours each day into the game. If you can't match that you are, at best, fodder and not supposed to have fun (the devs actually said that having fun is a secondary concern for them).
They are also soon releasing a arena game for Naval Action which makes me believe they have given up on this version considering the bad their decisions were lately.
If the game would cost around $5 you could give it a try. But the current price is just nonsense and you should stay away from it as far as possible.

Space Marine is one of the games I feel as though I get thoroughly dissolved into the game.  I am pretty sure there was a time when my wife heard me scream at the computer: "Booo ya, I AM A SPACE MARINE."  The controls are tight and the game just flows with you as you play along.  But a brief discussion on the game, in this 3rd person shooter you play as a Space Marine that has just arrived on the scene of an ork attack on a planet.  Your mission is to push back the tide and win the day, securing the planet for the Empire.
In short, this game has a lot going for it.  The visceral feel of combat has the biggest impact on the game in my opinion.  It helps set the tone for core gameplay that has you dispatching Orks in a ton of different ways, all of which are deeply gratifying to the player.  This feed back and gratification leads to the player feeling like they are a Space Marine!  To make a comparison, it feels like a Warhammer 40k version of Gears of War.  The gameplay isn't that dissimilar.
The core of the gameplay is really the heart of the game and I can't find much to criticize on the gameplay itself.  This is why I would recommend it to anyone that has any interest in shooters and/or scifi games.  To me it is a 4/5 and I would recommend picking it up on a steam sale however as it is a bit dated graphically.

A solid third person shooter. I appreciate that there is a health bar and no sticky cover. However, health pick ups would have been more useful rather than kills for health. These often prolonged kill animations that grant you health leave you exposed and you can lose just as much health as you gain in the process. Another issue is that the various pieces of cover you can use don't do a good job of protecting you, mainly from grenades. Grenades have awful trajectories and more than once I lost a portion of my shields to my own grenades because it hit a corner of rubble. Environments were a bit lackluster, I experienced a couple of glitches, one where I was stuck in a wall and had to reload a checkpoint, and in the other I phased through the map floor and fell to my death. Those were the only two I encountered besides the sound cutting off for split seconds a couple times--by no means game breaking. Other than, the checkpoints get a little cute. Sometimes you'll respawn right before the area you died in, and other times you're transported back to further back area and have to slog your way through a tedious mess of enemies.
The story is pretty solid, although the characters are a bit paint-by-numbers. The action was nice and fun, the variety of weapons was good. Environments were a bit lackluster and narrow. The variety of enemies was awesome and I had to shift tactics a few time. A lot of door opening and elevator action, which was more amusing to me than annoying. I make it seem like there's more good than bad, but honestly the good has more weight than the bad. It was fun, it was engaging for the most part, and by the end I felt attached to our lead character. Nothing incredible but by no means a bad game; try it out of you want to kil some time with a challenging shooter.

**Get This Game**
To the Moon is a point and click adventure game. You play as Dr. Watt and Dr. Rosalene two scientists from the Sigmund Corporation sent to help virtually fulfill John, a dying man's, last wish... to get To the Moon.
To accomplish this you use a machine (almost like the animus from Assassin's Creed) to go back through John's memories backwards starting from John's most recent memory all the way back to his early childhood memories.
In each memory you have to find an item that will connect you to one of John's earlier memories. This item has a barrier on it that has to be broken by finding items and talking to people that will give you different colored orbs that will unlock a puzzle which when solved will take you to the next stage. Through the exploration of each level you discover more and more of what John's motivation was for wanting to go To the Moon.
You can beat the game in one sitting if you want to. With a story line this good you might actually do it. The story will make you laugh, make you cry then laugh then cry some more when you see the ending of the game. The sound track is good and for the price it's totally worth it. Don't buy the game looking for a high graphic, high action game. This is a story telling game that takes you back through John's life and moves you emotionally. Get this game and see if you can get To the Moon!!!

cons: while the tutorials are great at explaining the basics of the game, there is a bit of a learning curve afterwards. i didn't find this to be too bad (i play EVE, and this is nowhere near that learning curve. i'd put it at about a Sim City 3000 learning curve). also the obligatory XNA framework stupidness.
conclusion: if you have a dedicated graphics card that supports DX10 (the GTX400 series and later should do, no idea about ATI though, sorry), then go ahead and get this. if you have a first gen Intel processor and an Intel GMA, hold off for now. i'm not sure if the Intel HD series will run this, but i know the GMA will not.
