If you are after a story that makes you cry, this is the one for you. I'll get to why I called this a story in a bit.
To the Moon has you take charge of two scientists who specialise in memory, the sarcastic Dr Watts and the more sentimental Dr Rosalene. Their contract is to fulfill Johnny's dying wish - to go to the moon. In order to do this, they must traverse through his memories to find out why he wishes to do so. As the story reveals more through you travelling backwards in his life (which is done excellently), you begin to understand. By the end, you are hoping so much for Johnny that it physically hurts. The story is worth the price alone. At the time of this review, it's €1.99 (a little more with the soundtrack, which I recommend) due to the Summer Sale, and an essential for everyone to experience.
As I said, this is a story. Gameplay-wise, there is not very much, except for one sudden platformer part that was really jarring to the point and click style and did not fit at all. The most difficult things you'll encounter are tile puzzles. It's very compelling to complete these in as few moves as possible. A running total of how many moves you've made over the game adds to the challenge. To the Moon is not very long, and will take at most 5 hours to complete, not including the DLC, which was kindly bundled with the game.
Given that the game was developed using RPG Maker, graphics are very bitty. Personally, I like this style, but it might not be to everyone's taste. Aside from a few cinematic animated cutscenes, it'll be the same style throughout. I didn't notice one very important plot point because of the style, but that's my only issue with it. I think it works with the story.
The soundtrack is beautiful. Composers (along with developers and pixel artists) are credited at the start of the game, which is a better way of crediting the creators. It's very clear that the composers truly cared about the story when they composed the soundtrack, which is worth buying with the game.
This story is a must to experience by everyone. It is one that stays with you, that leaves you crying at the end, emotionally and physically hurting. You need to try this, then introduce it to your friends and family. The price is slightly high for the length, but definitely pick it up when it goes on sale.

This is a game with a lot of issues. Almost every enemy has a self-heal and a litany of abilities that don't make sense. Wild boars with projectile attacks. Zombie torsos that are faster than zombies with legs. Crabs that heal and bless eachother. Personality traits determined through dialogue contribute to stats, and there is a lot of overlap ("compassionate", "forgiving", and "altruistic" are all different), meaning you don't know what dialogue choices will lead to what stat modifiers, and furthermore meaning that you won't always pick the dialogue choice you think best fits your character in lieu of trying to find dialogue choices that fit your build.
Sometimes battle element effects, which feature prominently in the game's combat, don't make sense; you will create an impenetrable smoke cloud that you cannot see through or even into, and yet enemies will casually lob projectiles through it at you. Sometimes you will be stunned by electrified water despite being some distance frome it.
Despite this, this is in my top 10 games of all time.
Combat, while enjoyable, isn't the main draw of this game for me. The focus on exploration, puzzles, dialogue, and problem-solving is what elevates this game.
When played with a friend, this game becomes an unforgettable experience. Especially with the dual-dialogue system. I'm reminded of Bioware's hackneyed branching dialogue system as they tried to immerse players in their games while giving the illusion of choice (with most if not all choices ultimately ending up with the same result). Not so with Divinity: Original Sin. You are given a plethora of genuine choices, and your companion may not see eye-to-eye every time. The amount of time I've spent bickering with my friends over what course of action we should take is no small amount, and the fact that with the dual dialogue system we can have an in-game component to that makes me feel sorry for anyone who played this game solo.
The story is a nice departure from most standard fantasy games. It's a little bit esoteric at times, but it's nice to see something different.
The difficulty curve is rather sharp at times, so quick saving constantly becomes habit. Also you never know when you might rub an NPC the wrong way when your friend decides to try to pick their pocket without your knowledge.
This game is a must have for any fan of RPGs or co-op games.

Game Dev Tycoon gives you the task of becoming a world-leading Game Developer. Starting from the humble roots of your garage and slowly you work your way up to becoming a full-blown video games company.  TL:DR at the bottom.
The basic task from the very beginning is to produce games. To do this you first name your game and pick it's basic genres. Then you move on to 3 stages of production. At each stage you're given a screen with 3 sliders that you control to decide the amount of time and focus you put into each aspect of the game (eg. Graphics, Level Design and Dialogues). After production is completed you gain experience points for both your character and the skills of the company.
After releasing the game your game is reviewed on a scale of 1-10 by 4 critcs. Higher scores will be awarded for a better balance of the features put into the game. A high score is essential for your company to generate sales and progress. A game report can be generated which will give you tips on where you should focus your developement time and if a genre/platform/target audience combination is a good one.
As you make games you will gain research points that can be used to research new genres, develop game engines, research new technologies and more. Other things that can be done is contract work (where you code for another company and gain research points), attend game conventions and market your games. There are also random events that can have an impact on your company depending on your decision.
Once (if) you grow big, you can move into a large office, hire employees and train them as well as opening up your own R&D Lab for hardware manufacturing.
TL:DR Overall this game is a great, simple yet fun and has intuituve mechanics that are easy to learn but difficult to master. I would definitely reccommend this game as it is definitely worth the money.

There's a lot of comparison between this game and Minecraft, and rightfully so. For an adult, this game is unlikely to unseat Minecraft as the king of block building games. Even with a LEGO pedigree, there's simply been too much development over the years that has made Minecraft into a remarkably flexible and powerful experience.
But were I a child, LEGO Worlds is exactly the sort of game that I would want to  play. It's colorful, fun, and extremely easy to jump into. Review as of update 1.12:
Personally, I actually like No Man's Sky.

The survival mode provides a real challenge that I find very fun, and base building feels very rewarding. No man's sky certainly isn't perfect,  but it also isn't the game that most of these negative reviews paint it to be.  Prior to 1.1 it was shallow and unsatisfying after the opening hours.  After 1.1 survival mode actually gave purpose to the entire game for me.
1. Life is actually decently challenging.
2. Buildings are more varied and not nearly as prevalent.
3.New resources, base building and freighters add depth and meaning.
4. Dwindling resources makes the tiny in game economy needed ( especially at the beginning.)
I know there is much more that needs to be done for it to reach even half of its pre release expectations. However,  I truly enjoyed the beautiful planets and music. The feeling that exploring gives you is truly the reason to play the game. That combined with game play changes in the update make this a thumbs up for me.
Judge the game for the state it is in right now.  Not what you thought it would be or what the hive of angry people are shouting.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a point-and-click adventure in which you are "the Scythian", a girl-warrior that has to find her way through ancient legends, shadows, dreams and reality, with help from a couple of people and "dogfella" (bark, bark). The game fully "shines" in its 8-bit graphics: this makes it "old-fashioned" compared to current games but this is part of the beauty of the game itself. You'll love or hate the graphical part: I loved it.
The music helps a lot in providing the right atmosphere for each part of the game. I discovered Jim Guthrie by playing at Sound Shapes on PSVita: the music here is very similar and enjoiable.
On the negative side, there are moments in the game where you feel lost and the next objectives (or how to achieve them) are not 100% clear. This happens especially if you put away the game for few days.
At the end I felt ... sad ... in finishing the game. If a game can raise this kind of emotions by putting together few pixels,
well, the objective is reached. Overall I definitely recommend this game, but this cannot be valid for anyone approaching this game.

In Sword and Sworcery, you're a warrior, The Scythian, on a quest to get the mystic macguffin. You meet a few folks, fight a few beasts, and solve some puzzles (mostly by clicking at the proper time or in the proper order). This is all framed as some kind of "therapy session", presented by "The Archetype", a Fourth Wall-breaking, cigar-smoking quasi-narrator.
The major issue with this game is its far too pre-occupied with being quirky and self-aware. If it were a person, it'd be that guy who confuses the simple act of dressing in a suit and drinking martinis with having charisma and gravitas. He doesn't know etiquette, doesn't have any sorts of skills, has no refinement to his tastes, but covers for it by downplaying the importance of all those things. He's too cool to learn the rules but still thinks he can break them. That he's too good to know that stuff. He has no game, but think's he's a player.
That's what I got out of this game. The gameplay is extremely rudimentary and poorly designed on top of that. Skin pulled across bare-bones. Exploration consists of tromping across a simple path through several screens, very slowly. You click on things of interest to gain to be rewarded often with throw-away lines delivered in that Dudebro vernacular ("We saw a grave on the hill and wondered what was up with that". Riveting).
Puzzles consist of going where the hint tells you. This isn't hard, it's just tedious and time-consuming, due to the aforementioned plodding walking pace. You only have a linear left-or-right path to take anyway. Once you arrive, you hold down the button for five seconds to make your Magic-Mode happen. You then click in an arbitrary fashion on things on the screen. Sometimes it's sheep, sometimes it's trees, sometimes it's birds. There's no logical connection to the objects and the puzzle. There's also no real logic to the order in which you must click them. It's just trial-and-error. It's about as difficult and as fun as stuffing a bunch of random toys into a toy chest so the lid closes.
Combat consists of a rythm game that's extremely rudimentary. You can block, or hit. Wait for the cue, hit the enemy, or block his attack. Sometimes you attack his attack so it's bounced back, and they might bounce it back at you. Repeat until someone screws up.
So on top of this gameplay we get a presentation that's way too satisfied with itself. When something pretends to be much more clever or intelligent than it is, that's the textbook definition of "Pretention".
Don't get this game, it's a waste of time.

Played the game twice, years apart, and I can attest to this much: If you go into this knowing little about the 40k lore, it will be an above average hack and slash shooter amalgam that goes away with cover and incorporates a setpiece-based execution-heavy hack and slash shooter game with an average story riddled with terms you won't understand that sometimes feels like there's more story under the surface and sometimes it doesn't.
Go into it knowing more about the existing lore, however, and the game rewards you with plenty more depth in its story, justifying and explaining much that doesn't make that much sense otherwise. The campaign is fairly short, but good. Multiplayer I can't comment on.
The graphics are very decent, and so is the sound, but where the game shines is the combat itself. Few games have weapons as satisfying as the Bolter and its shells exploding within Ork guts, the Power Hammer and most of all the Chainsword and its brutal execution animations (reminiscent of Gears of War's Lancer rifle, but who ripped off who, really?).
If you like 3rd person action games, it's a must have. If you like 40k, it's also a must have. If you like both, you're doomed to wait for a sequel that will never come.

Thankfully, we have a great back catalogue to draw upon, and this includes 2011's "Space Marine" from Canadian studio Relic Entertainment. To the Moon is a point and click adventure game. You play as Dr. Watt and Dr. Rosalene two scientists from the Sigmund Corporation sent to help virtually fulfill John, a dying man's, last wish... to get To the Moon.
To accomplish this you use a machine (almost like the animus from Assassin's Creed) to go back through John's memories backwards starting from John's most recent memory all the way back to his early childhood memories.
In each memory you have to find an item that will connect you to one of John's earlier memories. This item has a barrier on it that has to be broken by finding items and talking to people that will give you different colored orbs that will unlock a puzzle which when solved will take you to the next stage. Through the exploration of each level you discover more and more of what John's motivation was for wanting to go To the Moon.
You can beat the game in one sitting if you want to. With a story line this good you might actually do it. The story will make you laugh, make you cry then laugh then cry some more when you see the ending of the game. The sound track is good and for the price it's totally worth it. Don't buy the game looking for a high graphic, high action game. This is a story telling game that takes you back through John's life and moves you emotionally. Get this game and see if you can get To the Moon!!!

If you are after a story that makes you cry, this is the one for you. I'll get to why I called this a story in a bit.
To the Moon has you take charge of two scientists who specialise in memory, the sarcastic Dr Watts and the more sentimental Dr Rosalene. Their contract is to fulfill Johnny's dying wish - to go to the moon. In order to do this, they must traverse through his memories to find out why he wishes to do so. As the story reveals more through you travelling backwards in his life (which is done excellently), you begin to understand. By the end, you are hoping so much for Johnny that it physically hurts. The story is worth the price alone. At the time of this review, it's €1.99 (a little more with the soundtrack, which I recommend) due to the Summer Sale, and an essential for everyone to experience.
As I said, this is a story. Gameplay-wise, there is not very much, except for one sudden platformer part that was really jarring to the point and click style and did not fit at all. The most difficult things you'll encounter are tile puzzles. It's very compelling to complete these in as few moves as possible. A running total of how many moves you've made over the game adds to the challenge. To the Moon is not very long, and will take at most 5 hours to complete, not including the DLC, which was kindly bundled with the game.
Given that the game was developed using RPG Maker, graphics are very bitty. Personally, I like this style, but it might not be to everyone's taste. Aside from a few cinematic animated cutscenes, it'll be the same style throughout. I didn't notice one very important plot point because of the style, but that's my only issue with it. I think it works with the story.
The soundtrack is beautiful. Composers (along with developers and pixel artists) are credited at the start of the game, which is a better way of crediting the creators. It's very clear that the composers truly cared about the story when they composed the soundtrack, which is worth buying with the game.
This story is a must to experience by everyone. It is one that stays with you, that leaves you crying at the end, emotionally and physically hurting. You need to try this, then introduce it to your friends and family. The price is slightly high for the length, but definitely pick it up when it goes on sale.

Obviously I am fairly late to the game. Over the years I have read many a description on this game detailing its amazing satirical discussion on nationalism and propaganda. Finally, I have delved far enough to see what this talk was about. Indeed, never have I been subject to such a quality, subtle look into such profound concepts in a medium such as this.
The moment I stepped out of the vault and picked up that signal, Enclave Radio, I realized the incredible, obvious truth that has been staring us all in the face. The truth that we have been blind to, that has been filtered away by the media, that we touch on in tired history classes, only to forget as the tests come and go.
We are no longer true patriots of this great and mighty United States of America.
I stayed in Springville for hours on end listening to the eyebot echo the words of my pip boy, the words of that prophet... No... President, John Henry Eden. The only time I faultered was when I could break away from my computer screen long enough to realize that it was a new day and that I needed to renew my pledge of allegience. Eventually, only after being thoroughly certain that my pip boy would carry those great words, those chilling calls to action, no matter where I went, I did progress into the game.
And progress I did. Through a series of mistakes I somehow found myself in support of the Brotherhood of Steel, a confused group who I was only associating with in hopes of opening their eyes of the glory of the new government they simply didn't understand. Oh, but there was no mistake, was there? Not as soon as I had the glorious opportunity to lay eyes and ears on the greatest achievement the United States could hope to replicate: Liberty Prime.
I will not spoil things for my fellow patriots, to give them the chance of self discovery that I had. But let me promise you that not a day has gone by that I haven't spent readying my homemade mini nukes in preparation for the forthcoming final war against communism, painting them in the sacred color pallette of Red White and Blue as I sing the National Anthem and hum to the tunes between the Enclave Radio I have running 24/7, mounted proudly on my wall.
We may not be in an apocalypse that we can visibly see outside of our door, America, but we are without a doubt at risk of losing all that makes this country as free and superior as it is. Fallout 3 has shown me the truth. The Enclave, the Brotherhood, the great nuclear disaster... It is a message, encoded wisely into what so many regard as "just a computer game." And we must play that game. We must hear that message. And then we will know.

What keeps these MMO games alive and prosperous are the players, it is not supposed to be a single player, and it would be quite dull if it was.
Now players are kept in the game mainly through the social aspect of it, yes the nice features get you to try it but it is social aspect that keeps you going on..
I've played several worlds, and out of them all Europe world is the biggest and most diverse battlefield. In it you see people clash because of glory, because of land gain, because of vanity, because of the diverse human nature..
The players themselves have sort of hierarchy, from the casuals and farmers to the ones who spend massive amounts of time and money on the game. Now while it is appealing to have the long wars and big wars, for quite a lot of crowns is spend in them, it is the small players who give up for they cannot compete. and without them the hierarchy crumbles, when only the strongest remain, we pool ourselves into a single house and we "win", but we actually lost that joy of battle, and the one thing that kept this whole game fun.. the conflict..
If someone buys a charter in your territory, pops politics card and swaps everything, and when you try to fight him back he has fully built castle, well you must understand how this makes a little man give up. And even tho the carder will fill your pockets, he will kill the average players in the process, and without them world will become a barren wasteland, one man per parish, all in one house. It will die off.
What I recommend is: give the average and dedicated players a fighting chance against the big ones.
Some ideas:
1) Decay of goods in the parish
- As prices inevitably go down in the parishes as the goods are being sold, it becomes harder and harder for an average guy to earn enough to compete in the wars, with let's say 10%  or 5% decay of goods in parishes weekly you'd see prices going back up. And since it is percentage based, it will make these evening better.
Example: If there is only 5k apples in the parish, 5% decay means 250 will be gone. and would effectively bump up price by a half a gold or a gold 143 to 144 let's say. BUT if there is 150k apples, 5% decay will make 7500 apples gone and bump the price by a bigger margin, 73 to 82 let's say.. So the more goods there are the more it will be effected by decay, hence increase income, hence prolong the wars and give average guys fighting chance and would keep them in the game.
2) Repeatable quest / Quest Chains
- Quests get progressively harder, as they should, but it means there are no rewards for dedication and time spend if you just cannot complete those, especially in the times of war. If there are let's say, repeatable quests on daily or weekly basis, that would earn some rewards, ranging from small ones to big ones, we'd see more activity overall.
Example:
- Repel the wolves - kill 200 wolves (or 10 wolf lairs) => reward 2,000 gold or 300 faith
- Repel the invader: Rat - Kill 5 rat castles => reward 10k gold or a random card pack or 500 faith
- Repel the invader: Wolf - Kill 5 Wolf castles => reward 30k gold and 2k faith or a wheel spin
Also chain quests, for instance, if you construct the quests, 7 of them for instance, and put them in the separate tab, only ONE can be picked DAILY, and if you complete all 7 you get some reward or a bonus. Those quests could be:
Destroying AI castles, Trade quests, Production quests, Monk based quests, Donations, Supplying quests, etc.. 7 of them. Player can pick one per day, and after 7 days they reset, regardless if he managed to complete all 7. But if he does complete all 7, you grant them a wheel spin, let's say.
This would make players log into stronghold daily and give them something in return for the time put in.
3) Make room for strategy, increase unit diversity
At the time being, as you well know, only solder units used in game are archers and pikes, swordsmen are not competitive any more, other then as moat digging crews but even  then you'd want pikes and battle cry, and it will be more efficient. Swordsmen just die to fast in the attack to make any difference, and they are rarely used in defense as you'd prefer pikes to hold off the enemy while automated defenses and archers fend the enemy off. I say change things around a bit.
example:
- give pikes bigger health pool, give them higher resistance against melee attacks, oil pots and spike traps. make them less resistant against the arrows.
- give swordsmen lower health pool, give them less resistance against oil pots or spike traps, make them more resistant against arrows (they do have a big shield after all, in addition to suit of armor, that pikes don't have)
Due to the targeting priority of ranged attacks Sally > Archers > Captains > Swordsmen > Pikes
Archers will go after swordsmen first, and even tho pikes would be more vulnerable against ranged attacks, you can still achieve good results if you apply strategy => send a mixture of swords and pikes, and while swordsmen "absorb" the enemy ranged attacks, pikes can eat oil pits and spike traps, etc..
^
This is just an idea, needs more work on it
Add new unit in defense!
I've longed to see Crossbowmen added to the game. Make them similar to archers, lower range, higher damage, make people create their own strategies with them. Archers have range of 27 paces from the biggest tower (would be nice if we can get it confirmed), so make Crossbowmen have 18 - 22, and give them bit more of a punch, compared to archers. God knows defending castle is rather tricky, unless you card massively.
Increase passive and well planned defenses' resilience against the attacks, crossbowmen, strategy designs, add rolling logs or allow pitch to be placed outside of the white line and to be set ablaze to burn the foes. Limit the number of squares you can put pitch on so players cannot cover all of it in pitch, but must use it strategically.. etc..
Meanwhile, limit the amount of defensive cards you can play per let's say castle. You can only ever have 5 effects turned on, or 3 effects. So people get to choose the best card that suits their castle design, for instance:
- Big oil pot / moat castles => people will pick oil pot card, moat card and last stand
- Big massive stone castles => people will pick stronger stone structures, call to arms, ballista fire rate card
^
Still an idea that needs thinking about, could work on it, but this is raw idea.
Make a difference between carded and strategic defense less distant. At this moment you get:
Carded defense => can't touch this
Non carded defense => I got slapped so hard by 2 or 3 timed attacks that guy next to me in a parish lost two towers :)
During wars if you're not awake to card defense, you need to sleep by the hour, and it is exhausting. That is why people give up on the game... Let well built castle with strategic defenses be conquerable but costly to take, let people go to beds without worry of what might happen if they oversleep. I don't mind losing a village, but I wanna know it was worth it if it was built well.

To be upfront, I'm a fairly big fan of the tycoon style games and love playing them quite a lot.
Overview:
Game Dev Tycoon lets you start a gaming company in the 80's from inside a small garage. You start out with next to nothing and very little skill, working yourself through the years, video game platforms, and trends that are somewhat historically acurate.
Graphics:
There really isnt much to say here. Graphics are held in a very simple cartoon style. The game doesnt look special, but then again for what it is, there really is no need for it.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very....basic....at best. Every game is developed in the same fashion with very little input from the player. Each game that you develop will let you pick focus areas at different stages of the game. These stages are always the same, except the optimal focus changes depending on what game youre developing, for what platform/s you are developing and the intended audience. In order to get better you'll have to analyse each game after its been released on the market to find out how well the different combinations and focus points worked...or you could just look up the different combination tables online, seeing as they are always the same. Now, dont get me wrong, for the amount of money this games costs, youll likely get your moneys worth. I did. But dont expect too much after that. Its a game that you can play during downtimes, where you dont mind some mindless clicking here and there. It really doesnt require too much attention or focus. The biggest problem I found with this game, is that there really isnt a challenge. After developing a few games, you'll usually get the hang of what goes well with what, and where you should place the sliders. After that its really just developing game after game, until ultimately the game time runs out. Sure, there are some achievments that will require you to play on, but they really arent worth it. Once the last consoles and devices come out, theres nothing exciting to the game anymore.
Conclusion:
If youre looking for a small indie game with not too much of a challenge, this game is for you. It's worth the price theyre asking for, at least for me, but not much more than that. The idea and concept is great, but it doesnt feel like a fully fleshed out game to me.

It's still Early Access, so I'm willing to forgive that it's unoptomized at this point, but it is something to keep in mind for people with less powerful hardware. I have not experienced any crashing, however, so not all is negative on the technical front.

I bought this game on a sale after the foundation update came out so my review is based on how the game is after that update. I like this game, it looks good, plays decently and I've not encountered many bugs. This is a SINGLE-PLAYER space exploration game, so I don't recommend this if you're looking for multiplayer or action driven gameplay.
Even after over 30 hours of gameplay on Normal mode (got roasted when trying out survival - will try that again later), there's still so much to do. You can follow this Atlas path, or you can just wander around exploring new systems and their various planets, environments, plants and animals. You can hunt for riches by grinding materials and trading them and you can build your own bases with alien workers to further your income. The workers give you quests that unlock more builds or upgrades. If you like exloding or killing things then you can do that as well, sentinels and space pirates can be challenging, specially in numbers. So, you can basically do what ever you want in an endlessly big world.
There are of course some cons I need to mention even though the pros outweigh them for me.
For starters, the handling of spacecraft is annoying and when flying over planets there's some kind of a "safety cushion" that makes you unable to land or crash yourself. Instead you'll just hover over the ground and press the landing button for auto landing. This is specially annoying since you can't see below your craft, so controlling on what spot you land is very hard (like trying to land on a landing pad or next to a base, instead of randomly landing some 100 meters or more away from it). The crafting system might also need some overhaul, since you'll need an empty slot in your inventory when making an item, even though you're emptying 2-3 slots in the process. There are a few minor complaints here and there also but for the most part I can look past it because other aspects of the game are enjoyable to me and I'm optimistic that the devs will add more features in the future to expand this world even further as well as addressing the issues most complained about.

Despite its relative age among other games (about five years as of writing this, counting the original iPad/iPhone release), Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP maintains an air of timelessness. Between its unique visuals, haunting tunes, and brief but legendary story, Sword & Sworcery EP remains a game that should, and likely will, be played again and again for years to come.
Thrust with little to no explanation into the boots of the Scythian, Sword & Sworcery EP tasks you with recovering the tools necessary to thwart an ancient evil. It's not entirely clear just how happily the Scythian's tale will end, but it's clear it must be ended, one way or another. Despite taking place in a relatively small slice of a world, the environment reflects your progress, sometimes in great ways, sometimes more subtly, goading you silently on toward success. The subtle nature of said guidance often leaves the game feeling a bit confusing and the player wandering, to be fair. However, a careful eye and/or ear is often the key to overcoming obstacles, and if nothing else, just try everything.
It doesn't help that the game's social media integration is far less effective now that the game is hardly new. Back during its release, progress reports and hints flowed somewhat steadily onto Twitter, as sent out by the game as players made headway. Now, that trickle has all but stopped, making a look or two at a guide to the game a necessary evil, albeit a forgivable one. This sort of integration with the real world was an interesting experiment, however, as was the game's recognition of our world's moon phases, as based on your system's date settings. If you can, try and complete the game without messing around with your clock; it feels more rewarding to have done so legitimately, with time to think about things between sessions.
The game does quite a bit with a rather simple interface as well. Inputs are rather basic, which is to be expected given it was originally created for iOS devices before finding its way to the PC. Still, the timing-based action sequences can offer a bit of a challenge, as can finding the right paths to traverse between said segments.
Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP flexes what many would consider the definition of a "game," but does so deftly, and leaves the player with a unique experience to remember. Be it the melodies of the soundtrack or what the art direction was able to do with a fairly limited style, there's something for everyone to remember this by.

I admit, I was pretty excited for Minion Masters. I liked Forced quite a lot, and I was excited to see what sort of spin they would take on card games.
While the premise is good, with playing your cards and having them fight without your direct control. In fact, it's very fun to play with friends. We enjoyed messing around with stupid, gimmicky decks.
But that's not the meat of the game. You can't earn more cards by playing against friends; friendly matches reward no currency or even complete daily quests. You have to go into online play for that. Online play is ONLY ranked at the moment. There's no casual mode. There's no draft mode. Nothing. You just get to dive straight into ranked where your losses are punished.
There's no rank lock points. If you make it into silver and then lose a few games, you slide back into Bronze. And because there's no casual mode available, your only way to experiment with new deck ideas is to sacrifice your rank for it.
And in any ranked mode, people will try their hardest. It's only natural. The issue is that in most card games, the path to victory is the path to frustration for your opponent. The effective cards in Minion Masters simply aren't fun to play against. If they have Demon Warrior and you can't end the game immediately, they'll just snowball out of control and you'll end up losing to something you have no way to counter. Some of the aggressive decks demand that you have an immediate response in your opening hand or you lose instantly. I lost a match in 35 seconds to a swarm-based rush with a damage buff, and there was nothing I could do because I didn't have daggerfall in hand. The Rammer is a card that just runs at break-neck speed for your hero and begins chunking, with very little response available.
Ah, but you say, counters exist! You can play daggerfall against the swarms, and lightning bolt against the Demon Warrior, and Wall against the Rammer. But the deck is only 10 cards, and you only have 4 in hand. You can't have a counter to everything in your deck (or rather if you do, you have no way to win), and even with what counters you do bring in you can't guarantee having them on hand if they're needed for multiple purposes.
It's not that the game's imbalanced; while I think the balance is a bit off and could use tuning, that's what an early access is for. The issue is that the game is just frustrating. Your losses feel devastating and your wins feel more hollow than not.
If they want this game to work and feel good, they need to severely trim away some of the frustrating cards. When you're playing with the various basic and common cards like dragon whelps, grenadiers, scrat packs, crossbow guilds, the game is very fun. But the game is dominated by frustrating gimmicks instead of making valuable trades and back-and-forth fights for bridge control.
The game has potential, but for now I have to say that you should give it a pass. If you get it for free, I'd suggest you play through the solo challenges available and then never touch online play--the frustration isn't worth your time.

[DISCLAIMER: I received this game for free by registering my email on the dev's homepage.]
TLDR:
A spin on the known Clash Royale formula, featuring FORCED-style design. Overall good game, at times frustrating due to RNG.
Description:
"Minion Masters - Forced to Duel" is a Clash Royale-clone with toned down P2W, due to the removal of unit levels. Matches spawn about 3-4 minutes, though can be over drastically faster or slower, depending on the decks of both players.
A deck contains a total of 10 cards, those can  be either minions, buildings or spells. Each card in a deck needs to be unique, though you have two "wild cards" - each allows you to use an additional copy of an included card. allows you for example to use 7 different cards and 3 times the same, 6 differents and two times two copies of a card. (You do NOT need to use the wild cards, however I would recommend it)
The addition of a commander unit makes this even more diverse - at any given time you have access to at least three commanders, one of the being the one you start with and an additional two which are free to play for a limited time.
Interesting is that you can unlock everything (aside of a premium account which increases your XP gain after each match, doubles received gold for one year among things) without spending cash, including alternate arena skins.
PROS:
+ No need to spend cash for any kind of content
+ Constant balancing, preventing single cards from being overpowered
+ "Wild Card" system gives an interesting spin to the deck building
+ Comfortable match length of just 2 - 5 minutes at average
+ Variety of cards
+ Commander-system allows for additional customization
+ Basic cards are not useless, some of them are even competetive staples
+ Daily free token can give you some of the cash currency, without the chance being totally BS
+ Daily missions allow for fast cash...
CONS:
- ... but aside of those and the achievments it is very grindy to buy new cards, which makes progressing a chore at times
- If RNGsus doesn't like you, this game can be incredibly frustrating
- In comparission to other CCGs the learning curve is very hard on you
- Some strategies are less viable because there is no commander who really would support them, making them significantly weaker
- You cannot chat freely, rather they gave you Hearthstone emotes (I hate that. CCGs are games which invite you to socialize, something you cannot really if all you got are emotes)
YOU PROBABLY WILL ENJOY THIS GAME, WHEN:..
... you look for a short time diversion
... you don't really plan on playing it all day long to unlock everything ASAP - sometimes it is best not to play for a day or two so you have more missions to complete (you can save up up to 3 dailies at a time).
... you should generally like CCG/gacha games.
... you don't mind a certain level of competetiveness.

I personally believe games like this can have more emotional impact than a book, since the player controls the character instead of just reading about them. I rate this 10/10, 5/5, 1/1, whatever scale you want to use. 100% all the way.

is not what I expected. I'm not sure
I expected, exactly, but what I got is not it.
Let me start over:
is a rich and beautiful game, with a wistful, melancholic atmosphere weaving between joy and hope and kindness. The story is deceptively simple, about two people performing a service to a client, whose wish is to redo his life and go to the moon. The catch is, though, that the act of reliving life is virtual, only happening inside the client's head, and right before they die.
But the game has undercurrents that have their own undercurrents: questions about ethics, invasion of privacy, and agency pop out from time to time, and there are no good answers. Do you continue with what you're legally bound to do in a contract when you know it's the very last thing the client wants, but has no way to terminate the contract? Is it right to change people's memories, manipulating their choices and resetting them if things don't go right? Is it right to change the choices of others' in the client's memories, without the permission of their living versions? What if the other party in a certain memory wants to keep it private between them and the client?
doesn't offer answers, because there are none. But the questions are there, and you can't help but wonder, and wait for the other shoe to drop. The minisodes (2 so far) make an excellent job at digging into them.
The characters, I think, is what makes this game. Most of the game is interaction between Eva and Neil, the two doctors who do the memory rewriting in the game, and they're just charming. It's obvious they know each other well, like each other, and work well together, and I honestly can't wait to see what would happen to them in future episodes, even though that after minisode 2, I'm not sure it's anything good.
Shout out to the gorgeous pixel art (and non-pixel art!), writing, and music. All of these build up an atmosphere that just plain
, and serve the story very well.

A surprisingly good little gem of a game. Bought it for $2.50 on a whim during a Steam sale, but it's entirely worth the full price of $10 if not more so. It's basically a god sim where you control four giants that each have their own unique abilities to shape the land and create different types of animals and natural resources. With these giants your goal is to steer the development of the world and lead it to peace and prosperity. Along the way the greedy, dirty, little humans will try to stir up trouble and you'll have to figure out how to deal with those problems. You can either try and manage them, or just give in to your darker side and destroy the villages with earthquakes and other fun tools.
The meat of the game is in the complex relationships between different resources and making sure each village has what it needs to continue to grow. It can be quite difficult sometimes with only four slow moving giants to oversee a whole planet, and it requires some planning and thinking. So be warned, this is not just another clickfest where the game plays itself out for you and gives you a WINNER badge at the end. Great game.

The most recent massive update for No Man's Sky has added a whopping 3x the amount of content we've received at launch, but despite this achievement for Hello Games, it isn't the game they promised in the first place. But, don't lose hope, because this is called the foundation update for 2 reasons:
1. You now can adopt an abandoned base and make it your own, and customize it to your heart's content with few limitations.

Brilliant game, one of my favourites of all time.
First let's start with...
You play as a Captain of the Space Marines, who are some of the mightiest heroes of the Imperium of Man. And you can tell, not just from how powerful you are in combat, but from the way the world reacts to you - you are high status, and your presence brings hope. My favourite moment was when a wounded Imperial Guard guy slumped against the wall whispers "I got to see a Space Marine before the end" in almost religious awe, followed by a prayer to the Emperor to aid you. Really makes you want to go out and kick Ork a
ss for the little guys.
Now not everything works exactly according to the Codexes; for example, Titus (your character) starts with a pistol and knife instead of a Captain's usual loadout. This is just usual shooter progress, of course; you pick up more weapons as you progress and this is fine.
But for the most part, the way the game represents Warhammer 40000 is clearly a labor of love. Everything is massive in size, gothic, the way it should be on a Forge World. Love that crane the size of a skyscraper. :) There's never an infodump about W40k lore, but the background is filled with these little things that you'll notice if you pay attention. Like the automated announcements playing in abandoned factories and population centers, that have a vaguely creepy "1984" feel to them, letting the unfamiliar but observant audience know just what kind of a world and what kind of a Universe this is. My favourite is "If you are injured, return to your quarters; the Machine God will watch over you". In the middle of an Ork invasion slaughtering everyone. Very helpful, I'm sure.
So yeah. There have been some crappy games based on the 40k licence, but this isn't one of them. Relic's Dawn of War was a good example of treating the subject matter correctly, and so is Space Marine.
As to just how badass this game can make you feel in combat, just watch TotalBiscuit's review of the demo. His unstoppable glee makes me smile.
I spent more hours on the single player campaign than I'd like to admit, but it is the multiplayer that cemented this game as one of my very favourite games ever. Your abilities in it are scaled down for balance, of course - the jump pack in SP was overpowered as hell, and therefore only available for short segments of the campaign, but here it's a lot less destructive.
The combination of fluid melee-and-ranged combat, with all these wonderful Warhammer 40k weapons, and the possibility to play as an Assault Marine/Raptor, makes this literally my favourite multiplayer game that exists right now. It's just so much fun. Thunder Hammers and Meltaguns and Lascannons are powerful tools, but even the humble Bolt Pistol - my preferred ranged option - is a potent threat in the hands of a competent player.
If you're going to play Assault Marine, btw, check out my intro to the subject:
So as not to mislead - the multiplayer playerbase is small now, especially since Eternal Crusade came out and drained some people. That's why public games only happen in Seize Ground, which is the point capture mode, on classic maps (which is fine, because it's the best mode and the best maps). Also, currently it's harder to get games in European mornings; the multiplayer picks up in the afternoon and evening. Nevertheless, games happen every day and there's lots of fun to be had.
I got the DLCs and don't regret it - playing as the Dreadnought is awesome beyond description - but be warned: for the most part you won't get to play them. You'll only play the DLC maps in private games, duels or arranged games with friends. Make lots of friends, invite 40 people at once and you'll get a 4+ vs 4+ game. There's also Exterminatus (not the best name for co-op mode), which gets a more difficult version in the DLCs, and that one's quite fun too.
But you can get by just fine without buying them, since it's classic mode that keeps getting public games.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a generic third person action shooter. You take the role of a hardass white guy and meander through a series of narrow passageways that open up every 10 yards or so into a little shooting arena that fills with orks, who you then murder en masse so that you can hurry on to the next corridor or cutscene.
Even on Hard difficulty, this was so easy that it couldn't keep my interest enough to play all the way through. And it's not like I'm some god tier click-on-mans guy - just ask my TF2 teammates. The idea is probably that you're supposed to feel super badass chewing through hundreds of guys, mashing melee attack and spraying automatic weapons until the swarm of green turns into a pink mist. If that's your jam, more power to you, though I found it rather jejune.
Voiceacting is just as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as any other Warhammer game. Tough dudes saying gruff one-liners, angry orks repeating the exact same voice clip about how they are going to shoot you over and over, that sort of thing. WH40K has always been over the top but the RTS games did it to the point where it was
. This is just a boring b-movie action flick.
Graphics already look pretty dated, even though the game's only a few years old at this point. Color palette is just as brown and washed-out as any 2000's era shooter.
I very much want to like Warhammer 40k. Anything in the universe at all. But the tabletop game is tedious and only sperglords play it, the RTSes are basically only good for a one-time run through of the single-player campaign, and this is just a huge pile of meh. Your time is better spent elsewhere.

Introduction: Tom Clancy's The Division is an Third Person Open World Action Adventure MMO Set in Manhattan in the year 2030 after a deadly virus burned through the state of New York. The President Issued Directive 51 and Put the State into Martial Law. You are an Agent of the JTF and the Division fighting the result of the virus - Deadly Gangs, Escaped Prisoner’s, Contaminated Civilians and more.
Review: Sometime in the 2030s an Unknown Strain of the Smallpox Virus Known as "Green Poison" or "Dollar Flu" Among other Nicknames, was developed by Dr. Gordon Amherst, a virologist, as a means of population control and was distributed by infected dollar bills during the Black Friday shopping insanity. The Dollar Flu became so Out of Control that the Government Placed New York, More Specifically Manhattan Under Quarantine and a Martial Law. The Government then began Activating Sleeper Agents Who work for The Division to help the JTF (Joint Task Force" Restore Order to the State and City. The story takes the player through a 20 Hour Story Mode before Finally reaching Level 30. Like Most MMO's Reaching Level 30 is where the real game begins and the same is True for The Division. You will start out in Brooklyn which will be a very small "Training Map" that will introduce the player to the Very Basics of the Game then Story Events Will Take the Player to the Main Map Manhattan. There is lots and lots and lots of things to do in the division, you will never get bored. There are TONS of side missions and Events there is ALOT of lore if you like the story and the graphics are stunning so just walking around and exploring and enjoying the scenery can be fun all on its own. The game does feature a PvP Mode. To unlock PvP Mode you must be reach level 30 first. PvP Mode is held within The Dark Zone. Once a player enters the dark zone they immediately become available for other players to shoot at will. Shooting another player will mark you as a "Rogue Agent" Basically your PvP Flag is turned on and an Icon will appear over your character letting other players know that you’re a Rogue and your PvP Flag is on. Its screaming "Hey! Attack me! I wanna PvP!" lol. There is lots to do in PvP other than open world Fights. You can Go to an extraction Zone and Hijack Someone’s Cargo (Basically their inventory and Look) and put it in your own. You can Kill other players while they are doing Side Missions and annoy them. Whatever you want to do to start a fight with other players in the DZ (Dark Zone) Use your imagination because in the dark zone there are no Limits or Boundaries for PvP. Go Crazy. The population of players in the Division Are not bad but there not great either. Finding a player in matchmaking for a group can sometimes be very annoying and sometimes it’s an instant find. You can however do ANYTHING litterly anything Solo in the division as long as you have the right loadout. Nothing requires more than 1 player to start. The Servers themselves are Amazing. I personally LOVE the division servers. To be honest they are the best servers I have seen in a video game in a very long time. I have little to no problems with lag at all. No Connection Issues. Connecting to is very fast and non-problematic. The Servers on the Division are great. If you are worried about hackers and cheaters in this game, then you don’t have to worry because there are none of those in the division. The Division is a great clean game and Ubisoft done a great job at keeping cheaters out of the game.
Downloadable Content: The Division Includes some downloadable Content: Survival and Underground. Underground is a PvE Focused DLC that takes the player into the underground part of Manhattan, the overrun subway tunnels that have been converted into strongholds by gangs and bases by Military Gangs. Players can set multiple different modifiers on an Underground operation to make them harder and give them better loot. Survival is a Mix of PvP and PvE DLC that is just like it sounds: When a survival game is started the player(s) spawn stranded in the middle of Manhattan During a Blizzard with no gear or supplies, or comms and are infected with Sepsis that threatens to kill them in an hour. The only thing the player has is a pistol that has no ammo which you have to find. The objective is to find the Vaccine hidden somewhere in Manhattan and then get to the Dark Zone for Extraction. Players only have 1 hour to do this before the Infection kills them which results in game over.
Pro's:
-Open World
-Side Missions
-Activities
-Events
-Collectables and Lore to Find
-10/10 Graphics
-10/10 Server Performance
-The Game is Kept Updated
-The Servers are Great.
-DLC
-Con's
-The Community Could be bigger. It’s not dead but it’s not big either.
-More of the Population Speaks Foreign language than English.
Conclusion: The Division is an Amazing Open World Action Adventure MMO that will keep you infront of your computer for hours and hours. The Graphic's are amazing and it’s just fun to walk around and explore and enjoy the world. The PvP is just as fun as the PvE and the servers are GREAT. The servers are some of the best servers I have seen in a video game in a very long time. There are no cheaters or hackers anywhere and the story is good. There is ALOT of things to do including DLC and you will never get bored with this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves Open World Games, Shooters and MMO's.
Rating - 9.5/10

At the time of writing I'm at 3 hours of playing, so to clarify my thoughts are on the "early game", so to speak.
Reus is a fun, charming god game with beautiful art and gentle music. The main game mode gives you reign of a 2D globe for a set period of time (from half an hour at the shortest to two hours at the longest) and leaves you to achieve whatever goals you choose within that time, with the suggested goals that unlock new items being things like making a city that prospers using only animals and minerals, or making a particularly large city. The strategic element of the games comes from achieving each city's goals using the limited number of tiles around them by taking advantage of symbiotic combos, such as a predator that gets a bonus from being around smaller animals, or a plant that grows better next to mineral deposits.
While there is a free play mode, I prefer the structure that the goals offer, since they challenge the player to try new things and new playstyles. The limited time sessions are also a good design decision, since they avoid the weakness that some sandbox games have of dragging on for too long and becoming formless. I find that Reus is a good game to dip into for a session at a time, try a few new goals, relax a little but also think a little, and if that sounds like the kind of game you'd like to have in your library I would highly recommend it.

[DISCLAIMER: I received this game for free by registering my email on the dev's homepage.]
TLDR:
A spin on the known Clash Royale formula, featuring FORCED-style design. Overall good game, at times frustrating due to RNG.
Description:
"Minion Masters - Forced to Duel" is a Clash Royale-clone with toned down P2W, due to the removal of unit levels. Matches spawn about 3-4 minutes, though can be over drastically faster or slower, depending on the decks of both players.
A deck contains a total of 10 cards, those can  be either minions, buildings or spells. Each card in a deck needs to be unique, though you have two "wild cards" - each allows you to use an additional copy of an included card. allows you for example to use 7 different cards and 3 times the same, 6 differents and two times two copies of a card. (You do NOT need to use the wild cards, however I would recommend it)
The addition of a commander unit makes this even more diverse - at any given time you have access to at least three commanders, one of the being the one you start with and an additional two which are free to play for a limited time.
Interesting is that you can unlock everything (aside of a premium account which increases your XP gain after each match, doubles received gold for one year among things) without spending cash, including alternate arena skins.
PROS:
+ No need to spend cash for any kind of content
+ Constant balancing, preventing single cards from being overpowered
+ "Wild Card" system gives an interesting spin to the deck building
+ Comfortable match length of just 2 - 5 minutes at average
+ Variety of cards
+ Commander-system allows for additional customization
+ Basic cards are not useless, some of them are even competetive staples
+ Daily free token can give you some of the cash currency, without the chance being totally BS
+ Daily missions allow for fast cash...
CONS:
- ... but aside of those and the achievments it is very grindy to buy new cards, which makes progressing a chore at times
- If RNGsus doesn't like you, this game can be incredibly frustrating
- In comparission to other CCGs the learning curve is very hard on you
- Some strategies are less viable because there is no commander who really would support them, making them significantly weaker
- You cannot chat freely, rather they gave you Hearthstone emotes (I hate that. CCGs are games which invite you to socialize, something you cannot really if all you got are emotes)
YOU PROBABLY WILL ENJOY THIS GAME, WHEN:..
... you look for a short time diversion
... you don't really plan on playing it all day long to unlock everything ASAP - sometimes it is best not to play for a day or two so you have more missions to complete (you can save up up to 3 dailies at a time).
... you should generally like CCG/gacha games.
... you don't mind a certain level of competetiveness.

Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition Review
I spent 77 hours on Divinity: Original Sin and I spent another 94 hours on Divinity: Original Sin – Enhanced Edition.
And I liked it.
Many years ago I played an action RPG - Divinity 2 (aka Ego Draconis aka The Dragon Knight Saga aka Divinity 2: Developer’s Cut); it was a mix of an RPG and TPS and I really enjoyed it. The world, the characters, the style – I had a lot of fun.
Years later Larian Studio released Divinity: Original Sin. This game is an isometric RPG with heavy emphasis on turn-based battles. I really love this game and here is the list of reasons:
1.	It is beautiful. There were a lot isometric games published at the same time – Wasteland 2, Underrail, Age of Decadence and some others, but this game is a level above all of them. The game has absolutely stunning graphic. It looks like a AAA RPG.
2.	It has unique world. I really like Larian Studio’s style. They have their own universe, they fill it with many interesting characters and they treat it with humor. I really like the Pillars of Eternity, but it is a typical classic RPG – “and we have dungeons, and there are dragons in those dungeons, and we have dwarfs, and elves, and hobbits (i mean orlans), and there are powerful gods and they will meddle with our character...”. Sometimes I just prefer something really different and Divinity: Original Sin is in fact different.
3.	It has an amazing battle system. Many interesting skills and spells make the combat interesting and challenging. You can alter the ground with your spells and then add some effects from your thief skills.
4.	It has a lot of puzzles, it has a unique mechanic with teleportation pyramids (and the Teleportation skill), which can be used while travelling and battling.
There are several flaws in this game, of course.
First of all, some puzzles are not very interesting and require pixel-hunting.
Second – later in the game your team become too powerful. I believe it is a problem for the players like me who like explore everything and who gets a lot of experience and levels.
Third - most of the stuff you get is random items. I would like to see in their future games more unique items.
But these things weren’t able to spoil my impression of the game.
It is really good, it is challenging and fun, and I recommend it to every player.

You've been frantically searching for some ammunition, mysteriously left in a water-proof case in an oceanic labyrinth inspired by Bikini Bottom, Pirates of the Caribbean, and Sphere. You've got your crew, straight out of the Into the Blue, except there's only one female booty to ogle, but hey, everyone like's Alejandro's butt, too.
There's a minute movement in the water, a change of light that barely registers, but you're too busy staring at the shiny gold idol that's going to buy you that 50 footer you've always wanted, and all the champagne your ex-girlfriend insisted on wasting on a christening.
The torpedo that hits you is made of living steel, and it's covered in sandpaper. You've dropped your trusty underwater pistol (maybe that paranoia was justified, after all?) and now you're going full Prison Break on this fatal fish. It doesn't matter that your knife is only five inches long and you can't generate as much force under water. You stab, because that's the only thing you can do when there's a killing machine the size of a Nissan Leaf shaking you around like a plush toy.
Somehow...somehow, you survive. Your friend's toxic speargun made the shark sick, and it floats in front of you, a grisly ghost. It may not have taken your life, but it did take your peace of mind.
Now every time you look at something shiny and gold, you'll wonder if the shark is lurking in the shadows, biding it's time for the perfect moment to lunge. You see, these sharks have sentient human minds behind them, and as Jurassic World and Deep Blue Sea tell us, intelligent carnivores that move as fast as a moped are not a ♥♥♥♥ing joke.
tl;dr this is an asymmetric, omni-directional take on the multiplayer fps genre, and it's a lot of fun. Like Insurgency and CS:GO, it could probably use more stuff, but what's here is well-done, and that's more than can be said for any other asymmetric shooter.

If I put Pirates! and any of Akella's Sea Dogs installments on a scale, the needle would be pretty close to the middle. It's not that they are very similar, far from it, but both cover roughly the same bases, albeit with different focus and different strengths and weaknesses. Sea Dogs' naval combat and RPG depth are second to none while its side activities and conveyance are truly awful, and Pirates! is a brisk and fun game, very cinematic and varied, without much depth regarding character progression and so straightforward it feels too easy at times.
After deciding your starting year, skill focus, difficulty level and the nation you'll spawn as, the story starts with you and your fellow crewmen revolting against your cruel captain. From there on in the basic game loop is simple: go out to sea, pick a target, board it, sell ship and cargo, repeat. Combat is straightforward but still retains the staples of these kinds of game: wind direction, broadsiding, range, ball/chain/grape. Boarding is carried out in a symbolic duel between the captains, with the crew acting as their health points (although they can be defeated without running out of them). Ships can't be bought, only captured, but upgrades can be bought at ports (one in each), and the player can command more than one vessel, although combat is strictly one on one.
There is, however, more to it than naval combat. The tavern in every port serves as an information point where one can eavesdrop on rumors or collect information on buried treasure, notorious pirates or worthy cargo to sack. Sometimes those will lead to battles either by sword or cannon, sometimes they will lead the player into treasure hunts, and sometimes will give information on the whereabouts of the player's estranged family. While it's true that most of those activities will carry out the same way, they always give pointers for progression to those players not content with playing out the background simulation.
On that topic, Pirates!' map not only it's huge, but it also feels very alive. Cities will grow and dwindle depending on the commerce, attacks and people they receive, empires will react to the player's actions, and even cities can change hands. The player can also exploit the settlements along the way, sending pirate raids towards cities, escorting shipments, manipulating empires into amnesty, raising through the ranks as a privateer, attacking forts, sneaking into cities, marrying the daughters of governors, achieving ever larger estates age shifting the balance of power throughout the Caribbean. It's all very straightforward and needs drive from the player's behalf, but there's certainly a lot of things to do.
According to the difficulty one selects the game will become more complex, if not too much. There are three types of weapons to select on duels, pirate hunters will be on your heels more often, and morale will decay faster. After morale hits a certain point, the player will be forced to make port and divvy up the booty, where he'll be given the option to increase or decrease the difficulty, or end the game, wherein he'll be given a score based on his exploits during his career. The objective of the game, so to speak, is to get the highest score, so is a game designed to be played in 5-10 hour bursts and several times over, although the progression and objectives will always be largely the same, so while the incentive for replayability is there, the appeal is not huge.
Pirates! is a game dangerously close to becoming an all time classic, but it's simplicity and straightforwardness, while making it very accessible and appealing, hold it back from greatness. Just a tiny bit more depth to every aspect would've driven it over the hill, but as it stands, it is a very nice game to spend a couple afternoons with every once in a while. The graphics do certainly hold up, and the design of it all is well thought through and through.
8/10.

- Pros
1. Much larger campaign map (or so it feels) than the previous game.
2. Skaven, and soon to be Tomb Kings (♥♥♥♥ YES!).
3. New huge campaign that's focused on the great Vortex of Ulthuan.
4. Again CA knocks it out of the park with the unique playstyle of every race.
5. Improvements to magic UI make line spells a hell of a lot more usable.
6. Mortal Empires (post launch) adds all of the old factions (save for Norsca) so there's currently 12 encounterable races, and adds a new campaign that combines most of both maps.
- Cons
1. The Man-o-War license is really hurting this game now. High Elves and Dark Elves without Navel battles basically have most of the flavor of their factions sucked out. Luckily CA tried to negate this a bit by making the oceans of the world much smaller so there's less impact, but it could have used some old school navel combat mechanics like in Medieval 2.
2. Without the first game adding the Mortal Empires campaign and races this game seems a little lackluster of a choice compared to the first one since a lot of the hardcore flavor factions were introduced in the first game.
3. Campaigns in the Mortal Empires map are definitely grand, but the problem is that they tend to drag on. I haven't finished a single Mortal Empires campaign and I've put around a hundred hours into my Empire campaign. It's grand, but late game drags on in it.
4. Norsca. I hate to say it since they've been very upfront about what's been happening with the Norsca debacle, but unfortunately this game will have been out for nearly a year before we see content that was already in the previous title. This also includes the 30th anniversary patch. These two updates were huge, and made a lot of the factions more entertaining to play as with their units of renown. I understand that they had to redo those updates completely and that kind of work takes time, but it's still very dissappointing to have to wait that long for old content.
This game and the first Warhammer Total War are both awesome! This game gives you the Lizardmen, High Elves, Dark Elves, and Skaven races to play as with the Tomb Kings coming up in January as DLC. If you have both Total War Warhammers they combine in the Mortal Empires campaign, and while not at launch CA, the developer, has been very upfront about what's happening with this game and I'm very happy with their delivery of everything, save for the Norsca debacle. All of the DLC for the previous game was really good and added quite a lot of goodies so I'm more than excited to see what they come up with for this game. I'm a little worried since after the Tomb Kings there isn't any table top armies I could see them adding until game 3, but some people are speculating a Dogs of War army which I wouldn't be against.
This game needs a little bit more power than the previous title, but overall it wasn't to rough of a transition. If you haven't played a Total War game yet I would highly recommend looking at the system specs and making sure that your computer is up to the task. Even my machine with a 1080TI and 16GB of RAM and 3.55GHz of processing speed has moments of lag when in battles that have more than two armies involved.
With all of that said the first game ate up over a thousand hours of my time and I loved every minute of it. This game has so far eaten over two-hundred hours of my life. I don't think there has been a better Warhammer fantasy game. If you like dark sinister fantasy lore and want to see some epic armies duking it out with all sorts of monsters and eldritch horrors this is the game for you.

In conclusion, this is the best TW game so far, certainly worthy of a steam award

In fact, despite, even due to, its monolithic size many players will find the gigantic nature of the amalgamated Mortal Empires campaign to be too much of a daunting task and will find themselves spending the majority of their time playing through the Vortex with the 4 new playable races rather than attempting a campaign that could easilly take months of daily play to get through.
It is also important to note that Mortal Empires is only available to owners of both games and that any factions from DLC will only be available to those who either already bought them or buy them in the future.
Regardless of whether or not you make great (or indeed any) use of Mortal Empires; Total War Warhammer 2 is the pinnacle of tactical wargaming on any platform.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a generic third person action shooter. You take the role of a hardass white guy and meander through a series of narrow passageways that open up every 10 yards or so into a little shooting arena that fills with orks, who you then murder en masse so that you can hurry on to the next corridor or cutscene.
Even on Hard difficulty, this was so easy that it couldn't keep my interest enough to play all the way through. And it's not like I'm some god tier click-on-mans guy - just ask my TF2 teammates. The idea is probably that you're supposed to feel super badass chewing through hundreds of guys, mashing melee attack and spraying automatic weapons until the swarm of green turns into a pink mist. If that's your jam, more power to you, though I found it rather jejune.
Voiceacting is just as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as any other Warhammer game. Tough dudes saying gruff one-liners, angry orks repeating the exact same voice clip about how they are going to shoot you over and over, that sort of thing. WH40K has always been over the top but the RTS games did it to the point where it was
. This is just a boring b-movie action flick.
Graphics already look pretty dated, even though the game's only a few years old at this point. Color palette is just as brown and washed-out as any 2000's era shooter.
I very much want to like Warhammer 40k. Anything in the universe at all. But the tabletop game is tedious and only sperglords play it, the RTSes are basically only good for a one-time run through of the single-player campaign, and this is just a huge pile of meh. Your time is better spent elsewhere.

Reus is pretty much that- you have yourself some basic elements and landscape tools and use them to guide humans down the paths you want. The addition of timed matches and challenges to unlock new manipulations is brilliant because it means there are goals to strive for- and goals are essential when you're playing an almighty deity. After a few challenges and short runs of the game, you have more complicated matches, more elaborate goals, the ever-present danger of a population attempting to challenge you for a perceived slight against them. It's a game of simple controls but it's exceedingly difficult to master. Y'know, kinda like divine power would be. In a nutshell I strongly recommend Reus to any fan of God Games who wants a more involved aproach to divinity.

2. This is the foundation for updates to come, which looks very promising so far.
Overall, this isn't a terrible game, despite the reviews you see for it. The reason why so many believe that it is is because of the overwhelming hype surrounding it, and the lies that were fed to us by the devs. However, I feel that the devs are making amends, and they will continue to grab my attention and support if they keep up the free updates. I can almost guarantee that if this game was put out in early access, and if it wasn't advertised to♥♥♥♥♥♥ the reviews and thoughts on this game would be much different. That is if they didn't lie to us then.
Overall, I give this game a weak 6/10, but that can definitely change if Hello Games keeps up the good work. Seriously, though, please don't stop. I really want to see this game reach its full potential, and make do with all of its mistakes.

Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition Review
I spent 77 hours on Divinity: Original Sin and I spent another 94 hours on Divinity: Original Sin – Enhanced Edition.
And I liked it.
Many years ago I played an action RPG - Divinity 2 (aka Ego Draconis aka The Dragon Knight Saga aka Divinity 2: Developer’s Cut); it was a mix of an RPG and TPS and I really enjoyed it. The world, the characters, the style – I had a lot of fun.
Years later Larian Studio released Divinity: Original Sin. This game is an isometric RPG with heavy emphasis on turn-based battles. I really love this game and here is the list of reasons:
1.	It is beautiful. There were a lot isometric games published at the same time – Wasteland 2, Underrail, Age of Decadence and some others, but this game is a level above all of them. The game has absolutely stunning graphic. It looks like a AAA RPG.
2.	It has unique world. I really like Larian Studio’s style. They have their own universe, they fill it with many interesting characters and they treat it with humor. I really like the Pillars of Eternity, but it is a typical classic RPG – “and we have dungeons, and there are dragons in those dungeons, and we have dwarfs, and elves, and hobbits (i mean orlans), and there are powerful gods and they will meddle with our character...”. Sometimes I just prefer something really different and Divinity: Original Sin is in fact different.
3.	It has an amazing battle system. Many interesting skills and spells make the combat interesting and challenging. You can alter the ground with your spells and then add some effects from your thief skills.
4.	It has a lot of puzzles, it has a unique mechanic with teleportation pyramids (and the Teleportation skill), which can be used while travelling and battling.
There are several flaws in this game, of course.
First of all, some puzzles are not very interesting and require pixel-hunting.
Second – later in the game your team become too powerful. I believe it is a problem for the players like me who like explore everything and who gets a lot of experience and levels.
Third - most of the stuff you get is random items. I would like to see in their future games more unique items.
But these things weren’t able to spoil my impression of the game.
It is really good, it is challenging and fun, and I recommend it to every player.
