Sword & Sworcery features a female warrior on a quest to reunite triangles lost in a mysterious fantasy realm located somewhere between dream and reality. The intriguing story is divided into three increasingly long sessions, each briefly presented by monologue from The Archetype, with a shorter final one acting as a sort of conclusion.
Very appealing and well executed pixel art embodies artistic simplicity met with astounding precision and remarkable sensitivity. Simple but fluid animations infused into every corner of the world, along with subtle color shifts that gracefully enhance the liveliness of the scenes, create a mesmerizing environment unlike any other.
A solid soundtrack suits the mood perfectly, composed mostly of rock-tinged retro ambient ballads, properly extravagant mood trips, doom and gloom, and a wealth of high quality atmospheric sounds.
Dishearteningly and despite all the game does exceptionally well, there is too much to loathe about everything done wrong, or too peculiar to be enjoyable. Every time it surprised me with an awesome moment, of which there are a good few, it had to immediately remind me of its many glaringly frustrating elements.
Sword & Sworcery's totally awkward controls, obviously initially created for touch devices, do not play well in a mouse configuration, despite efforts made to ease the transition. Almost every design decision taken by the developer seems counter intuitive or ergonomically inefficient. Thankfully simple hints pop up from time to time to explain the more cryptic expectations.
Dreadful combat sequences require learning unavoidable patterns and hitting one of two buttons at the right moment, often with no clear consequence until repeated exposure. Later combat sequences can only be described as cheap rhythm games akin to playing ping pong. And waiting. Battles are exceptionally long for surprisingly so little action, as most of the time is spent waiting for a cue. Fights are so unequivocally counter-intuitive that an explanation comes after each failed attempt in the game's Megatome, a sort of encyclopedia chronicling important characters' personal thoughts.
The same boring and uneventful fights keep re-happening fairly frequently, without actual rewards, presumably to artificially extend playing time.
There are some funny and/or clever bits of dialogues and descriptions, though it eventually becomes banal to read blurbs drenched in juvenile hipster crass hidden among rare gems. Despite the intriguing setting and the very charming characters, the whole affair reads like an aspiring author's collection of best attempts at mystic alliterations and esoteric one-liners.
Most Sworcery puzzles mainly consist in (optionally) ingesting magic mushrooms to see specific parts of the environment lit up, then figuring out in which pre-determined order the game expects you to click to release sylvan sprites. I found no logic to these segments most of the time, so it turned out to be tedious guesswork for the more obtuse ones and deceivingly simple otherwise.
Parts of the game accurately synchronize with the actual moon's phases, marking one of the game's most unique and truly original ideas. Fortunately, the developers realized that being able to play entire sections of their game only once a month at full and new moons was a spectacularly bad proposition, and they built a way to temporarily alter the phases of the moon directly in the game, essentially circumventing the entire feature's purpose and value.
A few other minor flaws and annoyances include the main character constantly referring to herself in the second person, completely useless Twitter integration on every single line, slow character movement, and too often self-referential for its own benefit.
This game offers a beautiful world in which I would love to get lost for hours, if only it offered anything worthwhile to do. As it stands, its long list of frustrating elements far outweigh everything else I so desperately loved.

OK, first off, if you are looking for a game that offers real time strategy on a massive level where you face off with literally thousand of players (I am talking real people now), this is a game worth checking out. It's one thing to play a Real Time Strategy where you face off against multiple AI and/or with a few players, it is another thing entirely where you soley interact with people from all walks of life (remember, I am talking thousands of people) in a scope of a game that is the size of full countries and even continents. There is more to this game then constructing apple farms and land grabbing, a single poor decision can result in all of your villages being burned down by an entire House (a coalition of united factions) containing dozens if not hundreds of players, or just one lone player who did not care for you gold raiding his parish. The potential events are endless.
Stronghold Kingdoms is a game where Diplomacy and warfare go hand in hand to a level that the most shrewd and cunning strategist can be undone by a unsuspecting foe. One single misstep could mean the difference between being a King of a whole Country commanding armies of fellow players in a war campaign, or finding your self surrounded by enemies by waking up one morning to learn all your villages have been pillaged, ransacked, and razed (all of which are game features by the way). As for who could be responsible for this? A old foe you scorn long ago, a recent rival who seeks to usurp the power base you have amassed, or possibly a well trusted ally who has stabbed you in the back. In truth this game needs a Game of Thrones expansion of sorts, it is THAT indepth with it's warfare campaigns and politcal intrigue. As mentioned, the potential events you can experince are endless and impossible to express properly in a game review.
Now in terms of actual gameplay, it might not have the most top of the line graphics or all-star game engine at this time, but that is not the intended appeal for the game. The Gem this game offers is the scope and the depth expressed previously. With that stated, you basically have five modes of play that you will likely at some point or another partake in while playing Stronghold Kingdoms, these modes are "Research", "Village Contruction and Managment", "Castle Construction and Management", "Player vs. Environment" (things such as AI lairs that are run by a computer), and "Player Vs. Player". These main features have their own sub features but for someone totally new to this game who would be reading a Steam review, you don't need to concern yourself with sub groups at this time... besides there are already plenty of guides written covering such. In the end, these features while on the surface might appear fairly basic, can offer you literally hundreds upon hundreds of hours of enjoymeant with them alone. Not too bad of a deal with a game you only pay into at your hearts desire.
....And with that mentioned, time to address the big fat pink elephant in the room with dollar sign tattooed all over it. Stronghold Kingdoms is very much a free to play game which does not prevent you from achieving anything in the game a "subscriber" or "premium token owner" can do aside from a few things such as moving village buildings around and having a simplistic trading feature telling you which goods sell for top gold in location "A" while said good sells for rock bottom price in location "B". Aside from that, a Free to Play player can do and achieve that of anyone. Period.
HOWEVER! There is a "Pay to Win feature" now before you stop reading, pause, breath, and read a bit more to understand how the title is true but the definition is inaccurate. Stronghold Kingdoms is a game that is designed and true in everyway I have mentioned thus far, however there is one aspect I have not yet been able to touch on until this point. It's a game that is designed to have you keep returning to it in order to maintain not only your villages and castles, but the game it self. This is a game 110% designed around it having a strong and active population of players, without people playing it, there is nothing to do in it aside from picking apples and hunting helpless wolves in their lairs, who just want you to stop growing apples and spend more time breeding pigs! (not to much to ask, is it?). But seriously, it needs a active population, to help ensure this it has a gradual constructing-build-progression-system. Basic way to explain this is "construct 1 village building takes 5 seconds to complete, the second takes 10 seconds, the 3rd takes 15 seconds...... the 80th a whole freakin' day and a half!" this sort of system applies to things such as castle buidling and research but they work in seperate ways but to the same point. There are research option you have to increase castle build speed, village build speed, and research completion speed, again the three operate differently but the point of them is the same.
Here is where the "Pay to Win" feature comes in, or as I like to call it "Pay to speed this #$%^ up already!" ... better known as "Cards". Cards come in a variety of things but the majority of them focus on speeding the processes of the game up dramatically so you can achieve your goals faster and move onto other goals. To describe a few, cards which instantly give you things such as resources (so you do not need to wait to produce or steal them.. oh yea, have I mentioned you can steal peoples stuff? Mmm, dat pillage.), army speed cards so rather waiting 5 hours to reach a target on the other side of the map you are there in say a hour and a half (provided you have the army speed research done), village and castle construction speed, etc. In a effect it is a time saver but the advantage of "carding" to speed the process of the game up can give one a distinct advantage over others who don't, thus the "Pay To Win" common phrase but it is simply "Pay To Complete This $^&@ Today Junior!" Only a few cards make a player have a distince advantage over another in terms of combat / warfare and those are cards such as X2 to wall strength, handy to have but not god mode by any level. A half skilled player who is persistent enough, does his planning properly, and has some patients can beat a heavy "carded" castle.
If you are right now asking yourself "Is it possible to obtain cards without paying into the game or at least where I always need to do it?" The short answer to that question is... Yes! The game has over the years installed systems to give all players cards for free or for a short time investment. One common method is the "collect Your Free Cards" method, which is a option you see while looking at the campaign map on the near top left of your screen. Follow the steps listed to gain more free cards per week, maxing at 14 per week. Other systems are invite-a-friend, where you get crowns for a portion of anything your friends pay into the game if you invited them, treassure castles which gives wheel spins that have a chance of landing on card packs in a varity of quanities along with alot of other goodies, and quest rewards which either give wheel spins or just card packs out right.
With all that covered, is it easier to achieve your goals with card packs while playing the game? Yes. Do you need to buy card packs? Not unless you see it worth it. Can you obtain them throughout playing the game without dropping alot of $ consistently? Yes.
I would say that about covers my review for Stronghold Kingdoms, I could easily write and cover more about the game.... but while writing this, my House Marshal has finished debriefing me on my assignment to be dispatched with a buddy of mine to move far behind our enemy lines, go full swing viking rampage mode of pillage-ransack-razing the country side to instill fear while the bulk of our House holds the front lines from being over run by filthy Italians. One of the most beautiful games I have ever played and also one of the most mechanically satisfying. The introduction is intensely moving and the art is stunning. There are some difficult sections and although you can overcome most of them with a bit of powerup backtracking to get more health it is still a satisfyingly challenging game. The save mechanic is ingenious but is completely up to you. There are checkpoints but they are few and far between however the ability to generate a save point anywhere using part of a special meter which also unlocks certain doors is very clever (in the early game at least, once you have maxed this guage you will never run into the "do i save now vs. open this door" decision). Fundementally it is a metroidvania style gated progress game. There is backtracking but the more you progress/unlock abilities the faster you will move through the environments so this is rarely a chore. For those who want to collect everything be aware that each of the elemental temples will permanently shut after you leave it so collect everything within them before you retrieve the stones at the end of them. I played for 10 hours at least which was a pretty thorough playthrough but I feel this was a good length and the game did not outstay its welcome. I cannot recommend this game enough to anyone with even a slight interest in platformers it is one of the best games of the year!

This game was somewhat deceiving (though when I say that, I don't mean that in an entirely bad way). The game is barely what I'd consider a strategy game. It's much, much more closely a puzzle game. You basically are mix and matching different pieces of life that synergize with each other to complete objectives. It's almost like those element combining games mixed with Tetris, since you don't have much room to do all this. When I think of strategy games, I think of games like Civilization, Starcraft, DOTA 2, etc... This game even looks like an RTS meets simulation game by the videos and screens. But like I said, it's much, much more puzzle-like. I did not even remotely feel like I was playing with a simulation or strategy game. There's supposed to be some combat between villages, but I never got that far into it. I just wasn't having enough fun to do so.
If you like space management, puzzle games, then you would probably find enjoyment in this, but I like deeper, more accurately described strategy games, so I can't recommend it.

This can be a great game. I'll explain.
-This game's brick building system is amazing.
-There aren't that many bricks to use, but the ones that are there are usable for many things.
-Game looks amazing without being graphically intensive.
-The ability to edit every individual block in the seemingly infinite world. (someone get on this! Find the farlands!)
-So many vehicles, biomes, creatures, minifigures, and little items to unlock.
-Soon to be multiplayer.
-Great terraforming tools.
-Neat stud system where you unlock something, then buy it to spawn it infinitely afterwards.
-The items you unlock become spawnable on every map you create, much like terraria.
-Incredible movement animations for the characters.
-Awesome rocket launcher physics.
Some things can be fixed or edited.
-When you copy something, like a roof, and paste it on a house that is smaller than the roof, the generation puts land where there was something hanging off.
-When pasting and you have the outline of what you're pasting, there are some positions where you can't place it. (if an explanation is needed, I can make a video.)
-The panning camera stops working on occasion, fixable by restarting the game.
-When brick building, the panning camera might zoom out very far. So when you middle click on a block, it zooms very far out.
-When you dig with the drill into water, you fly into space. (Extremely funny the first time)
-Minifigures getting stuck in trees.
-can't make your own vehicles.
-No technic pieces or upside down/sideways pieces.(as of yet)
-The driving. I don't know what kind of "method" of driving physics this is, but holding forward, no matter what, should make you go forwards. When you are panned so you are facing your minifigure and "go forward" you go in the direction you are facing, or in that case, backwards.
-No first person.
There are so many more great things and gripes than I have mentioned, but these are the ones I have noticed while playing this game. Please don't mess this up! I have high hopes.

For an early access game, Lego Worlds sure shows a lot of promise!
Each world you play is randomly generated and shows you where you spawn, but there is so much more of the world for you to discover. The worlds consist only of lego bricks - you can delete just about every brick and place most "simple" bricks (e.g. 2x4 bricks) in any colour you want, but no specialist bricks (e.g. flags) can be placed. Hopefully the ability to place these specialist bricks will come out in the near future
As you play your Lego World, there are different objects, such as plants and cauldrons, that you unlock by paying in studs you can earn from destroying these objects, allowing them to be placed. Furthermore, there are npcs that you can unlock to play as, as well as using their clothes to create a custom character. There are also animals and vehicles that you can ride, which also must be unlocked
The camera is quite good when walking or riding around, but when building, it is not very precise, and difficult to line objects up. i have also encountered a glitch where shift+tabbing out stops me from moving the camera angle.
Building in the game could possibly be a bit better, perhaps more akin to the controls of lego digital designer, and as mentioned before, the camera prevents accurate block placement in many instances
Currently the game has no set objectives and also has little in the way of models and items. However, the current items and models are very detailed and useful, and I am sure that there will be hundreds of more exciting models that will be able to be placed
Ultimitely, the game has an array of exciting features and unique worlds, and is priced exceptionally well. Although some of the controls are a bit finicky, I am sure as the game develops further controls will be streamlined
This game is definitely a good buy if you are interested in the world building genre, and obviously if you like Lego

What do you think the game did well?
Compared to my experience with the classic version, the enhanced edition introduced more voice-overs for dialog and it trimmed the dialog text down. I felt the game guided the player better through the main story and various levels which helped prevent the player from completing a quest ahead of another. Several new spells and actions were added for more varied combinations of abilities. There were modifications to the main story which helped clarify it better than the classic version. New gear was also introduced to help ease the pain of combat, especially on high difficulties. A few crafting recipes were fixed and some new ones added. The side and the companion quests were by far the most entertaining for me as their stories pulled you in and sometimes surprised you.
What do you think the game could do better?
The Greek mythology of Pandora's Box is a great story but I felt like the game didn't really do anything different to make it unique or interesting. Some of the new spells and actions were consolidations or deletions which took away the middle-of-the-road varieties. Scoundrel additions were underwhelming and I felt like it nerfed the class more than helped it. The new Aerotheurge spell Storm is way overpowered as well as Lava Core from Pyrokinetic. The overall balance of combat has changed with the new spells and actions to favor the player, which can be entertaining for some, but not a challenge for others. With the new gear additions I as able to turn the Madora companion into an unstoppable Man-at-Arms by equiping her with all the immunity and high resistance gear.
Do you recommend this game?
I was entertained while playing and it was fun mixing and matching the new abilties as well as gear but I would say I am in the middle on recommending the game. I think some people will enjoy it while others will not but not a bad experience if you purchase the game on sale.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the Team-Based, Mulitplayer Action Gore-Fest known as Depth. Depth recently celebrated it's 1st birthday on Steam and has been around since November 3rd, 2014. It was released by Developer/Publisher Digital Confectioners.
(NOTE: This was a review from a game in my own Steam library, it was NOT provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:


The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Great twist on the Team-Based Multiplayer experience. You can be a diver or a shark. What more can you ask for?
4.5/5, Grab the 4-pack (especially when it's on sale)!
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Many of my friends know I am not a big fan of this style of game. I did play BF3 for a while and enjoyed it, and I did the CoD streams with Echo, but Team-Based Multiplayer games like this were never much more than average fare (for me). This beast, though. Man. This is what Evlove SHOULD have been. One team is the Divers, the other team is the Sharks. There are mutliple game modes, I spent most of my time in the Blood & Gold mode (divers collect treasure and defend themselves, sharks eat divers). You can earn money/evolution points and upgrade your weapons and items or abilities as a shark. Really, talking about a game like this is frankly a waste of time. It's something you have to play to enjoy. I typically am non-plussed by this style of game, but this one really is TONS of fun and took me back to the golden days of MultiPlayer gaming with my friends on Goldeneye and the like. This is cheaper, and better, than Evolve. The $24.99 or so that you can buy a 4-pack for during a Steam sale is an absolute steal. The graphics are great, the sounds add to the fun, the controls are simple. Add in neat skins and stuff (cosmetics), and it's a nice little game that seems to be picking up in community numbers. Give it a go and get in now while the community is growing. The Devs are active and the game still gets regular updates. This is the kind of game you cumulatively sink hundreds of hours to over time.
4.5/5 as it's still growing into that 5 that I am positive it will get to.
Happy Gaming!!!

Alright, so it’s not a secret that as I’m writing this, Warhammer 2 isn’t in the best spot right now. It’s a little rough around the edges, even if it’s not at Rome 2 levels. But this is a look at the game from a wide angle, to be sure, so let’s get started. With that out of the way: Warhammer 2 is (currently) the latest installment in the Total War series, which tasks you with managing vast campaigns and carrying out grand battles. This installment focuses on the New World of the Warhammer Fantasy universe, which brings two flavors of Elf (High and Dark), the rat-like Skaven, and the cold-blooded Lizardmen into the motley crew of races on offer so far (discounting the Tomb Kings, who aren’t out yet or part of the base game, but are shaping up to be really cool).
Opinions are pretty mixed about how the Vortex campaign works, and that’s fair. Personally, I’m a fan of it, even if I feel like it’s too easy to just ignore what’s supposed to be a failure condition (and believe me, you’ll need to ignore it on higher difficulties, where the AI outraces you to the end so quickly that you will be thanking the designers for making it almost impossible to lose due to a Vortex defeat even if it’s
possible), but Mortal Empires was the more appealing draw for me. This secondary campaign requires you to own the original Warhammer, but then adds the entire Old World into the mix too, giving you a ridiculously massive set of continents to conquer as your chosen races. Alliances will form, unlikely superpowers will emerge, and because Norsca’s not included yet, Surtha Ek will send 18 chariots and an infantry unit at you. It has a few performance issues, but I will admit that I’m slightly under-spec, and it’s incredibly satisfying to be able to mess with the whole world (with a few omissions).
At the same time as I heap praise onto this title, it’s somewhat obvious that Creative Assembly are spreading themselves a little thin. Warhammer 2’s “FreeLC” offerings thus far are well behind the timetable set by the original, not to mention the DLC has been slimmer (Beastmen were out 2 months after release, while we’ve waited nearly 5 for the Tomb Kings). I suspect this is due to the somewhat-rough shape Mortal Empires put the game in when it released, and only time will tell if they will make good on their promises or cut their losses. For what it’s worth, I remain confident the former is the case, and the game as it stands is definitely worth the asking price to me, being one of my favorite releases of 2017.

TWWAR 2 is such a great improvement upon what already I considered a great game in War 1.  Again each of the four new races are completely and totally different to each other.  AND completely different from all the other races in TWWAR 1.
I won't bore you with listing all the improvements, but It contains many hours of replayability within it and many new features added from the first to give you a different feel.  I hope that one day that CA adds actual ship to ship (Man-o-War) combat and multiple race army battles (like what you see in the intro trailer).  Be cool seeing a big battle royal all against all battle royal between four different races (for example) = TRUE WARHAMMER table top!  HA!
The massive Mortal Empires game map for those who own both games is HUGE.  Talkin tons of new gameplay hours playing any of the new races within it or any of the old races you got from WAR 1.  It's totally new experience as any race can grab any city.  You playing in it, you really need to pay attention to the whole world or you could find yourself completely overwelmed by lets say a massive norse & chaos invasion (haha) - yep it wasn't a pretty sight as I was fighting for my races exsistence.  Take note that the Mortal Empire map is slightly different than WAR 2's map.  They trimmed it up a bit to streamline it some.
When War 3 is released, you'll have a true Warhammer (names-sake) game.   Two races I know for a fact will be in there and that's:  Chaos Daemons faction and the Ogre Kingdoms.  Now the other two are a bit tricker, as there aren't anymore official recent army books for the others...  But I think I would bet we see Chaos Dwarfs, because their lands are in the north in the last map section.  Chaos Dwarfs are VERY different from their non-tainted kin, they use hob goblins slaves/cannon fodder (heh) for example.  And they got a unit that carries shotguns (blunderbuss).  haha
But the forth now that is where it's anyone's guess.  Now I bet we will eventually see the Tilian Mercs (that is why their main city isn't like others - prepping the way).  The orginal Dogs of War faction (Tilians) came out in the 90's, but was discontinued.  They are a mix-match of various specialized units of humans, orcs, dwarfs, ogres, etc.  They are the true first "regiments of renown" army - this is where CA got the idea to have them in the game for all races.
Another possibility is Cathy - but now your talking first & second edition original Warhammer (70's-80's).  But Cathy is also over in that map section (very far east).  A huge empire of Japanese syle units - they ARE pretty cool, won't lie.  haha
There's also a Amazonan race (all chick race) - never played them personally or even remember where they are located, but another old army.
There is also a Halfling army too!  But I hightly doubt this army is done.
Oh and I suppose you can mention Nagash - yes another Undead faction led by their original undead daddy (heh).  He would have a mix of both Vampires and Tomb Kings units, just none of their speicialized stuff.  But he'd have some his own special stuff (like a mummies unit with big two-handed mauls - ouch they hurt, heh).  But I wouldn't count on seeomg this faction seeing how they're going to release Archon the Black in the upcoming DLC.  But who knows...
But whatever CA decides to do, they got their work cut out for them in some serious researching and re-balancing.  Because Warhammer units & armies in the old days were much different than in the newer release days.
This takes allot of time and money to do all this - they are a business that has to show a profit to their Sega execs (who sets ALL the prices by the way).  NO business is going to stay in business for very long if they give everything away for free.  You people need to wake up and open your eyes to reality and get your heads out of Cloud 9.
They charge for the Blood add-on, because IF they add it to the base game, then they MUST make it a 'M' rated game, instead of it being a 'T' rated game.  I understand why they do it, though I think the impact of such things is small now-a-days seeing how they didn't even release WAR 2 in box retail game form (truthfully I think games should be released all over = more exposure = more sales).
All in all though, you will NOT be dissapointed in TWWAR 2, CA really stepped up to the plate and hit a home run with this game and I personally am very impressed by what they've done here.  Goodjob guys!!  I can't wait for Tome Kings!

This is a modern take on old school interplay RPGs. You have a party of four in a non-serious cartoony world with many modern day references. There were many places you can only advance after a skill check (Ex: perception of 8 or more). If you don't have the required stat you would never find hidden buttons or secrets in order to advance the main plot. You cannot respec your characters without losing all the skills you found from books. This means that you would have to find (or purchase) every single skill you lost during respeccing. The anxiously awaited, feared, dreaded "Mega-Patch" has been released.
Has it improved the game visually? Does gameplay profit from it? Should you buy this game now, if you have not yet?
Visually, the game has not changed; not that I could see, anyway. It still is very pretty to look at. Not at the technical edge, but still pretty, and mostly of high fluency.
Under the hood, there have been some changes. Quite a few. Certainly too many to review. Best read the patch notes, if you are interested.
If you have though of buying it, in the past but did not, because you were daunted, now's would be a good time, because with the patch all asstets and money were wiped from the existing players' inventories. So a level playing field. I cannot but suspect, that attracting "new" buyers into a "levellerd playingfield" might have been one of the motivators.
That aside, I cannot recommend buying it now. If you didn't like it enough 2 months or 2 years ago, you won't find anything in it now, that might justify buying it.
It still features the same dull, complicated, unintuitive, disorganized UI. It just makes me want to cry, for the lack of love over the last 24 months.
Gameplay-wise, the grind in this game is incredible. First money, then battle XP, then craft XP, and now money again. The devs have also introduced a new grinding feature - PvP and PVE marks. So the grind never stops in this game.
The economy has not worked properly so far. It's too early to tell wether it will now. But I wouldn't hold up my hopes.
Especially, because the one tool, which was avtually helped to make sense of the messy logic in the economic system, the trader tool, has been all but deactivated. So having "Excel" running on a second monitor to make notes, is almost a must.
Also, the announcement of Naval Action Arena (the lobby battle "light" version of the current Open World Sandbox), does not fill me with confidence, that there will be an Open World Sanbox Naval Action much longer - despite the developers' comments to the contrary.
This game is a pre-release version for now. It depends on a clear strategy being implemented. So far, I find it lacking in clarity, strategy and implementation. There has not been visible progress. On the contrary. Every development step forward in time, has been accompanied by two steps back.
If you were looking for an opportunity to be part of a development, as an active contributor, I fear, that you might be disappointed. The vast majority of "players" are simply disregarded. The only real contribution is funding. The proper development is done by a small group of players and devs.
Also, this title has suffered from continouosly decreasing player numbers (check steamcharts for confirmation), which spiked around patch announcements (to save what you could) or patch deployment (to see what has happened) and then rapidly fell to less than 200-300 players..
So despite the decent potential for the idea, of being an excellent niche title, which could have had a decent amount of devoted players, I do not see a bright future for it.
In the end, don't take my word for it. See for your self...if you can spare the hefty price amd a couple of hundred hours at least, before seeing and doing some really cool stuff, that is.

Like many online browser games of the "freemium" genre, Stronghold Kingdoms greatly favors big real-money spenders and gives everyone else--from small money spenders to the free-to-play majority--the shaft. This is not a game for someone who isn't willing to exploit every little fiber of the system or the fact that one is playing with real people, and therefore the smart player who cannot afford to spend hundreds of dollars to keep up with the big spenders must essentially lie, cheat, and backstab the majority of the player's adversaries--and at the same time, the big spenders with their awfully game-breakingly large armies are liable to do the same to you! Even if you chose to be a peaceful bystander.
On the technical side this game features doznes of technologies from four trees: Industry for resource production, Military for the army, Education for cultultural influence (which moves you ahead), and Farming for general agriculture. Their functions in the game are more or less obvious, but in order to use them effectively you must be willing to forgo wasting in-game currency on "useless" technology and find the best way to combine the usefulness of technologies.
The military is very simple: Peasants who are easy to draft en masse (expect to use these little guys a lot early on, and expect the premium players to never use them until they're spent), archers whom are fragile but can easily snipe enemies at a distance (expect to see big complex castles hosting these in their towers, which are protected by statkes early on and moats later on), pikeman for a balanced assualt and defense (early on these guys are impossible to get without spending real money, meaning you will not be able to use them for nearly a month while players who pay large sums of money will almost certaainly send these guys in waves in the first week!), swordsman who are basically the ultimate offensive unit, and Captains who serve as city-takers and leaders.
The castle construction part of the game is more complex and a bit fun when you're in-game rich enough to capitalize on the insane powers of tall towes and thick stone walls built in a maze with deliberate weaknesses in certain spots for the sole purpose of luring the attacking A.I. (even human enemies cannot control the battle itself, therefore the winner is essentially determined at the start) through your death maze with hailstorms of arrows!
Although the beginning can be rough, if you survive, you might see what I mean in the above.
However, this game is in real time, which means human enemies from the other end of the world hitting you in your sleep and real people waiting on you. If you cannot commit to serious play then don't play at all--"semi-actives" are almost always ignored, bullied, pillaged and eventually conquered by the 16-hour players.
Luckily the majority of the players don't like money-spenders unless they're in the same "faction" (i.e., a group of players who formed a veritable country with a government and political process and everything), and will therefore be willing to work with you in fighting the rich. Also note, the real fun comes from factions, as they have the real power (despite the fact Houses are meant to be groups of factions, they don't have any direct authority whereas faction leaders are practical dictators). In my experience the best role to play is that of a faction leader, but I highly recommend you find people to join you at least a month ahead of time. Otherwise you're putting faith in the random people you recruited in the local regions.  Also note being a dictator--or oligarch--requires you to invest much of your personal time and have extensive knowledge of the game (or at least a very good idea).
From the follower perspective, the game is much harder as it's very difficult to find a decent faction to match your desires. And if you join then leave too many factions you will almost certainly develop a bad reputation and be shunned by many. Therefore you might want to consider taking up leadership--even if it's small and weak, it's better to be the sole owner of a small-time business than a shareholder in a coorperation because you will at least learn from your mistakes and from them, do better next time (under a different name and account ideally).
In conclusion, this game is the epitome of Social Darwinism and it greatly favors people willing to shell anywhere from 30$ to 150$. With those who spent 150$ effectively buying out the game.
I have found it a massochistic pleasure, the challenge is punishing but the rewards are great, I'd give it a score of and 80/100 compared to most browser games and a 60/100 for games in general. This game will tease you with it's fun times and really bite you in the butt with it's jerks and big spenders, therefore if you want to play, you better bring your poker face and conceal don't feel.

As of the time of this review, the game is a solid experience.
However, I would like to say that the game does feel very samey when comparing it to Minecraft, or dare I say, Roblox. While the whole game captures that essence of a LEGO experience, it is hard to play it without thinking of those two games.
In the case of Minecraft, the presentation is fairly word-for-word. You are dropped into a blank world with its own ecosystem and inhabitance, you have no objective other than what you make of it. That is fine, after all it is LEGO, the brand is about exploring new ideas and creativity. Though some things, like the floating blocks, I find distracting, especially when some constructed objects respond to in-game physics, while brick-built objects do not. This is jarring to me as the gravity is clearly there. And where the game is lacking in regards to Minecraft is crafting. Though this is made up for with an in-game building tool.
Now with the case of Roblox. Everything from the character designer, items, and building, seems very akin to Roblox, yet much more refined. I don't have much to say in this regard because the experience is as solid as Roblox, perhaps even more with the added tubes in the bottoms of the bricks.
As a LEGO experience, I find it frustrating when building. The building is often compared to LEGO Digital Designer, an official tool for more experienced builders who lack the resources to bring their creations to fruition. I feel as though that team needs to be brought on to aid in this. The in-world building is interupted very often by the awkwardly inconsistent camera sensitivity, an issue that has harked on Tt LEGO games since they entered an open world experience. I found myself floating into hazards and dying, which both spooked me slightly, and frustrated me. That and the grid-snap is strange, as LDD functions on a tight grid snap that requires a good bit of movement of the mouse to separate the digiral bricks. Here the bricks are floaty, and do not hold onto others bricks for very long. Perhaps if the buidling was separted into its own system, or even if LDD importing was in-game, this issue would be resolved. For now, I will most likely be avoiding this all together in exchange for the pre-built structures.
Lastly, and this is just a nit-pick. The worlds in-game lack a sense of life. Skeletons roam the overworld at all times of the day, and while special mini-figures are locaton appropriate, those NPCs just roam. There aren't any settlements that really bring these worlds to life. And that always sort of bothered me with sandbox worlds, some of them just don't feel, alive.
Over all the game is a wonderful blank slate, definitely aimed at kids and AFOLs in the same way. Will it have the longevity that Minecraft has maintained? With enough up-keep, and community interaction, yes. Definetly. Now just to wait for the multiplayer so dedicated players can make recreations of LEGO Island and the Island of Mata Nui.

Do you like fantasy RPGs? Buy this. It's one of the best I've ever played.
The game world is a bit quirky (random bad puns, etc) which are sometimes tonally at odds with the story, but the pop culture references are rather entertaining.
The game is HUGE. Imagine the size of Skyrim, minus all the wandering around aimlessly. The world is big, but it's also dense. (Though there are a fixed number of enemies to kill for XP unless you get off on murdering townspeople. There are no respawning enemies.)
Combat is pretty fun. I like that there aren't any classes - each "class" is basically a skill you level up independently, then you find skill/spell books to learn abilities. Realistically, you're probably not going to have any generalist characters, but the fact you *could* is nice.
The one thing I would complain about is late-game spellcasting. Up until near the end of the game, spell casting is a lot of fun. Sometimes overpowered, but the enemy also having spellcasting makes that not so bad. But when you get high level and near the end of the game, enemies have enough health that your spell damage is kind of useless, and spellcasting really becomes buff/debuff and not elemental damage.
If you play D&D, you're probably familiar with people saying melee is a linear progression and magic is exponential. Well, in this game, they're pretty evenly matched, but the usefulness of magic decreases very abruptly near the end of the game. I ended up respecing my spellcasting character into melee w/ some support spells. I shouldn't have had to do that.
THAT SAID, I was probably 100+ hours in before I felt like spellcasting had stopped being useful, and if you aren't a completionist, there's a good chance you'd beat the game before it became an issue.
From a very personal point of view with the gameplay:
This game's essentially XCOM but without the cover system and the best elemental/environmental system I've every played with. I love this game.
An amazing game with fantastic devs play this game.

PLAY THIS - if you like puzzles, achievement and level unlocks, building and planning things
DON'T PLAY THIS - if you are looking for a God game with the usual fanfare of fancy spells and conflict
OVERALL - Recommended, assuming you like a bit of a development puzzle. Solid game, best played casually once in a while, interesting alternative take on what a God Game is.
At first glance you might be forgiven for thinking Reus is a god game. And at the start, in a very simple way - it is. But that's not what Reus is about - Reus more than anything is a puzzle development game, which just so happens to have god like giants striding around carrying out your latest puzzle solving commands.
You can probably stop reading here and decide whether you like progressive puzzles that require repeated plays to figure out. If you don't you can skip Reus. If you do, or at least you really like at least the theme of a God Game that's actually a puzzle game...
The first couple of hours of Reus will get you familiar with moving your guys around, creating the land types - and what kind of variations you can get up to, and most importantly of all will introduce you to the main element of the game - puzzling out the transformations of one resource type into another.
At this point you might leave the game alone. A light game. Couple of hours of play. I get it.
But, if you're the type of player that likes to build things that will see you progressing and unlocking new capabilities and achievements, that enjoys trying to optimise and plan a better setup, then Reus could lock you up for countless hours.
As Reus progresses your virtual world dwellers will demand ever increasingly impressive buildings to be built for them - and your job is to supply the required number of resources to do that. But resources are not just a simple task of sticking down a mine here and an animal there. In Reus there are dozens of resources - and most of them can only be utilised in a not so easy to navigate upgrade tree.
What you can build depends on how many successful projects you have built in the world - and therefore the upgrades your giants have in order to place ever better resources and upgrades, and also how far through the game you have progressed. Most of the upgrades and buildings will simply be unavailable to the starting player, and the game will need repeated plays for you to unlock achievements and unlock those better resources. It will often be the case that you will be able to progress so far - and then no more, as your paltry set of resources just don't have enough clout to cater to the demands of your meeples.
Reus has a lot of depth to it. The sheer number of resources available and their unique synergies with other things around them gives a huge amount of variation in effect. And this gives rise to a fairly interesting laid back game that comes down to puzzling out the best placement and interaction of what's available to you. But it takes time. Reus is going to eke out what it lets you play with so that you need to play it over and over again. As each unlock opens up new capabilities so you will be able to push the envelope and release a new set of unlocks and so on. As the depth of your unlocks increases so too does the time required to get your civilisations up to the point where they can start utilising them.
Nice progressive game mechanic, or cynical attempt at lengthening game replayability of an otherwise much shorter game ?
Overall Reus is worth playing, it's a solid game and has some nice depth to it - just how long you will be playing for depends on you temperament.

An oldie but a goodie.
Easy to play but deceptively hard to master, this, in my mind, is the definitive pirate game.
Not a very complicated game but highly addictive and very re-playable.
The eldest child of a wealthy and prominent family from the Old World, you were celebrating with the rest of your extended family when, in the dead of night, the festivities were interrupted by a powerful and corrupt Spanish Baron. Bashing down the door, the Baron and his men storm into your family estate and, for reasons as yet unknown, takes your family hostage. You, as a child, are able to hide from the vile Baron and only you escape with your freedom. Growing-up on your own without your wealthy family's resources at your disposal, you learned to sail, swordfight, and have a natural ability to lead. But you've never forgotten the Baron or your family, still his captives. One day, though, you hear a rumor that the Baron has set sail for the New World and taken his vast fleet with him. Hoping your lost family is traveling with the fleet, you go to a local tavern and sign-up with one of the Carribbean's four super-powers.
This is where the game begins. You create your character, define his name, set his profession, and choose a European nation to sign-up with. They each have their strengths and weaknesses and each will give you a different ship to start the game with. Your faction choice is not a PERMANENT one; you can change your loyalties as often as you like or even openly pirate everyone if you want.
-England, whose small but well-equiped fleet has secured a number of well defended ports. Their fleet is smaller than Spain's but is the most flexible in the game; able to do everything adequately but nothing exceptionally.
-France, whose strategic, but scattered, hold on the Carribbean leaves them in control of some of the most lucretive ports. Their hold on the Carribbean is tenuous when you arrive and they are threatened on all sides. With your help, though, France can grow into a power to rival Spain. Their ships are, generally, more formidable than England's but less flexible.
-Holland, the smallest yet wealthiest Carribbean power. They have few cities but they are all extremely wealthy and give you access to some of the rarest goods, items and upgrades in the game. They, generally, have the weakest warships in the game and could be regarded as the hardest faction to start with but their cargo ships can hold immense ammounts of plunder and, if you're willing to invest lots of cash into upgrades, they can be turned into surprisingly formidable pirate vessels. If left alone, Holland will usually be ousted from the Carribbean fairly quickly because they hold so few ports to start with but, if you support them, the Dutch are very VERY good friends to have. If you're nice to the Dutch, they will give you the tools you need to turn nearly any ship in the game into a formidable warship capable of challenging even Spanish Galleons.
-Spain, the dominant power in the Carribbean. They have more ports than England and France combined, the largest fleet and the wealthiest treasure ships. The Spanish are merciless to their enemies but can also be powerful allies. The slowest to trust, the Spanish are usually your primary target for piracy being that you'll encounter their ships pretty much anywhere on the map. At the start of the game, the Spanish will absolutely dominate all the other powers but, over time, they will become the targets of multiple wars and will slowly diminish. Eventually, near the end-game, Spain's military power will be a joke and, though they'll retain control of many cities, they will pose very little threat to the other nations by then. (Note: siding with Spain does NOT lock you out of the main storyline of pursuing the corrupt Baron as it is revealed that the Baron has gone rogue).
Buy this game! It's cheap, it's fun, it's easy to play. Some of the game mechanics are contrived and get tiresome after a while (the ballroom dancing and the fencing, for instance) but the grand-strategy of the thing is worth sinking time and effort into. From managing crew morale to knowing when to divide the plunder, when to take down rival pirates and when to fight make deals and when to break them, this is a deceptively nuanced game. Beware, though! Your character is NOT immortal. The longer you play, the older he will get. If you're careful not to get arrested or marooned too often and buy medicine from taverns from time to time, you can extend your life but, eventually, you will grow old. Though it takes a while, your character will eventually enter fourties and you'll start noticing his reflexes dulling. When you enter your late fifties, you will become too old to continue your pirate career and retire from piracy. You have a limited time to accomplish as many great deeds as you can (gain promotions, mass wealth, marry a beautiful governor's daughter, rescue your family members, dig-up burried treasure, etc) so you don't have much time to rest on your laurels! Simple and fun. Just play it!

Sid Meier's Pirates is an interesting mix of genres presented in a sort of "proto-sandbox" fashion: players take on the role of a swashbuckler living during the 17th century "Golden Age of Piracy". You may pursue the in-game story of searching the Caribbean Sea for their lost family members, but the game does not push this object on you but every so often, meaning that players are fully free to disregard the main storyline in order to make their own distinct niche out of Caribbean life. These activities include ship navigation and exploration, land combat (presented as a turn-based strategy minigame, ala Civilization), and courting noblewomen (presented as a rhythm minigame).
The graphics are colorful and have the right amount of cartoonishness to them, and the often upbeat soundtrack helps put a smile on my face every time I boot this game up. If any of this sounds interesting, I'd say to jump head-on into Sid Meier's Pirates, as I don't think a simple review conveys how much fun this game is, so much as sitting down and making of it what you will does. The seas are what you make of them!
Also, for those of you who originally owned this game on CD like I did, Steam will be able to read and use your old save files!

Great LAN game.  Not so fun against bots, but so much fun to play against/with your friends.  Co-op or PVP, but I prefer to play with people I know.  Its more fun terrorizing them :)
Pros:  Sharking is quite fun.  The four sharks are varied in playstyle and all are fun.  Divers have a vast array of mostly realistic underwater weapons, which surprised me, and diver vs shark appears to be fairly game balanced even if it doesn't feel that way as the diver (more later).  You will literally hear your friend scream when you maul them if you play on mumble.  Megalodon mode is Jaws:  The Game.  The AI is freakishly competent, even on Easy.  Humans are so much more intelligent, but as divers the AI is good about sticking together and they're crack shots.  As sharks the AI seems equally capable as actual real sharks.  And this is on Easy setting.  They're unbalanced above that, I find.
Cons:  Diving is terrifying.  Just completely insanely terrorizing.  You will be grotesquely torn to pieces.  You will flinch.  You will spin around, terrified that the sharks are behind you, only to find nothing there.  Its really pretty intense; almost too intense.  Its kind of a double edged sword; they set out to make diving terrifying, and god did they succeed.  As a diver, at the end of a round you feel like you lost even when you won, it is that terrorizing.  We take turns as shark and diver because while you may like diving, often you feel like you need a freaking break from being stalked and watching yourself be ripped to bloody chunks; and this is during a round where you win.  Being on the receiving end of a diver massacre sucks.  Hide and Seek mode, the shark has no enhanced senses, so we found it too hard find other players.  Tension but no release.  Megalodon mode, fun to play as/against Jaws, but don't do it with bots.  They're dumb and the shark can just kite and pick them off (the AI sucks on that one).
Verdict:  Awesome.  Best LAN game ever.  Have a party with your friends and eat them.  Its like Jaws or Deep Blue Sea:  The Game.  I doubt I'll play this game all the time, but it will definitely be fun to trot out on occasion.  It isn't complicated, though there is a knack to building divers and sharks, but it does what it does very effectively.  I still ultimately find the basic "treasure hunt" mode the most fun.  My friend and I played for five hours when we first got it; just looked up and the sun was down and we were late to life.
This game is great fun, it feels like it was the fun Evolve wanted to be.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
---------------------------
Pros:
- It's almost 100% LEGO (instead of typical CG non-LEGO backgrounds/structures)
- Lots of stuff to find
- HUGE world
- Great character customization
Cons:
- Build mode absolutely sucks
- It's boring
- It's pointless
- Camera is wonky at times
- Game is full-screen only
- It's nothing like Minecraft
I love LEGO and I love Minecraft and I have enjoyed almost all the TT LEGO games.
Having said that, don't expect this to be Minecraft with LEGO blocks. This game is not at all like Minecraft (in a bad way).
SUMMARY
It's mostly an exploration game. You walk across a seemingly pointless world, and find different objects, gain coins in the form of studs, come across characters that do nothing except give you extra clothing if you purchase them, and punch skeletons.
BUILD-MODE
The main selling feature for playing an open-world LEGO game would be the building. And in LEGO Worlds, building is awkard, pointless and ultimately boring. Structures, like houses can be found, gained into your purchase menu, selected and placed into your world. But the structure is automatically formed from an in-game animation, not built brick by brick as the trailer would have you believe. Once you place it, there's no real value to even having the house. It doesn't gain you anything, except a few new items like a car or swimming pool. But because you didn't build it room by room, you don't have any attachment to your structure so you just leave it there and move on to uncover more stuff.
Actually, you can technically place blocks and colour them, but it feels more like using a paintbrush than that feeling of building a LEGO house, that Minecraft does so well. So yes, you can build things brick by brick, but the game pulls you out of the regular "adventure" mode and puts you in an awkard photoshop-esq mode.
DESIGN
The detail is fairly nice for a LEGO game. Objects merge together frequently, which can unfortunately strain the visuals. The camera spins out of control at times. And there's a bizarre cinematic freeze-gameplay shot when you find a new character. There are also some areas where there simply isn't any LEGO, as if you're walking on unfinished ground.
THE PROBLEMS
The biggest problem with LEGO Worlds, apart from its terrible build mode, is there's no real reason to build anything. You have no use for farming since there's no hunger. You don't need to make weapons since there's no threat. You have no use to make mechanisms, because you can just buy a pre-built car or bike or whatever. Money is WAY too easy to get. And there's no real value in anything you find because the only fun is finding the stuff in the first place.
There are no objectives. Granted, this being an Early Access game, TT is sure to add objectives. But no objective I can think of, would make the gameplay worthwhile. And because the building simply isn't fun or meaningful, I can't recommend picking this game up.
Perfect exploration game for LEGO fans all around.

The jump from 2D to 3D can often times be a defining moment for a game series. The evolution of game mechanics and sometimes even the shift in genre can make or break its impact on old fans and new audiences alike. Some only play 3D Zelda games, some only play 2D Mario. Megaman Legends was something of an underrated flop, despite how much I loved it. That's just how it goes. And let's not even bring up Sonic. Sometimes the love for a particular franchise, a specific character or story, can't transcend the type of game. Some people are shallow♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥like that, only caring about their favorite game because of how it is on the outside. It's what's on the inside that counts. Just because your favorite series suddenly has different mechanics, you're gonna leave it for the next pretty game? How could you.
Surprisingly, all these beloved childhood characters aren't the only ones with blood feuds going on in the fanbase. Sure, they're the ones that are deemed "acceptable" to argue about. For the most part. Except Sonic, arguing about Sonic just disappoints your parents.
Fallout is another massive franchise with a split fanbase. Fallout 1 and 2 were highly acclaimed tactical CRPG's, with dedicated followings. However, after being acquired by Bethesda, Fallout 3 took the series in a new direction.
Fallout 3 is an action-RPG, feeling more like an FPS at times than a strategy RPG. Some say Fallout 3 ruined Fallout, making it essentially an Elder Scrolls with guns. Some say Bethesda is what saved Fallout from falling into obscurity.
While both are valid looks on what became of Fallout, I personally feel like they're both rather narrow-minded looks on the issue. Fallout 3 still manages to capture so much of the essence of Fallout, even if it's not a carbon copy of Fallout 1 or 2.
Much like past Fallout games, there's a huge emphasis on character building. The S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system is back, along with all of the other classic Fallout skills and traits. Over the course of the game you'll be leveling up and allocating skill points to different skills to improve your ability to sneak around, wield different kinds of weapons, or even stuff like persuasion or bartering. There are no bad skills to focus on, as the game is balanced enough to allow any skill set to be viable. Bonus traits are also granted with each level and give you a selection of unique perks to choose from, boosting your combat ability against certain enemy types, giving bonuses to different skills, or even allowing you to choose special dialogue options or use special skills in certain scenarios.
Fallout's karma system is back as well, allowing your character to be as unique as possible.
My character was Captain Sugartits, unstable mass murderer and crazed drug and sex addict. Captain isn't a title or anything, it's just a part of her name. You know how people can have two first names, like Mary Anne or something? Yeah, Captain Sugartits. Her father chose the name himself.
Her major skills were Sneaking, Lockpicking, and Science. She started out mild-mannered enough, but her thirst for science, blood, hard drugs, and violent lesbian sex drove her to massacre entire settlements. However, she gave like a hundred bottles of purified water to a homeless man overcome with radiation poisoning. So she was the murderous saint of the wasteland. She would enter any settlement and steal whatever wasn't bolted down, but the second someone talked to her with any sort of attitude she'd shoot up the town. She was quite unstable.
Fallout 3 manages to capture the spirit of the original Fallout in a beautiful way. Exploration and discovery is not spurred on by curiosity, or by demand. No one tells you to go explore. Fallout 3 has a massive, open world to explore. There are side-quests everywhere, secrets and surprises tucked all over the wasteland. But it doesn't hold you by the hand and guide you to each of these. No, exploration is driven by necessity. You're helpless and weak once you leave your Vault, and the means to defend yourself isn't free. You'll need to forage for weapons and ammo, forage for food and medicine, and forage for any other items of value to sell for whatever necessities you can't find from foraging. And it never ends. Even after you've found a powerful weapon, you'll need money or parts to repair it as its condition wears down. And what you're fighting will only escalate in strength, from mutated insects to corrupt leftover government weirdos. The struggle never ends. The struggle is real.
The karma system actually factors right into this as well. Before the Cap snapped and went on her rampage across the wasteland, staying armed and ready to fight was incredibly difficult. The only way I was able to arm myself to the teeth was from stealing everything, robbing and murdering whoever I could, and doing quite a bit of less-than kosher deeds. It really solidifies the idea of the world that you're in. It's hard to be good. There's not enough to go around, and it's a constant struggle to exist.
Fallout 3 is a masterpiece of smart game design, and still one of the best open-ended RPG's out there. Getting lost in the world of Fallout 3 is a blast. And most of all, it still feels like Fallout. The same style and charm is still there. Except you can't kill kids anymore, no matter how annoying the little ♥♥♥♥♥ are.
Not that I'D want to, I'm just saying. For realism's sake. If a deranged murderer hopped up on drugs and lesbians got talked down to by a little brat, don't you think she'd mini-nuke the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them? I'm just saying.
When it really comes down to which Fallout style I prefer though, classic 1 and 2 or the Bethesda-style in 3, I prefer both because they're both fun. Stop ♥♥♥♥♥ing you nerds.

Naval action, naval trading, naval everything. Beautiful ships and lots of features being added during EA. It's an open world game and is considered realistic. It is very time consuming and while bugs are minimal - the overall feel of the game is positive but mostly negative.
There is a decent variety in ships and every ship has it's own characteristics (speed, look, cannons,...). This way you can look for your own 'playstyle' and choose a ship accordingly. Every ship has 1-durability so a general rule here; don't sail what you can't afford!
Ship crafting is one of the next things the game has to offer. Unfortunately it's severely limited because of multiple features, requiring you to obtain multiple marks, resources and LH.  The new wood types diversify the ships being made but they seem to be rather limited because of realistic spawn.
You can be a trader, kill pirates or be a pirate. You can also discover the world of naval action. It's a very big open world; if you want to travel somewhere it does require you quite some time to get there. Average travel time is about 2-5 minutes to a nearby port / mission. Going further will go up to 15-30 minutes at least. That being said: as a trader you'll have to travel a lot. Trading is mostly an AFK OW sailing experience with one route being 30-60 IRL minutes of sailing.
The biggest pro here: the economy leans more towards player driven economy. Anyone can make a profit with a variety of goods and every player NEEDS a basic supply of goods to craft any ship (you can't solo). You can obtain a building for resources but you can't produce everything you need on your own. Joining a clan is highly recommended.
As a starting player you'll start in a small cutter and you'll have to do basic PvE missions; and buying new ships + cannons + crew is pretty expensive. If you're not in a big clan and can take NA as a 'second job' (time consumption) you're in for a game full of PvE missions and AFK trade sailing. You'll never see the big ships unless you wait for X months until some kind of supply is rolling in. There's no real tutorial or anything so you need advice from other players at some point. Beware for gankers (PvP) as they seem to be everywhere. I can't recommend NA for starters in the current meta; only if you have friends in-game or join a clan from the start.
As a fighter you are able to experience the best of naval action. Manual sailing is required to obtain advantages over your opponent. A good strategist wins every single time. From the sound of your crew to the sound of your cannons and the cloud being created by a single broadside. It's beautiful and you will enjoy it very much. You can do PvE orders, PvP and Port Battles (strategic PvP). Imo it becomes quite repetitive over time; especially the PvE content. PvP is one of the few things left which is really exciting.
Port battles are a more organized PvP experience; fight for a port to obtain it for your nation. Unfortunately ports can only be fought 25v25 - mostly only accessible by the most elite players. Joining a smaller nation might make you able to PB. Currently most ports are being captured and most nations are near each other's borders. Only a few ports will flip so don't expect to PB and earn conquest marks any time soon.
Every ship also has ship knowledge; to obtain additional stats for your ship (extra reload speed, sailing speed,...). See it as; if you're an experienced captain with a certain ship you have more experience in a certain area (not a grind...). It's a good 'tutorial' for any ship - it requires you to actually play with a ship for numerous hours. This will let less popular ships also be captained (which wasn't before). Each battle has a timer of 1h30minutes - on average a battle takes 15-30 minutes; bigger battles 30+ minutes.
There are 8 nations and 3 servers (Global, EU and PvE) which you can choose from and the biggest difference is their nation goods and the location. As for the servers; Global has no locked PB timerswhile EU does. Unfortunately you'll notice a lot of imbalance (due to overpopulation in one nation, underpopulation in the other). This will make the choice of nation very important; ask before you join and start playing.
This game is in EA state; meaning nothing is finished and everything is subject to change (including everything described in my review and others). You WILL notice bugs and flaws - but those seem to be rather limited. Overall the game feels 'finished'; there are a lot of features to experience already and they most likely work properly. Expect wipes; they do not intend to wipe earned XP and craft XP (only assets; money, ships,...).
Naval action is playable - but has it's flaws. For any casual gamer out there the game is not worth it; sailing requires a LOT of time and even fighting. That being said: if you can't afford to play it numerous hours (on average 2-4 hours straight) it isn't really worth it. It's very time consuming and you can't just AFK in the middle of nowhere, you need to watch enemy ships and have a logout timer. Population numbers seem to be pretty decent: EU has 800-1000 players while Global seems to hit at max 600.
My daily gameplay of NA: AFK trade sailing (NA and chill - YT) and repeatedly doing the same PvE missions (for ship knowledge, possible loot) over and over again to obtain gold. I'm not having fun; which is what a game should stand for, right?  For those who dislike the time consumption; there's a NA arena styled game coming this summer, without open world. It will probably offer the best NA has to offer: the battle aspect (and only that). I'm a small clan, lower pop. nation player: so this is where most starting players might start as well. Current meta is all about restrictions which isn't positive towards casual gamers.
% wise, NA would be 35% positive, 65% negative . Leave a comment if you have any questions (+ extra info).

Rozkol is an OKish top-down military game.
However, it has several disadvantages with its gameplay.
* When you hit R to reload, the weapon you're carrying should reload automatically - but you have to choose from an option wheel instead (which wastes time and is not necessary).
* When you have your gun at full sight, looking around, the cursor can swing wildly around (which can be really annoying when you're trying to target the guy who is shooting at you).
* You can't capture flags/points whilst you're in a vehicle - you have to exit your vehicle to capture a flag (you should be able to capture flags either way).
* You can't run.
* You can't take screenshots. The in-game guide says to use "1" to do so, but it doesn't work. The default Steam key of "F12" works, but it also simultaneously exits the game. Here's a pro tip: When you're winning a game, don't hit F12 to capture the moment - because you might just regret it.
Beware of mines; they are marked as a cross in a green circle - when I first saw one, I thought "Great! There's a health pack!" (that assumption didn't work out too well for me).
I'm just barely giving this game a thumbs up.
Even allowing for the style of game it is, I'd give it about a 5.5/10.
Try it if you want to, but don't expect a lot from it.

This fun, visceral third-person action game, is very true to its WH40K license. It sports massive violence, silly but serviceable plot, a genuinely satisfying, meaty combat and a horde of enemies to kill. It is rather repetitive though, and could get somewhat boring-ish after a few hours. Still, I'd recommend this game, if not for one fatal(for me at least) flaw - it has low FOV which cannot be fixed at all. I literally cannot play Space Marine for longer than half an hour per session due to nasty eye strain. You should totally try it out if you're okay with low FOV, but if you're like me - stay away.

This is a game you play for when you want to turn your brain off and bulldoze your way through hordes of enemies. The game stays true to the source material and really makes you feel the part of an Adeptus Astartes. The sounds are great, the visuals are acceptable (though given the games location, I was pleasantly surprised with how they created variety), the story is pretty standard for a Warhammer 40K title with a twist that I admittedly didn't see coming, but where this game truly shines is in the combat.
The guns are all fun, mostly portable with a couple turret sections scattered here and there, though eventually you find the ones that you stick with for the remainder of the game, *cough* Lazcannon *cough*. The melee weapons and the jump pack though are the ones that make you feel like an angel of death with the Chainsword, Power Axe, and Thunder Hammer all available for use. Executions are both the most satisfying and bloody kills you can get, but also the way you get health back something especially important on the higher difficulties.
Ultimately, this is a fantastic title which offers a surprisingly challenging campaign on Hard and all the blood and gore you could ever want.

This isn't a game as much as it's an experiment funded by the Canadian government. If you're transcendent, you'll recognize everything from the "archetype" to the binaural "song of sworcery" to dream-walking to cosmic friends. And once you're nice and tranced out, the woodman starts talking (or "suggesting" rather) about bloodsports and watching animals kill people downtown.

Nothing made sense, there was no story closure, no character progression, the game mechanics had no logic, no depth, there was virtually no interactivity so I might as well have watched a let's-play...  Pretty graphics and soundtrack, but that's it.
With some games, even if the gameplay isn't stellar, a player can derive something from the feeling of being in control of the character that they can't get from watching a let's-play (The Stanley Parable is an excellent example of this), but that's not the case here.  There's nothing.
The controls are point-and-click.  You guide the character around on a leash and solve "puzzles," and by “puzzle” I mean "click arbitrary things on the screen in an arbitrary order."  What sort of things?  Click all the ducks, or click all the trees, or click all the bushes – in a specific, arbitrary order.  It's just trial and error, with no rhyme or reason.  If you think perhaps I'm exaggerating, I don't blame you, but I'm not.  This game really is that mediocre.
Occasionally you'll have to fight something.  Combat in this game is an extremely simple rhythm game.  It's tricky-enough to be a little frustrating, and bare-bones-enough to be boring.
The world that you explore is simultaneously small and tedious.  There are maybe three dozen locations.  They're all pretty, and backed by a great soundtrack, but devoid of things to do.  Around half of the locations are completely purposeless, and serve to do nothing more than take up your time as your character (slowly) walks through them on her way to the place you're trying to get to.
To be perfectly honest, I'm fine with games having decorative content that's just there to immerse you and give you a place to chill out.  Trouble is, these locations actually GET IN THE WAY of gameplay.  I don't want to spoil too much, but there's a sizable chunk of the game that you spend walking back and forth between two locations at opposite ends of the map, and I am completely baffled by that design decision.
Now we have to talk about the story and dialogue, and...  Oh boy...
The game opens with a man who appears to be a shrink sitting in a plush chair.  He breaks the fourth wall and speaks directly to the player as his patient.  He refers to the game by name, describing it as a “therapy.”  The game is broken up into four “therapy sessions.”  If all of this sounds horribly pretentious, that's because it is.  The therapist (referred to as “The Archetype”) even subtly hints that if you aren't enjoying the game, it's because you aren't approaching it with the right mindset.
The Archetype persists throughout the game, constantly giving you “hints” (more like outright telling you what to do next) and breaking the fourth wall.  There is almost no opportunity afforded to the player to suspend disbelief.
Most of the game takes place in a fairly classic fantasy setting, with swords, shields, monsters, ghosts and spellbooks.  But the characters, inexplicably, talk like modern-day stoners.  That's the most accurate description I can give.  Even the dog.  No, really, even the dog.  It's not funny or clever at all.  At first it's quirky, but the novelty wears off as you meet more characters, and discover that every single one talks in the same way.  It's like reading a fanfiction that's trying for self-depricating humor and falling short.  None of the characters speak seriously, and it makes it that much harder to get immersed in the game.
Anyway, that was my experience playing Sword and Sworcery.  I finished the game, and I kind of regret it.

I honestly had to think about whether or not to give this one a thumbs up. I loved it all the way through, but some of the negative reviews here have some points. For one thing the game is terribly short - though it says 'small world' in the game description. Another is that the click to move is often considerably slower and more clumsy than I would like, and finally the humor is hit or miss. Sometimes it puts a grin on your face, other times it's eye-roll worthy.
With that said, this is roughly the equivelant of an indie prog-rock concept album, only instead of lyrics you get gameplay. Most of the puzzles involve clicking and experimenting with the environment while 'meditating' and are all in themselves relatively simple. The combat involves some reflexes, but has set patterns which can allow even people with slow reflexes to survive it.
The star of the show is the music - play this with a good set of headphones and enjoy the atmosphere it creates, don't play this game if you like to rush, and don't go expecting shakespeare instead of beowulf. I found it a really fantastic experience that was definitely worth the price of a movie ticket. I would take a chance on it - there is always the refund.

I like
