It's like one of those weird but unique toys that you see on a commercial. "Easy to learn, Hard to master."
Not for the squemish as it is very bloody and gory for that extra realism. Expect to see plenty of torn off limbs, skin, and shark chunks.
Graphics and sound are excellent and the game is optimized pretty damn well.
Graphics menu tells you how each setting affects your quality and impacts your system.
Community is usually very friendly although there are a few major aholes (typically 1 faction-onlys that have near four figure hours logged) (be nice to be able to blacklist and avoid games with those toxic few...)
It is very skill based as the time to kill is much faster than you'd expect for both divers and sharks (seconds-milliseconds).
It progresses as you earn money/evolve like going from all pistols to all awps on csgo but without a round system.
Progression is very fast then very slow. You unlock the popular stuff first then the very specialized stuff MUCH later.
For both the divers or sharks your performance must be flawless if you want to avoid dying.
Tons of strategy potential for both teams based on maps.
Can choose which maps you want to play on. (choose ones biased towards your side if you're new.) Only one feels 100% fair.
Devs steadily making the game more fair and you can occasionally play with some of them. (Cause the community is a bit small)
Can use memes in chat like awkward seal and what I assume is a tsundere shark. Pro/Con depending on who you are.
No anti-shark chainmail like irl but sharks can get "armor"
Surround sound headphones almost required for divers as sound is your cue for where the sharks are.
The biggest problem with the game is that there is absolutely no balance. It's not uncommon for two lvl 100 sharks to go up against lvl 1 divers and because the community is currently miniscule you'll likely get matched with the same people again and again. (Be nice to restrict heavily winning teams to low level weapons/evos since it's no fun to club seals or be the seal.)
You might get mad that one of your teammates leaves and gets replaced by a bot but the bots are like lvl 50 divers or lvl 20 sharks since the shark bot only knows how to attack nonstop but very rarely makes a mistake. Sometimes it's an upgrade.
Still, with its balance issues, immense skill gaps, and simple gameplay it's still my favorite multiplayer game for with or without friends. Extremely fun to play a private match with friends and bots at your desired skill level. (yes you can no bots 1v1)

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
---------------------------
Pros:
- It's almost 100% LEGO (instead of typical CG non-LEGO backgrounds/structures)
- Lots of stuff to find
- HUGE world
- Great character customization
Cons:
- Build mode absolutely sucks
- It's boring
- It's pointless
- Camera is wonky at times
- Game is full-screen only
- It's nothing like Minecraft
I love LEGO and I love Minecraft and I have enjoyed almost all the TT LEGO games.
Having said that, don't expect this to be Minecraft with LEGO blocks. This game is not at all like Minecraft (in a bad way).
SUMMARY
It's mostly an exploration game. You walk across a seemingly pointless world, and find different objects, gain coins in the form of studs, come across characters that do nothing except give you extra clothing if you purchase them, and punch skeletons.
BUILD-MODE
The main selling feature for playing an open-world LEGO game would be the building. And in LEGO Worlds, building is awkard, pointless and ultimately boring. Structures, like houses can be found, gained into your purchase menu, selected and placed into your world. But the structure is automatically formed from an in-game animation, not built brick by brick as the trailer would have you believe. Once you place it, there's no real value to even having the house. It doesn't gain you anything, except a few new items like a car or swimming pool. But because you didn't build it room by room, you don't have any attachment to your structure so you just leave it there and move on to uncover more stuff.
Actually, you can technically place blocks and colour them, but it feels more like using a paintbrush than that feeling of building a LEGO house, that Minecraft does so well. So yes, you can build things brick by brick, but the game pulls you out of the regular "adventure" mode and puts you in an awkard photoshop-esq mode.
DESIGN
The detail is fairly nice for a LEGO game. Objects merge together frequently, which can unfortunately strain the visuals. The camera spins out of control at times. And there's a bizarre cinematic freeze-gameplay shot when you find a new character. There are also some areas where there simply isn't any LEGO, as if you're walking on unfinished ground.
THE PROBLEMS
The biggest problem with LEGO Worlds, apart from its terrible build mode, is there's no real reason to build anything. You have no use for farming since there's no hunger. You don't need to make weapons since there's no threat. You have no use to make mechanisms, because you can just buy a pre-built car or bike or whatever. Money is WAY too easy to get. And there's no real value in anything you find because the only fun is finding the stuff in the first place.
There are no objectives. Granted, this being an Early Access game, TT is sure to add objectives. But no objective I can think of, would make the gameplay worthwhile. And because the building simply isn't fun or meaningful, I can't recommend picking this game up.
Perfect exploration game for LEGO fans all around.

I'm always looking for a new (new to me, anyway) game to run on my now aging mac mini with its HD 4000 graphics.  The other day I picked up Divinity: Original Sin -- Enhanced Edition.  And it runs flawlessly on my Mac Mini, that is always a plus.
So far I've put about 25 hours into the game and have not yet completed it.
The game has a great story line, Characters are very customizable in terms of Abilities, Skill and Talents.  Combat is tough but not unbeatable with a little smarts and a restart or two.  Quick save is a must... use it often.  The game also has auto saves at various points which I really like.  Dialog... there is lots of it... take the time to speak to your partner, companions and hirelings.  The game is voiced and that's a nice touch.  Talk to everybody... you never know when a local citizen or talking clam has a quest with XP and other rewards.  Also you can trade with just about everyone you meet though their inventory and gold might be limited.  The game is visually pleasing and if the stock game isn't pretty enough for you there are some mods that will improve the aestetics some.  Explore... most buildings can be explored... and don't forget the basements and cellars.  Crafting and blacksmithing is pretty easy if you have the skills and materials.... recipes can be found in books or you can look them up on the internet.  The maps are large, with lots of places to explore.  But large maps means it takes time to move around.  If the stock movement rate just doesn't do it for you there are modes to help that too.
Now there are a couple of things I don't like, nothing game shattering but anoying... like the limited number of portraits available for the PCs.  I really would  just prefer a symbol if there's not a portrait that matches the looks of the PC's.  I've already mentioned the movement rate and I added a mod to fix that.  Then there's the lack of control of the camera.  I wish it could be set to follow the PC instead of having to move and rotate the camera, though to be fair my son told me "I'm just not use to console gaming and if I was familar with using a controller it wouldn't bother me.  And finally, finding objects.  Yes, the 'alt' key will highlight some objects but not all and even when it does so many blend in with the invironment colors that its hard for these aging eyes to see.
Other than that I will give this game a thumbs up.  As I move through the game towards completion I'll come back and give an update especially if I find something else of note pro or con.

I'm really enjoying Minion Masters, it's a great 'filler game', what I call a game that's quick and easy to start up and play, but in depth enough that it takes a while to learn and master and playable while doing something else passively on the other screen =)
Something I found really rewarding was in situations where I was on the ropes and defeat seemed imminent only to be able to pick myself back up, shout RAWRRR FER FREEDUM! and charge the enemy until victory was secured!
It's a card based table top combat game where the goal is simple, destroy the enemy base and defend your own. It's simple, challenging, rewarding and enjoyable. However i'd be lying if I said the game blew me away. It didn't bring any new concepts to the genre and I would like to see some map variety.
With that being said though, what this game does, it does well. It delivers an enjoyable real time, card based combat experience with enough variety, content and initial support to keep you interested for several hours, and for 20 euros you can't go wrong if you enjoy intense PvP.
Pros:
-Animations are gory and fun
-Graphics are clean and simple, but not too simple
-Card variety and deck building is satisfying
-Match-making seems very fast and puts you against equally skilled opponents
-Heroes are well balanced
-PvP matches have no chat ability so no player toxicity is possible. (There are smilies though!)
-No problems with performance at all
Cons:
-Perhaps a little expensive for the simple premise of the game.
-Only 1 map design
-Only 1v1 matches (would be good to see 2v2, 3v3 and 4v4 matches at some point)
-Deck building is a little simplified

A timeless era, miniaturized on screen, but certainly expansive in scope and scale. This is one of those games that you can pick away at, village by village, farm by farm, castle brick by brick.  Or, this is a game that you can get swept up in, by either trying to stay out of the eventual fighting by opposing Houses and Factions, or by jumping in headfirst to join the slugfest between hundreds of live opponents.
SK asks for patience as you develop, perform missions, gather resources, and build your villages and castles.  Developing growing and successful villages, leading to resources used for castle building, can test even the most patient of players.  SK's game system admittedly offers those that can play "cards" an advantage in this all-important economic progress aspect of the game, enabling players to accelerate the pace of their development through the use of in-game cards.  War fighting and other combat related aspects of the game can provide a similar challenge.  Attack a computer-generated target without proper resources and troops, and you risk a punishing war of attrition against an inanimate foe that constantly regenerates.  Attack a human player with a similar lack of war readiness, and you risk being annihilated by foe and potentially countless hordes of opportunistic foes alike.  Attack or counter-attack with good strength and patience-driven readiness, and the glory of a 2D face planting of your enemy is yours.
SK is essentially a winner-take-all game, with a twist.  Players can attempt to stay neutral (my 10-year old son named his village "Be Nice to Neutrals" and has so far survived).  Or, players can join a House and one of its many subsets (Factions) to wage either diplomacy and/or warfare on your enemies.  The game can seem unbalanced at times on the latter, as players seem to gravitate toward joining the strongest House out of fear of getting wiped off the map or shunned to the ash heap of Houses that are periodically eliminated as the game progresses.  SK game designers would be well served to add 2nd place, 3rd place (etcetera) awards to Houses (like mine) that seem to start the periodic map resets at a numeric disadvantage to the one or two Houses that are immediately in the lead.
Overall, SK Is a solid game for those that want a 2D game that they can enjoy either semi-passively -- or quite aggressively.  It basically comes down to this:  What you put into it, you tend to get out of it.  And, as the game offers a very deep strategic experience, if you are fortunate to join a House and Faction that is well connected (we use Raidcall to communicate in the House and Faction that I am in), SK can offer even some very enjoyable operational and tactical experiences as well.

Downwell is an interesting take on rogue-lite style games. Your goal is to fall down the well with your gunboots, shooting or jumping off of whatever is in your way to do so. Of course, this is MUCH easier said than done.
This game has a simple control scheme, but getting a hang of controlling the game itself may take some time. Simply, your only controls are moving left and right, jumping, and shooting downward. You do fall pretty fast, so it's important to make sure you keep control of your guy, as well as trying to find as many platforms as possible. For the most part, the controls are responsive, but I've only had a few instances of taking damage because of slight input lag.
As you progress, you'll notice some side rooms, as well as shops. In these areas you can discover bonuses such as large piles of gems, or gun modules that change which gun you use, as well as provide you with a certain boost. In the shops, you can buy little pick-me-ups with the gems you collect like health foods or extra charges for your gun boots. After completing each level, you are allowed to select from a number of upgrades that power you up in someway, such as explosive jumps or protective gear to save you a hit point.
Big warning, this game is hard. If you want to get all the way to the bottom, be ready to face a lot of trial-and-error, because this game is unforgiving if you make mistakes, such as moving too fast or not reacting quickly enough. Also, you don't start with much health to begin with, and if you die, you have to restart fresh from the top of the well, losing anything you collected in the last playthrough.
However, all the gems you collect do contribute to a total gem counter, which alters the gameplay in different ways, and also unlock palettes, which change the color scheme of the game itself to suit your tastes. Add all this on top of randomly generated levels with each playthrough, and you'll find yourself with a different experience each time you play; sometimes you'll get lucky and stock up on the best items for you, other times you may not get what you need right off the bat and have to make it work.
In conclusion, Downwell is simplistically good for a time. It does get repetitive after extended play, but if you want a challenge, it's worth a try. If not, then you won't be missing too much with this game. Either way, this game is good for killing a small amount of time.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery is easily one of the most unusual, nonsensical, gorgeous games I've ever played. As I write this, I'm still not entirely sure how to describe what exactly it was I experienced.
The general gameplay consists of you searching beautiful low poly. highly detailed environments for strange creatures known as 'sylvan sprites' by clicking multiple points in the environment. The game gives very little direction as to what parts of the environment you should be clicking and the direction that the game does decide to give you is delivered via nonsensical, highly confusing messages through in game twitter like updates from the few characters.
While I presume these messages were meant to contain hints, half the time I couldn't decipher what was random nonsense and what was the game's way of trying to point me in a particular direction. This resulted in me randomly clicking my way through most of the puzzles, which worked out fine except on a handful of occasions.
While the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired, it's everything else that makes this game worth experiencing. The writing, while cryptic and often times silly, sets a very laid back tone as you quest to save this musically infused world.
The charming art design combined with the beautifully composed music gives this game a sense of style like no other and I often found myself in awe of the relationship between the two.
The story isn't partiuclarly deep or complex but the quirky and episodic nature in which it unfolds makes this a game worth seeing through to the end.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a simple and quirky mouse-driven adventure game with an excellent soundtrack and deceptively captivating art style.
There's really not much else to say when it comes to this game. This game does not overstay its welcome and does an excellent job of setting the player on a vague adventure through a forest where they must find magical triangles for no clearly defined purpose. This game's humor is extremely self-aware, and is often juxtaposed by the game's sense of epic art direction. Speaking of the art, it's hard to hide that this game uses a sprite based style that is actually more impressive than you might first think. Animations are extremely fluid, and you'll find yourself captivated by pixel art that looks fairly mediocre in stills yet springs to life in motion.
More important than anything else is this game's atmosphere and theme. This game has a wonderful soundtrack that plays many nature-inspired tunes while you walk around solving nature-inspired puzzles in your quest to find the magical Trigon. It's a difficult feeling to describe, which is why I have to recommend feeling it firsthand. There's something very earthy about the way this game presents itself.
However, if I had to find pick one gripe about this game it'd be the "Moon Mood" system in Session III. Regardless of how you decide to manipulate this game to utilize it, a gameplay-based way and system manipulation-based way", the process is tedious and puts an unnecessary damper on the game's overall pace. However, it is a minor gripe when the rest of the game is so captivating.
Overall it's extremely easy to recommend this game. If you're looking for a relaxing puzzle-adventure game with an excellent soundtrack this is an easy must buy! Especially when it's on sale!

Naval Action in a nutshell (imho):
The BAD:
Devs have still not managed to find/settle on, a satisfactory OpenWorld RPG system.
Introduction of new features have been few and far between.
Game is difficult for new players and difficult to play solo (but it is an MMO after all). Some kind of clan affiliation is necessary (at least to start with). Becoming self-sufficient takes a lot of time investment.
Player base keeps declining then resurging then declining again while RPG mechanics are being worked on, before and after each big patch.
Success of Open world game remains in doubt while upcoming 'Legends'  arena version lurks in the shadows.
Game is currently brutal, Eve Online type players are used to it but WoW types are shocked with realisation that the game does not hold your hand and hostile players are constantly hunting you down. (This could go in the 'GOOD' section of course, depending on your prefs)
Lack of guides and tutorials make it a tough game to learn.
A lot of grind to get the things you need to be able to compete at a high level.
Sometimes requires very long sails which can be boring as there is very little else (in game) that you can do.
The GOOD:
Looks great. Ship models, skybox, sea scapes. weather and sound are all excellent.
Huge Openworld really gives a feeling of distance across the map.
The BRILLIANT:
The Combat Engine - simply gorgeous. Simple to use and yet the tactics are infinitely complex and requires oodles of skill to execute. Easy to understand but difficult to master. A steep but seemingly never ending learning curve.
So many things to consider: Wind, Manual Sailing, Rudder and Turning, Gunnery, Ammo types, Penetration, Distance, Angle, Speed, Leaks, Armor, Sails, Masts, Structure, Crew Assignment, Boarding, Repairs, etc etc etc. Neglecting any one of these often means death, but a good Captain can snatch victory from the jaws of defeat and overcome overwhelming odds. The best I have ever played.
This game has it's problems yes, but the combat engine alone makes this game worth trying, 100 times over.
If they finally sort the RPG mechanics it will be a true gem.

This is the fighter that has really got me into fighters.
I feel like I'm actually pretty good at this game, since the tutorial does an awesome job of teaching you, as I was a convicted button masher before playing this, and you can translate that skill to other fighting games (more so ones with six button layout).
The story, at first, is nothing to marvel at. But honestly, you need to put time into the game and appreciate the characters, and then you'll like the story a bit more.
The art style is absolutely brilliant, being very anime-inspired, but not crossing that border in a sense. There will be boobs and butts, but if you are mature you'll learn to deal with it.
The online play is reasonably solid, and has lag compensation, which is a godsend if I want to play with my foriegn friends.
While there isn't that many characters, there are more being added thanks to a very successful IndieGoGo campaign, and there is variety and contrast between what's there already. You have Filia, an amnesiac with a living head of hair named Samson, to Peacock, a child that was mutilated and turned into a experimental death machine, with a passion for cartoons. There is even a man (believe it or not) named Big Band, a massive cyborg with pneumatic weaponery themed after brass intruments, and a mysterious blob named Double who is a doppelganger that borrows various moves from the rest of the roster.
It has some fancy extras, including an amazing art gallery, and one of the hardest challenges known to man.
From there on for me, it was really just experience and practice and then I could get good and beat up my friends and rub it in their face.
If there is anything that has really impressed me with this game, it's the dedication of the people at Lab Zero, who want to make this game as awesome as possible. If I wasn't a metaphorical hobo, I would give all my money towards this game and be happy that that money is going towards a good cause. But that's just me.
The summary: great characters, great art, alright story that takes time to apprieciate, great extras, awesome devs (luv ya <3), and in my opinion the best PC fighter to date. And this series is only in its infancy, mind you.

This game directly targets issues I have with procedural sandbox games like this.
First, there aren't stacks in your inventory. Once you find something, you pay Lego coins to unlock it and it can be remade indefinitely. This helps with the issue of farming for resources. Every destroyable object drops Lego coins so you never feel like you are hunting for resources.
Second, once you find something you pay for it and its yours for the game! If you want to spawn 20 cars on top of each other you totally can. The only limitation to this is that there are a few special items you equip (all in the same menu) and others for customizing (also a separate menu).
My final happiness from this game comes from a separate build mode. When you don't have to worry about how close your character is and if you can draw in that box or not, it really makes things better. Instead you get a cursor the shape of the tool and go from there. brick removal is similar, and placing decorations is simple.
The only problem I have (besides glitches of course) is that there isn't multiplayer, and that is being worked on currently so I can't even complain!
All and all its an extremely well done engine with lots of potential...I can't wait to see the finished product!

Sid Meier's Pirates is a classic remake of a classic. The games legacy often speaks for itself, and while some aspects havent aged well, you are hard pressed to find a better pirate game on the market. Mostly because there are so damn few.
The game is a bit bare in the gameplay and features department, even for 2004, it will get very repetetive very fast, and odds are you will see every minigame by hour 3.
The minigames also have very few variations, dancing practically has none other than slightly different moves depending on nationality of the dancers, and around 6 swordfighting scenes, you will see each about a dozen+ times. I find them visually enjoyable, but in terms of gameplay they are just frustrating, the fencing in particular often feels like the enemy is reading your inputs, and the timing for defending/counter attacking is split second, early on you can just spam attacks and it will absolutely float you, but then you get old and slow, and having never learned to properly fight results in a lot of save scumming for certain fights.
You have to forgive some flaws due to its age, and being a remake of a 1980's PC game forgives the lack of content, but it does have some flaws that are annoying even by 2004 standards.
Travel speed is my biggest gripe, the game is time based, your character ages, and after a certain point you are forced into retirement (theres ways to keep going forever, but its not really "intended") and if you have to travel east...you just get to watch yourself get older just trying to traverse a small portion of the map. The wind is always blowing west, and unless you can take good advantage of it when it leans north or south, traveling east can be a snails pace, even with speed upgrades.
My other big gripe: you cant remap keys, at all. I despise the control setup, particularly use of the numpad and mouse in gameplay, I hate having my hands so close together. Its a PC game, no reason it shouldnt have customizable controls.
The game had some performance issues, particularly a flickering I experienced early on, though that can just be a result of old software running on modern hardware, nothing that made it unplayable however.
The game also has one thing going great for it: charm. The art style, animations, its fun, cartoony, and gets you in the mood for swashbuckling.
Sid Meiers Pirates, even today, is the second best pirate game I have ever played. (The first being Assassins Creed 4, if not just because its more modern, has more to do, and has damn good combat) Its still worth a playthough, even if its a bit old.

There are a slew of reviews praising this game, so I won't belabor the point. Instead, I'll just point out some of its most unique and best features.
1. Full character customization. (Of your first two characters, that you create at game start, plus you can level up your later hirelings/companions any way you want.) While there are classes, those only come with a set of starting abilities and stats (that you can change completely in character creation if you want) and starting gear. Mix and match the skills and stats you want. It's a cRPG-lover's dream.
--P.S. If you want a full 4-person party of completely customizable characters from game start, there is a mod on the Nexus for that :D
2. The environmental interaction, particularly in combat, is top notch. Water douses fire. Fire sets oil barrels to explode. Lightning turns steam clouds into deadly static. It's terrific. If you don't have at least one mage in your party, you're missing out on a lot.
3. You can pick up and move things with telekinesis! It is extremely cool! And you don't have to cast a spell or something to activate it beforehand. It is ALWAYS on, as long as you have points in the Telekinesis skill. Just click on what you want to pick up or move, and presto! It was really cool to feel like an actual wizard or psion.
4. The voice acting is fantastic. (At least to my own non-professional opinion.) Lots of nuance, lots of quirkiness, very animated tones.
5. I highly recommend taking the Pet Pal perk on one of your two main (starting) characters. It lets you talk to animals, which introduces you to a lot of the game's quirky humor, and can occasionally provide very useful hints! (It's pointless to give your hirelings that trait, however, as animals are snobby and will only talk to a main character.)

I want to start this review by saying that I absolutely love Roguelikes. I'm pretty sure it's my favourite genre, and I've played a fair amount of, IMO, the best ones there are. Downwell is one of my all time favourites, and I found out about it simply because a friend casually mentioned it.
In this game, your character jumps down a well to save the world from evil (I think?). This means the only way you can go is down. There's very little chance of backtracking, even if you bounce on an enemy's head, since you don't get much vertical distance. In this game, your main weapons are your feet and what you shoot out of them. You can get different weapons via rooms that appear as you go down, that can also contain a shop or some gems, this game's currency. Keep in mind that when you pick a new weapon, you lose the one you were using.
There are four worlds, each containing four levels. At the end, there's a boss. When you end a level, you get to pick from 3 upgrades. Levels go by pretty fast, which makes this a perfect game in case you have 5 minutes and want to play something. It's also great for the sentence "just 5 more minutes...", as it's very easy to press that reset button and start a new run.
I've praised the game a fair bit, but it does have it's downsides.
It's considerably easier than most roguelikes. For perspective, I have 60 hours in Spelunky, and I've faced Olmec (the first, and normally last, boss) three times. In Downwell, at 3 hours I've had 2 fights against the boss.
This is probably more of a neutral point if anything. The fact that it's easier means that inexperienced players can hop in and not get as frustrated compared to something like Spelunky or Crypt Of The Necrodancer. But it also means that more experienced players might just beat normal mode with ease. There's a hard mode that I haven't unlocked yet, so I can't tell you how much that affects the game.
It's fairly lackluster content wise. You unlock some "styles", which are pretty much different characters with some changes. For example, the Boulder Style starts with more health, but you get less upgrade picks at the end of a level (2, down from 3). There are also filters to make the game look different, but my experience with them was negative, they were mostly distracting or ugly. Other than that, you have the same 4 worlds ending on the same boss every time, with no opportunity to spice it up.
All that being said, the game is amazing. Consider the fact that, during the sales, it's at 1 Euro, you have no reason to not get this game if you enjoy roguelikes.
Verdict: 8.75/10. Get this game.

Fun, rather old school game, set in the WH40K universe. What I like:
- Great gunplay..the weapons have nice sounds, both ranged and melee weapons.  Melee weapon combat has a well executed sense of weight and when you hit an enemy hard, there's a brief slo-mo to add more sense of ludicrous force. The Chainsword's roars and the eventual rough flesh tearing sounds never get less awesome either for example.
-Blood and gore..there are nice execution animations for stunned enemies and the blood splash and dismemberment are well made, though there's not many dismembernent variations.
-Fluid, brutal and just damn intense combat. No cover shooter stuff. Mostly you fight hordes and I wouldn't have it any other way. You can smoothly switch between melee and ranged combat.
No regenerating health ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t! You have a Halo style infinitely regenerating shield, but health is static and there isn't medikits or the like to heal you..you must stun an enemy and perform an execution, it will restore either about 33% of total health or even about 60% depending on executed enemy's type.
Overall great sound design. Explosions, the Orks' trademark WAAGH and whatnot.
What I rather don't like:
Simplistic plot, not saying though it even needs to be complex.
Only 3 factions in the game..could have been lots of extra awesomeness potential if more factions were in the story.
In conclusion a fun 3rd person shooter with intense combat, the plot is not to be minded, the sheer catharsis of the combat makes up for it.

S:S&S is a game that tries too hard.
Its visual and audio style are both incredible, and the game is a joy to experience, but it quickly goes downhill once you start trying to actually do something.
The controls are the first thing that hits you. It becomes immediately apparent that this is an iPad game. 'Replacing touch with a mouse is clumy, but I can deal with that,' you say. And so you deal with it. The controls don't seem to get more intuitive, but at least they're workable.
Then you get to a girl named Girl, and that seems quirky. And this quirkiness stays pretty consistent, which means it gets a little annoying. There's a g-man that says a bunch of big words that essentially mean nothing, a woodman that states the obvious, and a dog that barks. Whatever, you've seen iffy writing before, and you continue.
But then you realize that you're incredibly slow. Annoyingly so. Most of the game is spent waiting for your character to slowly meander across the beautiful pixel landscape. You can only explore an area the first time through, but this game will keep sending you back and forth through it. So you deal with it.
This slowness carries through to your interactions with things. Everything needs to be clicked and held, or maybe rubbed for a while. Or strummed or touched just right, or poked a few times.
Which brings us to the puzzles. If you can call them that. You click and hold on a thing (for a while,) then you have to interact with... something. Sometimes that something glows, sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes you need to slowly walk over to a mushroom and eat that first before you can see the thing you have to do something to. And once you figure out what you're interacting with, and how to interact with it, you have to divine what ORDER to interact with those things. I could find no rhyme, reason, or explanation to how this worked. It was pretty much just random clicking that eventually got me through.
'But this game is rated Mostly Positive in user reviews!' you say. And yes, it is, so you keep going, thinking that there's gotta be something incredibly redeeming about this game.
Perhaps this is so highly rated because it wallows in how artsy it is. Everything about this game is artsy. Yes, it's pretty. Yes, it sounds good. Yes, it's pretentious. But that doesn't make it good. Anyway, you think this, and continue on to...
The first boss. Now, combat up to this point has been pretty simple. There's been a wolf that you block attacks from, and it seems like you can't hit it, though it's never explained why not; and there was a statue or something that you blocked and then hit while it was stunned. That was actually pretty okay. But the boss? Oh no, it doesn't follow the few combat rules laid out up to this point.
So far, the player has been shown that you are capable of blocking god damn anything with your shield. So the boss betrays your trust with an unblockable attack. You fumble your way to finding the solution to this little problem and make it to the next step. Now the boss triggers an audio cue, at which point you tap the block button and dodge to the side. THIS IS NOT INDICATED OR USED UP TO THIS POINT. Until you dodge, you don't even know that dodging is a mechanic. This is terrible design.
Zelda gets blasted for overusing the new toy and throwing it away at the end of a dungeon. But do you know why they do that? The entire dungeon is spent training the player how to use said toy before offering a final test of the player's skill in the form of the boss fight. S:S&S throws this entire concept to the wind and throws random crap at you and laughs when you don't pick it up immediately.
I think the boss is supposed to be beaten through trial and error, but 'trial and error' and 'figue out the new mechanic on the spot' are not the same thing. And since everything takes so damn long (the boss's first attack is over a minute after you triger it, every time,) it's really hard to keep pushing yourself through this encounter.
I certainly didn't.
And that is why I do not recommend this game. Maybe get the soundtrack and poke a Let's Play or something, because it's really pretty and sounds great.

It's a very solid fighting game, it's not 3rd strike or Tekken 3 or another fighting game with 3 in title but it's good nonetheless, and here's why.
Character roster is not robust but it still covers a variety of playstyles, all rounders, zoners, grapplers and speed characters... To put it shortly, despite the lack in numbers every character feels different from one another.
This game has best tutorial I've ever seen in a fighting game. It doesn't just show you which buttons do what, this tutorial will explain you every little thing about how this game works and how each character plays and when you're done, there's still a lot of space for creativity and improvement.
Story mode is... fine. I'm honestly not a big fan of it, story itself is quite predictable and largely based on one or two standard tropes that many fighting games use. Final boss felt a bit disappointing for me but it's kind of a hit or miss situation. Some will like that there's a special character that is very different from anyone else in a very fundamental way but I personally prefer when at the end you face just a character from the roster like everyone else you've been fighting before. Also at the time I was beating the game it seemed like the only way to beat the boss on higher difficulties was to just cheese her out and that's not really fun in my opinion but it was some time ago and by now people probably got much better at the game and found out other, more interesting ways to beat the boss.
Multiplayer... I wish I could say something about it but I only managed to play it once with some guy from Australia (and I live on the edge between Europe and Asia) with both of us having ping over 150 or something like that... not exactly enjoyable expirience (though i have to say lag compensation was rather nice even in that dire situation) but it was the only expirience avaliable at the time. I recommend you check out something like steam charts if you buy this game for multiplayer, and check if you have some sort of community for this game in your area.
Visuals and sound are very good. Background music is not distracting and yet very charming, reminds me of something Yoko Kanno would've composed but it still sound quite unique and recognisable. Animation and art is beautiful and smooth, yeah there are boobs and butts but they offend as much as Switzerland. There are plently of stages and all of them look amazing. Game looks and sounds very good, period.
And to finish it off, gameplay and controls. They are both very, very solid. I use a fight stick and it works like a charm, as it should,  obviously. Keyboard is also fine though, it's much harder for me to play on keyboard, but I don't see why you wouldn't be able to get good results with it after some practice, though I have to say fight stick is real sweet. Game mechanics are way beyond what you would expect from an indie dev, gameplay feels very polished and refined, every time I lost I knew that it was my fault and what that fault was and that's a big deal in any game.
So yeah, this game is good, I liked it, pros overwhelm cons and I wish this game sells even better so there would be more people to play with.

I have been seeing alot of people complaining about this game recently and I feel I need to write a review that tells the truth and isnt bias, or an opinion that isnt purely based on anger due to the wipe. So I have probably around 150+ hours into this game. Now this might not be alot compared to some others with considerably more hours than I, but I still have had fun and enjoyed this game tremensouly, and my opinion counts just as much. Naval Action is one of my favorite games that will always be fun to me as I am interested in naval combat from that era. Now most people I have seen are complaining about the wipe. I have been playing this game since day one release on steam. There has been a wipe in the past and we lost literally everything that time. We lost our XP, Gold, and Ships, and that seems like a bad thing but it was nice because it gave our group a new begining. We were able to restart and grow the group and participate in the new things the Devs introduced into the game. So lets go over some "Pros", and "Cons" about the game.
PROS
- The ships and authenticity are amazing, and the Devs should be proud.
- The level of detail that goes into the game and the ships is amazing.
- The Devs truly care about the game and want this game to grow and thrive with frequent updates and fixes.
- Game is optimized and I had little problems with running the game even when I had a GTX 560.
- The game is easy to learn and user friendly.
- The community is mature and helpful, even between factions, and I have rarely seen toxic chat if at all.
- The graphics and the sound effects are amazing as well.
- New ships and new things being constantly added to keep the game fresh and interesting.
- XP system encourages Teamwork within the faction.
CONS
- The game is quite grindy when you first start out. It takes forever to rank up and earn XP. There are alot of ranks and its hard to go from a cutter and work your way up through the ranks to Captain larger ships.
In conclusion, the game is amazing, I recommend this game to anyone and would love to see this game flourish. The Devs really care about their game and want to see it succeed. So often nowadays early access games are garbage, and cashgrabs. Naval Action is not one of these games and the Devs "will" and continue to make the game better. The server wipe is not a bad thing, people duped and cheated some things, plus the ships durability and everyone had so much, it just makes sense to wipe and start over. The wipe is only affecting assests, the important thing here is that we keep our ranks. Gaining money and new ships is not hard to do when you are max rank. It wont be that hard to achieve everything again. The fact that people are complaining about it and giving this game a bad rep about something so minor is honestly childish. It is extremely easy to gain ships once you get passed the grindy XP gain. In the end its your money, and your decision, but I would highly recommend this game to anyone that is thinking about buying this game.

A timeless era, miniaturized on screen, but certainly expansive in scope and scale. This is one of those games that you can pick away at, village by village, farm by farm, castle brick by brick.  Or, this is a game that you can get swept up in, by either trying to stay out of the eventual fighting by opposing Houses and Factions, or by jumping in headfirst to join the slugfest between hundreds of live opponents.
SK asks for patience as you develop, perform missions, gather resources, and build your villages and castles.  Developing growing and successful villages, leading to resources used for castle building, can test even the most patient of players.  SK's game system admittedly offers those that can play "cards" an advantage in this all-important economic progress aspect of the game, enabling players to accelerate the pace of their development through the use of in-game cards.  War fighting and other combat related aspects of the game can provide a similar challenge.  Attack a computer-generated target without proper resources and troops, and you risk a punishing war of attrition against an inanimate foe that constantly regenerates.  Attack a human player with a similar lack of war readiness, and you risk being annihilated by foe and potentially countless hordes of opportunistic foes alike.  Attack or counter-attack with good strength and patience-driven readiness, and the glory of a 2D face planting of your enemy is yours.
SK is essentially a winner-take-all game, with a twist.  Players can attempt to stay neutral (my 10-year old son named his village "Be Nice to Neutrals" and has so far survived).  Or, players can join a House and one of its many subsets (Factions) to wage either diplomacy and/or warfare on your enemies.  The game can seem unbalanced at times on the latter, as players seem to gravitate toward joining the strongest House out of fear of getting wiped off the map or shunned to the ash heap of Houses that are periodically eliminated as the game progresses.  SK game designers would be well served to add 2nd place, 3rd place (etcetera) awards to Houses (like mine) that seem to start the periodic map resets at a numeric disadvantage to the one or two Houses that are immediately in the lead.
Overall, SK Is a solid game for those that want a 2D game that they can enjoy either semi-passively -- or quite aggressively.  It basically comes down to this:  What you put into it, you tend to get out of it.  And, as the game offers a very deep strategic experience, if you are fortunate to join a House and Faction that is well connected (we use Raidcall to communicate in the House and Faction that I am in), SK can offer even some very enjoyable operational and tactical experiences as well.

First of all don't get fooled by my play time on this game. I normally play through the stand alone client and have 2 years of experience. Now taking about the game... i can honestly say this is one of the best mmorpg games i have ever played. Although the graphics look like it's from the late 1990s, the fact that this requires so much communication between players especially in wars, makes it so much addictive even without decent graphics.
It is free to play but as all f2p games are, there are special bonuses for people who pay. There is no premium account here, rather a premium token which grants the player several bonuses like research and building queues, auto trade, scout and recruit troops. These are generally in from of 7-day and 30-day tokens which can be bought but there are 2-day tokens which are given in the tutorial and some quests. The fact that free players can have these 2-day tokens from quests in multiple worlds makes them at level with the payers. Also another thing that is bought are cards. Now these give massive boost to almost everything in the game. Free players do gain cards by completing quests, but this is nowhere near the amount of cards bought by payers. This is where the games get very pay to win. A f2p player can easily get frustated at this and leave. But there is a way to carry on. A f2p player just needs to communicate with the payers and ask them for help. Most will gladly agree and also invite them to factions if the player is active. Now in a faction, different people gather together and can help each other out in times of need whether its war or building up. Lot of f2p players complain that payers can get their villages, castles and armies up in seconds with cards. This is true and very frustating for a f2p, but through communication and diplomacy, you can get resources to make the same. But the drawback is that it does take a lot of time. The fact that there is no limit to the amount of cards that a player can purchase is a very serious drawback to the game for f2p players. The only way to get round this is to leave pvp to carders and play the role of a supplier or monker to the fighters for f2p players. This creates the necessicity for lot of communication and that is one of the strong points in the game. In war, helping others with resources and monking(influencing) requires so much communication, that one is able to lose sleep! However the chat system is pretty flawed and people don't use the mail syestem that much because it takes too much time. That's why people use 3rd party programs like teamspeak and skype to communicate.
You can have many villages and that too with of different types which grant special resources, research different technologies, create different armies, battle the AI, wolves and other players. The main goal is to win the age and you can only do that if you are in a faction/house. So this is not a solo game and requires teamwork. It is possible to succed as a f2p player if you know the game mechanics very well and communicate with others, but if not then you can get very bored easily. The most inetersting part comes when war takes place, as you feel the urge to be online almost all the time lest your villages get destroyed by the enemy and also to take them out while they are offline! And as stated before this requires huge amounts of communication which can help us create new friends. The faction and house is literally like a family when you play for long with them.
Altogether this is a great free to play game but not close to the best. If you can spend some cash or dedicate enough time this will really become very addictive :) I would recommend this to others who want to play strategy games and have a lot of patience.

This game directly targets issues I have with procedural sandbox games like this.
First, there aren't stacks in your inventory. Once you find something, you pay Lego coins to unlock it and it can be remade indefinitely. This helps with the issue of farming for resources. Every destroyable object drops Lego coins so you never feel like you are hunting for resources.
Second, once you find something you pay for it and its yours for the game! If you want to spawn 20 cars on top of each other you totally can. The only limitation to this is that there are a few special items you equip (all in the same menu) and others for customizing (also a separate menu).
My final happiness from this game comes from a separate build mode. When you don't have to worry about how close your character is and if you can draw in that box or not, it really makes things better. Instead you get a cursor the shape of the tool and go from there. brick removal is similar, and placing decorations is simple.
The only problem I have (besides glitches of course) is that there isn't multiplayer, and that is being worked on currently so I can't even complain!
All and all its an extremely well done engine with lots of potential...I can't wait to see the finished product!

This is a game that's well under-rated. It's not a Black and White style god game, so you cannot go into this game expecting that.  Reus is about transforming the world to help humans achieve projects, and in turn unlock new rewards. Its a game of transformation and optimization.
The "campaign" consists of 30 minute, 60 minutes, and 120 minute plays. To unlock the higher timed modes, you have to complete aforementioned projects, and unlock developments. I found that unlocking developments can be done just by playing - it was harder to try to target a specific development.
While that makes the game sound easy on its face, the true fun of Reus is in its complex symbiosis system. Everything in Reus interacts with the world differently. Blueberries and Chickens will form a symbiosis, and grant more powerful combinations than any one on its own. Reus' challenge is to discover how plants, animals, and minerals work together to form food, wealth, and technology - the three primary resources for completing projects. The symbiosis system is constructed upon the interlocking resources each giant can uniquely create, the varied aspects each giant has to augment a resource's innate power, and the upgrading of a resource to a more powerful tier. These three factors mean the Reus world is constantly changing, and as a player the challenge is to adapt your world so that greater unlocks can be achieved. It is not possible to succeed relaying on any one giant, or on any combination of basic resources and aspects.
Added to this are additional, secondary, factors. Natura, danger, and awe augment how some resources act and how human villages respond to the world. These secondary factors are just that, secondary. I've played several games without any awe or danger, but in those games the humans became greedy and went to war with each other, or would attack the giants. As these challenges arise, the giants are equipped with a couple destructive powers.
I feel Reus is amazingly well balanced, and no playthrough will be the same twice. The game has a large number of symbiotic combinations to discover, and as the player acheives new developments, new resources are unlocked. I would remind any new players to use the spacebar, and take the time to plan your developments. A 30 minute game seems like a short period of time, but one can easily spend several minutes planning a move, and a few seconds letting the game unpause to complete that before pausing again to plan.
I'll end with the only significant negative: at time of writing, Reus does not have Steam Cloud support! This bothers me the most, because I feel Reus is a game where a single "profile" or sorts is best. Because so much time can be spent crafting an optimal world, I don't relish the thought of re-unlocking developments whenever I migrate from my desktop to laptop. As a casual game, Reus needs cloud savegame support.
Regardless, I highly recommend Reus. Don't let its seeming simplicity fool you.

During the wait for Fallout 4, I bought the Fallout 3 ultimate edition on sale for $10 (US), mainly to get myself even more worked up and salivating for a new installment that boasts everything we love from the series with so very much more. I thought I was putting down ten of my hard earned dollars for a trip down memory lane, but 52 hours of gameplay later - I rediscovered a masterpiece.
I put close to 200 hours of gameplay into Fallout 3 when it was initially released, way back when, in a period I like to call my "console days". I hated computer gaming, thought it was for idiots, and played Call of Duty and Halo all the time. I also enjoyed 25 cent PBR night at the local bar and subsisted mainly on pizza. Basically, I was an idiot (not due to pizza - pizza rocks). Fallout 3 was an enlightenment to me. Never before had I been so drawn into a multimedia experience. I remember staying in on new years alone while my room-mate and friends went to the bar because broken steel had just come out. I tell you all of this because Bethesda churned out the best interactive multmedia experience I have ever experienced and all of these years later it still blows me away.
I reserve this section for negative comments: Fallout 3 is not compatible with anything after Windows XP. Bummer. But wait, I have Windows 10!? Oh yeah, some clever group of modders have fixed that problem. There are excellent "how to" tutorials in the community section on Steam. Don't worry about it. Also, the game randomly crashes. Just randomly out of nowhere, all of the sudden, without warning - crashes. Expect it. I have had no more than 20 crashes in 50 hours of play. Also, Steam doesn't recognize that I am playing Fallout 3 when the game is running, only when th launcher is open - so it looks like I've only put 0.7 hours in the game.
The positives: Amazing storyline, massive amounts of choice - from where to go, what to do, and how to do it etc., loooooooooooots of stuff to do and see, loot, loot, loot, loot, hilarious voice acting, impressive (still) graphics and design, Liam Neeson.
If you have never played Fallout 3, get it. If you have and it's been a while, get it. It didn't change my life or anything stupid like that - but it definitely improved my life.

What a fantastic game, truly. I haven't been this addicted to a game since Witcher 3 first came out. Early on, around level 3-5 the game was a bit tough, learning about the various status effects and combat (pro tip: when you want to attack, hold the attack button, default control, to reduce misclick chances), but at level 12 I'm cruising pretty easily through.
The gameplay is sometimes a bit weird. My favorite so far is combat with 3 ice elementals when one repeatedly hits my support enchanter from a solid 5 ap move away, eventually killing him because I thought he was hitting the tank directly in front of him. Silly me.
The default UI seemingly has no way of opening bags during sales/purchasing at vendors which is really unfortunate. The bags themselves are super useful. I like putting my arrows in one, which I then drag to my spell bar for easy arrow access.
The spell effects are really cool, and the variety in classes and game length ensures great replayability. I haven't had a chance to play co-op just yet, something I'm hoping to do soon. Can't wait to troll with static cloud arrows.
The music is also pretty cool overall, very catchy and again a good variety. I usually leave music off but I don't mind it in this game.
If you can get through the first few hours of learning the UI, map, combat etc, then you'll be rewarded with a great RPG experience (pro tip 2: the default builds are usually pretty bad. Also, dagger rogues are pretty bad early on).
Edit - 85 hours update. The honeymoon is definitely over, and several consistent annoyances have made themselves apparent. Misclicks due to shifting character models are the least of it. Some abilities, such as Elemental Tortoise or Ranged Precision Aura, sometimes show their activation animations but don't actually activate. Naturally they go on cooldown as well, so you can look forward to 2 rounds without them. I didn't notice anything in the gameplay that would suggest a reason for this (enemy aura blockers, for example).
Autosaves are too uncommon, usually only happening before large or important fights. DO NOT FORGET TO SAVE FREQUENTLY. This completely ruined a co-op game with a friend, after we got focused and neglected to save, then had to go back about 1.5 hours and at least 1 level up worth of playtime. All motivation to play this game died that night.
Speaking of having to load saves, I don't understand why when both main characters die, you are forced to load a save rather than use those handy res scrolls on your followers.
There are probably a few more that time away from the game has caused me to forget, but at best I'd currently rate this game about a 7/10, and now I'll be very carefully investigating Divinity 2 before I make the plunge.

It's rare for me to come across a game where I can't cite at least one major flaw, but Ori and the Blind Forest is something even rarer. Not only can't I name a major flaw, but I'm struggling to find any flaw at all, and while that may sound ridiculous, please keep in mind that I'm not saying the game is perfect... Although it pretty much is. As far as Metroidvania games go, Ori is the benchmark that all previous & subsequent titles should be measured against. It achieves everything it sets out to do with flying colours, surpassing its contemporaries in ways I previously deemed unimaginable.
Very few works of fiction can transmit a real emotional impact in such a short period of time, but Ori manages to do so within the first ten minutes of the game starting. Not only does it manage to hit such a high note very early on, but somehow continues to carry it throughout the game, without it ever feeling shoved in your face through pages of dialog or lengthy cinematic cutscenes. There's some highs, lows, and bittersweet moments all expertly told through exciting gameplay, incredible art, and perfectly matching music.
I'm not new to Metroidvania style games, nor am I new to platformers, so while I can appreciate that the game doesn't do a whole lot new in terms of gameplay, I still found myself smiling with glee as I unlocked new abilities. Controlling Ori is an absolute dream, with the movement being some of the best in any game out there, accompanied by some charming abilities, perfectly balanced to give a challenging but fair experience. It's never not enjoyable, and regardless of game length, that's something worth applauding.
And the art... The art! There's obviously games out there with more technical gizmos going on behind the image, but I can't point to a single more beautiful game than Ori and the Blind Forest. A simply unforgettable, beautifully designed world with a variety of locales and an insatiable attention to detail left an impression on me like few games could ever dream of. What's even more amazing is that the OST, while stunning in its own right, matches up with the art perfectly to create something truly special.
When breaking Ori down into its core components, nothing sticks out as the weakest link. It's a combination of excellence, united together to form one of the greatests gaming moments.

Total War: Warhammer II offers three things over and above the original Total War: Warhammer which I think make it worth buying:
1. a bunch of new races, units, etc.
2. an engine which allows you to take over any settlement instead of only those for your racial type, but does distribute penalties in a way that doesn't make all areas equal for you.
3. the 'Mortal Empires' campaign mode that allows grander strategic games with any of the races from this or the original.
I do have two main gripes however:
1.  mission objectives are now such that completing a campaign has become a real slog, not only (predictably) in Mortal Empires, but in the basic game.
2. I'm also enough of a fanboy to be unhappy about some ways in which the game isn't faithful to Warhammer lore. Now, one aspect of this is the failure to include factions that should be found on this map, but are now coming in DLC e.g. Tomb Kings, hopefully Araby. My bigger lore gripe then is about the implementation of Skaven. Admittedly it's hard to see how they'd implement this, but in the lore Skaven exist under almost every non-Skaven settlement in the world in their own subterranean settlement, with only a couple of settlements of their own. In this game, there's no nod to this at all: Skaven either control or are not present in a city, just like any other faction. The only difference is that if Skaven control a city it appears ruined, which is a nod to Skavenblight's status in the lore. Moreover, Skaven have to travel around on the surface, unlike in the lore where they ought to be able to travel around underground and attack cities at will – this to my mind would be the appropriate implementation. I apologise for my nerd rage, but couldn't help posting this.

A slow paced point-and-click adventure with side-scroller elements, I'll be the first to admit that this probably isn't the game for everyone. But I love it.
Reasons I love it?
- killer soundtrack. Seriously, even if you don't want to play this game, pull up the OST and give it a listen. It's one of my favorite soundtracks to listen to while I study or write papers.
- the dialogue is hilarious. I've read a lot of reviews which pit the writing as pretentious hipster nonsense, but I just don't see it. The game got more than a few chuckles out of me. I mean, two of the characters you encounter first are Dogfella (a dog) and Logfella (a lumberjack).  I dunno, it tickled me senseless.
- the Grizzled Boor. This guy is a nut, seriously how do you guys come up with this♥♥♥♥♥♥lol. Uh uhuh uh uh uh.
- the pixel art style is deadly. The first couple of times I loaded up the game I distinctly remember letting out a few involuntarily audible moans of "cooooooool"
- the gameplay and puzzles are directly tied to the actual phases of the moon. THE MOON. How neat is that? The entire game should, in theory, take you at least a full lunar cycle to complete. That is, unless you can come up with some way to alter the moon's phases yourself, you cheater.
- the combat is easy-going, which may or may not appeal to you. It's all personal preference, you know?
- the puzzles were challenging, but not impossible. Once you get into the rhythm of the game a bit the solutions will come easier to you. I'm a huge puzzle nerd though.
- great for touch-screen devices, if you're into that.
- it's refreshing to have a female lead, honestly. She's just trying to complete her woeful errand, you know, doing her own thing, being a heroine and such.

Overall, I'd have to say this is one of the quirkiest games I've ever played, and I sincerely hope you like it as much as I have.

Fun, rather old school game, set in the WH40K universe. What I like:
- Great gunplay..the weapons have nice sounds, both ranged and melee weapons.  Melee weapon combat has a well executed sense of weight and when you hit an enemy hard, there's a brief slo-mo to add more sense of ludicrous force. The Chainsword's roars and the eventual rough flesh tearing sounds never get less awesome either for example.
-Blood and gore..there are nice execution animations for stunned enemies and the blood splash and dismemberment are well made, though there's not many dismembernent variations.
-Fluid, brutal and just damn intense combat. No cover shooter stuff. Mostly you fight hordes and I wouldn't have it any other way. You can smoothly switch between melee and ranged combat.
No regenerating health ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t! You have a Halo style infinitely regenerating shield, but health is static and there isn't medikits or the like to heal you..you must stun an enemy and perform an execution, it will restore either about 33% of total health or even about 60% depending on executed enemy's type.
Overall great sound design. Explosions, the Orks' trademark WAAGH and whatnot.
What I rather don't like:
Simplistic plot, not saying though it even needs to be complex.
Only 3 factions in the game..could have been lots of extra awesomeness potential if more factions were in the story.
In conclusion a fun 3rd person shooter with intense combat, the plot is not to be minded, the sheer catharsis of the combat makes up for it.

This game is beyond frustrating, and not in a good way like Lost Souls. Hardly 5 minutes of play will go by without me yelling out a curse word, as the obtuseness of the interface continues to be the most deadly enemy in the game.
Obviously this game had a lot of promise, which it didn't fully deliver on. Maybe they'll patch-in multiplayer someday...
In terms of actual gameplay, Normal and Survivor modes are just variants of the crushingly familiar and boring fetch missions and scavenging/crafting that plague so many RPGS and open world survival/crafting games. Creative is a bit better, as it dispenses with resource grinding, but eliminates even the weak story.
As for the 'story', sure a formation of ships just flew overhead. What species were they? What are they doing? The only way to interact in the game is the painfully slow to navigate NPC/merchant screens. There aren't even dialogue trees. The universe is huge, but there is literally nothing happening in it aside from you. Where's the conflict? Everything and everyone just sits in place until you come by, unlock yet another empty discovery, and leave. There's lots of places to go, but very little to see. Perhaps the developer could have spent more time on quality rather than quantity.
I can't even figure out what effect they were trying to accomplish with the space travel. Everything is just a brightly coloured fog, and orbital dynamics, altho indicated, seem to serve no purpose. In-system navigation is non-existant, you just kind of drag your viewpoint around the screen, hoping to find what you're after eventually. Which I guess is OK, because every place you could go is exactly the same. It makes it frustrating to try to find a good planet to set up a base on though.
The controls are too loose for a combat sim, there's nothing even close to dogfighting. You can have a couple different weapons, but you have to manually toggle between them and only fire one at a time. I think the combat in Spore was more thrilling. Speaking of controls, the entire game is designed for consoles. They've done a decent job of changing tool tips and such, but navigating inventory etc with a mouse it becomes clear that no effort has been made to adapt basic functionality for mouse and keyboard users. Just to exit the game you have to go to the options menu, like whoops, I guess the developers don't know that on a PC you sometimes would want to exit a program. Just a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥port, all around.
There's also just random frustrations thrown into the mix for no apparent reason. Journey Milestones, anyone? I suggest adding a Journey Milestone that unlocks for every 5 Journey Milestones you're forced to endure. Or, if you're going to make the game unplayable for 15 seconds every time I walk a bit, try selling it as adspace and pay us to play the game. And what's up with ships? There's no library of discovered vessels, no customisation options, and no correlation between size and cargo capacity. I had one that was literally just a thruster with a cockpit on it, and it had more cargo capacity than a freighter. There's no handling or performance changes between ships and you can't even use them to interact with the environment!
My overall conclusion is that this game is not worth buying at AAA prices. Maybe for $5 I'd recommend this game for someone that wants all the bright colours and 'wacky' landscapes of Spore without the creativity, or Elite Dangerous without the combat or thrill of space travel.
I'm still playing because I want to like this game, and I spent $200 on a new GPU to run it. One day in though, and I think the Factorio demo was a more fully-realised, polished, and entertaining game.

I purchased this game in December of 2014. I have played it through all the various phases, wipes and resets up to its current state of early access. The truth of the matter with this game, as well as any other, is it can only be as good and enjoyable as you make it...
First of all, this is a work in progress. If you are expecting a polished, perfectly performing game, you will be disappointed and I recommend to you to wait until final release to purchase.
This is a game in development. You can expect resets, asset wipes and bugs. The developers will change things to test and see if they work. Your playing of the game and giving feedback in the forums helps the developers to adjust and perfect their game. The developers are engaged with the player base on the forums and many of the changes to the game have been from player suggestions... some good... some bad...
Much has been written as far as the "toxicity" and poor attitude of the developers... I would venture to say say the level of toxicity and poor attitude of the player base is 10 to 100 times worse. I am frequently stunned at the level of "I want...", "I deserve...", "Give me or else..." whining, complaining, and moaning.  And when they don't get their way they try to hurt the game by trolling bad reviews...
While there is currently no tutorial lessons for new players, the community in game is generally very helpful, just ask in game or search YouTube. Tutorials are being developed. The UI is kind of clunky but that has been marked for fixing last before release.
Initially, only 10 ships were promised. There are over 40 ships (with more in development) in the game now, all beautifully modeled and tuned to sail uniquely, each providing a different sailing experience.
There are various missions to do including crafting, trading, tournaments, PvP and PvE combat, large and small battles... and more content is being developed.
The open world is large and beautifully modeled and time is managed in a way that you can experience much more of it than if you were playing in real time.

Sid Meier's Pirates! was developed by Firaxis Games and released Jul 11, 2005.
Sid Meier's Pirates! is a part-strategy game, part-managment game, part-sailing/naval simulator game, part barbie-dance game, part RPG, part open-world-game, and even has stealth and questing elements.
The story starts off with the protagonist
as a little boy, and his family is abducted by corrupt noblemen. Then fast forward to being full grown on a ship off for adventure... Then becoming the captain of that ship.
BAM!
Cut scene's are over, you are now in control over what you do. Will you save your family? Will you pillage every ship you come across, will you rise in ranks with the different nations, will you hit on every Governor's daughter's
... the choices are up to you. Maybe you'll do all the things like I did, or maybe you'll only do one of them and retire from pirating.
The whole game is controlled using number pad keys. You can use a mouse or  trackpad if you're playing on a laptop, but the game itself recommends you use your number pad keys.
There's a lot of layers of complexity for Sid Meier's Pirates!. I actually had heard about the game while it was still rotting in my steam library waiting for the day I would actually download and play it.
I actually had only heard good things about it, and after playing through, I can totally see why people praise this game so much!
Lets cover what you'll probably spend most of your time doing in the game: raiding enemy boats, and dueling enemy captains. Once you set out on the high sea's, you'll notice the boat tends to move better depending on your direction and the direction the wind is blowing.
If I didn't attack the enemy ship from above wind, normally they could escape me
Again, mind you that the controls are with the number keys. so you turn your ship right and left with 4 and 6, you can change your sails with 8 and 2... and you can toggle between three weapons: 7, 1 and 3. lastly 9 changes your view, but I rarely found a reason to use it.
While engaged in a duel you can choose between three attacks: 7, 4, 1. and Defending against the attacks: 8, 5, 2. and naturally you can taunt with 6. (if it sounds compliment, don't worry, it's really simple, 7 will do a "chop" attack, 4 is a thrust, 1 is a slash. 8 is a jump defense, 5 is a Parry, and 2 is a duck defense.
As long as you start out on an easy difficulty the game will help you know when to defend and what to defend with... Actually I suggest you start out on an easy difficulty in general, until you learn the basics, you can always increase the difficulty whenever you destribute the spoils in a city.
I started out by sailing the SS Anne, I saved my Sister and plundered many a ship. The SS Anne, she was a small ship, the first ship I took over when I started the game. I saw no need to switch flag ships because I could just sail into enemy ships and take the fight to a duel between captians!
This worked well for me until that fateful day... The day I met Captian Kidd on his Brig of War... I sailed directly into his ship and discovered quickly I had bitten off more then I could chew, but alas, it was far too late, I was locking blades with the Captian, but only with a crew of 20-30 so men to back me up... up against Kidd's 100-150 men.
You see, the reason having a big crew is important, is because as you lock blades with the enemy captain, both crews slowly tick down. If you cannot defeat the other captain fast enough you lose the dual, regardless of winning status.
In summary, I lost the SS Anne that day and was stranded on a desert island and later picked up by another ship in my fleet.
...Later I was to come back and defeat Captain Kidd, and steal his ship. I renamed it to the SS Sucker Punch and beat the rest of the game with it. Saved the rest of the family, beat the "boss" evil NPC, Married and English girl from Kitts, and retired from pirating to become a Bishop. (actually I still have the save, so I could go plunder a bit more if I want a higher score and to retire as a Governor...
I've only scratched the surface of the kind of crazy stuff on this game. Unfortunately it has a terrible case of the PlayStation2 face, and doesn't support 1920x1080
. That's really all that I have to say negatively about the game.
After upgrading my ship and getting all of the personal upgrades I was started to get bored with how easy my game had become, so next spoil distribution I kept going up in difficulties until I realized I had to chose the dueling sword, and could no longer dance with the beautiful girls because there were no helpful light up cue's in the bottom right of my screen...
Basically what I'm saying is, if you think the game is too easy for you, increase the difficulty and it'll add MORE features, more strategy, and more complexity to keep you interested focused and getting more.
