This is a stain upon game design. You play a magnetic moron who sticks to pavement and shoots clip after clip into spongey terminator badasses wearing wife beaters. The AI should at least be praised for their advanced team strategizing, as they often pincer the player, or force you to retreat. During this retreat though, you will lack full control over your character, who insists on sticking to the wrong surface just when it matters the most. You never really have full control over your character, to the degree that you hold A near anything and he literally slides into position (what is next ubisoft? hold A as your guy does everything for you on screen? hold down A till its over?).
The campaign "story" has been reduced to just a map and picking objectives that give you lines on screen to follow that lead you to rooftops, sewers, garages, and basements of the beautiful new york city, where you get to have an annoyingly voiced character talk long windedly at you over the radio, typically interrupting any conversation you might be having with your actual human friends. Of course if you have no friends, the enemies call you names and the friendlies can't stop giving you compliments, so that should make up for any socializing you might be missing out on. All the hub safe houses are functionally identical, despite their efforts to make them look different and have a unique personality for each quest giver. The entire game feels like copy pasta that has stretched the gameplay thin. Just like in ubi's other game, Wildlands, every new zone you enter gives you the exact same objectives, just rethemed. They are seriously just copy pasting and then changing a few things and they don't think we will notice... cause they think we are all moron casuals.
The world itself is amazing. It is a shame that they did not spend as much time on gameplay design as they did on the world itself. It is a shame that so many people spent so much effort to fully scan and model New York, only to have the game design team poop all over it. Every distinct location in New York is recognizable, but the quest writers decided they should put all the most iconic locations as pointless encounters or side missions, while the main missions have you going into boring places like the storage rooms, or basement underneath Grand Central Station, but never actually inside that recognizable main room with the arched glass.
The worst part of this loot shooter though, is the loot. They tried to copy the loot systems of your Diablos, Warcrafts, and Borderlands, and about the only thing they got right was the colors. They completely bungled the tiers, because they seem to think everyone deserves to be decked out by end game. You level up every 5 minutes, faster than you can even get used to your new gun before you replace it. No point of spending money, only to have your item obsolete within 5 minutes. All items are just copy paste of a small subset of items, with increased stats for each level. So ya, your level 16 ak47 will be better than your level 15 ak47, but it won't be worth the price at the shop, because your level 17 ak47 will drop 5 minutes later. Filthy casuals seem to love the intellectually unstimulating item hose strapped to their face!
OK, I was wrong. There is a worse thing than the loot. It is the inventory management. I am not sure how they could screw this up so seriously, given the dozens, if not hundreds, of examples of games doing it right. The entire thing is backwards or inside out, where you are going into menus within menus only to do things that could have been done in a single screen. Something as basic as equipping a new gun (every 5 minutes) is made into a process so annoying that you would rather just wait out the next gun (5 more minutes) before it is worth your time to actually swap it. And if you are foolish enough to ever use the loadouts system, then you are stuck having to now also add the new gun to loadout every time. And really, the guns are not worth the effort it takes to swap them, because it doesn't matter if your gun does 32k damage or 34k damage, cause the enemy has 5 billion health.
But, but... there are high damage slow shooting 5 clip snipers, and medium damage 10 clip snipers, and fast shooting low damage 20 clip snipers.... isn't that... no. no. just no.

Good likelihood of being recommendable in the future, but today, it's not.
The worlds are procedurally generated, but they all end up as islands. The draw distance seemed low, so I couldn't tell in-game that there was another island nearby. From the menu where you choose your world, I could see much farther and tell that there was another island I could get to. Frustrating, though, that I can't tell beyond that without exploring oceans -- a painful process when there's no good ways to keep track of distance and such.
Run around your island, discover the pre-made features - trees, rock formations, one or two fun unique things here and there. There are various forms of a single baddie that you can easily defeat, some vehicles, some ridable animals, etc.
For building, there are a couple things:
- building with individual bricks is immediately and unfailingly tedious. It's just like any other game-building tool that lets you put items in 3D space from a 3rd person perspective.
- placing pre-designed shapes -- the afore-mentioned trees, rock formations, that you discover, plus some other odds and ends. It's not as painful as placing bricks, but I didn't feel motivated to do more than a couple buildings and plants.
Using the vehicles and ridable animals is fun, but it's tricky to get close enough to features to "discover" them, and it's tricky to pick up the in-game currency when it drops.
Mouse and keyboard worked OK, but I ended up mostly using an Xbox 360 controller. Did not figure out how to cycle the top-left menu with the controller, so had to switch back to mouse each time I wanted to do that. (I may have missed an instruction prompt -- this might just be my fault.)
It's open world, but in this early stage it's a little
open. There's not enough motivation to keep playing. No multiplayer (yet?), and no real in-game goals/achievements/quests/etc.
Many people are comparing the game to Minecraft. Minecraft's first person perspective and 1 meter cubes allowed for much easier building of pretty much any basic idea you have. Building from individual bricks in Lego Worlds is painfully tedious. After placing a couple blocks, I immediately had no interest in trying to hand build any larger structures. It would be
interesting to see if a first person perspective mode can make Lego Worlds' building modes less painful.
I'm interested in seeing what the game will become, but I'd call this a "wait and see" for now.

I've been playing the Total War series since Shogun 2, and this is my favorite installment probably since then. I really enjoyed the campaign of the game and respect the effort of the developers to make a Mortal Empires map for owners of the both games even though they make so much paid DLC. To anyone paying their respects to the CA team and sticking with their installments, this is a worthy purchase and you probably already have it. To those who haven't yet played a Total War installment but have a fantasy or RTS liking, this would likely be worthy of your time and you may easily sink a few hundred hours in.
The balance of the units in this game is very well established allowing for a somewhat competitive matchmaking system in the RTS battle genre. The races feel fleshed out and the vortex storyline pushes you to move faster than in any other Total War game thus far.
With some people getting salty about the DLC, just remember that CA is a company and that they are actually acting more lenient with this game's dlc than those before. Tomb Kings will be a large DLC as the Tomb Kings are huge in the Warhammer lore, and it would be a shame to not give them justice and CA knows that. Blood DLC is free if you have pack for the first game, but I see how this may come as an annoyance to new players.
I've run into a few bugs along the way, but I feel that most of them have been patched and they have been minimal to affect my gameplay experience. There is a thriving modding community and lots of free content out there. The game is not perfect, but the performance is pretty damn good compared to some of the other installments. I have long loved the RTS genre and feel that it is losing it's steam, but hopefully as CA trucks on we can revive these beautiful games.

A point and click game designed for iphone users with plenty of social media intergration, chatspeak ingame dialog, and confusing puzzles which they intended for the user to repeatedly come back to at different times to see if the solution presents itself. As a PC user, this is less than thrilling or entertaining. Sure it's got good music and they definitely have an interesting art style (which I don't like but I'll give credit for the attempt) but there's little else going for it. The story unfolds slowly, and it wasn't enough to keep me paying attention. Dialog and descriptions are always either really weird and nonsensical or written as if you got a text message from someone else on an iphone, which strikes me as really lame. As you scroll sideways occasionally you'll get in a fight or a puzzle. Fights are a mess which probably didn't need to even be in this puzzle game, but whatever. Puzzles sometimes require different touches or gestures which would seem natural to an iphone gamer, but not to a PC user. In addition the puzzles often give no clues or really vague clues as to their solution. Puzzles are really obtuse. In fact, as I hinted earlier, the game is connected with your clock and calendar, and certain puzzles can more or less easily-or sometimes not at all- be solved at specific times of day or phases of the moon. Again, this would be more interesting if I was on a phone playing 15 minutes at a time, a couple times a day.
I dunno, some reviewers say it's a masterpiece, but the only masterful part about it is the music. Maybe I'm wrong, but even if a game is boring or frustrating, isn't the dialog and story supposed to keep me interested to push through? Well, didn't happen here.

I wish they would have stuck to the good old card game formula we all know with this one. The polished look is something I find missing in most other card games out there and I would be so hooked on this if it was just like any other card game - turn based and without a battlefield that units move around on.
However they tried too hard to make something different. Nothing feels natural, the slowly regenerating mana bar, the two bridge set up that allows whoever holds them to gain abilities for their hero unit, the placing of units on the battlefield. It feels like a bunch of different mechanics thrown together without them really fitting together.
My biggest gripe with the game is how hectic is and that you can't control your units. The unit ai is pretty dumb, often you will see your units stuck on an enemy they hardly deal damage to while another enemy they could have easily defeated picks them off one by one. The developer says this is a game mechanic that the players need to learn but to me it was nothing but frustrating and didn't add anything to the strategic layer of the game. Talk about strategic, I think the developer tried to make it count where and when you place your minions and to a degree it works but the game is just too hectic and the battle fields are too small for this to really work. For example your units can be attacked by the enemy while they are still spawning, so you are forced to think about where to place your minions. The problem is that the battlefield is just way to small for this, which makes enemy minions reach your hero too fast and gives you too little room and time to properly do attack routes for your minions.
And don't get me started on the pay model. It's insanely greedy. You earn between 5 and 30 gold pieces per match depending on if you win or not. It takes 1000 gold to roll for another card. You will often roll a card you already got multiple times. There are several currencies, shards, gold, candies... experienced f2p game players will know this is all to make you pay for the game. I think we all know these kind of "free to play" games by now that are addicting but only enjoyable if you pay. I don't think I really need to explain this further, it's not f2p done right.
Over all I can't recommend this game. The developer tries to bring in new strategic layers to the existing card game formula but at the same time takes away on the strategy part by not giving you control over your units and basically turning the game into a hectic clickfest that is normally decided by how lucky your card draw is.

Steam really needs some sort of middle ground review besides a simple Yes/No. Normally I would recommend this game to anyone, but seeing as how there are a thousand other recommendations for this game, you already know it's good. You don't need me telling you that.
Rather, I'd like to use this space to point out some of the issues I had. Note again, the game is still great, but man oh man, these few points just frustrated me to no end. I hope if the developers make a sequel they could work on a few of these points. Damn I sure want them to because this game is so beautiful,
My main issue? The story falls apart so completely in the end. It completely undermines everything I did in the game and left me feeling very unsatisfied, almost angry, when the credits rolled.
A few other, more minor points
- The difficulty curve is just... I don't know, odd. Most of the game will bore hardcore players, while the first gauntlet will crush casual players. Not to mention that it just strangely gets easier and easier as the game progresses, with more and more saves available to you and enough health to just tank through everything.
- Powerups can be hidden in parts of the game YOU CAN NEVER RETURN TO!
- Too many redundant abilities. Why do we need wall jump and wall run? The latter seems to exist entirely so we have FOUR different kinds of charge/dash abilities, and they all use different inputs! There is something to be said for games that can be challenging without overcomplicating their mechanics.
- Just a little too short. Really, it feels like this game needs about an extra 30%, maybe one more area and temple.
- When I got the breathe underwater power, I realized I already had finished basically the only underwater section, so I wouldn't have minded they expand on that area especially.
Again, I'd actually recommend this game because it's just so beautiful, with 2D art even better than the Rayman games in my opinion. The gameplay is fun, and the world is colourful.
I can't believe I am saying this, but if they had cut out the story, I would have loved this game so much more.

Really though, Downwell is an amazing indie title for its price. Being one of the indie titles that has a android mobile release (Looking at you Crypt of the NecroDancer), it'd be worth it if it were $10.
It's easy to pick up and just play, no 30 minute story cutscene telling you what's going on. Just go down and shoot stuff with your gunboots, it's that simple. The movements are fluid, the shooting is spot on, and all the gun modules are balanced in my personal opinion. Once you go down to the depths of the well, it progessively gets harder with you, the player learning how things work and adapting your play style to fit that criteria.
Remember how I said the gun modules are balanced? The upgrades aren't, in fact only a small portion of them are actually useful.
For example, knife and fork. It works progressively, yes, but more often than not you'll not touch the enemy at all or you'll try to go near it and get hit by another enemy.
Also, the game is a tad bit short. It'd be neat if the game had a looping mechanic like Nuclear Throne does. However, this is a $3, so it does have its limits though.
Also, jumping on enemies has really awkward hit detection sometimes. You can land a little bit to the left or right side and sometimes get hit.
Would I recommend it? If you haven't seen the thumbs up, then yeah. It's a great and simple indie game I think some roguelike fans would really enjoy.

Good likelihood of being recommendable in the future, but today, it's not.
The worlds are procedurally generated, but they all end up as islands. The draw distance seemed low, so I couldn't tell in-game that there was another island nearby. From the menu where you choose your world, I could see much farther and tell that there was another island I could get to. Frustrating, though, that I can't tell beyond that without exploring oceans -- a painful process when there's no good ways to keep track of distance and such.
Run around your island, discover the pre-made features - trees, rock formations, one or two fun unique things here and there. There are various forms of a single baddie that you can easily defeat, some vehicles, some ridable animals, etc.
For building, there are a couple things:
- building with individual bricks is immediately and unfailingly tedious. It's just like any other game-building tool that lets you put items in 3D space from a 3rd person perspective.
- placing pre-designed shapes -- the afore-mentioned trees, rock formations, that you discover, plus some other odds and ends. It's not as painful as placing bricks, but I didn't feel motivated to do more than a couple buildings and plants.
Using the vehicles and ridable animals is fun, but it's tricky to get close enough to features to "discover" them, and it's tricky to pick up the in-game currency when it drops.
Mouse and keyboard worked OK, but I ended up mostly using an Xbox 360 controller. Did not figure out how to cycle the top-left menu with the controller, so had to switch back to mouse each time I wanted to do that. (I may have missed an instruction prompt -- this might just be my fault.)
It's open world, but in this early stage it's a little
open. There's not enough motivation to keep playing. No multiplayer (yet?), and no real in-game goals/achievements/quests/etc.
Many people are comparing the game to Minecraft. Minecraft's first person perspective and 1 meter cubes allowed for much easier building of pretty much any basic idea you have. Building from individual bricks in Lego Worlds is painfully tedious. After placing a couple blocks, I immediately had no interest in trying to hand build any larger structures. It would be
interesting to see if a first person perspective mode can make Lego Worlds' building modes less painful.
I'm interested in seeing what the game will become, but I'd call this a "wait and see" for now.

I absolutley love Fallout 3. The main story was great, they got Liam Neeson to voice your dad, and it got me into the Fallout Series (I might go back to play the first 2 at some point, but I don't know.) Although, you will probably have to mess with the options in order for the game to work, the game is buggy and can crash sometimes, there are guides that show how you can fix this for the most part, so check those out. Other than that, I can't say much else about it, but I'll give a rundown of the DLC's.
If you didn't know much about Fallout's Lore, there was a war that happened between America and China. The Chinese took over Anchorage Alaska, where the remaining oil is kept, and this is about you playing as a soldier in Anchorage Alaska, with you being one of the two surviving in a squad. You can find 10 pieces of intel around the map. It gives you a nice little perk that ups some of your abilities. At the end, you unlock a special room in the current location where you and the Outcasts were trying to enter. You and 2 other Iutcasts are attacked by the remaining Outcasts who want the valuable pre-war technology all to the Outcasts. So they attack you, and the 2 other Outcasts fight them back. Unfortunatley, those two died whilst I was getting the loot so I never got their dialogue options.
Anyway, the loot you get is a really good set of T-51b power armor, a Gauss Rifle, grenades, mines, you even get a unique Chinese Officer's Sword. But it had more potential. It didn't get much in the way of stuff. It was you sneak into a missile depot, kill chinese guys with a guy, and destroy giant cannons. Then you go and take some other bases and it all ends with you disabling a minefield, and then confronting Jingwei where you can make him suicide, or kill him.
You go to a destroyed Pittsburg. People are dying from a disease and a baby is immune to any sort of mutation, or disease. You could join a slave revolt, or prevent it. Either way you get stuff.
Borken Steel extends the main story. You watch Liberty Prime get Destroyed at the Beginning, then take revenge by destroying a mobile platform. You get some good loot out of it, and it increases the level cap. This also introduces new Enclave Armor, new enemies, and lots of other stuff, even a ghoul trying to scam other ghouls to buy Aqua Pura (which is literally pure water) mixed with the dirty water.
To summarize, this is an extension for Fallout 3's storyline. And it lets you continue post-main quest.
You go to an island and kill inbreds. I can't say much else about it other than the guy who takes you to the island ends up cutting out your brain.
There were Aliens in Fallout 1, Fallout 2, and because they were referenced in Fallout 3 (via the Alien Blaster(s) and also the Firelance) now you get abducted by them. You meet a Slaver, a little girl who somehow is eternal, a US Medic working in Anchorage, a Cowboy, and a Japanese Soldier. There is also a Dead Astronaut. Anyway, I recommend doing this DLC First considering you get lots of good early-game gear from it.
Overall, the game is very pentiful with content and despite the bugs, and glitches I love it.

However, after the player's father, voiced by the one and only Liam Neeson, leaves the Vault in a chaotic fashion, thrusts the player into the Wasteland, exiled. You then adventure into the ruins of the former nation's capital, your only goal is to find your father and figure what exactly happened back in the Vault, and why he left.

I recently picked up Warhammer 40k: Space Marine because I was in the 40K mood.
In this game you are put into the shoes (power armor boots?) of space marine captain Titus of the Ultramarines as you help fight in a long, bloody, and seemingly hopeless battle to save the forge world of Graia from falling into the hands of the enemies of mankind.
The grimdarkness of the distant future is everywhere in this game. It captures the feel of the 40K universe well with graphic imagery, disturbing hints, an overlooming feeling of dread, and yet a light of hope admist the carnage. Of course being a Warhammer 40K title it does get gory and disturbing at times.
The story is simple, yet complex. I am not going to spoil anything, but the story and characters are written well enough that the ending leaves you wanting more. Perhaps one day we will get a sequel, because the story needs to be continued.
I would reccomend this game to anyone who likes 40K or wants to get into the 40K universe. Some hardcore 40K fans might complain about the space marines not being portrayed as "zealous" enough, but personally I loved seeing a more human side to the 10 foot posthuman supersoldiers who violently "purge" their enemies in the name of the Emperor.
Gameplay-wise, it plays out like other shooters such as Half Life or Gears of War, except there is a greater focus on melee in certian areas. It is pretty straightforward, you move, shoot, swing your sword, and use your surroundings to your advantage. Be sure to get the power ups, because the enemies get harder and harder as the game progresses. It's simple, but very fun and it will give you something to do for the week. And it is worth coming back to play again as well.
8/10: Give this game a sequel!

Space Marine is a fun hack and slash/ 3rd person perspective(the camera is right behind your' character) shooter game set in the Warhammer 40000 sci-fi universe. The game is simple, intense and sometimes frustrating, and makes you feel like a mighty astartes without going overboard. For example, when you walk or run, you can hear the booming footsteps of your character, but it doesn't sound cheesy or deafening, and the weapons seem godly powerful, but again not cartoonish. the music is instrumental, and pretty good, especially the more battle themes, but there is no sound galery, something that Is definately a good idea. The game doesn't have a save file system, but there are many checkpoints that you can start from to replay a certain part. A lot of running between fights, but there is plenty of detail to examine, some of it gruesome, but truly paints the grimdark setting well. In the beginnning, u can look up and see ships continuously getting shot down, gunfire and explosions in the distance. The "voice of Graia" the voice that anounces things like when you get a new weapon sounds callous and serious for example, lines like "Public disturbances will NOT be tolerated", help to paint the grim, brutal sci-fi setting. The final boss is a let down gameplay wise, but the story makes up for it. You feel like a hero, arriving in the imperial guard's darkest hour to save the day, and the cutscenes and dialogue portray this well. Titus is a true hero, doing what is right, even if he will be betrayed by comrades and punished by the inquisition for it.
Recommend it, fun and intense. Wish the campaign did not become so difficult towards the end, means you can't have as much fun and take the combat as lightly.

I don't understand why so many people praise this game so much. To me, this is just a fair game. I actually prefer Attila and Rome II to this. Yes, it has so many great features but most of them are new textures and new factions which look very cool at the beginning. But the strategic value of the Totalwar franchise is actually reduced.
Pros:
+ 4 new factions with heroic quests. Different factions with unique play styles. This is a huge plus for a strategy game.
+ Vast and detail campaign map and battle. The boring siege battle is boring. Don't tell me to count on Mods because from now on CA will not give us full siege map anymore.
+ Cool and good animations especially monsters.
+ Level of difficulty is fine to me. AI seems to respond better in battle.
+ Great sound performance. I love the music so much.
+ Coordinate battle with allies is now improved a bit.
+ Mortal empires expansion is free for those whose bought TWWH I.
Cons:
- Another game with 1vs1 combat animations. Please get rid of this, CA. There have been many issues with this kind of combat. Units do not charge routing army (guarding button is just for decoration). Routing army now run with a speed of god-like cavalry. Your units can never kill half of them.
- Naval battles are gone. They use auto-resolve to simplify all. CA actually does not how to make naval warfare.
- Vortex feature is not good for a strategy game. Everything is about rushing. I don't like the intervention army mechanism.
- Still 20 units per army. It has already been 10 years. Large-scale battles are impossible. Each reinforce unit will join battle after another one routed.
- Rally feature turns you into the crazy mode when dealing with huge AI armies.
- Very slow army build due to poor economy balance.
- Very small amount of units while defence towers are small Deathstar ion cannons.
- Now to complete 1 turn. It takes you at least 30-60 secs in the late game. The map is huge but you will find it boring to conquer. The answer is below.
- Many factions are just copy-pasted of each other. Why do you like to create so many small factions like that? What a waste of performance on those tiny factions like those.
- Diplomacy is still the same. No improvement at all.
- Prepare for the DLC whoring next year.

We’ve had something of a resurgence of more classically styled CRPGs, and Dvinity: Original Sin was at the vanguard, being one of the first real Kickstarter success stories. D.OS is in many ways a fantastic game – but I’m surprised at how its glaring flaws get glossed over by professional reviews.
Let’s start with the good stuff – D:OS is an incredibly polished, expansive and absorbing RPG with clever tactical combat, entertaining writing and impressive character customisation and crafting mechanics. The core of the game is definitely the combat – the story and characters are serviceable and work to move things along, but ultimately anyone expecting serious, epic fantasy should temper their expectations – like all Divinity games the tone is mostly silly and irreverent, and shares more in common with Fable than Pillars of Eternity. I personally found the voice acting charming, but I can see how it’s menagerie of regional UK accents could set teeth on edge, especially when you’ve heard about the man with many cheeses for the 300th time.
The tactical turn based party combat is the real crowd pleaser here, and mostly it’s brilliant. Nearly every fight is set up for multiple angles of approach, and characters (especially magic users) have an enormous amount of options. Enemy variety is top notch, with very few repeated foes throughout – there are no lazy palette swaps here. The money shot for D: OS is environmental usage and inter party synergy – a clever player with an optimised party could make it rain, cover the ground in oil, set fire to the water oil/mix and then electrify it leading to stunned, burning enemies over a massive area. When it works you feel like the cleverest person in the world.
Which brings me neatly to one of the game’s biggest issues - class imbalance. You may have noticed that at no point above did I mention hitting someone in the face with a sword. Mages are extremely powerful, especially initially where it can feel like melee characters and archers are little more than cheerleaders. Knife wielding rogues in particular are a sad joke, requiring huge amounts of investment and setup for relatively meagre gains, all the while being incredibly fragile. Exploiting the environment is a large part of why D:OS is so compelling – a large portion of the tactical combat involves combining elemental powers to create choke points, block line of sight or inflict massive AoE damage. Mages are the ones who can most readily do this, and vs early undead enemies (resistant to arrows and swords and weak to fire) they seem overpowered to the point of absurdity. Mages also bring healing spells, exceptional crowd control ability as well as summoned creatures to tank better than a dedicated tank while providing additional throwaway offense.
Thankfully later on the balance of power definitely shifts as the damage potential of mages drops off due to elemental resistances on enemies, and you will find your warriors and archers picking up the slack. Unsurprisingly this is very much the game’s sweet spot, before the difficulty takes a nosedive after level 15 when you start summoning meteor strikes from the heavens. Warriors bring unrivalled single target DPS as well as solid survivability to the party, while archers become very versatile with a stockpile of crafted arrows alongside some nasty single target DPS of their own. Mages settle into a more supportive position of crowd control, summoning as well as party buffs and healing. Rogues sadly never stop sucking.
However by far the biggest problem with the game, and the one that I’m sure has led to more players giving up than anything else is the dreadful pacing of the first part of the game coupled with non-existent signposting. After a short tutorial dungeon, you get to your first major city and the first order of business is solving a murder mystery, with almost no indication of how to proceed or why you should care. D:OS is defined by it’s excellent, tactical turn based combat and depth of character building. You will be seeing none of this for about five excruciating hours, and attempts to leave the city to explore are met with a deadly faceful of skeleton wing-wong.
The thing is, you never have to do anything like this ever again. I’m not against this style of quest, especially in an old school CRPG, and around halfway through the game as a palate cleanser after a large combat section would have been a perfect change of pace. As it is though it gives a completely unrepresentative and unflattering first impression, which is a real shame as less patient players may miss out on a real CRPG gem.

Minion masters is honestly a really cool idea for a game, and i think theres so much that could be done with the game. however, as far as gameplay is concerned i cannot say minion masters has gotten any better, rather worse from when i started playing it. now lets get into some of the issues:
------
Rock Paper scissors gameplay -
Well, maybe not entirely R-P-S style gameplay, but close to it. in the current incarnation there are decks that just eat other decks with no real fighting chance given to the players. you essentially hit the queue button, and then a "you lose" screen appears the moment you get into the game. well... i wish, rather you attempt to see if you actually can muster anything against a deck that you simply lack the tech answers to.
Now yes, this does exist in other tcg games, however, countering in those is different. where in hearthstone and other such games a deck being countered still has a 30-40% chance of victory, they are just simply unfavored. in minion masters its a whole new level. things like dragon's nest decks are completely unbeatable unless you have the right tech options against it due to the nature of flying minions and how they are easily buffed. however there is one way to beat that...
----------
AGRO IS DOMINANT -
Like in every bad tcg, agro in this game is both braindead, and entirely too powerful. the nature of bridges in this game reinforces a style of constantly pushing down your opponents throat, and the aoe affects of most spells being able to hit masters further pushed the thought process that running your dudes into your opponent as hard as you can is a good option. there aren't really great decks that beat this style, at best they have decently solid win rates, but nothing staggering. the result is: if you want to do well, play an agro deck. and the leaderboard decks being mostly agro is representative of that.
-----------
IMBALANCES ABOUND -
hey you guys know milloween. shes been out for a long while, and still isn't even halfway viable. 1 of your 9 characters in your game has been sitting in the gutter and 2 of your 9 heroes have long sat at the top of the pile (apep and king puff) and no big changes are being made to actually stop this. and from a competitive stand point, this is hell. it kills creativity and experimentation because the other architypes the other masters are meant to embody simply dont hold a candle next to the few that are too strong.
Card balance isn't steller either. there are a whole slew of straight up awful cards, and a whole host of absurd ones. and most of the issue comes from just how incompitent the devs are at balancing.
AND I MEAN INCOMPITENT.
take for instance call to arms, a card that was reworked, and now sits in the gutter.
or crossbow dudes, who were nerfed to the trashcan, watched as an op ranged unit filled the same mana slot, and then slightly buffed to still being unusable.
the examples go on, but the developers seem to have this keen inability to actually be able to put something in relatively balanced states when they change it. its either nigh useless or absurd when they try to do any decently large changes to something.
-------
WILDCARDS
JUST
WILDCARDS
you know what no one in the community wanted? tripling the grind to obtain all the cards in the game. you know what the community wanted? not methods to trump deck creativity by allowing people to stuff their decks full of an overpowered option that over centralizes the need for tech options against certain decks to fight back.
no one wanted wild cards. they came out, ruined the balance, forced x3 crossbow dudes, and only really served for decks to skip over interesting cards, instead focusing purely on stuffing decks with overpowered garbage that can't really be dealt with if they blow their tech options on the prior 2.
to this day i have no idea why wild cards were added, as they only seem to cause issues with the balance system, and further cause strains with what they can release. before wildcards, a broken card was okay, it was just 10% of someones deck, and it could be countered easily. after wildcards, a broken card could be 30% of someones deck, and you aren't going to be able to answer it unless your deck is similarly including large numbers of tech options to fight it, and thats simply not fun.
for an indie studio with a small team and a limited supply of testers, this is absolutely mind bogglingly insane to put in. unless things are balanced to a really solid point, things can easily overcentralize now, instead of just being a minor part of the meta, its puts a much bigger emphasis on balance and when its not met, losses feel unfair, and wins feel unearned.

To the Moon is a short and sweet title that will take you on an emotonal rollercoaster. I would greatly recommend this game as it is beyond worth your money.
To the Moon will take you throughout a man's life and will have you explore his memories so that you may help him accomplish his last wish -- To go to the Moon.
Along the way your emotions will be flowing out of you like a

To the Moon plays off of older style graphics to bring you beyond amazing writing and connection to the characters. The gameplay is somewhat repetitive as it mostly consists of moving your character throughout a space and exploring an area from John's memories, but the writing and subtle music absolutely makes up this. Overall, this game is WELL worth the money and I strongly recommend playing it.

I absolutely adore this game! The pixel art is gorgeous and the music is fantastic (I often listen to the soundtrack as background noise, Jim Guthrie did an amazing job), and at a play length of only a few hours the game is just long enough to leave the player satisfied without being bored by hours of no substantial content.
The writing is really fun and has a great juxtaposition with the setting which I love. Even though the story is set in a fantasy land and you play as a Scythian warrior there's a really modern feel to the way things are written and characters interact. It's interesting having the main character (who, might I mention, is a woman! extra points!) using "we" instead of "I"; for example, in the beginning there's a part where you can examine a girl sitting in a field, and the main character says, "Far from the war-ravaged steppes of Scythia we met a dark-haired girl in a sunlit meadow." It's a great way of really drawing the player into the game! Almost every line of dialogue also has an option for posting to your twitter, I never used it but if that's your sort of thing it seems like fun.
The controls can be a little weird to get the hang of at first if you're like me and don't bother looking at instructions, especially playing on a PC since the game was originally made for a touch screen. Once you get the hang of them though they're super easy. I love that the combat system ups the difficulty not by introducing new things to the combat but by simply reducing your health bar as the main character gets more tired and worn down. It's a unique way of creating more urgency without simply making the bosses do more damage, and I think it's a great way to play into the story.
If this game is your kind of thing, I'd definitely check it out!

Overall I recommend the game, but please take note it has some issues that can break the enjoyment for some people.
The art style is lovely and the music is fantastic. It incorporates the soundtrack perfectly with the gameplay. Seeing the story and adventure unfold was very enjoyable. Now for the negatives. The game has a LOT of back-tracking, and by the end I was forcing myself to continue until the end. It can be very unclear what you need to do to proceed; at one point I had to check a guide to realize I had to summon a lightning bolt to crack a tree (the game never, ever hinted I needed to do this). There is a lot of aimless wandering as you try to figure things out. The combat is extremely basic, but to be fair that's not the focus on the game.
I'm happy I played it, but it definitely stretched my patience at times. It took me about 3-4 hours to beat it in one sitting.

Fallout 3 does many things right. The most important of its strengths in my opinion, however, is its ability to immerse the player in an atmosphere filled with choice, unique experiences, and a world worth exploring.
The Fallout franchise has always done these things right, but Fallout 3 brought a new atmosphere and a new set of mechanics to an already great model. These mechanics all work extremely well and make Fallout 3 a revolutionary game. The combination of the dialogue system, V.A.T.S., and the functionality of the Pip Boy make gameplay smooth yet still very refreshing. The primary narrative is strong and supports the immersion of the gameplay, while the entirety of the wasteland is filled with areas full of depth and story that is present in almost no other game.
Revisiting Fallout 3 has only confirmed the undeniable strengths and with each playthrough, the player will surely find new areas and characters worth exploring and experiencing. For these reasons, Fallout 3, along with its predecessors, stand alone in their own sect of games. Along with these strengths, Fallout 3 added a certain undefineable charm as it broke into the 3-dimensional realm. NPCs, the world, and the physics make playing the game a real joy and keep a smile on your face the entire time.
Fallout 3 is a must-own game and represents a special era in gaming in my personal opinion.

Gameplay, graphics, sfx and performance are all good. It's reasonably well balanced and has usually short queue times.
It's a good game if you need a quick break from another game and it feels original and refreshing. But take note, it's PVP only!
What it is about:
Sharks vs divers. The divers collect gold that is scattered around and use it to buy equipment to defend themselves against the sharks. The divers will follow a bot called STEVE to drop their gold into. The sharks eat divers and buy upgrades with those kills and must prevent STEVE from reaching the surface again.
The first team to run out of tickets (lives) loses.
Sadly this game has a few cons that impact gameplay a lot:
- Leavers during matches are annoying. Bots take over their place but it's not exactly great. It happens frequently and w/o penalty.
- Players are matched based on first come first serve. You as a level 1 can be matched with 5 other players who are level 100. Also skill levels are not taken into account at all. This generates a
of bad games.
- Lag is extremely horrible in this game on higher skill levels. It is almost always there even if you only play within your own region. You shoot a shark, it takes no damage at all. You dodge a shark, you get teleported into his mouth on the other side of the wall. You get the point.
If you love playing Shark the game is pretty good. Most of the time you can carry solo.
If you love playing diver and you are an experienced gamer, you require friends to play with because otherwise you will go nuts by teammates doing nothing but feeding. Just like in a moba. But worse. They literally swim around, alone, don't shoot sharks, don't collect gold. And those people may have 20+ games in their history... Unbelievable and frustrating.
The reason for there being no matchmaking system present is (from what I understood) that the devs want to keep the queue times low. The downside is of course that 9/10 games has at least one total newbie swimming around in your game, wasting all of your tickets and contributes literally nothing. Not his fault, just... no decent matchmaking...
- Overall I do still recommend this game.
- I do not recommend it for casual people however, people will stomp you over and over and you probably will lose interest rather fast.
- I do not recommend this game if you prefer being a diver while also having a short fuse.

I remember playing this on my old Xbox Original as a kid and loving the hell out of it. Now after playing it as an adult I can still say the same. However it's not without some pretty evident flaws.
The graphics are dated but that's to be expected. This game came out in 1987. Some 15 from then it would be ported to the Xbox Original where it was still widely loved. And some 20 years later it would end up on Steam. Still critically acclaimed. If you've made a game that's obviously dated but still super fun and memorable, you officially made a perfect game.
The combat does take a bit of reaction and timing however once you get the trick down you'll realise how basic it is. It's still made plenty fun however by the neat little details in the battle. Sometimes you can pick up stuff from the stage and smack the opponent with it. And some of the victory scenes after each battle are very satisfying to watch. You'll laugh when the opponent get's side-swiped by a box. It's not all good news however as I've noticed there is NO POINT to using any other weapon other than the rapier. The other to weapons don't matter in a battle that requires speed. Kind of a waste sadly.
Travelling the world takes some amount of patience, planning ahead and a bit of luck. You need to plan your arrivals into certain ports to keep your supplies in stock, your ship healthy and your crew satisfied. And you also need to be careful about what ships your ready to battle and what factions you want to please. It's not all about "Find the treasure, get rich, die happy." You have objectives you could do to give yourself a much better retirement. You have to find your family who were kidnapped, you have to get married to a mayor's daughter, You have to get rich, you have to really please one of the factions cause they'll give you more land which you'll eventually use to build your mansion and retire and ofcourse you've got legendary pirates to beat to become the no.1 most infamous pirate. This may sound like way to much to handle but don't worry about it, this game does allow you to tackle these things one at a time.
Overall the game is fantastic. It may not be graphically pleasing but honestly if that's what you care most about then your probably a treadmill hypocrite. And no one likes hypocrites. Despite it's shortcomings it's still a fantastic game and I truly hope it get's a sequel or even a remake one day.

In all honesty, this game scratches that niche of grind gameplay with an atmosphere that i personally enjoy. The Dark Zone remains a cluster of cancer, horrible ideas, and good times for PvP I highly recommend the new mode/s.
TLDR; 7/10 buy this game ON SALE for like 20-25$ and get a solid 2 weeks enjoyment out of it then move on. Story is decent if you dig and get into it, graphics are a shell of what they were advertised as, game modes are mildly diverse and challenging, PvP is decent but ingrained in meta.
Graphics;
If you're looking for a game with graphics that make you stop and go "Oh wow that's amazing" move on, this game has decent graphics that get by but don't break any boundaries or impress anyone.
Game modes;
Story- The game is mainly comprised of missions that are divided up into three categores; health, armor, and tech/attack. Each of these missions will have leveled enemies to give you a sense of progression throughout the game. But the order in which you go through these missions is horrible. For one of the missions you START the mission in a low-level low stakes mission to take out the main base of one of the 3 major factions in the game. Then afterwards you will proceed to do harder and harder missions to take out more of said faction where the "lackies" are harder to kill than the very boss given to you!
{Update} There has been an update giving us a much much harder version of this run, but you can still murder the mission at low levels with ease in the initial story. +2 for effort, -1 for timing.
Underground is essentially a semi-randomized dungeon crawler addition that plays on cheap puzzles, tight corridors, and small objectives that can last as long as you make them due to a selected difficulty/challenge ability. This game mode will keep you busy for awhile, but there is a small interim point where the loot and the effort don't match up for awhile while you grind your way to the better rewards.
The addition of a hardcore surivival mode has made for some interesting times, high stakes coordination, and tense moments running from safe-house to safe-house. The snow is beautiful, and almost gives us a call back to what the game was intended to look like rather than the turned down version we have now.
New PVP modes have made the game more fun, standardizing many stats and dmg in order to level the horrendous balance previously seen in the game. A tutorial explaing how to optimize kits beyond youtubers would be a welcome addition.

Well FINALLY! A decent take on a FPS Warhammer 40K! It looks great, feels great, moves great and is (depending on difficulty and/or single/multi-player game selection) as easy and/or hard as to be... - You guessed it: great!
The Story is simple and deep at the same time. Lots of shout-outs to the lore and the board game. There's a few things missing, but I'm gonna forgive it, simply because I understand the Devs' problem that they had to keep it all progressive and over-the-course-of-the-game-like.
The graphics are so blocky and ugly that they're stunning. (Warhammer 40k fans will get what that means.)
The enemies and combat is in-your-face gory and brutal, as it should be in the deep dark universe of Warhammer 40k.The Arsenal of Weapons is not only cool, it stays true to the lore... The characters work incredibly well, and grow juuuust enough during the game that you're feelling bummed when it's all over. (SEQUEL!!! - I doubt it, but, I, for one, would welcome it.)
Right... So, down to cases.
Pros: 5/7 - Nice, simple, deep, developing, engaging storyline; decent, believable characters (I know you're hoping for more, Devs, but let's be honest. This is Warhammer 40k. Even decent and believable are BIG words of praise for story purposes.) ; Graphics are as they should be. Not pretty, but stunning in their dark, blocky, vast, gritty ugliness; Good Funfactor is excellent. Stomping, Chopping and Shooting Orks and Chaos Marines is SOOO much more fun than it sounds. And It actually gets harder and more fun in multiplayer once you take the time to get into it; Very Nice Replayabillity, (there's ton's of difference between single-and-multi-player-games, and the difference in difficulty settings-vs-feel in the campaign is visible enough that it makes several consecutive playthroughs viable.)
Cons: 2/7 The money-maker, unfortunately, is in effect in the multiplayer. (Look Devs, as much as I applaud you wanting to provide assistance to those unfortunate few who don't have the time, talent, skill, or dedication to "earn" the assorted skins, weapons, gadgets and-what-not, BUT do have REAL money they're willing to trade you to GIVE it to them isn't really endearing you to the rest of us, who like a challenge, who like to play and rank up and stuff. I understand you're running a business, I really do, but it's discouraging and more likely than not to make me quit the multiplayer than not.) ; Things are a liiiitle repetitious. The variation in topography and architecture makes it less obvious, and the progression in the singleplayer campaign to bigger, badder, better trained-and-equipped-enemies is all well and good, but while it IS fun to "SMITE THE INFIDELS" "FOR THE EMPEROR!" and all that, I'm not gonna lie. Sooner, rather than later, it'll get old. Thankfully there's tons of content and good ground for replayabillity here, but given the fact that competitors are already vying for top FPS spot in the Warhammer (40k and otherwise) theme, the Devs might wanna consider upping the ante on this title. Soon. More content... More Factions, (Guardsmen, Eldar, Tyranids?) maps, an expansion, whatever... - Theres room to grow here, people, and you know it.
(Oh. Incident'ly... I'm gonna go ahead and ask where the "Powers" are, in the game. You know... Psychers or whatever they were called in the boardgame... Every faction had them, more or less... They would probably rock the Multiplayer if you balanced them right... Just saying.)

Reus is a strange story of contradictions. On paper it's about controlling a pack of world shaping titans, and crafting the planet to your will. Each new forest or ocean is a place to drop animals or minerals, and before too long the humans arrive like unwelcome houseguests. Caring for the pests, helping their cultures thrive becomes the mission of the titans.
Theoretically that sounds liberating. Build an entire planet, shape its cities, and if they ever get a little uppity or violent, simply turning their city into a new Atlantis is always in the cards.
Well, if you don't mind seeing all of your hard work go away, that is. My problem with Reus is that it's actually very restrictive. The creators had a divine plan for how various minerals and animals work to make the best bonuses, and as the game gets longer, the ability to create variety or personality vanishes. There is only ever one path to success in the later stages, and that holds Reus back from greatness.
Still, it's visually pretty, and the whole power of being Gods is worth a few dollars.

I purchased this game in December of 2014. I have played it through all the various phases, wipes and resets up to its current state of early access. The truth of the matter with this game, as well as any other, is it can only be as good and enjoyable as you make it...
First of all, this is a work in progress. If you are expecting a polished, perfectly performing game, you will be disappointed and I recommend to you to wait until final release to purchase.
This is a game in development. You can expect resets, asset wipes and bugs. The developers will change things to test and see if they work. Your playing of the game and giving feedback in the forums helps the developers to adjust and perfect their game. The developers are engaged with the player base on the forums and many of the changes to the game have been from player suggestions... some good... some bad...
Much has been written as far as the "toxicity" and poor attitude of the developers... I would venture to say say the level of toxicity and poor attitude of the player base is 10 to 100 times worse. I am frequently stunned at the level of "I want...", "I deserve...", "Give me or else..." whining, complaining, and moaning.  And when they don't get their way they try to hurt the game by trolling bad reviews...
While there is currently no tutorial lessons for new players, the community in game is generally very helpful, just ask in game or search YouTube. Tutorials are being developed. The UI is kind of clunky but that has been marked for fixing last before release.
Initially, only 10 ships were promised. There are over 40 ships (with more in development) in the game now, all beautifully modeled and tuned to sail uniquely, each providing a different sailing experience.
There are various missions to do including crafting, trading, tournaments, PvP and PvE combat, large and small battles... and more content is being developed.
The open world is large and beautifully modeled and time is managed in a way that you can experience much more of it than if you were playing in real time.
I paid $40 for this game. It was some of the best money I've ever spent on a computer game and this game is still under development.

Hello Games has done a good job with this update, adding the huge capital ship sized freighters (which you can build inside and summon at will), base building on planets (with pretty standard building pieces and decorations, but look nice in its artstyle all the same) more resources to collect (for example, killing animals no longer collects carbon, but mordite) and some general fixes and graphical upgrades like motion blur and temporal aliasing.

The survival mode makes the game so much harder, as life support runs out much faster, and resources are more scarce than before. Creative mode makes you a god, completely invincible and with unlimited resources and money, allowing you to just explore and build wherever you want without having to worry about running out of resources or units.
Bearing in mind Hello Games said this update was the first of many to come, I'd say it was a pretty good start, and if all the updates are to this standard then this game will be awesome within 2-3 more updates. Personally i wish Hello Games would add multiplayer as a priority, so we can finally "find each other within the galaxy" as this would only make the game far better than it already is.
Overall: Still not entirely the game that Sean Murray promised, but it's on the way there, and it's nice to see Hello Games didn't take the money and run.

I purchased this game on a Steam sale for ~$35.
I've had a lot of fun playing No Man's Sky, but I had low expectations going in and did not play prior to the Foundations update. There's not a ton of depth with what is presently available; the game is predominantly about exploring a procedurally generated universe and scavenging the necessary resources to do so. I find it a relaxing exercise in wandering and poking my nose around in new locations.
To characterize the game overall I'd describe it as broad, but shallow. There's a lot of planets to explore, but they have a relatively small number of themes to draw from. There's crafting systems with discoverable recipes for many gameplay mechanics, but the recipes for any individual mechanic have 4 or 5 elements. Xenobiology produces some interesting looking races, but they generally fall into one of three or four distinct types. More depth in each of these dimensions will make them feel more substantial and the universe less samey-feeling.
The idea is interesting and should be rewarding to play for people who can appreciate slower paced games and a focus on explorative gameplay.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the single best titles I've played this year. From plotline to mechanics to pacing and even artistic design, Moon Studios nails eveything on the head.
As a game that is centered around its platforming mechanics, Ori manages to set up a movement system that is seamless in transitioning between different types of terrain. I found myself flying through sections of the map at incredible speed with abolutely no lag time between running, climbing, gliding on updrafts, and jumping. The animations are a little weird in that while the game runs at a silky smooth 60fps, Ori's actual animations aren't quite animated at such a high framerate, giving him a slight stuttering animation at times. This does not, however, detract from the mechanical qualities of the game.
The game is played out in a single, huge map, with no method of fast traveling between locations. If the player wishes to get all the way from the west edge of the map to the east, he will have to traverse the entire distance. While this lack of a travel system may seem disconcerting, it doesn't take TOO long to get across places, given Ori's incredible agility. There are very few automatic checkpoints in the game, mainly just at the entrances to "dungeons" or escape sequences. Other than that, the only checkpoints are manually placed by the player as they progress.
Platforming games are always a delicate balancing act of being either too forgiving or too difficult to progress, but Ori does a great job of melding these components together, provided that the player remembers to set down checkpoints, or they may find themselves going back 5-10, even 15 minutes depending on the sequence they are currently completing. My only concern here is that players new to the genre may find that the open world isn't too difficult, but walking into a dungeon will instantly spike the difficulty of the game, and escape sequences for unfamiliar players can be downright frustrating, but in my opinion, this is perfectly okay, as players can use the open world to refine their freerunning skills.
Combat in the game is very straightforward, with a basic rapid fire attack, a charge attack, and then various freerunning abilities that double as attacks as well. The bash mechanic, learned fairly close to the beginning of the story, is the games flagship attack, giving Ori incredible agility and ability to manipulate foes against themselves. There wre some sections that showed that the mecahincs surrounding combat weren't perfect, but no part was ever so bad to be game-breaking in any way.
Progression in the game is accomplished through three methods: Life cells that increase Ori's maximum health, Energy cells that increase Ori's maximum energy capacity, and Ability points, a kind of experience/level system. Filling the experience circle or finding an ability orb will grant Ori an ability point which he can then use to upgrade one of three trees: Combat (increases damage output, damage radius, and number of targets), efficiency (decreases costs, increases regeneration from finding health and energy), and utility (miscellaneous quality of life upgrades as well as revealing map points of interest). All upgrade paths are achieveable in the same playthrough, but in a given situation, I found myself regretting taking certain upgrades over others early on. None of these upgrades are actually required to complete the game (as there is an achievement for actually completing the game without the use of them), but boy they will absolutely help.
I really cannot stress enough how beautiful everything is in the game. Ori and the Blind Forest is an absolute masterpiece when it comes to artwork and sound design. According to the developer, background assets are only used once, meaning that the art team actually produced an enormous amount of individual pieces for the game. The orchestration is phenomenal, rivaling the beauty and power of many AAA titles, with varying takes on the main theme of the game. The build up into the first escape sequence, activation of the escape part, and the ensuing music will make the game feel instantly epic. I found myself in the first escape yelling at Ori to "GO GO GO" as the world came crashing around him.
From an animation perspective, this game is a shining example of the real power of the Unity engine. When I think of Unity, I usually think of small indie games, but with the level of detail put into each and every animation, from the way plants move in the wind as a shockwave hits them, to the individual animations of every enemy, I have yet to find a glaring fault with anything from the art department.
The story of the game is fantastic, told in both real time and flashbacks. There are a couple interactive cutscenes, in which the game doesn't actually tell the player that they are in control, and so it takes a second or two to actually get going. I will warn you now, if you don't take to sad stories well, the game will drop a feels bomb on you in just the prologue alone, and continue to do so a couple more times through Ori's journey. The story itself is very somber, but tells itself extremely well, even making a villain that I could not only empathize with, but almost agree with their decisions. Even the ending was fantastically told.

I first ran into Stronghold Kingdoms just after lauch. I had been a fan of the franchise for several years already. I had already played a few 'MMORTS' games already, though, and was a bit burned out on the type of gameplay necessary to keep from getting steamrolled, i.e. sleepless nights, missing work or school, constantly watching from your smartphone... well, you get the point. The change from the high competition to strong cooperation was such I actually felt let down and dropped the game after a few months. (I will note that I did not make a strong effort to find a faction or join a house in the glory race, and so I had missed out on a huge section of gameplay that would have kept me playing.0
I recently picked up SHK again and started playing and noticed some of the changes that had been made. I played a few weeks and noticed some of the core things weren't really different, though. If you don't join up with a faction/house, things are pretty boring. I should note that is unless you just decide to be the thorn in everyone's side, and of course, that has its own levels of excitement. I joined a house on the latest server, USA 2, and things are promising to be interesting.
The one big addition to the game I have really liked is the quests. For people completely new to the game, it gives some direction as to how to play and what to do. For all, it's extra rewards that help you get established in the game faster and something else to compete over. They start off easy and build up to the difficult or very time/resource intensive.
My final complaint about the game is that the honor cost of attacking smaller players can still be prohibitive. This is what gives the game its more laid back style, but makes it difficult to deal with the annoying players that deliberately don't level up and constantly harrass with cheap troops just to annoy those around them.
Overall, I give SHK a thumbs up as it can keep a properly-minded person entertained for hours and days at a time without requiring you to sit and stare at your avatar 100% of the time. For those easily addicted and like to micro-manage each minute: play at your risk.

Alright, where do I begin with this... this is probably the game that has hit me the most in an emotional way out of anything I ever played. Not because of how incredibly sad it is, because it's not. Though some scenes are incredibly sad and bittersweet (and the music makes it oh so more effective), there's plenty of entertaining scenes and funny characters to balance it out. And even though the story is incredibly well crafted and covers such a wide array of feelings, from fear to joy to sadness to that massive clump in your throat and the downwards pull in your chest, there's one aspect that hit me more than anything before. It's something not everyone will be able to understand, in fact only a small subset of people will (not because they're dumb, it's just a unique situation only few people have been in)
MASSIVE spoilers after this part, you been warned!
So, one of the main characters, River, has a pretty obvious case of autism, most likely aspergers. It slowly gets revealed as the two playable characters (who somewhat remind me of Tiehl and Boerne from a german police show no english person will have ever heard of travel back through the life of the dying old man, and it never gets fully confirmed, but the signs are quite obvious. And that journey back in time, the first subtle and later quite obvious hints, are what really got me. Because they reminded me so much of my own childhood and brought back so many half-buried memories of my young years that I sometimes just stopped playing entirely for a few minutes, thinking back at my past. I was lucky enough that my condition was discovered while I was still young. I went to therapy for a few years and it helped me integrate enough to survive in this wicked world, but River wasn't as lucky. I haven't ever been able to relate to a fictional character so well before. I don't really know how to describe the experience. All I can say is that it was a good one.
But even all of that aside, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone. The gripping story, the lovable characters and of course the beautiful pixel graphics (I'm a sucker for SNES graphics, what can I say) and the lovely music are way, way more than enough to put this game in my list of favorite video games. It's the cherry on top in the form of this astonishing throwback into my childhood that elevates it into at least my top 5, if not to the very top. I can't wait for the sequel they teased at the end of A Bird's Story, and I hope Eva and Neil will finally kiss by the end of it :p

For one thing, the game encourages you to take your time playing through because if you play through this game honestly you're meant to take a solid month to finish it. Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a unique game (if it can be called a game). It's more of an experience? The main focus is not the game itself but the pixel art and the clever use of sound and music. The music always matches the mood of the action giving you upbeat and epic tunes during battles and soft ambient tunes during exploration. In fact, battles were my favorite parts of the game (though there were few). They battles are simple patterns of attack and defense but they still prove to be fun and sometimes a bit intense.
While there are some definite good aspects of this game, there are other aspects that have me torn and make this game somewhat difficult to recommend. First of all, when playing this game, you have to remember that it was intended for mobile devices and tablets. I didn't understand that at first and was instantly frustrated with the controls. Touching and tapping has been replaced with mouse controls. It's still a bit confusing but you get used to it. My second gripe is that you as a player have very little idea of who your character is, what she is doing, and why (you understand more towards the end but for most of the game, you will be confused). It's important to check your surroundings, interact with characters, and listen to what they say (though they can be deliberately cryptic at times). This bring me to my next complaint... This game works fine, it looks good but there was something that kept bothering me and I couldn't quite figure it out until a couple of other users pointed it out in their own reviews. The game feels pretentious. Something about the overall presentation... The flashing of the game's title every now and then in-game, the flowery language of the archetype narrator, the fact that your character is known a "The Scythian" while other characters get names like "Logfella"... It's difficult to place the blame on one aspect but something is not quite right about this game's overall atmosphere.
Overall, this is not a bad game. And maybe I'm wrong and this atmosphere was not the intention of the game's developers. So if you're into point-and-click, adventure, and music type things... Then give Sword & Sworcery a try and decide for yourself. It's a unique experience that you won't find elsewhere.

Pros:
+ Intense, non-stop heart pounding(literally) underwater action
+ Fun cooperative gameplay which requires serious teamwork and synergy
+ Simple and engaging objective (survive and protect for divers, kill on sight/hinder for sharks)
+ Surprisingly well-balanced even though teams are asynmetrical
+ Fast matchmaking
+ Good AI with difficulty levels also make for great solo play
Cons:
- Matchmaking could be improved. Instead based on region, skill could also be a factor when matchmaking. That way, there will not be a case where 2 newbie sharks are placed in a situation where the hunter becomes the hunted, or newbie divers getting rekt with a score of 0-2X. Though I'm not sure how this skill-based system could be implemented without introducing ranks and MMR and all that boolsheet.
Suggestions:
<> I think it would be great to be able to view all the weapons, upgrades and their damage statistics under a gear tab or something, same goes for the sharks and their evolutions. And it should also show what other upgrades I have yet to unlock. Basically a view only version of the in-game shop placed in the main menu.
<> I think it would be cool for divers should get $$$ for earning medals like Kill Joy etc., same goes for sharks getting upgrade points when they get a medal as well. More sense of achievement ya know.
<> More maps and more modes. They need not be as balanced as blood and gold, some can really casual. Maybe a mode where the divers only have a live but start with $5000 to buy whatever they want, and they have to get from point A to point B(their boat) with the 2 sharks on the prowl. Or heck, even a mode where every diver start with harpoons. Or both sharks are Megalodons. Or a map in total darkness in the abyss. Possibilities are close to endless.
Overall, a great game to play with friends or even with public. Just have to add in more content and address some of the issues I mentioned and I'm sure it will surpass the likes of Evolve or L4D2 Versus, at least in my opinion. As it stands, I would give Depth 8/10.

Huge amount of content, this is incredible for an early access game (I've got it as soon as it was released, but the game works perfectly well already). Scenery and elements are very diversified. You can find all sorts of animals, vehicles, buildings, tools, toys...
The procedurally generated worlds are big, beautiful, varied (many biomes, climates, terrains, ..) and really feel like Lego bricks. With some vehicles and animals, you can fly (e.g. the eagle, the plane or the dragon!). You can swim, there are boats and submarines, ... This is a paradise for explorers. My daughter explores and uses predefined buildings and vehicles. I've played a bit more with the brick-by-brick way to build things, (but she doesn't let me play often with the game because she wants to play it all the time herself).
The stability of the game is perfect. No bug at all (no crash, no clipping, no weird thing happening, everything behaves as you'd expect). I'm amazed that this early access game is more stable than most games that have been released for years.
The editor is one of the best I've seen so far, though the camera is not optimal yet : Brick-by-brick building is really easy to use, tools (for larger terrain changes) slightly less so but still very handy.
Minor defaults, list of small things to fix:
When typing the name of the world at the beginning of the game, it assumes I'm using an English (QWERTY) keyboard and I'm using a French one (AZERTY) which can be mildly confusing
Vehicles get stuck easily. Once stuck, you've got to use tools to delete or smooth out parts of the terrain to get your vehicle out of trees and cracks of the terrain.
Submarines should be able to dive (and swimmers too): the left ctrl key should let you go underwater (like with a descent of the plane). At the moment, submarines are like boats with a different look.
When building something brick-by-brick, the camera doesn't help. You should have a better (full) control of the camera rotation and movements. Sometimes the camera falls under the ground, most of the time the camera adjusts itself in a less-than-helpful location...
All in all it's already a great game and it has the potential to become an incredible game... Keep up the great work!
