Minion masters is honestly a really cool idea for a game, and i think theres so much that could be done with the game. however, as far as gameplay is concerned i cannot say minion masters has gotten any better, rather worse from when i started playing it. now lets get into some of the issues:
------
Rock Paper scissors gameplay -
Well, maybe not entirely R-P-S style gameplay, but close to it. in the current incarnation there are decks that just eat other decks with no real fighting chance given to the players. you essentially hit the queue button, and then a "you lose" screen appears the moment you get into the game. well... i wish, rather you attempt to see if you actually can muster anything against a deck that you simply lack the tech answers to.
Now yes, this does exist in other tcg games, however, countering in those is different. where in hearthstone and other such games a deck being countered still has a 30-40% chance of victory, they are just simply unfavored. in minion masters its a whole new level. things like dragon's nest decks are completely unbeatable unless you have the right tech options against it due to the nature of flying minions and how they are easily buffed. however there is one way to beat that...
----------
AGRO IS DOMINANT -
Like in every bad tcg, agro in this game is both braindead, and entirely too powerful. the nature of bridges in this game reinforces a style of constantly pushing down your opponents throat, and the aoe affects of most spells being able to hit masters further pushed the thought process that running your dudes into your opponent as hard as you can is a good option. there aren't really great decks that beat this style, at best they have decently solid win rates, but nothing staggering. the result is: if you want to do well, play an agro deck. and the leaderboard decks being mostly agro is representative of that.
-----------
IMBALANCES ABOUND -
hey you guys know milloween. shes been out for a long while, and still isn't even halfway viable. 1 of your 9 characters in your game has been sitting in the gutter and 2 of your 9 heroes have long sat at the top of the pile (apep and king puff) and no big changes are being made to actually stop this. and from a competitive stand point, this is hell. it kills creativity and experimentation because the other architypes the other masters are meant to embody simply dont hold a candle next to the few that are too strong.
Card balance isn't steller either. there are a whole slew of straight up awful cards, and a whole host of absurd ones. and most of the issue comes from just how incompitent the devs are at balancing.
AND I MEAN INCOMPITENT.
take for instance call to arms, a card that was reworked, and now sits in the gutter.
or crossbow dudes, who were nerfed to the trashcan, watched as an op ranged unit filled the same mana slot, and then slightly buffed to still being unusable.
the examples go on, but the developers seem to have this keen inability to actually be able to put something in relatively balanced states when they change it. its either nigh useless or absurd when they try to do any decently large changes to something.
-------
WILDCARDS
JUST
WILDCARDS
you know what no one in the community wanted? tripling the grind to obtain all the cards in the game. you know what the community wanted? not methods to trump deck creativity by allowing people to stuff their decks full of an overpowered option that over centralizes the need for tech options against certain decks to fight back.
no one wanted wild cards. they came out, ruined the balance, forced x3 crossbow dudes, and only really served for decks to skip over interesting cards, instead focusing purely on stuffing decks with overpowered garbage that can't really be dealt with if they blow their tech options on the prior 2.
to this day i have no idea why wild cards were added, as they only seem to cause issues with the balance system, and further cause strains with what they can release. before wildcards, a broken card was okay, it was just 10% of someones deck, and it could be countered easily. after wildcards, a broken card could be 30% of someones deck, and you aren't going to be able to answer it unless your deck is similarly including large numbers of tech options to fight it, and thats simply not fun.
for an indie studio with a small team and a limited supply of testers, this is absolutely mind bogglingly insane to put in. unless things are balanced to a really solid point, things can easily overcentralize now, instead of just being a minor part of the meta, its puts a much bigger emphasis on balance and when its not met, losses feel unfair, and wins feel unearned.

In terms of fighting games, Skullgirls is by far my favorite.
The team are balanced, and the combo system allows for individuality:
Not every team you see will play the same way, and each match therefore different from the next.
Learning to play the game is easy!
The tutorials are expansive and user friendly, even for people that are new to fighting games!
The community is very supportive and provides feedback on gameplay to help newer players advance.
The character list may be relatively small when compared to other games.
However upon further exploration you will find the differences between each character more than make up for it.
No one character is anything like another in terms of moveset, strategy, etc.
So whatever playstyle you prefer, there's bound to be character for you!
The team system allows for endless possibilities in terms of competition and strategy.
Teams are well-balanced, and so a team of 3 is just as good as a team of 2, etc.
Playing solo is not punished, as you are compensated for your lack of teamates in terms of damage and health.
Much awaits you in the world of Skullgirls, and it's only getting better!
But don't take my word for it, try it out for yourself! You won't regret it!

Basically, it's a 2D platformer in which you control a ball or better, the ball itself moves according to gravity 'cos you can only manoeuver through WASD keys the screen.
Ok, do you have in mind the application Windows uses to view photos? In the low bar you can rotate them of 90° degrees? That's what this game does. Left and right keys and the ball (ok the game says that's a deformed creature called The Stalker, to me looks like a badly designed ball) will keep on falling or will float in the air while you go from point A to point B avoiding spikes, flames etc.; of course, while you progress other things are added such as mandatory directional arrows, Mario-like fading blocks, exploding tiles and so on.
The game itself is hard and challenging, but overall it's not new at all and it's really badly designed. Every level looks the same, the background is the same and so on. The soundtrack and sounds in general are truly awful.
The controls aren't so buggy but ovearll if this game was free, ok, it would surpass many Flash games out there but since it isn't free, I don't think this will add something to your collection if you've been into these kinds of minimalistic Flash gravity platformers for years.

No Man's Sky- the modern day pariah of the gaming world.
*ORIGINAL DRAFT - AUGUST 12, 2016*
No Man's Sky is a first-person space exploration game developed by Hello Games, the creators of Joe Danger and Joe Danger 2: The Movie. This will be a personal review of the game's overall performance; flaws and successes. It was, and still is, the subject of much controversy among critics and fans alike. Delays, fabrication of in-game features, and a devastatingly awful launch all contributed to what is widely regarded as the biggest gaming flop of the past five years.
Let me start out by saying, I'm no stranger to waiting for things. Final Fantasy XV, The Incredibles 2, Doors of Stone. In a lifetime of waiting, I've developed no small amount of patience. I caught my first glimpse of No Man's Sky way back in 2013, on a livestream of VGX. The highly saturated, retro-futuristic world design was the first thing I noticed, followed by the game itself. It touched the adventurous chord in my spirit, and it immediately shot to the forefront of my imaginary wishlist. Alas, I knew it would take years more to finish development, so I mentally shelved it until a time when it was once more relevant.
As it happens, that time was midway through 2016, when the game finally garnered international attention. Until then, it had been flying relatively low under the radar. Hello Games had partnered with Sony, and it looked like a release date was finally in order. The date June 21st was slated for the eventual release of the long awaited space sim. This is, I feel, where things started to go downhill. Spurred by the immense hype train, Sony and Hello Games began to reveal more and more incredible features. That is, until around the beginning of June 2016. If you were to watch a number of interviews with Sean Murray, creative director of Hello Games, with each being closer to the release date than the last, you'd notice something. He seems to shy away from answering questions about certain, unofficially announced features.I believe the June 21st- August 12th delay was Sean Murray realizing that his game would be far from complete, and urging Sony to give his team more time. It wasn't enough.
Now, let's go over the pros and cons of the game itself.
Pros:
-Gorgeous visuals
-Enormous game world
-Fantastic setting/idea
-The language system
-The feeling of discovering something new
Cons:
-Abysmal graphical performance on all settings
-Lacked depth
-Many redundant or unimportant features
-Many incomplete or missing features
Now, I know the pros list was longer. But believe me, the cons list possesses a much larger sphere of influence. No Man's Sky suffered from the classic conundrum of being a mile wide and an inch deep. The first few hours were powered solely by the wonder of discovery. Flying around different planets, meeting the alien races, learning their tongue, mining for resources to upgrade your ship, suit and multi-tool. For me, this initial phase lasted ~30 hours. For others, it lasted 45 minutes. Despite perhaps having a bias, my eyes were not closed to everything wrong with the game. I did feel somewhat betrayed, and disappointed about the lack of content. Was it worth $66.49(CAD) on launch? No. Would I have recommended this game on launch? No. Would I still have pre-ordered and played on release day, had I known the state the game would be in? 𝑌𝑒𝑠. If that confuses you, it can be answered with one simple word: interest. I had a feeling it wouldn't live up to its vision. In fact, I prepared for it. But I had to play it, just to be sure. There was my interest, and then there was Hello Games/Sony's interest. They wanted to know if people would buy/play it. And they did. Sure, it's not the shiniest of business practices, but it worked. Hundreds of thousands, if not millions of people played, streamed, and watched the game's first few hours. Shortly afterwards came the angry mob.
One of the biggest hiccups in the game's launch was the PC performance issues. Powerful rigs were running the game on low with 40FPS maximum. On lower end PCs, the game was barely playable, if at all. Incredibly long load times, severe tearing, and Gsync enabled by default without an option to disable it in-game were just a few examples of the game's poor technical state on PC. Hello Games quickly released a few fixes, bringing performance up to a bearable level. But by then, their fate was sealed. Prior to the November 27th 1.1 update, if I checked the stats for the Steam version of No Man's Sky, there'd most likely be less than a thousand players, compared to the 200k+ on launch. The game was dead faster than an anti-vaxxer's child in the slums of Namibia. Moving on to the next topic, the November 27th 1.1 update; the Foundation Update.
The Foundation Update has been an absolute blessing for this game. It added in a number of missing features from the initial launch (larger space battles, the buying of large ships, base building), and gave a shot of steroids to the graphics section. My moderately powerful Lenovo laptop used to get 20-30FPS on minimal settings, now it's getting a solid 50-60FPS on medium settings. The improvement is monumental. I completely understand the skepticism coming from this latest update, but if you have not refunded the game already, I urge you to give it another try. Hello Games straight up lied about their game, and that's unacceptable. However, this update is a huge step in the right direction. Without a release date looming over their shoulders, the team is free to work on updates and fixes for the game. It will take a lot of time and effort to make No Man's Sky into the game we all thought it would be, but it can be done. Listening to Sean Murray's boyish awe when he talked about a childhood fantasy of space, and the passion of the team at Hello Games has instilled a faith in me that cannot be quashed. They have invested far too much of their lives on this dream to give up now. All we need to do is have a little patience.
*EDIT, AUGUST 11, 2017* See? Was I wrong? It's been a year today since No Man's Sky released, and our patience has been rewarded time and again. This game's several major updates have transformed it from a shell of what it should have been to a rising star position among space exploration games. The game we were all expecting has started to take shape, and it'll only get better from here.

Visually astounding, Ori and the Blind Forest is a game that should not be dismissed by any true fan of platformers. The first 10 minutes will strongly attatch you to the story, and the gameplay is some of the most fluent and interesting platforming I have seen. Did I mention its beautiful?

I'm about 5 hours into this game and I'm in love.
From the get go, you're pulled in by beautiful music, smooth graphics, and stellar atmosphere.
Although I didn't cry during the opening, I did tear up a little bit.
From there on, you're thrown into a large world (with no load screens) full of secrets and beauty. You can go anywhere as long as you have the correct skill involved, whether it's double jumping, gliding, or bashing walls. If you can't get somewhere, odds are you're probably not supposed to go there yet. So far my favorite part has to be bashing, you get the skill once you find the water element and it makes you feel really really cool.
The platforming is very smooth, and it's quite easy to pick up. The difficulty does ramp up and I have had a few times where I need to run a course several times before actually getting through it. Combat is very simple, you just click a bunch near enemies, although when you get more abilities, you can do some more complicated maneuvers.
Going into more depth about the whole atmosphere of the game, it's just freaking amazing. Did I mention the music because I have to mention the music again. I freaking love it. Seriously considering to buy the soundtrack so I can lull myself to sleep. I get really depressed at times, to the point where I don't want to do anything, and it makes me feel at peace. Which I think is really saying something. The graphics are beautiful. It looks like it could be a painting. It doesn't feel like anything was just copy and pasted. Probably the Ginso tree is my favorite part of the level design. In short, everything just feels in place.
I really enjoy the skill tree. It's something simple, and completely optional what you go into. You don't want to see hidden secrets? You want to find them by yourself? Then don't invest in the middle tree. Don't want to do much combat? Just invest in the combat tree and make it simpler. The whole game doesn't seem like it even requires the skill tree, but it's there as an option.
I think my only complaints about the game is that there's a lot of back tracking for extra goodies, and the story is nothing really new. Find the elements to save the world. It's still not a very big issue. The story is simple, sweet, and gives you an objective, nothing really more. The reason to play the game is in everything else. As for the extra goodies, they're completely optional. Yes, they will make the game a lot easier in the long run, but it's up to you whether to go back for them or not.
Tl;dr, this game is great to just immerse yourself in the atmosphere. It's not too hard but just enough for a little bit of challenge.

After around 2 and a half hours into Ori and the Blind Forest, and after experiencing the panic and reward of a wonderfully climactic escape sequence, I can say this game has completely surpased my expectations. I bought this game expecting it to be a beautiful platformer/explorer that focused more on the visuals than actual gameplay, but once you begin experiencing the increased difficulty and the unforgiving perscision found a couple hours in, the game becomes much more.
The gameplay, which some critisize for being "floaty" or innsensitive to mid-air imput, fits perfectly well with the lightness and the theme of your character, Ori. The movement Ori undertakes in itself is contrasting the harsh, flat motion that the enemies in the game have, and within 10 minutes of playing, you become used to the movement system. The in-air motion is also easily controllable, but only to a certain extenent. Your take off from jumps have to be accurate, as there is only a limit to the forgiveness you'll get for flinging yourself too far or coming up too short. This however, will come as no surprise to those that enjoy platformers.
Visually and Audibly, the game will knock you to the floor. With artistic background and appealing environments, Ori and the Visually Impaired Tree Family creates areas you not only crave to explore and traverse, but also to occasionally stop and observe. During your times taking in the visuals, you'll also have the beautifully composed sound track playing along with you. Each track fits perfectly into the situation, and each adds to the gameplay experience.
As for difficulty, this game does not mess around after the first hour and half. After allowing you some time to master the mechanics as best you can, it will steadily begin ramping up the difficulty with not only dangerous situations, but it will also increase puzzle difficulty, often forcing a pattern of trial and error in order to finally complete a room or area. This difficulty however is not implemented falsly or unfairly, and instead plays off of your ability as a player. This allows skilled platformers to still complete rooms and areas on the first try, which is a great sense of accomplishment as well. If you as a player do not enjoy the feeling of earned success after repeated failures, this game may not be for you. You'll have to learn in order to get further in this game, so if you came for a game you can buy, beat, and brag about, you should probably turn away now. This game is too much of an experience for that.
Overall, this game has sold me. While not quite perfect, Ori and the Blind Forest has left an impression on me, and always pulls me back in for more gameplay after I take a short break. It's direction is perfect, and doesn't impede and over interact with the player like most modern games are trending towards. It reminds me of the older Mario Games, where you're given a story, and purpose, and set off to figure out everything else over time. On top of all else, this game is extremely fun, and if you enjoy platforming at all, or enjoy challenging games, you should buy this game.
9/10

TLDR: the developers don't take criticism well, are biased against American players and do not punish cheaters whatsoever. Take your money elsewhere, this game is just about dead.
When I started playing this game about a year ago, it quickly became one of my favorites. Since then however, it has been continuously and completely ruined by the developers. It has been over 4 months since the last public patch, and it shows: there aren't more than 200 people online at EU or NA prime time.
The attitude of the developers towards their player base is outright toxic and quite frankly a PR nightmare; they don't deserve your money. First of all, there is an enormous bias against players from North America: the devs blame them for the issues in the game,  and accuse all Americans of being unwilling to fix the game for them (that solution being that they don't play in the US prime times).
Recently an announcement was made basically stating the game will become more 'hardcore' than it already was: the developers will strip nearly all Quality of Life (QoL) features from the game. This means players will have to put insane amount of hours in to just be able to find and/or fight an enemy.
The reality of it is that there aren't nearly enough players in the game to support that 'hardcore' view, and these changes will only drive more people away. Players naturally went onto the official forum to announce their displeasure with the game's direction. After this blew up into the dev's faces, about 300 posts were simply removed - including a lot of constructive ones, but also the Game's Producer basically insulting individuals.
The developers just didn't seem to care anymore, so I posted a silly YouTube video in the feedback thread (among those 300 removed ones) as a metaphor for how the devs test and announce new features. They decided to permanently ban me from their forum AND FROM THE GAME(!) because of this, even though a moderator removed the post literally within a minute (so nobody even saw it). A friend of mine who posted a picture of a pizza and another YT video got the same treatment.
Keep in mind that this forum is in no way connected to the game or Steam; it's a completely seperate account (with the username being the only means of comparison). Now, I would fully have accepted a permanent from their forum - despite the game's producer insulting and ridiculing certain players consistently himself. That would be their right after all, but a permanent in-game ban for something so trivial is unacceptable and in breach of the Steam TOS.
Maybe worst of it all, is that meanwhile cheaters who duplicated ships and resources (for unfair advantages) for many months remain unpunished - despite the developers claiming they would take action. Instead they changed their policy to accept exploits and cheats of any kind, as long as you report them before they decide to ban you.

This game has it's ups and downs.  Challenging, but rewarding.  Basically you'll start from scratch starting from a single village scouting for resources, creating weapons for your armies, adding new buildings to your villages, researching new technologies/upgrades and designing castles.  Eventually you'll have multiple villages and sizable armies where you will join with others to attack enemy factions.
If you can get into a friendly, helpful faction things can be easier for you.  Unfortunately, one of the biggest downfalls for SK is in order to compete with hardcore/longtime players you will have spend cash on this game.  Buying cards and tokens can get pricey so I'd recommend trying out SK for a week or three before throwing money at this game.  Even with a card edge don't be surprised on losing resources, villages, etc from a enemy faction or from some who is having a bad hair day.  I've seen strong and skillful players lose everything and have to start a new village from scratch.
This game is slow paced and you will need patience in order to get the most out of it.   If you like faster action paced games then SK might not be the  game for you.  If your into teamwork, slower paced thinking strategy with an added touch of cunning and skulduggery then this game might be for you.
The game does have it's positive points.  One of the more interesting aspects is the research tree.  The research tree is huge and it will take you many months to go through a sizable portion of it.  Careful research planning is vital if you want to survive in SK.  Another interesting aspect are monks.  If you don't like the direct frontal approach of fighting players monks give you a more subtle Machiavellian way of messing with enemy factions.
Despite it's problems I still enjoy playing this game and plan on playing in the near future.  I've had people ask me if they should try it.  My response is try it out for yourself.  You've got nothing to lose and everything to gain.

This is one of the best strategy games I've ever played. I only have 172 hours down. But that is like 1.5 playthroughs. The game is that dense. And it's challenging as all hell. Playing at a lower difficulty is, I assume, fun. But once you turn that difficulty notch up, ohhhhh boy; get ready for some fun.
It's maddenning. It'll keep you up til 3 am. It'll have you saying "just one more turn" for two or three hours. It's an incredible strategy game. It's not your 15 minute drop in PUBG accessibility to be sure. But once you start mastering all the nuances of the game, the turn based strategy and the frenetic pace of no-pause real-time combat, you'll realize you have a battle world where you can literally commit any strategic act you can imagine. And that's just the first few turns. By the end of a proper campaign play through your empire will expand over a continent or more, you'lll administer almost 100 cities, and you will have a dozen 1000-1500 man armies that are constantly conquering in your name. Every army will have a leader. You specialize your leaders in ways that truly matter. One of my favorite talents is "lightning strike" because it rewards me for outpositioning my opponent.
If you're more of a barbarian strategist, you can have 3 or 4 Carnosaurs consuming your enemries. You read that correctly. Dinosaurs. Eating your man-sized enemies. The Dark Elves take slaves which boosts your income. If you are a sadistic tacitician, a nice massive slave-holding can sustain a fantastic end-game conquering strategy. It's all up to you.
If this sounds like your type of game, you won't be disappointmented.

I never could have imagined that I would get so much raw enjoyment out of Downwell. Even after playing for just a few hours total, I would definitely go the extra mile to say that Downwell has one of the best kinds of ''Game Feel'' I have experienced thus far, where the mechanics of the game altogether work in harmony with each other.
Gameplay wise it draws inspiration from another popular rogue-lite platformer, Spelunky. Both in Downwell and Spelunky, you venture down into the perilous depths of the underground world, collecting valuables, finding power-ups and upgrades and defeating all sorts of critters and creatures along the way. But what differentiates Downwell from Spelunky, is that Downwell focuses more on the combat aspect, both enemy and player wise, where enemies left undefeated pose an actual challenge for the player later on, which encourages players to defeated as many enemies as effeciently as they can, so that later on they have more practical experience on each levels unique enemy types and have more gems to buy health and upgrades from shops located in set levels.
When it comes to the presentation, Downwell excels on all aspects in my honest opinion. The game has a very clean and charming pixel artstyle with high contrasting colors helping everything pop from the levels. The game also sports a  chiptune soundtrack that is very pleasing to listen to whils't playing, because the tracks also help to create the proper atmosphere for each stage. The sound design makes every action, from shooting your gunboots to simply jumping on enemies and collecting gems, feel incredibly satisfying and rewarding.
TL;DR: Just buy it. Its dirt cheap, fun as heck and the quintessential ''pick up and play'' rogue-lite on Steam.

Huge amount of content, this is incredible for an early access game (I've got it as soon as it was released, but the game works perfectly well already). Scenery and elements are very diversified. You can find all sorts of animals, vehicles, buildings, tools, toys...
The procedurally generated worlds are big, beautiful, varied (many biomes, climates, terrains, ..) and really feel like Lego bricks. With some vehicles and animals, you can fly (e.g. the eagle, the plane or the dragon!). You can swim, there are boats and submarines, ... This is a paradise for explorers. My daughter explores and uses predefined buildings and vehicles. I've played a bit more with the brick-by-brick way to build things, (but she doesn't let me play often with the game because she wants to play it all the time herself).
The stability of the game is perfect. No bug at all (no crash, no clipping, no weird thing happening, everything behaves as you'd expect). I'm amazed that this early access game is more stable than most games that have been released for years.
The editor is one of the best I've seen so far, though the camera is not optimal yet : Brick-by-brick building is really easy to use, tools (for larger terrain changes) slightly less so but still very handy.
Minor defaults, list of small things to fix:
When typing the name of the world at the beginning of the game, it assumes I'm using an English (QWERTY) keyboard and I'm using a French one (AZERTY) which can be mildly confusing
Vehicles get stuck easily. Once stuck, you've got to use tools to delete or smooth out parts of the terrain to get your vehicle out of trees and cracks of the terrain.
Submarines should be able to dive (and swimmers too): the left ctrl key should let you go underwater (like with a descent of the plane). At the moment, submarines are like boats with a different look.
When building something brick-by-brick, the camera doesn't help. You should have a better (full) control of the camera rotation and movements. Sometimes the camera falls under the ground, most of the time the camera adjusts itself in a less-than-helpful location...
All in all it's already a great game and it has the potential to become an incredible game... Keep up the great work!

I've played this game for more than the 7.3 hours that it says I have. And everybody is saying "Oh it's amazing!" and yes, yes it is, but in it's current state it's lacking a main objective, yes you can build but there's only a few types of brick in the game currently. So I'm going to voice my suggested improvements, the pros and cons. Not in that order.
Pros:
Amazing Graphics, like seriously the game looks incredible for an Early Access
Brilliant controls, it's just like playing a LEGO game in a sandbox.
Great exploration, exploring is fun and enjoyable, but can get tedious since that's all there is to the game apart from building at this moment.
Lovely building, there's no shortage of colors and all things considered the building mechanic is good.
Child Friendly, surprise surprise, a LEGO game is child-friendly, what I mean is that it's a game marketed at Children, with grown up appeal, such as the building possibilities, but the children can have hours of fun riding dragons, blowing stuff up and driving around, even jumping is super fun, just doing parkour and all that, you can climb any surface.
Cons:
The game lacks an objective, like it's too sandboxy, which is good but there's not much aside from exploring and building.
Lack of variety, as I mentioned earlier there's a lack of types of brick, I mean they're likely to be added later, cause most bricks 'are' in the game, but you can't place them except for the props. Like you've got the plate pieces, the block pieces,  and the ramp pieces, but none of the bottle, stick, cylinder, arch or stud pieces.
When building, the minifigure you play as has a knack for putting his big building gun in the way.
Lack of use for the currency, this will probably change, but right now the only use the in-game currency has is for buying the stuff you find so you can spawn it anywhere, but they're one-time payments.
Suggestions:
More brick types
A Survival themed mode, where you mine bricks and use them to make stuff, but no hunger bars.
More features in terrain generation, right now most terrain is a bit bland aside from props but still detailed.
Maybe some optional physics? So things crumble, I don't blame them for not adding this in.
Vehicle-building, this is a fairly desirable feature for LEGO enthusiasts.
Themes that should be added: Star Wars, Space (The old one), Atlantic, LEGO CITY, Haunted (The old LEGO horror brand thingy), Pirates and Cowboys.
Which should be optional in the generation, so you can make that perfectly generated world.
More may come soon.
Final rating: 7/10 for current product. 10/10 for Early Access product, I play a few Early Access games, few of this are this promising from the getgo, so goget this game now and watch it grow and your inner child return.
Parents, get this game for your LEGO loving child and they'll love you. It's a steal at this price.

(Review from 6th December) Well, it's no secret that No Man's Sky let down countless people around the globe on release. People expected much more content and expected to be able to find each other in-game (aka: multiplayer) and eventually most quit and gave very low reviews. We all know all of that already so no point going into the details.
Anyway, the devs recently released The Foundation Update. Adding much needed content like: better inventory management, base building, and much more (for free, of course, as they should have). They added that the update was also "... a foundation for things to come." This leads me to believe that the devs are aware of their mistakes and are hard at work to rectify them.
I'm playing the game post-update and it does seem relatively okay. I think it doesn't yet justify its price, but you could wait for a discount. i bought it on a 40% discount so i guess it's acceptable. I'll keep playing to see how much it could keep me going before it gets boring. If they keep it up and release more free content, I believe this game could really be worth a second look and could get its players back.
As long as i see that the devs are doing what needs to be done, I'm actually gonna give this game a positive review.
Let this review be a foundation for things to come!
(Edit from 23rd August) As of the recent update, it seems like the devs really are making up for the sloppy release. Countless improvements and additions have already been implemented, improving the general gameplay and atmosphere of the game. Multiplayer is finally starting to come together. It's very limited at the moment, but the improvements these guys are making for the game are not to be taken lightly! This is becoming the game we all hoped it would be! This game is no longer a joke! The devs aren't just in it for the money grab! Get this game!

Okay so I played this game while it was a free weekend and I played it again...IT'S COOL! :D
Why? I'll tell ya:
1) I know most people would assume that the reason why other people play this because it has boobs, well...touche. However that's not really the case... I guess. The art style I really like and the design of the game is really anime inspired, the kind I like to see in other art...things.
2) The gameplay is pretty good its the standerd fighting game controls. But if you play this on a PC I recommend you get an arcade stick with a USB plug you can plug into your computer because the controls will be confusing and difficult as hell when it comes to combos. It will make your hands sore if you don't have a joystick.
3) The tutorial needs work too, it dosn't really address to keyboard controls for those who don't have a joystick or can't afford one. But it still provides information on how to move around and how to fight in some aspects.
4) The character designs are pretty cool too along with their stories. I loved the looks of these characters, my personal favs to me are Valentine, Ms.Fortune, Painwheel, Cerebella, & Filia.
5) Some other problems in the game are here and there but nothing too serious and to be honest I'm not one to have gamer expearence so I'm not sure what problems are worth addressing here since their not too seirous.
6) The music is pretty good too. The music in the game is composed by Michiru Yamane who did the score for the Castlevania games. So if you ever played the Castlevania games and admire her music in the games then you should check this game's score out yourselves, 28 tracks and pretty good ones too.
7) Online mode is another fun aspect of the game, like any other fighting games like Street Fighter or Marvel vs Capcome, it has sessions from other players you can join or you can create your on session to fight other players and go into Spectate mode when it's not your turn to fight yet.
So that's all the things I can cover up for you. If you are a fan of fighting games and ones with style and replayability then this is the game for you. And if you want to support this game go join the Indiegogo project here:

The open world and the RvR meta-game is where Naval Action leaves little middle ground between love and hate. Personally, I like playing in a clan and dabbling in grand strategy, but I get my main kicks out of ship combat. As such, the major mechanics and balancing shifts that took place on the strategic, RvR level do not tick me off as much as they understandably did some players who are in it for the strategic conquest before anything else.
Thus buyers will need to beware that the game is in Alpha, and therefore the center of balance is still shifiting around (particularly on the strategiclevel). Rather, meaning I have to re-think standard recipes every now and again keeps me on my toes.

I've played the game a couple hours. Here are my thoughts:
Eye of the Vortex Campaign: It's dramatic. The legendary lords feel truly epic, and you get a real sense of their powerful personalities in the world. From the brotherhood of Teclis and Tyrion, to Mazdamundi's sequenced striving, the world and theme-building is top notch. The Lizardmen tech trees and name locations feel epic, and borrow on the mystery of the Mayan and Aztec systems in the best of ways.
Like anything, the modding community adds some really refreshing value to what's already existing in the vanilla game. They compliment each other very well, and getting into Warhammer 2 really shines when both the developed game and the game community are taken together. There are many great TW youtubers out there who really enhance the game experience, and CA seems to truly recognize and honor that.
Constructive criticsm of the game world: I feel that the inclusion of the Lizardmen and High elves added some much needed light. Each faction has its positive and negative aspects, but balance isn't always achieved. Sometimes the dark is so dark that it doesn't have anything to contrast itself with, which leads to staleness. This game strikes the balance fairly well, with no race being completely good or completely bad. Even the Skaven make up for their evil with humorous battlefield conversations.
It fails in others. Some characters are so evil that the idea that there'd be any sustainable elements is completely impossible. Even Gengis Khan was reveared perhaps as much as he was feared.
I encourage the game developers to look to add more positive elements, such as reforming the Dilemma system of the Treasure Hunting. It didn't feel so much like Treasure Hunting as it did "don't accidentally choose wrong". Some choices that sounded interesting, like "Follow the mysterious stranger", ended up quite literally in a dead end. What could have felt inspiring felt deflating, instead.
Also, the AI cheats. It diminishes the player's struggle to manage armies and economy, when an AI power can pump out 8 armies and rule the landscape with little or no hinderance. Checking the savegames in save parser reveals that some factions can have a massive standing army with a turn income of -99999, which would be impossible for the player to emulate. So as a player it feels like you're playing with special rules the other races don't have to follow, which seriously diminishes the reason to struggle.
CA's Total War is a great place to be in gaming. I'm proud of the game, and honorably recommend it to anyone looking to experience a new love. It's a sincerely great movement in the right direction, and I pray that in the 3rd game, we see an equally balanced presentation of light and dark, positive and negative. It gets right a lot. My inner child -- who collected the figures and hung out in Games Workshop stores -- feels pleased.
Best wishes, and Happy Holidays.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a subtle, beautiful, dark, compelling, and funny adventure. With gorgeous artwork and soundscapes, witty modern language, a meta sensibility, and a fantastic lunar cycle mechanic, I can't stop thinking about this game.

Three years ago, I wrote a joke review for this game just saying "Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is an indie game", with the joke being that it looked like the samey pixellated trash that was flooding the indie scene at the time. But now I actually got around to playing it, and I've found that it's actually exactly what I expected it to be.
You don't really do much in this game. Your goal in each area is to find the sprites "hidden" in the area, though they aren't particularly difficult to find. Then you do a quick "puzzle" ranging from things like sliding ducks to their mother to engaging in trial-and-error to find the correct sequence of clicking on trees. You do this a few times and then occasionally fight a boss that plays out kind of like the first Ganondorf fight from Ocarina of Time, where you deflect a missile attack back and forth until it hits it. You meet two characters along your journey and you can see their thoughts, along with your own, in the megatome (a magic book that you find early on), and they're interesting enough to not make you feel like you wasted time reading them but they rarely go beyond that level. The game disagrees, of course, and even if you tell it that you don't want to participate in its twitter functionality early on it's still going to put a tweet button beside every line of dialogue and constantly remind you that social media is going to play an important role in the game (spoilers: it doesn't, at least as far as I could tell).
If the controls were changed at all from the iOS version beyond letting you use your mouse, I couldn't tell. Almost everything is done by clicking and holding, or clicking and holding and sliding, and other things you would expect from a touch screen game. I didn't think it was possible to make a simple point-and-click interface unintuitive, but they've proved me wrong. You can move by either double clicking the area you want to move to or holding and sliding, but holding and sliding produces a constant humming sound that goes against the music, which is presumably the whole point of the game. The music is admittedly good, particularly one part where you can listen to the composer play the guitar while clicking on things in the environment to make your own rhythm alongside him, but a significant portion of it seemed to just be ambiance. It set the scene well, but it isn't something that I'd want to listen to outside of the game, though I'm not sure if that was the point or not.
So in the end, my review 3 years ago was probably better left unchanged anyways. In the time it took you to read all this you could've done something else that takes a minute or two to do, and you still probably wouldn't have touched this game either way for $8. Maybe we'd all be better off if I had never returned to Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP after all these years.

I'm really intrigued by what I just played. Sword & Sworcery is a strange mix of funny self-awareness as a game and art project; pretty pixel landscapes and nice soundtrack; all mixed in a plot that goes from the super-serious to the super-casual in waves. The game is never out-right comedic, but you can tell from screen to screen where you're supposed to relax and where you are supposed to be tense. What fascinates me is how even with its pixelated characters the game manages to make you feel stressed, afraid, rejoiced or frustrated as you go.
One of the game elements that is constant throughout the story is the lack of a expectations on what is possible and what not within the environment. I found myself unable to judge if I had any agency in this or that environment or situation, which in this game, is a good thing. You feel great when you realize that you CAN interact with this or that element, and once the creepy monster starts to chase you, this lack of understanding about where are the game-boundries makes you feel trapped and powerless as you desperately click everything on screen while moving away as you trying to figure out what to do next.
Granted, this lack of context did made me go for an online guide once I couldn't figure out how to wake up one or two of the Sprites. But overall, if you have enough curiosity and patience, you will get the hang of this strange little world without external help.
Another thing that I found really original about this game is how the difficulty raises as the story progesses. We're used to getting more health and power in other titles, allowing you to combat fiercer and bigger enemies as you go. But in Sword & Sworcery you get LESS health as the main character's well-being begins taking a toll on the quest, which makes formerly easy challenges suddenly stressful and difficult. This increase in vulnerability goes counter to the power-trip most other games makes you go through, and that alone, I found it to be really cool (as well as REALLY nerve-wrecking as I faced old enemies).
That being said, this is not a fighting game per se. Sure, the fights are the parts that require most eye-hand coordination and skill, but the puzzle solving and exploration take a similar toll in your brain. I found it very balanced how much emphasis it was put onto each part of the gameplay.
Oh, another thing I liked: At the end of each "chapter" the narrator takes you back to the main screen, telling you to take a break before continuing. I found this to be cool in terms of story-telling, and oddly considerate for you as a player. It made me wish more games would suggest that kind of pauses for their players.
So overall, this is a very strange, charming, deep, stressfull and rewarding game all at once. It's a bit short compared to other titles, but by the end, you'll be glad by every minute of it.

Game is designed around the 'hard counter' fetish. There's several layers of how units interact where something can be 'trumped' by several other units for different reasons, which *sounds* cool, except, when you build your deck and try to play a strategy, the swingyness of the luck overrides any decisions you make. Say you have a solid 3-minion combo that can be effective against anything--whether you get all those cards together at the right moment is luck of the draw. Placement makes another level of what seems like it should be skill, but in practice, just makes any internet interruption potentially defeat what you wanted to do. Thought you placed your units in the right spot at the right time? Nope. You had an internet hiccup, and your units appeared a fraction of a second later on the other guy's comp, and now your hard counter is dead before it gets to act.
It's not fun to explore the deck building process. It doesn't feel like there's a plan you can pursue that has its own integrity. When I play a good CCG, or a Starcraft Tug of War map, I like the feeling that I can see the way the early, mid, and late game play out, and how I have to balance snowballing against an early advantage.
I've watched people take me apart, and I've done that back to some people. But it feels like this is about who can counter, first. It tends to make for games where you sit and stare at each other for the first 20+ seconds of the game. Maybe if you *had* to pick an opening play or there was some kind of unit that was continuously spawning--that you got to pick, then it would be less a matter of figuring out how to drill down on the rock paper scissors and play that straight up.
There's reactive spells, but they mostly have delays which seems like a poorly considered antidote to the issues with lag. Somehow, the minion playing seems very time intensive, but the spell casting which should bridge that gap ends up showing up so late that it's far less attractive. There are many spells and minion effects which are random, which means it can unfairly win you or lose you the game.
Minion AI seems like hit or miss. Deck building seems to get me nowhere. I guess there's a 'right answer' that I'm not aware of.

EDITORS NOTE: This Review was oringally posted in janurary of 2016. The Review reflects the game and prices at this time and does not cover the 2v2 mode or any changes since that time. Since the time I wrote this review the price has also dropped,
Okay. So I played a fair amount must have done over 100 games and I feel I'm ready to write a review. So the game is pretty well designed it looks good and has been themed well each of the 'hero' units look pretty awesome. The issue comes from the route wheel.
To explain; The game has 3 currencies.
Coins - They are used to buy spins on a roulette wheel
Shards - Used to buy cards or champions
Candy(premium currency) - used to buy champions and arena skins.
Obviously having Free to play elements isn't a bad thing if the game is balanced in such a way that doesn't punish players for not paying out but this game isn't balanced that way.
Coin System Explained
to spin once on the wheel you need 1000 coins. Per a match you're looking at between 20-30 coins (each match lasts about 3 and a half minutes on average in my experience and getting into game about 1 minute. To make the maths easy Im rounding to 5m / match.
Okay so here is the break down 1000 coins is about 28 games. 28*5 is 140 or about 2 hours 20 minutes. Now this would be an acceptable amount of time to wait, for a 100% new card but; The game wheel has old cards. old cards give you 25 shards. and they also have shard squares (0-2) that give 50 shards.
Shards system and buying cards Explained
You can buy cards with shards. They have various prices but most cards that are good are 125+ with the extremely good ones being 2000. Given that you get 0 - 50 shards per a spin. lets just average it to 30 as the 25 shards in my experience are more likely than a new card or a shard. so you're gonna need 5 spins to get a decent new card at 125 cost and if you want 2000 cost cards you're in for a huge grind
Candy system explained
Candy is the premium currency of the game costing real world money;
325 Candy costs $2,
750 candy costs $4,
1650 costs $7
3350 costs $14
This candy can be used for 2 things one of them is buying spins which cost 160 candy for 2 spins or 725 candy for 10 spins.
The other thing is unlocking new hero units. there are 6 in the game and they can also be purchased for shards.
To put this in perspective. you can pay $4 to gain what is equal to 23 hours of play time. So it's a Pay to win game rather than a pay for a slight boon. This is unacceptable as it gives a huge advantage to the people willing to put in just a few dollars. think about this. You have 2 people. one has $14 one who doesn't the one who does gets 3350 candy and spins it all giving them 44 spins or about 4 days worth of game time over the other user. Despite these two users getting the game at the same time the user not paying the small money is at a large dis advantage.
Gameplay
Going onto the game play its self. Its pretty fun. It's like a more tactical version of hearthstone or other card based games.  While those games are slower the tactical nuance of this game is in the timing. choosing when to play or wait to get more mana. This leads to experimental deck play where you build to counter certain styles of play. such as swarm users being countered by area attackers. flyers being shot by range ECT. This is a good and fun core gameplay concept
Over all Balance
This is why it disappoints me that overall the game is poorly balanced. There are certain cards that are just much stronger than other cards. there is a huge guy called colossus. big and slow attackers. This type of card is normally countered by a swarm style card as it attacks slowly But unlike most big slow attacks with massive damage but slow attacks. this guy hits in a frontal cone.  this means that the swarm is dispersed in one shot. Is there counter play? Yes. There are 3 ways to counter this big guy. the first is to CC them with a stunner and the game provides you with a base stunner... but the base stunners have Very low hp and there is multiple ways to kill them to free up the big guy again. from area ranged attacks coming up behind to get rid of the melee to flyers doing the same. the spell fireball or beam of doom or even having the archer as your hero unit (as his shots target the closest thing and getting rid of the big guy takes a lot of focus) and you can even send healers behind to keep the big guy healthy.
So I said there was 3 ways. the other is a ranged flyer attacker, this gets rid of the area stopping them as that's normally ground based (with 1 exception) but the other ways stop it.
This brings us to our second over powered card Ghost.
Ghost costs 3 points and takes control of an enemy unit. given this guy costs 9 there is a low chance of having guys instantly behind him so... you use ghost and boom the titan is now your titan.
Ghost is another over powered card. it takes control of enemy units and costs 4. This wouldn't be so bad but one of the 6 hero units in the game summons as his 1st and 3rd ability big units. and yes even though they only get one and its meant to be this guys primary power. for a 4 cost you can turn him boss unit against your foes.
Both ghost and colossus cost 2000 shards to buy so, though I make it sound simple; put these cards in your deck) unless your either lucky or have spent money on it. this is a very card process to do.
Now there is a reward system along side just playing. which is given upon reaching a certain rank and leveling up  which gives a fair boon towards gaining a spin (as normally it does give 1000) and combined with the steam buy price the leveling up candy can help you unlock every champion to try different play styles.  these systems are good but they do not offset the great power of buying. as I continued playing I found a lot of cards was stronger than the others to the point of you should just have them. there are other cards I haven't mentioned by name that are just generally strong.
Overall I would rate this game a 3/10 It has a good Strong core concept that is a pretty fun to play experience by the fee to pay elements and the pay to win experience within the game tilt the game to the point where it feels less like skill and more like being lucky. If you're looking for a cute quirky card game I recommend waiting till this game goes full free to play where then you might be able to get some enjoyment out of it. but in its current state I cannot recommend this game to anyone who isn't willing to put extraordinary amounts of time into a game or spend more than the asking price to get artificially boosted to the point they can match players.

This game is barely alpha. It's a bad knockoff of Pirates of the Burning Sea.
The interface is barley above a DOS level program and lacks even rudimentary functions to get you started. Combat is an exercise in frustration as NPC's are lethal while you can barely hit the broad side of a barn.
Can this game be more enjoyable? Certainly, but not without a ridiculously steep learning curve that discourages anyone but a masochist from playing it.
All it is, is a wooden ship combat simulator, and not a very good one at that.
I accept that its in alpha test and it just embryonic right now, but there's no excuse for basic gameplay functions to be absent, like a working map function or a proper ship description. I am constantly told by the rather limited population that I will learn in time.
Sorry, but if a game is not enjoyable from the get-go, it smacks of a failed attempt at cloning a far better version of another  put out years ago for the sake of capturing dollars. Lack of a finished game is one thing along with bugs, but an unenjoyable alpha is hot mess.
I will continue to test the game and explore its limited gameplay value and change this review if the game changes as time goes by, but for now, avoid dropping retail money on a barely finished product. I'm sure I'm going to be roundly lambasted for this by the 50 or so people playing it.. so be it.
UPDATE : Ok, I've now invested more hours in the game and I'm to at able least kill things and keep from getting killed all the time.
That's something.
But bottom line, the game is little more than a combat simulator, having no strategic or true MMO flavor to it-- its just mindless killing or getting killed and scraping up enough materials to build your fleet.
Hardly worth the time you have to invest in it , to get good.
A fresh interface instead of something out of the DOS era, and some true tools for players to interact and customize themselves would help enormously. Also a decent starting tutorial game which provides some immersion is needed before I could recommend this game to others for forty bucks.

*Down, Down, Down*
This game is incredibly well designed! I genuinely felt like everything I did was my fault, every little bit of damage and messing up combos. It helped train my reflexes.
To start, you'll notice the fact that there's no story. Sorta. You jump down a well, fighting frogs and turtles, bats and worms, demonic space monsters and snails. The usual. Then, suddenly, the area begins to change, and now you're fighting skulls and ghosts. Beware Child! There's bony people skeletons everywhere! Scary, right?
The upgrades are rather varied, and you will find a playstyle that suits you- for me, it was to just to go a full gem build, collect as many gems as possible and buy my way to the end. Luckily, there's an upgrade that makes it so shops appear at the start of every area, making this a valid strategy.
As you continue on, dying and dying again, you'll begin unlocking new colours and characters, and soon you'll unlock a character that will easily trump every other one. For me, it's 'boulder style', which gives you +2 max health but lowers your upgrade choice by 1. As you always got 3 upgrades to choose from, reducing it to 2 helped a lot in giving me less choice, which ironically made choice easier.
There's always a flaw, though; for me, it's the fact the final boss feels... easy. at least, on Normal Mode. On Hard Mode, You'll NEVER get to him to find out. I literally beat him 5 minutes ago, and it took me 5 minutes to beat him. I also found that getting to the final boss was easier than the area before it. Maybe that was the design choice? Who knows. To be a fly on the wall at Devolver Digital.
Now, as is life, my opinion may not sway you. I really don't mind- it's your choice! However, for it's current price, I got my fun out of it within the first hour, so if a nice time waster is something you're looking for, I heartily recommend it. The achievements are balanced and possible, the colour palettes are fun to try and unlock, and the characters are willing to do anything they can to get you to use them. Overall, it's another awesome game from an awesome company!

This game is a brilliant game to sit down and play after a long day at work or school. You really feel like you are a Medival Lord ruling over your personal empire and helping your fellow players along the way. The game has a brilliant community feel to it, and it would be great to play with your friends. You could work together, help eachother and fight together.
Here is a small summary of a few of the main game features:
Your Village: When you spawn into the game for the first time you aquire your first village, this can be customized to your liking. Your villages can be captured and taken over by other players and you can add you your village total by capturing other villages.
Your Castle: When you spawn into the game you have no castle, and you must build yourself one using stone or wood. This is your defence and without a good castle you will not be succesful.
Trading: You can trade with Parishes, Counties, Provinces and Countries for gold. You can also trade with other players and give them some assistance.
Attacking: When attacking you can Vandalise, Pillage, Ransack, Raze and Capture. When sending a attack on a player, you will lose some honour, however when attacking a AI castle (Wolf Lairs, Bandits Camp and Castles) you gain honour for each opponent you kill.
Scouting: When scouting you can scout resources from the map and scout other players villages to learn there defences.
Monking: Monks can be used to change the game and are probably your houses strongest and most effective weapon. They can be used to protect your villages, monk players into Parishes and much more.
Research: Research is the most important part of the game. You may research new technologies or improve other ones by using the Research Points you gain by ranking up.

Listen, honestly. Before the update, I had a decent amount of fun with the game because of it being this awesome new space-exploration & survival game. Fast forward 4 months later, they released the Foundation Update (1.1) and it honestly filled a lot of what I thought was empty about the game. The planets look more varied, you'd find some barren planets and then you'd find some beautiful lush planets (Some of the barren planets are very pretty though, mind you.) The biggest new addition in my opinion has to be the base building. I'm personally not very creative when it comes to base building, however, the building mechanics are REALLY simple and easy to use. The resources you mainly need to build is Iron, and that's abundunt in space asteroids and on most planets. I've been playing this update for around 10 hours now and I'm still having so much discovering new things and upgrading my base.
Lastly, the three new modes introduced are Normal, Survival, and Creative. NMS has defintely upped the difficulty of the game and my first experience was in Survival, and man oh man, let me tell you. In Survival, they start you about a 10 minute walk away from your ship and you have to repair it AND make your way towards it and it's just hell. I died around 8 times trying to get there and once I got there, I felt so rewarded to finally get off my radiation filled planet. There's other features of Survival that make it super difficult, but you should play the game and find out for yourself.
I can honestly say this game is starting to finally shape itself into the game I wanted it to be originally (Excuse the name pun) and hopefully they don't leave us in the dirt for 4 months again and THEN release an update. I want Sean Murray and Hello Games to communicate with us and make this game what it was meant to be.
TL;DR: Game is much harder and base building is just great, three new modes (Normal, Survival, and Creative) were introduced and they're fantastic. Sean and Hello Games are finally starting to make this game to what people wanted it to be. If you don't already own the game, I wouldn't suggest buying it JUST YET (If you have the money, go for it) Just wait a little til more updates get released and see if you can trust them again.

General overview of the game from my perspective and experience.
I'll focus only on foundation update.
The foundation update gave us two new difficulties. Survival, which is the most important one. And Creative, which is kind of useless in my view.
Survival difficulty gave the game a new edge, it makes it really hard
, especially if you spawn on the cold or toxic planet. And you have to use all kinds of tactics to get from one place to another. All the elements except the iron and carbon became rare. Your ship takes 100% thruster fuel per launch and pirates spawn a lot and do a lot more damage than before. And all that made a game even bigger grind than it was before. Your shields and pulse engines both use iron now thus you have to fill your inventory with it all the time. The difficulty of the first planet is really fun and challenging, that is, until you gather all the required stuff to make your first take off.
After you make your first take off, you're back to the same ol' grind that the game was in previous patch without almost any change except scarcer resources. The only difference is that most of the planets you'll visit are in some way hostile.
I replayed the start on both hot and toxic planets because I found that initial beginning very fun. After realizing that it's the same thing after gathering enough things to leave the first planet I just deleted my Survival save and started a new one which put me on a hot planet.
To make things worse, quests are basically a must do, because without some of the tech from quests you can't mine certain resources and/or collect some others.
Base building is just a complete barebones right now. You can make some buildings that mostly require iron to be made. You get to make some basic domes and a way to connect them. Inside you put some terminals and get some NPC's from the space station to work in your base. Then you do some basic half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quests for them to unlock some new tech - which is mostly useless and only made to make you grind more resources for different quest givers.
So far the base building is complete barebones and nothing worth noting as of yet.
In a game such as this, base building is pretty much the last thing we need, since after all, the point of the game is to
. And the problem of outposts and buildings everywhere is still present, and it kills the point of exploration when everything is already explored.
Now you can land on freighters and purchase them. Only to be able to summon them in any system you're in, so you can put your resources in them. They're basically just big boxes for storing resources. And they just sit where you spawn them and never move from that place in a certain system. They said that a player will be able to purchase and fly a freighter, but at the moment that is still not in place.
Our own spaceship still lacks a ton of things. They all act the same, the spaceship controls are still pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and completely unchallenging thus fighting pirates in Survival every few pulse jumps just becomes a chore after few attacks.
Ships still can't have their cargo slots expanded, so you have to change and upgrade your ship all over again if you want to increase the amount of slots it has.
You still can't rename them, you still can't change their color.
The game is still as beautiful as it was before, planets look very cool for the most of the part and you can get some very nice and amazing screenshots and views.
You can even check some of my screens to see what I'm talking about.
Basically, the game is beautiful, most of the effects are very nicely done.
- Survival is awesome on the starter planet.
- After the inital few hours in Survival, the game loses it's challenge and is back to the same old thing, and it will bore you fast.
- If you were bored of the initial game, this will only give you a few more hours of fun.
- Base building is at the moment useless.
- Freighters serve no real purpose.
- Still missing a lot of promised features, and instead of adding some of them, they added two
features out of the three new ones.
- Quests are okay, but they're just
- Quests are forced on a player.
- Spaceships still can't have cargo hold upgraded nor their name changed.
- It's pretty much still a 60 euro screenshot/scenery generator.
- So far, I still can't recommend the game.
- This is a step in the right direction, it means that they haven't stopped working on this game and I give them that as a big plus and hopefully they'll be adding more new features every few months.
- Hopefully, those features will actually have a real purpose unlike most of these that were added now.

Let me say that while I don't feel as if I'd recommend this game, I'm not claiming it was a wholly unenjoyable experience. It just might not be what a lot of people are looking for, and the number of positive reviews are a bit misleading.
Positive:
-Some well-crafted storytelling, I'll admit.
-Good worldbuilding, some clever ideas.
-Positive representation of autistic characters, not a lot of misinformation that stood out to me that might have ruined that.
Negative:
-Short.
-While the story is inventive, it is also linear, and I hesitate to call To the Moon an "interactive storybook" at all, but that's the best description I can think of because it kind of falls short of being a game.
-Moving around is a chore. The characters are often slow, and you inexplicably bump into things on the map sometimes that are arbitrarily solid. (You can walk through cars, but not over flowers? Really?)
-Puzzles are simple and boring. Does not feel like much at stake. They don't really add much to the story by being there other than giving the player something active to do.
-Gameplay mostly consists of walking around and clicking things until you click on something "important." Click on enough important things and you can unlock the simple tile puzzle and move on to the next memory. There's nothing really fun about it.
-On that note it would have made sense for the game to be more passive. The components that were there seemingly just to make it "like a game" felt out of place.
-IF YOU USE THE INTENDED CONTROLS (the mouse) YOU'RE GONNA HAVE A BAD TIME. You click somewhere for the characters to go somewhere, but they often don't quite reach entirely, maybe because of an obstacle, and so it feels like the characters are never going where you want them to go. Getting to objects is exhausting. When I discovered you could use the traditional arrow keys to move and the space to interact it was a life saver.
-Too much dialogue, I hate to say. Wayyy too much bickering between the protagonists bogs down the whole game. Way too much melodramatic prosey monologuing at times, too, taking away from the impact of actually beautiful and important dialogue. Just too much. It's clumsy. You spend much of the game inundated in wooords.
-What's worse is the characterization is weak at best. Most of the characters don't have much in the way of personality, which you kind of expect from this kind of game especially if it's supposed to be carried by character interactions.
-A lot of it... was not funny. When it was trying to be funny. A lot of inward groans to be had at the unnecessary snark. (There were funny parts to be had, definitely. Most of the annoying stuff was in the dialogue between Watts and Rosalene, who as I already said, spend way too much time bickering.)
-This is a bit of a personal nitpick, but I wish, if they were going to make a game about asperger's, that they might just name it outright. I don't understand why everyone was so cagey and vague about River's "condition," it struck me as unnecessary.
Verdict: If you are going to get it, get it on sale. Then stick it out past Act 2, because that's where the story starts picking up and you don't have to put up with the puzzles and junk. Don't approach it expecting much in the way of a game, or much in the way of replay value. It's a decent story, not decent enough for me to wholly recommend the experience, but not bad enough for me to say there was nothing worthwhile about it, either.

Pretty much everything you read about this game is true, both good and bad, but it most certainly does not deserve all the negative reviews that dominate the top of board, at least one of them written by someone who still plays the game. Go figure.
This game is in early access. It is not finished and some things you might take for granted - such as a tutorial - simply don't exist. The players (some of them) are helpful enough but it takes ages to talk through - or write in chat - all the game mechanics you will encounter in your first few minutes playing. If you are thinking of buying this game, do read forums, game guides, check out youtube and so on to find at least the basics of how to play so you don't entirely swamp Help chat with questions when you start.
The devs and chat and forum moderators are ... erratic. Sometimes it seems like Geppetto has carved this beautiful game, but he grew old, tired, blind or something and left it to his wayward apprentices to finish. There must have been some great vision to have got this far, but until recently it seemed to have been lost with a history of abandoned trials (which players predicted would fail, and they did) finishing up with three grand announcements about a server wipe, allocating crafting resources to the 25 Port Battle winning participants, and merging the PvE and PvP servers. The server wipe was widely accepted as a good idea and is planned for 20th April 2017, and I think it is to the dev's great credit that the other two ideas have been withdrawn. The PvE server will now stay for at least 18 months after release, followed by a review (and quite honestly I will be surprised if release is in 2017 - I think there's quite a lot of life left in PvE, but your guess is as good as mine).
On technical points the devs actually seem very good at listening (despite what you might read), but they are sometimes poor at communicating and they appear to have a total blind spot when it comes to humour, particularly it seems from American players (I think they don't pick up very well on American cultural references). If you post anything funny that could possibly be misconstrued as an accusation (against them or a fellow player - it doesn't matter) you can expect a week's forum ban. They are very heavy handed.
The playerbase is also sometime overly aggressive, misogynistic and unsympathetic to people who like to play in a different manner from them. But this is an MMO so it goes with the territory, I'm afraid. However this is almost certainly the best age of sail game you have ever played so if the only thing putting you off is that it is an MMO with all that entails, perhaps the PvE server might be for you. People are polite there; there is no aggression - literally at the moment: no other player can ever attack you and right now AI ships won't attack you either (but you can attack them). This will probably change so there is some form of AI aggression (this is an early access game so things change - I really cannot repeat this enough), but either way it opens the possibility for playing the game like a sailing sim, roleplaying or whatever takes your fancy, things you cannot usually do in a combat-orientated MMO.
Personally, crafting is my thing so I play on a PvP server, where there is real demand as well as risk. The crafting system isn't yet sorted so - as with so many other bits of the game - don't come here with too high expectations, but the 20th April server wipe will bring changes which look good from here. I look forward to finding out.
Finally, if you are reading this before 20th April, don't think you need to put off buying the game till after then. Start before and you'll keep your combat and crafting xp and be given 4 free ships after the wipe. Come on in, the water's lovely.

Arguably the best Total War I have ever played. Is a stark competitor with some of the best like Rome and Shogun 2.
Granted a bit more complicated to deal with than the past historical titles, this is also THE MOST intuitive Total War in terms of tool tips and gameplay basics. So much information has been readily made for the player's access than in past Total Wars.
Each faction plays differently in both the Multiplayer and the Campaign with all having their unique faction mechanics that will affect how you play on the campaign map on the battle map.
I've always had my gripes and so has the rest of the community  on the topic of lords, generals, and heroes. This game addresses that and also makes them one of the most exciting things in the campaign. Specializing your agents to your playstyle is now as easy as it's ever been. Agents that mostly specialize in sabotaging enemy armies that will most often stay on the campaign map, to Casters and Nobles that will join you and you armies onto the battle map to buff your troop with spells and abilities or debuff your opponents. That's also not to mention the powerful magic that can be used to wipe out vast swaths of your enemies on the field in fiery brilliance.
If you are a fan of Total War: Get this game.
If you're new to the series: It certainly is a decent jump off point though I would reccommend a historical title like Shogun 2 or Rome 2 first, to whet your taste for the concept of Real Time Strategy the Total War way. You can get those at a fairly decent price these days with some of CA's deep discounts.
Be wary though. For someone who has played these Total War games for years, I only caution you on the use of CA's DLC strategies. They are often exploitative. I'd wait till those go on sale for deciding to purchase them. As I did for the Wood Elves and Beastmen factions.
