As a long time Warhammer Fantasy fanboy this game is everything I could have asked for. Overall and TLDR it is a all around great game. If you like Total War games or even if you thought they were just okay in the past, you need to pick up this game. The High Fantasy aspect of the army rosters adds an element to the game that is just not present in any other total war game.
PROS
-The singleplayer campaign has enough playablity to make it worth buying the game alone.
-The campaign management is easy to learn with a great tutorial system but not so easy that it doesn't feel unsatisfying.
-The combat UI is easy to navigate and control.
-Tons of High Fantasy races with their own unique army lists.
-The armies are true to lore and cannon of the Warhammer universe.
CONS
-STOP calling the Mortal Empires campaign free content. One of the biggest selling points of the game was the fact Total War Warhammer 1, 2, and 3 were going to be a trilogy that slowly encorporating all the best aspects of the previous game including all it's content you previously bought. Calling the Mortal Empires campaign free content is like calling the sauce free with an order of McNuggets. It's why we bought the nuggets we knew we were going to get the sauce with it.
-The Huge initial investment of $60 USD for each game and the roughly $10 USD per race DLC's makes this a hard game to just pick up. (Kind of like the tabletop) if you find it on sale somewhere though, it's worth it.
-The Auto-resolved battles don't put enough emphasis on unit type when determining who wins. If I take 18 units of low-tier spearmen (An anti-calvary unit) the AI with 18 units of low-tier Calvary will win since it puts more emphasis on the calvary as an individual unit and not taking into account that the spears are a direct counter with a bonus vs. that unit type even though the spears have lower stats.
If you're a fan of strategy, his game is not to be taken lightly. It offers a wide range of choices that impact your course of action at every turn. The sheer depth of this game is astounding.

Though a bit more taxing on computers than the original, Warhammer 2 comes with clear graphical improvements, some quality of life improvements, and an overall better experience.
The vortex campaign, exclusive to the Warhammer 2 experience is one of CA's best designed Total War campaigns to date with a very clear overall objective. The geographically based power struggle between non Lothern factions is tense, and the shift away from a land domination campaign is a fresh addition. There are some gripes with the multiplayer campaign, specifically with "Intervention armies" that can be sent to give your buddy a terrible day, but other than that, it is well tuned and engaging.
The mortal empires campaign on the other hand I would hold off on for the time being. Many of the old races have not caught up to snuff with the newer ones in terms of gameplay mechanics and it will be some time before they are caught up.
The multiplayer scene, is in my opinion one of the main reasons for choosing Warhammer 2 over other games. With the addition of the Mortal Empires patch, all of the old world races are avaliable for play, and the game is in one of its best states of balance at high levels of play. Some factions are lagging behind of course, but there is nothing stopping you from picking up your favorite and doing well unless that's Bretonnia.
All in all, I would say
Vortex Campaign 8/10
Mortal Empires Campaign Old World Factions 5/10, New World Factions 8/10
Multiplayer Scene for Good Players 8.5/10, Average Players 7/10
Campaign would be a 9/10 if they allowed for more than 2 players in multiplayer campaigns.

First of all, I recommend this game only for people who are EXPERIENCED in playing time management and strategy games. I do not recommend this game for people who rarely play them or who aren't used to them. This game is way too challenging for my taste, but it may be appropriate for more skilled players. The impression the videos gave me was that the game was cute and easy going, up until war broke out among the neighboring tribes, but the needs between the villages are so demanding that I could not keep up. I was very over whelmed. I really admire how the tutorials eased you into the gameplay, but it didn't do a good enough job of preparing you for managing multiple things at once because once I got into the actual game, I felt thrown into disorder. The fewer number of villages you have, the easier it is. I tried to limit myself to only two villages, by not giving the requirements for them to spawn. However, regardless of this, they were still popping up! I had to run around maintaining four or five different villages, and I thought it would be easier than that but it just seemed to be too much.
The biggest thing that made this game so difficult to me is sort of an infinite cycle. Each village has a project it wants to be built that needs to be completed in a certain amount of time. In order to complete the project, the village needs so many resources (food, wealth, or tech). In order to increase the amount of resources, you have to spawn things like animals, herbs, plants, mines, ect that will yield the desired resource. However, to get enough resources, you need enough space within the village borders to spawn them. The villages will expand their territory automatically over time but after several different playthroughs, my villages expanded extremely slowly and in most cases, they just stopped all together and barely expanded. I simply had no more room to spawn anything else, therefore I couldn't get anymore resources than what I had. Even when I would with apply "upgrades" to make the items produce more resources, which are called attributes in the game, I still sometimes wouldn't meet the quota. So with insufficient resources, the time limit would run out, and I wasn't able to complete the projects the people wanted done. This was especially hard when I had four different tribes to tend to who all wanted projects completed. These demands and limitations really restricted gameplay. There's just a lot going on at once in this game that's hard to handle.

This game is basically Clash Royale with hero avatars, so a bit like Clash Royale meets HearthStone I guess. It plays a lot like Clash Royale but there are two bridges in the game you need to control, the longer you have them under your control the more exp you get which enables your hero to do get some skills. IMHO it's a vast improvement over the Clash Royale game because each hero you has a a distinct playstyle, this leads to a lot of varieities in decks you play against. One thing I don't like though is deck slots are locked till lvl 20, it's a pain to make decks or search for the card you want.
I find the business model to be both fair and a bit unsatisfying. On one hand you get a pack a day, there is dust to craft cards you need and there is a "free rotation" on heroes. On the other hand though, the "pack" is really just one card so buying power stones isn't that satisfying, once you have a decent collection good luck getting new cards as you will just get duplicates which will get dusted. I bought 10 power stones and got dust and a crappy card.  Another thing is you still need to buy heroes separately, of course you can also grind for it using freemium currency but this game isn't exactly free to play so why are we paying more stuff for heroes? If this is the business model then just make it F2P outright, they have a promotion giving out free steam keys for people following their newsletter which essentially makes this game free, but for the average Steam player who has no idea there's such a thing he'll be paying for the game, and then pay for it again in micro transactions. At least right now though paying $13 gives you the Premium upgrade for free so you're getting something for your money and players who didn't get a free steam key don't feel like they got ripped off.
Even with these gripes though the game is still pretty good and addicting, I find it to be much improved version of Clash Royale both in mechanics and business model. I highly recommend it.

Sometimes games aren't games, but a collection of systems.
What this means is that the game has its own internal logic, and the world acts acordingly. Chopping a lock door breaks it open. Electricity can spread through a pool of blood. Summoning an oil slick underneath a burning enemy ignites the oil and creates a pillar of black smoke that blocks line of sight.
Divinity: Original Sin has intellectually engaging turn-based RPG battles. The same fights can come out radically different due to how much the terrain can change with blood, lightning, poison, water, oil, and fire pouring unchecked throughout the battlefield. Coupled with great visuals, this game is always enjoyable to play, and because the systems are fair, it rarely feels frustrating. Character customization can go out into a fair number of directions, although several of my characters felt somewhat samey towards the end due to having a lot of spell overlap, but perhaps that was because I had a heavy magic-user party.
The biggest flaw is the first couple hours when you're running around a city investigating a murder. The game strays far from its strengths, with effectively no combat if you approach it in a rational manner. But after that is completed, the whole world opens up, and you can head out and explore and enjoy the excellent combat. The crafting system can feel tedious at times, as forging dozens of swords and selling them in bulk rarely feels engaging or heroic. The story will be hit or miss depending on your preferences. It can be rather light-hearted at times, which is dissapointing to those who prefer more serious storytelling. Personally, I enjoyed it for what it is, a fun break from the combat and exploration.
These are ultimately minor flaws though it what is one of the best computer roleplaying games of the past ten years. If you enjoy cRPG's, and if you enjoy combat that rewards creative solutions, pick this game up.

This is one of the best games I have played in quite some time. Not without it's minor flaws (more on that later) But all the same. I'll start by telling you what type of gamer I am. In the past, I haven't enjoyed rpg games such as Chrono shift or Final Fantasy. I did play Dragon Age: Origins and heavily enjoyed the world, characters, and story. But I never finished the game due to my distaste for the combat.
So let's start with the game's combat system. I won't go into detail about how it works, but the elemental system is incredibly satisfying to use. There is a lot of creativity to the combat due to this system. Whether that be throwing down pools of oil to keep melee attacker's away from your backline or something as roundabout as sending a spider that bleeds poison into a large group of enemies so that you can blow up it's carcass.
The storyline has been good. The main quest so far has been full of tropes but It has done this in a self-aware way, so it works well. For me the side quests have been the real meat of the narrative, sometimes even affecting the world in unique ways.
Multiplayer is great, I would still recommend it to a solo player, but this game feels like it was deigned for 2 friends. The individuality that comes from multiplayer is one of my favorite features of the game. We've started the game over 2 times due to having a poor party compisition. (I Reccomend making a melee warrior and a pyro / geomancy mage.)
And during these playthroughs we've been able to role play very well. On one of these playthroughs my friend was a rogue who would pickpocket everyone and steal anything that he could get his hands on. Meanwhile I was a charismatic people person who would sell them back their belongings.
The game does, unfortunately, have a few weaknesses however.
-Inventory managing is tedious, plus the game WILL NOT hold your hand for the crafting. I recommend using a guide.
-Some stats and abilities are, unfortunately, not worth getting. And along these lines the early game is pretty brutal, so if you've wasted stats then you will feel it when combat happens
-Some puzzles were made for two players and end up being quite tedious as a solo player. The banter between the two main charcters also doesn't work well when you get to choose both character's responses.
That's about all I can say about the game. I haven't beaten it yet but I feel I've gotten my monies worth and more from this excellent game. Bring on number two!

The developers have created a graphically beautiful world with complex combat mechanics that approach realistic big ship sailing and age of sail battle better than any I have seen. The potential is there for a rich player experience. However, one should realize before purchasing at this Early Access stage that it is currently more potential than reality. Don’t get me wrong: you can have a lot of fun playing Naval Action when in battle. However, most of the peaceful activities such as trading and crafting can be more of a drudgery than a joy. That could change though. THIS IS AN EARLY ACCESS GAME. That means that mechanics, rules, and even some basic paradigms of the game are changing. Many players don’t think they are changing fast enough. Others hate the changes and want things left as they were.
One of the biggest impediments right now is just low player population. As Naval Action gets closer to release or after release, hopefully the population will get higher. Many problems with the game are a direct result of not enough players around the world to make PVP action readily available, to fill player battles, and to truly test a player run economy.
If you’re the type of player who wants instant shooting action, this game will probably never be for you. If you are primarily interested in PVE play, it may never be for you as well since the developer’s stated priority is PVP play. While PVE is available right now, it is unclear how much development time it will get in the future to make it a richer experience. If you are the type of person that after dedicating time in a game which is in testing and development you’ll get all huffy when things change or when a wipe is necessary, you should probably wait until release. We’re testing here. However, if you are interested in this period of history and want to literally experience the fun and pain of a New World, you should give Naval Action a try.

Firstly, do not buy this game. I know it looks awesome, but it's not. Now lets get into the reasons why.
GAMEPLAY
I had originally been watching this game since before the open world was created. It looked incredible. I thought this was the game I had been dreaming about for ages. I bought it as soon as it became available on steam; however, life got in the way and I never really had a chance  to play it until half a year later.  At first, I thought the game was great. However, I soon realized that this WAS NOT the game I had been watching for almost a year. First, I was thrown into a poorly designed open world system that slows every aspect of the game down. I had no idea how to get started or what to do. Thankfully, the community was there for me. As I slowly (and I can't emphasize slowly enough) worked my way up to larger ships, I became increasingly annoyed. Where was the huge PVP combat? Where were all the other players? When do I get to fight a ship that isn't a bot? All of this was supposed to exist in the game, but didn't. Granted, I sometimes saw allied players, and I had also encountered gank squads composed of high level players camping outside ports. But I never saw any of the real PVP combat I had drooled over on youtube. In the current build of the game, You will spend 90% of the time sailing, 5% in port, and 5% fighting incredibly overpowered bots that will hit your
ship no matter how far you are away. PVP is a joke, simply because there is none. Henceforth, I shall refer to the game as Naval Inaction, as that should be it's proper title.
UPDATES
In Naval Inaction, updates are unreliable. The devs refuse to listen to the community, WHICH IS CRITICAL in an early access niche game like this. Instead, the devs continue to pursue their idea of what the game should be. The only problem is they don't know what their game should be, or where to go from here, so they keep pushing out updates that don't focus on anything specifically, so nothing is ever fixed. The community of this game has several great ideas of where the game could go from here. Unfortunately, however, the community is almost never listened to, and so Naval Inaction continues to remain in limbo, progressing nowhere while experiencing a steady decline in player population.
The devs also are also known to release unreliable information about upcoming patches. For instance, a gamewide shipwipe was announced in late 2016. The devs claimed the wipe would occur in December or January, but no wipe has happened yet. To my knowledge, the devs have not released any information about this failure.
EDIT: The devs released information about the shipwipe on the community hub two hours before the time of this edit.
DEVELOPER ABUSE/CENSORSHIP

"
Potter Stewart

"
George Bernard Shaw
If you have read other steam reviews, many players are accusing the devs of censorship on the Gamelabs forums. Some reviews provide proof of censorship. While I personally have not experienced censorship, I feel I must bring up this topic. Developer censorship of differing opinions is a serious problem. In my opinion, people who have purchased this game (which is not a cheap) have a right to express their views freely. The developers have a responsibility to respect and listen to their playerbase, not throw it in the back of the closet. Without the players, afterall, the developers would have nothing. If the developers truely care about their product they must respect the rights of those who purchased it. This is why I think the Developers DO NOT CARE  about their product any longer. The game has gone nowhere for almost 3/4ths of a year, despite several updates. At this point, I feel the game has been abandonded and the devs are hoping people will continue buying the game. This is essentially fraud, but the devs avoid this by providing low-effort patches every few months. Naval Inaction is seemingly nothing more than a scam at this point in time.
CONCLUSION
Do not buy this game. It is not worth the price, and the developers do not deserve the money due to the behavior they exhibit towards the community. If you really feel you must buy this game, buy it, leave a negetive review, then refund it.

Right off the bat I want to just say: this is great game and I've never spent so many hours with any one steam purchase.  It's early access so there are of course some problems and the Devs can be a bit tetchy at times but it's nothing like has been made out in recent Steam reviews and obviously Early Access means things are changing all the time.  The UI and clan mechanics are a tad basic atm but that's prety minor stuff, escpecially when you consider extremely polished battle system and the quality of the ship models.
So the game tries to simulate/gamify being a sea captain in the late 18th/early 19th Century and it does a pretty good job of this.  Obviously it's not a true simulation, the scurvy and weevilvs have been swapped out for live map coordinates and a teleport function if you get really lost, but that's probably for the best.  There are two modes, the Open World which is a large map of the Caribbean where you sail from port to port and the battles.  The battles are phenomenal: beautiful to watch and exciting to play with a realistic flavour absent in SO SO SO many other pirate/sailing games.
The game offers various playstyles but I mainly play RvR (Realm vs Realm) where you sail for one of the 7 in-game nations (+ Pirates) and attempt to conquer ports off eachother.  Not all factions work the same way but most have clans that work together to conquer or blockade ports, diplomats that work out deals between the factions and some people who pass it all by and just go sailing the open seas looking for enemies to sink, ignoring RvR completely.  There also are competitions, both dev and player run for people looking for a quick consequence-free ship battle.
Some of the best parts of the game aren't even dev made and that's communities and the culture built up around the game.  There is some toxicity of course, and that's a shame, but it represents a small part of the game experience compared to the vast majority who are courtious and polite and for the most part passionate about history, sailing and just having a good time.
For example: at the moment there's a guy putting out weekly Youtube videos following the battles and conquests on the game with specials on tactics and ships and other assorted game topics.
Thee's another guy making a 3D model of a British 2rd rate from 1768 who posts regular updates on his progress
and like them there are lots of people doing really cool and interesting things that make the culture around the game a fantastic added benifit.
As I said before it's an Early Access game so there are some kinks to be ironed out and that is what's causing the most amountof angst both in the forums and in the Steam Reviews.  It's a game that lots of people are passoionate about so when things head in a certain direction they don't like people get salty.  There's also been a few atempts at using bad steam reviews as a way try and influence the Devs against certain decisions.    I'm not saying that's the reason for all the negative reviews but it's a factor in a few of the most recent ones. The devs can get a bit defensive but personally I wouldn't say they've crossed a line or been rude to people who hadn't first been rude to them. People get salty because they care about the game and they care because it really is a great game.  It's not going to be everyone's cup of tea but if you're on the fence about this one I'd say give it a go.

Depth is an asymmetric multiplayer shoot 'em up or shark 'em up with 4 divers vs. 2 sharks. Despite Depth's simple gameplay, there is so much to master. For instance, sound is a huge part of the divers' gameplay. You can hear sharks sprint-swimming and lunging around the outside of the room, which you can take advantage of by guessing what entrance they'll use, or if you're ballsy, go out and kill them before they even get in. With sharks, you NEED to plan your exit strategy before entering rooms the divers are in. Sharks take less punishment than you might think, so you need to be quick and hardly give divers the chance to land hits on you. If you have friends, Depth is perfect for you (not that it isn't good if you play solo). If you only have one friend, play shark! If you have more than one, play diver! Depth's asymmetry is great for different sizes of friend groups. And trust me, teamwork in depth, for both sharks and divers, is scary for the opposition. I've been addicted to this game for a while now, and if you're on the wall about picking up Depth, I highly recommend that you do. I've definitely gotten my money's worth out of it.

I had relatively high hopes for this game after finding several small gems in the most recent sale, but I am very dissapointed in this. The jist of the game is that you control several giants, each with their own powers such as creating oceans, mountains, wildlife or minerals, and you try to create an environment in which a human settlement will start up and hopefully thrive. While this sounds like a fun god game, unfortunately, for me it was boring and cumbersome.
The main problem, as well as the real draw of the game, is that each ability that your giants have can synergize with another ability, meaning that if the two are together, they will produce more food, science, or minerals. While this good be a very interesting mechanic, allowing you to create strands of synergizing areas for a town, this element is stifled by the fact that each village can only have two plots of land on either side of it that it can use, so even when you have 40+ abilities to choose from and syergize, you can only do to synergies, then that place is done. On top of that, the giants move very slowly, for no apparent reason, meaning that the game takes much longer than it should to get things done, which can be a problem when each world has a time limit on it.
Ultimately I feel this could have been a very good game, but the fact that the giants take so long to get places and the creative and strategic ability of the player is limited by the small areas around settlements puts this game out of my mind as I move on to better games.

Overall I really think this is a game worth playing, especially if you like online competetive games.

Sid Meier's Pirates! (slight spoilers) - A boy lived in a nice home with his family. As they were eating dinner, an evil man stepped in to kidnap them all, but the boy got away. He survived for years on end to eventually enter a tavern to join a crew. He had the choice of joining one of four nations: the Dutch, the English, the Spanish, and the French. This is where the player takes over and joins.
Joining a particular nation only affects your starting ship as you can easily switch your allegiance to another nation or fight for no nation at all. Of course if you stay with one nation and rise through the ranks by sinking enemy ships and helping them with tasks, you will get perks such as free upgrades and repairs. Not to mention, all of your faction's towns have a governor with a daughter. They range from plain, to attractive, to beautiful. Plain and attractive women are easy to romance while beautiful women take skill. Skill in what you say? Dancing. It's actually pretty tough and I've noted that some people have ways to cheat it. You get various rewards for completing dances and can eventually marry.
On your ship you can board other ships and make their ship your flagship, sink their ship, or take it to sell or keep. There are some nice ships to get such as the prized "Ship of the Line" crewed by the English. To get it you have to make the English hate you by taking their ships and assaulting their towns. Don't forget to pick up crew at a tavern, you'll need a lot to take on those bigger ships!
Town Assault works differently from the rest of the game as in you take your crew to assault a town. It's kind of like a chessboard but it works quite differently. Other than towns, there are also Missions, the religious kind where monks live. They help you make friends with factions that hate you, and grow towns that you want to grow. There are also other types of settlements such as small faction towns, pirate havens. and indian villages.
Other features include a top ten list of pirates, that you can kill and get good loot from their ship, as well as renown. You can also take their secret treasure by buying their maps. Remember your wife? She can give you a different map as well, a map to a secret city which will give you a literal ton of gold. The MAIN point of the game though is to rescue your whole family, so don't forget! I've enjoyed this game a lot though, so I'd give it a 7.75/10.
TLDR - It's a good game, buy it.

Skullgirls is an indie, 2d fighting game with the most lovely animations and characters ever, plus great gameplay. Some people came for nostalgia, some people came for the girls, but everyone stayed thanks to the amazing fighting gameplay it offers.
- Characters and Story
Believe it or not, this is a big part of the game actually - i have never played a fighting game with such likeable roster and interesting story. I expected the classic cutscenes where the character just "wants to be the best fighter ever!" and boy, i was wrong.  I started the game playing mostly with Valentine (the sexy nurse ninja) and Cerebella (Circus superstar with Vice-Versa, a hat with two superstrong arms) and their stories are already engaging (at least for a fighting game), but the most fun i've had was with Peacock. Her story mode was an emotional roller-coaster, oscillating between hilarious scenes that had me laughing out loud and moments that had me almost crying. While other fighting games have a bland roster with no personality (sometimes characters are just a recolor of others), in Skullgirls i can see that every character had a lot of love put on them during development. They're fleshed out, they're lovely, they're great.
My only complaint: The roster could be bigger. But hey, it's an indie game, so i'll let that pass.
- Gameplay (The Part that Really Matters)
It's perfect. That's just how i can sum this up. Responsive, fast-paced, varied and very fun. If you like fighting games, this is right up your alley - it reminded me a lot of Guilty Gear and Marvel VS Capcom games, with aerial combos, several flashy ultra attacks for every character, insane combos and switching between characters of your team mid-fight. With a twist - you don't necessarily have to play a team, you can play with a single character or two high-powered characters instead of a crew of 3, if you want to sacrifice versatility in exchange for more power for your favorite character. Oh, and another fun addition - You know in Marvel vs Capcom when you were about to defeat one of the enemy's teammates and he switched? So, in Skullgirls you can punch out one of his characters and force another one to come back, at the cost of 1 level of your Blockbuster (special moves). Neat idea right? Another thing i loved is how several of the characters play in a really interesting way. I expected fighting game tropes (the ryu clone, the combo guy, etc) that every fighting game is plagued with, but every character in Skullgirls fights in their unique way. Some of them may remind you of someone else (Like Parasoul reminds me of Testament from GG), but they always have their own, original traits and twists.
- Audio and Visuals
Flawless! I love it! The soundtrack does not disappoint, fitting the stage and gameplay (i especially love the
), and the character's voices really impressed me. There is a very wide array of lines for every character, making sure they don't repeat the same sentence even when you repeat the same attack, and they call each other's names when switching teammates mid-fight, they have several unique lines to greet every specific character AND for their victory animations. Usually in fighting games the audio gets a bit repetitive after a while, but this is not the case. I actually still hear new lines whenever i play.
And the visuals? Oh man. Maybe this games' biggest selling point? The hand-drawn, high-framerate animations are absolutely amazing. Reminds me of Darkstalkers actually - the likeable characters and excellent animations. Again, when i played with Valentine and Cerebella i was already impressed, but the highest point so far was Peacock ; she's downright hilarious when fighting, following that classic Disney animation style, very cartoony and fun. I think the visuals, together with the gameplay, are the best parts of this game - and they should be, that's exactly what matters in a fighting game.
My only complaint: Every character has just one victory animation. (and one for time-out). Although they're not sooo repetitive since they have several lines to say, i wouldn't complain if we got more.
- So, Should i Buy this Game? (TL;DR)
Do you like fighting games? If you do, YES. Buy Skullgirls and you will not be disappointed.
You don't like fighting games? Well, you're about to. Skullgirls will get you in the genre, guaranteed. I actually suck at fighting games (my specialty is shooters), and this game entertained me a lot. It's worth your money and more - I actually regret buying it on a sale, they deserved more money from me.

This game still has some issues - there is no denying that.  Many of which that were in my previous review still remain.  The developers can't seem to come up with a decent economy system that benefits the majority of the player base, not just the super hardcore players.  This game has always been a niche MMO and it requires a certain kind of player that is willing to invest the time - this is not a casual game. The main admin does seem to have been trying to make amends and the moderation of the game forums seems a bit more fair and he is stating to ask the right questions as to what needs to be fixed and why, this current patch is a very much needed step in the right direction.
I cautiously recommend this game and hope to see more players pick it up and sail the map.  Be aware of the faults and the "interesting" community on the forums and hopefully if you're a US or AUS based player you land on the GLOBAL server and things will be fine.

Played this on Android before. Twice. This will be my third time playing it. I have a lot to say about it.
It's not quite a point-and-click adventure. It's not quite a hack and slash. It is a strange emotional experience, that is based in the fantastic but sprinkles in a bit of the mundane just to keep you grounded. It's a somewhat short game, but it demands you to space out your experience, even asking you to wait entire IRL moon cycles before progressing in some cases. In the first section of the game, the narrator will actually tell you that the first play session will tak you 15 or 20 minutes, and when you finish you will even be kicked back to the main menu just as encouragement to not play it all at once. I kind of wish more games did stuff like this, too many games are built for open-ended gaming sessions, but S:S&S parcels out the gaming experience in discrete amounts.
The strangely proportioned pixel art people might be a little off-putting at first, but it forces you to see them not as they look but as what they represent. And the music is excellent, and is incorporated into the gameplay and game events masterfully. The music will entice you, provoke you, threaten you, and calm you. Everything about this game is like falling into a trance.
Gameplay-wise, there aren't really any difficult puzzles, and the combat isn't too complicated (though sometimes those trigons will get the better of you). When you do mess up, the game punishes you swiftly but not harshly. When you lose a fight the worst that happens is that you have to regain your health and then try again. It feels a little odd playing this game with a mouse though, as it is very clearly intended for touch controls.
The story starts out intentionally vague. You play as a warrior referred to only as the Scythian, who was sent far from her home to complete a woful errand that somehow involves a book called the megatome. The dialogue is mainly related to you indirectly by the omnipotent narrator, who sometimes will appear in game to make an appearance just to break the fourth wall. In fact a lot of the dialogue and environments is just a little cheeky and breaks the fourth wall. There is twitter integration, but it's not very obnoxious and it's only referred to once in the beginning if you choose not to use it.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. But with one caveat: if you have a touchscreen or tablet and a good pair of headphones, play it with that. You can get this on Android's Google Play Store, and probably on the iPhone app store as well. I played it on my phone, though I much prefer the way it looks on a full-sized monitor.

Definitely a shorter game, but that can be expected from a ported iPhone app. The game mechanics themselves don't do much for me, mainly because it was optimized for touch screens. The music and art style, however, are absolutely beautiful. Being that the art was the reason I bought the game, I was not disappointed. The music fits in amazingly and sometimes interactively with the current action of the game, and the game is as beautiful as the store page suggests.
Also, the game is split up into episodes that provide great stopping points, so rather than doing my usual "Power though the indie game to reach 100%" race, I've been taking my time and enjoying it much more than I might have otherwise.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery is quite unlike any other game you'll play. It's uniqueness is what makes it so quirky and lets it stand out. Sometimes for the better, while other times being a bit frustrating.
This is an 8-bit style abstract puzzle-adventure, stylised like an album (if that's possible). You follow a lone warrior, as he meets new people in this strange wilderness, while trying to find some ancient tome to defeat an evil thingy. It all sets up pretty standardly.
The little surprises came from the sprinkled humour in the ways the warrior interacted with the environment, and the inner monologue that followed. The sarcasm, and style of speaking was reminiscent of a teenager talking to friends, as opposed to fantasy speak ("We were like groan not another fetch quest amirite?")
Controls were not entirely intuitive to figure out puzzles, mainly because this was primarily designed for the smartphone interface. You would come to a new area, and see a shining light, for example. The way in which you interact with it may be to click it, or attract other things to it, etc. This game doesn't go out of it's way to explain how to complete a puzzle, but rewards exploration. This could be frustrating for some, if you're like me who is sometimes impatient.
The minimalistic style is cool, and Jim Guthrie's atmospheric soundtrack fits in perfectly.
Overall fairly simple and short, this game is good to spend a few hours in.

"To the Moon" was a great experience!  Here's the best way to describe the story --- it is a mix of the movies "Inception" and "The Notebook" illustrated through Super Nintendo graphics.
As many others have noted in their reviews, "To the Moon" is for a very specific audience.  Do not come into it thinking it will have great game play, state of the art graphics, or 40+ hours of play time with replayability.  This is more of an interactive movie experience; there are elements of point-and-click game play involved, but nothing that will make your brain swell or raise your blood pressure.  If you do not care for emotional/inspirational/romance movies, this also may not be for you.
With all that being said, if you come into "To the Moon" expecting what it is, you will not leave disappointed.  It is a complex journey that shares the power of the human spirit, illustrated through one man's life (from childhood to his death bed) and his pursuit of dreams versus love, and overcoming regret and loss.
It's a sobering reminder that many of us will lay in a death bed some day (whether old age, accident, cancer, etc.) and the questions will be...will you be at peace, or will you question everything that was your entire life?  It's also a simple reminder to enjoy the simple joys in life with the ones you love with what time you are given with them.
"To the Moon" was a great piece of art that I was glad to experience.

This game has some surprising depth to it (no pun intended); as you play it more, you start to realize that EVERYTHING has multiple purposes. The complexity in this game is found in the mechanics; you have to strategize and find your playstyle because every option has benefits and drawbacks (I mean, you can even choose from 4 different playstyles before the start of every run, and each one is useful in their own ways). Do you want to keep your combo going to get greater prizes, or do you want to keep stopping early to maximize monetary gaines? Do you want to change your weapon just to get extra health, or is it not worth changing your gun? The game is inititally fun because of the gimmick of going down instead of left to right, but then the game becomes even greater once you understand all the all the little decisions that can fit in the span of split seconds or impact the rest of your run.
Besides the clever execution, the game is just hard; plain and simple. It's like a weird combination of a platformer and a bullethell; it requires fast decision-making skills and reflexes, and the hard mode you unlock after defeating the boss totally changes the game. I definitely recommend this game (though prepare to rage sometimes; it'll happen).

Downwell is a roguelike, fast-paced plattformer with retro graphics.
You jump down a well and shoot or stomp enemies, which are dropping red crystals when they are killed. The crystals are needed for buying stuff at the shop and maintaining the weapons boost status. The weapons boost is needed to kill the enemies more quickly.
In each level you have the chance to strengthen you character with multiple weapons upgrades. After each level you have the chance to choose between some (mostly) passive upgrades. Like most roguelikes, if you die, you have to start all over again.
There are also different play styles (e.g. More life from the beginning) and color palettes to unlock permanently.
Positives:
+ Entertaining, fast-paced, satisfying and addictive gameplay
+ Different weapons/passive upgrades
+ It's difficult enough but not really frustrating
+ Funny enough to come back and give it another try
Neutral:
o Retro graphics and sound with Gameboy feeling
o Watch the trailer. That's exactly what you get.
Negatives:

This game is hard. It will kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you don't look through a walkthrough, or if you're not comfortable exploring every single crack in every single crevasse.

Sometimes you go to the next area only to find out you have to complete 8 dialogue-only quests to get enough experience to level up to fight the next area.

So if that's the game for you, I'd recommend it. If you aren't a hard-core RPG fan, turn away.

This game could be amazing. It has everything it needs to be good, but there's a huge, huge, huge, huge, huge problem up-front.
The game sucks.
The creators obviously have no idea what scaling is, and they expect you to be familiar with the game and min-max right out of the gate. "Did you not pick the right skills, stats, and weapons at first level? Oh darn, guess you lose as soon as you get to the first combat zone outside of the city gates." The zombies are preposterously powerful, and each fight *requires* multiple attempts all the while cheesing fights.
People try to defend it with "There are ways to succeed" and "Just do X" but the problem is that *you can't.* You're already a couple hours into the game, emotionally invested into the characters because of the admittedly-good writing, but lo and behold you can't respec (at least not this early in the game.) Did you decide to do a dual-wield build with one of your starting characters, and not realize that you will miss *every single attack*? Darn, sucks to suck. Did you think it would be cool to have a battle mage? Sorry, not optimal, you lose.
And don't get me *started* on the unintuitive follower-gaining system.
If you talk to an early character you can get as a follower (who you effectively need if you didn't set up one of your initial characters as a ranger), your primary NPC ally *actively says no to inviting her to the party* unless A.) You happened to know the right "attitude" to give her in character creation or B.) you make her go stand 20 feet away while you recruit the new person, after which she's completely fine having this character in the party. You might be thinking, "Oh, that's not too bad." Until you realize that nowhere in the game is this given to you as a hint at any point in time.
I want to love this game because it has good writing, deep lore, and (when you're not being overpowered in a 4v8 against higher-level enemies that can rez and heal one another all the while perma-stunning your team) fun combat. Unfortunately, the people who made this game have no idea what scaling and combat balance are.

Sid Meier's Pirates! (slight spoilers) - A boy lived in a nice home with his family. As they were eating dinner, an evil man stepped in to kidnap them all, but the boy got away. He survived for years on end to eventually enter a tavern to join a crew. He had the choice of joining one of four nations: the Dutch, the English, the Spanish, and the French. This is where the player takes over and joins.
Joining a particular nation only affects your starting ship as you can easily switch your allegiance to another nation or fight for no nation at all. Of course if you stay with one nation and rise through the ranks by sinking enemy ships and helping them with tasks, you will get perks such as free upgrades and repairs. Not to mention, all of your faction's towns have a governor with a daughter. They range from plain, to attractive, to beautiful. Plain and attractive women are easy to romance while beautiful women take skill. Skill in what you say? Dancing. It's actually pretty tough and I've noted that some people have ways to cheat it. You get various rewards for completing dances and can eventually marry.
On your ship you can board other ships and make their ship your flagship, sink their ship, or take it to sell or keep. There are some nice ships to get such as the prized "Ship of the Line" crewed by the English. To get it you have to make the English hate you by taking their ships and assaulting their towns. Don't forget to pick up crew at a tavern, you'll need a lot to take on those bigger ships!
Town Assault works differently from the rest of the game as in you take your crew to assault a town. It's kind of like a chessboard but it works quite differently. Other than towns, there are also Missions, the religious kind where monks live. They help you make friends with factions that hate you, and grow towns that you want to grow. There are also other types of settlements such as small faction towns, pirate havens. and indian villages.
Other features include a top ten list of pirates, that you can kill and get good loot from their ship, as well as renown. You can also take their secret treasure by buying their maps. Remember your wife? She can give you a different map as well, a map to a secret city which will give you a literal ton of gold. The MAIN point of the game though is to rescue your whole family, so don't forget! I've enjoyed this game a lot though, so I'd give it a 7.75/10.
TLDR - It's a good game, buy it.

This is a very good strategical and casual game, and a king amoung pirate games. It's story-driven, and there isn't a whole lot of choice-making, and there isn't much of an item system (ie no inventory) but there are still collectibles, armor, swords, guns, all the likes to buy from the mysterious merchants in the corner of taverns. Being able to take and pick from multiple different types and grades of ships is a good part of the game, along with making your own sails and choosing which flag you'll sail under. The naval combat, in all honesty, is slow and boring, so if I were you, just board them already! Don't sit there and fire cannons, they barely do anything. Boarding is less extravagant than most other pirate games. Basically you pick your sword (Go Rapiers!), which can be upgraded with new sets of swords you can buy, and defeat your opposing captain in a Hollywood-style match of sword fighting before your crew gets murdered. Should you win, you will be deserted or captured somewhere, and be left with little to nothing -- this is when the saving slots and loading come in handy, cause who the heck actually serves prison time in RPGs? If you beat the captain, which won't take much time to master doing, he will be everso conveniently knocked off his ship, once again, in a Hollywood cinematic style. This is especially true when facing a famous pirate such as the cliche Blackbeard. There are plenty other times in the game where you'll need your valiant swordsmanship, so be prepared for that. Other than that, it's working up the ranks of kingdom militaries, winning the heart of a governor's daughter (or a few, if you're into that...), finding your lost family members (NOT a spoiler, btw), and pillaging and exploring as you see fit. Don't forget to do some special missions along the way, trust me, they're actually fun and not a waste of time. Just try not to get too frustrated when searching the endless jungle lands for treasures and buildings, because you'll start to make so much more sense of the treasure maps you pick up as you go. There's more that I could say here, but you're probably already itching your mouse to hit that Add To Wishlist button, so I'll letcha go.

Should we accept a classic as a classic after the era it became a classic in stops being classic? This is the classic question that I would love to finally classify and I shall provide a vintage standard and time-honoured solution to this problem.
Pirates, classically, are known as the typical scurge of the usual seven seas we are all familiar with. However, this classification is typically unjust. Sid Meier's classic experience, Pirates! focuses on the most representative of all classical periods of piracy, namely the Golden Age in the Caribbean of pre 1730 vintage. I want to point out that typically, a classic pirate crew of this day would not be a simble group of your usual scoundrels, but in fact much closer to the democratic nature of classical liberals. While I don't believe that the classic game Sid Meier's Pirates! represents this class of pirates in a standard manner, it does make a good attempt at showing how Piracy was a reasonable and standard career choice in this era.
Now for the typical pros and cons;
+Classic arcade combat
+Classic lost family story line
+Classic famous pirates (collect the skulls of all 9)
+Classic ship designs
+Classic game
-Classic repetitive gameplay
-Classic ugly charachter models
-Classic scurvy
Overall, this game is a classic that still stands the test of time. A true classic for video games!

Ori and the Blind Forest is more of a video game than the prologue might lead you to believe.
It is an action-platforming game that features a world map, swimming, gliding, combat, and various abilities you can find in the world. As you progress, you can spend Ability Points to unlock nodes on the ability tree, providing Ori with additional abilities and increasing his strength.
The start of the game is somewhat slow, and areas of the world are, of course, unreachable without certain abilities. The game's difficulty ramps up with each new area, and you must take advantage of the abilities you gain along the way to succeed.
Maximum vitality and energy are increased by finding objects in the game world, and inexperienced players may find Ori's initially low survivability to be limiting. Using the game's Soul Link mechanic, however, a player can attempt an area multiple times, allowing the player to eventually master using Ori's various capabilities.
The artwork and soundtrack are stellar and very much contribute to the game's atmosphere.
Overall, Ori and the Blind Forest is a game I highly recommend.

Having played each iteration in the Total War series I feel comfortable saying that this has been the best one they've created thus far.
The game came with a boatload of content with the four races and their campaigns and each is highly detailed and nuanced in their particular gameplay mechanics, aesthetics and play styles. There are a pile of improvements to help smooth off some of the edges seen in the first game and it's been one of the most bug-free pc gaming experiences I've had in a long time.
As an owner of both game 1 and 2 I also got the benefit of the free side-content combining both maps into the Mortal Empires campaign which has also been quite a lot of fun. There have been some minor teething problems but considering no strategy map has ever had that much unique content in it before it's no surprises, plus they've been swift with ironing out the major issues.
On that note, the game is getting continued and regular support and on top of that initial gigantic free content drop (albeit only for owners of both games but hey, we bought both games), there's likely going to be a bunch more of it coming as with the first game.
They've listened to feedback from the players and have improved the game and the content they're bringing out, the main campaign is great and the free side-campaign is also pretty fantastic so you can't go wrong with it really. If you like fantasy and complex strategy games, this'uns for you.

Sometimes it pays to be pretty. Especially if your personality is akin to that of a differently-abled llama.
The pixel art is great, no doubt. However the scenery soon becomes repetitive and the initial charm of the landscapes diminishes.
The clunky, unintuitive contols frustrate often. In particular, a chase scene quickly goes from tense and urgent to mouse-throwingly-irritating. As you try to escape, your mouse clicks "grab" the screen, dragging the scene in the opposite direction of the one in which you were attempting to move. Throw in the painfully glacial pace of your protagonist and navigating this lovely low-res world becomes a chore. Essentially the gameplay itself is pinned upon almost a singular mechanic, initiating "scorcery mode" and activating the environmental surroundings through mouse clicks in a specific order to release Forest Sprites. It's simplistic at its core, but often obtuse. You may however consume mushrooms to highlight these specific points of interaction, but maybe 'shrooms is how we've ended up here in the first place.
For all the emphasis on the soundtrack or the "EP", the tunes here are generally uninspiring, background ambience. A grating bell-dong accompanies every scroll of on-screen text that feels quite unnecessary. Although, the grunts and cries of your protaganist during battle sound fierce and have a Link-like charm. There's also a rambling, awkward monologue from a character that was somewhat amusing.
The attempted casual, modern style of the text is an innovative idea, but feels forced. The word "super" is repeatedly thrown in front of adjectives, endevouring to be current.
In spite of all this, I found the choice of a female lead character to be a commendable one. It's just a shame she doesn't have more to do.
The parting announcement S:SS leaves you with- "Your woeful errand is at an end." Indeed... Indeed it is.
Super disappointing.

First off, this game has amazing visuals and has an absolutely amazing lego landscape. And i do enjoy this game, i just have some complaints to note before it comes out of early access.
The building is off and im always struggling to place bricks. You can never get the right angle and its just awkward at most. You get individual bricks to use but they take so long to build with that it isnt even worth it. You can place  multiple bricks at once but there is only cube shape and sphere shape, and you cant change the size. There is also no way to be accurate with placing. The landscape editing is good though, and i enjoyed altering my surroundings. but why build when the game gives you no motivation to do so? There is nothing to protect yourself against, There are no penaltys for anything you do.
The game makes you explare ALOT, but there is nothing else you can do except that. And what happens when you have already seen all that you want to see? I only played this game for 2 hours and i saw everything. All there is to do is look around and mess with items.
The reason the game makes you explore alot is so you can collect all of the items from the multiple biomes, i do actually like this mechanic though, it was fun to explore while it lasted, and even though i didnt use the items it was fun to get them.
The Characters I collected fun to use because they give you different abilitys, like as the vampire you can turn into a bat, or as the wizard you can shoot fireballs. I enjoyed unlocking all of the animals and vehicles too, i used these alot. I used them to get around, blow things up, and just have fun in general. But the placeable items i got, i never used because the game gave me no reason to.
The camera is also really weird and is not fit for building or moving around. you have to hold right click whenever you want to move the camera on your own, otherwise, it just stays in this one position behind you, that does not work well in a game where looking around is all you do.
The game is cool in the concept where you can enter in coordinates and pick the world that you want, this also means that you will be able to get the same word as one of your friends. Or you can just press random until you find a world that looks nice. I actually liked this part.
My final verdict is that this game is a great concept, but it definitely needs editing, and is just not worth your money at this early stage. Maybe when this game gets out of early access it will get better.

Diary of Sir Reginald Fopsworth
Day 1
Friday, 5th of June, 2015
The dive went splendidly. I landed safely on some shrubbery and set about exploring these strange lands as soon as I had found my monocle, which must have come loose in the fall.
This new world truly is entrancing. The landscape changes so quickly it is almost dizzying. I spent most of the afternoon admiring the plant life and various natural, colourful formations, collecting plans for my research. I realised early on that I would need some form of transportation to get around given the sheer size of this place, so as soon as I came across a rather amiable horse (I named the sturdy fellow ‘Chestnut’), I hopped on his back and rode off into the sunset towards a lush-looking forest, hoping to continue my exploration in the dark.
This, as it turns out, was a grave mistake.
As night fell, strange skeletal creatures started to emerge and rove about the forest. In my naivety I approached one, dismounted Chestnut, and tried to strike up a conversation. This bizarre character would have none of it, and instead challenged me to fisticuffs. I refused to engage and tried to talk some sense into it, which seemed to work at first. It eventually lowered its arms, and for a second it seemed to smile -- strangely, sickeningly, disconcertingly.
Then, all of a sudden, a number of these creatures ran out from the trees and formed a gang, which then proceeded to chase after poor Chestnut. The brutes pummelled and hit him with their white claws, uttering strange shrieks and screams as they went. I ran after them in horror and made quick work of them – clearly these awful beasts do not deserve any mercy. Sadly, when I looked up from what was left of them, Chestnut was nowhere to be seen.
I retreated with a heavy heart to my initial landing spot for the night, where I am writing now in a small brick lodging. I don’t know what became of Chestnut. I have seen some of the horses here miraculously make their way up into the trees, so I can only hope that Chestnut will take refuge in the forest’s canopy until sunrise.
These lands may be beautiful, but they are wrought with hidden dangers. The skeletons’ vicious, bloodthirsty cries are still ringing in my ears, and I expect I will have a fitful sleep.
My only consolation is that I have learned an important lesson today: Never, ever trust a skeleton.

I can't remember where I picked this up, I'm pretty sure it was a bundle because I got a Steam Gift key as well. I know its been given out in a couple giveaways already.
Anyway, this game has promise, but it's sorely lacking in content at this stage of development. On the plus side, it runs well on my laptop (2 year old mid range gaming laptop), the gameplay is easy to pick up, graphics are decent. On the negative side, they expect a $20 buy in and the game is almost nothing but micro transactions from then on. You can earn rewards by playing, mainly gold with a daily chance for gems shards (for crefting cards) and rubies (the premium currency). From there it's set up like a MOBA, you have to buy heroes and arenas (which are purely cosmetic so why do they cost money?). And you collect cards to use as minions. Very basic 2 lane set up, control the center points to increase mana production, dispatch minions to defend your hero and attack the enemy hero. Progression seems slow even with the "Premium" upgrade, there's no story or interesting flavor text to make the heroes and minions seem interesting, it's just... meh. If you get a free key it's worth checking out, but I don't think it's worth the asking price for the premium upgrade. Maybe keep an eye on it for future development if it improves.

I just wanted to write this because there are so many negative reviews out there, and I have been really enjoying this game so I wanted to kind of off set them.
First, Let me start with the areas in which this game can improve.
No tutorial
Slow gameplay
Expensive
While this game doesn't have a tutorial, there are plenty of youtube videos out there that will help you get started and many more that can help you with strategy and other things you may be wondering about. I do think that the programmers are planning on putting in a tutorial, but just haven't gotten around to it yet, since there are other bugs and whatnot that they want to fix first before implanting that. They probably are going to add much more options (like fishing)   that would change the tutorial.
Slow gameplay is another thing that people always go to when making this game look bad, but the fact of the matter is that the ships in this game game go about 2x faster than real life. The fastest ships of those times couldn't even go as fast as some of the early ships like the cutter/privateer. So really, this is fast gameplay compared to what you would do in real life, and I think it's actually nice and realistic and I wouldn't change it at all if I were one of the devs. For the people who complain about this clearly have never sailed before and can't really appreciate this game.
The game being pretty expensive/not a great value is the only valid comment I've seen that is kind of true. I bought this game after watching many youtubes, after talking to some friends and other people. I knew that it had some problems when I bought it so I wasn't unhappily surprised to find them. The price is what it is, and while it is quite expecive you just have to know that going in, you have to be able to put up with that.
Now on the areas that are already great:
Realistic Sailing
Fun, realistic battles
Good Graphics
Trading
I've been looking for a game that has real sailing angles like this, made by people who have actually sailed before, or done a lot of research for years, and so far, this has been the only game with all of that stuff. I'm not sure if the devs are going to make the sailing more realistic (i.e. making sailing angles on some ships from close-hulled to close/beam reach), but I'm ok with how it is now.
Again, the real sailing angles sort of ties in to how the battles are more fun/realistic for someone who does a lot of sailing, but also I like how you can really have control on how you attack and scope in your opponents before releasing a full broadside, or how you can switch between grape, ball, and chain cannon ball types. These are things that you don't find in some ship games that I just wanted to point out.
Other things I liked included fishing, trading, and the good graphics. Fishing is the only real way to make money at the beginning of the game, so I found this to be a great addition to the game. I also really enjoy trading, because you can make a lot of money on it by doing nothing but buying and selling at different ports. For people that would like help for finding good deals at ports, go to
. This a very helpful site because you can also find many other helpful things on there including ship blueprints, the materials you need to build diffent modules etc. I also found the player base to be very friendly and helpful.
I hope that this review has helped inflict opon your decision to buy or not to buy this game. This game isn't for everybody, but I just wanted to show the other side of this one sided forum.

Downwell is a fantastically frenetic action-platformer with snappy controls, wonderful 2-bit pixel art, and a bizarrely fascinating world.
Combat is quick and satisfying, and the game bundles health and ammo boosts with weapon types to encourage you to try new weapons.
The game's characters and setting are weird as heck, and I love them for that- every new area is a joy to experience for the first time.
Getting to the bottom of the well is a mysterious challenge like nothing I've ever seen; there are no checkpoints, so to beat the game you have to go through every single level without dying once. That level of near-impossible-challenge intrigue is something a lot of roguelikes pass up in favor of "rogue-lite" mechanics, so you don't see it all too often, and it works perfectly here.
It isn't without its flaws- most of the unlockables you get through multiple runs are simple palette swaps, and there are plenty of times when not getting hit is almost impossible- but the good far outweighs the bad.
Heck, I haven't even beaten it yet, but that doesn't matter: I love this game, and, if you're an action gamer with a penchant for pixel art and tough-but-fair challenges, you will too.

The 'original' Divinity Origin Sin was easily one of the best RPGs I had ever played. The game was mechanically one of the very few rpgs out there which stayed true to it's meaning. With the Enhanced Edition, the developers went back to their original masterpiece and cleaned up some of the rough areas which they really didn't have to do - yet they did and they did it for free.
The game has the classic good vs evil setup. One of things which I grew to love about this game is among the serious nature of the narrative, there is an equal measure of quirkiness which gave it it's own unique style.
The game is a CRPG at the core: Turn-based and a party of no more than 4 at a time. However, there is one aspect of the game which levitates the game among it's peers, the way how everything reacts with anything. Elements plays a huge part in the game and for it's part the game hands over complete control to the player (and enemies) on how elements behave with each other. For e.g. Calling in the rain brings water and makes everyone Wet. You can now zap them with electricity for a more powerful effects which stuns everyone foolish enough to stand over the puddle of water created from the rain. Or use the Wet status on your enemies and fire an ice spell to quickly turn them into ice. Once they are in ice form, they are more suspectible to Crushing Damage. You can then call in the fire to melt the ice to water, more fire will result in water vapor. If you you hit the vapor area with electricity, the vapor will turned into a crazy space of electric clouds, stunning anyone caught inside of it or stupid enough to get into it. The elemental system is one of the highlights of the game and can make the battlefield very unpredictable.
The Enhanced Edition of the game also introduces a full voice cast from top to bottom. The original edition only had a few voice options. I didn't expect the voice to be as good as they are in the newer edition. They also tweaked some parts of the game and completely reworked the ending for the better. So thank you Larian.
The game's greatest strength is how free-form the gameplay is. As a player as you gain knowledge on how the world reacts to every action, you are free to manipulate it as you wish. You can easily created situations which  the developers might have never intended for, yet it does not break the game, only makes it that much more interesting for the players to be as creative as possible.
I highly recommend this game. It is one of the most mechanically-perfect RPGs I've ever played.

I had to spend about a full day trying to find ways to get the game to operate on my system without lagging, since there are no graphics settings offered to players. You need to have one of the best graphics cards in order to play this game on a resolution higher than 900. To top it off, I had to watch all of the cutscenes on youtube rather than in the game itself, since the game would always crash due to overload whenever a cutscene played, and I had to skip them.
The beginning of the game is fun, getting simple powers and abilities and adventuring and learning of the rather good story. I spent a good amount of time completing the map and getting all the extra stuff because that's how much I liked navigating around the creative world.
However, in my opinion, as soon as I reached the Misty Woods, the gameplay took a turn for the worst. Trying to get through the puzzles was relentlessly difficult in comparison to the first area, and the controls became increasingly difficult to handle (it started to seem that shift was the only button that did anything and everything). I became lost after every turn, which I'm sure was the point of the area since it had lore of people becoming lost in it, but it turned from Ori and the Blind Forest to Ori and the Walkthrough. It took so many deaths and so many hours that I couldn't handle it anymore and gave up.
If you're a lover of platformer puzzles and have a good graphics card, I'd definitely recommend this game to you. The story is cute and the graphics are fantastic, and all the sounds Ori makes are to die for. Otherwise, I would not recommend this to normal, laid-back players.

Remembering all the combinations of things you can do is a bit overwhelming at times, but the achievement system (which reminds me a lot of Viva Pinata) keeps you focused and on task.
Controls are awkward at first, but you will adapt quickly, and the pause feature means you aren't fighting them with no recourse. Music is mainly background, only the opening theme sticks with me. And while gameplay may dry up when you run out of achievements to get, that hasn't happened to me yet.
Overall it's a pleasant game, that does what it does well, and doesn't try to recreate the genre.

This game's greatest strengths are its moving narrative, and a soundtrack that enhances the mood perfectly. At its heart, the story is a bittersweet romance; generous doses of quirky nerd-culture references and make-you-think mystery make it well-rounded and distinctive. Much of the comic relief comes from the banter between Drs. Rosalene and Watts. At first I found their sarcasm and silliness grating, but eventually as they come to care about their patient, Johnny, their wisecracks are put into balance and cease to detract from Johnny's story.
The puzzle- and hidden-object-based game mechanics are simple, but that's a good thing, because it was supposed to be subordinate to the story. That said, the gameplay does have some flaws. The mouse controls sometimes lagged, and I found some of the maps to be cluttery and hard to navigate. But overall, the game mechanics did their job of getting me to notice the little details that contribute to the story.
I completed To the Moon in just under 5 hours, mostly in a few long sessions, because I didn't want to put it down. It made me feel all the feelings. <3
Did not think a beautiful emotional narrative could be executed with RPG Maker, 10/10. A must play if you love story rich games. I am looking forward to playing the minisodes soon.

I didn't experience the tear jerking moment I'd read much about in the forums and expressed personally to me by a close friend. Also, I felt some moments in the game were a little lengthy, perhaps to prepare for an emotion-filled moment. Sometimes they could be for comic. Example [spoiler ahead], after Rosalene collects the roadkill, Watts excuses himself from the house and again when he passes Rosalene. It seemed pointless.
Nonetheless, it's a sweet story game with beautiful piano music accompanying most scenes which I find is easy on the ear.

To The Moon is one of those games wants to tell you a story, and uses gameplay simply as a storytelling device. I gave it a go upon a friend's suggestion, so here are my thoughts.
The story is fairly compelling. Right from the start you're given its premise, though not the reasons for it. The subject of the story is a dying man, who on his deathbed, requests to "go to the moon". You play as a pair of memory-modifying wizards/technicians who try to give the man his wish. Throughout the story you learn of his motivations.
I felt that the dialogue is a little at odds with the tone of the story though. The humor borders on slapstick, and frankly, detracts from the melancholic narrative. The dialogue isn't a particularly strong point either.
The two characters you control are not nuanced. One is your typical bossy girl, the other is your typical comedy relief guy.
Nevertheless, the overarching story really is quite good. Despite its flaws, I found myself wanting to get to the next level in order to progress the story.
I think that's as much as one can expect for a story-focused game.
Gameplay consists of a fixed isometric view and grid movement. The majority of the gameplay involves collecting orbs (memory links) and then solving a simple puzzle to proceed to the next part of the story. It's repetitive and does not add any value to the story. Really, I feel like To The Moon would be better served as a visual novel. There are a couple of different gameplay sequences throughout the game, but again, none of them felt necessary.
The music is really good! I'm not well versed in this genre, so the uncultured me would define it as classical piano.
Came for the story, left full of feels.

Hi there folks,
I have put a few hours into this game now and I really enjoy playing it, however due to recent negative review I have decided to put some things straight;
My time in naval action has been turbulent, it is probably the only way to describe it.
First off, I started the game and asked myself "What did I get myself into?". I was a long way off from understanding the game and it's mechanics but enjoyed sailing my little cutter for about 20 hours, in which I did little more than sailing from port to port and get 1 or 2 missions done per hour.
After playing the game for about 50 hours total I had stumbled across a clan, they took me in and provided me with a couple of ships, which I sailed into PVP and PVE alike. The thing that most people try to justify here in their negative reviews is that they hate the fact that there is "FORCED" PVP, which is definitely not the case. As such you are presented with the choice of playing on PVP 1 EU, PVP 2 US or PVE 1. So they try to justify the fact that they get ganked lost their ship and what not...
My answer to those people is; Stop crying, grow a pair and hit them back twice or thrice as hard. This game is about Naval Warfare (Action) during the Age of Sail, of course people will sink you and gank you and shoot the hell out of you. But hey, welcome to Naval Action.
Then onto the next important point that people were trying to justify the long sailing times;
Why on earth would you complain about this, this is what makes the game so unique, it requires you to put in some time and effort to build a ship of your own. Or to trade and make a lot of money by doing so.
Overall, I would say that yes the game needs some improving of course (No one is perfect). But the majority of the game is there, I would say with a bit of polishing on the UI it could even be released however, as they have stated they still want to add more ships and finalise the conquest features before they even think of releasing the game.
I would definitely recommend this game.

Played less than 30 minutes. Learned all I need to do:
PROS
-Great graphics
-Realistic ships (minus the fact that no crew can be seen on deck which looks stupid)
-Combat and sailing mechanics are challenging but realistic
-Helpful player base, but insanely small (all servers have around 50 per grouping meaning the max player count was around 150, even though it's likely because it's morning, I highly doubt that the playerbase is much larger than that)
-Lots of depth
CONS
-It's not an MMO. It's just a sandbox sailing game. There's no real involvement with building up your ship other than trying to get the next, best ship.
-The player base is tiny.
-Way too much time investment for little payoff. There are no tutorials, no help files, and the suggestions you get from chat are to watch YouTube videos or the Wiki.
-Devs seem to be super shady.
All in all, it's not worth 40 bucks. At all. Not for a game that expects you to do all of the work to learn how to play and what to do. There are better games out there with similar themes (Blackwake for example) that are better supported, have more players, and developers that aren't afraid of critiscism.

Okay, so, let me throw out some context for this review:
The reviews here are mostly negative. So much so, that when I bought the game, I literally set a timer while playing to make sure I didn't exceed the max play time before I could get my money back. THAT'S how bad I expected this to be from the reviews. I was pleasantly surprised. Most of the negative reviews recently have been due to interaction with the devs. I can't speak on that as I'm not on the forums, so I have no real community exposure.
I was brought to Naval Action because I've always loved the age of sail. I previously bought Assasings Creed IV just for the sailing ships. It was fine, but the inability to really change your ship was frustrating. Then I bought Tempest, which was okay, but not really pretty, and not very clear. I decided to give Naval Action a try. Now, the interface is poor at best. It looks like the 1990s. It's a bit sad. There is no tutorial, so, good luck figuring out what you're supposed to actually DO or how to do it. Fortunately for the devs, there are enough people in game willing to help explain things that it's not unplayable. But they should probably do something about that, because they can't rely on their playerbase to do everything for them. Then there's the graphics. This game is gorgeous, no question. Additionally, I really enjoy that it's not just point and click warfare. You think about the wave motion, the winds, you can't instant-stop... it's a VERY enjoyable game if you simply love sailing ships. Don't get this if you want a quick-click arcade pirate warlord game, but if you have a passion for sailing ships, it's worth the buy!
UPDATE: After more time playing this game, and with the post-wipe changes, I have to say, I cannot recommend this game. It's become the ultimate grind-simulator, as well as isolating anyone who isn't a European player. They failed to actually whipe clans on their previous PvP servers, meaning anyone wanting to change servers from what became the EU to the global server, would have to raise hundreds of thousands of gold to start over, essentially locking them in to the new EU server. To compound the problem, players can only participate in conquest (A necessary part of unlocking additional ships) during the EU prime-time hours.
