It´s currently in dev limbo, slow and small updates, not the nicest of Devs but a small and helpfull community. If you are willing to stomach the really steep learning curve, invest some time into this game and are able to make friends and join a gaming group, you´ll have some decent fun in challenging PvP matches.
The solo-experience is rather bad, NPC Ship combat ranges from pretty decent to downright abysmal, trading and crafting are basically Travel Simulator and looking at Excel-The Game.
The open map... serves its purpose. it´s big, it has a lot of ports, islands and NPCs to make the vast Carribean sea feel somewhat alive but that´s about it. You can fish while you travel, but the fishing is a completely passive process based on RNG.
The Combat feel is unparalleled. The ships handle great, it feels very realistic and hitting a full broadside, watching the splinters fly and seeing the enemy sinking is really damn satisfying.
So: If you´re coming for the combat: Prepare to stomach a steep learning curve and sometimes tedious NPC fights to be rewarded with splendid looking, well modeled ships and a nice community trhowing PvP events from time to time.
If you´re coming for the sailing: It´s only the "real deal" in combat, the world map sailing is basic WASD maneauvering.
Don´t come for the rest, that´s not really fleshed out (yet)
Conclusion: Do not buy this at full price. It´s not worth the money in it´s current state and the propability of reaching such a state is there, but it will take time, likely lots of it. Grab for a Tenner on sale if you are in dire need of age of sail naval battle simulations but that´s about it, after all it´s still alpha/beta/hatever you call the early access state limbo steam does nowadays.
Do i recommend it? Yes-no. The battles are fun but incredibly challenging, they can take well over an hour, expecially in smaller vessels with 4-6 guns per side. Large-scale Big-ships-brawling is damn sexy tho, but it takes a harsh grind to get there.
5/10, room for improvements, might be improved in the (near) future.

The gameplay is great, but after a while you learn a few words that are "overpowered" that you probably constantly will come back to over and over. In previous Scribblenauts you could only complete a puzzle with a certain word a certain number of times. I would like to see that brought back because it is quite easy to beat the game using a small vocabulary. I think this detracts from the gameplay since you aren't forced to try new words and get met with the feeling of surprise when something interacts in a way you didn't think of.
The game provided some challenges, but often had manufactured difficulty in places where the game was looking for one particular object, even though other objects with similar properties could have logically been substituted. As an example, there is a man in one level who asks for help finding the fountain of youth. Well, even though the Fountain of Youth, and Youthful Fountain can all be spawned in game, he doesn't care about the Fountain of Youth spawned right in front of him, since he is looking only for a specific object.
The "unlimited" in this game comes from the idea that they have incorporated adjectives as well as so many new nouns into the game that you can basically do anything. However, as I mentioned, there are still only a few that you will use frequently. "Invincible, Fast, Small, Big" etc. all come to mind. There are also still a few words that it doesn't recognize. I hope that future versions continue to build off this premise and find a way to give us limitless possibilities while still encouraging us to use new words. Additionally, I would hope they can make more objects "interact" with each other. For example, if you spawn a dog and a cat, the dog will generally chase the cat. Well in the same light, I should think if I put a curious scientist next to a suspicious lever that he would trip the switch for me. - Gameplay... 9/10
As I mentioned, you can beat the game very early. There are a ton of levels, but you only have to complete a few of them. If you consider all the extra levels, replayability is great, if you consider replayability after beating all the levels, then it is pretty poor. You are only left with collecting "object shards" which are difficult to track. If it was easier to see them, I would like to tackle them (and probably will at some point) but the fact that you have to go through 5 menus just to see them, and then track through multiple pages makes it not worth it.
I hope that future versions continue to build off this premise and find a way to give us limitless possibilities while still encouraging us to use new words. Additionally, I would hope they can make more objects "interact" with each other. For example, if you spawn a dog and a cat, the dog will generally chase the cat. The cat chases the mouse, etc. These interactions are there. Well in the same light, I should think if I put a curious scientist next to a suspicious lever that he would trip the switch for me. A few of these items could be worked on in a sequel of which I really hope there is one. This game is great and deserves to be an established successful series.
Plus, its one of those games and developers that you are "rooting for" because of their creativity with bringing a unique and fun game to light. - Replayability... 8/10

You get individual bricks to use but they take so long to build with that it isnt even worth it. You can place  multiple bricks at once but there is only cube shape and sphere shape, and you cant change the size. There is also no way to be accurate with placing. The landscape editing is good though, and i enjoyed altering my surroundings. but why build when the game gives you no motivation to do so? There is nothing to protect yourself against, There are no penaltys for anything you do.
The game makes you explare ALOT, but there is nothing else you can do except that. And what happens when you have already seen all that you want to see? I only played this game for 2 hours and i saw everything. All there is to do is look around and mess with items.
The reason the game makes you explore alot is so you can collect all of the items from the multiple biomes, i do actually like this mechanic though, it was fun to explore while it lasted, and even though i didnt use the items it was fun to get them.
The Characters I collected fun to use because they give you different abilitys, like as the vampire you can turn into a bat, or as the wizard you can shoot fireballs. I enjoyed unlocking all of the animals and vehicles too, i used these alot. I used them to get around, blow things up, and just have fun in general. But the placeable items i got, i never used because the game gave me no reason to.
The camera is also really weird and is not fit for building or moving around. you have to hold right click whenever you want to move the camera on your own, otherwise, it just stays in this one position behind you, that does not work well in a game where looking around is all you do.
The game is cool in the concept where you can enter in coordinates and pick the world that you want, this also means that you will be able to get the same word as one of your friends. Or you can just press random until you find a world that looks nice. I actually liked this part.
My final verdict is that this game is a great concept, but it definitely needs editing, and is just not worth your money at this early stage. Maybe when this game gets out of early access it will get better.

Diary of Sir Reginald Fopsworth
Day 1
Friday, 5th of June, 2015
The dive went splendidly. I landed safely on some shrubbery and set about exploring these strange lands as soon as I had found my monocle, which must have come loose in the fall.
This new world truly is entrancing. The landscape changes so quickly it is almost dizzying. I spent most of the afternoon admiring the plant life and various natural, colourful formations, collecting plans for my research. I realised early on that I would need some form of transportation to get around given the sheer size of this place, so as soon as I came across a rather amiable horse (I named the sturdy fellow ‘Chestnut’), I hopped on his back and rode off into the sunset towards a lush-looking forest, hoping to continue my exploration in the dark.
This, as it turns out, was a grave mistake.
As night fell, strange skeletal creatures started to emerge and rove about the forest. In my naivety I approached one, dismounted Chestnut, and tried to strike up a conversation. This bizarre character would have none of it, and instead challenged me to fisticuffs. I refused to engage and tried to talk some sense into it, which seemed to work at first. It eventually lowered its arms, and for a second it seemed to smile -- strangely, sickeningly, disconcertingly.
Then, all of a sudden, a number of these creatures ran out from the trees and formed a gang, which then proceeded to chase after poor Chestnut. The brutes pummelled and hit him with their white claws, uttering strange shrieks and screams as they went. I ran after them in horror and made quick work of them – clearly these awful beasts do not deserve any mercy. Sadly, when I looked up from what was left of them, Chestnut was nowhere to be seen.
I retreated with a heavy heart to my initial landing spot for the night, where I am writing now in a small brick lodging. I don’t know what became of Chestnut. I have seen some of the horses here miraculously make their way up into the trees, so I can only hope that Chestnut will take refuge in the forest’s canopy until sunrise.
These lands may be beautiful, but they are wrought with hidden dangers. The skeletons’ vicious, bloodthirsty cries are still ringing in my ears, and I expect I will have a fitful sleep.
My only consolation is that I have learned an important lesson today: Never, ever trust a skeleton.

Seriously can't recommend this game enough.
This might be one of the best RPG's ever made.
TLDR;
- 2-Component crafting system means it's possible to experiment and actually make things rather than needing to rely on cheat guides. TONS of recipes. Combine almost anything.
- Elemental system is really cool. For example, if someone's standing in a fire, they're less likely to freeze if you hit them with a frost bolt. If they're already frozen, it does more damage. If they're standing in a puddle, the puddle freezes and you slip if you walk on it. If you're standing in a puddle and are hit with electricity, everyone standing in the puddle gets hit.
- Very rewarding and varied levelling system. Gaining a level is a really big deal and you really feel the effects of progress. Skills, talents, and traits add a great variety and customization.
- Very challenging, and takes some time to really learn how to use the battle system effectively (Won't add spoilers here), but it's a lot of fun once you do.
- Best consumable system EVER. Your battles rely on consumable items as much as they do your skills. Grenades, scrolls, and arrows can change a battle.
There's really too much to write. The ony downside is that the start of the game has you running around town a LOT before really getting into battle, which can get boring. Don't get discouraged after town if you start losing fights. Play with the elemental system, use your consumables, and take your time with your turns. Learn to quick-save and load! (F5 and F8)
Seriously buy this game if you like RPG's. This kind of gameplay is what made Final Fantasy so epic.

I am a bit conflicted about whether or not I can recommend this game wholeheartedly.
First of all, I'm an amateur at fighting games. I used to play some street fighter and a few other fighting games that came out on a couple consoles, but I was never anywhere near "good" by any competitive standard. So keep that in mind.
So, where to start...
The art style and world construction are both excellent. The game takes place in a fantasy world of the 1920s or '30s, populated by animal people as well as humans, and of course the martially minded female characters who possess varying levels of magic or otherwise supernatural abilities. As you can see, the art is heavily inspired by Art Deco, and while the world itself is rather fanciful, both the setting and the art feature heavy dark tones. The soundtrack is spot on, in my opinion, featuring nice 1920s style lounge jazz with silky smooth female vocals. Then, of course, there's the fan service, but I don't think I need to say much about that; I'm sure you already know what you think of that all by yourself.
Unfortunately, the writing for the story sections is pretty flimsy. I don't know anybody who gets into a fighting game for the story, but if you're going to do it I think you should probably do it right. Especially when it's just a few terse lines struggling to tie together two fights, a little bit of good writing goes a long way.
And, what about the gameplay itself?
I think that the story and arcade modes are beginner friendly, and both modes are fun when you've got a little time to kill. Not only do the various difficulty levels help you find your own, but the challenges were such that I felt I was learning more about how to use my character of choice effectively. With the move encyclopedia (accessible in battle), and the practice mode, I think there was a good effort made at making the game accessible and learnable by those newer or not as dedicated to fighting games, like myself.
Also, there a number of cool features, such as the ability to choose one character, or a 2 or 3 man tag-team for your versus battles (with each character having 1/2 or 1/3 of max health, depending on the choice), and in 2-round battles the winner keeps their health from the first round, gaining an additional bar when that's depleted.
The multiplayer is really the meat of any fighting game, though; this is where it all hinges. And I do think that the multiplayer can be really fun against someone of a similar skill level, at least when you're both low to mid-level (more on this later). However, the multiplayer infrastructure is set up in such a way that finding someone of a similar skill level is the exception rather than the rule. It selects based, it seems, only upon ping (and not terribly well, even just by that standard. Expect a lot of 260ms ping fights). The result are a lot of really one sided fights that aren't any more fun for the winner than the loser (even as infrequently as I get to be the winner, haha).
Additionally, playing the online multiplayer has raised some doubts about whether Skullgirls is likely to be much fun among the top level players (although I can't really say, not being one). There has been some talk of anti-juggle protection, but regardless of what that actually means a player who knows what they're doing can throw you around until the cows come home; that is to say juggle you, in the ways that leave you completely vulnerable. Once they get you into one of these the result is invariably 60-90% of your max health gone before your character is able to stand up, and then the rest is just mop-up duty. Doesn't this mean that play between two high level players is entirely focussed on who gets in the first hit?  Maybe I'm just too bad to see or know the way out of these juggle chains. It's hard for me to say.
The online multiplayer also lacks any sort of communication, which is definitely best for a fighting game (communication would almost certainly just mean insults and yelling), but it also means that there's no way to develop any community or ties within the game, and means that there's noone giving any advice to those who aren't so good.
Finally, this game is being patched and updated fairly regularly, but it's not an early access, so you can't expect much of this to change in the future.
Conclusion; I DO recommend this game for more amateur players, but only if you're going to play it with friends (or only solo, but where's the fun in that?). Serious players, choose for yourself. The problems that I've listed may be in every fighting game, but that doesn't make them any more likely to attract new blood to the genre. Is this why only the most pigheaded of the competitive seem to play them seriously?

Clearly a love-letter from a seasoned fighting game player to everything that makes games fun for him, Skullgirls doesn't do much that's genuinely new. What it does do is tie together all sorts of disparate mechanics from other games into a well-balanced, cohesive whole that that is constantly updated to make sure it remains fun. And all this is completely ignoring the stunning hand-drawn art, endless little quality-of-life touches and fantastic netcode.
Skullgirls is probably my favourite fighting game and I wholeheartedly recommend it to any fans of the genre, especially those who enjoy MvC, KoF or airdashers/anime fighters.

Skullgirls is a different breed of fighting game. Instead of the common "mash the buttons until I win" formula that is prevalent in games like Smash Bros., Skullgirls puts a special emphasis on attack combos and chaining.
Now I'm no master when it comes to fighting games, my place is more rogue-likes and RTS, but Skullgirls is an excellent way to enter the wonderful world of fighting. The tutorial is vey well put together, and training mode helps you peace together new strategies and get a feel for each character's play-style. Gameplay is good, but I'd suggest tying it yourself or with a friend before you take my advice.
In terms of art direction and style, Skullgirls is an odd animal. All characters and backgrounds are hand-drawn, in a way that mixes anime with that of more Western cartoons. There is also a very big dash of Pre and Post-WWII Deco artstyle. Essentially you can imagine Bioshock banged Kill-La-Kill and Mortal Kombat decided to get in on that, and then this is what their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child was.
My only true problems with the game is that its roster, even with its upcoming DLC characters (Big Band best husbando) is pretty small. The original cast only numbers a meager eight characters, with all DLC characters there is still only about twelve. Hopefully more can be added over time. Despite this, all the characters are fairly good, and bear unique playstyles that you can slowly master.
I'd definitely recommend this game to both beginners and veterans of the fighting genre.

Tom Clancy's The Division is a cover based looter/shooter. If you liked the Borderlands series this could be something you should try out. The entire game takes place in New York City and someone has released a mutated small pox virus and is killing everyone! Your job, in The Division, is to find out who released this and put a stop to them.
First and foremost this game was fun, LONG, challenging and rewarding. I enjoyed Borderlands so this one was a no brainer. The game took me roughly 60 hours to 100% complete. I completed all the quests and found all the collectables.
The difficulty in this game was all over the place. At one moment you're over powered and the next you die in two bullets. If you get surrounded chances are you'll die. There are safe houses all over the world so if you do die and there isn't a respawn point you won't be too far away. During your adventure there are loot boxes all over the world and all the enemies drop loot too.
Loot consists of two primary weapons and a side arm. There are backpacks to hold more gear and armor pieces like gloves, chest pieces, knee pads and more! Gear is standard like you've been accustomed to throughout other games. You have your grey gear (worst), then green gear, blue gear, purple gear, yellow gear and finally a pinkish color gear (best). Each progression in color provides better stats and additional perks. Finally, there's cosmetics. Cosmetics don't provide any benefit and is strictly there for looks. These drop in loot boxes and from enemies as well.
The cover based system was something I'm neutral over. Sometimes it works fine and other times it didn't and when it didn't I died. In example: When I was in cover and I wanted to move in cover I'd sometimes come out of cover. I also had certain times where my skills wouldn't work. It must had been positioning while I was in cover. As you level up in the game you can pick different skills, talents and perks to use and change at any time for FREE! You can also repair and build up a home base. You'll get more skills doing this as well.
You can pick skills that make you a Tank, DPS or a Healer. When you reach end game you will get gear that have set bonus'. When you reach this part this is when the grind comes in to play. There are daily missions and weekly missions. Each give you random gear to help complete your gear sets. You can do a lot of the game solo, but certain missions will need to be done through the matchmaking system. You can use the matchmaking system to queue up with 3 others (4 in total) to play through the games "dungeons".
I hated the matchmaking system. While leveling I'd queue for a match, but start before anyone joined. I only got lucky a couple of times for someone to join my game. All other times no one joined or joined at the very end of my 20-40 mins session. By the time I reached end game this didn't change and was sitting idle in matchmaking for quite some time before I just cancelled out. In my opinion the matchmaking system needs to be reworked.
There is a PvP system and an area strictly for it called The Dark Zone. You can solo the areas or group up just like in PvE. There will be random NPC's that you can kill in The Dark Zone, but real people are in there too so watch your six! If you find gear/weapons while in the Dark Zone you must signal a helicopter to extract your findings. While the helicopter is extracting you must protect it. If you die during this process you will lose PvP experiance and the gear you found will drop and can be picked up by anyone.
There are a lot of things to do once you reach level 30 (max level), but you must wait until then to do so. All the DLC is locked behind level 30. As I previously said it took me 60 hours to get there, but that's because of completionist. I wished they'd space end game DLC out better instead of only at the end.
I had a lot of fun regardless of the problems I had and the enemies could at times take way to long to kill, but a good game nonetheless. The game regularly goes on sale for $20, but you can also grab the gold edition which includes the base game with all the DLC for $38. That price is well worth it as you'll get plenty of game time and even more so with friends playing coop. Worth a single playthrough and definitely a try. 8/10

With just shy of 600 hours in game, I can tell you the game is fun and has a solid structure.  However they have some very glaring issues that need to be resolved before I can recommend the game or even return to playing it. As well I held off writing this review for months in hopes that the devs would fix these issues.
Before I continue, you need to understand that most players join the in game nation that they reside in. US joins US, Brits join the Brits, Spanish to Spain, and so on.
1st, RvR (primary endgame content) is locked out between the hours of 9pm est and 3am est. This means if you are a US based player that does not log in till after 9pm est, you are not allowed to participate in any RvR port battles at all.
2nd, Due to the RvR system, Port Battles can take place during time that are not optimal for a faction. Ie. Attacks by US nation just prior to the lock out at 8pm est is very early in the morning for defending nations. Or other nations attacking the US in the middle of the work day.
These two issues have created friction between nations and players both in game and on the forums. US/AUS players are upset that they are unable to play end game content during their prime time. And non-US/AUS players are upset that port battles can take place during their night.
Due to the size of the player base, Avg around 450 to peak of under 900 players online and the large map, regional servers are not really an option. (don’t be fooled by the NA server, it is mostly dead and still follows the same Lock Out rules above.)
In addition to these issues, the devs of the game, have been mostly silent on the issue. The last they said is that they are thinking about reverting back to an old mechanic of Port Timers. However this mechanic left the game with very similar issues. Ports can only be attacked during the defending nation's prime time. So US/AUS players are unable to attack EU ports and EU players are unable to attack US/AUS ports.
Outside of these issues, the game is overall fun, again the game is overall fun!
Pros:
FUN!, Who doesn’t want to captain a ship during the great age of sail?
Combat is a blast, well designed and in depth, solid damage models and does not feel arcady.
Graphics/Smooth Gameplay: Graphics, yeah they are not the best. The game runs on unity, however the graphics look good for a game that runs as well as it does in early access.
Sea gals!
Cons:
The aforementioned Port Battle mechanic, IE. end game is broken.
The Open World is empty. Aside from a few NPCs, that don’t attack you (devs said they will change that), there is not much to do in open world. Most development has been on PVP. So if you are looking for PVE, hold off.
Pro & Con:
This stuff is good and bad both at the same time.
The trading mechanic is solid and can be fun. However it barely if at all impacts the game. Ships and good ships can be built simply by having the correct buildings in the correct ports. No need to trade with friendly/non-friendly ports.
Crafting as well has a solid base, however needs to be flushed out. Crafting can be done by anyone and everyone so being an expert crafter doesn’t really feel special. If you have the mats, you can build just about any ship.
Diplomacy, again, solid base but needs to be worked on. You are either allied with a nation or at not. Being at war is the same as not allied, you can attack them, they can attack you. War means nothing.
Community, the community can be an awesome group of guys or a really whiny pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They are highly opinionated and passionate about their play style, I’ve seen (and sad to say partaken in) several all out brawls on the forms. That being said, I know some really awesome guys from both inside and outside of my alliance. And without naming names, they have a top notch RP player that adds a lot of depth to the game.
In short, the game is fun and has a LOT of promise, however it also has some broken mechanics that means I can not play the game as intended. Till those are fixed, I can not recommend the game.
Note, the devs have said they hope to come out of Early Access soon. Once done I’ll definitely be revisiting and updating my review then.

Bought this original cause of Empire Total War and Darth Mod's additions to it, though while the ship combat is enjoyable and reminiscent of Empire, the overall gameplay is severly lacking. The combat gameplay itself isn't bad, and at times enjoyable even.  Ships sail like proper ships, you can adjust sails individually to pull off specific maneuvers, guns feel solid, ships feel proper for their class, crews are quite a bit lacking specially compared to Empire but they do exist there to provide a semblance of not sailing a ghost ship.
Though the issue occurs what happens outside of combat, the UI is primative though that's really nothing that can't be easily fixed.  The game is grindy, quite grindy and overall trys to play like Eve Online.  Deaths matter quite a bit, your ships have durability and once that's gone you lose your ship, it is open pvp though there isn't quite the base there to support it.  PVE is mudane, you spend couple minutes sailing to some designated spot to fight a ship that will spend that entire battle just running away from you which is a valid strategy but doesn't quite make for fun gameplay.  Once that's over you get a trickle of xp, barely some gold and sail back for a couple minutes to rinse and repeat for slow progression.  The game does somewhat allow you to play above your level cap in return for paying into a essentially gold sink in the form of crew members, but the paltry rewards never quite make it worth it.  Beyond that there is a semblance of a crafting system, though it isn't anything spectacular or interesting.  Overall PVE is simply just a chore.  If you're playing for the PVP you may have slightly better luck out of the experience, though pvp relies heavily on the people, but without a proper fundation to build the pvp on your experience may vary.
Really a shame given how enjoyable Empire's ship battles were, but in the end this game at it's current state is and unpolished, endless grind that never really seem to get anywhere.

is a game some of you might already have in your library, through a bundle of sorts, and that you never got around to play, because you think 'It's a bundle game like thousands of others in my library'. You are making a terrible mistake.
I had this game for months in my library and never even considered playing it despite it being very short. A very dear friend of mine talked me into it as she discovered my taste in video games, telling me I wouldn't regret it. After a little research, I realized she was not the only one to have only good things to say about the first game of the studio
, as the Steam reviews were close to all being positive. I decided to give it a spin live on my stream, and I really don't regret it.
is the result of a very delicate alchemy which gives the expression
its full meaning. The graphic style will bring gamers in their thirties back to their teenage days, as the game was developed with
, giving it this very nice SNES look. The story itself will put you in the skin of two doctors who will go
on the memories of an old man, exploring his memories, from the most recent to the oldest.
The game is very short, it took me around 4 hours to complete it, but the clock is the last thing you will be looking at. You will totally be absorbed by the game and it wouldn't surprise me if you'd play it in one go without even realizing it. The story can't be compared to any other, it's totally original and you can't stay indifferent to what's going on. The game mixes humor with tragedy, in a delicate brew that will leave you totally hooked and desperate to know what happened.
This game is not very lighthearted, and tackles issues which are currently being debated in most of our societies, like the right to be different, or what it means to stand out, or even the choice to live and die when you want or the way you want. Those pretty heavy topics are nicely compensated with the humor brought by some of the characters or the very funny situations they end up in, but believe me, you won't be laughing at all when the credits will be rolling. The story writers found the perfect balance between laughter and tears, and they definitely made that game the jewel it is.
Because everything is not perfect with this game, as the gameplay can be pretty repetitive (explore a new area, find mementos, solve a puzzle, explore a new area) and you only get to play two characters who spend their time exploring or solving puzzles. But the game mechanics are only here to serve the story, and as you just want to know what happened, you'll pardon everything. The 16-bits graphics might also push away the younger audience, but they give the game a unique style and even manage to make you relate with some of the items (the platyplush made me want one in real life).
This indie game is definitely a must play. It proves that you don't necessarily need extravagant marketing budgets or shiny graphics to produce quality entertainment. Its story is continued regularly through
DLCs and I can't wait to see another game with the same heroes.

Because it's so touching and emotional to me that I know I need to devote one entire sit-down play session to it when I play it again.  I need to be alone.  I need to be in a good mood.  I will cry again.  I'm also hoping this gem gets what it deserves and is released on consoles, where I feel it will get a much bigger audience to try it.  It begs to be played by SO many more than have.  Anyone that has ever played a relatively simple game or more, needs to play this and experience it.  Hell, even people that haven't played games need to play it.
To the Moon is a journey that you won't soon forget.  It is sad.  It is funny.  It is charming.  It is unforgettable.  It is totally worth your time to play.  Set down the Call of Duty's, put away the MOBA's and let WOW go for a day.  Play "To the Moon" and be a better person for it.  Its one achievement for finishing, may just change you life.

In short: It's DosBox emulated. It works, your joysticks might not, and, no, you don't get high-resolution support.

I think it got this game sometime in '97 or '98 in one of those special PC gaming magazine publications that would pack a CD-ROM game once in a while for a pretty good price. I remember I got a bunch of other ones this way like MegaRace, TekWar, Cyberia and LA Blaster.
Terminal Velocity was the kind of game I'd run looking to have some fun for ten minutes but end up playing for an hour or two. The graphics and sound effects were awesome and the gameplay felt great, blowing stuff up on an alien planet with sick weapons, flying a lightning fast ship. Sometimes I wouldn't leave a level without wasting all the enemies and would waste time trying to fly out of the atmosphere into space while grooving to the amazing soundtrack.
The story is set in the year 2704, when the ASFAR (Alliance of Space-Faring Alien Races) of which Earth is a member, suddenly starts a war with Earth by having their fleet ravage the planet. You fly a powerful starfighter, the TV-202, in a series of missions to defeat the enemy. In Episode 3, you learn that a huge supercomputer known as X.I. (Xenocidic Initiative), located on Proxima Seven, is responsible for the war. Your final mission is to eliminate it. A hidden mission can take place after the main plot only in the CD-ROM version where you must investigate a sudden metamorphosis of an unknown nearby planet and destroy the force that changed the face of the planet. It is revealed here that this force drove a man named Sy Wickens into insanity, and how the X.I. Supercomputer had "accidentally" digitized Sy Wickens' persona.
The game is broken up into 4 episodes. The first of which was released as shareware early on. Each episode consists of three planets, or areas you have to complete. Episode 1 has you attacking a massive space cruiser in the Wolf 359 system as the final mission, and in Episode 3 you have to destroy an asteroid that is overrun by enemies in the second mission. Once you completed all missions successfully, you'll be sent to an alien world for a secret mission with no information given.
You can fly with six degrees of freedom and at low speeds without falling. Your craft has no inertia, meaning its course can be changed instantly. There are seven different weapons, ranging from guns, blasters and rockets to homing missiles and a rare secret weapon, and only the first blaster type will never run out of ammo. Additionally, it possesses powerful afterburners that allow it to move at very high speed, which is useful in order to evade attacks, but sacrifices the ability to return fire temporarily (they can be selected like weapons, and if they are, the fire button will ignite the afterburners). The craft is able to survive some hits, and even some collisions with the terrain, including tunnels.
Each of the 27 missions consists of several objectives: enemies that must be destroyed, tunnel entrances and exits, checkpoints and an extraction point.
The game's multiplayer featured eight players over LAN, and two players over modem. Since at the time voice chat was not a common option and typing was difficult in a fast paced dogfight, the game had a dozen pre-recorded clips that could be played as taunts by pressing certain keyboard shortcuts.
Developed by Terminal Reality and published by 3D Realms, it was originally released in 1995. Terminal Velocity is an arcade-style flight combat game, with simpler game controls and physics than flight simulators. It is known for its fast, high-energy action sequences, compared to flight simulators of the time.

A big improvement and i'm glad to see such positive reviews.
-The DLC Policy (Skip if you just want to hear my opinions of the game atm.)
I think people now finally understand the direction CA is going in which is good. Content is being worked on constantly and released as DLC. However unlike games made by say paradox said content is released into your game despite you not paying for it. Meaning when they release a DLC that fixes current factions and adds another. That new faction is still in your game and all the changes are in your game despite you not paying for it. However you will not be able to play the new faction.
Now let me reiterate what that means because people still seem to get annoyed by that. That means if they produce a new unit for a vanilla faction and give you a brand new faction they've worked on. You will receive that new unit and overhaul to your existing owned faction. Any overhaul,units,changes to factions you do not own. Will be in your game however you will not be able to play them directly.
Which means you're receiving a hell of a lot of free content if you choose not to pay for new DLC. For example the original Total War 1 factions are getting an entire overhaul to bring them on par with TW2 factions. They don't need to do this, this won't be locked behind a pay wall and you'll receive it regardless of not owning any DLC.
I imagine they will indeed do the same again for all TW1 and 2 factions when TW3 releases. Meaning despite the massive dlc and expansions they continue to work on, you can indeed experience all of these changes without owning them.
That's the key difference between CA's current model and paradox games as an example.
- The game what i think.
Overhaul TW2 is a massive improvement you can definetely feel the difference between a TW2 faction and a TW1 faction. Which worried me as what if your favourite faction was released prior to TW3? With the news every single faction will be overhauled free of charge as the game is molded and upgraded all those worries have dissipated.
So playing now does feel like playing WoW it's great it's amazing Mortal Empires could as well be the finished game (with some AI improvements which will be released next year.) But you'll be playing Vanilla WoW with expansions on the horizon think of faction DLC as patch content. Each new faction will change the dynamics and behavour of the map. Super powers in one game will be lesser powers in the next. With expansion content new powers will arrive and others will be weakened. This can have problems e.g Wood Elf release making them roll over everyone like the fourth reich but that's whats fun about playing right now!
Yes you could wait for the finished experience or you could enjoy these games atm where a faction will be released and change your entire dynamic of the game. I imagine the finished product may very well have some sense of status quo with particular factions rising to the top every game. Like Dwarfs atm. So if you're on the fence about buying now think about what you'd rather have?
A stable game which doesn't change everytime has all the content and patterns? Or a random chaotic map which changes with every release and playthrough.
I am of the latter which makes me hope the final product will have some sort of Civ-like map tweaker so you can experiment with the different factions.

Reus is a strategy, building game.  In this game you play god or earth.  You have control over 4 giants to manipulate the world as you see fit. The game takes place on a 2D world where you move your giants around to perform tasks for you.  The giants you control have different aspects, forest, swamp, ocean, and rock. These giants are used to create biomes and build your environments around your desires and the villages requests.  Once you create a biome and place an animal, plant, or mineral a village should be attracted to that biome.
After a while the village will make a request depending on the biome and area around the village. These will vary depending on the project and are selected randomly based on what is around the village. If the village is next to an ocean it has a greater chance of doing ocean projects. These projects require certain levels of food, wealth, or tech to complete. The giants are used to place plants, animals, or minerals within the villages influence to meet the required number of each resource.  There is another way to improve these numbers that is through synergies, or symbioses.  An example is if you select lets say a Blueberry plant it will tell you that it needs either a Strawberry or Dandelion next to it to produce more food.  These symbioses range from so much of x being used, x being in influence area, x being next to x, or so much of the nature attribute existing on that tile.
Each of these giants has it’s own little niche that it fills.  The ocean giant creates oceans, these create a wet zone around the ocean for forests and swamps. The ocean giant can also create domestic animals. The ocean giant also has the powers to improve plants, providing more nature, an animal improvement herd, which provides more food, and crystal aspect, that boosts wealth and awe. It also has the ability to heal your giants and provide an aspect boost to tiles.
The rock giant creates mountains. These produce deserts on non-watered tiles away from oceans, or prevent water from getting over them. The rock giant can place minerals in the ground that provide either wealth or tech. It also has the abilities to upgrade wealth of minerals, nobel aspect, or the tech value of minerals, seismic aspect. The rock giant also can improve the wealth of animals with exotic aspect. To cap this his final skill is earthquake one of the combat abilities.  This can be used to stop armies or punish, or destroy cities.
Next up we have the forest giant.  The forest giant can create forests next to oceans, it also can place food plants.  It has improvement aspects of leaf, which improves nature, and fruit, which provides more food on the plant. Another aspect is the aspect of hunt, this makes animals provide food and threat to help keep villages from waring. The forest giant has to powers on of migrate that lets you move resources around, and fertility that grants a higher chance of providing higher level aspects on the tile it is cast on.
Finally we have the swamp giant. The swamp giant can create swamps on tiles next to oceans, and can plant herbs that produce tech. The aspects that the swamp giant controls are exotic, that works the same way as the rock giants, toxic which gives plants more tech, reaction which gives minerals more tech, and predator that gives animals more wealth and danger. The swamp giant also has an ability muck bomb, this is another attack ability that can be used to destroy armies.
You have access to build 3 different biomes, these are swamp, forest, and desert. To create these different biomes you need to do different things. For forest and swamp you need to place them next to an ocean to get water.  deserts you just place a mountain and you will get a dessert that is pointed away from the closest ocean.  These can be placed on the other side of the world and a desert will still be created. In each of these biomes your towns generally have a specialty but you can do what you would like with them.  Deserts towns generally want wealth, swamps tech, and forest towns food.  You can do specialty towns with a town next to the ocean and they gather from the sea or mountains on either side. These last 2 are required for a few unlocks.
At the start of the game your giants usually will have only 2 things unlocked to unlock more of them you need to complete projects that are randomly generated by the towns you have. Once you finish a project you get an ambassador from that village depending on what giant collects this ambassador depends on what gets unlock or improves something already unlocked. For example to unlock the forest giants fruit aspect you need to get a forest ambassador. To improve the fruit aspect you need to collect another. For the final unlock you need 3 forest ambassadors and 1 other ambassador. It’s hard to get the final unlock on the smaller worlds since there is only room for so many villages. The aspects will affect any resource that it is associated too. But depending on the aspect you add and it’s power you can unlock different resources that have different symbioses.  You need to be careful when upgrading tiles that you can get the new synergie or that the upgrade is better than what you would have had with synergy.
Main game play is set by “eras” at the start of the game you pick how long you want to play for.  At first you can only play an era that is 30 min long, after you unlock some achievements you can play the 60 minute era, the final era is 120 min era. After completing these you can go into free play mode but anything you achieve here goes towards unlocking other items. The achievements unlock upgrades to your resources so even though you could upgrade them the game will tell you that you need to improve humanity more to use it. So at first it is better to do the 30 min eras to complete as much as possible and the go up when you need to get the longer achievements. Doing this will make the longer games a little easier since you will have a few more things unlocked to use.
Overall this is a great management/strategy game and I would recommend it.  The only downside is that you only get certain things for finishing achievements I wish a little more was open before things were locked away to achievements.

Reus is far more complicated than it is on first sight. Though that the core elements are simple, and easy, to understand, especially the effects of synergies/symbiosis have to be mastered first so that you can actually dare to build the higher tier projects.
The unlock system is simple, complete an achievement, and if it contains a reward you get a new feature on how to upgrade your plants/mines, etc. Each era (or game) is parted into 30, 60 or 120 minutes lengths, which unlock as you progress in levels. There are 3 levels, 2 to earn, which give access to new ressource options aswell.
Each giant has different abilities, in addition to their normal powers like planting bushes or other ressources, that become available as soon as this giant takes a certain ambassador onto its shoulders. Those are gained by completing building projects. These abilities give you access to moving ressources around or higher damage values for attacks (which you need to defend yourself, if a village becomes too greedy) or upgrade a ressource with either aspect of science, wealth or food, which are the only three ressources needed in the game. You can have up to four ambassadors on each giant.
You can activate different modificators before starting an era, that make gameplay much easier for beginners, but you are then unable to complete higher tier achievements, to unlock the last upgrade stages of ressources. This, in my opinion, adds just the right amount of difficulty. (Yet, I still gained 2 achievements in this alt mode, that were tagged as not achievable in alt mode, cough.)
There are five terrain types, consisting of forest/grassland, swamp and desert, with mountains and water/sea being the last two, though there are no villages to be built on either. Village types are, as you could guess, three, habitating the forest, swamp and desert. Every village in the different terrains wishes for different projects, and they also have a main ressource aswell to finish those
Even though, that the game is cheap, and definitely worth its price, i would really like to see more updates, with more combinations, more natural ressources and upgrades.

The short version.
The game looks good during fights, but the UI is useless, the open world pointless, and progress impossible.
This was once one of the single most promising games on Steam and now a year after launch is worse than I have ever seen it. Had it stopped develoment in the alpha arena test mode it would have been a far better game.
The long version
Once upon a time I purchased this game. Months later I got an alpha key to the testing phase where the game was an arena slug fest between the ships and you could slowly rank up and try more out to test the physics.
Since then everything has gone downhill. My Yacht does not change that and neither did 3+ years of patience.
At first it was a fairly solid game I would have been happy with. Honestly if they scrapped the open world or brought back the arena I would be happy. There is some sort of large pvp mode still in the game but after a year of open world trial I have yet to get it to work.
The UI is almost entirely useless and is entirely confusing. Menus simply exist and action buttons trigger with no explination as to what they do. If you somehow manage to get into the open world expect an eternity of endless sailing with no sort of guidance what so ever until you are beaten to death or simply get bored. The open world itself is ambitious and stunningly large but it is 100% empty and you are reduced to watching a sprite of the boasted ship models lumber through waves like a lazy flash game. The game didnt even include a map for months. With transit times impossibly long and the rewards of travel limited to whatever you can scrape up from the miserable and primitive trade system there is no point to going outside of the ports.
The highlight of the game is still combat. Where before the ships worked moderately well now they have complicated things with crew, officers, upgrades, and quality. Some of this is neat, other things simply add further confusion to the already abysmal UI. After more than a year the upgrades still display bugged. Officers skills do not work. Crew refuse to follow orders or suddenly abandon tasks. There is no feedback to anything you do and any sort of repair is guesswork. After loading into an admirality order combat mission today only one of my chaser weapons loaded, it took more than 20 minutes for it to finaly be useable. Speaking of weaponsm if you somehow manage to get a new ship good luck trying to figure out what type of gun to use on it. There is next to no way to tell without buying and equipping them.
The visuals of this game are still lovely, within their context. The open world is an ugly mess, cities as far as ive seen look entirely the same. There is 0 customization that I am aware of. Crews stand on deck doing a single animation loop eternaly despite the condition of the ship or orders given. The ships themselves are gorgeous, but only in battle, out at sea they are significantly reduced sprites. Inside a port you cannot see anything but a name and a terrible unity basic UI.
Sadly not recommended until significant changes have been made to the game. If I were you I would scrap the open world or put out the arena as a different game. I honestly just want to go back to brawling.

I don't like platformers, rogue-likes/lites, schmups or procedural generation, but I love this game and seems to do it really well.
First and foremost, while the game is challenging, it is easy to jump into. This is a game I wish was on the Switch so that I can play it wherever I go. The gameplay is simple and easy to learn but hard to master. The furthest I've gotten is level 2-3 and I've died a whole lot but I still want to play more. Unlike most other games in this genre, I don't hate redoing the levels because the journey back is just so exhilarating. It embodies the term "replayability" in its purest form -- not for some arbitrary extra content or for completion's sake, but for the sheer amount of fun you can have while playing.
There's something about the verticality of the levels and the ability to just dash through to the next level at breakneck speed without knowing what awaits you that makes the experience very satisfying. You don't have to kill any of the enemies if you don't want to, you'd only kill them for gems that you use to buy upgrades should you choose to. A very simple, cheap and highly entertaining game with a ton of replayability.
I have not experienced any of the technical issues that other people have reported. The only negative I can think of, and this is really a nitpick more than anything, is that at later levels when there are a ton of enemies swarming around you, it is difficult to tell which pixel are you or where you are. This is mostly due to the very simplistic color palettes that both your avatar and enemies use. It would have been better to use a different color scheme for the avatar to make him stand out.
EDIT: I have just played the mobile version of Android and while the game itself is still great, simulated controller schemes don't feel as good as a physical controller. But that is just my personal preference. You do you.

Very rough.
Firstly, the game, unlike its analogies in the genre currently is aimed at very young audience, and not because of the theme, or graphics, but how it functions. The controls are horrible for someone who wants to have control.
But let me start with the requirements. First thing that came up as soon as I loaded the game, is advice to turn graphics down because my config was apparently not enough to run it at, thou it exceeds the minimum requirements by far. Advice to devs: make the game to recognize the system config and configure the grafphcs on the load.
Now back to controls. Most annoying thing is inability to have a control of the camera, it always slips to the default view. Yes, I get the idea that the same control handles both camera and character movement, but that is a very bad design. Put camera on middle mouse and frekking fix it.
The only place where controls win is sticky combat. I maybe a little lazy, but when it comes to coop with other controls, or rather lack of them, I totally appreciate that I dont have to struggle to keep my char faced the right way in order to hit an enemy.
Those controls will be good for a child who doesnt really care about precision and is happy with game doing half of the stuff for them. If controls were a little bit more precice I may have tought on looking forward to updates, but right now Minecraft stays on my machine just for letting me to do what I want, not what devs think I want to do.
Further on, for me, as someone who has a large experience with first person the movement keys confuse. If I use AWSD I expect my character move backward when I press S, not turn around, while my camera sticks in same direction. Either turn the camera OR make char move backward.
Menus are very inconsistent and totally NOT intuitive. On one menu you only have to ESC in order to exit it, in another you got to look for a special button. Every time you have to think, what menu you have opened now and what way will you close it.
Very annoying that there is no option to delete a world from save, and lack of option to start new world instead of trying to find a fine location in the generation the games suggests.
Loving the vehicles. Not so much for mounts, the controls there seem to be little bit more rusty, and there is absolutely no information of what kind of attack the  particular mount has. Same goes for character classes and use of inventory items. The is no indication what so ever of when does mage is using a fireball destroying a building I have been working on for half an hour and when is it a melee attack. There is no indication on what weapon is equiped and it it is going to make a big hole in my castle. I also didnt find a way to unequip a weapon. which again adds a lot ofannoyance with terrain destruction weapons.
Much annoyance of inability to remove the set building or at least to make it stop spawning indefinite number of vehicles.
Liking the thing about lego blocks, their size in scale to character, ability to make so many things and the idea of building out of them. But controls lack in this area too. Most horrible is constant uncotrollble camera spins, which you have to wait for to finishing playing the animation each time you switch from terraforming to building menu. Considering that the option of removing wrongly placed blocks exists only in terraforming menu, this becomes a nightmare.
As for gameplay it looks like this: first time you log, go explore, collect blocks and coins and then can build what you want in any new world, if camera allows. Use coins to unlock some additional objects found in the terrain. I dont know if it was ever intentional to make this to be sort of survival game, but it doesnt work to be a survival at all and in this sense is nothing to be compared to minecraft genre. It is a virtual lego constructor with elements of mario 3d combat, exploration, and horrible navigation and controls system (at least on PC).
If I was to change anything beside fixing controls and navigation, I would encourage the player to keep exploring in order to build something, for example. spend conis on construction isntead of unlocking blocks. I also was expecting from terrain a little bit more than just collecting the coins and dying in lava. Its beautiful, but absolutely useless.

"Space Marine was where 40K explained that the "Gears of War" were actually the little hinges on a pink handbag. Gears of War is a whack-a-mole simulator with fewer colors. You learn someone's true nature in the moments before their death, and in Gears of War, that nature is "cower." The regenerative health system in cover shooters means that the smartest move is huddling where no one can see you and not doing anything until you feel better. That's not a battle strategy, that's hibernation. That crisis response tactic is one couch and a pint of ice cream away from both watching and being Ally McBeal.
The Space Marines don't have a cover button, for the same reason they carry guns instead of white flags made of frilly lace panties. Health recovery is via execution -- if you take a second to kill an enemy with a particularly brutal move, you recover health. That's badassery as a core gameplay mechanic. When you're about to die, your impulse reaction becomes "diving at the enemy to destroy as many as possible" and "wondering why that's not always the case." It's made very clear that if you ever have full health, you're not doing it right. You're not playing endless shooting galleries; you're an engine of war powered by enemy blood." -Luke McKinney, 26 Jan 2013

To sum up this review right away, I will say this is one of the funnest time-wasting pseudo-sandbox games I have ever played. Now onto the real reason why:
Scribblenauts has you playing Maxwell, a little boy with the ability to make anything appear, change, shift, etc. with his handy dandy notebook. His sister Lilly is sick with some weird disease so he has to go out into the world and find little shards of star thingies called "starites" which will hopefully make her all better.
This game is part messing around with whatever strikes your fancy (aka a sandbox), part puzzle, and part adventure. It also requires a little bit of thinking and creativity to get past some head-scratching or seemingly impossible tasks. This game is designed to tap into the ingenious little child you once were, where the possibilities to accomplish anything were endless and only limited by your imagination. You need to get a ball off an old man's lawn without touching the lawn itself? Fly yourself over the lawn in a helicopter and pick it up! Need to get past a killer robot? Dress yourself up in a suit of armor to deflect the attacks!
The art is adorable, the animations seemless and what is humorous to note is to watch how the objects you've brought to life interact with other objects, creatures, and people long after you've set them free or completed a mission. I find myself accidentally unleashing less-than-friendly little beasties on the unsuspecting populace, much to their depleting heart bar and my wry schadenfreude.  The music also fits well with every place you go, perfectly setting the tone to where you are and what you're doing. I have not had the chance to mess with the object editor but from what I can tell by popping in and taking a look around it only adds to the possibilities of further customization of your little adventure.
It is at times so easy to earn starite shards that I sometimes feel like I'm progressing too fast and not enjoying it for what it is, namely a pleasant time-waster, as I've said before. Personally, I find that you can tell a lot about yourself by what beings you bring into the Scribblenaut world to solve your problems. For "man's best friend" I always type in some breed of terrier, and when I can afford to I always use sponges to clean stuff up. Is it familiarity or my lack of thinking outside the box that makes me lean towards these choices? Who knows.
This is a fun game that unlocks the imaginative kid in all of us, and for kids that know their way around a computer this is the perfect game for them to play, too.

After investing 324 hrs into playing TWW2 I finally feel justified in giving a honest opinion.
Is the game good?
Well yes and sort of. The Vortex campaign is phenomenal and a welcome break from the usual "paint the map my colour" formula the TW series is known for. It forces you to act quickly and decisively, trust me, when 3 different factions are having picnics outside your settlement and the majority of your forces are rampaging elsewhere, you kind of need to face these threats. Auto resolve isnt going to help so using every underhanded, sneaky trick with crappy garrison units really tests your mettle.
The ME campaign.......is a love hate relationship. Imagine if you will a mail order bride with perfect pics and no morals or another beautiful women (Scarlett Johansson, Peta Jensen, your mom before she had you) now imagine they packed on a substantial amount of weight, chronic foul breath and can't even make a proper sandwich. That's ME for you. Now that doesnt mean it's total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it just means it needs to shape up a bit more. CA are on top of it and are keeping the community in the loop regarding it's progress, I salute them.
Is it worth paying full price?
for the Vortex campaign alone, yes. the factions are rich, detailed and immersive albeit not 100% lore friendly. It still provides hours of fun. For the ugly duckling that is ME.....only time will tell but I remain positive that this flatulent slob of a lady will soon be a sensuos, scantilly clad, uber chested witch elf, dual daggers in hand!
So to wrap up
if you already have TWW1 with all the DLC buy this diamond in the rough! if not, buy TWW1 and play that untill ME is out of it's "beta phase".

Bought this last summer and played a little bit. At the time, the game was struggling, with server populations dropping. It felt very grindy and I posted a negative review.
They recently did a server reset, and I decided to give this another go. They have split up the XP and crafting systems to encourage varied gameplay. There are PvE marks, PvP marks, and Conquest marks that are part of what you need to make different kinds of ships. There are also more kinds of missions, including solo matches against AI, fleet battles against AI, epic events, delivery, and war effort supplies. And that's just battle options: crafting and trading have depth to them now too. There's just more to do!
I also switched from the PvE server to one of the small nations in PvPGlobal. We had a dutch raiding party show up and try going for a few of our traders near our capitol port. One of the traders got on Teamspeak and the clans mobilized. Next thing you know, the raiders became the chased as a fleet of Surprises and Trincomalees went after them. It was great fun! I worked with an allied pickle who happened to be in the area to take on another surprise in my first real PvP battle.
The game, while still clearly in development, has improved since last year. I'd recommend it!

This game is good. Level up, hunt new gear, decide what class you prefer to play and work as a team. Many gear sets and weapons can be collected, recalibrated and mods added to give you that control over how you want to load yourself up in either PvE or PvP.
Save weapons with specific talents and keep gear sets so that you can change your play style. Change specific character talents to run best with your chosen skills or to benefit the team more. The variety of choices you can make is what gives this game it's playability. You can go nuts and look for the ultimate set up - wether it be solo running or a team player build.
Probably also one of the few games that communication will be critical - so get a mic!
PvE can be fun. Once working through missions you can then start playing them at harder difficulties as you progress your gear level and therefore unlock better gear. Incursions are the superior missions (like raids on MMORPGS) that require more skill and a lot more effort. Then you have survival, underground, dark zone (PvP) and last stand (PvP).
By now if you've read the other reviews you probably know what this game is about. I'm writing this to say that after over a year I rejoined and it's a lot of fun. Quite a few things to choose from to ensure you don't get bored doing the same daily grind missions whilst the flexibility of running different classes keeps things fresh.
Then I got hooked onto Last Stand....
Love it, and hate it at the same time. Love it for all the right reasons: fun, quick, fast-paced action where all maps are objective-based and 90% of your team only care for their K/D ratio - working alongside your teams to take points or to surround a single player and watch him try to dance around a flurry of bullets and not die. It's glorious, it's frustrating - it's fun.
Only thing that let's this game down? Cheaters. PvP dark zone and last stand are awesome fun until you run into them - and you WILL run into them. Not enough being done to keep these bellends from spoiling games. Don't let this stop you from enjoying this game though, there's lots to do and lots of customisation to choose from. Play how you want to play it.
One thing that I also advise to stop the unstoppable boredom of the grind setting in is joining a division community. You'll find this game a lot more fun moving in a team of friends. Only so much playing solo I could do before getting bored to death.
Great to play with friends, it does get repetative on the end game, but if you looking for a easy to roll group game with your mates this one is worth looking at.

Skullgirls' combat system is very unforgiving especially to new players. There is very little room for error in an SG match.
First off, the combat is very fast paced and relies on 50+ hit combos that leave you with roughly 50% HP left. That doesn't sound so bad, but it doesn't end there.
Metagame relies a lot on resets. This means that getting hit by combos leaves you in a defensive position just right beside your opponent. And from there you have a split second to guess his next move or else you get hit by another combo again.
Did I mention almost anything starts a combo? Overhead moves, instant airdash overheads, special moves, and even normal grabs can lead to combos that shave off roughly half your life. So after losing half your life from the first combo, you have only 1 or 2 chances to properly avoid his next move or else you get hit again by another combo effectively killing you or leaving you with roughly 10% HP in just a couple seconds since the start of the match. Skullgirls seriously needs a better combo break mechanic and/or more HP on it's characters as there is very little breathing room if you're on the losing end of the match.
Another frustrating thing about SG's online play is that you spend more time waiting for an opponent rather than actually playing against him. Keyword there is PLAYING. Because spending the match sitting there while watching your opponent use your character as a combo training dummy does NOT count as playing (again, little room for error).
Skullgirls' visuals and sounds are amazing however. The HD hand drawn high frame sprites are impressive. And the overall character and background design along with the music fits well with the Gatsby era theme.
Beautiful and very relaxing.

This is not a hidden object game, nor is it an adventure - not one that you would expect to see on Steam, anyway.  Rescue Lucy is kind of an escape-the-room Flash game.  You know the type - click on everything and see if you can pick it up, or if it will do something when you click.
The box on the bottom left manages your inventory.  Click on that box and select which item you'd like to have in your hand.  Some items need to be merged, which the game will walk you through.  It's pretty much the only instruction you'll get... everything else is click and see.
Enter a room with something scary and you'll have four seconds to take it out or leave the room (it won't chase you.)  If the counter reaches zero, your character will scream, and you'll be back on the intro page.  Just click on Continue Game and go back in - prepared this time, hopefully ;)
The inventory can be fiddly, you have to hit your enemies in just the right place (aim for the chest!) or it won't do any good, and there were some nonsensical solutions, which are a pet peeve of mine.
I generally don't like to write negative reviews, as it's all a matter of personal taste, but I can't recommend paying for this game.  There are plenty of similar games on the 'net that are just as, or more enjoyable, and they're free.
Sorry, devs, I have to give a thumbs down on this one.

Made in a time when flight sims and sci-fi action were THE genres. The game is pretty good, but it was the first in its series, and many of the obvious faults, such as the somewhat bland level design, were objectively improved upon in the later games Fury3 and, my personal favorite, Hellbender.
Apart from one crash, the only problem I encountered was an awkward control situation. This is emulated through DOSBox, which seems to have issues with input hardware detection. Worst case scenario is that the game ignores the analog control of joysticks and gamepads. Instead, it will recognize these motions as regular keyboard presses, and this is a pain for steering. Mouse controls sort of work, but take a lot of tweaking to get just right. I personally found the best option to be a gamepad, steering with the directional buttons and controlling thrust with the right analog stick.
Other than that, this is a blast to play. Fun, fast, and quickly self-explanatory, it just feels good to shoot stuff, and it's entertaining enough for a bit of replay, too.

Having played all games of the series: Terminal Velocity, Fury (cubed), and Hellbender, I still prefer this game to any other, due to its semi-freeform gameplay where you can follow the nav points, or just randomly fly around and shoot anything in your way. (In reality, the game wraps around seamlessly so you'll eventually get where you should be). The gameplay is simialr enough... It's basically you fly around a planet, make occasional forays into the tunnels which turn, rotate, spin, open-and-close, and otherwise make things difficult for you.
For its days, the 3D graphics were fast, and furious, and far less claustrophobic than Descent, which is restricted to tight tunnels. Other than that... you shoot ground installations, airborne targets, ground tanks, turrets, and occasional bosses.
Being an ancient DOS game, peripheral support was good for its day, horrible for modern peripherals.
If you get this in a bundle, enjoy. But I wouldn't pay $6.99 for this, even for nostalgia.
Still the best.. like back in 1997

I've played nearly every Warhammer 40k game to date but this one is easily my favorite. The combat is simple and loose but very intense and enemies come at you with everything they're got. It makes you feel like one BAMF but more than that it makes you feel like you've earned it. If you've played very many WH40k games or are familiar with them at all really, the plot will feel pretty predictable. I wouldn't go as far as saying it's weak, but honestly it's not the story that's going to keep you playing. I can't say I've encounted very many bugs in the game either. Overall it's a neat peek at the WH40k universe, a great way to get the space marine experience, and a downright excellent stress killer.
As for playing online, unfortunately the player base is just about dead and only one PvP mode is actually played anymore. The game is honestly pretty underrated and most people have simply moved on over the years since it's release. Matchmaking for either PvP or co-op survival can take anywhere from 10 minutes to 45 on a bad day. On the bright side, just about everyone I've run into playing online have been really pleasant and there's very little whining and moaning like the 9 year olds you'll find populating the majority of matches in games like Call of Duty. Really it's just a bunch of WH40k nerds that just enjoy playing the game.
PvP is fairly balanced, nothing like the cluster**** you'll find in similar WH40k games like Eternal Crusade. As you progress, you'll unlock new weapons you can use and all armor unlocks are cosmetic. There is a perk system but the really nice perks have to be earned with weapon and armor challenges. The effects are nice, but they don't make you vastly overpowered and it's not uncommon to see players with noob gear whooping maxed ones. Armor customization is pretty neat and all in all it's a fun challenge working towards unlocking them and building your own look.
The co-op survial mode is definitely where I've had the most fun in this game. It takes a really solid team to actually make it the whole way to the end and also beat the bonus wave, but it's one hell of a ride if you do and a lot of fun with friends. If a team doesn't work together, a whole match can fall apart before you know it. If your team gets wiped out, it allows you to start over from the last "checkpoint" and most are more than willing to keep trying over and over to beat it. Players can drop in after it's started if someone leaves the game, which is good because it's pretty hard to beat without 4 players. Like PvP, it can take some time to find a full group through matchmaking though.
Due to the lack of player base online, I highly recommend you skip the Dreadnaught and Chaos Unleashed DLCs if you buy this game. There's few enough players as it is and even less that actually have those DLCs. It's a shame because Chaos Unleashed's co-op maps are actually a lot of fun, but unless you have friends you can coordinate a game with it's just about impossible to get one going through matchmaking. I would also skip the armour set DLCs since you can customize your space marine to look nearly identical to them anyway.
The Space Marine game was originally supposed to be a trilogy, but with Sega acquiring Relic and sticking mainly to strategy games, it's pretty unlikely it's ever going to happen. Personally I'd love to see it and support the idea, but if you're wondering if you should expect more it's probably safe to say no.
