It's really hard to rate the Division based on face value alone.
Firstly, let me start by saying that this game is an RPG style game; not an FPS or TPS. Yes, it has the movement and shooting styles of a TPS; but one headshot won't down an enemy in this game (unlike Ghost Recon: Wildlands).
Alright, now that I have sifted through most people who won't buy this for that very reason (and yes, there are many of those people); let me say this that is game has taken the RPG genre to a new level. I'll break down the game for you into 4 segments: Graphics, Story, Gameplay and RPG elements
GRAPHICS 10/10:
Oh, does this game look gorgeous! Based on a post-apocalyptic (non-zombie) city of Manhattan; this game's graphics look gorgeous! From the sweres leading to hidden quests and missions; to the beautiful Madison Square Garden; to the massive Times Square; this game has made New York look great. But it's not just the big things that matter, the little things do too. Things like shooting glass will leave small fragmnets on the ground, shooting or hitting buckets of paint will make them fall and spill paint on the ground, and many more small things are what make this game look amazing. Planning to buy DLC, my opinion is get Underground. It has random generated worlds that look very nice and present a challenge.
Story 5/10:
If you play a game solely for the story, then I'm sorry, you'll be very disappointed in this game. The story revolves around 5 factions fighting for thr city: The Rioters, The Cleaners; The Rikers; The Last Man Battalion and The Division. The rioters are people in the city who like to break things. The Cleaners are people who like to burn things (literally). The rikers are people who like to shoot things. The LMB are soldiers who were part of the team that tried to contain a masive virus and failed, so they angry. You are part of this Division and as you play through the story you have to take down the leaders of all the factions to reclaim the city for the people. The bad thing about the story mode is that you don't feel that it is a story. It feels more like a series of big quests surrounded by mini-quests. You aren't driven to complete quests.
Gameplay 7/10:
I like the gameplay of this game and its a little difficult to understand at first. There are 2 major zones in the game: The City and The Dark Zone. The City is where you have your PvE encounters and all quests and story missions are included. The Dark Zone is the PvP area, and I generally dont like it. Why? Watch VideoGameDunkey's video on the game and you'll see why. Apart from that there are many enemy types: Standard, Rusher, Heavy, LMG, Sniper, Officer, Leader, Agent. Each of them have a unique attack style; and are different from faction to faction. For example. The Rioter's Rusher is a guy that runs to you wuth a baseball hat, whereas the LMB have a military guy running with an AA-12 (autoshotty) towards you. As far as your player model goes, there are a few times you glitch into the map, and if you dont have a fast PC, you might run into areas that haven't loaded in textures forcing you to slow walk until it loads in. Firing guns are really cool and the assortment available is crazy. Over 60 weapons spread over shotguns, sidearms, SMGs, LMGs, Assault Rifles and Sniper Rifles makes you want to try 'em all before you pick your best.
RPG Elements 10/10:
There is SO much to this game that makes it a unique experience for you. I'll break this segment down for you into 3 major categories: Weapons, Gear and Abilities.
Abilities: The smallest of the bunch having 3 areas to itself called Abilities, Talents and Perks. You get Abilities by unlocking certain areas of the Base of Operations. Talents and Perks also get unlocked as you further improve the base of ops. You have 3 abilities per skill group (read next section) and 1 ultimate ability
Gear: 2 areas for this category: Appearance and Gear. Apperance is 100% cosmetic and doesn't affect your game in any shape or form. Gear on the other hand chnages your playstyle completely based on what you equip. There are 3 areas for you to spec your gear into: Firearms, Stamina and Electronics. Firearms acts as a sort of multiplier to the base stats of the weapons you carry (aside from the perk stats and talents you equip). Stamina makes you moer tanky and improves health regen. Electronics boosts your ability power, health and skill cooldowns. So specing into 1 or 2 areas will yeild different gameplay style for each and every person. Want to take out a boss in less than 10 hits, spec into Firearms and watch his health drop! Want to become the bullet sponge, spec into Stamina! Want to hide in a corner and have your abilities do the work for you, spec into Electronics. If you are lucky, you could even get exotic gear which gives you a special stat or talent not found on any other item. This is where is gets crazy: Gear Talents and Gear Sets. Once you cross the Grey, Green, Blue and Purple tier of items, you get into GOLD tier. Each Gold tier item and Gear set item comes with a unique talent that is RNG. Aisde from that is comes with 3 number values in Firearms, Stamina and Electronics. Even more, there are Major and Minor stats that each gear item gives you. Gear sets are crazy. Collect 3-4 pieces of gear and use them and you get a massive and unique ability for you to use. Deadeye for example makes EVERY hit you shoot with a DMR or SR a critical hit. So damage is just crazy. Classified Gear sets are even better. Get 6 pieces of classified gear and you get all boosts of the regular gear set with addition bonuses for using the 2 extra gear pieces.
Weapons: This is where it gets crazy. Over 60 weapons including 15+ legendary (exotic is the name in-game) weapons. Each weapon comes with Base, Major and Minor stats. Base stats are those like weapon damage, fire rate and mag capacity. Major stats improve on that by adding crit damage, crit chance, armor shred, etc. Minor stats boost you even more with damage to elites and so on. Additionally, each weapon can be equiped with attachments that not only gove you a numbers boost to the weapon, but in some cases actually help you out in the game! For example, you have a 10 round mag in a M44 Carbon with a 12X default scope. If you find or craft attachments for the weapon you get major and minor stats from each attachment, like an ammo boost per mag from an extended mag, or increased optics from a 15X scope.
Overall, I love playing the Division. I have played and hit end-game with 1 of my 4 characters 100% solo. Playing with friends, however, is where so much of the fun in the game lies!
My rating for the Division: 9/10. with friends 11/10

8.75 / 10
(Also if you buy it now, any new characters would be free DLC)

Skullgirls' combat system is very unforgiving especially to new players. There is very little room for error in an SG match.
First off, the combat is very fast paced and relies on 50+ hit combos that leave you with roughly 50% HP left. That doesn't sound so bad, but it doesn't end there.
Metagame relies a lot on resets. This means that getting hit by combos leaves you in a defensive position just right beside your opponent. And from there you have a split second to guess his next move or else you get hit by another combo again.
Did I mention almost anything starts a combo? Overhead moves, instant airdash overheads, special moves, and even normal grabs can lead to combos that shave off roughly half your life. So after losing half your life from the first combo, you have only 1 or 2 chances to properly avoid his next move or else you get hit again by another combo effectively killing you or leaving you with roughly 10% HP in just a couple seconds since the start of the match. Skullgirls seriously needs a better combo break mechanic and/or more HP on it's characters as there is very little breathing room if you're on the losing end of the match.
Another frustrating thing about SG's online play is that you spend more time waiting for an opponent rather than actually playing against him. Keyword there is PLAYING. Because spending the match sitting there while watching your opponent use your character as a combo training dummy does NOT count as playing (again, little room for error).
Skullgirls' visuals and sounds are amazing however. The HD hand drawn high frame sprites are impressive. And the overall character and background design along with the music fits well with the Gatsby era theme.

Review Divinity Original Sin: Enhanced Edition
I give Divinity Original Sin: Enhanced Edition an overall score of 8 out of 10.
Gameplay: 	8
Music:		8
Graphics:	9
Originality:	7
Divinity Original Sin: Enhanced Edition did hold up to my expectations of the game. This is one of the best reviewed RPG games on the market and for good reason. The player starts out on an epic adventure, and the adventures never stops. One of the things I like the most about this game is the mystery part of it. As a player, you basically have to do detective work to do most quests. I also liked the dialogues and the fact that you can choose your own dialogues and the dialogues can have influence on your character traits.
Gameplay: The gameplay is easy especially if you are an experienced RPG player. But the game itself is hard, much harder than I expected it to be. It is very unforgiving to the new player, which makes making progressing even more satisfying. Other than the combat is enjoyable, would be better if there were random mobs or easier ways to gain experience to progress the caracthers.
Music: The music is good, not the best that I have experienced so far in gaming, but not the worst either, hence the 8.
Graphics: The graphics are very good. I like especially the detail in the scenery. One aspect I like about the graphics of the game you can move the camera around the map without moving your character so that you can gain a basic idea of the area (only works with explored areas).
Originality: I find this game oddly familiar when I play it. I was a huge fan of the Baldur’s Gate series and this game reminds me of Baldur’s Gate a lot. It has some similarities mixed in with turn based combat which makes it more tactical. But for the hardcore Baldur’s Gate players, most players used to pause the game in combat so that they can implement their tactic for each specific combat situation.
Hopefully this review will benefit people wanting to know more about this game.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery, while linear, proves to be over-the-top and out-of-the-box.  While fitting into the pixelated art style that is becoming more popular by the minute, this game may be the only one to pull it off in such a gorgeous and vivid way.  Bright colors, unique environments, and the cute little creatures of the forest are all implemented perfectly and without excess noise to drown everything out.  The graphical content of this game never ceases to disappoint.  From a tiny village, to a waterfall going through the middle of the woods, and even a concert venue with a bear, Capybara makes everything work and keep you wanting more.
Sword & Sworcery tells the tale from a Scythian woman’s point of view as she steals a tome and proceeds to fight a towering specter, numerous small triangles that form a larger triangle, and even that mysterious bear inside a tree that is much bigger on the inside. Using the tome to read your, and everyone else’s, thoughts from second person, this title provides a fun and humorous way to keep you coming back.
While this game is short, it is split into sections.  To prolong this game, I recommend playing each session on a different day.  As short as it may be, Sword & Sworcery is a fantastic game with a wonderful soundtrack and is for anyone who likes adventure, pixel-art, art in general, or just having a good time.

This is a game that on it's surface seems simple and♥♥♥♥♥♥easy, but as you delve deeper it actually harbors a very strategic element that comes a pleasant and much needed refresher in a world were every AAA seems to be trying to "outgrey" each other.

This game's budget price justifies its existence.  It is a god game, where the player controls 4 teraforming giants who plant resources on a planet.  Villages form to take advantage of those resources and give missions (called projects in game) to the player, usually revolving around having a certain amount of resources and tile types.  Complete a misison and get an ambassador which empowers a giant letting them built more advance resource types.  To really succeed, a player needs to take advantage of resource "synergies."  For example, you develop a deer node, which gives substantially more food if near certain types of plants.
There are catches.  Villages that grow to quickly may declare war on other villages and wipe them out, depriving the player of a possible mission/ambassador.  If villages get really greedy the may declare war on your giants and attack them!  At some point, it is better to just destroy the village.
The game is at first a lot of fun with a ton of unlockable achievements that let the player unlock new game modes and new resources.  However, the unlocked 2 hour mode is necessary to get some of the more difficult achievements, and is simply to long.  Furthermore, the harder achievements require players to make carefully planned decisions regarding which ambassadors to pair with giants.  So, the game becomes outright tedious.  Spending 2 hours or more (with pausing) only to discover you missed unlocking that one achievement is very disapointing.
Still, a player should give more hours of enjoyment out of this game than the standard FPS single player campaign.  Combine that with a budget price and you have a cheap way to entertain yourself for a week.

Although it seems like a god-game, this is more of a puzzle. With your population divided into Forest, Swamp and Desert villages, and each one having specific resources, and each of them having specific Reactions and Evolution, the game quickly turns into a lot of thinking about where to put your resources, as your villages demand more and more.
While that would make it a really enjoyable game, the unlock system, where you need to complete in-game achievements to be able to make upgrades, puts a dent in the fun, as some of them are annoying or plainly against common sense(Such has having a Village declare and/or win multiple wars).

Tom Clancy's The Division is a cover based looter/shooter.  If you liked the Borderlands series this could be something you should try out.  The entire game takes place in New York City and someone has released a mutated small pox virus and is killing everyone!  Your job, in The Division, is to find out who released this and put a stop to them.
First and foremost this game was fun, LONG, challenging and rewarding.  I enjoyed Borderlands so this one was a no brainer.  The game took me roughly 60 hours to 100% complete.  I completed all the quests and found all the collectables.
The difficulty in this game was all over the place.  At one moment you're over powered and the next you die in two bullets.  If you get surrounded chances are you'll die.  There are safe houses all over the world so if you do die and there isn't a respawn point you won't be too far away.  During your adventure there are loot boxes all over the world and all the enemies drop loot too.
Loot consists of two primary weapons and a side arm.  There are backpacks to hold more gear and armor pieces like gloves, chest pieces, knee pads and more!  Gear is standard like you've been accustomed to throughout other games.  You have your grey gear (worst), then green gear, blue gear, purple gear, yellow gear and finally a pinkish color gear (best).  Each progression in color provides better stats and additional perks.  Finally, there's cosmetics.  Cosmetics don't provide any benefit and is strictly there for looks.  These drop in loot boxes and from enemies as well.
The cover based system was something I'm neutral over.  Sometimes it works fine and other times it didn't and when it didn't I died.  In example:  When I was in cover and I wanted to move in cover I'd sometimes come out of cover.  I also had certain times where my skills wouldn't work.  It must had been positioning while I was in cover.  As you level up in the game you can pick different skills, talents and perks to use and change at any time for FREE!  You can also repair and build up a home base.  You'll get more skills doing this as well.
You can pick skills that make you a Tank, DPS or a Healer.  When you reach end game you will get gear that have set bonus'.  When you reach this part this is when the grind comes in to play.  There are daily missions and weekly missions.  Each give you random gear to help complete your gear sets.  You can do a lot of the game solo, but certain missions will need to be done through the matchmaking system.  You can use the matchmaking system to queue up with 3 others (4 in total) to play through the games "dungeons".
I hated the matchmaking system.  While leveling I'd queue for a match, but start before anyone joined.  I only got lucky a couple of times for someone to join my game.  All other times no one joined or joined at the very end of my 20-40 mins session.  By the time I reached end game this didn't change and was sitting idle in matchmaking for quite some time before I just cancelled out. In my opinion the matchmaking system needs to be reworked.
There is a PvP system and an area strictly for it called The Dark Zone.  You can solo the areas or group up just like in PvE.  There will be random NPC's that you can kill in The Dark Zone, but real people are in there too so watch your six!  If you find gear/weapons while in the Dark Zone you must signal a helicopter to extract your findings.  While the helicopter is extracting you must protect it.  If you die during this process you will lose PvP experiance and the gear you found will drop and can be picked up by anyone.
There are a lot of things to do once you reach level 30 (max level), but you must wait until then to do so.  All the DLC is locked behind level 30.  As I previously said it took me 60 hours to get there, but that's because of completionist.  I wished they'd space end game DLC out better instead of only at the end.
I had a lot of fun regardless of the problems I had and the enemies could at times take way to long to kill, but a good game nonetheless.  The game regularly goes on sale for $20, but you can also grab the gold edition which includes the base game with all the DLC for $38.  That price is well worth it as you'll get plenty of game time and even more so with friends playing coop.  Worth a single playthrough and definitely a try.  8/10

I had heard of Skullgirls a while ago, didn't purchase it because I had never really bought into the 2D fighting genre.  Then I had some spare change, decided to give it a go simply because the artwork was incredibly impressive.
This game is so much deeper than it appears: from a first glance, it's a bunch of scantily clad female characters duking it out through clunky stories with little to no exposition.  But in reality, it is a beautifully animated and well constructed game with intense gameplay (depending on your level of ability), limitless combo possibilities and very challenging gameplay that can be difficult to pick up, but rewarding when you finally get the knack of chaining combos together and holding your own against tougher AI's.
A word to the wise, however: if you're thinking about lobby/online play, don't do it until you're incredibly seasoned.  I've only been playing this game a couple weeks, I've tried two online matches, haven't gotten a single hit in.  The players there are incredibly skilled and competitive, and have mastered chaining, cancelling and all the techniques to maximize their damage potential, so practice as much as possible until you've mastered a character or two before you try it out, otherwise it's honestly a waste of your (and their) time.
Overall, fantastic game, definitely reccommended.

If you’ve played any Tycoon game, you know the basic premise.  The theme is what’s attractive here – developing the very games that we enjoy.  You start off as a single nerd in you garage developing simple games for either the PC or what is supposed to be a C-64 (most of the major platforms between the 80’s and today are represented, albeit with altered names), and slowly grow into a major publisher.  Players gets to add staff, upgrade offices, research technologies, attend trade shows and even engage in a little corporate espionage.  Like many of the best games, Game Dev Tycoon is very easy to learn but rather difficult to master.
Pros:
-A fairly good game engine that requires both financial planning and resource/talent management.  There is no one 100% sureshot way to win the game, and sometimes luck does factor into whether a game will be a success
-Absorbing game-play without being tedious
-Good sense of humor throughout
-Multi-platform, and no issues so far on my Linux machine :)
Cons:
-Graphics are pedestrian … not that it matters that much for this type of game but maybe in the future they will include character / office customization?  Maybe the ability to import logos?
-Some of the major platforms are missing.  No 16-bit computers? (Amiga, Atari ST)  How about the TurboGrafx 16?  That had a fair following.
-Ironically, there is no option to customize delivery platforms according to the game – like using Steam (“Smoke”?) for smaller games instead of shipping them on disc
Verdict:
-Totally recommended.  I hope they plan a sequel.  Definitely worth your tenner if you have any interest in all at Tycoon games.

ALL MY ASSUMPTIONS WERE VALIDATED!

Rescue Lucy brings back the atmosphere of the old and cheap Fighting Fantasy books, but even its decent-ish graphics cannot justify its price point, despite the free DLCs.
First and forefront: Rescue Lucy is a roughly 10-15 minute long Flash game (with two similarly sized free DLC), so any play time over that means the owner was waiting for the cards to drop. As for the content…
There is next to no plot besides what the store page already states. The game plays more like a cheap barebones old Fighting Fantasy book: you wander through a haunted manor, where each room contains either a key-like item, something used as a weapon, or an enemy. Find weapon, use it on specific enemy, and get next item/key to move on. Pure trial and error, repeated a few times—not particularly bad, but only as a short time-waster at large discounts.

Not scary, not challenging, not fun.
So funny story, the first time I died in his game, I had no idea I was in a room with an enemy. I entered a room, the floor was covered with the usual hidden object/adventure game detritus, a gnome with glowing eyes stood stock still in the middle of the room, and a countdown timer appeared in the bottom right corner. Timer hit zero, and that was game over. I did manage to kill one enemy, but it was pretty unsatisfactory.
I think this game's greatest sin is that you don't have context for anything. No reason why you're poking around this house, only thing that tells you if you're in danger is that timer, and all you can to to progress is just click on everything. Your only clue that you did something right is that an item appears in your inventory or an obstacle disappears.
For a flash game from 2000 or so, it might have been just mediocre. In this day in age, it's not even worth the time to install it.

What a weird little number. It comes across as a sort of mix between a hidden object game and a free browser title, but without the ridiculous, tacky charm of the former, and the inoffensive price tag of the latter. Instead, what we get is a little bit of a master class in what not to do with your game design.
In Rescue Lucy you'll move around static screens that make up an old house filled with monsters and a light sprinkling of puzzles. The monsters themselves are a kind of puzzle, as you have to figure out the right item to use against each one to defeat it. I actually really like that idea and think it's an interesting approach that could be really fun and gratifying, but this is where the first showcase of bad design presents itself... The game's item management is g*ddamn awful. Awkward at best, bafflingly unintuitive at worst - finding, understanding and using items is a complete mess and ruins anything good the game might have built up in its favour.
You'll start by tapping at various points on the screen hoping that something you click on will actually be an item you can collect. Then fumble about in the inventory to either equip something you think might possibly have a use somewhere, or else awkwardly try combining items into something more helpful. From that point on, you click on objects and monsters and hope the item you've equipped will work on it and allow you to progress, and if you fail to either kill or escape from a monster within a five second time limit, you'll die before respawning on a previous screen. But as if all that wasn't painful enough, the game's own sense of logic is one of pure imagination.
Some things are pretty obvious and make sense, like using any number of keys you might be holding to open a locked door. But then you get things that are utter gibberish, like using a skeleton's finger to open a door, or killing one type of ghost or spirit with a book of incantations or some such, but then finishing off another one by throwing salt at it. It's hard to tell exactly what the game is thinking and far too often you'll have to rely on total guesswork to push your way through.
The game also comes with two additional pieces of free DLC. These are strange little oddities in themselves as they're wholly unconnected to the main game in everything bar style and offer little else beyond extended playtime as they peak and dip in quality, entertainment and frustration just as much as the main title, improving in some areas, then completely sh*tting the bed in others.
Even if this
a free browser game, I wouldn't be in any huge hurry to point anyone in its direction to try it out (although, given how short each slice on offer is, maybe some people will find some throwaway value in it). But as a product that's on sale and looking to prise you away from your money, I really couldn't tell anyone to invest in this.

Right off the bat I should say that I did notice a few slight improvements in this game compared to Warhammer 1.  Slight enough that it's hard to specify, but it did seem better.
One major problem though.  When I play a Total War campaign, I very methodically secure territory before branching out, always keeping armies within reach of the approaches to my capital.  Pretty basic idea, right?  This game (at least the Vortex campaign) doesn't care about secured territory or approaches to your cities.  It will just spawn 5 full stack armies wherever your armies are not.  The main instance I'm referring to wasn't even "Intervention" armies that the enemy sends when you're doing your Vortext ritual.  You can somewhat anticipate those.  It was 3 Chaos armies, a Skaven and a Dark Elf (I was High Elf).  At that point, the whole campaign is broken for me.  There's nothing strategic about that.  It's not even a challenge, it's just a nuisance the game randomly throws at you.  I'm hoping the Mortal Empires campaign will be better because I do love the Warhammer setting.  In Shogun 2, after you become the Shogun, all of your allies turn on you, and you're suddenly fighting wars on multiple fronts.  THAT is an example of how a Total War game can offer the player a memorable, believable, and surmountable challenge without completely breaking the game mechanics.
Even without the Vortex campaign, a lot of things are missing compared to playing a past Total War campaign (and not naval battles, I can do without those).  360 degree seige battles are the obvious thing to point out.  I'd have to play another old campaign to fully place it.  The campaign map is "bigger" now, but it used to feel more open, and more... strategic.  The Warhammer 1 and 2 maps both feel too constrained by the landscape.  Territories are divided up so that any given territory never borders with more than 2 other territories.  The only strategic option on the campaign map is navigating bottle necks, there is no possibility of using neighboring territories to envelope a turtling enemy.  I can see how it's somewhat necessary for multiplayer campaigns to keep things segmented, but it makes a single player campaign feel contrived.
On the battle map, I miss some of the more advanced controls you had over your units.  Yes, every now and then I actually liked to use the "move forward" function to advance a unit or a formation.  I miss being able to spread individual units to mitigate missle damage, do cavalry wedges, spear walls, etc.  I understand they don't want it to become too micro-heavy, but I think they could have left most of those controls in along with the addition of spells.  Morale also seemed to have a much more reliable and straightforward function than the new "Leadership."  I played some Shogun historical battles earlier today and yep, units start to waiver after taking a cavalry charge to the flank, much like you'd expect.  But if that cavalry runs off to ruin someone else's day, that waivering unit can still potentially recover and regain control of the fight.  Battles don't turn into random scrambles with units kiting back and forth.  You wouldn't believe how refreshing it was to see that.
I wouldn't blame you for thinking this was a negative review.  Nor would I blame you for thinking it was a Shogun 2 review.
All in all I would say I still recommend this game, with a few caveats.  If you're interested in it, it probably won't disappoint.  It's undeniably polished and well-made.  Most of my gripes are subjective and might not bother other players.  It seems to trade authenticity and complexity for a more streamlined experience.  It's a common trend in video games, especially niche games grabbing for a larger audience.  They can't just make a new title with all of the same mechanics, so they opt to make the experience more accessible, but it always comes at the cost of some defining characteristics.
Basically, I wish I could have the graphics and the setting of this game, mixed with everything else from Shogun 2.  Shogun 2 is the best in the series IMO, but I haven't played every single entry in the series to compare.  If you're dying to try a Total War game, and not in love with Warhammer, then Shogun 2 is in the sweet spot for replayability right now.  Still looks amazing, and runs great on modern PC's.  Shogun 2 is the perfect zen moment in the series where everything came together and it looked as good as it played.  From Rome II and beyond, they started to look better than they play.  Thankfully this game is at least better than Rome II.

As a fan of point-and-click games, I tend to enjoy playing even short ones. This is only true if the games are fun, though. Rescue Lucy is certainly not fun. It is "fun"ny in some ways, mostly unintentional ones, but its sheer badness makes it very difficult to recommend. Hence, I do not recommend it. But I am going to explain all of its faults in loving detail, all while questioning myself as to why I subject myself to playing these types of games and writing reviews for them.
Let's talk about the price first. Rescue Lucy costs $2.99 at the time of writing this. That would not be a bad price for a game that lasts a couple of hours. Heck, if it is a really good game, even an hour or so might be justifiable. But no. Rescue Lucy takes about seven minutes to beat if you know what you're doing. I can confirm this because developer had the brilliant idea to record a walkthrough of the game... AND POST IT ON THE BLOODY SALES PAGE. Watch that video and there you go, that's the entire game! Hope you had fun with it!
Now let's say we cut it some slack with the video thing. What if the player doesn't see the walkthrough? How long does it take then? The answer is: it depends on how well you adapt to insane troll logic. There are a lot of stupid things you have to do. You will probably eventually figure out these things by randomly clicking around until you stumble upon the right answer. This makes the game seem longer. But let's face it, the length alone makes it difficult to claim that it's worth even a dollar, much less $2.99. If anything, Rescue Lucy should have been free. I traded a bundle game for it that I wasn't going to play, so I don't feel like I lost anything from getting Rescue Lucy, but I feel sorry for anyone who actually bought this.
So the game has the courtesy to show you how to pick up an item and how to combine items. Other than that, you're on your own. That is unfortunate, as some of the things you have to do are extremely absurd. For instance, the game does not warn you that the monsters waiting in the mansion kill you in five seconds. No kidding, you enter a room, timer ticks down, if you don't get rid of the critter by then, you instantly die. You can usually leave the room after seeing a monster to gather your bearings, select the right item, and walk back in to stab/melt/salt it (yes this is a thing). Sometimes, though, the arrow to go back is not present. Those rooms require you to click on a door, and in those five seconds, you may not realize which is which.
Let me speak of my experience in the first few minutes of the game. I get the idea that this is a point-and-click game. I go into a room. A short dwarf/gnome/leprechaun/who the heck knows is standing in the kitchen. A timer in the lower right-hand corner is going down from five seconds. I look for the arrow to go back. It isn't there. I try to go into my inventory. I am inside it and then a young girl's scream echoes through my headphones. And I'm dead. After going over how stupid this is, I think to myself, "Well, I didn't get very far, it'll be easy to get back at least." No kidding, because it turns out that you don't lose any progress when you die. You get sent back to the front door, but every item you have is still there, and every item you used is still gone, having fulfilled whatever purpose they served. I walked back into the room, gave the whatever-it-was a penny, and it left. Because apparently it was really, really, really easy to bribe it to not eat my seven-to-ten-year-old protagonist.
This first experience left me fairly sour. But that's not all the offensive things Rescue Lucy does. For one thing, the mouse does not change when you move it over things you can interact with. Hovering over a key does nothing until you click on said key. For obvious items and doors, this is not much of an issue. But there are things you can interact with that you might not think to click on until you go pixel hunting. Not having the mouse change is awful, especially since this game has no hint system. I may not like using hint systems, but games like this really should have one. Unless you count the walkthrough, which is more of an instant win button than a hint system.
The tutorial also forgets to mention you can combine more than two items, which left me quite miffed about the whole thing. It probably didn't want to touch the clunky item system any longer than it had to. I don't blame it for that. Having to click on items so frequently to switch them in a separate menu gets tedious, short game or not. The game also commits the sin of not saying what the flipping items are. You get to see pictures of them, but some of them are hard to identify by sight alone. Better hope you use it in the correct place when randomly guessing!
I will note that this is the first game I have ever played from Steam that uses Adobe Flash to run it. I wouldn't care if the game ran well on it. As it is, the game runs mostly fine. There are some odd graphical errors I got at certain points. It could have been worse.
The music loops, and there is only one track of note. I actually kind of liked said track. I didn't mind it looping since I don't get tired of music I like. I wouldn't be surprised if it drove some people insane, though. Graphics-wise, welcome to the game's one strong point. The art is very pretty in several parts. It's actually the main reason I wanted to give Rescue Lucy a try, and the drawings did not disappoint me. Some of the monsters and their death animations look silly as can be, but otherwise, they're nice scenes to look at.
I guess I should mention the story. Lucy the dog runs away and little girl protagonist enters a spoooooky house to find her. She then dies terribly in five seconds to one of the monsters. The end! Or, if you use the continue option/go in prepared/get extremely lucky with the monster encounters, you hopefully find your dog and save her. It's an incredibly basic narrative that only serves to say why the protagonist is going through this house. It works fine for that. What doesn't work is the terrible English translations. No clue how the other languages fare (and there are several of them), but gosh, a proofreader really should have gone over this. The only saving grace there (besides the hilarity of these butchered lines) is that there's barely any words at all. No characterization, no plot beyond the bare bones, you're here just to beat the dumb thing in seven minutes and idle for cards for an hour and fifty-three minutes after that. Because yeah, it has cards. It doesn't have achievements. I honestly don't care whether they have them or not. Neither seem worth it for this rubbish.
(This is also another one of those games that seems to mislabel its cards. The game refers to the dog as Lucy, who you are rescuing, yet the cards call the dog "The Dog" and the protagonist "Lucy." You can tell how much they cared.)
Rescue Lucy has two free DLCs. Congrats to the developer for getting the hint that the content should be free, but they somehow manage to be even worse than the base game. I'll save my complaints on those for their respective pages.
If you are a radical point-and-click gamer who gets this game in a bundle or somehow obtains it for free, maybe it's worth going through Rescue Lucy just to say you did it. I don't think it's worth it even if it was free. It's not the most offensive game I've played, but there's almost nothing going for it and almost everything going against it. If you're morbidly curious about how bad some of the puzzles are, watch the walkthrough. Or if you just enjoy hating life, play it yourself. To people who want an actually good game that will make them feel warm and fuzzy, Rescue Lucy is not for you.

If you're looking at game like this, then you will probably enjoy this one.  It's as competent a Metroidvania style platformer as you can get, and it really isn't possible to get much more beautiful and detailed as the environments in Ori.  Unfortunately simply being the best at things makes the game rather difficult to praise, since anything you can say about it sounds like it applies to countless other games, even though that isn't the case.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a Metroidvania game, but it's focus is more on navigating the perpetually twisted and thorny environments of the forest rather than fighting enemies.  The forest's more violent residents tend to serve more as springboards or unwitting passage openers for Ori than any real threat.  This is fine though since Ori is wonderfully quick and agile, making travel through the forest a joy, and the game provides plenty of times where you will need all that agility, making you never feel like your abilities are only for show.
The other main draw of the game is the detailed environments.  The creators obviously put great thought into how they could make different sections of the forest be different from one another, which sounds silly until you play the game and realize how dull forests have always been in other games.  Every square inch is filled with so many different kinds of plants that I'd need a botanist's help to describe them, which is to say nothing of how the game uses water, rock formations, light, and climate differences, as well as less mundane elements such as fire and ghostly mist.  Appearance isn't the only thing that's detailed, as the game boasts a wonderful soundtrack that plays up the different atmospheres and emotions of the sections, and sound effects that made me realize how sad it is that in most games walking over different types and thicknesses of wood would all sound exactly the same.
The only bad thing I could think of to say about this game is that it's short, which should come as no surprise seeing as it's a platformer and highly detailed, two elements that never signify length.  Of course the game is only twenty dollars rather than the sixty of other games that often find themselves making excuses for their length, but it's still an understandable reason for someone not to buy it.  Despite that I would highly recommend it to anyone who thought any of the elements I described sounded interesting, as this game represents those elements finally realizing their potential in a game.

Well, having been played nearly 200 hours in WH1 and 110 hrs+ in WH2, I would like to share some of my experience with the general gaming community.
Experience in WH1:
First of all, why would I mentioned the game in first title of the trilogy? Well, it's because the map in WH1 was stitched into WH2 under the massive campaign called Mortal Empire (ME).
My initial experience in WH1 was great as I was pumped to be exposed to the warhammer world which I have never even heard of. I was amazed with all the sieges, underpass, field battles, cavalry charges and so on. But after like 50+ hrs, things get boring after you have tried most of the races and there seems to be nothing new anymore. The event triggered gets pretty routine and predicted, the game wasn't dynamic at all. But still it is a decent game.
Don't get me wrong though, I still hate Creative Assembly for charging us the fee on the Blood and Gore graphic effects.
Experience in WH2:
Man the vortex campaign, that was exciting. Four major races clashing together to control the god damn whirling vortex on a continent called Ulthuan. I was so excited that I even get my graphic card upgraded from gtx 950 to gtx 1070 to fully enjoy the ultra graphic settings.
The event was unpredicted, traits on lords and heroes gained are based on actions taken, the ocean is not dull anymore when its fill with treasures and attrition as well (except that there is still no naval battle, meh). Each continents where the 4 major races rest has its unique weather and terrain effect.
Though that I am more than happier in WH2 than WH1, it is not without any cons. The capitals model is not distinct enough, for example, the two legendary lords starting capital on the similar race looks the same. There is not much challenge after you completed the vortex, the buffs are just too epic. I also dislike the fact that I can't have the legendary lords of the race you confederate with, which is a massive meh for me.
Mortal Empires:
Now this is the craziest stuff I have ever heard of. The idea was brilliant the game studio combine the map from the first and second title of the game. I will not discredit CA just because they have some bugs here and there. I mean come on guys, they gave you the extra campaign to spend another hundreds of gaming experience here for free. They could have just walked away after the vortex campaign and move on to the third title of the trilogy, or even get you to put in some bucks for the extra features. If you don't get what I mean, just head back to WH1.
I can't complain.
Overall, well done CA.

So basically there are two types of video game franchises:
There's the type which you need to play every single game to get the full story/optimal experience, like Half-Life, or Hotline Miami.
Then there's the type in which every game is basically the same in plot/gameplay, and you only need the most recent or most highly-rated game, like COD or Assassin's Creed.
This game falls under the second category. It's pretty ok, but Fallout 4 is going to be a vastly superior experience, and Fallout: New Vegas was pretty good, so I'd skip this if I were you. I like the open world and the cool side quests, and plot, but the graphics are out of date (the latest Half-Life game came out a year earlier but it looks so much better), the gameplay could use work, and the weapons just have no "oomph" to them. Compare it to Wolfenstein: The New Order. That game has some real badass weapons, you'll see what I'm talking about.

An atypical fighting game, but one of the best that you can play to introduce yourself to the genre.
HELL YEAH!

Skullgirls is a well-rounded, well-balanced 2D fighter with a roster of memorable characters. There's little overlap between characters (save for the "joke" character Fukua and Filia), but team mechanics can be manipulated to make any of these freakshows a threat.
With a solid tutorial system and a community that thrives on teaching new players how to be successful, Skullgirls is probably the best entry to the world of fighting games. Many of the techniques used in this game translate to other games, but if you're not versed in the genre it's very easy to pick up and learn the combos needed to be successful. I really wanted to like this game. Critics seemed to love it and everyone compared it to old Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale games. I really gave it a try and tried to like it... But it just didn't do it for me. The problems were small, but many. I'll list them below. Also, keep in mind, I was very interested in the co-op play.
*Dialogue issues with multiplayer - In multiplayer only the person that initates dialogue sees and hears the conversation. This is, unless the other character clicks on the target to watch the dialogue. This manually action often takes a few seconds and it means you often miss the beginning of the conversation, but that's not the worst of it. Since players often read faster than the audio, they'll skip ahead before the audio is done. This means you have to read aloung, no problem normally but... With every dialogue choice the watching player is kicked back to the very beginning of the conversation, forcing them to scroll quickly down to try to see what choice was made and keep up.
*Long winded dialogue - The frantic nature of the dialogue would be forgivable if it was short in concise, but it's rather robust. I would typically consider this a virtue, but found myself finding the amount of conversation very tedious. And, if not the one talking, very difficult to keep up with.
*Rock, paper, siscors - Social skills in this game (Intimidate, Bluff, Diplomacy) are all a game of rock, paper, siscors. This isn't a metaphor. You actually choose one of those and the computer randomly chooses one. Your skill merely determines how many "points" you get for a victory. While essentially random, this is worse than random... It gives you the illusion of some kind of control and just makes conversation frustrating and time consuming.
*Item durability - I'm find with equipment breaking, but in the middle of the first dungeon? My sword was trashed shockingly fast. I did find another weapon, but that was getting eaten through pretty quickly as well. And, despite being a couple hours into the game, I still had little idea how to repair items. I would've expected a quality sword to at least stand up through a few quests... But found myself wondering if I'm supposed to carry three or four weapons just in case.
*Movement speed - Kudos for making such a large world. With big towns that make a degree of sense... But... When I'm not in combat, can i move a little faster? I feel like I spent 50% of this game walking around from place to place.
*Inventory management - Limits to inventory seem to be primarily on weight, as you can place containers within containers and gain limitless squares. Which makes me wonder... Why do we have a "square" based inventory system? Why not just a list with a weight total?
*Storyline - I didn't find it particularly clear what we were doing in the first place. Hunting magic users? There seems to be a lot of them, even some random townsfolk. The horrible way to dialogue system is handled in multiplayer didn't help, I missed a lot fo bits speed reading behind my co-op partner. It did seem like instead of starting small with a little quest or job and getting you immersed in the world that there's just a huge cosmological catastrophe you have to fix pretty soon. And all of this at I point where I wasn't even sure where to buy a decent suit of armor.
*Other small issues - Some NPCs, which I assume you are meant not to fight, have tons of action points and can do 10+ things before you can act. Don't mess with the average townsfolk, they aren't just strong in groups (they know flippin' magic!).
Maybe it's better single-player? I don't know. All I know is this is the only game I've every requested a refund for. It wasn't granted either because I spent three hours really trying to like it. So I write this to try and save others the money. This isn't Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale. Yeah, it's the cloest you'll get nowadays... But not close enough.

After spending many hours in the game starting new game after new game I finally beat it and figured to review it. Divinity Original Sin is all those things that people defined it in the tags, but what they forget is that it is difficult. The game requires the player to keep track of where everyone is and where they are, and, to an extent, remember what they say. There are no quest markers in D:OS, there are no "go here" arrows, and there definitely is no hand holding. This is what makes the game fantastic. It poses a challenge that is difficult enough for the player to have to think tactically throughout encounters and to keep track of their gameplay, rather than mindlessly skipping through dialogue to follow the waypoint to the next checkpoint. I'll be the first to admit I probably spent way too much time in some places than I should have
. The best party is you can play this game with a friend. It can be pretty easy to feel burnt out if you get stuck in a game, but having someone there to suffer throught it all with you makes it that much better. I highly recommend buying this game if you are interested in RPGs and enjoy the tactical turn-based combat.

This is not a game, it is a naval simulator, do not expect to succeed or to have a fun time. The game sets you up for failure in the true 1800's naval warfare fashion. Do not expect your Cid Meier Pirates experience, the game play is so slow you will not realize your mistake until it is too late to return it.
The simulator is so accurate it does not allow for enjoyable gameplay. After sailing across the map for hours constantly checking your co-ordinance with the map, there is no "You are here" mark, you might find an enemy that is of lessor strength then you. Upon activating an instance with that ship of lessor strength, for a ship of equal value I never encountered and ships of a higher value destroy you out right, the ship immediately begins to flee. The pursuit will take up to a hour and half and usually ends with you either facing into the wind unable to pursue or a larger ship entering the battle and destroying you. The canon reload time is extremely fast for naval standards or remarkably slow when compared to the pace of other games. Battles are long and usually end in failure, ideal for those of us who don't rely on success to release dopamine. Who wants to succeed to have a good time when it is far more realistic to fail.
The in port actions are not explained within the game and reading through the tutorials I have learned that there is an optimum way of doing things, no competitive tactics or free choice involved. If you want to do things your way you will waste time and lose harder.
Overall, as a simulator this product is amazing! Remarkably true to life, it offers all the frustration of life on board ship at the turn of the 19th century. Be prepared to spend hours sailing and still more chasing after your opponents for little reward, a tiny amount of experience and to end your days haul up on a lee shore. After all, the mariners of the past spent their entire lives chasing after fortunes that were just over the next horizon. We can't all be Admiral Nelson and this game certainly drives that point home.

Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery is one of the most imaginative and beautiful games I’ve played in a while (that’s just my personal preference). The game is like one of those “Where the f*** do I go” kind of games but, I don’t mean that in a bad way as you may think for the quotation sentience. The pixel visuals are really nice. You don’t really have full control of the characters but, I think it make you feel and take in the world and environment more. It’s a funny game but, at the same time, I felt, some sort of serious connection to the character as I got further into the game. I felt… something… at the game ended, which I can’t really explain nor did I expect. Every now and then you trigger random battles, which personally, I really like. At first I didn’t know what to do but you get the hang of it pretty quick.
The game tells you nothing. I like games like that. It doesn’t take your hand and flat out tell you what you need to do next. Other characters in the game give you clue as to what to do next and you take it from there.
Overall I love this game. It’s one of those games that makes me wish I could make my own game. I know a few people wouldn’t but, I would say it’s worth the money and if I didn’t have the game (as in if I had played it at a friend house) I would buy it for myself. Even if I finished it. The gameplay was at times as challenging as technical platformers in the vein of Super Meat Boy, but was rarely even a fraction as frustrating; the worlds and the soundtrack have both been so beautifully crafted that there were times I almost didn't want to finish a segment, just so I could listen a bit longer.
The controls feel incredibly responsive, leading to a flow-like experience as you jump from platform to platform, particularly during the dungeon escape sequences (which were definitely some of the best scenes in the game). There are platforming staples like the wall jump and double jump, but there were also a handful of unique mechanics that brought something special to the game, such as being able to redirect yourself in midair by bouncing off enemy projectiles. The puzzles definitely felt fresh throughout the entire game.
This is a game that has made even my most stoic friends experience a full range of emotions, without needing more than the barest threads of dialog. Moon Studios has done an excellent job of contextual storytelling, and distilling a tale down into it's purest elements.

If you don't know anything about 40k, this is a pretty good introduction.
The gameplay is pretty simple, you're a genetically modified super soldier in absurdly bulky power armor, with guns that shoot miniature rockets, and a chainsaw sword, there are orks, a lot of them, in space. Kill them all. For the Emperor.
You can move surprisingly fast despite being a literal human tank. The guns handle well and have good range.
The melee is pretty simple with only a few combos, but it feels good and you can wade into crowds of the green barbarians swinging your chainsaw sword, or giant ♥♥♥♥ off hammer.
Of course, the orks aren't pushovers, the basic ork has a respectable amount of health and is still dangerous in numbers, the ones with guns and rocket launchers can kill you pretty quickly if you're not careful. And the bigger ones are pretty tough too.
There's also no health kits, to get health back you have to perform a special melee kill on an ork after stunning it. These are quite gruesome and very entertaining to watch. There's also no "Glue yourself to a wall" system, because you're a brick shithouse. Cover is for cowardly xenos and heretics.
Graphically speaking, it's not bad considering it's age, though some of the textures and particles definitely do show. Enviroments are large and open, and there can be dozens of enemies on screen at a time.
A solid game overall, kind of short, but it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
MP is apparently dead though, but that's not really my problem.
8/10, would purge xenos in the name of the Emperor again. Deserves a sequel.

Too much MMORPG and not enough RL.  This game defines bullet sponge.  I understand the need for that in multiplayer, it's meant to be a multiplayer game, and that would be awesome if it scaled... or something?  Single player is hell, which I'm okay with because I think multiplayer games should promote multiplayer combat, but when coop is still a struggle then you might have to look at balancing or scaling... I dunno.
They seem to promote spray and pray over good marksmanship because of the bullet sponge design.   There's not even selective fire on your automatic weapons and even if there was you'd suffer because of bullet sponge enemies.   In every fight you basically have bosses or captains or whatever (white, purple, yellow), they're like Megatron, but not cool robots, but normal looking dudes and they just casually stroll into you as you mag dump into their amazing, otherworldly armour plates.  Mmmm... lame.
Initially when you first start playing, the presentation seems very realistic but the gameplay is far too MMO like without the benefits of an MMO.  No open world, no open tapping where other players can dynamically join in and help you, but mobs that will just stomp you into the ground.  It's artticially inflated difficulty where your tactics and marksmanship play a minimal role.
Anyway I'm still going to give this a thumbs up because they seem to be working hard on it, and there's so much potential.  Also I think so many people are expecting different things from this game without getting to the core issues.  They need to either make this game more realistic, where marksmanship matters, or make it more MMO like with an open world, and open tapping, etc.  You can't have both.  You can't have MMO based enemies in a non-MMO game unless you scale them properly.
TL:DR - A very realistic presentation with awesome cover mechanics, and some of the best graphics I've seen.  All this is hindered by meh gunplay with unrealistic bullet sponge enemies meant for an open world MMORPG.  Single player and coop suffer with bad or non-existant scaling.

Skullgirls is a well-rounded, well-balanced 2D fighter with a roster of memorable characters. There's little overlap between characters (save for the "joke" character Fukua and Filia), but team mechanics can be manipulated to make any of these freakshows a threat.
With a solid tutorial system and a community that thrives on teaching new players how to be successful, Skullgirls is probably the best entry to the world of fighting games. Many of the techniques used in this game translate to other games, but if you're not versed in the genre it's very easy to pick up and learn the combos needed to be successful. Once you have the muscle memory you'll be nailing your opponents to the wall.
Online play tends to be a bit unforgiving, but lobby play lets you find players of similar caliber and hone your skills.
Definitely recommended to anyone interested in exploring fast-paced fighting games.

Good turn based RPG that is fun solo or with a friend.  Start by creating 2 characters, find 2 side characters in the first town, go adventuring with your party of 4.  Plenty of interesting quests, characters and dialogue throughout.  Combat is fine for the most part.  Plenty of skills & spells to learn.  The game gives you descriptions for pretty much everything, including a quest log for guidance.  The game doesn't hold your hand though, which I like.  The game assumes you're not an idiot and can figure out how to have an adventure.  Apparently based on some of the negative reviews, they shouldn't have assumed this.  Unlike many other games, this one will punish you for making bad decisions, especially if you've been given one/multiple warnings not to do something.  Game does have flaws though.
1.  UI can be annoying occasionally.  Sometimes you'll accidentally walk during combat and waste AP when you tried to click to attack an enemy.  Sometimes you'll mean to click on something in a town and accidentally steal an item resulting in the entire town getting mad at you.  Also annoying is that your side characters will get mad at you if you purposely/accidentally attack them and will leave your party forever if you do it too often.
2.  Once you hit the high levels (12, especially 15+) and can start learning master skills, the game becomes a cakewalk.  Enter battle, use master skills, battle over in 1 round.  The late game is not well balanced or even remotely challenging, this includes the endgame area as well as the endgame bosses.
3.  Quicksaving every 5 minutes, just in case, and having a hard save every time you finish a session are your friends.  Game can be buggy here and there.  Getting the teleporter pyramids is a start game quest that somehow never triggered it's completion and was in my quest log the entire game, even though I had them.  Plenty of other bugs, usually not gamebreaking, that you'll run into as well.  Somes traps will instantly kill you, so be prepared for that.
4.  Random loot drops & vendors whose equipment gets better based on your level makes finding loot meaningless.  It's also time consuming going through it.
That said, enjoyed the game alot.  I've never had as much fun stealing paintings in a game before.  Especially funny is when you kill a vendor that you've sold paintings to & 20+ paintings pop out of his corpse.  Also that stupid seeming rain spell that I bought early on as a joke that turns out to be OP early game and useful throughout the game.
I'm not a cRPG player. This turn me into one.

UPDATE:
This game has several horribly implemented “puzzles” that will have you searching the internet for walkthroughs. The world builders/designers re-use several art assets so you won’t have any idea if you are looking at a pressure plate, a harmless drain or a trap when you are wandering aimlessly through the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥content. For the most part, combat is enjoyable but there is no continuity from one fight to the next. Some fights are completely unwinnable using the Classic difficulty and you'll have to build a wall of crates, barrels and baskets to prevent the AI from overwhelming your party while other fights (later) are no challenge at all. Fighting a boss? Watch with irritation as your character’s special abilities are countered with immunity (immunity to knock down, immunity to freeze, immunity to bleeding, etc. etc.). As I progressed closer to the end game I found myself getting more and more angry with the non-intuitive design decisions. I don’t know if I will bother finishing this game as I am running out of drywall in my house to beat my head against.
Changing to do not recommend.
UPDATE AGAIN:
The last several hours of this game are a flipping joke. You can't take a step without having to consult a complete walkthrough. There is a really important quest to resolve the attack on the Homestead (The End of Time) that doesn't actually exist. This means you get to level 21, think you are almost done, but find yourself stuck at a closed door unable to proceed. Thankfully there are 25+ complaints about this bug and a few threads included unapologetic comments from developers stating how to progress.
It is as if everyone on the project gave up on game play making any sense and figured players would give up as well.
Side Note: Notice that none of the people that gave this game shining reviews have more than 30 hours of game play.
If it were not for one of my friends playing co-op I would have given up 50+ hours ago and moved on to something that was actually fun.
LAST UPDATE:
The last few hours of the game FAIL TO WARN YOU that you will no longer be able to teleport back to the End of Time. Customarily there is a popup that would tell player that once they enter an area, they won't be able to leave. This game did not provide this information and we have given up trying to defeat the VOID DRAGON (the last fight).  I'm not buying anything from Larian Studios moving forward.

The game has a reasonable economy system which is constantly being tweaked by the devs to make it fit the server population, mostly with success.

The game will leave early access during 2017, and there will be a wipe before launch, so you might be better off waiting until that to buy the game. The current state is pretty solid, but there are wipes hanging in the air - port wipes (where every port is returned to the original owner realm), and a full assett wipe before launch. Not a complex game, but fun and stylish. The level design and story progression are completely linear, and all visuals and dialogues are set in the cliché universe of Warhammer 40k - however, I like that dystopic sci-fi world. The game is not very hard either, as soon as you understood which weapon to use in certain tactical situations and when to pop your fury buff. A special mechanic is how to regenerate health: Not some food or med kits lying around guarantee your survival, but executing stunned monsters in close combat, which means that your regeneration is not handed out to you, you have to work for it, and I like that, too.
The most remarkable thing about this particular W40k game, apart from the excellent sound effects and voice acting, is your character. It is not a story of "rising from nothing" and becoming a great hero - you already start as one. You are a captain of the Ultramarines, the genetically enhanced elite force of the Emperor in his war against the enemies of mankind, aliens and demons. You are a respected leader amongst your battle brothers, and as every Space Marine has a part of the Emperor himself in his genes, common humans in the Imperial army refer to you as "My Lord" and bend their knees to you. This setting makes it plausible that you are an invincible power armored fighting machine who can single-handedly defeat hordes of opponents with your arsenal of ranged and melee weapons. Plausability is good for immersion, and besides, it feels good to be revered a little!
I was a bit underwhelmed by the final boss fight. After several waves of mobs you already encountered before, you switch to a falling scenario and press buttons prompted to you on the screen. You win by - clicking your mouse as fast as you can. That feels cheap and breaks the immersion almost completely.
With a little more variety in regard to the mobs and a more creative ending, this game could have been very good - like this, it is just "good enough": 6.5/10 from me, for the solo campaign. I have not tried multiplayer yet and cannot comment on that part of the game.

Fallout 3 - Has an inability to run for longer than 20 mins.
OH BETHESDA!

In truth, I've dedicated somewhere in the range of at least 400-500 hours to Fallout 3 across my life, including the PS3 version. Running the game through Fallout Script Extender prohibits time from being logged, but I've dedicated a lot of time to the Capital Wasteland, and yet I've only completed the story once, never explored evil karma, and have only finished two of the DLCs. There is just such a grand level of exploration in this game that it's hard not to daydream about your second, post-apocalyptic life whenever you're away from it.
Though I found myself hard-pressed to engage in the original isometric Interplay titles, Bethesda's 3D take on the setting brings it all to an atmosphere that's borderline life-like, and was the foundation for Obsidian's New Vegas, my all-time favourite video game. Truly, Fallout 3 was a major part of my childhood, and remains a heartily recommendable action-RPG to this day, though I fear a vast majority of its content will become invalidated with the impending release of Fallout 4 (unlike New Vegas, Fallout 3 does not have the combat, dialogue, and variety to survive a direct successor).
Questlines are sparse and relatively linear, with only a couple of different outcomes for most, and many towns simply don't make sense (a village actually built around a bomb, a civilization made exclusively of children, an underpopulated and undergunned slum surrounded by raiders and mutants). There is limited weapon and enemy variety, and navigating sewers and metro tunnels can become enragingly confusing. However, on the flip side, the action is a gory delight, and all of the environments are lovably crafted down to the smallest of details, even if the world abides by its own bizarre sense of logic.
An easy argument in favour of this game is the modding community- an outlet for solving essentially every negative I have listed. However, it is also a display of Bethesda's oftentimes lackluster game design, and does not help anyone seeking a purely vanilla adventure. Overall, anyone looking for a game that's rich in content variety, solid RPG mechanics and a believable world should likely be pointed toward New Vegas (which I more strongly recommend regardless), but otherwise, this is a nice time sink until Fallout 4.

Now, I shall conclude this review with a nigh-perfect score of 8.75/10.

Allow me to sum-up the entire game: The best way to get into fighting games. Skullgirls is a fighting game where you play as eight different women (more if you get the DLC characters), and you battle each other. Each character feels and controls different from one another, and they can be played differently. You can use Peacock as a long ranged fighter, or as a close-up counter machine.
Skullgirls shines in two major parts: the tutorial (I'll get to later), and the controls. The controls are great. With or without a stick, doesn't matter, you'll have a great time. I haven't tried with the mouse and keyboard, but I don't plan to do so. Arcade sticks are the best to play with, if you can afford a great one. If you made one for PC? Great. You'll love this game. Have an XBox 360 controller? Great, you'll love this game with that, too. Also, mapping the controller of your choice is easier than picking which controller to play with. At this time, I've been playing with the Logitech F310 Gamepad, and it's been working great with me.
Now, the tutorial. Honestly, if you wanna get into fighting games, and know how to play them, start here. The tutorial has all of the terms, details, practices, and everything you need to get started. The only thing you need to know is which button does what. It'll tell you do to a "heavy punch", not to press RB. If you know how you mapped the controller, you're already off to a good start.
So far, if you're wondering how the soundtrack and graphics are, it's just awesome. You can get the soundtrack of about $10, which to be is worth it. The animations are all hand-drawn, and look so life-like. The games does run at a good FPS, so seeing what you're opponent is about to do before they do it is great. The backgrounds are beautifully done. You can't help but look at how amazing they are. Heck, they have them so you can get them as your background for you Steam Profile background. It's that good.
Overall, is Skullgirls worth it? Of course it is, and it's hard not to say yes to a game like this. Great controls, great score, great graphics, outstanding characters, and just an amazing time. If you wanna get the game, get it for the $15. It's well worth it. Go buy Skullgirls.

To the Moon is a beautiful, touching, and genuine game. It was easy to settle down with my computer and fall in love with every aspect of the game.
The art style is very unique. It's pixel art, so it's very simplistic in some ways, yet still very complex in others. It is so beautiful, and I found myself admiring all of the different scenes all through the game.
As far as gameplay, there were times where running around trying to figure out what to do next was very tedious, but it was easy to figure out with a little bit of thought. I never found myself stuck for very long, so I'd be back to moving along in the story in no time.
Now, my favorite aspect of the game: story. At first, I wasn't really sure where it was going, but when the final piece of the puzzle was revealed, I felt how much had truly gone into weaving such a tremendous story. It is applicable to real life, it made me feel for the characters (and love them), and when I finally finished the game, I was left with a calm feeling of completion.
I recommend this game to anyone who wants to cry their heart out and still feel like they loved every second of it, because even though the story is sad, it is also thought-provoking and moving. I've taken a lot away from this game, and I think you will too. I eagerly await its sequel because, well, I've fallen in love with our two main characters and can't wait to see what happens next!

Let me tell you right from the beginning: in my opinion this is the best game of 2015.
The graphics and the soundtrack are magnificent! But it is their collaboration (also including the story) that produces an atmosphere I have not seen in a game for years. This is one of those games when you find yourself standing in an area, just looking at the screen and listening to the music.
What is best about this game, though, is the gameplay. Staying true to the Metroidvania style is captures the player with its focus on exploration over fighting. Not to say that there are no fighting sequences, there are and they are masterfully done and do not impede the game’s flow. Yet, the main focus is on finding all the hidden objects and exploring the entire map. It does have its fair share of backtracking, though only if you wish to have 100% rating at the end and even then not to an extent even closely to Metroid titles for instance. Even when you are revisiting areas you never feel like it is forced upon you, as you might just leave it out.
As for the length, this game took me about 9 hours on my first play-through. It can be finished in even less than 3 though (there is an achievement for that). But do not think that it will stop being fun once you have finished it. This game just does not get old. Maybe it is because I am so amazed by it, but I have played through it 9 times and would still pick it up any time again.
All in all I can highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys sidescrollers, exploration games, Metroidvania style games and atmospheric games. Let us hope there will be more like this from Moon Studios.

I played Warhammer Tabletop (Chaos Army) and this game can give you a similar kind of feeling after winning a Multiplayer Battle... i.e  it takes time to build and perfect your army & strategies & become a good player but a win can feel very rewarding, just like in Tabletop. However, unlike the Tabletop, TWW2 battles happen very fast as this is an RTS (Real time strategy) game and not a TBS (Turn based strategy) like Tabletop is and as such it did seem a bit frantic to me at first. I got used to it pretty quickly though playing TWW1 and if you are famililiar with other RTS games then u wont have any problems in that sense.
Sun Tzu once said. So trying out all the various different races is something well worth doing so you can find out how to defeat them and I also found this a lot of fun in Custom Battles & Multiplayer Battles. What I especially like about the Multiplayer mode is that there doesn't seem to be one single build that can beat everyone (like in some games) so that makes it more enjoyable and there are no real options to Pay2Win with micro-transactions. Granted, some factions/races are stronger than others but in the right hands even the weakest factions seem able to win.
The game also has extensive campaign options (solo or multiplayer) including all the Races from TWW1 (well nearly all... Im looking at you NORSCA!) which I also found very enjoyable in Mortal empires mode. The Vortex campaign offers something different to TWW1 with the 4 new races and the Mortal Empires campaign is pretty epic in scale and ambition from Creative Assembly. I'll admit that the Mortal Empires mode has had some teething troubles but it's to be expected from something as ambitious as what CA are attempting here by combining 2 seperate game maps alongside all races & DLC factions. They are updating and fixing bugs with the ME Reprisal update so it's all looking good from my perspective and it hasn't prevented me from enjoying the game immensely.
In summation:
If you are an RTS or Wargame fan & enjoy planning deep strategic builds and playing frantic, fast paced battles with micro management of units/forces then i highly recommend this game in Multiplayer mode.  Campaign mode/battles can also be great fun but there is less emphasis on army builds & deep strategies there as the main focus is on Empire building which many people will also enjoy greatly.
If you are looking for more of a slow paced, Tabletop style TBS (turn based strategy) then you can still find it here in the various campaign modes & by playing those campaign battles in slow motion if you really want to. However, for a true TBS you will need to look elsewhere...
Enjoy!
