I kept meaning to write a review about this game since it came out, but procrastination got the better of me.
I originally played the freeware Hydorah several years ago and liked it enough to give the developer, Locomalito, some donation money. When I heard Super Hydorah was being made, I of course jumped on it as soon as it was released. 
The traditional horizontal shooter style reminds me the most of Gradius. Spefically the Gradius IV/Gradius Gaiden era of the series. This also extends to the music, which has that funky jazz fusion/rock vibe. The controls, gameplay mechanics, and power up system is simple enough where you can dive into it immediately. It provides a good challenge but isn't overwhelmingly daunting. It has multiple paths and several hidden secrets to keep you invested in it. I especially like the fact that you can save/load your progress and pickup on where you left off at any time as you traverse through the multiple paths to the end. 
Overall, I'm going to echo what was mostly said about this game already and say that it is very well crafted. The dev was obviously mindful of the elements that make a good traditional shooter and was sure to craft that into this game. The Gryzor87 composed soundtrack is great too. "No Mercy" in particular I enjoy. For the shooting game fan of any type, this is definitely a must have game.

This is the sickest traditional shoot-em-up I've ever played.
Super Hydorah is oozing with quality. I won't bore you by talking about how great the artwork & music are, just look at the trailer & demo for those. What I would like to mention is how incredibly dialed in the game play is. These guys have mastered the art of making 5-10 projectiles a serious threat, they don't need 5,000 bullets to do that. The game design carefully rewards spatial awareness, reaction time & tactics, over rote memorization and extreme precision. It's difficult, you're gonna die a lot, but the deaths come with minimal frustration. Almost every time I've died, it's provoked a shrug and a "Alright that was a fair call" sentiment. I would say this game is both more difficult, and more fair than any of the great classics, gradius 1/2/3, salamander/life force, etc. 2 player mode is great, if you've got someone that will sit on the couch with you for some good old fashioned gradius fun, definitely give it a try.
The ship uprade system is overall very good. The weapon choices you have before each level are meaningful decisions. Death only knocks a little bit of power off your primary & secondary weapons, which is a lot nicer than sending you back to the stone age every time you fly into a wall. It's difficult at first to build up many speed & special attack upgrades, but the game is managable even when your ship has lost most of it's power. I've had to resort to killing most bosses on my first play through with a peashooter and no speed upgrades left.
I've got a couple minor nitpicks, but they're mostly subjective stuff and shouldn't discourage anyone from trying the game out:
1) I wish there was a little more red & blue color on the ships in 2P mode. When you're flying level, there's only about 5 pixels of identifying color which can make it difficult to tell them apart, especially if your housemate is RUDE and insists on equipping the same weapons as you for each level.
2) It's a little difficult to experiment with special weapons when you're a beginner. I see the need to decrement your special weapon charge count by one on death, that's a good call. But maybe you could be kind enough to only decrement us down to 1 in stead of all the way to 0. ;)

Super Hydorah is a fantastic horizontal shoot 'em up with varied levels and weapons, a killer soundtrack and great graphics. As a fan of games like R-Type and Gradius / Parodius I'm very happy that this game exists and even more that the old freeware version got the "Super" treatment. While the game borrows many elements from classic titles, it feels fresh and unique. Unlike most other shooters of this kind, Super Hydorah supports analog controls. At first I wasn't a fan of this, but after a while I got used to it and even with maxed out speed upgrades you can still maneuver precisely. There are also secrets to find in each stage.
Shoot 'em up veterans will have no problems blazing through the game and even a 1CC run is achievable for most players. That's not to say that the game is easy. The levels are challenging, but fair. Checkpoints within levels and a save system after each stage help newcomers. There are unlimited continues, but if you run out of lives you get send back to the start of the level. Some stages are pretty long and new players might have some trouble beating them. But with the right combination of weapons, sub weapons and bombs every stage and boss can be conquered.

The original Hydorah is free. Go play it. It rocks.
This game is like that game, except Super. Super as in expanded upon and re-balanced in every way you could probably ever want. Shields are just as available as Turbos and Powers, there's more indication when those and the level-up pieces are about to change, the regular bullets are more visible, your controls are better, etc. There are more levels, more weapons, and many changes made to adapt to this. Additionally, there are some changes made to the old levels and even a few bosses just because they could and should be made. If you like Hydorah but don't own this game, you are cheating yourself.
And if the final boss of that version lowers your opinion of the game, then just... don't worry. This version fixes it.

Music: The soundtrack. The soundtrack the soundtrack the soundtrack. Soundtrack? The. Soundtrack.
Sound Effects: I don't think I have ever commented on sound effects. I mean, voice acting, sure, but that to me is its own category. I also want to cater my chatter to the games themselves since oftentimes something stands out on its own and needs to be talked about. That said, the sound effects are crisp, elegant, real, magical. I think crisp is a delicious word; it makes me happy. Crisp. That was the first thing I thought of when I watched the Steam Release video. It carries throughout the game. Moments where there is little music are made vibrant by the sound effects. Not an "oh I hear birds, how realistic" or "oh the people in the distant market, I can hear them!" vibrancy. It goes deeper into an almost trance inducing simplistic beauty. It dances in your mind. It dances with your mind.
Story: Simple. At least to me it wasn't terribly deep, but I admit that I didn't spend an enormous amount of time in the game. The writing is superb though. I was pulled into the mystery of the game mostly becasue I didn't feel I had to be playing the game to be a part of it. The story became part of my own. The woeful errand is mine.
Gameplay (A): The controls and actual gameplay are brutally straightforward and it works. I felt good about accomplishing things but it was more of an "Ah-ha! Got it!" feeling than an "I did it! I can't believe it! YEEEEAAAAHHHH!" feeling. That said, the last part of the game gives you the latter feeling.
Gameplay (B): The way it incorporates into life would have been more engaging if I used twitter. Still, this game got me to actually make a twitter account, so that was something. I haven't used twitter since, so...yeah. Anywho, even despite that element being wasted on this guy I found the way this ties into the real world to be the best thing ever. I am sure some people will think it is lame, but I loved it. I don't want to ruin it, you can always look it up if you want, but it is astronomy related. Nothing complex. Nothing you can't google your way into knowing. But I was enraptured.
Graphics: Obviously not for everyone. I loved them. It manages to be pixel art while also being art. Not all pixel art games are terribly pretty, but this one is. Nostalgia doesn't even have much to do with it. It is an art style and I love what they have done with it.
Overall: I bought it, obviously. I watched the release trailer and knew I had to. I am recommending it. I bought the soundtrack. I fell in love with the mystery and ambiance of this game. You could read a hundred reviews that say this is amazing and you may think it is insipid. I tend to buy indie and sale games that spark my interest. I love trying different games to find ones I like, but a lot of them I don't fall in love with and I am ok with that. If you want to invest some effort then look at my library, my reviews, and what I have spent time playing, then decide.

"The worlds got smaller on release, it used to be large/infinite and now its more limited."
When this game had Infinite Terrain Generation/Super Large Worlds (bought it when it came out and didnt ever reach the end of the world so I dont think there was one at the time) It was so laggy. The reviews rolled in about no one being able to run it at a higher quality without a computer powerful enough to give people radiation (basically the best computer in the market for those who dont get what Im saying.) So they fixed it by reducing the world size to just one large world and it ended up running a lot faster.
When it released, it came out with world size options. You unlock the larger sizes when playing adventure mode and completing the quests. This game now runs well on my Dinosaur of a computer, where the only thing even remotely current is my graphics card and everything else coming from 2004.
and speaking of Quests....
"They added quests to unlock characters and now I have to give up something or complete a building in order to get it instead of getting it for free."
Wow, does anyone know that this is how all games work? Here, let me give a demonstration on how dumb it was to get stuff for free.
What if you bought a game and began to play it, only for it to immediately tell you "Congrats, you won the game," Without you ever having to play a level or even press a button. Does it feel rewarding? No, of course not. The things that games are supposed to do is make it feel like you accomplished something. If this game were to just down right hand you everything, it would be pretty boring wouldn't it?
Also, if you're super lazy about building, you can just spam bricks inside the build zone and build a poorly made roof over the build zone. Works every time.

Legos...its in all likely hood that you still have some laying around in a box somewhere in your home like me.  Our world building sand box got its start with Minecraft, and since then we've all been wondering just when the Lego company would jump on the band wagon.
Well it looks like they finally caught on and now we have a game toat lets us play with Legos once more.
Now this game obviously isn't complete yet since it is in early access, but there is potential.  For those of you who play minecraft, don't expect the same experience here.  First off the controls are very different and you are moving in 3rd person.  The look in general is like that of any other Lego video game out there except that the world is obviously built out of Lego's.  This gives it a look far different from other Lego games and at the same time makes it that much better looking than Minecraft - also you can use a PC enabled XBox controler for it.
When you start playing you have only a limited selection of minifigs to use.  As you explore you will come across more minifigs running around.  You can either just walk up to them to collect them for use, or you have to defeat them in combat to collect them.
And speaking of collecting - stud collecting is still here like it is in other Lego games.  You collect studs from the environment and spend them to unlock minifigs you've collected, weapons, vehicles and other things.  Least to say there is going to be more stuff coming to fill this all out.  You don't however have to collect blocks individually by harvesting them from the environment, their all there right off to use.
As for building, there are a number of prebuilt sets that you can just select and essentially choose where you want to put them.  But there is also an option to change the landscape, and not just by using vehicles.  You can add land mass, take away from it, and even control the shape to some degree as well as the color through painting.  You could even use this process to build structures to some degree.  You can also choose to build with individual lego pieces rather than large groups often chosen for altering the landscape.
But don't be mistaken, while it holds alot of promise its not perfect.  The game needs a good graphics card to run it at its best, but even with reduced graphics settings the game still looks good.  The real downside is the fact that you can't really do any intricate building yet.  There's no doors, windows, joints, or other special peices that would allow you to build impressive Lego models like say an X-Wing, or a Ninjago vehicle. Leisurely paced, story driven, fully voiced, PvE heavy, turn based rpg.
If reading this wall of text is too daunting then you may not like Divinity: Original Sin.
Divinity: Original Sin is full of dialogue and for players who skip this feature are in for a world of hurt. Players who skip dialogue and avoid npc interactions on a first play through will be digging up online walkthroughs within an hour or two of gameplay. Not to say that the game is impossible to aimlessly wonder through but the dialogue gives valuable clues for main quests and side-quests. Ignoring the dialogue will leave a first time player totally lost as to which items to look for and which npcs to talk to in order to advance quest-lines.
Dialogue is one of the pinnacles of D:OS. The world comes alive with every npc having some sort of story that actually connects them to the world. Listening intently brings worldly rewards as npcs in one town may mention a connection to a town or dungeon later down the line. Players may also key into sub plots or long backstories which further fortifies how connected the world really is within D:OS.
Unfortunately one of the major downfalls with D:OS is the quest log and general vagueness of quests. Listening to all the npcs and making mental notes about sub plots can make it difficult to remember what to do next; especially when returning from a good night's sleep. Quest logs are rather vague and barren leaving it up to the player to think long and hard. While thinking long and hard about quest lines is intended to be immersive, the amount of vagueness and lack of specific information in the quest logs can be frustrating. Generally the quest logs are there to jog the memory but do not serve as much guidance. For example a quest log to retrieve a cat's collar fails to tell which beach it was lost at or how the collar was lost. Fortunately most of the time for the main quests players will be following the strings of combat encounters that progress the overlying story.
Combat is at first a steep learning curve especially on the difficulty known as Tactician (1 above normal). The environment plays a large roll in damage potential and strategy; not knowing how the environment works is a big problem. Both the player and the npcs are capable of creating and abusing the available environmental hazards to their benefit. When the environment is under control the players can then use their vast, or small, arsenal of skills and items to strategically strike a victory. Most skills and abilities are diverse enough to make each character unique and able to provide something to the team. The game really comes together when the players coordinate their skills with the environmental hazards.
The downside in combat however is the UI and the visuals can be problematic. The UI Combat Indicator consistently bugs out and fails to accurately display health or who is next in line for the turn based combat. Environmental hazards are often difficult to see or impossible to know where the line is drawn between safe and hazardous. Enemy targets can move out from under the cursor during their idle animation which can make targeting them difficult; mishaps cause players to click-move around the target thus wasting Action Points instead of the intended click-attack to use Action Points to deal damage.
Ultimately D:OS is a great turn based classless system. The dialogue is extensive and the world is tightly interconnected. I would recommend D:OS EE as a nice leisurely paced, story driven, fully voiced, PvE heavy, turn based rpg.
Other Thoughts:
*As for the crafting system, I have not actually tried out yet.
*Skill Tooltips are not always clear
*Players can not view what enemy buffs do.
*Online Wikis seem unfinished, outdated, or straight up incorrect

A really clever game, fusing concepts from platformers, shmups, and roguelikes in a way that feels natural and sui generis. It's hard to believe Downwell isn't the latest entry in some long-established genre. Recommended only for people who love fast-paced action games, as this one demands intense focus and excellent physical execution. That's the core of the game, actually - gravity is always pulling you just a little too hard as you fall down a procedurally generated shaft, zooming through deadly hazards faster than the speed of thought. To control your descent, you have gun boots with limited ammo that stall your momentum, and whose bullets have complex and varied effects on the various structures and monsters populating the shaft. There's a combo/chain system, and randomized items, but the core action is reading the level design as fast as possible, and knowing exactly when it's too much and you need to back off for a millisecond. Totally compelling.

I am not gonna say anything that has been already said. Super Hydorah is a top ten game. Level design, secrets, arms, music, difficulty... All amazing and very well balance.
I would like to mention the continue system, if you understand the philosophy of the developer and the connection his work has with the arcade world, you will understand this system.
When you lose the game you will have the option to continue, if you decide to continue you will lose different things: some ship upgrades, points, you will go back to the beginning of the stage, and also you will see a different ending if you finish the game.
This punishment creates tension on your game play, similar to the one when playing arcade games with real coins. And this is brilliant, the way you play changes dramatically. You feel the rush when you are about to die, you know there is a punishment if you don't perform well enough. If you could continue without consequences like in most of the present games you wouldn't have this feeling.
Locomalito is an archeologist of the video games art. He studies let's say what video games have existed till a particular year, then he released a game that could fit perfectly on that year, thinking on the technology limitations of that particular time. He mimics, pixel art, sounds, style, game play, etc. You can see some examples of that on his catalogue: a master piece for ZX Spectrum called " l'Abbaye des Morts " (it could have been released on 1986), an arcade cabinet called " Death came from Verminest " (it could have been released on 1981). Who would take the time in creating such a games and self imposing the visual technical limitations of those specific years? not to mention doing that for free.
Super Hydorah is a really good game, but also you will appreciate its full potential if you have a well understanding of the Video games as an art form.
And you can apply all I said here to the music, Gryzor87 has done an amazing job, if you don't believe me just wait till you arrive to the level called Verminest on Super Hydorah.

A super well done retro shoot em up. It clearly takes heavy inspiration from games like Gradius, but while feeling modern and polished.
If you have experience with Gradius and liked it, you'll definitely like this. (I personally find it much better and far less frustrating than Gradius.)
If you don't have experience with games like Gradius but ya like shmups, this can still very well be quite appealing for you.
So, onto some basic things the game has:
Your GUNS. You have various weapons at your disposal, specifcally: A Main weapon, a secondary weapon (like mines that shoot below you) and a bomb or active weapon that you get charges to use via a certain powerup. Most levels gives a new weapon unlock upon completion to add to what you can choose from. This can lead to some unique loadouts and even some neat synergies.
POWERUPS. There aren't many, which is fine for a game like this. There are little green orbs and red orbs you'll come across often. When you max out on either your fire power/fire rate will improve. Then there are the main big "3" power ups that you kill special enemies to get. This powerup, when dropped, alternates between a shield, an active weapon use, and speed/mobility upgrade.
Usually, you want to get a shield if you lack one as it protects you from a hit before dying, and then go for the other two. You can have a total of three active weapon charges and the same goes with the speed upgrades. And when you die you lose some of all your power ups.
LEVELS. The levels (from what I've done so far) are very well made and even hold some secrets. They all feel fair and I never felt a death wasn't my fault. Every boss is significantly different from the others and the pacing of the game is very nice as is the difficulty curve.
There are a lot of levels as well. This is an obvious gud thing. And as it says in the features list, the order of what levels you go through are non-linear! There are some branching paths in the level select screen so you can go through one set of levels or the other. There are also some "special" levels which are designed to be extra difficult but also reward a neat item.
AN OBLIGATORY CONCLUSION.
They set out to make a modern Gradius and succeeded in every aspect. It's difficult but fair, and is one of the best shmups ever made I'd say. Heck, I'd say it's easily THE best I've ever played if we're talking horizontal shmups.
And it's worth mentioning that the art style is perfect for capturing the retro look in a crisp, clean way. The soundtrack is also well done and fits perfectly with the game.

The first RPG Maker I ever tried, and it still lives up to its reputation, a bit. After trying this, I tried fan translations of RPG Maker 2000 and 2003, but I won't talk about those since these two are also for sale legitly now. Anyway, back to the RPG Maker on this store page.
It's the first one to have a scripting feature, using Ruby (RGSS 1 version). I'm not much of knowing anything about the Ruby programming, so I can't exactly tell you how it's done. It was an interesting addition to an RPG Maker, and it saves time from Eventing, though Eventing is still an option.
The Database, though not quite as simpler as RPG Maker VX/ACE and RPG Maker MV (I've tried those too), You can make characters, Items, etc. Like the other RPG Maker programs, but not as much, in the system thing. The Vehicle system from 2k/3 isn't there, an that means that there's no way of riding a boat, unless it's either an event, or there's a script (and there is one) that adds this feature back in.
There are three layers for making maps, which is an upgrade from 2k/3's layer system. However, you can use the same amount of tiles as you can on the first layer, the entire tileset is available to you. And of course, there's also the event layer too, and that can use tilesets for a space as well, so it's pretty neat to make a hidden passage, or a moving object with events with.
The default Battle System for the game(s) you make is rather unique, though uses the front view style as in RPG Maker 2000 instead of using the sideview from RPG Maker 2003, what makes this one unique is that you can see your character's in the battle screen, and see the animations, damage numbers, HP, SP, status, etc. instead of just reading text. If you don't like the default battle system, there are scripts available that change this.
RPG Maker XP can import PNG and Jpeg images, as well as a bit more picture formats, though later RPG Makers do the same, RPG Maker XP was the first RPG Maker to do this. You cannot have videos during gameplay, however. That feature was removed, but found a revival in RPG Maker VX ACE.... Sort of. It's more complicated than RPG Maker 2k/3.
Unlike RPG Maker VX ACE and RPG Maker MV, There are no DLC for this software because it's not needed! There were no need to have people pay for DLC in the first place, I'm looking at you RPG Maker VX ACE/MV! This means that you will have to find free resources from the internet and credit the creator(s) of said resources.

As someone who created one of the larger (in terms of game world) commercial games in RPG Maker XP, I must say that this engine is much more versatile then people give it credit for.  First of all, most of the engine's Ruby source code is directly editable, meaning your only limit is your coding skills.  Second, and this applies to all RPG Makers, if you provide all original art, your game won't look like an RPG Maker game (especially if you tweak the UI and systems a bit.)  However, while I do think RPG Maker XP stands on it's own, I would recommend everyone starting new projects to use RPG Maker MV instead, since it can target many more platforms and uses Javascript instead of Ruby.

I've had a lot of fun playing this game, so not reccomending it is something that I do not take lightly. However, I played it long past the point of it being fun and the fun times that I had with it are a distant, albeit a very fond memory. About a year ago, this game was magical. Its world was new and full of promise and possibilities. Most of the people were new to the game and we were all growing in it and shaping its world together. We were all more or less equal and equally searched for good fights and interesting places. The time I spent progressing through ships was pure magic for me; each time I could man a progressively larger ship was exciting. Each time I managed to sail vast distances and find the place I was looking for was pure satisfaction. Then things changed. Some changes made life easier for people and eliminated certain challenges - such as the grid and coordinate system that made traveling vast distances effortless. Other changes drove people from the game. For me, personally, the biggest change was in the players themselves. The novelty wore off after a few months, and soon there were gank squads (pa)trolling different waters and looking for easy targets while running away from a challenge. Finding fair fights became a chore. Trading became a chore. Crafting became a chore. The game itself became a chore and for a while I treated it as such. I would log in, do my trading run or mission grind to raise funds, buy some resources, do some crafting, escape a gank squad, and log off... lather, rinse, repeat... I remember playing Hydorah a few years back.  It was a free game made by from what i know just 2 people, the game designer and a musician.  Despite the game being rough around the edges you could see they were really talented at making these kind of games.
So i was really excited to play this, and it pretty much lives up to what i had hoped.  Super Hydorah is a horizontally scrolling shoot em up in the tradion of Gradius and many others.  If i had to pick a shmup it's most like it would be Gradius Gaiden.  It has awesome pixel art, with authentic looking sprite rotation and zoom effects that look straight out of a 32bit shmup.  It has fantastic variety in levels, and extremely good music.
Unusually for a European made Shmup it has properly balanced gameplay and none of the usual mistakes that are associated with Western made shmups seem to be present.
My only very slight gripe is the ever so slight judderiness that your ship has when moving vertically, it's only very minor and the problem can be reduced by tinkering with the games aspect ratio.
So to sum up if you like these kind of games or just want to appreciate a game made out of love for the genre with great art and music, you should defintley try this.

The old games we remember -- many of them actually kind of suck. That's why Cursed Castle EX and Super Hydorah are so great. They have a nostalgic look to them (the CRT effects are good too) but play better and have more depth than the actual games of old.
One thing the old games excelled at was pixel art. They did amazing things with limited resolutions and palettes. Most new "retro" games try but fall far short of the quality of the classics. But this game looks fantastic, on the same level as the best arcade and console games of the 80s and 90s.

The game itself is pretty solid and fun, the variety is good, campaigns run for a long long time (though you may frequently snowball eventually, making the challenge negligible past a certain mid point, especially with races with strong eco), and essentially plays like any standard total war game - but with additions instead of reskins.
However, similarly to other total war games the diplomacy system it's is greatest weakness and thus there are only really two ways to actually play.
1) You play a horde faction, like Beastmen or Chaos, and you just sort of declare war on anyone and everyone willy nilly when it suits you, because if you try to build an alliance with multiple factions (say you want to make a big alliance of norscan tribes, beastmen, orcs, skaven, etc) your allies will just randomly declare war on each other - since there is no way to make or force AI to ally with each other (but you CAN for whatever reason ask them to break their alliances with other factions), so ultimately there is absolutely no point even trying.
Sometimes I ally with Clan Moulder, a skaven clan that starts near the Chaos starting position and try to help them establish themselves so the other races wont resettle the lands I destroy, but aside from that it is what it is.
2) You play as a faction that actually occupies cities and whatnot, and that have an economy that isn't based around murder bonking every living thing that happens to be in the general dirction you are going.
What you do instead is sign non-aggression pacts with anyone you can trade with, get them to trade with you, and always ALWAYS refuse any sort of alliance whatsoever.
Why? Because for starters, your allies declare war on each other left and right, which is a huge problem if you were somehow assuming that one flank was going to be safe and protected by an ally when it actually isn't going to be at all, and second because your allies will constantly get you dragged into wars you don't want to partake in.
Naturally you'd say "Well of course, you're signing an alliance with them, wars happen", and absolutely, I agree, but then we get to the way the AI calculates WHEN to declare war.
See, the AI, will frequently declare wars on AI's (and also you) who are arbitrarily calculated to have a weaker military power than them, and I say arbitrarily because apparently this doesn't take into account things like, how strong the enemy garrisons are, or what kind of troops they are dealing with (and the strength of troops in auto-resolve is another thing too, a total mess).
So often times an AI will feel like they are hot stuff, declare war on another AI, instantly lose all their armies, and suddenly reduce themselves to mewling for mercy, because quite frankly they aren't all that great at strategy and don't seem to understand the concept of homeland defense.
One would then think, "Well, play on a higher difficulty? That oughta do it no?", well see, I do, but the catch is that the AI doesn't improve on higher difficulties, it just gets more cheats to help it thrive more.
The reason the AI never seems to deal with rebellions, and why they have the ability to conjure full army stacks out of thin air with a non-existent economy, is because they are given these cheats, cheats that increase income, reduce army upkeep (by up to 40% iirc on Legendary, which is HUGE), public order bonuses, research bonuses, etc etc.
Would I RECOMMEND the game?
Sure man, it's a fun and feels a bit different from say, Shogun 2 for sure, and you'll get a decent experience if you want to play a fantasy RTS where you can play as armored knights with wicked axes claiming skulls for khorne, or a greenskin tide, or space lizard people, or tree hugging elves, cannibal ratmen, etc, the theme and setting is very special, and the sheer scale of the game, and the active mod community makes it even more so.
But don't expect the AI to be god knows what in this.
Once you've established yourself ingame, you'll begin to snowball like crazy, and probably, like me, restart your campaigns over and over because you just get too bored to actually finish them with all the auto resolving and turn waiting you end up doing.
Work of art, if you the only complain about this game i have is that there are so many factions you have to wait a long time before it your turn again! 10/10

TL;DR:  After playing Warframe and then a bit of Destiny, I started to really get in the mood for shoot-and-loot type games. I bought this and haven't regretted it. If that's the type of game you're into, this game delivers in spades - this is the most fun I've had with a video game in a long time.
PROS:
- Great gameplay. The weapons and skills you get work smoothly and aren't a pain to use. The snap-to-cover system works great (most of the time. More on that in a moment) and is very fluid. Enemy A.I. is (most of the time) intelligent, and does its best to try to flank you, making moving around to find new cover a must. The loot system is also very rewarding - I am constantly finding new and better gear not just from bosses, but also from regular thugs on the street. Even random civilians. I'd say that this game even has Destiny beat in that regard.
- Great level design. This game's version of New York feels very real and lived in. Almost every building you walk into or alley you turn down feels unique (very little in this game feels like a copy-paste job). The game's sense of scale also makes it feel like you really are walking around a big chunk of a large city.
- Great visuals and sound - This game is beautiful. Everything from the character modeling to the shadowing, even down to posters on the walls were crafted meticulously. If you've played GTA 5 on PC, then you'll have a good idea of what I'm talking about. Many kudos to Massive Entertainment's art department. The sound is great too, with guns sounding realistic and powerful. Superb voice acting and ambient city sounds are also a good plus for this game.
- Active development - I'm a bit late in the game (only just started playing it a week or so ago), but Ubisoft seems to be releasing content for this game on a pretty regular basis. Recently they added new PVP game modes and soon they'll be adding a new area to the map to explore. Can't wait to see what else rolls out.
CONS:
- Glitches - This game can be pretty glitchy at times. Among some of the ones I've ran into so far are: getting stuck in boxes, my character not responding to my instruction to switch cover, Enemies randomly stopping and doing nothing in the middle of combat, the screen gltiching out in the equipment screen, my weapon disappearing from my hands in the equipment screen, and the sound (but not music) cutting out. There were also a few times that the game crashed, but ever since the 1.7.1 update, it hasn't done it.
-Server Lag? - Not sure if it's because I'm currently in the Pacific region and the servers might be stateside, but I will occasionally run into issues like enemies teleporting forward and back and getting shot before the enemy's muzzle flash goes off.
- Mediocre storyline - The story is by no means bad. It fact it can be pretty engaging at times, (that mainly has to do with the side content, like the phones and journals you find laying around) but this is your basic government agency fighting bad guys to restore order type of story. It's been done a thousand times before. The voice acting is great, but none of those voiced characters are particularly engaging. And unsurpisingly your character is the typical voiceless protoganist.
- Little music variety - The music in the game is great...whenever it plays. You'll often be left with upwards of 30 minutes with no music whatsoever playing. It mainly only plays during combat, during the transition from day to night and when you go into an Underground mission. I would have liked to have seen just a bit more tracks playing when I'm just strolling down the street.

Probably my favorite fighter currently on steam (though it seems ASW has added some titles recently).  Overall a fantastic game that I would highly recommend.
The gameplay itself is great, with the only real issue being the limited roster (hopefully to be fixed with the addition of more dlc characters which are free for a short time).  Each character has a number of combos they can preform and no two players will likely play a character the same way.  Additionally, the ability to control 1,2, or 3 characters in a match adds more depth by adding the options for assists and comboing with meter attacks (meter being known as "dramatic tension" in skullgirls or something like that).
The gameplay can be a bit complicated (not unusual  for a fighter) and new players can be quickly overwhelmed if they jump into an online match right away (most opponents will be better than the AI opponents on nightmare difficulty).  Thankfully, skullgirls has an indepth tutorial system that is probably the best I've seen in a fighting game.  It covers every major gameplay element and serves as a wonderful introduction to the basic principles of 2d fighters.  Seeing as many aspects such as blocking and mix-ups are done similarly in Skullgirls as they are in many other fighters, the tutorial system makes Skullgirls an excellent place to start for those wishing to break into the genre.
The soundtrack of the game is excellent and does a good job at setting the mood of the game.  It isn't the most memorable, but it is certaintly better than average and a few tracks in particular stick out.
Visually the game excells.  The character models are drawn beautifully as well as the backgrounds and attacking frames.  The character design is excellent and left me with no misgivings as to the success of the game in the male demographic.
Overall, I'd put this at about an 8.8/10 making it my favorite fighter currently on Steam.  Would highly recommend.

What I always liked about this game was the simplicity of the experience. You're a Space Marine. There are orks. You kill orks. For the Emperor.
If you don't already know Warhammer 40k, here's the deal: 40,000 years into the future, the human Imperium worships their God-Emperor (he didn't exactly want the job of being called God), and spans a million worlds. There's several alien species which would be happy to exterminate humanity (and each other), as well as a sort of parallel-dimension-spirit-world that can corrupt things on this side.
In this, you play as a Space Marine: A genetically and surgically augmented supersoldier who can live for centuries (but will probably be killed in battle before then), and has some thoughtful extras like three lungs and two hearts and their skeletal growth includes their ribcage fusing into a essential a solid sheet for better organ protection. Then they're put into armor that makes them even stronger and faster. Right, you play as one of them. And you're given a gun that shoots small rocket-propelled grenades designed to penetrate then explode inside the target, and given a chainsword (that is, a chainsaw with a hilt).
Gameplay switches between God-of-War-esque Beat-em-Up action and over-the-shoulder-shooter very smoothly, and it needs to; you'll run into mixed groups of ranged and melee enemies pretty quickly. Difficulty is a surprisingly natural curve, too. You'll see enemies who need specialized moves or combos to defeat--you might encounter one by itself the first time, and then after that you'll run into a group of three or four. As the game goes on, things escalate and early-game enemies aren't ever quite obsolete. Another nice touch is your health regen is accomplished by doing execution-type kills on stunned enemies. There aren't health pickups; if you're on low health you have to charge something and prove hard enough.
This is one of those definite "grab it on sale" games. Gameplay is simple, but it's fun and challenging.

My major 'problems' with this game?
1] I have a party where only one member has a healing skill ... for just 10%. This results in after a (tough) fight; healing spell, wait for (relative long) cooldown => repeat 10 times or (much) more. I have spend way more time waiting on the damn cooldown after combat than in combat itself. Maybe with a different characte/party setup things would be better, but I fear I'd end up with a party that is great at healing but sucks at other things. In essence I do not trust the balancing of this game.
2] The elemental subsystems. Nice idea, but it breaks down too easily and too often and is used way too much. For example you WILL end up in situations where you have no way to counter/negate a certain element ... so you're 'stuck', or muddle through hoping for enough luck with the randomised damage. For example the party AI is such that party members walk through harmful substances when there is an easy way around it. So to me, instead of an interesting tactical component in combat, it ends up as an irritating subsystem.

First off, let me say to those poor souls that have not been buying this game due to bad reviews, i am sorry. Here is why you should give this game a true chance, and I think you will find most people whining on here just wanted easy game play.
-First and foremost, the teleport thing. I am tired of seeing people cry about teleporting in here, then in game rage quit because they got caught and couldnt teleport away. The teleport only works every 3 hours, and it only teleports you to your main capital. You can however move from outpost to outpost once you have docked your ship in a city with an outpost to another outpost, in a sense teleporting. This is simply due to the time it takes to sail, do you really want to sail for 5 hours to go to somewhere that only requires you to be there for 2 minutes for?
-The TRUTH ABOUT THE DEVS.
The Developers of this game are not all English, so of course there is sometimes a slight language barrier. However i have dealt with and happily worked with these Devs since January of 2016, and let me tell you. These guys work hard as all heck to get it right. They believe in taking the time it requires to test everything out, from extreme to extreme in order to find a balance and the best possible way to allow for pvp in the pvp servers, and give good pve in the pve servers. I have lost several ships to glitches (its Early Access it happens) the devs know that, and they completely brought those ships, and everything on it back from Davy Jones' locker several times for me and several other players.
The devs on this game take a lot of crap from players that dont understand how to test a game completely with a smaller playerbase, it really is as simple as that. The devs want to try everything out because honestly, this game while not the complete first of its kind, has reached a point where no other sailing game has ever gone before or even gotten close to. It is required of the smaller dev team to work on one thing at a time from most to least important to find balance, try radical things to see what happens and how to fix any errors in game and to truly know how to further develope the game.
-This game has so many great things, my favorite is the AMAZING GRAPHICS. And i mean truly breath taking graphics. For once in gaming history, the screenshots on the store page need to be taken down because they are not good enough to show what this game looks like on med-high settings.  With the amazing graphics also comes the support of and almost a symbiotic relation with the physics engine, its awesome, needs some work, but its still awesome none the less.
THE BAD...
-If you dont enjoy a grind.. This game forces you to do well and do it often in order to advance ship wise and crafting wise.
-Like i mentioned, the updates take a bit, usually once a month for major updates, but patches come for the next 3 days generally after a major update. I think its worth it.
-Right now the player base is small, and this game needs a larger player base, i am writing this review to help that, everyone on this game wants you to buy it and join their nation, the mroe people that play, the more fun this game truly is. especially in the pvp server.

Downwell is a simple game, with a very simple premise; you grab your gun boots and fight your way down an expansive randomised well. Presented in a very simplistic art style and music straight out of the 8-bit gaming days, Downwell’s gameplay is the main focus of the game with concepts such as story being obsolete. You find yourself equipped with the ability to move, jump, and shoot your might gun boots, which you then use to fight your way down the well's shaft. This game is a good time with addicting gameplay, various weapons and powerups to try out, and tons of replayability with its roguelike level generation, there is a lot of fun to be found in this little package.

First off, this is a great game, and for the price of £1.99, you'd be mad not to give it a go. Downwell is a game you must play in short bursts every now and again to truly appreciate, and while some people deem it addictive, I don't see it. Luckily, the game is fun enough to be able to play for tens of hours, however there is not much keeping you attatched to it. This is actually a good thing, since the fast paced repetitive action is indeed very repetitive, by the millionth run in a row it starts becoming rather dry.

Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
A fun, but shallow game. Lack of depth/challenge and any sort of immersion take away from the overall experience. The original Escapists is much more fun and there are far better zombie survival games available. Wait for a 66-75% off Steam Sale. 2.5/5.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
The Escapists : The Walking Dead was released on September 30th by Team 17 Digital. Obviously this is the same team that brought us the original Escapists game. A fantastic little game in which you live out day to day prison life while plotting and executing an escape. This game is exactly what it sounds like. They've taken the walking dead franchise and dropped it into the Escapists environment. Replacing prison life with life as a survivor living in a survivor camp. A lot of the same gameplay elements from the original are present.
You play the game as Rick Grimes. As i just mentioned, a lot of the gameplay elements will be familiar to those gamers who have played The Escapists. You've got a schedule to keep. Theres roll call, you have your meal times, some daily chores and of course you have free time which you can use to find and craft items and weapons. There are also tasks which you must complete in order to move to the next map.
Much like the gameplay,  the graphics and sounds are very similar to the original Escapists. In fact, the graphics even appear to be slightly improved. The control scheme also is improved upon from the original with a few slight changes. It is easy to say that, all in all, the actual basics of the game itself have improved.
Unfortunately, the game just misses the mark. I enjoy the original Escapists much more than i have enjoyed this version. It simply falls short for me as a zombie survival game. The levels seem shorter and easier than they should be and there dont seem to be very many of them at all. It simply seems much....shallower than one would expect. This gamer simply cant justify a rating any higher than a 2.5 out of 5. This gamer advises waiting for that magical 66-75% off on a Steam sale before biting.
Happy Gaming!!!

[TLDR AT BOTTOM] I don't recommend buying this game and here's why.
First off, I've enjoyed two campaigns so far with nearly 200 hours played as of writing. For $60 I would agree it's worth it. In the end however I regret supporting Creative Assembly and the continued dumbing down of what was once my favorite series.
Some of my most endorphin pumping moments I've experienced gaming are owed to Rome 1 & 2. Moments like being vastly outnumbered sweating each second desperately trying to deploy my spare unit of pikemen in a spear wall formation to stop an imminent cavalry charge at my flank meanwhile bringing down my own hammer (cavalry) into the defenseless flank of the enemies line.  Trying my best to form both units of heavy calvary into wedge formations and time the impacts of their combined charge just right as to trigger mass panic amongst the heart of his infantry undoubtedly resulting in a chain reaction as one after another his panicked units begin to mass route.
Or that time I held off an entire army with one unit of Hoplites in spear wall formation at the gates of a city while I moved several units of heavy cavalry around the city walls smashing into their bottlenecked flank which crushed so many of the enemies units he no longer had a chance of winning. Then repeating it again, and again as each of his allies besieged the same city.  By the end I had crushed insurmountable odds which left even my healthiest units having suffered over 50% casualties.
What I'm getting at here is the depth of the older titles. Warhammer 2 has no depth. Majority of the units do nothing more than move around and change their single formations shape. I can't recall seeing a single unit with formation options available to them. Why CA? Why remove depth from battles? You imbeciles stripped battles to nothing more than forming lines and flanking. That's all every battle comes down to.
Yes, I'm aware you have an assortment of spells available to some units but what fun is that when you can only cast ~5-10 spells depending on some nearly random factor (winds) and it's pretty much pointless in most cases to field more than a single spell caster leaving you at most ~7 spells in your arsenal nearly half of which identical to other classes (healing, debuff, magic missiles of various sizes/colors). But HEY! It looks great when a fireball hits sending units airborn.
Yes, I'm away you have dragons and stuff. I'll agree they add a new element of strategy... to the really bad AI mechanics they never seem to improve.
and city sieges... what the heck??? A single wall? That's it? I'll spare sharing whoever reads this wall of text the stories I have of sieging entire CITIES using tactics I can never use in against a single wall and tie this up.
They stripped nearly what feels like a majority of what gave Total War series depth and made things a fun challenge and left us big pretty map with nice graphics, spells, flying units, and a half decent story. What a craptacular trade-off we got. Oh, and how we're buying 35% of the game at full price and expected to shell out for the other 65% as ~$19+ DLCs!!!!
I wish I could refund this game. Creative Assembly has turned into Electronic Arts.
[TLDR] Creative Assembly continued stripping down of this series is sickening. Not a single unit formation, sieging reduced to a single wall? Battles come down to moving a line of units into another line and flanking. Wash, rinse, repeat. Comparing Warhammer + Warhammer 2 to past titles and it's easy to see they're dumbing the serious down. Removing it's depth. Why? Heck if I know. Looks like they're chasing the dollar.

I've played most of the Total War titles and was greatly enthralled with how they pushed for accurate representations of realistic forces throughout history. My favorite is Medieval II. One of Medieval II's virtues was the ability to confront super elite forces (aka mounted knights in full armor) with a large rabble of peasants with spears and have a decent chance of winning. Battles came down to planning, tactics, and command-and-control (often through placement/movement of the general for morale purposes). Another major boon was the large number of factions you could play as (England, France, Scotland, Poland, Egypt, etc), there was about 15 or so kingdoms you could play, making replaying a fun task that I still enjoy today. When I played Total War: Warhammer 1, I had MASSIVE problems to the point that I felt compelled to write a review on it. Well, here we go for Part 2.
I'm going to skip all the stuff I covered in the review of TWW1, and focus on the thing people really have been talking about since this abomination was released to us...the Mortal Empires DLC. This is perhaps the biggest "♥♥♥♥ you" CA has given its customers since Rome 2. This is at best a situation of "one step forward, two steps back" and at worst THE BEST REASON NOT TO BUY THIS GAME. For those who don't know, CA has embarked on an ambitious project to create a game with a global map split across one game and two expansions, but with a campaign mode that allows players to play with/against all the other factions in the Warhammer world. This has since changed from one game with expansions to three separate games with DLC free for anyone who owns the previous titles. Okay fine. When TWW2 came out, it didn't even have the ME as part of it. Annoying, but I can be forgiving. Once we DID get the TWW ME DLC, oh man did everything implode.
For reference, in TWW1, CA did a power creep by expanding existing factions (Bretonnia) and adding new playable factions to the game. The same goes for legendary lords who lead the factions (both those that existed on release and those added). This got so bad that CA even had to go back and revamp the orginal legendary lords to make them worth bringing as an attempt to rebalance at least the big wigs of each faction. With the release of TWW ME, we now get to experience all the original factions and heroes AS THEY WERE AT THEIR RELEASE OF THE FIRST GAME!!! Unbalanced is an understatement. Furthermore, they left out one whole playable faction (which seemed very popular) from TWW1. We were told by CA that they are working on it and will have this fixed by Chrismas this year. Well instead we received an expansion for Rome 2: Total War because, you know, THAT'S what people are playing nowadays.
Basically this game is like going to a restraunt, having a waiter (CA) spill food and drink all over you, then look at you and say, "I'll be back later. Let me check on my other tables." Not only do I not recommend this game (because mods from the community are mandatory imo), I would advise everyone to boycott TWW3 when it comes out unless CA shows some really good business practice and unfuc'ks themselves.

Truly an underrated online-only action role-playing shooter on the market, this game seriously needs more people in the community, why you ask? First ignore the mixed reviews, most of the negative reviews were from earlier stages of the game, back when it was first released the game felt rushed, clunky and glitchy but after surviving and constantly getting better every update, the game is now truly one of the best online role playing games out there. What exactly is Tom Clancy's: The Division? The game sets place in a post-apocalyptic New York where you set foot as a division agent, fighting off factions who want to take the city for their own, fighting allongside the JTF and other agents, story mode is truly captivating and challenging, you can team with up to four agents and complete one mission to another, the fun never ends. Once you complete the main story and reach level 30, this is is not the end in fact, this is only the beggining of a truly different experience, past this point is where your agent has the potential to become truly powerful, there are four main things you can do after passing level 30 and these are:
-Dark Zone: The Dark Zone is a PVP and PVE area within the city that requires a strong agent to survive, team up with friends to explore the city and get better gear or run in solo and stay under the radar, whatever your choice is Dark Zone remains as intense as ever. In the Dark Zone, be careful of rogue agents who plan to kill you and take your loot, kill hard enemies and bosses to gain Dark Zone XP and rank up all the way to rank 99, the posibilities for Dark Zone are endless.
-Incursions: The Incursion is a more hardcore PVE mode where you or accompanied with a group of agents must fight off waves of enemies with high health and armor, the difficulty is indeed challenging, but the rewards are worth it.
-Daily Missions: Complete extremely challenging daily missions by yourself or with other agents, note that like incursions, these missions are far from easy and require a lot of communication to get through.
-Underground: Descend in the dark to fight off and clear groups of enemies by yourself or with a group of agents, Underground like other PVE modes is challenging and require a lot of communication to get through, the Underground also features its own level cap where you can go all the way to level 40.
If you are looking for a good online-only action role-playing shooter then this is a game for you. For the price this game is at it is truly worth it.

On with the review.
Pros:
- Multiple layers of strategy, (Positioning, timing, your deck, etc.)
- Very generous level up and Rank rewards
- A brief, in-depth Tutorial and rewards along with it
- Very short match-making times, and highly accurate
- Balance for the most part seems fair currently
- It is not P2W. You can gain everything with reasonable time
Cons:
- Very rough around the edges, but expected in Alpha
- Some design and artwork appears derivative
- Deck possibilities are currently limited, but will improve obviously
Conclusion:
The game even right now offers a great deal of fun, and minimal frustration. As you can see I received it for free, so I didn't buy the Premium pack, and have won the majority of my games (Currently at Bronze 3 at level 18). The strategy is very fair, and even Common cards can shutdown or answer expensive high-cost cards. To be more clear, superior decision and strategy absolutely WILL trump a deck that potentially counters your own. The game is very skill dependent, much more so than traditional TCG's, as the added layer of positioning and real-time decisions increase the possibilities of misplays and superior decisions alike.
The game is very fair, and generous, and offers a warm welcome to anyone interested in trying it out.

In short: Skullgirls is a classically styled 2D fighter in the a vein similiar to the MVC series. When I say it is classically styled, I mean that in more ways than one; the gamplay is reminscent of a blend of KoF, Street Fighter 2, MVC, and a dash of Tekken, the music is all Jazz and Blues influenced, and the opening of matches is themed like a '40s movie. If you are unfamiliar with fighting games, the game features an extremely in-depth tutorial series. More advanced players will dominate online matches; don't even think you will win a match until you've logged close to 50 hours. The story, arcade, and survival modes are, in my opinion, enough to justify buying the game on sale ,but if you are confident in your online abilities, then it is easily worth full price.

I'm new to steam, this is the first game I bought and i completely regret it. If I wasn't as new to steam and was more aware of steams refund policy, (no more that 2 hours play refunds are invalid) I would have refunded it immediately as it took me 4 hours to get it to work.
N.B Never leave the game running in the background, even if not actually any further than the play screen. It took me over the 2 hour return limit just to get the game to start running, and I was only on the Load page with no clickable features!
As I was past the point of being able to refund by the time I Instead I persited with the glitches that would normally accompany a free to play game or a beta version.  This is a great regret of mine as I only persisted because I had paid for it. Apparently I have played the game for 51.7 hours. I have actively played it for no more than 10, but Load screens, and back ground pauses count.... OF COURSE!
I'm not going to comment like many have on the misleading nature of The Escapists brand compared to this, I don't have a measure for comparison. Personally I thought it was fine as a stand alone game if you like the style of game that require exploration rather than, games which challenge you to complete ASAP. Also this game is truer to the comics than the tv show. Which makes it interesting for me, though TV-only might dislike some missing charectors.
But the glinches and errors are constant. The lack of ability to save except when the evening hits means you can loose large amount of progress when a glitch happens. I have felt like i have repeated 50% of what I played due to having to restart. I know I have reapeated large segments.
Glitches include:
- Not loading. - It wouldn't load for a while.
- Not closing - the amount of 'force closures' I have created is rediculas.
- Charectors who follow, targeting mechanism appearing for no reason.
- Charectors who will not stop following you for an extended period dispite dismissals.
- Game failing to register daily tasks as complete, most notably evening head count.
- Invintory box vanishing completley. (This stops you from preforming daily tasks)
- left click fails to work, this prevents game saving at end of the day and all interaction with charectors.
- Desks seem to 'lose' items when they are stored in them. I have 4 boxes of ammo dissapear on me.
I cannot believe this game passed the beta test and was considered fit for sale with this number of errors.
I am utterly fuming.
It is not worth the money.
It needs overhauling.

Your refund policy is fundementally flawed if non-actve game play i.e load screens, count towards the total and prevent a refund. It is penalising people who have patience and try to resolve issues. All I have learnt to do is have a tantrum and demand a refund immediately when I have any small issue.

I assume people downvoted this game due to issues right after release or Uplay problems, because there's nothing wrong with the game itself. The Division is pretty cool, and a real AAA title.
It's a third-person-shooter, with RPG elements and an open world, that relies strongly on cover-mechanics.
Whenever you get into a fight (which happens constantly) you'll find some cover, hide behind it, and use one of your 3 weapons and/or your special skills to take all hostiles down. One could argue it gets repetitive--and it does, just like any other game or, really, anything else in life, does--but...
- You have 3 weapon slots, and 6 armor slots. You'll get loot from enemies and chests, and frequently improve your gear throughout the game. TD is not a fantasy game, so there's no fantastic spells nor effects, but it has sentry turrets, seeker mines, healing stations, and more. Weapons and higher-tier armor also have some particular special effects that give you some useful extra bonuses when you meet the condition to activate them (having X or more of one or two of your 3 main attributes.) The gear is good enough to make you feel rewarded and keep looking for stuff.
- The AI in this game works pretty well. Enemies will constantly attempt to flank you, snipers will stay as far away as possible, dudes carrying close-range weapons will rush you. Some have grenades, others deploy sentry turrets, and they all move constantly. This makes the fights a lot more interesting.
- I'd say TD has the best map design I've ever seen in a game. The amount of objects spread over the world is incredible, locations are very well furnitured, there are several interesting and beautiful places, a lot of different cars spread over the streets (and they lower when someone shoots their tires, and their doors and hoods open/close as well, which is neat.) It's scary to think about the amount of work Ubi put into making all the models and textures for this game, it was obviously a
, and it makes the game much more realistic and pleasant.
All the types of cover you can use, and the way they're placed everywhere in the game also make it so that every encounter is somewhat different from the others. They managed to make this work very well.
- It's a Tom Clancy game, you know that. So you know the writting is flawless, and realistic. The only unbelievable thing in The Division is that although New York was affected by a deadly virus, it wasn't a muslim who released it.
It's worth noting that the voice-acting is great as well, just like the game's graphics and sounds (I just don't have these as my top priorities, so I'm not making an exclusive topic for them.)
- I'm not sure any other game has ever treated multi-playing as TD does. You can form a party of up to 4 people, and go together or spread out all over [a good part of] New York. You also see other players inside Safehouses, and you can invite any of them to your party. You can matchmake, and find random players to play with. You can choose to matchmake only when doing main missions. And, finally, there's...
- This is a place you can go any time, a place where the best loot can be acquired. All enemies there are "Superior" (I'm not sure how the game calls these ones) or Elite, and other players will also be there, whether they're in your party or not, whether they're friends or foes. In the DZ, you can kill other players to still their loot, you can wait until they hang said loot on an helicopter's rope for extraction and steal it, or you can be the victim of such felonies yourself. More often, you'll run into friendly people (at least so far I haven't run into any hostile players there myself) and just start exploring the DZ together, helping each other. It's pretty cool. You're out there, in the most hostile of environments, getting r*ped by NPCs, then you see another player, and you don't know if you can trust each other, so... you wave to them. They wave back. And just like that you are friends, and your time in the DZ will be much easier from now on.
- The Division is not easy. You'll die a lot, all throughout the game. Sometimes, specially during main missions on higher difficulties, you'll have to plan how you position yourself and deal with each fight, or you may be stuck there for a long time. And this is awesome. Games are supposed to be a challenge and require some skill, so you can get a sense of achievement when you succeed in doing something. Easy games suck.
- After 40 hours playing, I got none whatsoever. So... yeah, that's a good thing.
- The main problem in TD is that playing solo is a lot harder than playing in a party. One friend is enough--so get out there and find yourself one. I had to do that.
When playing solo, all the heat will be on you. Basically, you'll get hit every single time you try to get out of cover to shoot. And some enemies in this game do a LOT of damage (snipers sometimes do like 4/5s of your HP in damage with a single shot.) Partying with someone will allow you to share all that heat, so you actually get some windows to aim at and shoot your enemies. You can play TD solo, it's perfectly possible, but it's a lot harder.
- Long ones. With 8gb RAM, it takes my computer about 3 minutes from starting the game until actually getting to control my character. 12gb of RAM probably smoothens this out a lot, but the game
heavy.
even though I do hate Ubisoft myself to a certain extent--for ruining the Prince of Persia, Heroes of Might and Magic and Anno franchises--I gotta say there's nothing wrong with The Division to justify the Mixed feelings Steam reviewers directed towards it. If there once was, it's gone. And if you enjoyed Freedom Fighters, Gears of War or any other game of the sort, you'll like this. TD is better than all of them.

Downwell is proof that a solid concept is the most essential element in game design. The one-line concept for both Downwell is exceedingly simple:
You're falling down a well and your only weapon is guns attached to your feet.
Downwell nails what a lot of retro games miss: that the concept should be interesting enough to carry the whole game by itself. Convoluted systems and mechanics aren't necessary. The game is so fabulously simple I can explain all the mechanics you really need to know to somebody who knows nothing about video games at all right here in the review. Use the arrow keys to move left and right. Jump with spacebar. Spacebar in midair shoots your foot-guns. Colored stuff is interactable. There you go, the game is well designed enough that everything else can be trial-and-errored or even intuited the first time you encounter it in-game, and to me, that intuitivity is one of the lost arts of game design.
Apart from that, Downwell is very challenging. It's demands some unreal reflexes out of the player and if your reflexes are pretty blunt that might be a turn-off. Art and music are both good. If I had to pick some cons out of this game, it'd be technical stuff, such as BGM and SFX volume not having separate sliders, windowed mode not being resizable, and fullscreen alt-tabbing being pretty awful considering how light the game is. Overall, highly recommend, especially for the price.

TL;DR
Downwell is a vertical, bullet-hell rougelike with quite a bit of difficulty to it. You play as a kid with gunboots, falling and shooting down a massive well past lots of different monsters. Ghosts, floating eyeballs, turtles, things like that. The game's controls are very solid, and movement is a lot more fluid than it looks. You can bounce off of walls, smash ontop of enemies to chain combos, or just land on a ledge before moving on. And certain 'styles' allow for different runs, such as the Spinning Arm, which allows you to only find gun types (a good thing), but shops are much more rare.
And the soundtrack is pretty great, too. Downwell's soundtrack reminded me of Hotline Miami's, (Another Devolver Digital title, may I add.) in how fresh it felt. The songs were perfect for each respective stage, and they really help make the game special.
Downwell is just a really great game overall, and took me about 15 hours to 100%. I'd recommend it for sure; and I mean, the price really makes this game a steal for what you're getting.

I'm only putting this as not recommended for the current build (As of October 6th, 2015). While the game has good points, right now there's some flaws that make it so that you would be better off waiting for a while to get the game. Hopefully in a few months all the kinks are worked out.
That said, I DO enjoy the game! The game still feels super Escapist-y, you have a schedule, you do chores to keep down the zombie meter (Replacement to the Heat meter), there's a lot of crafting in this game, but with being ported into the 'Walking Dead' world, there's also a story, that follows the comics more closely than the tv series. I've not seen the comics, so I can't confirm how close it is myself. Other reviewers might though. The levels are short, but it doesn't feel unnecessarily short, as long as you take the time to explore each level without rushing through to the next.
Unfortunately, some of the flaws become noticeable as you go on-your AI is pretty bad. Sometimes, if you go up into a vent with allies following you, instead of staying with below the vent entryway like they usually do, occassionally they'll attempt to follow you in erratic ways, usually leaving the building you're in and running face first into a bunch of zombies. That is unfortunate. On top of that, sometimes the level design feels almost spiteful. Duct tape is just as scarce, but now you need other items too, and you'll find occassionally they're just as scarce. Now I'm all for Nintendo Hard games, but requiring several hours of searching desks every day to find that one item that'll let me open into a room containing a key so that I can open a door to get the one item I need to advance -one- quest to the next feels a little unfair. But maybe that's just me whining :P
I did however encounter a glitch in Alexandria. I cannot seem to reproduce it, but after hours in that level, I saved, exited the game, and then the next time I came on, I was no longer Rick, I was playing as Abraham. I also had HIS stats and his items. So I lost a few really nice items I had in my inventory, plus one of the two items to complete the quest I was on, and I also lost the several days in game it took to max out Rick's stats-Abraham's were in the 30s. Luckily nothing was changed in my desk (though it changed to Abraham's desk).
All in all, the game feels like....hmm. if I were to use a metaphor, it'd be like a game made by 6 people, and 2 of those people, regularly do unpaid overtime, because they really feel strongly about the game, they want it to be the best possible experience, two of them just do what they're paid to, no more, no less, and then the last two devs just...kinda sit in the back and play another game all day. There's great polish in some places, decent in others, and some places it just falls right off the wagon.
I want to be clear though-I don't think the devs -actually- did that, hence why I phrased it as a metaphor. Every situation is different. Stuff happens. But unfortunately, the game does not feel worth it's price right now. Maybe in the future, but until then, get it on sale, or wait

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

This is a game I played the whole way through with my daughters. I manned the keyboard and mouse, but they solved all the puzzles. Simple childlike solutions are a valid approach to just about all the game's problems, and really the fun for an adult comes from doing things creatively in silly roundabout ways, and seeing if the game likes your style, as the challenge is just about nil.
The premise is, the game presents you with loads of challenges in a globe full of different climates etc. Generally, people have a problem that needs to be solved. You are armed with a magic notepad that will create anything you write into it, and you can also use this to add adjectives to most objects or even in-game characters. So, you write in: "Polka-dotted yellow cryptozoologist," and suddenly a spotted marigold gentleman in a jacket and hat will appear that has a keen interest in monsters. Then you can create "Bigfoot" and he will appear, and the former will walk over to investigate the latter.
The game's problems occasionally require a bit more knowledge than a six year old can muster, including awareness of mythology, pop-culture or some complex relationships. However this can turn into a really great teachable moment as you can guide the kids through deciphering the answer, or take them through the process of learning the answer by quickly opening up a browser window and doing some research. In the cuddly context of the game, the knowledge feels useful and they seem to absorb it really well, and it's usually at least referential of practical info.
Additionally, Scribblenauts Unlimited is the first game in the franchise that allows the player to make their own objects that they can later create with the notebook. While the amount of nouns the game recognizes is staggering, it's still quite amazing, considering there's loads of copyrighted or rated-E objects the game won't let you make, or just wacky stuff that isn't real or too specific for the game creators to have included. These objects are built on templates of objects that already exist, but they can be modified in every way visually with a simple layering / coloring system, and you can then further modify them by defining their relationships with other items, audio, etc. etc. I've used this to make stuff like Mike & Sully from Monsters Inc. (Cryptozoologists find them fascinating, by the way, check out my Workshop items if you want'em!)
The only part of the game we haven't finished is an extra portion where there are loads of various interactions the designers want you to uncover. These are like achievements and are called things like "Liar Liar Pants on Fire," so if you create a Criminal and a Lawyer in the same location (or otherwise anybody that pop-culture deems to be known liars), the influx of localized liars will automatically create a pair of pants that happens to be ablaze. There are literally hundreds of these things, ranging from the amusing to the obscure to the complicated, but at the very least they illustrate all the fun special cases that the designers went through the trouble to make happen. In a game that's all about making whatever you want, I appreciate that the designers took the time to make stuff interact as you'd expect, and this is a great way for them to pat themselves on the back by showing you how to get them all to happen.
I recommend Scribblenauts to game designers and anyone with kids, or anybody that likes a super easy activity that lets you be creative.

This game has stunning details and graphics. The game movement is very, very smooth; I don't see much of this lately.
