I wasn't expecting much from Skullgirls when I bought it, but it more then exceeded my expectations after playing the game for more then just an hour. This is a six button fighter that can be played with normal powered teams, a strong tag team, or an overpowered single character. The option to be able to choose how many chatacters you want to bring into a match allows you to play the game in a numerous of ways, and brings different learning curves.
The in-game tutorial is the best I have seen in a fighting game, to date. This is a good place to start with fighters, just for the simple fact that it tries to teach newcomers the nuances of the genre, and not just combos. Although, there are plenty of advanced combos that require precise execution and memory, that put games like MvC and Blaz Blue to shame, if you are interested in high-level play.
Controls are fluid and responsive, any time my fighter did something I didn't intend for her to do, I knew I was at fault and that it wasn't due to bad mechanics. Combos are easily to learn and execute but like all fighters, require some time to learn. I have tried playing with a Keyboard, Gamepad, and Arcade stick, and can say you will probably need a pad or stick to play this game. Don't get me wrong it is very possible to play with a keyboard, (and from personal experience, actually kinda fun) but it will be hard to play characters who rely on Z motions.
The 2-D sprites are detailed and animated fluidly. The developers did a good job incorporating each characters personality into their fighting styles, if you can appreciate such things. Each character even has their own animation and properties for their tag ins and outs. (something I wish Marvel had)
Even though most people probably don't go into fighters looking for a story, the game does feature a story mode, that has suprisingly good lore, and interesting characters, with a final boss that may well rival Shao Kahn. So even if you are looking for a single player fighter, there is something to be found here.

I enjoyed playing Superbrothers, but it was the kind of game I only wanted to play for thirty minutes at a time. That might have more to do with the genre than the game itself, though.
The best part is undoubtedly the music. The delivery is good too; just experiencing the world is half of what the game is. Visually it is hit and miss; the pixel art looks great however there are often parts that are too detailed and stand out for it, such as the sprites. And the combat reminded me of Quest for Glory, which I enjoyed.
The game doesn't try to hold your hand too much, thankfully, but reading over the Megatome can always put you on the right path (and adds to the experience besides).
What I didn't like was the very obvious touchpad controls. They work completely fine, but the game could have been made more enjoyable with better mouse control rather than just substituting the mouse pointer for a finger. Also the blatant twitter integration was groan-worthy... but I could accept it with the way they presented all of the dialogue.
Ultimately I'd say that if you are interested in Superbrothers that you should try to catch it on sale. It is good, but completely skippable.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is one of those unique gems that just plain works. The art direction is both bizarre and beautiful, and the soundtrack is one of the best I have ever heard in gaming. The story is so simple yet insanely deep, and the ending is one to think about for a long time. Although it is a short 4-hour campaign, it is very much a deeper game than the majority of AAA games on the market. Superbrothers is just plain brilliant.
But on the flip side, the controls are pretty bad on PC/Mac. Unfortunately, the game was original designed and released on iOS, and it suffers in transition. Moving the screen around, zooming in and zooming out, and combat are all much more complicated with the mouse than with touch screen.
But despite the bad controls, this is very much a worthy investment and one of the most unique and powerful indie games I have ever played. Definitely a recommend!

It's still very much an early access game. I think I'm going to run out of pre-loaded content before too long, but the ability to make your own models through the LEGO Digital desiner will certainly add a lot of lifetime to the game!
Lots of people have claimed it is a "Minecraft killer," but it's definitely a very different experience at the time of this review. What surprised me was the "survival" gameplay has far less risk than Minecraft. Yes, you can die from enemy attacks or falling in lava, but you do not lose your items, just 2,000 studs, which is a very small amount. You also do not have to worry about food or fall damage. There is currently not resource management/crafting game like Minecraft, where you'dcollect blocks/ores and craft your materials and tools. You find item treasure chests chests in towers/igloos/treehouses.
Once you encounter characters (defeat hostile NPCs), decorations, or vehicles (ride animals or drive vehicles once to unlock the purchase option) that you find in the world you can purchase them (one time stud fee) for unlimited use/placement. This is very much like Minecraft's creative mode. You can use the pieces of lego characters

For example,  I found a helicopter, a plane, and a lot of tool items within the first two hours.
There are good terraforming tools, which will really come in handy for base building!
Currently this game is single-player only, but when they add they add multiplayer, I think it will really shine!
Adding more content (more biomes/items/characters) will really give players a lot of replay value.

Performance-wise I had some issues using mouse/keyboard controls instead of a controller. There was also some lag as new biomes/chunks loaded.
As many have said, DLC content pricing/value will be very important for this game.
tl;dr: This game is definitely reccomended to LEGO fans, especially those that enjoyed the Traveler's Tales LEGO movie games (Star Wars, Batman, Marvel: Superheroes). For those a bit more hesitant, wait for it to go on sale at $7.50 or $5, or wait for the multiplayer it's definitely worth it at that price.

Today, i got this game as a gift. I won't lie, i was expecting something worst then what i tried. But even still, this game does not match my personal criteria.

When i played this game. I found it intresting and realistic... I found it has some awesome things that get me going, and also found some things that just don't work for me.
I started to play this game around mid day on my b-day. 04/06 Australian time.
When i was playing, i realized their are really some cool features that i found quite impressive. All in all. I played about 40 minutes this morning.
My reasons to dislike this game?
*The camera is terrible, and you have to manually rotate it where ever your looking. It feels quite awkward when your fighting, and running around.
*Their was very minimal resistance when playing the game, and i felt practically invincible, because when i died their was no loss or gain. And considering their were next to no enemys to fight, only people to kill...
*I had no sense of achivement when i found new things to buy and place, as well as when i was killing animal's, people, machine's and of course destroying the world.
*The Bob cat felt like a piece of rubish,  i could not get it out of a hole i dug, as well as the camera went spastic when trying to get out, or dig further.
*The car that has a drill on the end was the first vehicle i found, all well and good till i hit a small pocket of lava and the whole thing just blew up. It felt quite weak, considering a drill should take alot more pain then the rest of the vehicle, and considering the vehicle does not feel quite so powerful.
*I found a chest. I got a Musket rifle out of it. I discovered i could hit the chest forever, and have infinite lego credits at my disposal, considering i wanted to destroy the chest which was practically invincible... Till i genetated new terrain.
*Man, did i love the dragon. It locked onto every plant in the area, and double clicking caused him to tail spin or bite! Forward: I played this game with a Xbox 360 controller.
~Pros~
- Absolutely breathtaking visuals. Every frame is a work of art.
- Superb sound design, with exquisite attention to auditory detail in all aspects.
- Beautiful, emotional soundtrack. Compliments the tone and feel of each part of the game perfectly.
- Gorgeously fluid and detailed animation. Makes you feel like you're flying through the world rather than running.
- Some notably interesting abilities that are a fresh deviation from the usual platforming arsenal.
- Skillfully integrated and intuitive save system compliments the games style perfectly.
- Excellent game design. At no time is any one previous ability rendered useless by later ones.
- Controls like a dream.
- Difficulty is just right. It's challenging (sometime very) without feeling unfair. Learning curve is gradual and forgiving.
- Charming, family friendly game without feeling dumbed down or deliberately cutesy.
- Made me cry like a baby.
~Cons (AKA Nitpicking)~
- The game is on the short side. Expect 8-10 hours, though every moment it lasts is brilliant.
- Little replay value. There's no New Game Plus feature or playable/unlockable post-game content.
- There are a couple points-of-no-return throughout, making it difficult to clear 100% on your first run.
- I can imagine trying to accomplish some feats late-game would be incredibly difficult with a keyboard.
- Visual effects can become so bright and dazzling at times that you may lose track of your character for a second.
- Left me with a crippling lonliness in my chest after the game was finished, realizing my adventures with Ori were over.
If you enjoy Metrovania style games (2D, free exploration. action-platforming sidescrollers), and appreciate the unique, spirited artistic styles seen in such works as Spirited Away and within games like Okami, then you should love this game.  It's truly a breath of fresh air and a ray of light in the otherwise largely stagnant and blind game industry of today. Just be sure to play it with a PC compatible controller (which is really something you should consider investing in if you're doing PC gaming, anyway) to prevent mechanical control issues from staining the game experience.
Ori and the Blind Forest is really best approached as an experience as opposed to a video game. If you view it as such, I feel you'll come away from it with the most wholesome, satisfied experience possible. Either way, it's  certainly not a game to let pass by.

Warhammer 2 is warhammer 1 in everything from graphics to the gameplay, literally nothing changed. I would treat this not as a game but an expansion pack to the first Warhammer, because you will get the best experience with both of them. The normal campagin is good, I really liked some of the new mechanics they implemented. The battles are the exact same thing you got in the first warhammer, which I don't like, I think the more realistic battles of the historical Total Wars were much better. I can run this game on Microsoft Surface pro 4 so that is a good thing. But the best part of the game is the mortal empires. So what you get is a giant campaign map that includes both the map and the factions of the first and the second warhammer. So a mortal empire game for the first 50 turns (or someting like that) is gonna be a normal campaign, I started as the empire and the first 80 turns was just the normal empire campaign from the first warhammer, and I mean it when I say Excatly the same. So after you got a port and a strong postiton on the old contitnent, then you can start colonizing. This is game fixes all the issues of Empire: Total War with a big map. And then the fun begins, having foothold in diffrent continents is like playing a new faction, but at the same time you have to keep your♥♥♥♥♥♥together on the old contitnent so everything doesn't collapse on you. Mortal Empires is an actual well-made grand strategy game, it doesn't have anything close to the level of detail in Paradox games but let's not forget that this is still a total war game. But I really like Mortal Empires because it feels like kind of a tribute to Total War: Empire, and I played that game a lot despite all of it's flaws. So what you get is Warhammer 1 with new factions, a few new mechanics (really minor ones) and a new map, as I said, this is more of an expansion pack than a stand-alone game. In fact, it's hard for it to stand alone. So, I do recommend this game, but if you want to get the best possible experience, save some money and also buy warhammer 1, and if you can't, then you will still have a lot of fun playing this on its own.

This is a hard review to give. On one hand the totality of the content offered here is impressive and offers countless hours of gameplay from the main campaign, the massive mortal empires, or the endless custom battles and the steam workshop. However it comes at a price....a steep monetary price to access its full potential. Which brings me to the difficulty of reviewing this game and ultimately giving it a positive review in spite of its cost.
First, before reading any further, I must warn the potential buyer,  to enjoy the game in its entirety, specifically that offered by the mortal empires campaign. You must make a hefty investment.
$60 warhammer 1
$75 warhammer 1 dlcs
$60 warhammer 2
$195. That is the investment needed to be made to enjoy the entire game. Even if you are to avoid certain dlcs, you are still left with a game that will cost you $120+. This is where my ire is centered at, and my trepidation at giving this game a positive review.
I find, as I'm sure many others would agree, the practices of the total war franchise, and the game industry as a whole ahorent. Warhammer 2 with its mortal empires dlc, is the game warhammer 1 should of been. This is now the finished game that should have been released to fans. Currently mortal empires offers the experience any total war or warhammer fan would love. A massive fantasy world map, countless factions, detailed units, lore, real time action, grand strategy. This is a jewel of a game, but the cost cannot be ignored. The trend in gaming seems to be to release an unfinished game, then charge for patches/dlcs, or micro transactions to receive a finished product.
Now I am not a dinoasaur who is going to rant about the good ol days, where $50 or less bought you a game in a large box, complete with a nifty little booklet and plastic cd case, and maybe a $20 expansion at most. Realistically, $60 is reasonable in comparison to the amount of recourses used to make modern AAA games. I find that a season pass serves as a middle ground between a company losing profits, and micro transactions shorting the consumers.
However no total war game offers any of this. In fact they take a different route, offering some $60-100 of dlcs with no option of purchasing a season pass. Simply look at all major past total war games from ETW on, and you will see the increase in the amount of dlcs and there overall price. While additional factions or campaigns offer high quality content, they do not warrant the cost of purchasing another $60 game. Total war and sega owe it to its consumers to offer up a realistic season pass that doesn't squeeze its customers for every penny.
You might be wondering where the review of the game comes into play. Well the total war series has consistently delivered on all of its game, even with the most mediocre being enjoyable. I have been a fan since shogun 1, and have owned every one of there games since then, yes even spartan total warrior. Warhammer 2 is no different. A plethora of factions, units, heroes, lore. This game delivers on all fronts, which is why it would be petty of me to not reccomend this game.
However the recommendation comes with a warning. Be prepared to drop well over the $60 price tag to obtain the full potential of this game.

Beautiful game - a fantasy lover's dream come true.  The engine and gameplay are tight, multiplayer is fun, competitive, and realitivly cheese free.  It has insane rats driving giant hamster wheels and aztec dinosaurs riding bigger dinosaurs.
There are some problems with the Mortal Empires campaign - the massive grand campaign combining content from Warhammer 1 and this game (and requires Warhammer 1 to play).  Most of these are due to the Warhammer 1 factions not really being as developed and fleshed out as the Warhammer 2 races; CA is working on this and I believe an update is coming this month.  Even with that disparity, the campaign is still a blast to play, even with Warhammer 1 races.  I think much of the blowback on this front is overly dramatic and unfair.
Multiplayer is where this game truly shines, however.  The quick battle ladder is a ton of fun and the community is very helpful.  Warhammer 1 had quite a bit of cheese with people spamming heroes, but all that is gone now.  There are still people who will bring cheese to the battle (basically spamming one or two types of units - very powerful and tough to counter if you are not brining an army specifically designed to counter), but this is VERY rare (in 40 games I've seen it twice, and that was early on... most of those players are probably long gone).  The battles are fast, fun, and don't require a ton of APM to do well - expereince and knowledge trumps click speed.
If you like fantasy, buy this game.  It's a great time to get into Warhammer as there is a ton of great content here and a ton more coming down the pike.  If you do get it, don't hesitate to hit me up for a game.  I'm not a great player by any means, but I'd be happy to help you get started in multiplayer.

I loved Total War Warhammer 1! I have played Total War since Rome Total War and it was the best Total War Experience yet.
Vortex Campaign: Total War Warhammer 2 is a big upgrade over Total War Warhammer 1. 4 really fun races with a great campaign map and numerous quality of life improvements makes this just a better quality experience that I can highly recommend.
Mortal Empires Campaign: I was looking forward to the Mortal Empires campaign and that has been a bit of a disappointment so far. I have played a couple of fun campaigns, but many of the improvements from Total War Warhammer 2 has not been ported to ME yet for the old races and there still are several bugs. Stranded in Time is a typical tablet game: a 90-minute trip that won’t tire you out with any sort of difficult puzzles, but fun enough to pass the time with.
Stranded in Time is the type of game you usually find on tablet app stores: a very simple, casual point ‘n’ click with a small cast and a short story.
Everything about this game is as simple as possible, down to the three main leads, their conversations, and even the plot—it may sound super exciting to go on an expedition under the ruins of a temple to find some ancient advanced machinery; but in reality, the whole thing is like a longer Saturday morning cartoon episode.
Even the gameplay wants to make sure that the player can just relax. The point ‘n’ click mechanics are kept as simple as possible, and the few puzzles are only intimidating if one never saw them before. But even then, there is an infinite hint and skip button, further proving that this game wants nothing but to provide some cheap and casual entertainment for about an hour and a half.

There are these orangey tan mushrooms that as soon as they see you they run far across the board (at your max speed) and start creating literally endless amounts of gates that each summon several creatures before the gate disappears.  If these creatures hit you with their melee, ranged or charged attack, you'll take damage and get teleported to some random spot on the board.  If you are teleported into the attack range of any of the summoned creatures, they'll get a free hit on you and teleport you again.  The only way to clear these boards is to get super lucky and either get teleported right adjacent to one of the mushrooms and kill them in 1 hit which isn't always possible depending on your class, item loadout and the amount of xp you've managed to accumulate on that board.  Oh, and the charge attack doesn't have to even hit you to cause you to teleport.  The teleport effect has a couple block range so side stepping the charge causes you to avoid the damage but you still get teleported, potentially starting the chain of taking damage and teleporting.
So because of the endless teleporting mobs you can never catch up to the mushrooms and clear the floor & the tide of enemies will very quickly overwhelm you.  Up to this point it's been a fun little casual timewaster but I am now giving it the finger and uninstalling.

Ah, the Division. This game is pretty much all about semi-tactical semi-realizstic shooting. Cover-based infantry combat with guns. There are vehicles that can be fought on certain, end-game missions, but none that a player themself can use. There are no rocket launchers, player-usable grenade launchers (although there is a launchable sticky-bomb that only requires a cooldown to use.)
As far as the combat goes, the game is great. The gunplay feels good. The tactical orientation of the game requires you to think to succeed (or be overly well equipped) and there's plenty of gun variety and the RNG is ever creul but lower limits keeps it mostly in check.
Character development is a bit iffy, as far as I'm concered. Yes, there are clear benefits to leveling. There any many "skills" that can be unlocked for active use in combat to turn the tide to tip the balance in your favor. Enemy difficulty also ramps up as you raise level. But the main thing is that at higher levels you can use the higher level guns and gear, which is of course, better than equivilent lower level stuff. But talents, skill mods, unlockable slots are the most you can directly see from the level differences. Other than that, leveling and base upgrades don't really give you much in the way of more tangible feeling development.
Then there's the role playing element. Which is to say, one of the worst parts of the game. There are pretty much next to no choises aside from which parts of the base to upgrade first (which thus gives you skills and skill mods you can use) when to get those upgrades (not if, eventually you'll get all of them and the resource limit is well beyond what is needed for everything) and when you run off through the giant, mostly empty city to deal with the many side quests, encounters, and run into countless helpless people and then those other guys with guns. Your character has fewer lines than Link in the Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time. You get no option to say anything, nor make any choices that have any real outcomes on the fate of the city. You're just a sleeper agent from the Division, activated in the second wave, given a terrible weapon and armor, and told to do whatever it takes to ensure continuity of government.
Fights happen with much empty content in between simply because all fights are dnagerous. While you can easily succeed as long as you are skilled, properly equipped and experienced, and trying hard enough, you must try. Even in a simple gunfight with some jerk with a pathetic little handgun on the street. As a direct result, the developers cannot throw enemy after enemy at you while out and about, and thus you'll spend much of your time running toward the next fight, pushing the little button to advance the mission you're on, and sometimes chekcing if that thing that guy you just shot is better than what you already have.
Which is my next point: the entire game is a constant grind, with the intent of finding equipment that is beter than what you already have. Even up to and through the endgame, you will still be checking if that shiny new high-end drop is a gun, one that you like, and if so, one that is better than the one you're already holding. It becomes an endless cycle.
But the part where the shooting, the thrown and launched grenades explode, you use some weird SHD tech to pull a tiny healing robot out of nowhere that rebuilds itself after a half-minute or so, and a lot of people named Alex, Chains, or Dylan, or some nameless crazed sanitation worker falls over and take whatever they wer epolite enough to leave behind... all of that... is fun. The fact you can't just fart and annihilate every enemy that crosses paths with youforces you to actually try if you want to succeed, especially on higher difficulties.
In summary:
Because the combat is fun, and the RNG grind is satisfying when something useful actually shows up, I do recommend this game.

Goodness, there is so much to say after just finishing this game. I'll try to make it a succinct review. First of all, I want to express just how much I loved Ori and the Blind Forest. It is a masterpiece that I attribute to their breathtaking visuals, mesmorizing music, excellent heart-tugging story, and challenging gameplay. I've lately been having difficulty finding a game to truly capture my attention, but Moon Studios blew me out of the water with this work of art. I sat down and could barely manage to peel myself away once I started.
The visuals were astounding with vibrant colors poured into every bit of the game. I sometimes would just stop and just stare in awe at the magnificient flowing waterfalls, captivated by the sheer detail that was put into this game. I honestly had so much enjoyment exploring and listening to the music as I went.
The story was great, and I won't say more than that because I feel it is something that should be experienced.
Now, before I say anything about the gameplay... I will say that I haven't played a platformer game in probably 5-6 years. It has been a long time, and to be honest, I'm not much a fan of them. But Ori and the Blind Forest just executed it so well. The controls were crisp (I am a Keyboard and Mouse user), and everything just flowed perfectly. There were some difficulty spikes, but they came with new techniques which were introduced for you to practice some. I probably died some... 200+ times. It seems excessive, but their saving system makes things not seem like a grind, and I was constantly progressing even despite hurdles as I moved on.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a wonderful game, and I definitely recommend others to buy it. (Hence this review, which is actually my first. I've never been moved so much by a game as this one.)

Stunningly beautiful, thoroughly enjoyable metroidvania games. Some of the powers you unlock are obvious (double-jump and the like), but some are fairly novel and fun (the "bash" ability allowing you to launch yourself infinitely off of enemies and bullets). Has a gorgeous, natural/outdoors feel to it, and there's lots to explore.
There's a story, and it feels like it's on the verge of intriguing, and wants to tug at heart-strings, but in the end it's really kind of bare-bones, and completely superfluous to the game. The heart-string-tugging bit is right at the beginning, before actual gameplay, so there's zero time to invest emotionally, and they switch to a cop-out "twist" later anyway so it feels kind of meaningless.
And, some of the most intense levels get shut down afterward with no way to get back in, and yet contain items you could conceivably collect, so it's possible to be prevented from fully completing the game. I think the things you can get in such cases aren't actually tracked/trophied, but that doesn't really lessen the harm, to me.
But the graphics, animation, gameplay mechanics, and challenge, are fantastic, so this game gets a big thumbs up from me.

The
game making software for begginers.
I bought this engine about a year ago, but have only started using it recently.
It is very easy to use, but you are still able to customize most features of the game, through tilesets, the database, events, and RGSS (RPG Maker's scripting language/system)
It was designed to make RPGs (which it does fantasticly), but with a know-how using events and RGSS, the possibilities of this engine are pretty much endless.
In my opinion, it's the best entry in the series, plus, it's also cheaper than VX Ace, and much MUCH cheaper than MV (the newest one)
There are pros and cons to XP, but I feel as if the pros outweigh the cons. It comes with the BEST runtime pack out of ANY RPG creation software, which you can use for free, which is another thing;
You can publish pretty much anything you make with this, on the Workshop or even on Greenlight, and you'll never even have to pay royalties to Degica.
Also, the charachters are very nice, but that's just my opinion. I have and use XP, and VX Ace, but I feel as if the characters in XP look much better. VX Ace uses chibi sprites, but XP uses taller, more proportionate ones. You can also import your own sprites, tilesets, scripts, sound effects, music, and just about any other audio or graphic you'd need.
If you don't make graphics or music, there's also many free ones just a good search away.
It is great for begginers because there isn't much to learn. However, there is some stuff to learn, which is a con;
Learning RGSS really is a pain, and mapping can be too if you've never used a different RPG Maker before. That's the only place though where I feel like VX Ace is better.

The two scientists are fleshed out well and are fun to watch, however the old man, who we are supposed to care deeply for, ultimately feels shallow by the end. Regardless, there are extraordinarily touching moments throughout the runtime. It's only about 4 hours long, so I'd wait for it to go on sale, but if you can get this game for $5 or less, definitely pick it up. It's an interesting story and has some very touching moments.

If you are a Linux user running an AMD card, avoid this game. I bought it long ago when it was announced that a Linux port was now available, with the hope that with time, the developers would work out the kinks of getting the game to run properly on Linux.
As a Linux user, I have learnt to cultivate enormous patience with developers working on Linux ports of games out of gratitude, and understanding. So when the game failed to even launch, I did not push the issue.
The MESA developers have pointed out in technical detail that it is a game bug and not a Linux driver issue:
There has however, been zero indication that Larian will be fixing this bug. I am unsurprisingly, rather displeased by this turn of events, and will most likely not be buying anything from this company ever again until they deliver on what they promised, which is proper Linux support.
At the time of writing, the Divinity Original Sin 2 still does not have a Linux port, which indicates that Linux support is on the low end of things to prioritise for these developers. Spend your money wisely.
Update: Just in case you have encountered this issue, there is a way to actually play the game, but it requires you to build a shim for the game, and modifying the runner.sh file in the game folder.
The file and instructions can be found here:
I remain unamused that one has to literally learn how to compile software on Linux to get the game running.

More than recommended. It seems simple at first, you have a few cards in your deck, 4 of them in your hand all the time, you continously acquire mana which you spend to place them somewhere in the battlefield, then most of them start walking towards the enemy and they fight whatever they meet on the way.
It's simplicity is deceptive, to be really effective one needs to know many things and make good decisions quick. At heart it's a game of countering as the trailer suggests, but to effectively counter you need to know the cards in the game well. On the surface it might seem enough to know which card is able to damage which, but in reality their placement and even the timing of casting them matter a lot, sometimes an effective counter is nullified just by placing it half a second earlier then you should place them. Of course it matters what cards you have in your deck as they can be built for synergy and also variety to be able to counter whatever comes your way, but in my limited experience how you play them is more important.
It's one of the better examples of the easy to play, hard to master concept and a lot of fun for a game that you can play using just a mouse in a minute or two.
I recommend, hands down. Don't care what others say.

Sproggiwood is a turn-based roguelike game that won't make you feel frustrated every time you die. It has six different classes and various items, which add variety to how you finish a level.
What I like the most is the enemy behavior design. The monsters are difficult not because they're strong stats-wise, but because they do certain things.
The game could be better if they optimized the UI and controls for PC. But now it just looks like a lazy port from its mobile version.

Sproggiwood is a top-down roguelike with a heavy emphasis on random chance and gold grinding. Each level, you select from one of several characters, each with a unique set of abilities. Some of these characters cannot sustainably fight the constant influx of slimes the game throws at you from the first level to the last. Slimes tend to multiply when you kill them, unless you kill the offspring quickly. Since some characters are not good at fighting multiple enemies, fighting them only makes the situation worse. This can be mitigated by buying upgraded gear for each character, which is either randomly picked up in levels (and only lasts for the level) or bought for a way-too-long-time's worth of gold. The controls are meant for a tablet or phone. I would not recommend this game.

Fun, addicting, turn-based, rogue-like-ish, cute graphics, and it has a Frog Boss so of course it's a good game ;-)
The story is kind of weird but the gameplay is what I like.  And a game that doesn't take place in a dungeon for once!
Each level is randomly created into corridors and rooms and big areas.  You have the "fog of war" meaning that when you start everything is black except for a small circle of light around you.  As you travel you light up the level and it stays lit.  So you don't know if you're going to run into an enemy when you round the corner.  It's turn-based so when you make a movement on the grid, then the enemies make their moves.  You can sit there surrounded by enemies and they won't do anything until you make a move, so you have time to develop a strategy if you want.  Some enemies are annoying because they duplicate themselves.  After a few levels there is a boss and there are different themes for the areas and bosses.
After a successful run you appear back in your town.  You can spend time messing around placing buildings, trees, etc.  Also this is where you upgrade your gear and abilities.  If you want everything you will have to replay areas you've already been through.  Which was no problem for me because it was more killing and looting!  YEAH!  ARG! RRR!
Music & Sounds: it's been a while since I played it but I don't remember anything annoying.
Graphics:  I LOVE LOVE LOVE Them!  All the characters are so cute, even some of the enemies I have to remind myself they are the enemy and I must kill them, but they're so cute!
tldr:
Rogue-like
Turn-based movement and combat
Cute characters
and FROG BOSS!  (what's not to love!)
Casual rogue-lite

1. Eve Online style MMO - things are difficult to acquire or create but the reward is wonderful
2. Like the age-of-sail period - the game has a lot of sailing to do.
3. Enjoys clan social interactions
4. Being part of shifting clan politics
5. Like hardcore PvP conflict that has some real loss - 1 life ships (like Eve Online)

This doesn't feel anything like The Walking Dead.
After the tutorial you very quickly realize that, fun game as "the Escapists" was, it's mechanics have nothing to do with survival and don't translate well.
You are constantly trapped in the daily routine cycle, doing tedious work that isn't improving your situation in any way - a core mechanic that prevents you from playing the actual game!
Crafting is working as in its predecessor, though again it doesn't feel like surviving when you have to craft a pickaxe to break through a wall to find a key to open another door... I've found a few interesting items though no idea and hints how to craft them so far.
The game daily respawns loot inside containers (so literally next to your bed - survival, yay), so the only motivations you have to go out is to find the damn key that prevents you from progressing.
And the level design is horrible. Long roads that make the short amount of time between routines even shorter, rooms you can get trapped in and have to reload a save, and those damn locked rooms that can only be entered with the right key that is hidden somewhere. I constantly get the feeling that everything has been designed for length instead of fun.
TL;DR - Prison break mechanics don't make for a fun survival game.
If you haven't played "The Escapists" get it instead.

A short point-and-click adventure game with a few puzzles.  This is not a hidden object game, though it does have some similarities to them.
Olivia is visiting her uncle, who is an archeologist, and ends up going along with him and his young assisstant to a site at the ruins of an old church.  Once there they discover that the workers have disappeared!  And they discover something never seen before.  There is some funny dialogue.  The overall tone is light-hearted.
The game is played by clicking with the mouse to find objects on the screen, and clicking on the sides or bottom of the screen to move to the next area.  There is a hint button if you are stuck and don't know what to do.  There are also a few mini games that appear, but you can skip them if you want.  Certain areas of the screen sometimes pop up with more detail, like a part of a shelf, and usually there's a special item there you have to interact with.
The items you find are stored in a backpack which can be opened and closed by the zipper (very nice idea there!), though sometimes you have to close the backpack before you can exit a room because you can't click at the bottom of the screen while the item tray is up.  I had no logical problems with the items and their uses, unlike most hidden object games I've played (in one game you have to find scissors to cut something even though you already have a knife that could have suited that purpose).  It's refreshing to play a game that doesn't make me go "Oh, seriously?" and facepalm.
The graphics are nice.  Very colorful.  Objects are nicely defined, sort of like cartoon or comic book.  I prefer this style of art to the more realistic style because in this type of game I want to know what I can click on.  I've played some games where I didn't know what something was or that I was supposed to click there until the hint button told me.
No voices.  And I really don't remember the music, if there was any.  If there is music it was very bland and did not stand out.  Or else I had my volume down.
Total time playing according to Steam is 1.8 hours.  I did have a little problem figuring something out so some of that is wasted time going back and forth trying things.  So it might be an hour or little over for fast players.
It's a good price for the length and content.  Actually I've seen similar games priced higher, so this one is a bargain.

A good story mixed with a dreadful game. The gameplay is dull and the controls are awkward. In some sense, it's actually impressive how they managed to screw up the controls in such a simplistic game.
The story might be a bit cheesy and short, but good. Not worthy of any awards, but good. The story is the main selling point of the game, no two ways about it. The game is described as a "story-driven experience" and tagged as "story rich", so as you might expect the gameplay takes the back seat. But there's the problem: the game itself is so bad that it serves only as a distraction to the story. Every moment I spent actually playing the game was only so that I could continue the story. I would have prefered only the story, with no game at all. In other words, a movie.
So do I recommend it? Well, maybe. If you are willing to suffer through a bad game while being told a good story, then sure. If you want to support the developers, then sure. But if you want a good game, then stay far away from this one. Everything this game has to offer has been done much better. If you want a point-and-click game, there are plenty which are actually good as opposed to this one which is bad. If you want a puzzle game, same thing. And while the story is good, there are plenty of better ones. Just read a good book or watch a good movie. Even some games have better stories. This game is hilariously over-praised.

First of all, props to Larian Studios for making an phenomenal game. I can say that the minds behind this game are pure genius! Quests are almost non-linear (except for the main ones of course), and I just admire the branching systems of quests (as well as their respective consequences!). The skills and abilities system may prove to have a brutal learning curve for some (and yes, you can never have that one perfect character with all those attributes). In this game, I really learned the value of having multiple (and also very frequent!) saves. Teamwork and strategy is really crucial in this game. Even the normal/classic mode is somewhat unforgiving for me already (what more with the Tactician and Honour modes!?!).
What I don't like about this game is just the rock-paper-scissors system of winning arguments. A bit troublesome if you ask me. I just wished they had thought of something else in lieu of this probability system. Nonetheless, everything else is excellent! Definitely recommended for those who love gruelling, hardcore RPGs!

The AP system is marvellously well conceived, as well as the skill tree and the attributes actually matter in this game. Hokay, so, I've decided to re-review this game, as per the comments below requesting I do so.
I tried it again, and I am willing to admit that:
1- I was probably wrong to judge it so quickly and harshly, and
2- There are elements that bug me, but we'll get to them
So, the game: the game is actually pretty fun. I loved the idea, and I still do. What I didn't realise was how important using doubles in games are, nor how important it is to have certain types of cards. Now that I do, I'm getting through issues pretty quickly and easily. It does take a bit of learning, but I will state what I have always loved:
I love the fact you draw your minions from cards, and not just always have them, making you think on the fly and when creating decks.
That being said, I'm still not sold on the marketing idea of random creatures, but I am happier now that I see a crafting system. That does help offset the rng that can mess you around, as well as knowing it's not the rarity of the card, but its usefulness.
All in all I think the game is fairly fun to play, nice and simple for a quick romp, but for me at least, I feel a bit of a lack of staying power, and so will play it on and off as opposed to religiously. We'll see how well that goes in terms of things.
However, I also know there are elements I have yet to play (draft and such like) so I will also need to try that, and observe how dailies are done in this game. Otherwise, I am enjoying it more than I was before.

This game is the most fantastic game I have in my Steam Library. I revisit it every year to play through again. This game might not have the most thrilling gameplay, but it is simple and beautiful, and has one of the best soundtracks you'll ever hear in a game. I'd definitely recommend it for anyone who just enjoys games that make you feel happy and relaxed. But be warned, there is a lot of walking involved

The graphics may look lo-fi from a screenshot, but in game everything trembles to the touch, or else sways and flows of its own accord, suggesting a living, breathing world. What's impressive is that the effect is often achieved by the animation of just a few solitary pixels. Combined with some atmospheric sound design, the result is a world where every detail of every screen begs to be pored over. The music evokes all the right emotions on cue, and the presentation and language of the game is quirky and original. The gameplay is somewhat rudimentary and clearly designed for touch devices first and foremost, and yet Sword & Sworcery EP remains one of the strongest and most captivating interactive audio-visual experiences I've played in some time.
The game tries too hard to make it's fake-retro style into something artsy, but it's real flaw is that the gameplay is somewhere between non-existent and bland.

I love the art style and way the game unfolds. Some parts might have you thinking for a bit; a good thing. Check it out if you are in any way interested. (or maybe check out the mobile version instead?)

Playing this game was one of the simplest, happiest experiences of my entire life. I can't explain it, exactly. SB:S&S EP is a retro pixel point-and-click game. But I think it's also best described in the game's own terms: as a drug trip, and perhaps even stranger, as an album. The music, the art style, the gameplay, the transmedia interactions, and the bizarrely perfect anachronistic speech mode all suit it perfectly and combine to form something totally unique. It took me almost a year to finish this game. It was something I had to be in the right frame of mind for. I don't regret a second of it.

This game is a bit different as it early on demonstrates its uniqueness through its use of pixel graphics and catchy tunes. The thing about it is that it does not feel retro at all, but particularly modern. The game was originally developed for touch devices, so the controls are a bit simplistic. It feels like a point and click adventure, although you are free to move around anywhere you like. However, the story it tries, and succeeds to convey is quite beautiful. You are a rather unknown adventurer starting a journey to retrieve a book. Not treasure, not a weapon crafted by gods or demons, but a book capable of giving you knowledge you require. It is your job to take that knowledge and venture on a journey with the book’s guidance in order to achieve the dream of becoming a hero. That journey is marvelous and wonderfully complemented by its atmospheric soundtrack composed by Jim Guthrie, the same person who wrote the soundtrack for Indie Game: The Movie. This game is one I recommend to anyone in search of a great 4-hour long quest.

Ah, the Division. This game is pretty much all about semi-tactical semi-realizstic shooting. Cover-based infantry combat with guns. There are vehicles that can be fought on certain, end-game missions, but none that a player themself can use. There are no rocket launchers, player-usable grenade launchers (although there is a launchable sticky-bomb that only requires a cooldown to use.)
As far as the combat goes, the game is great. The gunplay feels good. The tactical orientation of the game requires you to think to succeed (or be overly well equipped) and there's plenty of gun variety and the RNG is ever creul but lower limits keeps it mostly in check.
Character development is a bit iffy, as far as I'm concered. Yes, there are clear benefits to leveling. There any many "skills" that can be unlocked for active use in combat to turn the tide to tip the balance in your favor. Enemy difficulty also ramps up as you raise level. But the main thing is that at higher levels you can use the higher level guns and gear, which is of course, better than equivilent lower level stuff. But talents, skill mods, unlockable slots are the most you can directly see from the level differences. Other than that, leveling and base upgrades don't really give you much in the way of more tangible feeling development.
Then there's the role playing element. Which is to say, one of the worst parts of the game. There are pretty much next to no choises aside from which parts of the base to upgrade first (which thus gives you skills and skill mods you can use) when to get those upgrades (not if, eventually you'll get all of them and the resource limit is well beyond what is needed for everything) and when you run off through the giant, mostly empty city to deal with the many side quests, encounters, and run into countless helpless people and then those other guys with guns. Your character has fewer lines than Link in the Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time. You get no option to say anything, nor make any choices that have any real outcomes on the fate of the city. You're just a sleeper agent from the Division, activated in the second wave, given a terrible weapon and armor, and told to do whatever it takes to ensure continuity of government.
Fights happen with much empty content in between simply because all fights are dnagerous. While you can easily succeed as long as you are skilled, properly equipped and experienced, and trying hard enough, you must try. Even in a simple gunfight with some jerk with a pathetic little handgun on the street. As a direct result, the developers cannot throw enemy after enemy at you while out and about, and thus you'll spend much of your time running toward the next fight, pushing the little button to advance the mission you're on, and sometimes chekcing if that thing that guy you just shot is better than what you already have.
Which is my next point: the entire game is a constant grind, with the intent of finding equipment that is beter than what you already have. Even up to and through the endgame, you will still be checking if that shiny new high-end drop is a gun, one that you like, and if so, one that is better than the one you're already holding. It becomes an endless cycle.
But the part where the shooting, the thrown and launched grenades explode, you use some weird SHD tech to pull a tiny healing robot out of nowhere that rebuilds itself after a half-minute or so, and a lot of people named Alex, Chains, or Dylan, or some nameless crazed sanitation worker falls over and take whatever they wer epolite enough to leave behind... all of that... is fun. The fact you can't just fart and annihilate every enemy that crosses paths with youforces you to actually try if you want to succeed, especially on higher difficulties.
In summary:
Because the combat is fun, and the RNG grind is satisfying when something useful actually shows up, I do recommend this game.

The Escapists: The Walking Dead is an aptly named amalgamation of the prison break indie game, The Escapists, coupled with the smash hit comic book and TV series, The Walking Dead. It takes all of the original game's mechanics and fits them into the world of Rick Grimes' undead uber-brand. As expected from a game set in that world, instead of escaping from prison, you're in charge of a group of people struggling to survive the onslaught of the zombie apocalypse.
It follows the story of the original comic books pretty faithfully, although it often feels like a cheap skin applied over the top of something else, which is, of course, essentially what it is. What this means, though, is that The Walking Dead license serves only as a framework for its setting rather than providing the game with a coherent and unified narrative and mechanical paradigm of any substance. That said, it's easy to see how the mechanics of the original game may work in this scenario, and these have been faithfully brought over to the follow-up game – both good and bad.
The Escapists: The Walking Dead is essentially a time-management game where you must methodically execute a series of everyday chores and objectives in order to both keep the other survivors happy and to keep the walkers out. Simple tasks such as taking attendance in the early hours of the morning or doing the laundry are mandatory exercises that determine the threat level of the undead making their way into your little sanctuary.
An ability to suspend your own sense of disbelief is an ongoing requirement to find enjoyment with this game. You must be able to ignore the audacity that mopping the floor on a daily basis somehow relates to the likelihood of being overrun by walkers. You must also be able to accept that when another survivor asks you to return their bar of soap that a walker has stolen, only that very bar of soap will be accepted. No other bar of soap, no matter how clean, will suffice – they only want the one that has been mauled at by a dirty walker.
Considering the burdensome nature of these demands, the game begins to feel like a chore in itself. These laborious quests are pretty much mandatory in order to progress within the game since completing them is how you earn in-game coins which are used to purchase components and items from vendors. These ingredients take up a significant role within the game since they are required to craft new items such as weapons which are needed both for yourself to survive and those under your command.
Sure enough, items can be found riddled throughout the world, but the randomized locations of these components mean that the game often feels like it's going out of its way to make things difficult for you. The aim is to gather the right ingredients to craft new items, but these combinations are often illogical, and unless you can find a written recipe outlining the algorithm to success, you have to rely on a trial-and-error strategy of lumping anything you can find into the crafting screen. This is time-consuming, too, since the limited nature of your inventory means that most items found need to be left where they are, leaving you having to remember the different locations of each item. It's like playing a game of Pairs, except on a much larger and more complex scale.
Not everything about The Escapists: The Walking Dead is negative. The game has a charming 8-bit aesthetic, and the soundtrack sets the tone well – you will often find your foot tapping along to the groovy beat. It's not all bad, but the negative aspects far outweigh the positives. This is the kind of game where a slow, methodical approach is best served, but it feels more like a time-waste than a compelling game that rewards you for your efforts.
The Escapists: The Walking Dead is a visually charming game with a standout soundtrack, but its gameplay is shallow and repetitive. It follows the narrative of the original comic books, but uses them only superficially without any real depth or engagement with the license. It has its moments of fun, but more often than not is a frustrating time-sink made up of trial-and-error mechanics with little sense of reward.

Game Dev Tycoon isn't complicated to learn or to play, and it's almost completely text and menu based. For some reason, though, it's completely addictive. If you're looking for something more casual than Software Inc., this is for you.

Story and Gameplay
At the beginning of the game, you name your game studio and you start making games as solo projects. As you progress throughout the game, you can hire more people and eventually get better offices so you can hire more people. When you start, you’ll only have a few options and a few platforms. Eventually, you’ll gain research points and you can use those to upgrade stats, research new genres, and new engines/game mechanics. When you are making a game, you can pick your audience (E, T, and M), budget, and what platforms your game will be on. Once you learn what combinations are good, this game becomes pretty easy. Pretty much, this game is all about making games to get money and then researching so you can make bigger games and make more money.
Graphics
There really isn’t much to talk about when it comes to graphics, this game just has a certain art style. To me, the art style isn’t unappealing, but I feel like it could’ve been better. Despite that, it does not take away from the fun that you can have with this game.
Overall
Game Dev Tycoon is a great indie game and I highly recommend if you are into these types of games. I had a ton of fun with this game and I will continue to put more time into it. If you want a game where you manage a game studio, this is the one to go with.

There's a moment early on in Scribblenauts when you're faced with a puzzle with an entirely easy solution. Instead of that solution, you want to do something creative and crazy. The idea is in your head, but you know it won't work: there's no way the game developers even thought of putting a <insert thing> in the game, and if they did, they wouldn't have made it a way to solve this puzzle. And then it works.
That moment is different for everyone, and describing mine (giving a theremin to a homeless guy so he could start a band) wouldn't really explain what makes it so special. It's a moment everyone needs to experience for themselves.
Scribblenauts is a sandbox game. Sure, there are puzzles, achievements, and even a plot, but for the most part Scribblenauts is a game where you want to put the craziest things into the world and see what happens. The puzzles facilitate this well: any adult should have no problem solving them (they are, after all, designed for young children), but if you're like me you will find yourself motivated to think of the most ludicrous solution, with the hope that maybe you can outsmart the game. Need to put out a fire? Firefighter is a boring answer; try annihilating it with some antimatter!
Playing out pure sandbox fantasies is amazing too. Watching what happens is what makes the game amazing. Give God a magical squirtgun and he'll use it to turn Cthulhu into a dove—then promptly discard the weapon, pick dove Cthulhu up by the neck, and start bashing him on things. It's an inexplicably amazing experience.
The game shines when your crazy ideas play themselves out, but it's not perfect at it. Finding the holes takes a little magic away each time, and reminds you that the game can't actually function without being programmed to. If something is missing in the game you might be able to find it in the Steam Workshop (or build it yourself), but it's doubtful it will be quite as epic as finding that yes, the developers did in fact think of it.
My main criticism is the adjective system. While it's amazing when it works, and it can be a lot of fun to add an adjective to a random citizen and watch them change their behavior because of it, it's not without fault. Many if not most of the available adjectives seem to have minimal effects short of thought bubbles expressing them, if they even have that. Why doesn't my "vengeful" hunter attack people? What makes her vengeful? Further, some objects do exist in the game that are multiple words, and making these is tricky when the game assumes if you have a typo you meant to type "Adjective Noun" instead of a two word noun. Some of these are entirely confusing: "flying broomstick" is a seperate object from spawning a broomstick and adding the adjective flying to it, for instance.
Still, these moments hardly detract from the rest of the game. It's an amazing and well worthwhile experience.

Sproggiwood is a real Nethack game on the lighter side. It is somehow perfect for me, and I have been sinking lots of hours into it. It is a great way to kick back after work: have a multi-hour dungeon delve that has a 80-90% success rate of beating the boss monster. The game keeps me engaged by making me think through each movement. And the movement and attacks are FUN, which is most important. So many games look good in the description, but the game mechanics are dull once you learn them. Sproggiwood does a great job keeping the mechanics challenging with new monster abilities and new character abilities. I obtained a grappling hook (pitchfork actually) that drags my hero toward the monster, and another character has a sword that pushes monsters around when he uses his charge ability. It is so fun using these and coming up with new item combos that take advantage of the new equipment. The game also has a base-building component, when I am chosing the advantages all my characters will have by buying town buildings. For me, this game has a lot of the things that make it a joy to play a computer game. I am glad that I took a chance on it!

I have very little time to play games nowadays. I typically don't ever finish a game, and when I do, to me that is the true sign of a real good game, a game I would make time for, a game to lose sleep over.  Total War: WARHAMMER II is such a game.  I played through both the Vortex and Mortal Empires Campaign, and both were engaging and fun.  I am a Total War Veteran (started with the first Medieval), but have never been too keen on the battles themselves.  I typically just play the strategic part of the game without being too hands-on on the battlefield.  In TW: WII, I actually wanted to play the battles.  I wanted to see the units, how they would match up, how different stacks had different results, etc.  I think the result is much more varied than when using all humans, for obvious reasons. Oh, and did I mention Dragons?
The graphics are solid, the game is not too heavy on the resource management (you can choose factions that are very low-maintenance) and the factions and lords are interesting enough.  There are four factions you can choose for Eye of the Vortex, and everyone except the Norsca (as long as you own the DLCs) is available for the Mortal Empires campaign.
As a con I would say there's not a lot of cohesion on the Mortal Empires side from a story perspective, it feels a bit thrown together. However, I love the ambitious nature of the massive Campaign, which I completed with the Wood Elves on my first run.  I played through the Eye of the Vortex campaign with the Dark Elves, and both factions felt very different, almost like playing different games just by switching factions.
Minor annoyances like restrictive camera angles or distances can already bve handled with mods, and I am sure the Creative Assembly team will continue to improve on the game as they put out further expansions.  I was rteally disappointed that I couldn't play Mortal Empires with the Norsca, because I had bought the DLC specifically for that purpose. I will have to wait until May for that playthrough I guess.
As a final thought, I definitely recommend this game.  I have finished both campaigns, and I still want to play it.  I have Battlefront 2, Destiny 2, ME: SOW and FIFA 18 gathering dust because of this game, so that should tell you enough about how addictive and enjoyable it can be.  Mind you, I am not a big Warhammer fan, nor do I really know the lore outside of these two games.  I don't own any other Warhammer game, so I come into this with the perspective of a light Total War player, and not a Warhammer player.  If you have never tried a Total War game, I would say this is one of the best ones to get into as a newb.

How not to like? This game is absolutely one of the best new-gen RPGs I've played. It stands at incredible high standards, giving me the sensation of quick yet tactical combat that I haven't felt since Dragon Age.
The AP system is marvellously well conceived, as well as the skill tree and the attributes actually matter in this game. Character building and customization is a great advantage, even though it doesn't offer that much customization in appearance, it lets you build a character in pretty much any way you want while still maintaining its effectivity (Beware; It's not because it IS viable and/or effective that it is effective in every situation. A Water Mage might want to get more supportive in the early levels, because the whole zombie area is under heavy rain, which makes the enemies resistant to water while they're wet.).
And most importantly: Different from the Souls series, enemies aren't complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You rarely see an enemy that's got 10 times as much health as you, but still deals about the same damage you do (More than enough to kill you in two or three punches,  which he can actually do in a single turn), as most of them are of similar health and damage. Their only disadvantage in relation to your group is the massive amount of abilities you'll have, compared to 1 or 2 of most mobs.
I give Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door a 4/5, just a solid RPG.

Gameplay: The ships have a nice balance between action and simulation. Wind profile and hull design are taken into account... and improving all the time as the game devlops. Available nations to sail for are; USA, Britain, France, Denmark, Holland, Spain, Sweeden, and infamous Pirates!

Comunity / Moderators; Ive been playing this game since it began in closed alpha... these guys in game are some of the funnest and funniest players around! The community has been more than fun to work and play with and able to voice opinion easily.
Pros: Immersive sandbox world of immense proportions! Good sounds. Good variety of ships to buy/craft/steal. Ecconomics for those who want to be a trader captain. While I recommend this game, note that it comes with a caviat. ONLY BUY THIS GAME IF YOU HAVE A CONTROLLER.
While I have no issue with 2D fighters, there is one problem with this one that makes a lot of the more powerful game-changing moves unusable. The fact that this game started out on a console that then moved to PC means that the arrow keys have to take place of an analogue controller. This makes the rotations required for a lot of combinations very difficult to use if you're relying on your keyboard. I needed several attempts just to get consistent quarter turns, several more attempts for the more complicated rotations and a full rotation is downright impossible (for me at least).
If you have a lot of experience with 2D fighters (or a lot of patience to try mastering the controls for this one), then the keyboard controls shouldn't be too big an issue for you. However, if you're new to fighting games on the PC, I would seriously recommend getting a controller if you want to play Skullgirls. It's a good looking game, but it is an example of how making a cross-platform game can have some unfortunate drawbacks.

This game comes so dangerously close to perfect. Arguably the most beautiful 2D platformer you've ever played Ori and the Blind Forest stuns with details -- swaying plants, perfect mood lighting, a veritable army of colors on screen at any given moment. How visually stunning this game is can't be stated enough. It's like having your eyes injected with unicorns on LSD. The story is simple, well told, and emotionally effective. The gameplay is more or less spot on with the occasional erratic control flub. Combat is basic but fun. Secrets are numerous and sometimes rather clever. You're likely to die often, but generally this isn't a problem as you're able to consume energy to establish a "spirit link" to save when you like - almost always. The skill tree is basic but useful though by game's end you're likely to have all trees near maxed if not fully completed.
Ori's problem is that every point that makes it succeed to brilliantly is completely thrown out the window in the sequences after waking a spirit element. The screen floods with effects making it hard to figure out where to go, what to do, and where Ori is admist the chaos. You've overcome with instances of one-hit kills exacerbated by occasionally buggy game elements (primary the dash n' bash targets) that cause you to die. And, worst of all, the save-as-you-go establishment is tossed aside in favor of you repeating these gaunlets over and over and over again from the very beginning until you can execute them flawlessly. What should be dramatic life or death struggles against a tide of chaos degenerate into an absolutely infuriating experience that fails the player on every level. Your reward for completing these is a save file with a shiny icon and the inability to load your completed game. Did you want to explore the world or maybe trek back to nab a secret or two you might have missed? Too ♥♥♥♥ing bad -- play the game from the start again. A great big middle finger in your face.
As much as I'd would love to recommend Ori and the Blind Forest these details deride the entire experience leaving a foul taste in the mouth by game's end. It's like Davinci was creating the Mona Lisa but decided to use human excrement to paint her hair. Tragic.
tl;dr 10/10

I work with both VX Ace and XP for event scripting work. While there are quite a bit more different graphic packs available for VX Ace, and the format is a little bit easier to learn, it's worth it not to discount XP. XP is cheaper, and you can really do quite a bit more graphically with it.
The main difference you hear about is XP's layers. You have three graphical layers to work with, (foundation, middle, and top), as well as an event layer that goes over all of that. I can thus stack graphical objects closer to one another in XP. I just put them on different layers. The frame rate is 20 lower than VX Ace, (40 instead of 60), but if you were going for the feel of the old Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior games, this is much closer than Ace. Regarding those layers and objects, if I want to create a castle armory that actually feels well stocked, I'd use XP instead of Ace. Ace has an easier scripting wizard for events, but there's an awful lot of online scripting available from the RPG Maker XP forums that improve your XP functionality by a wide margin.
XP and Ace both give you battler backgrounds, as well as an increased sprite size over other programs in this series. XP is from 2004, and is thus seven years older than Ace, but a lot more scripting has been done with this engine, so it isn't impossible to find help and support for whatever your project requires. If you think to yourself: "Gee, I'd really like it if my game had this feature..." ask around, someone's probably written the Ruby code for it already.
I would also point out that if you bought this software direct from program publisher Degica's website like I did, their licensing support has been super helpful getting me a steam key so I could use the Steam Workshop. (They got back to me with a working key within an hour of my first email to Licensing Support about it). This is an all around well supported program from what I've experienced in the last month since my purchase.
Bottom line: If you don't mind a steeper learning curve than VX Ace, (but there are lots of video guides out on YouTube),  and your game project isn't designed with ultra sharp graphics or fast action sequences, XP is well worth your time. You'll be spending a lot of time in techy forums figuring out how to ad scripts and coding to your program, but it's not a terribly difficult program to work with.
Reviewer Qualifications: I have used VX Ace to analyze scripts/test alternate scripts for game articles on The Last Sovereign's wiki, and I am the current script debugger for the AloneXP project. (Both are adult RPGs).

The fact that the Warhammer series for Total War will be turned into a trilogy shows how far Sega/CA are willing to go with their money grabbing. This isn't worth anything more than a DLC price and even then that's pushing it. They've chopped up one game into 3 separate pieces and then have the gall to turn around and say "Hey guys! If you've already thrown money at us twice, then don't worry! You can now play both games on one map! Aren't you lucky?"
It doesn't matter if it's a somewhat fun game to play (and that's purely because I used to collect High Elves as a child), the fact so much content has been removed and that the map is tiny doesn't excuse Sega/CA.
Naval battles? Gone.
Large map with diverse cities, towns and villages? Gone. You know get a rather small map with either "city" battles or field battles.
Town/Village battles? Gone. If your settlement doesn't have walls then you're playing a generic field battle. No more luring in armies to the streets and ambushing them or flanking them.
Full city battles where you can attack from any angle? Gone. You're given the corner of a city to attack and that's it.
Faction managing? Gone. You don't have to worry about food, loyalty, faction politics or sanitation. It's all been removed.
It's rather sickening that people are rating this game so highly purely because it's a Warhammer game when content that was part of at least the last 4 TW games (Shogun 2, Rome, Attila and Medieval 2) has gone.

While I think it does very little to show itself as anything brand new compared to other Rougelikes, it's a short and sweet enought that it's easy to tell if you enjoy it from the first hour alone. And yeah, I enjoyed my time with it.
Dungeons are short, which means they're easy to beat, but the lack of a lot of levels means if you don't care about replaying the levels, you won't get much out of it. However, the main meat of the game comes from the replability in most of the dungeons from the class system. Each class has it's own set of skills, and you can level them up as you kill monsters in the dungeons. The cool thing about this is that you can run though the game in multiple ways and strats based on the current situation and your starting class, so not only is the map randomized, your skills will change based on what you'll find useful in the situation at hand.
The biggest issue I have is the item system. See, the thing that gives this a "Rougelite" element is that your skill dosen't go up with each playthough, instead, you earn items by finding them in dungeons, but they are not auto-unlocked; you must buy the items in the store after finding them.
The problem with this is that gold is minisucle in the earlier dungeons and these items can get expensive really fast, so you'll have to go to a higher areas, but that means you're using a class that has more equipment unlocked, becuase your new class will get destoyed if your items suck. So pretty much this is saying the game can get grindy really fast. Sproggiwood is a decent enough roguelike, although the price point is a little high. I managed to pick this up on sale for 3 bucks, but had I payed the full $15 price, I would have been very disappointed. The 'city building' mechanic is very misleading- it's more like a map editor and it has no impact on the game itself. Perhaps the development schedule didn't permit the completion of this feature, but leaving it in the game just feels like a way to boost a feature-list. Combine this with the limited number of skills (I think there are 4 per class) and equipment, and the brevity of the game and it just feels incomplete. To be fair, I did play the game on easy mode, so the shortness is my own fault, but I just thought there would be more to the game.
That said, the graphics are appropriate. There are no mind blowing cut scenes or anything, but the colorful 2d imagery fits well with the cutesy, simplistic storyline. The music is nice, and it reminds me a lot of Secret of Mana. There are only a handful of tracks, but they never get repetitive considering how short the game is. The enemy mechanics can be a little annoying, but on the whole that just seems to make defeating them that much more satisfying.
In conclusion, if you're looking for a short, colorful roguelike to kill a little time, then I highly recommend this, but you should definitely wait for it to go on sale.

TLDR
Like Clash Royale for PC, mixed with some elements from Hearthstone.
'Minion Masters' is a game that mostly can be defined as a competitive/duel - RTS, as you battle an opponent in a heads up minion spawning game and see who can crush the opponent's hero/base first.
The game is primarily inspired by the Clash Royale game for mobile and borrow some game design choices from Hearthstone or MOBAs to add another level of complexity to the game.
The game follow the rock-paper-scissor-lizard-and so on structure to bring balance to the game, with the added complexity of a hero/base that has a set of abilities that become available the longer the game progresses. These are in most cases significant 'timing-windows' that players play around which just adds to the interesting play-styles and diversity in each game.
Games last about 5 minutes at max, and that is probably setting it too high, as games are incredibly fast paced and quick thinking is adviced. Queues are pretty immidiate at the early levels and I never felt like I was being matched outside my league.
It's free to play, and the standard load-out of cards are pretty strong, so you can get a ton of game-play in without taking another bank-loan. Weekly free-hero rotation, as you probably know from LoL or HoN, allow you to try different heroes(bases) each week before you commit to a purchase.
Unfortunately you cannot duel a friend yet, although it will be out soonish.
- Overall a great experience, little time between updates and fixes.

Here's the deal: I liked this game. Yeah, it's a mobile game ported to PC and that does mean it isn't technically flawless. But man, I remember staying up in a room with no air conditioning in the middle of summer playing it and being like...two hours late for something because I wanted to finish this in one sitting.  I think I was meeting Mike for something. Mike, I'm sorry.
On the whole it's a really well made and fun adventure game that does a fantastic job at telling its story in a world that's filled to bursting with mysterious and enticing tone. The whole experience is truly evocative; a quest that will somehow lead you straight to peril, a la Shadow of the Colossus. The story itself is compelling and the game does a wonderful job of doing as much storytelling through the beautifully realized environments and haunting sound design as it does through actual text.
And here's the cool thing about that. Sword and Sworcery swings almost all of its weight in those departments to create an engrossing experience. Why do I care about the world? Because it's simultaneously beautiful and enticing, it beckons for you to explore it. How do I know it's not just goofy? Because the music and the design of each area inform you of the mood there, you can tell when you're supposed to chuckle and when you're supposed to be on edge. Why do you press on? Because it looks like a quest-y video game, what else would you do?
Where does it fall apart? That's why I want you to play it. Personally, I think the narrator breaking things up is a bit to cheeky for the tone of the game (at least as I remember it almost a year later). Yeah, some of the combat controls are a little wonky, yeah the movement can be a teeny bit frustrating. But really, I want you to play this. I want you to understand what good design is: bringing all aspects of the experience together to create something that you want to spend time with, characters you feel for even if you don't know them well, and provide you with a story that you remember vividly enough to tell your little nephew at a camping trip 6 months after finishing it. It'll provide you with that wide-eyed childlike joy of exploration and the bittersweet joy of completion.
If this does convince you to buy the game, message me after it's done. I want to talk about it. So bad.
