A cute and simple little roguelike. The basic mechanics are pretty easy to grasp; there are 6 progressively-unlocked classes with 4 skills each, and character progression where you gain XP to unlock and then upgrade skills happens on a per-dungeon basis, rather than overall. Between individual dungeons you use money from the last dungeon to buy permanent items or unlock bonuses, and you can also build a little village that nominally acts as your home base. There's also a paper-thin story, and a progressive series of dungeons with an increasing variety of enemies to deal with.
I enjoyed the simplicity and the clarity of the mechanics, and the process of picking out items that best matched what I wanted to do with each class, though the keyboard controls were a bit awkward at times (sometimes WASD and the arrows are interchangeable but sometimes you need to use one or the other, for instance). The setting is kind of whimsical in a nice way, too, though it's a shame the village-building systen is purely cosmetic. Overall, it's a fun little game to play while you're doing something else at the same time, like listening to podcasts.

At first, I thought Sproggiwood was okay. Not great, but okay. The gameplay (especially the combat) was overly simplistic, but worked well enough. The writing, while rather bland and boring, was by no means terrible.
Then it introduced me to the town 'system'. What I mean by this is that there is a town, which you can customise with purely cosmetic buildings, and buy stuff from, but otherwise it serves no purpose.
Then I was introduced to what seems like the games core concept; items you find in dungeons are only usable for that dungeon. If you want to permanently keep them, you must buy them. Okay, that's an interesting concept. The game also has multiple classes.
I only played the Farmer and the Archer, but their skills seemed fairly similar. You have a ranged attack (Pitchfork throw/Arrow) an escape tool (Scarecrow/Roll) and the kill-lots-of-things-at-once (Pumpkin Bomb/Piercing Arrow) and a fourth ability that requires you to be a much higher level then I ever bothered to attain (levels are also reset at the start of every dungeon.) This is where things quickly went downhill.
At the start of the second dungeon, I encountered an enemy that killed me in about 3 turns with a charge attack, which I had no way of avoiding in the narrow corridor I was in. After about eight more playthroughs of my health slowly being dwindled down by enemies whose tactics were clearly designed to chip away at your health, forcing you to grind for one use hp potions, I made it to the boss. In a game where you are encouraged to avoid taking damage, the second boss of the game is designed to force you into a head on tactic, as it has a charge attack in a room full of narrow corridors.
This may just seem like complaints about difficulty, but these issues (combined with its obvious mobile design. There's actually an option for Mobile or Tablet display) made me realise that if I played any more of this game I'd likely grow bored of it anyway. Shallow gameplay and an intentionally tedious grind do NOT mix well.

Those were my initial thoughts on Lego Worlds when I'd played it a while ago when it was in Early Access.  Having purchased the game in June 2015 it was early days and the game while in many ways looking diferent than it does now still had the same sort of asthetics the I can't remember the exploration aspect being part of the intial early access builds I think it was just a choice of procedually generated worlds for you to explore but I may be mistaken.
One thing that has changed hower is the expansion of the game, you are now able to explore new worlds, collecting Gold Bricks expands your rocket ships ability to explore the far flung reaches of the legoverse and strange new planets.  There are initially a couple of very easy 'learner' planets to get to grips with the tools and to learn the controls and how to build/create then once you are done with them the game lets you lose to explore and build for yourself.
I must admit that in my first three and a half hours I did a lot of exploration of planets (and getting lost remembering where people where to hand in quests lol) but it was really good, the controls seem much easier then the earlier version of the game, the tools give you a range of different things you can do, from discovering items, people, creatures and buildings to unlock and use in your own worrld; changing the landscape to fit your creative whims raising and lowering grounds and changing surfaces, to a wide range of different bits and pieces to allow you to build once you unlock them and much much more.
My opinion on lego worlds is exactly the same as before but now seeing the finished product I can't see any reason not to recommend this game, it is a lot of fun to play, build and explore and will keep all ages entertained.

While later versions of RPG Maker are considerably more capable and user friendly, the one thing I prefer about this version is the ability to "Resize" your own sprites. The size of the sprites is directly proportional to the size of the image, so if you want a taller character he'll be taller ingame.
This is not a magical game maker, they've done the programming. It's up to you to make the game. Triggers, story, characters, all yours. While plenty of content is provided right of the bat, I prefer to create my own images and music. This can either be done in menu, or simply by moving files into the appropriate folders.
If you've used level editors, you should be able to flow comfortably into the interface and you can do almost anything, however this has no option for cutscenes. That being said, reasonable quality images can be imported (640x480 or less) Nothing you make will ever be graphically impressive, but it's really not the point. If I'm correct the amazing title "To the Moon" was made using this software.
The item/character customization is pretty much complete, I was actually able to create an accessible book using dialogue chains. Heck, you could even write a "Choose your own adventure" with the dialogue chains. Every stat is alterable as well, even the amount of experience required to level up. If you want to be in depth enough, fight animations and sounds can be replaced.
Just bare in mind, there is nothing casual about this process, it is time consuming, but if it's your thing, it's time well spent.

This was on my wishlist forever and when I finally played the game it was worth every penny. It is a really fun modern, tongue-in-cheek, turn based RPG. You create 2 characters to start off with and end up recruiting 2 more as your party battle to save the world.
Two key points to note are:
- This game does not take itself seriously at all. If you want a straight faced, deep plot then look elsewhere.
- This game does not hold your hand. You must be willing to experiment and discover things by yourself (or consult a wiki!)
Turn based RPG veterans will find the default difficulty a bit easy. Tactician mode is recommended.

+ Lots and lots of silly humour - you get to talk to animals and help Walter McWishing Well look for his brother :)
+ Fun and tactical turn-based combat
+ Streamlined but interesting character development system, giving you plenty of choice to customise your party
+ Crafting system allows you to buff/enhance items and create entirely new ones
+ Challenging puzzles
+ Co-op mode available as well as single player
+ Full voice acting on every single line of dialogue makes the game very immersive. An impressive amount of work must have gone into this.
+ The enhanced edition lives up to its name with smooth, polished and bug free gameplay
+ Pretty graphics and rotatable camera
- The pacing of the game feels slightly off. The beginning town of Cyceal could do with more hints to ease the player into the game. At times I ran around not quite sure what to do. The mid game has a few too many trash mobs with little variety. The end game has a section which is full of puzzles, one after the other - I found that a bit exhausting.
- NPCs repeat their lines far too often and it gets irritating. Luckily there is a mod that fixes this - I highly recommend QuietDayOnTheMarket mod by Abraxas1990
Also check out the FastMoveSpeed mod if you are impatient.
- Inventory gets cluttered with lots of junk items that are useless.
- The game does not hold your hand. If you love to experiment and spend time trying out different crafting combinations, you will love this. I personally got annoyed by all the undocumented crafting combinations that were available. I highly recommend the use of a wiki to save time.
- The game does not tell you that in order to advance the plot, you need to use certain quest items. Also you must save a certain amount of quest items to succeed near the end of the game. (Trying to avoid spoilers!).
- The storyline is not the greatest so don't expect anything mindblowing.
- One particular area in the game felt slightly unfinished (Sacred Stone I'm looking at you!). Trying to be heroic resulted in reputation loss.
- Insta-kill traps and forced stealth sequences were a bit annoying.
If you have any interest in RPGs you NEED to check this game out. Divinity Original Sin 2 is on my wishlist :)

If you are a fan of any sailing combat game then this game is an absolute must have. It provides a whole map of opportunity. If you don;t want to test or see the unfinished game then simply wait for release.
This game is still in testing. Many negative reviews I have read seem to be by players complaining that the game isnt finished, well of course it isn't finished it hasn't reached launch date yet ! If you bouhgt the game early it was to put money into the development, gain a 'Testing position' if you wanted it and a freebie or three at launch.
There are currently PVE and PVP servers setup for the testers to populate.
The game has been designed to immerse the player in accurate combat simulation from the age of sail. Great ship Models, Wind and sailing effects. Changeable weather. Detailed and very agreeable firing and damage system.
In addition to the combat the game gives the opportunity for trading, in depth crafting of ships, consumables and ship upgrades modules.
Rank advancement of you as the captain and personal development of your 1st officer to add depth to your tactical style.
Opportunity to take part in port battles for ownership of ports and resources, open map warfare where a mixture of player squadrons or solo ships can engage each other. International treaties between player nations. Missions and AI squadrons for those more pve aligned.
Ship combat is excellent, visual from the deck, telescope or the crows nest view, control, models, real sailing and damage systems give this game a huge thumbs up. I won't even mention the effect a sub-woofer produces when a 1st rate fires off a broadside.  Ships can be upgraded with modules but within reason giving you a slight style of ship without 'magic' or unrealistic benefits.
The Devs are always open about their plans and timelines and achieve most milestones as well as listening to their player base when feedback can and does influence game content and mechanics.
As testers the current player base can still see areas of improvement all of which are on the Devs "To Do" list prior to release.
My only mini gripe whish is far outweighed by the many positives, is that although set in the Caribbean I do feel I am usually sailing up a foggy and muggy English channel. More sunlight and bright skies are to be hoped for in the future.
I wish Game Labs well and am pleased I have been able to have so much time and fun in the game as a tester which far exceeds my usual time spent in a full release game. Bring on the Final Launch, looking forward to adding another 1100 hours. :)

Recommended for those looking for a sailing game, to be on the sea and get lost in the romanticism of the age of sail.

Starting out, there's not a whole lot to love and to latch onto. The graphics appear to be taken straight from the Atari, the controls are clearly limited, not enhanced, by the original touch screen interface, social media is brought up as a potentially important part of the game from the beginning, and the first characters introduced are creatively named Dogfella and Logfella. However, by the end of the first session, all those things had taken on a different light. The sprites stopped looking like a handful of rectangles and became real characters, the touch based controls resulted in a more direct interaction with the environment, and the names gained a weight which made them seem natural. All this started with the music. It seems to slip right into these inadequate forms and make them into what they should have been. Once that happens, this game goes from a mess of hard corners and half measures to a truly worthy experience.

If you want to know what the game gets right head on over to the ‘recommend’ section, there is no need to repeat the praise – much of what it deserves – here. This review instead is all about the impact of a studio overpromising and eventually under delivering on an idea much more than the actual game. Let me explain, from the get go of TW:WI Creative Assembly trumpeted the idea of a grand strategy game spanning various instalments but – critically – stitching together for an even grander experience. This was the reason I bought every single TW:WI DLC, and went so far as to pre-order TW:WII, in order to make the most of the grand campaign when it finally came around. The anti-climax to this studio induced hype was of course Mortal Empires, a “free” DLC for owners of both TW:WI and TW:WII. Apart from it being a bug ridden mess and without key updates to the original TW:WI races (where is Norsca?!), the much hyped up idea of a grand campaign map was in reality a lacklustre and severely downsized version of what could have been a truly breath-taking focal point for the series. Instead it feels like an afterthought, a box that had to be ticked to keep the plebeians from rebelling due to low public order. I have never pre-ordered a game before, and thanks to my experiences with TW:WII I shall never do so again. In the end I can only vote with my wallet, and unless some drastic action is taken by the studio execs I for one won’t be spending another denarii on any future TW:W releases. Burn me once…

All ya'll thought ya'll knew games? Nah you don't know♥♥♥♥♥♥about games! So here's my review of Ori and the Blind Forest.
Where to start though? If it had beautiful art, that would have been enough. If it had solid controls, that would have been enough. If it left me wanting more, that would have been enough! Ori and the Blind forest does all three for me and more than that.
So about Ori and the Blind Forest, it's a metroid-vania style game, which if you're unaware means that as you play the game you unlock new abilities and skills that allow you to visit places you couldn't get to before. Like gaining the ability to double jump up to a higher place or ground pound through an obstruction. There are some games that do this okay (Terraria), some do this really well (Shovel Knight), but Ori does it absolutely almost perfectly. Getting the little items and upgrades for my health and energy were challenging but not impossible which can be attributed to the excellent controls. Fortunately this game takes more after Castlevania more than Metroid and as such the opening of the map is MUCH more organic. It's not perfect, mind. there are some locations that close off forever and if you didn't get all the collectibles say goodbye to 100% completion. An intentional design flaw made to punish those who just can't deal unless they have 100% of something, which I'm thankful for in this game. If you're playing to 100% the game then you've obviously forgotten what video games are for.
Now onto the controls. Typical WASD, space, shift, e, left, and right mouse key. At the beginning, all you have are these but as you go you get better skills from these spirit trees that make more of the game accessible and running around the map more easy. It's also worth noting that moving around is fun as hell late game. I found myself getting into a rythm bouncing off enemies and projectiles and super jumping through terrain, killing all the enemies in the room and landing on the other side of a spiked area completely unharmed. It's this near perfect mix of speed of progress and difficulty that makes it so engaging. It's got that Sonic the Hedgehog smooth as butter kind of movement.
As far as game mechanics go it doesn't bring much new to the table except one thing, making your own save points. If you have enough energy you can make your own save location. It's not exactly anything more than a quick saving feature made less efficient but I thought it was pretty nifty. It is from these save points that you buy upgrades for yourself with spirit orbs that you collect from enemies and upgrade orbs hidden throughout the map. You have three upgrade trees: Utility, Combat, and Utility ++. Utility does things like double the energy, life, and spirit orbs you absorb. Combat is pretty obvious. Increase the power of your shots, increase the number of enemies they can hit at a time, etc. And Utility ++ is kind of a hodgepodge. You can tell they were struggling for a third tree because basic design law dictates that a repition of three is the most attractive. But Utility ++ is like adding a third jump to your double jump, recovering life every time you make a save point, etc. Also the skill "trees" are more like skill twigs at best. A single line for each tree, no branching, or choosing this or that skill. But that's okay. The upgrade system might be my least favorite part of the game but that's okay since everything else is polished to a mirror shine.
I'm not going to talk about the story much because this is a story that deserves to be told by the game. So instead I'll give the premise. You are Ori, a spirit of light working to restore life to a now dead land. Some sad things happen some happy things happen. You ain't getting no more. BUY THE GAME!
Now on to my favorite part, the artwork. Jesus William Christ the artwork. Beautiful, vibrant color, outstanding design, and the animation... just... there are no words for all the emotions this game made me feel through the art alone. The animation is just so gorgeous there are no words in existence to accurately depict how much I love it. You have to see it. Not to mention the sound design. I have never heard quite as beautiful a sound design as that. A lot of games treat music as just white noise not to be payed attention to and really only meant to occupy your brain. (Terraria, Call of Duty, freakin Borderlands!) I actually found myself staying in certain areas just to sit and listen to the music. And when you get to event areas the music picks up the pace and gets your blood pumping like crazy as you're bombarded with massive amounts of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and you're just trying to stay alive and you want the music to calm down and just as you're ABOUT to die... you make it out and this relieving music plays and makes everything all better. There were times when my arms were jelly afterwards. It's a game that engaged me and made me feel things, and that is miles more than I can say for a lot of other games like Borderlands or even Skyrim. (Not to say that either was bad) I'm even rereading over this and this paragraph doesn't accurately describe how much I loved the artwork. So I implore you not to take my word for it and instead go look for yourself.
I'll go ahead and wrap up my thoughts with this. It probably sounds like a cliche at this point but I believe in one general truth with video games. That is that there are two types. The first type being one that was made so that the creators could add a new golden sex dungeon to their money palace because they have a product that they know people will buy regardless of it's quality (The Sims or any EA games or Call of Duty or Halo 4 and 5). And the second type being one that was made because the creators had an idea that needed and deserved to be shared with the world. (Bastion, Dark Souls, and XCOM: Enemy Unknown) And Ori and the Blind Forest is definitely in the latter category. So here's what I would like for you to do. Find about $17, go on steam, and buy this game. No. Stop. Don't torrent. Normally I'm okay with it, but Moon Studios deserves your support for creating this, dare I say, masterpiece.

I picked this up at random during a sale drawn in by the cute art style and rouge-like tag. Note I have a personal weekness for rogue-likes and enjoy the live fast die young nature of the genre. Oddly enough many of the issues other users have mentioned as cons I find to be pros (see below for more detail). Overall Sproggiwood is quirky, charming, albeight somewhat short.
* Graphics: Cute and minimalistic without crossing into the highly abused 'pixel art' catagory that is common in rogue-likes
* Music: Matches the graphics in charm. Nothing groundbreaking but rather subtle and ambient
* Complexity: The game is strikingly easy to learn while sitll allowing you to taylor your playstyle based on your class. Be prepared to die nonetheless (especially on savage mode)
* Replayability: the game rewards you for finishing each dungeon with each class. That said you could still beat all of the dunegons with all of the classes fairly quickly on normal mode. Up to savage for more of a challenge.
* Length: The game is overall rather short espically if only observing the dungeon count
* Price: The base price is a little high for what you get compared to some other popular rougue-likes on the market. However if you're a fan of the genre and can find it on sale I'd strongly reccomend picking it up
TL:DR: Cute. Short. Would reccomend if you get it on sale.

Sproggiwood is a post-marxist critique of the late capitalist state. Clog is an examplar of the proletariat, a working class individual who has not befallen the seduction of the commodity fetish. While he treads in gold, this is not for the betterment of only himself but rather for his civilization. "From each according to his ability, to each according to his need" is the philosophy of Clog. In contrast to this is Sproggi, a natural intellectual, deceitful, manipulative, but using these tools to guide the otherwise directionless proletariat (Clog) toward the creation of new worlds and new civilizations. This eco-utopian marxist allegory easily belongs with the likes of Marx and Gramsci.

Also, the turn-based combat is pretty good.

If you're going for a co-op RPG with a lot of fun mechanics, this is a decent start. If you're going for a co-op RPG with a decent storyline, this is NOT IT.
Honestly, there's a lot about this game to like. There's a ton of debuffs, and you can design and play a lot of different types of characters that work well, so there's no 'best' way to play (which gets a big plus from me), and some of the later abilites make you feel nice and powerful.
However, there are a couple big issues for me, and one is the story. Yes, I realize it's supposed to be goofy and cheesy, but there's a difference between cheesy and awful, and this swings back and forth like crazy. Okay, I do like a lot of the side quests, and a few of the jokes made me laugh out loud, but good GRAVY that main plot.. I'm not going to say anything spoilery, but it's the most cliche feeling story that I can't remember anything else being like. It's odd, I can't tell what kind of cliche it IS, it just feels SO HEAVY in that regard.
Another is, there's several quest bugs, and we're in the last zone of the game, with about 4 quests we can't complete because we did it in the wrong order. Not the BIGGEST deal, but it's still an issue.
The other major bugbear is that there's one large... dungeon, I'll call it, that once you finish the plot in it, you can't go back in it at all. Didn't finish looting? Too bad! Kind of annoying for the completionists. This 'can't go back' thing also crops up in one of the side quests I mentioned above, which is why we couldn't finish that one.
Oh god, I almost forgot the voice acting. I know the Generic Fantasy Accent tends to default to 'British', but can we at least have a consistent British accent? It sounds like random people were just taken off the street and told to say stuff in a British accent... some are okay, but some after a while I was just screaming at the screen "SHUT UP I DON'T WANT YOUR POTIONS F--- OFF"
... Still! It's worth getting, if only for a look at the well done battle system, and a few of the other things. And if you want something to laugh/groan at with friends.

Here is my approach:
Starting in 2003 with Pirates of the Caribbean by Bethesda with I was obsessed by sailing games. Although the game got the franchise forced on it - which you really could feel - I was hooked from the first minute on. On the lookout for some mods to make the experience some kind smoother, it was Naval Action which caught my attention instead. The time I discovered it was still in greenlight status and yet I was eager to play it from the looks of the impressive pictures.
I started my journey in Naval Action in early February and sank a bunch of hours so here is my attempt to give you an overview of the game BUT let me tell you from the start:
The grind to the top is hard and time-consuming but working your way up you learn more and more about the game - cooperating with other players helps immensely. It has a very steep learning curve and no ingame-tutorial whatsoever. You will have to look up quite a bit of things but the community ingame is mostly helpful as well - as long as you dont ask about very basics. And if you let it happen you will meet a lot of nice people collaborating.
- Age of Sail | sandbox sailing simulator
- a sandbox game, and will require you to make your own fun.
- mostly clanbased niche-game / rather unfit for casual players
- dynamic and slow paced action
- player-driven economy
- vast openworld-map of the Caribbean with close to 400 harbours
- as close to realism as possible in battles and sailing
- basic crafting system so far
- various ships from 7th to 1st rate
- no fancy UI so far
- unfinished but work in progress descriptions
- Sweet Graphics and Soundeffects
- plenty possibilities ingame: Trading and Crafting, Missions (PvE), Duels and battles (PvP)
- rare but epic and relentless battles
- various possiblities for cooperating with other players
- little to none Endgame-Content
- very repetitive (portbattles and missions)
- long journeys with nothing to do
- combat can take a long time and end in chases up to 1,5 hrs
- AI sometimes has unfair advantages
- shrinking Playerbase and therefore less PvP
- crafting is extremely time consuming atm (It is already beeing
)
Coming to NA I was never really the “clan person” but Naval Action showed me how nice it can be. Since you sometimes have a lot of time to kill sailing for a staging, missions or trading it can be fun just talking to other players. A clan is no must-have but it definitely brings more possibilities to the game. Most of the nations also have common Teamspeaks where you can meet up and organize with other players.
- different ingame chat-channels for different matters ( nation, global, help, ...)
- very active forum
- most nations have set up TS for collaborating
- Mostly helpful players ingame and on the forums
- chat and forums are monitored and toxic players are dealt with
- Few active players
Naval action is developed by a small team, so dont expect a high pace of developent. BUT the game is formed by the active help of the community.
- one of the best Age of sail games with a lot of potential
- work-in-progress / active development
- sometimes drastic changes
- sometimes one step forward, two steps back
- sometimes groundbreaking new content
- expect changes both good and bad
- content is getting updated frequently
- Constant contact with the playerbase
- Open for criticism and suggestions
- mods and devs have a open ear for problems regarding the game and its mechanics
- few content in the last patches
- patch notes have few details
- no really clear agenda atm
- devs are sometimes too emotional interacting with players
Do you like being part of an evolving game in early access, like to try new content every month (or so), you can spare the 40 bucks and like the Age of Sail you should definitely give Naval Action a shot. But be warned you will have to sink a lot of hrs into this game to actually achieve something and expect changes both good and bad.

I've had two playthroughs of this under my belt, one vanilla and one modded. Don't let my play time fool you; since I use a mod for Alt Tab in this game, it doesn't count my hours I've actually played. First time I did around 50 hours; second time with mods is at 100 hours and still going. First time around was incredibly enjoyable but some features were a bit annoying. The story immediately feels immersive and unique, with a more relatable set of characters than Oblivion (which has a similar engine - it even has the same animations for dog attacks and sheathing/unsheathing melee swords). It pays to research how to build a character before investing in your SPECIAL stats as they aren't easily increased - basically, charisma is the least important, at least in my eyes. I'll point out pros and cons of vanilla and modded versions below, just like I did for Fallout: New Vegas.
Vanilla
Pros:
-Fascinating, large open world packed with loads of content
-(Arguably) fun hacking system that requires some brain power
-Exp system feels streamlined and motivates you to explore more
-Being able to snipe - with headshots
-Good dialogue and voice acting, with SPECIAL stats and skills contributing to available options
-Dogmeat returns!
-Cool armour and weapons, especially the Power armour variants and energy weapons
-DLCs are great, especially Operation Anchorage and Mothership Zeta. The Pitt in particular breaks the monotony of being too powerful in late game by stripping you of your equipment for a limited time. Operation Anchorage is a good DLC to do early as it gives you powerful equipment.
Cons:
-Too slow movement speed, thought it doesnt' seem to change much between light and heavy armour
-Main quest feels too small (as usual for Bethesda), though the Broken Steel expands it to a better length
-Level cap too low! You'll stop being motivated to explore (most likely) when you hit it, and therefore rush to finish the main quest without exploring half the wasteland.
-Combat not as dynamic and intense as a true FPS - also I tend to miss sniper shots because of some object blocking me despite the target in clear view. Melee combat also relatively boring as most enemies use guns.
Modded (main mods I use are Fallout Wanderer's edition, Darnified UI and Weapon Mod Kits):
Pros:
-Improved combat dramatically. It's much easier to aim properly at bobbing heads of enemies when time is slowed down in bullet time. This also makes sniping easier and less frustrating. A quick grenade hotkey also makes them more useful.
-Adjusted options to slow experience gain to an appropriate level. I chose 50% and was on level 25 when I started the final DLC with most of the main quest still to go - a good pacing percentage.
-Ability to sprint is a godsend
-Makes weapons and armour more diverse and even cooler-looking
Cons:
-Requires you to know how to install mods (I'd recommend Gopher on Youtube for help)
-Has caused a couple of strange bugs in quests, though solutions from the community and the pc console let me work around them
-May lower your performance, though Fallout Stutter Remover alleviates this, depending on the types of mods you use
All in all, as good or even better a game experience than Fallout New Vegas, and different style from the previous Fallouts makes back play in sequence a likely route for me to take in the future.
And I have to say I've always been a fan of the weapon and armour designs. I still love the look of Power Armour, and I loved my modded Gauss Rifle as a sniper weapon in the end. Mothership Zeta was the most visually impressive, with a lot of time and effort put into the area design.
I particularly love open world RPGs, and therefore loved this game. Others who aren't a fan may not enjoy it as much as I did, but modded properly, these games are some of the greatest gaming experiences you'll have. 9/10 vanilla, 9.8/10 modded.

A really difficult but fun roguelike platformer. The gunboots are brilliant: they simultaneously kill enemies and slow your fall, but the most important part is the fact that their limited ammo makes you work to build up combos. You see, killing enemies without touching the ground builds up a combo, which can earn you money and health. The safest way to play Downwell is to take it slow, hopping from ledge to ledge, but the combo system encourages you to instead recklessly fall through the level, bouncing on enemy heads and only using the gunboots sparingly to keep from falling onto a ledge or hazard. When you manage to keep up a combo for an entire level, it feels amazing.

An indie gem, Downwell nails everything about what makes tough as nails platformers from the 8-bit era a true joy to play. All the mechanics in the game works overtime to create one of the most challenging and unique games I've played in years.
If you like mastering challenging but fluid controls, and appreciate retro pixel-art, Downwell is for you.

Sooo Minion Masters. A game from the company that created FORCED (Superb co-op game with friends btw) and FORCED shutdown (Somekind of a card arena brawler, which TotalBiscuit enjoyed). Minion Masters has to be something different right? Well it is!
Minion Masters is essentially Hearthstone which plays more like a fast-paced RTS than a card game. You don't have turns, your only limiting factor is mana which replenishes over time. You only have 10 cards in your deck but instead of dissappearing after being used they are re-entered to your deck. You draw cards each time you spend one. The objective is to destroy the enemy's altar and master by using any means necessary. Matches themself generally last around 2-4 minutes and can be dominated in less than a minute as well.
The card types are minions, spells and buildings. The first two function similar to Hearthstone but the last one can be different. These are structures you plant on the map and they slowly decay while performing its' abilities.
Instead of Heroes the game has Masters which each have a different passive attack (this essentially functions as your altar's defensive turret). Some attacks are small range ground AoEs while others are ground-air single target attacks etc... In addition the masters have other abilities which are unlocked through gaining XP during the match. XP is earned passively as the match progresses and also for controlling the two bridges in the middle of the map. These abilities range from adding new cards into the deck to improving the range of your ranged minions. The purpose of the abilities is to end the match and avoid stalemate thus they are very powerful. Each Master plays completely different and you must adjust your deck to favour that Master. Three of the masters are on the free rotation and you can purchase them permanently through crafting materials (earned by playing) or rubies (microtransactions).
Minion Masters is fun and fast-paced 1v1 duel game that has similarities to RTS and Card games. It shines compared to its' competition by removing turns and rewarding for quick thinking and fast decisions. Ever had that Hearthstone match where the opponent spends 95% of his/her turn every time? Well do that in Minion Masters and you are going to lose in under a minute.
PROs:
+ Easy to learn, hard to master. NO TURNS.
+ Short and intense matches (1-5 minutes), a single mistake or a good counter can turn the tide.
+ No casual mode, every game is a ranked game (exception friend matches).
+ 2-3 "free" cards each day by completing the daily. You'll get a decent deck running a lot faster than in other TCGs.
+ Card crafting + duplicates into crafting resources.
+ Rewards skill and tactics, higher rarity cards are not like legendaries in HS although still powerful.
+ Very polished and constant updates considering it is early access v 0.11~~.
+ FREE after launch (free keys still going around for EA).
CONs:
- Balance Issues (although very typical for ErAc games).
- Reliance on dailies: The game rewards you very poorly for playing (even with the premium option they offer). ~30 matches for a card with premium, ~60 without, dailies are worth 2-3 cards. So essentially you need to play closer to 100 matches with premium to equal a single daily -> Much rather ONLY play with dailies.
- Sometimes even too punishing, very difficult to come back after making a bad high cost play.
-----
If you are looking for a card'ish game without TURNS to play for 30 min - 1 hour a day then Minion Masters is probably the best and only choice in the market even in its ErAc state. You can play the game for free by getting a key from giveaways/friends or waiting until it launches. The 20$ premium DLC package allows you to play instantly with some additional goodies. While this might be a bit steep, after this purchase you most likely don't need to spend a dime on the game, ever. Unlike *cough Hearthstone cough*.

I wholeheartedly recommend this game. Think you might not like it due to the (apparent) prevalent focus on boobs and butts? Give it a shot, the smooth gameplay and the surprisingly interesting story and the excellent voice acting and the overall presentation might just sway you to end up really loving the game.
I like fighter games quite a bit, but not on a competitive level, really. Never had the need to be the winner of a tournament or even play online too much. I generally keep to local play against (or with, if the game allows it) a few friends. The most enjoyable part of a VS fighter, to me, are the character designs, animations, and the fun factor when playing with a person next to you. The following is from the perspective of such a person - I won't be talking about online play or communities or pro tier gaming. Just what's interesting and what's fun.
I prefer games like Melty Blood and Guilty Gear - easy to pick up and impressive to look at. The gameplay of Skullgirls is quite similar to Melty Blood, I'd say (except less air-oriented :P). The characters are generally very fast and mobile, the attacks can be linked freeform, and the matches can be extremely furious and quick. There's quite a few really clever additions - the automatic infinite combo breaker, the tech colors, the way the blocking works, it's all simple solutions to problems that plagued other games.
The designs in this game were offputting the first time I've seen it, quite a long time a go. It seemed like sloppy fanservice without much heart. Then at some point I had the chance to try it out, and starting right of the bat with the menus, my opinion began changing. Bought it after only a few fights. It's just that good.
The presentation is done in an art deco manner, like an old cinema, and it really works out well. The music fits, the backgrounds are strange and varied, the mood is quite unique. I just enjoy what I see and hear from the moment it boots up to the moment I quit the game. There is a surprising amount of disturbing imagery, though. Some artwork is really not for the squeemish.
The character animations, in particular, are extremely well done and quite imaginative.
Don't let the small roster fool you. The characters are interesting and differ significantly one from another, sometimes even down to the inputs for basic moves. Squiggly, for instance, has the capability to _move the screen_ temporarily, which is something I've never seen done before. The future characters promise lots of very unique abilities as well.
I can pretty safely say that this is my favourite VS fighter at the moment, and probably will be for quite a while. It's great fun, even solo, and even more with friends.

Sproggiwood is best described as a Lite Roguelike — it’s got all the fun elements and none of the permadeath, making it a really pleasant, stress-free game to play. It’s also funny and has adorable art and I just really enjoyed it. I think I paid $6 and got 24 hours of playtime out of it, and it’s totally worth the money. The plot is weirdly bleak but told in a kind of funny way, which offsets that it’s actually pretty depressing (and now that I think about it, that’s a pretty big feat, considering… but I don’t want to spoilers). It’s really an awful story told in an incongruently cutesy way (and the more I think about it now, having finished it, the more I realize just how depressing the whole thing was), but it does work, I think, especially since it doesn’t take itself too seriously. More importantly, though, it’s really fun, and I thought all the classes were done cleverly and the powers were different enough that experiencing a dungeon with each felt unique. I had a good time doing a completionist run, and was sad when it was all finished.

Sproggiwood is a cute, enjoyable game.  It doesn't take very long to play through each level, which consists of a few floors and a boss.  It's great if you're looking for something you can pick up and put down easily.  Much of the modest length of the game comes from replaying the levels with different classes.  Doing so nets you extra gold, which you can use to buy gear and bonuses to make future runs easier.  You unlock items for your charcters by finding them while playing, but you only you only keep them for the rest of that level unless you purchase them back in your town.  It's not really critical how you spend your money, since there is no penalty for dying besides starting the level over again, and you can profit even on runs where you die.
The only real difference between the classes is the four available skills. I only used 2-3 per run as you must choose where to invest points.  The game's strength is that the classes' skill sets are different enough that each one has its own distinct strategy, but simple enough that it's easy to pick up a new class or change classes on different runs.
On the downside, each class's weapon and armor bonuses are drawn from the same pool, so there is no functional difference between the their gear.  Even choosing a character with what would logically seem to be a ranged weapon does not grant you a ranged attack until you get a ranged skill.  Also, the town-building aspect of the game is quite minimal and feels unfinished. It was cute seeing different creatures added to my town as I progressed but there's not too much more to it.  This is not a base-building type of game.
I played through about half the levels with all the different classes and really enjoyed it.  Once I got a bit bored and decided to just press on to the end, the game was over pretty quickly.  The gameplay is fun but the replayability is going to vary from player to player.  Overall, I'd recommend buying the game when it's on sale.

I had gone where the little arrows told me to go, and done what the little text boxes told me to do, but that's about it. I want to like this game, and I want to see the poetry in it, but no poem I've ever read requires me to sit through two hours of holding down a mouse and watching a pixellated character walk across a screen just to get to the good bit, wherever it may be.
If you're into atmosphere, or you want to stare at pretty pixels while relaxing background music plays, buy this game. If you want to play a videogame, don't.

'Ori and the Blind Forest' is without a doubt one of the most wonderful games I've ever played. It brought me back to a time when videogames were still full of wonder and awe, and I didn't just rush through a tired obstacle course to unlock the next item or level, but lingered and explored because I wanted to, because I never knew what was around the next corner. It made me feel like a child again. Simple yet engaging and beautifully touching, with gorgeous music and art direction, it was an absolute masterpiece of story telling. I only wish there was more of it, as it's cursed with the same drawback as a good book: once it's over it's over, and there's nothing left for it but to read it again if you're so inclined. But it's a magnificent journey while it lasts.

Not much to say about PROJECT XINATRA.  It's not good game, though for the price it's not a particularly bad game either.
I was hoping for something along the lines of Xain'd Sleena or maybe even Exolon but it lacks the diversity of the first and the atmosphere of the second.
First off there are no graphics options.  The only screen resolution available is whatever tiny 4:3 ratio'ed one that Xinatra was developed in.  The graphics are somewhat mismatched with a variety of texure resolutions (the character seems to be lower res than a lot of the other assets) and styles.  The art is functional but not inspired and looks a lot better in the small Store screenshots than on a large monitor.
Gameplay is where PROJECT XINATRA really falls down though.  What little I played felt like a chore rather than a work of passion.  The collision box is sometimes wildly different from the graphic on-top of it.  This is true for enemies and static platforms.  I regularly fell through platforms as they're shorter than apparent.
The gunplay lacks the ability to fire up, and becomes annoying when coupled with the small collision boxes mentioned above.  The default weapon is woefully underpowered.  Most of my play time (more than a half) stems from the first boss.  I ran out of green ammo shooting the lava balls before I reallised I could shoot the lava vents, however the default gun does so little damage I got bored and gave up.  I later retried and won with the green gun in about 20 seconds.
The non-boss music is okay, and the keys can be rebound.
Again, there really isn't a lot to say about PROJECT XINATRA.  If it gets significantly better; I was unwilling to spend the time to find out.

PROJECT XINATRA was developed by two guys from a small indie company called "DemonVideogames".
The game works with SNES, Xbox 360 controllers and with a keyboard. You can also rebind keys for all three. I'm more than certain that it also works with the NES controller but I have not tested it...Yet. Neither have I tested any of the PS or Logitech controllers.
The game itself is a classic run 'n' gun side-scroller and it plays just like an old-school NES/SNES game. You can move left-right, crouch, jump and shoot. That's all folks! The only issue with the gameplay is that you can only shoot straight forward and diagonally up. You cannot shoot straight up and that is making the first "boss" fight a real pain in the behind.
Other than that it plays just like your classic run 'n' gun game. It's really enjoyable!
There are, however, couple of grammatical errors. "From now on your are going to be on your own..."
Graphically the game looks quite good (Remember. It's supposed to be an "old-school" game). Sound effects and music and visuals are all quite decent and fit for the SNES era feeling. I've encountered one game breaking bug tho. I once missed a jump, fell and I should have died. I didn't tho. I was trapped below the screen and could keep walking to the right. However I couldn't kill anyone, get back on the ground to reach the next level nor could I kill myself. I had to alt+tab and close the game. This and the spelling errors are the only issues i've had with the game so far.
Will update the review once i've finished the game.

This game is awesome !
You get to play beautifull ships in an eve online mmo type environment. Graphics are quite good and immersion is great.
Pros :
- Naval combat gameplay is great. You have to deal with wind, gravity, penetration, waves... You can damage enemy's sails to harm he's speed, his crew to harm ship handling and canons reload and his hull to sink him. This mix allows a wide variety of tactics, skill is extremely important and you can surprise your enemy by mixing things up.
- You can play any way you want. Trade, craft, play pve for lvl ups AND practice (very important before you start pvp).
When you pvp you can play as a soldier in the army and work together in the conquest of enemy ports, as a privateer and kill players in hotzones to harm enemy nations, or as a pirate type hunter boarding traders for valuable cargos.
- A cruel world : When you loose a battle, you really loose something if you cant escape ; your ship, your cargo, your mens, your officer... But not everything. Ships have several "lives", same for officer, and if you dont play like a fool, you'll manage... But this sensation of "real death" in defeats brings immersive tension to fights.
- I cant list everything i love about the game... Just too many.
Cons :
- An unfinished product : Interface is ugly, rules are changing from patch to patch, but it's all about the early access state of the game. I have no doubt the game will become more user friendly at release.
- The relation between OW accelerated time and battles real time. When you sail in open world, time passes faster, your ship moves faster etc. Obviously because if it was not, sailing from one point to another would take way too much time. But battles are played in "real time" so the devs have to find a way to make things fair about this, because you can not allow a player who is 5 hours of real sailing away from his clanmate to be able to join and help him in 5 minutes. Which means the game has to pull some artificial engagement rules to make things fair+fun+realistic. And, this is not polished yet in my opinion but hopefully it will come.

Fallout 3 was the first Fallout game I played and reinvigorated the respected Series from the late 90's. Fallout 3 made the jump from 2D Isometric CRPG to full 3D RPG FPS. It was extremely commercialy successful and won many GOTY awards. Despite its flaws, I feel that FO3 earned this grand recognition. It is one of the best sandbox RPG's I have ever played and was a step up from TES: Oblivion, Bethesda Game Studio's previous title. Fallout 3's strengths is its vast, detailed, and stylish world and art design, as well as its completely freeroam nature. It does a superb job drawing the player into its world. Where Fallout 3 stumbles a little is in its character writing and plot, two aspects of the game that Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas shone. There are a few moments of greatness for storytelling in Fallout 3, but I feel they are few and far between. This makes Fallout 3 feel more like a Sci-Fy version of Oblivion or Skyrim. Many fans of the other Fallout games  were put off by this, though I dont think they give it the credit it deserves. In conclusion, I can say that Fallout 3 is certainly worth your time and money.

A really difficult but fun roguelike platformer. The gunboots are brilliant: they simultaneously kill enemies and slow your fall, but the most important part is the fact that their limited ammo makes you work to build up combos. You see, killing enemies without touching the ground builds up a combo, which can earn you money and health. The safest way to play Downwell is to take it slow, hopping from ledge to ledge, but the combo system encourages you to instead recklessly fall through the level, bouncing on enemy heads and only using the gunboots sparingly to keep from falling onto a ledge or hazard. When you manage to keep up a combo for an entire level, it feels amazing.

An indie gem, Downwell nails everything about what makes tough as nails platformers from the 8-bit era a true joy to play. All the mechanics in the game works overtime to create one of the most challenging and unique games I've played in years.
If you like mastering challenging but fluid controls, and appreciate retro pixel-art, Downwell is for you.

This is when you start to realise that in order to progress you are going to have to slow down your advance immensly in order to deal with the frustrating and seemingly endless amount of Chaos armies hell bent on destroying your towns appearing out of nowhere. This game is a rougelike where the layout of the levels determines your success so much there's barely anything you can do.  You could either have a level full of easy slimes and just breeze through it, or get the super annoying exponential growth slimes and before you know it you can't move for slimes and you may as just restart. It's bad design all the way through. For example. there's one enemy who can dash all the way across the level in one turn to kill you. Helpfully, a sound plays whenever he's about to do that. Unhelpfully, half the time he's off the screen and so you just have to pray he's not about to dash into you.
There are 6 different classes, which are pretty much all crap except for the archer. Why? Because he's the only one you can actually avoid taking damage with. To attack an enemy with any other class, you have be standing right next to them. And enemies attack every turn. So it's impossible to not take damage. And the archer's one ability that takes the game from "brutally unfair" to "slightly less brutally unfair" you only unlock after killing some number of enemies. And if those enemies have high damage, you're screwed.
Moving on to the bosses: They're crap. They're just regular enemies except they have 40x the health and have some other special ability that basically screws you over. The only strategy for them is "come into the room with full heath and pray that he doesn't run straight for you".
There are also these shrines which allow you to "pray to the gods" and get some reward. Half of the time this reward is actually something bad like "hey you like frogs right? Those enemies with unlimited range and some weird attack pattern? WELL HERE'S 50 OF THEM". Sometimes the shrine just says "Haha you're not getting anything lol".
Finally: There's a "quest" "system" but the extent of these quests is "complete the next level". You can rearrange things in your town, which is boring and accomplishes nothing. There's this sheep enemy who runs away from you and spawns a bunch of doors to hell which create gigantic swarms of enemies that stop you from moving, and then kill you. The slimes create these slippery trails of slime, but I thought they were weird teleporting things because the slime slip animation is non-existent. You just get teleported to the other side. There's this guy in town who if you accdentally click on makes you go through like 50 dialogue boxes just to get back to the game. The menu font is super large, and has options for "mobile mode". Occasionally when trying to go from one place to another these mushrooms will pop up and attack you if you don't hit them, forcing you to move tediously slow or face losing a round
If you want this kind of gameplay, Crypt of the Necrodancer is what you're looking for. The entirety of the time I played this I thought "I wish I could be playing Crypt of the Necrodancer right now". In case you don't know, Crypt of the Necrodancer is like this game, but music based, and not crap. It's also slightly more expensive, but that's a small price to pay for a non-crap game.

This is a pretty solid dungeon-crawler game. At first it seems hard until you learn what to really do.
What I love about this game is the fact to unlock items in the shop, you need to find them first which makes you want to explore and not just rush for the exit.
This also gives you a reason to play each class from the start, to unlock better gear as you can only buy gear for them once you found it and you cannot find gear for another class unless you are activly using it.
This way you cannot just buy the best gear and slash through dungeons with a new class you just unlocked.
Each dungeon also keeps track of which class you have completed the dungeon with which is helpful to those who forget which class they done in which dungeon.
The controls are simple and using items or skills is just one click away.
You can choose the difficulty at anytime in the options menu so you don't have to start a new game just for certain difficulty-based achievements, this makes it more fun and less of a grind for achievements.
-----------------------------------
My only gripe with this game which may be a nit-pick is the fact you don't keep your level up each dungeon. Once completed or you died, you lose items you had (unless bought from the shop) but also your level up. So you will be unlocking the same skills for each dungeon everytime.
Not a big flaw, I see why they kinda took this route, after all it is not an RPG where you keep everything and leveling up is not hard, heck you tend to level up around 5 times even when you are rushing for the door.
-----------------------------------
Otherwise, I don't really see anything bad about the game. It keeps it simple and is a nice introduction or even fans of the Pokemon dungeon series may like this. It is not too complicated to where anyone can enjoy it and put it down whenever you like.

I needed a break from 4X/Strategy games that require a lot of attention, so I picked up Sproggiwood on sale for a few hours of distraction, which it did. I therefore recommend getting it on sale. The videos of my attempts are below so you can decide whether it is worth getting at full price.
I would classify the game as a casual game, which each "quest" lasting 15-30 minutes, so you can just pick it up and play for half an hour, then put it down to do something else. As other reviewers have mentioned, the early quests are linear, and are all of the same type (go kill the boss). The "dungeons" are procedurally generated, so they vary each time.  According to the game, there is a decision branch somewhere further down the path, but I  have yet to reach that point.
The story and graphics are well done, cute, and humorous. The monsters and equipment are great as well.
I initially thought that you can build the village to affect the main game play, but that turned out not to be the case. There are buildings that are automatically built each time you unlock a character class, and buildings that you can put down strictly for decorations.
Between the randomly generated dungeons and the six character classes -- each with their own equipment -- there are quite a bit of replay values. I can see myself spend about 20 hours total on the game (6-8 with the main character class and the rest trying out the different classes/equipment.)

As of right now, I have played almost 5 hours of LEGO Worlds. What do I have to say about it? It is awesome. Now of course there are some flaws in the game, mostly because it is still in Early Access. But I am %100 sure that by the time it is fully released in 2016, that it will be %100 awesome.
Let's start with the cons:
1) The camera controls are a bit wonky. Sometimes when you're climbing up mountains are walls (especially when you are inside a building) the camera will try to follow you in the most absurd of ways. For instance, while I tried to scale a mountain on horseback, the camera went into the mountain side and stayed there until I reached the mountain's peak. Often times inside of building with small rooms you will be staring at the building from the outside while your character runs in circles inside.
2) Weapons:
a- You seem to be unable to fire a gun from horseback.
b- If you have both a melee and a ranged weapon equipped, switching between the two is a nightmare. Enemies that are some 4ft away will get blasted with an rocket launcher while you were planning on swinging your katana. Meanwhile you get hit with the full spectrum of the rocket's explosion.
c- Aiming can be difficult especially in close quarters with multiple enemies.
3) Mouse:
a- Sometimes the mouse will vanish for no reason at all. (Happened 1 time to me but I have read some of the other reviews).
b- On one ocassion I lost complete control of the camera. Clicking and holding the right mouse button did nothing.
4) Building:
a- I found it rather hard to line up structures when I was using the "add block" tool.
b- Sometimes the pain tool did nothing at all. Spraying blanks.
c- The "undo" and "redo" tools only seemed to effect paint for some reason, not actual blocks.
d- Maybe we could use some sort of measurement tool.
e- I couldn't get a large area to be completely flat because the "flatten" tool can't be set to flatten everything to a singular height but rather flattens land to an average height compared to the land that you are trying to flatten. (If that makes any sense)
Niether Cons nor Pros. Inbetween.
1) Map.
a- We could use a map.
b- I want waypoints to mark where I built my hidden base or my communal town.
c- Maybe some kind of fast travel, like a pay to use portal or something.
2) Minecraft!?
a- crafting. I want to be able to make my own weapons like in Minecraft (or even cubeworld).
b- Maybe some like forges and stuff. That would be awesome.
c- Crafting clothing. YES.
Pros:
1) Terrain.
a- The way that biomes blend from one to the next is smooth.
b- No two biomes of the same type have the same look. Every area has different hills and valleys.
c- The way that the game looks is just very aesthetically pleasing. (opinion)
2) Building
a- The ability to build ad destroy anything is just awesome.
b- The fact that you can construct anything on such a fast and large scale is almost terrifying. (especially when compared to Minecraft).
c- Besides the problems I listed in cons, I found building farely easy to use and almost smooth.
3) Spawnings.
a- I did run into several situations where horses spawned in trees. But, other than that, the spawning of mobs was nicely generated.
4) In game buildings
a- The seasonal home that you can build is essentially a free and easy way to make a ton of coins. If anyone didn't already know that.
b- The buidlding that the game gives you are nice, but I think that we could use some more buildings to correspond with certain biomes. Maybe we would have to buy them with coins or something, but I do feel like the  buildng list was pretty barren when it came to diverse homes.
Now I know I didn't mention a ton of things. That was inevatible. Maybe I'll edit this later. However, it is now time fr my overall rating.
Get the game. If not for the reason of actually wanting to shape how the finished product looks. Get it because in less than a years time, the price will have jumped up. For all we know it may be $30 or even closee to $60. I sure as hell don't want to pay that much when I could have spent $15.
Now other than that, the game is awesome and fun. There is an endless amount of exploring and building you can do. Get out there and do it.

I'd call it a very good RPG. You can manipulate most of the objects in the world.  Can't open the chest?  Pick it up and carry it to your sanctuary until you can find an unlock spell.  Can't reach a ship's deck from the docks?  Throw a pyramid, then use your other pyramid to teleport up there.  You really do have tremendous freedom, and a lot of spells that affect the world in interesting ways.
Consequently, it has a lot of puzzles, traps, and difficult combats, so if those are things you hate, stay away.  It is also text-heavy and you may be confused if you are not interested in reading a lot.  I like all of those things, so it works for me.
Combat is often a puzzle, too.  To give you an idea of why the turn-based combat is so great, here's an example of something that happened in-game.  We summoned a fire elemental to block our enemies from moving forward.  They attacked it and wounded it severely. Next, we lauched a fireball, which hurt the monsters, set some of them on fire, and healed my elemental.  Then we cast an oil spell, which immediately caught fire, burning and slowing them.  Then their archers moved close to the fire field, so we cast a rain spell that put out the fire and created a smokescreen so they couldn't shoot at us.  This kind of combat synergy is pretty common in D:OS.

I'd like to start by saying this is a niche game and still in development. if you are looking for an assassin's creed pirate gameplay experience then... walk away. If you are looking for more realism and tactics with a mmo aspect to the game then you might have a winner!
Naval battles: let's start with that as it is focused on the golden age of sails 17/18th centuries. they are awesome...
You have access to many ships as you level up in the game. Some are fast and manoeuvrable other strong with great fire power. Each ship has a purpose (hunter/scout/ fire power platform etc.) They all have advantages and drawbacks, it is up to you to focus on the good aspect and play accordingly to get the most of your ship! Playing with others in different ships will allow you to build tactics to win an engament.
PvP can be very intense but beware of ganking not so fun^^ so open your eyes while sailing in open world.
The graphics are nice and the ambient sound during battle are immersive.
Crafting and trading are available. i'm not going to lie.. it's a long process and it takes time. But if you are into that it works well. To sum up, you need ressources to build ship parts that will ultimatly be used to build your ship. Ressources can be bought or produce in ports and every ports produces specific ressources. So you will have to sail a lot to gather the much needed ressources to craft. If you can't craft well trade for what you need by sending contacts in ports.
The open world: it's huuuge! it encompass the south of the USA, the mexican gulf, cental america and the north of bresil (and all islands in between). sailing to one point to the far opposite point of the map will take hours!! fortunatly you can open ports docks to fast "warp" your captain from one area to another (without the ship). Each area is controlled by a kingdom you can choose from when starting the game (GB, USA, Spain, France, Deutch, Sweden, Danemark and the Pirates)
Kingdom vs Kingdom: As said earlier on, the game has a mmo part in it. it is represented by nation fighting each other over control of ports.  Going to war (or allying) is acheived by a round of vote inside the nation. Once the votes are closed well, you know who is going to fight you.
To capture an area, you need to flip the targetted area by increasing the hostility level in this area. This can be acheived by PvP and  PvE mission. Once the region is "flipped" a porty battle is open (46hours after the flip). This is the occasion to have a 25v25 players fight! (very intense). Nations will organise to attack or defend. This can bring epic battles.
Capturing an area has a strategic value as ports produce ressources needed for the craft of your ship. It also gives different bonuses to your ship.
Regarding the UI, it is indeed a basic Unity menu but it doesnot hurt the game mechanics nor the pleasure of sailing. Moreover it is the last step you take in game development. Why spending hours of work in a UI you will have to change constantly as the game evole (The UI will be released  before launch. and that the intelligent thing to do).,
As a beginner,  you might get a bit lost starting as there is no guide provided. But a quick google search will give you access to many player's guide and "how to" explaining the basics.
Regarding the play time needed to evolve (carft / make money etc..) well this game has a MMO aspect to it so yeah it takes time. This is why the game is best played within the comfort of a clan/guild or with friends. As you can centralise and put your effort together to gather ressources and craft ship. Crafting in this game imply that you organize yourself with other to reach your goal. if you can't produce a ressource, trade for it, find people providing the goods, many people do that. Making money is very easy and can be obtain by doing mission or trading goods between port. Furthermore it is always fun to hunt enemies with group of swashbuckling lads!
To suml up: It is a slow pace game, beautifully designed (very stable for a beta) The game is still in devlopment and the devs are making changes and are tweaking it but imo they are going into the right direction.

Naval Action is an odd creature.
I've played this game for almost 250 hours and in that time I've enjoyed myself immensly, but I've also encountered many issues.
The developpers spend a lot of time on balancing ships. They obviously make a bunch of mistakes or balance it the wrong way, but that's normal and in the end it always gets rectified. I've not done that much PvP but from what I've seen so far it's looking a lot better than at launch. The biggest issue here is that there's no reason to use the smaller vessels in this game. Once you unlock a larger ship, you ditch the old one. They tried rectifying this by making most port battles limited to the smaller vessels, but in the end people still play the largest ship they can when they can. It's not an easy thing to solve mind you.
The graphical team have done an excellent job on the ship design. Most of the ships look very good, there's no way to argue against that. But that's where it kinda ends, which is my first issue.
Other than very detailed ships there's not much else. One of the largest playerdriven events in this game hasn't been properly updated for months. When you go into a portbattle you're still fighting a couple of random towers in the middle of the ocean, and whilst an update to this was promised many months ago, we've yet to actually see any chance to that.
I remember the concept art being shown for actual forts and the like, but ever since then, nothing. If you bring it up on their forums they usually don't reply to it.
The cities you go to when you need to go to port are pretty much all the same and are largely a result of copy pasting. Which wouldn't be that bad if it wasn't the only thing other than ships that could make the game look and feel authentic.
Another glaring issue is the user interface. It's♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's harsh but that's pretty much the essence of it. It looks really bad and is never once explained ingame. New players who buy this game, log in to the game and see the user interface are instantly turned off and who can blame them. My real question here is, why the hell has there been no attempt to even upgrade the interface. The usual response from devs and other players is: "They're going to do that on release". To me it's a bit of a cop out and in a game that is hemoraging players and has difficulty with player retention, small things like this are very helpful. First impressions are key, especially since you can now refund the game within the first two hours.
There are other smaller issues, like the whole officer thing. They add in perks that are helpful in combat. Perks that are helpful in crafting. Perks that are helpful as a trader. Yet they only allow you to recruit and train one officer whilst it's clearly intended to allow you to have multiple officers. Why this is the case? Nobody knows.
However, the thing that is the most baffling of all, is the devs reaction to critisicm and the apparent willingness to buy positive reviews from their players by promising new content if a certain amount of reviews is reached. This is why you should most certainly take any positive reviews for this game with a grain of salt. And whilst yes, you never said the reviews had to be positive, saying that: "Positive reviews will make us work harder" makes it obvious you meant give us positive reviews.
Recently they posted a reaction to a negative review. The most striking thing that was said, was that the responses of the admins on their official forums were not always representative of company policy. But if someone with the tag 'admin' says on your forums that a feature is getting pulled because of critisicm, then it's YOUR job to make sure that employee doesn't post stupid things like that. It's always easy to, after the backlash, come out and say that he/she didn't speak for you, but the damage at that point is already done, and from my experience dealing with the devs of this game, it isn't that much of a stretch to believe the devs capable of pulling a feature because they got some critisicm.

The multiplayer, when not dead, is full of griefers and hackers and is generally unpleasant. What with that one single Deathmatch running constantly (For the other modes you really do require a dedicated group or friends to match up with). But really, who cares when the Single Player Campaign and the Co-Op mode is soooooooooooooo GOOD !
Great story, great action, The violence is completely over done and over the top. Even the method in which you heal yourself is beyond brutal. Most definitely one the most under-rated games of the last generation. A fantastic Third Person Shooter and a personal favourite with solid mechanics, awesome guns that both perform and sound great (seriously, I can't think of any other game where the weapon sound is as awesome as this. Even your standard side arm gives new, fresh insight into the term "hand cannon"). Giving you all the help you'll need to face down the onslaught of an Ork Waaagh !
In the MP / Co-Op the customisation options are numerous and many, As well as being able to choose straight paint jobs from Space Marine chapters of the 40K universe. The Multiplayer itself, instead of being a tactical ground shooter as it probably should be. Just turns out to be half a dozen or so game modes. Where any advance you wish to make is usually thwarted by hammer wielding Space Ninjas. Something which I have never really found a decent footing with. The MP does serves somewhat of a purpose though. As it is the only mode in which you can unlock extra perks and special bits of armour. Though you rely on these extras in the Co-Op, Exterminatus mode. The Multiplayer is the only place where you can obtain them for use. Which is a bit inconvenient and bad planning on Relics part. Multiplayer tends to be pretty much dead. And when it's not. The games are usually squalid affairs, mad rushes of chaotic nonsense in which team communication is non-existant. Running a gauntlet of God Mode kids and aimbots. The major downside of all this is, if you want those weapon perks, then you'll need some good friends to MP with. Either that or go about it in the boring way and do a bit of "Perk farming".
Although nice to have. The Weapon Perks themselves don't really add all that much in the Co-Op. It's all really down to how you utilise your loadout and what you're comfortable with using. It certainly won't make things any easier. As the Exterminatus has to be one of the toughest Co-Op game modes out there. No matter how experienced you get. Victory is never a sure fire thing and these three sets (one as DLC), of four horde arenas are an absolute nightmare. Relic really wanted to make you feel that you survive it rather than "Kick its @$$". And provides you a hellish slice of button bashing, trigger pulling warfare. That puts your tiny four marine team into a green-meatgrinder for 21 Waves of unfettered violence.
Some might say that the Single Player campaign is a little on the short side, rolling in at around 8 to 10 hours. But that just means that it doesn't out stay its welcome anytime. Keeping the story snappy and to the point, but leaving plenty of room for wanting more
. And if you can't already tell from the Store Page Vids and Screenies, the graphics and animations are more than competant. Can't praise this enough.

I am not someone who writes reviews, but I feel like this game deserves me taking time to do a quick one.
First off, I think this may very well be in my top 10 games of all time, and that is with over 25 years of pc gaming experience.
I am not someone who has fantastic reflexes or plays shooters normally and I do not enjoy pvp. So why do I like this so much?
It is not because graphically the game is stunningly beautiful, but that certainly is a nice bonus.
I think for me it is because it allows you to play with your brain as much as with your reflexs. AI is challenging but not frustratingly so. The feel of your character in the world is also spot on, there is a realstic weight and speed to all the things you do.
If you like experimenting with different builds and play styles The Division has that as well. It is hard not to be a horder, collecting gear, weapons and mods, if you enjoy this aspect of the game.
I rarely pvp, and I think there has always been some frustration with this aspect of the game from those that do. But I can say that if you are just trying to get missions done in the dark zone, the pvp aspect will give you a whole different feeling.
The gear ceiling has capped out now, so loot means very little to me anymore. The global events will add a modest improvment to gear so that may be another carrot to some.
The odd thing is how much I enjoy pve Survival. Spawn with a sickness, and start the search for gear both to stay warm and to fight. Yes there are static spawns that people learn, but even that becomes part of the strategy, trying to decide do I waste time trying to get to X whe I am badly positioned to do so?
It has gotten to the point were I will jump on and try different runs, just competing with myself to beat my personal high score, or see how fast I can get out, or never take medicine, or just play the role of trying to help others. If survival was released as just a stand alone game it would be better than most of the games that fall in that catagory today. With just a few modifiers it would easily stand against a game like Battlegrounds,
Wishlist for Survival:
Some sort of leaderboard for keeping track of various records.
The ability to spawn tiered hunters, for instance Tier 1 would be one hunter Tier 2 would be two and so on.
Because gear doesnt matter for people that just play survival, an option to earn a token for encryted caches would be awesome.
Solo or Team only instances of survival.
Even though I dont genearlly pvp, a battle royale mode would be awesome.
Underground is not a good DLC and currently there is no reason to go there unless you are pursuing commendations.
Last Stand is good if you like pvp.
For those that like them, the emotes are awesome in this game and the cosmetics are great as well.
I have wandered all over the road on this review, but I hope it helps someone on the fence about getting this game. I have now played it through on PS4 and PC.
