Pretty graphics and music. And the floatiest controls of any game I have played.
The character is meant to be some sort of super agile squirrel spirit - but it floats through the air in interminable jump animations, during which there is no ability to steer. The mechanics of this might involve some kind of obscure 'aftertouch' to do with how long you hold the button down before releasing it controlling how high you jump - but gosh darn it I just want to jump on two simple platforms and go up a tree, not master a radical new control system.
At least that's what I think they were getting at in one line of the "emotive" deliberately broken-English tutorial voiceover - which during the first few stages are on a par with Papo&Yo for laying it on thick. These voiceovers are delivered by a sort of floating battery that has to be recharged whenever you save. Whatever.
The dire controls are like what would happen if you took Sonic the Hedgehog and how he runs and jumps... and put him into the tightly packed levels and dodgy hitboxes and glitchy controls and utterly unforgiving environmental obstacles of... Manic Miner.
I bought this because I thought the story would appeal to my toddler. But my toddler wouldn't have had much opportunity to wander round the environment and watch squirrel-thingy gathering fruit with Totoro No-Face, before having to do a jumping-over-timed-fireballs skit whose three, just three, platforms are equivalent in difficulty to the entire last stage of Trine. Wall jumps consist of inching up a wall in small random jerks and then hoping you manage to pull the other way during the split-second in which the character can receive a control of any kind, and that at the same time the incoming fireball happens to be somewhere else. On landing safely, it's usually necessary to use one of the oh-so-post-console portable savepoints. These are in short supply and use up the same talking-battery-narrator energy needed to open half the doors.
Since you play the ghost of a departed squirrel who might also be a leaf from a mystic tree (cringe), maybe they could have had insta-respawning instead of this agony. I also wondered if perhaps I had done something wrong in the pretend-interactive opening sequence and Totoro No-Face was supposed to survive and throw me past literally every single platform segment.

It's kind of sad to see the game in this state, it had so much potential, but I think the Devs simply just bit off more they could chew. Relying too much on word of mouth what the game has mainly lacked so far is exposure and time. The game still needs polish and it really lacks it. Sure it is in Early Access, but its very hard to say if the Devs will keep on pushing for this game after its failed release on steam. If you play this game currently, you will hardly see a soul until peak hours. The terrain still glitches, there still seems to be a lack of variety in combat, They have introduced one new weapon from its alpha which is the lance and shield, and it seems utterly broken due to its long melee range, although I cannot say if its balanced in a pvp perspective because yet again there is no one to fight. I have not played on European servers myself, but with the amount of lag I will be experiencing doing it. I simply don't think there is a reason to go out of my way and trying to boost my ping on a game that is half baked at best.
They have released new biomes, boss fights, and new character models for mobs since the Alpha, but the new models seem to lack some amount of continuity. Like they tried stuffing too many enemy types in one small biome. Which in turn makes the assests in the game kind of lacking. For example, The revenant faction seems to be made of zombies, wandering humans, bug people, giant zombie behemoths, mages etc etc. And they all seemed to be focused in one area. Which kind of makes it seem they took a bunch of random assests that didn't fit and plopped them into one area. I guess the one good thing about the mobs is that they gave them variety in attacks, but none of the attacks are telegraphed, so you never know when to dodge an attack so 90% of the time you will be hit by an enemy's stun.
The combat is still kind of Clunky to the point where it still feels that your basics are point and click and not actually skill shots. The normal control points still take too long to control. It takes a total of 5 minutes, which might not seem like a lot of time, but for a game where there are hardly any people and the world feels pretty small, it kind of is. The one thing they did change was that you have to baby sit the control point so monsters don't destroy it, which kind of sucks because from a PVP standpoint you're forced out in the open and you're just a sitting duck while people will converge on you, rather than carefully hiding in the brush for a surprise attack. (but since there are no players then there really isn't a point here) Then from a PVE standpoint it kind of sucks killing weak mobs for five whole minutes that don't offer anything except for equipment exp which every mob drops in this game+more. I haven't attempted any of the group content or the harder control points because either im pretty sure from my past experience they all work the same way with the harder content, but with the group content... you already know what I will probably say about that.

The Exiled (formerly Das Tal) looks amazing and the gameplay and graphics remind me of Nostale, which was one of my favourite childhood games that was ultimately ruined by its publisher "Gameforge". Unfortunately The Exiled lost quite a bit of players and attention when the devs changed the name from "Das Tal". However, in essence the game has not changed and is still a fast and fantastically fun skill based isometric PvP game. You basically fight over important areas in the world like bases and even animal carcasses as you try to get resources in order to control larger portions of the game world. Everything in The Exiled is PvP based and the game world is harsh. PvE mobs are smart and players can ambush you at any time, and often from anywhere as there are plenty of places to hide.
Basically think of DotA2 or League of Legends but with cartoony graphics and instead of killing forts, controlling minions and doing the same thing all the time, you are fighting other players directly over important things in the game world, or just killing them for fun. Classes have a lot of difference and combat variety. You have archers, warriors, guys with long sticks and of course spellcasters. It's awesome. There are tons of combat effects like slowness, bleeding, poison and the game has a massive stealth aspect as there are plenty of places to hide and wait in ambush.
Put simply, The Exiled is fun, and has so much potential and literally all it needs is more players. Seeing as it's free, I suggest everyone to go and play it. The game is in 'Early Access' but it's free, so you literally lose nothing by trying it out. In addition to that, for an early access game all of the mechanics are there and the game is fully playable with very few bugs.

Sproggiwood is a turn based tactical RPG with roguelike dungeons.  The first thing that struck me about the game were the adorable visuals, but what really makes Sproggiwood stand out is the hilariously quirky writing! Most roguelike games have a very limited story. Sproggiwood takes the time to develop the plot a bit, so you know exactly what you're trying t accomplish as you make you way through the dungeons.
I don't want to discuss the mechanics of the game too much because a big part of what makes roguelike games enjoyable is the sense of discovery as you play. You start each dungeon at level one with the option of being equipped with your choice of items that you already collected and subsequently bought in your town. This helps make luck a bit less of a factor in your dungeon runs, but it also slightly hampers replay value.
The only criticisms I have are:
The tutorial is not robust enough to give a full understanding of the controls/mechanics
There is a lack of endgame content, once you're done getting items and experimenting with the classes, there's very little feeling of progression
Reccomended for:
Fans of turn based tactical RPGs like Front Mission and Fire Emblem
People who find leveling the most fun part of MMOs
People who like cute things
People new to the roguelike genre
Avoid if:
You find endgame the most fun part of MMOs
Overall Sproggiwood is a fun, adorable game. A worthy addition to the roguelike genre that's a great starting point for those intimidated by the high difficulty of traditional roguelikes!

With its very soft on the eye aesthetics, charming music, and big friendly UI, Sproggiwood is a difficult rogue-like to place in regards to its peers. It wears the trappings of all rogue-likes, simple mechanics that hide a more complex, strategic element (especially in the later levels), procedural dungeon crawling without the sometimes overwhelming expanses of an overworld landscape to navigate, a focus on items and gear found as loot instead of crafting, and some light RPG elements.
But where it steps away is how forgiving the game is. It mixes a hybrid of permanent death with a progression saving 'village' from which new expeditions using previously unlocked levels of gear are possible, so dying means you go back to the start of the dungeon, rather than back to the start of the game. Even when you die in a specific dungeon, you keep the small amount of gold you might have accumulated, potentially allowing you to unlock a new item back in town that'll make successive attempts easier.
Additionally, Sproggiwood has a light hearted story running throughout, and I found myself often amused by the quirky, humorous shenanigans of Sproggi, the charming if hopelessly misguided spirit who seems to be at the heart of everything going on (and going wrong!) in Sprog. And although it is a short game compared to many other rogue-likes, and certainly less full in some ways, everything in Sproggiwood seems to fit well. Nothing seems out of place, or unbalanced that I've found, and I suspect it's precicely that quality that makes the game so appealing. Everything feels nice about the game. It's like a spoonfull of ice-cream for the soul :D
So, in conclusion: Sproggiwood is a fun, cute, and forgiving roguelike. It is perfect as an introduction to the genre, and offers more than enough hours of casual fun for serious rogue-like fans to be worth considering for the price.

After my initial romance with sproggiwood, I realized pretty swiftly that the difficulty was well below anything that required strategy. The total enemy encyclopedia including bosses must total something like twenty? Thirty? Theres slimes, spiders, goats, sheep, creeper farmers, wisps, mushrooms, frogs, and a single fish monster. Then theres a boss for each of the nine "different" levels.
Dungeons are about three floors a piece with a total of usually 4 to 9 rooms per. Maybe fifteen minutes to clear a dungeon? Though honestly certain classes can go for about five if you dont care about the money involved (and quickly you wont.)
I will say this. The music, the environmental effects, and the scrolls and potions were a ton of fun. This is a great game until you realize how small it is, and how completely lacking in replayabillity. I buy rougelike games, like dungeons of dredmor, because of the sheer amount of replayabillity they offer.
However, sproggiwood doesnt have the story, or the deep gameplay necessary to involve itself with such a shimmering and drawing game description here on steam. By all means, buy the game if youre easily satisfied and are a total beginner when it comes to RPG titles or rougelike genre games.
But steer clear of sproggiwood if you've already cut your teeth on anything else! This is not an engaging title in any sense.

This game made me realize that being bigger and having beautiful graphics is not always better.  More than anything else, game developers should strive to give us games that are both memorable and satisfying.  A game that makes you feel and experience something extraordinary.
To the Moon is not gorgeous in terms of graphics.  What it lacks in graphics, it makes up for its interactive story telling.  It lets you take part in a tale that is both hearthwarming and incredibly tragic.
The story immerses you and engages you to fulfill a dying man's (Johnny) last wish to go the moon, by altering his memory and replacing them with alternates ones.
What really made the journey interactive is how you put together bits and pieces of his memory and various highlights of his life and love story with wife (River) in order to progress forward in the story.
You will also be carried away by the games soundtrack, specially its main theme also entitled - To The Moon.  It really enhances your game experience and sets the mood in every game sequence.  The game, however, is relatively short, but the game content is what all that matters to me.  The game's message about life and death and the joys and difficulties we might or have already experienced did struck a chord.  In the end all we have our just cherished memories of our loved ones. The moral of the game is' if we had the chance and the ability to change our past, Will you do it?  Maybe some for me.
I really recommend this to a mature audience or even someone who needs a break from the run and gun games we have in our games library.  Kudos to the game developers for giving us such a wonderful game.  Can't wait for the next installment.

Characters are nice, controls are fine on keyboard (I have never had an arcade pad, so IDK if that would be better), and story makes sense (eg. Ms. Fortune not liking Cerebella due to the fact that Ms. Fortune hates the Medici mafia, and Vitale Medici is the adoptive father of Cerebella), but is sometimes boring.
Overall, the game is very fun to play, but I don't really care as much for the story EXCEPT for Peacock/Patricia (Peacock's name before her body was mutilated and becoming a robot) and the relationship between her and Marie (the current Skullgirl in the game), due to the fact that both of them were orphaned during the war and forced into slavery by a group funded by the Medici Mafia.
Also, some characters will have dialog pre-battle between the two of them (Watching from a video, Leviathan (Squigly's parasite), comments that Samsom (Filia's parasite) has gone "too far" and when Parasoul is defeated, she mentions to Filia that she is being "...used."). Overall, the game is great, but the story could be a TINY bit more fun/polished, then it would be SUPERB.
EDIT: It has been months since I made this review, and I now am going back to give my second thoughts on this game: The game is practically the same, but now that I have had the time to play most of the characters, I can appreciate the story even further.
I never mentioned the tutorials in my previous review, and I can say this in 3 words: Greatest tutorial ever.
I enjoyed playing Skullgirls with my good friend NoblePariah when we would go 1 v however many he chose. Everyone has a style of gameplay that they are most comfortable with, and mine would be fast and furious, so Ms. Fortune happened to be one of my favorite characters.
I also had the opportunity to play the Skullgirls Endless Beta, and I am loving the fact that the devs are working on Eliza as of 6/12/2014.
In the end, this is a game worth it's money and time, and definitely a good game for first time players of the fighting genre.

I’m playing multiplayer with some cool guy from a great discord server. We decided to play the LA mod. For some reason, it loaded up the harbor city 5.04 map. I really, really like that map, and I really, really like the LA mod. So cool. I guess..?
Anyways, so we are playing, and the other guy gets a callout to a gas explosion. No big deal, we do this all the time. At the same time, I get called out to a group of about 9 people fighting, and, ANNNND a bomb alert. So I’m panicking a little bit, I decide to go to the bomb first. So I apprehend the suspect (I barely did), switch back to the fight, get everyone into the MCU. And I go back to the bomb... It went off. Seconds later, I found out it lit a nuclear plant on fire. Luckily, I had a hazmat on call only about 90 meters from the explosion. The injury toll was at about 15, I think… So he called some first responders to the scene, and in the meantime, I got to treating the contaminated. They just kept walking in, some of them more than 3 times. I decided to call police to the scene. They did a good job at keeping the decontaminated out of the cloud of… Something… But there was a problem. I walked 2 police officers into the gas by accident. I thought to myself, no big deal, I can just decontaminate them, and if they collapsed, I could just decontaminate them, and then send them by ambulance. I was wrong.
Both officers collapsed, and by now, the toll of injury was at 27, and the response was at about at its 10 minute mark. The hazmat decontaminated them, but I couldn’t get an ambulance until the rescue was almost over, by the way, I kept them alive via a truck of medics.  By the 20 minute mark, the fire was still raging, and I was waiting for the gas and fire to clear, so I could rescue the other 25 people. That didn’t come until the 40 minute mark. Finally, the gas cleared, and the fires were out, and I moved in. I was greeted by a lot of dead people. I went into a hotel near the blast site. 7 people dead. Found the bombtechs body, and finally, 1 living civilian. 3 people out of 27 lived. 2 police officers, and one civilian.

Out of the depressing parts, onto a list of the things that made me laugh. I was yelling at him for an ambulance, he asked what kind, and I said, and I quote, "WE ARE DEALING WITH A CHERNOBYL SIZED DISASTER AND YOU ASK WHAT KIND OF AMBULANCE I WANT?" I got an ALS ambulance. When trying to land the helicopter, I didn’t see a hazmat fireman on my landing site, so I landed somewhere else, thinking I was crazy. To this day, there is still 1 person I never found. Weird. To top it off, it took me like 4 minutes to find that guy who planted the bomb. I felt like an idiot when I saw that he only moved like 4 blocks. In short, B U Y  T H I S  G A M E. Pretty graphics and music. And the floatiest controls of any game I have played.
The character is meant to be some sort of super agile squirrel spirit - but it floats through the air in interminable jump animations, during which there is no ability to steer. The mechanics of this might involve some kind of obscure 'aftertouch' to do with how long you hold the button down before releasing it controlling how high you jump - but gosh darn it I just want to jump on two simple platforms and go up a tree, not master a radical new control system.
At least that's what I think they were getting at in one line of the "emotive" deliberately broken-English tutorial voiceover - which during the first few stages are on a par with Papo&Yo for laying it on thick. These voiceovers are delivered by a sort of floating battery that has to be recharged whenever you save. Whatever.
The dire controls are like what would happen if you took Sonic the Hedgehog and how he runs and jumps... and put him into the tightly packed levels and dodgy hitboxes and glitchy controls and utterly unforgiving environmental obstacles of... Manic Miner.
I bought this because I thought the story would appeal to my toddler. But my toddler wouldn't have had much opportunity to wander round the environment and watch squirrel-thingy gathering fruit with Totoro No-Face, before having to do a jumping-over-timed-fireballs skit whose three, just three, platforms are equivalent in difficulty to the entire last stage of Trine. Wall jumps consist of inching up a wall in small random jerks and then hoping you manage to pull the other way during the split-second in which the character can receive a control of any kind, and that at the same time the incoming fireball happens to be somewhere else. On landing safely, it's usually necessary to use one of the oh-so-post-console portable savepoints. These are in short supply and use up the same talking-battery-narrator energy needed to open half the doors.
Since you play the ghost of a departed squirrel who might also be a leaf from a mystic tree (cringe), maybe they could have had insta-respawning instead of this agony. I also wondered if perhaps I had done something wrong in the pretend-interactive opening sequence and Totoro No-Face was supposed to survive and throw me past literally every single platform segment.

To begin this review, let me say that I went in with a positive attitude. The game opened up and I was informed this game was free to play "listed on steam as such as well". At the bottom of the main menu, there it was... the words "Your free trial will end on June 3rd". That was unexepected, but I decided to go through and see if the game would be worth paying for after the trial period anyway.
I started out in the tutorial (obviously). The controls were fine, the graphics were nice, and the ability to try out all the starting weapons at the start was great. I enjoyed using the shamans staff (oddly...I usually would have gone with swords or bows) and went on my way through the tutorial. The mobs were very easy, killing them just by standing behind a small pebble that wasn't phasable. I thought, at that point "eh, this is the tutorial...of course it'll be easy". That's when I hit the "Extract from the Dead Animal" or "Extract from the Meteor" part of the tutorial. Essentially, think of these as "Capture Points" in which you have to stand around the dead animal...to claim it. While you're doing this, monsters will spawn and try and kill you or the capture point. The dead animal point wasn't too difficult...but the meteor one was a different story. The meteor one spawned monster eggs, that had a 30 second timer to destroy. That doesn't sound too bad in itself, however it took forever for a single player to destroy one, while more and more kept spawning around you... I thought I would be fine later with this since I'd probably get stronger... so I managed to look past it. I completed the tutorial and began my venture.
Once in the main game, I looked around for a bit then headed off to do some of my objectives. I ran into some mobs and fought them carefully, since I was no longer in the tutorial. However, I eventually ran into a mini-boss (or rare spawn) and found that he too was stuck on a pebble, and small tree. I used this to my advantage, and killed him in 5 minutes (yea it took a bit longer than I wanted. I was just holding my left mouse button down and using my "Q" every time it was available (damage over time skill). After killing it, I noticed just how easy the PVE is. I killed everything, let everything swarm me, and just watched them get caught on things. The pathfinding of the enemy mobs is just horrendous.
Moving on from the mob difficulty, the game is dead...Like, dead dead. There was only 1 other person speaking in the server, and I had not seen another player at all. The 1 person only asked "Is anyone even on?!" in which I replied "I am!". He had been on for 3 hours without having another player speak in chat or even to be seen at all... This is basically a solo game, or co-op with friends game. The PVP aspect is ... at this point non-existent. We partied up, but never got to find each other since the games map does not provide you with information or a marker to show where the other party members are. He eventually got tired of the game and asked me if I knew about any good games.
After he left, I played for a bit more and managed to get to level 14. A message at the top of the screen stated that my progress in level has placed me "85%" higher than other players of the game. I checked the leaderboards with "L" and confirmed ... I was already #14 . That was disappointing.
I played a little longer still and went to gather resources from dead animals and meteors... but this time it was much harder. The meteor timer (for capturing) was 5 minutes. 5 minutes of standing there, shooting eggs before they hatched. This was just a tedious and boring task that eventually overwhelmed me with eggs literally everwhere around me. I managed to finish the capturing of the meteor however, but I thought this was ridiculously long and boring as hell. The same with the animals dead corpse capture point. It was also 5 minutes, however the enemies started getting progressively harder. It started with simple little monsters (like in the tutorial), then came raptors and Hungry Thogs (Pig like things). The raptors were freaking brutal and the pigs were just annoying. I managed to survive and gather my reward from the dead corpse, but realized at this point that there's not much else going on for the game. With the dead playerbase, there is nothing but boring capturing points and mob hunting.
This game is a no-go in my book.
3/10

Game is actually quite fun; But it appears that there isn't anyone else playing.. So.. Unfortunate, As It has a fun premise.

** The Good **
+ Action combat system similar to League or Battlerite
+ Open World
+ Interesting and deep settlement construction system
+ Fair variety of builds and skills to use
** The Meh **
- Tutorial is fairly stoic and requires *shudder* ...reading
- I was able to climb to the top 3% of players after a mere 30 minutes of play
- Very dead game with only about 15 concurrent users (but the community can be grown)
- Not a whole lot of direction in the game aside from a MMO style killquests
** The Bad **
- Undeniably cluttered foliage that makes much of the environment look odd
- Foliage also creates a lot of very random collision material that is easy to get stuck on. Like, REALLY easy. (Not really a great way to put the map together for a pvp focused game, imo).
- Not a whole lot of content aside from capture-the-point hoard mode activities
- Can't really see too much of a point in picking any class. It's really a matter of which animations you like to watch. They all have everything you need to sustain yourself without offering too much of a tradeoff
- Enemy camps seem to be designed to be raided by a mob of players at once, given that the respawn timers on enemies is about 4 seconds.
** The Ugly **
- Seriously, the foliage. Eyesore city.
- Fairly certain there are no safe zones for pvp, including the area you're spawned into- there's also only one world spawn for players. What could go wrong?

This is a painfully underrated game. While it didn't get off on the right foot due to some internal server bugs, I strongly suggest you give Das Tal / The Exiled another try. While the population of the game isn't the greatest, only you can change that. The game is a blast with friends, especially once you make more in game and find some rivals. The village sieging is very fair, and it's nearly impossible to get offline-raided if you play the game even somewhat actively.
The art style is somewhat reminiscent of League of Legends, and the controls are very similar to Battlerite. There are five weapons (Scythe, Bow, Staff, Totem, and Spear/Shield), and four armor types (Cloth, Robe, Leather, and Splintmail), allowing for a grand total of twenty different classes, and an endless number of unique character builds. New weapons (Sword, Dagger/Cestus, and Sling), and new armor types (Backpack, Hide, Tattoos, and Fur) are also being added into the game at a later date, bringing the eventual minimum combinations to a whopping 64!
PvP is the heart and soul of The Exiled. The combat system is very simple, aiming skillshots at your enemies with various effects... but, there's friendly fire. I play a Ritualist Guardian, a tank whose job is to dive behind foes and stunlock them with a variety of AoE CC abilities. If I miss, I've just stuck an ally in my black hole along with my enemies, essentially protecting the enemy team from my combo. Healers have to worry about this too; if they try to heal their ally whose gotten up close and personal with their opponent, they may end up accidentally healing the wrong person! This adds a unique little touch to the game, which I happen to be a big fan of.
Finally, the gearing is incredibly fair. You may tweak the HP, Mana, Movespeed, Cast Time, Cooldown Reduction, Physical Armor, and Magical armor of any piece of gear by a fixed amount. If you boost one stat, you must reduce another by an equal amount. The difference between a +0 and a +8 item is simply how hard you can tweak these stats, and very little else.
All in all, just download the game and make some friends; it's worth your time. 9/10, needs more people playing it.

Downwell is about as close to a perfect game as you can get. It has an amazing sense of flow; it's simple to grasp, but has endless depth and it has tons of replayability because despite being intuitively simple it's just incredibly polished.
But what makes this special, I think, is that it's a game that melds traditional "ultra-hard" mechanical inspirations a-la super hexagon or VVVVVV with a gameplay system that really adjusts to the skill of the player and allows for a large variety in gameplay styles. This is not a game that punishes you for not doing exactly what the game tells you to. It does not kill you instantly and respawn you instantly with a souless "try again" until you conform to what it wants you to do. It lets you have adventures. It lets you teach yourself how to play in the most wonderful way. This game is the only game I have ever played where I felt not only the rush of beating something immense, but haven't been frustrated at it.

This game made me realize that being bigger and having beautiful graphics is not always better.  More than anything else, game developers should strive to give us games that are both memorable and satisfying.  A game that makes you feel and experience something extraordinary.
To the Moon is not gorgeous in terms of graphics.  What it lacks in graphics, it makes up for its interactive story telling.  It lets you take part in a tale that is both hearthwarming and incredibly tragic.
The story immerses you and engages you to fulfill a dying man's (Johnny) last wish to go the moon, by altering his memory and replacing them with alternates ones.
What really made the journey interactive is how you put together bits and pieces of his memory and various highlights of his life and love story with wife (River) in order to progress forward in the story.
You will also be carried away by the games soundtrack, specially its main theme also entitled - To The Moon.  It really enhances your game experience and sets the mood in every game sequence.  The game, however, is relatively short, but the game content is what all that matters to me.  The game's message about life and death and the joys and difficulties we might or have already experienced did struck a chord.  In the end all we have our just cherished memories of our loved ones. The moral of the game is' if we had the chance and the ability to change our past, Will you do it?  Maybe some for me.
I really recommend this to a mature audience or even someone who needs a break from the run and gun games we have in our games library.  Kudos to the game developers for giving us such a wonderful game.  Can't wait for the next installment.

This is a casual roguelike with very pleasing graphics and a fantastic soundtrack. I found the challenge sneaks up on you as the first level lulls you into a sense of ease, but the difficulty ramps up somewhat unexpectedly and not in a bad way. You slowly find yourself taking more careful steps as you play or you start dying a lot.
It's not a traditional roguelike in the sense of true permadeath and endless junk inventory management. You gain equipment to take with you and unlock classes through the story as you build up a small village, something akin to Rogue Legacy's method of increasing danger while increasing player resources. There's no inventory. You get one weapon, one armor, one consumable, and one accessory. In your village, you can purchase these items to have available for adventuring. Each class (there are 6) has a separate weapon type and armor type and you unlock new ones to purchase in your village through adventuring as that class.
You get one chance to clear a dungeon. If you fail, you can start over with a new procedurally generated dungeon that ends in a boss fight. Each dungeon is themed and increases in difficulty at every chapter. You gain gold during your delve which can be spent on upgrades in the village. Previously defeated dungeons will spawn new mobs as the story progresses, which reflects plot developments within the main story.
The turn-based combat is where Sproggiwood really shines. It feels like a roguelike in the sense of grid-based, turn-based combat, but the enemy and character skills will keep you on your toes. Skills cost stamina to use and killing enemies rewards stamina. It quickly generates a feeling of chess where you're trying to outmaneuver your enemies. Purely bashing your way through the dungeon is not viable. You will need to use your class's four skills cleverly to avoid damage and keep your stamina up. Your gear will have special effects that will help you in the dungeon. Unlike traditional roguelikes, your decision about where to move to, or not move, is very key to survival. There's slimes that create bomberman style explosions when defeated, slippery puddles, and a host of other effects. Spiderwebs will make you lose a turn. Goatmen will charge across the map to ram you. I find the combat in this game to be a very fun exercise in proactive and reactive thinking.
Finally, the story is a fun read. It's humorous, well-written, and makes sense within the Sproggiwood universe. You will quell the dissention of a blob social philosopher, deliver messages of peace (by any means necessary), and generally bungle your way to victory.
The devs are responsive on the forums and have ideas for post release. I'm hoping to see the addition of an "endless" dungeon, but even so, going back and replaying previously beaten levels with the various classes really offers a new challenge, ultimately providing quite a bit of replay value.
I would be inclined to point out bad things about this game, but for what the game is designed to be, it does everything very well. I honestly can't think of anything bad to say about this game.
Ah, yes, I thought of something. The village decoration. A point I forgot about. You can apparently decorate your village with pleasing aesthetics, such as placing a bridge over the river. I'm not sure why the devs added this content and I have not really done much with it. I won't begrudge giving the player the ability to decorate his village, but it seems to have no real purpose in the game and I'd much rather the devs work on the actual gameplay than playing village dress-up.

The combat and abilities are neat, but it's much too easy. Not nearly as deep as Shiren the Wanderer, and that game is already a simplified roguelike. Not enough meat.
The town customization is also frustratingly bland.

A fun moderate-length adventure game that makes up in silly humor what it lacks in depth.
The Sproggiwood story is pretty haphazard and absurd; mostly it just exists as an excuse to crawl through the dungeons and as a platform for the absurdist humor.  The humor is good, although nothing to write home about; I don't think I ever laughed outloud, but I almost always played it with a smile plastered across my face.
As for the combat system, it's just barely deep enough to carry you through the length of the game without getting overly repetitive.  Barely.  There is definitely a learning curve, as you figure out the skills, weapons, and armor, and how to use them all properly in tandem with each other (not to mention learning how to defeat the tougher opponents).  But that learning curve does plateau; thankfully, for me, by the time it did so, the ending was in sight, so the grind never felt overly repetitive or mindless.
So if you're looking for a Zelda-lite adventure game with a sense of humor, this game is for you.  On the other hand, if you are the type of player who loves dying a lot, who immediately turns the difficulty of all your games to 11... then, be warned, you might find Sproggiwood pretty easy.

The crafting system could use some tweaking, for instance they could add a project tracker where no matter what tab you are in on the crafting menu you can see what you need in order to build that new ship, and with the low player base getting a new ship can be a pain sometimes, but it has potential. The battles are very fun, and it is very satisfying to set an enemy ship on fire and watch as it sails next to one of its allies and blows up, although it can be quite anticlimactic when you fire one broadside and sink the ship, because you got lucky and all the shots went under the water line when the ship was rolling away from you.
I have 60 hours put into the game and have yet to see one bug or crash.
I would say it is better quality than some games that are already released, and Naval Action is still in alpha testing. As others have said the biggest issue is probably the UI. The UI is very simple and easy to use but it isnt very pretty. If you dont mind having a very minimalistic UI in your menu screens, then I would definately recommend this game.

Judgement :
Downwell is a simple concept executed flawlessly. It's incredibly rudimentary in its design, but this simplicity and forwardness is what allows it to work so well. It's lean, and everything in it is running multiple functions for the sake of streamlining how the entire game controls. This may sound like a negative, but Downwell was designed with mobile devices in mind, which is one of the reasons that it is presented in a portrait style, and its mobile home is why it has only three buttons. However, this does nothing to detract from how it plays, and as someone who played it on both mobile and PC, I can say for certain that here is where it shines.
A lot of what I want to say on this game is covered by Mark Brown in a series he makes called Game Maker's Toolkit. His video on Downwell succinctly covers what about the base design allows Downwell to function so well, and I highly recommend watching the video, even if you're not too interested in the game right now.
Link:
Now, since he covers a lot of what I would cover at this point, I want to talk from the perspective of someone who got
at this game. I told myself that I would beat the game completely before I wrote this review, and that meant completing Hard, which I just managed to do.
And by God if Ojiro Fumoto (the developer) didn't make me ♥♥♥♥ing work for it.
As Mark said, this game demands that you play by its rules. It forces you to play fast and loose, and by the time you've cleared the game on Normal, you've started picking up on the bonuses speed and style confer, with combos providing health and ammo increases.
When you start attempting Hard, you'll realize that those bonuses are not just nice, they're mandatory. This game demands that you think while it's going by at 100m/s. You have to plan how you want to approach each part, and which powerups are likely to result in success. For something that looks and feels so simple, it has real depth to it (pun intended). Getting good at this game becomes a test in pure reaction speed and muscule memory. You start subconciously remembering how everything is supposed to go on a good run, and you'll begin realizing how well the visual feedback keeps the player informed. As speed increases you spend less time trying to recognize enemies, and just begin reacting without thought. When you get going fast, this game almost becomes zen in its playstyle, with you effortlessly bouncing off enemies and blasting others while you descend.
Downwell is a testament to the idea that a simple concept can be wholly engrossing. It didn't need flashy visuals, a budget the size of Montana, or even dialogue. Its arcade like gameplay managed to pull me in with what it has, and it did it for very, very little cash.
At the end of the day, the question is whether Downwell is worth your money or not.
And it absolutely is.
The fact that it's only $3 just makes this an even easier recommendation, even though I would've recommended it at $10. It's great, it really is, and if you can appreciate a challenge, you'll find plenty available for you here.
Really, for less than the price of a half-decent sandwich, you'll get one of the best little gems out there. A mechanical masterpiece, and a game I'm likely to still dive into now and then for years to come. It takes little time and little money to give Downwell a shot, and it's worth every penny and second you give it.

Don't let the small play time on Steam fool you. I've been spending hours on this game through the Android and Vita versions, and those are exactly the same game you get here.
Downwell is a very addicting Roguelike experience. The goal of the game is to go down a well as far as you can without dying. Sounds simple, right? Well, the game is not afraid to show you that it's not messing around, as it can overwhelm you with enemies as early as level 1, and the game only gets harder from there. I myself have never managed to get past world 3 (out of 4 worlds in total, not counting the ending boss fight), even after I managed to accumulate over 150,000 gems over the course of playing the Vita version, and unlocking all of the play styles on both Android and Vita. The game does have a pretty high learning curve, but once you know how everything works, you'll start managing some pretty good runs.
Unlockables are pretty nice. Collecting gems counts to an overall total, and when you die or complete your run, the gems you collected will count towards a progression bar that levels up when you reach a certain milestone. Every time you reach that milestone, you'll unlock either one of 4 additional playstyles that each add a different set of rules for your run, which can increase replayability and experimentation, or one of dozens of pallete swaps that change the color scheme of the game. Rather than all of them be "red turns green" however, the palletes can also consist of screen alterations inspired by game consoles and 8-bit visual styles, or even just be very random screen changes. Just be mindful that some of them may cause the game to be a lot harder because of them being incredibly bright or consisting of a single solid color, making damageable enemies hard to distinguish.
My only real complaint is that the combo system doesn't feel very rewarding, to an extent. How the combos work is that for every kill you get while airborne, it gets added to a combo, with the count showing after you reach 5. When you reach 8 kills, you get 100 gems once the combo ends on landing. Hitting 15 gives you an additional gun charge along with the 100 gems. Hitting 25 gives you a free point of HP along with the previous benefits. The problem I have with this is that this is really it. You don't get any additional rewards by getting bigger and bigger combos, even if you were to hit numbers as high as 600+ (which is possible. Look up videos on Youtube). This does suck up any incentive of getting combos higher than 25 unless you're just going for the acheivements or bragging rights. What would've been nice is that for every 50 kills you get in a combo, or even 100, the rewards you get are added by 1. For example, if you hit 50, you get 200 gems, 2 charges, and 2 hearts, and hitting you 100 gives you 300 gems, 3 charges, 3 hearts, and so on. That would be a nice incentive for racking up higher combos, especially in a game that encourages players to stomp on enemies to stay airborne.
That's really my only negative, and it's more of a nitpick than anything else. The game is still very addicting and fun to play.

I'll start off by saying that, like many other reviewers here, I LOVE this game. I've spent at least 200 hours on my old console and simply could not stop playing. The Fallout universe is one of the most fascinating and fun places you'll ever visit in your gaming experience. The game itself deserves no less than a 10/10, bugs aside.
This, however, is not a recommendation of the game. I'm urging any PC gamer, Fallout fan or otherwise, to NOT buy this game as it stands. If your OS is anything newer than Windows 7, you won't be able to run this game. Period. The store page warns that it's "not optimized" for anything Windows 7 or beyond, which is a bold understatement. Instead, it should warn that it is simply unplayable on newer OSs.
There are numerous fixes floating around the modding community or through other programs and some youtube tutorials can help you get it up and running relatively quickly, but this is still an unnecessarily annoying issue.
[See EDIT] Recently, a Limited Edition PC Fallout Anthology has been announced and put up for pre-order in the wake of the Fallout 4 hype (which I snapped up as soon as I could, of course), so I'm hoping that Bethesda will have a compatibility patch in time for its release, which would only seem sensible if they're selling it in 2015. If not, it would be a huge insult to the fans of this great franchise.
I'll revisit this review when I get my Anthology and hopefully have better news, but until then, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME ON PC.
TL;DR: The game is ****ing fantastic, but unplayable on PC. Buy New Vegas instead or wait for Fallout 4.
EDIT: The release of the anthology sadly saw no compatability update. Such a shame. It was still worth it for the collector's case and the great older Interplay games, but it still feels like a bit of a cheap shot that Bethesda would sell something exclusive to PC that isn't playable on any recent PCs. To be quite honest, I'm insulted. Apparently, it doesn't take long with mods to get the game running, meaning that the inclusion of a simple update to fix the issue is well within the realm of capability for Bethesda. Sure, some other simple mods fix some of the other numerous bugs, but the game is almost 8 years old so I can let them slide. We can't expect them to fully support a fix for every bug after so long. But one would think that a game-breaking issue would be addressed before the inclusion of the game in a recently released edition. I'm disappointed, Bethesda. *End rant.*

For the most part, Fallout 3 lives up to the hype.  I had a great deal of fun with this game for the first thirty hours of play or so.  The RPG character development is strong, the FPS aspect is great considering it's an RPG, and the VATS system which is a combination of both is unique and adds a certain cinematic appeal to combat.  And of course, the perk system adds a certain excitement to leveling up that wasn't standardized for RPG gaming yet at the point of this game's release.
The open world is exciting to explore as you seem to run across all kinds of events and quests that (as far as I could tell) you weren't handheld and led to from any other place in the game.  The main storyline and the enjoyable DLCs lead you to the far corners of the map, though additional quests are plentiful.  Multiple quests also seem to offer something entirely unique, especially those related to the DLC, where you'll unlock special perks and otherwise unobtainable weaponry - weaponry which often has its own mechanics that differentiate it from other gear in the game.
My only complaint with the game, and this may be self-inflicted, is that as I neared the end and started playing the different DLCs it seemed to begin to drag.  I ended up having to push myself to start the game up, even though I, generally, enjoyed my time playing the game even then.  This could be related to your character becoming drastically overpowered if you allow them to in the higher levels.
All in all, a great game and one that I highly recommend to RPG and Post-Apocalyptic fans.  I secondarily recommend this game to FPS, as the gunplay is fun, but it won't blow your mind if that's solely what you're hopping into the game for.

This is basically the same game with a few better mechanics.
+ Firing require additionnal aiming, affected by the sea.
+ Graphics are much better
+ World map is much larger, it has pro and cons but I believe it is better like this, players will be able to "own" regions since it would be really hard for anyone to quickly travel across the entire map for defense. It could easily take up to 6-8+ hours to cross the entire map.
+ Economy is more simple, which is a bad and good thing. Everything is viable so there is no chance everybody end up producing the same thing like in other games due to the cost effectiveness. At the same time it remove a little of depth.
+ Devs are creating events with special rewards / blueprints.
+ Roles are more flexible, players can be at anytime a privateer / trader / navy officer.
+ Can customize cannon pounding of each deck
+ Damage is realistic, constantly shooting a mast will destroy it, same with rudder, crew etc.
+ Navigation is pretty good, you can  control each individual mast, assign crew in sailing, repair, gunnery, survival, boarding.
- UI is really ugly, in fact we keep discovering context menus or label that are actually clickable. At least, it quickly become the least of our concern.
- Maybe it is not actually a con, but I know there are mortar ships in the game and while I have not personally been able to used them or see them in action, I am pretty sure they aren't a good addition to the game since the completly move away from the standard fighting style.
Neutral : I am unsure whether or not update progress is fast yet since I have recently started. It look like the devs added a lot of content since then however the game still really feel like an alpha after 6 months. I would assume it could have been faster but I do not know the size of the team, at the same time making sure everything is tested throughly isntead of rushing through everything is a good thing.

Considering that this game is in Early ALPHA, I'd say it's quite an experience!
On my first exploration day I managed to capture (by grape-shooting crew) 2 ships: a Lynx and a Snow. This shows the freedom given to the player. Where in many other games gaining a new ship requires boarding, in Naval Action you can Craft it, Purchase it, Win it after a fight or, as said, Board it.
The graphics are beautiful, the sounds are realistic and the controls and mechanics are enough intuitive and bearable even for someone like me that knows absolutely nothing about sailing and sailing-games.
Of course, a long way lies ahead before this product will reach its final shape, but given the fair amount of fun I had today, I do feel optimistic.
Recommended.

The most obvious flaw of the game is its repetitivity. Throughout the story different weapons and enchancements become available, sure, but essentially the gameplay situations themselves are becoming more and more of a deja vu as you proceed.
There are some refreshing moments, like jetpack riding, but they are like dessert, before which you always get to eat another full pot of cereal. Perhaps, it would be less noticeable if the game would turn out to be less absurd by both the terms of WH40K canon and mere common sense.
Overall, the singleplayer part of the game is just not worth the pain. The multiplayer has a lot less sharp edges and generally allows more diversity, but still looks like a semi-serious wannabe-Warhammer game, with power armor painted all colours of rainbow (acceptable for Chaos, but nonsense for loyalists) and a pretty standard, though entertaining, gameplay. There is also Dreadnought assault, but finding an active game is extreme luck. Whoever finds himself a fan of the 40K universe should probably only buy this with a major discount.

Lego Worlds is in pre-alpha stage so I’ll be comparing it to the game that inspired it. A pre-Alpha state of Minecraft when it was also just creative mode in a web browser. Where water would destroy your homes in a second.
Understanding that it’s a very early alpha you still get the general idea of the game. At first I absolutely love how you’re falling out of the sky into your world. However the world isn’t infinite, and it’s oddly shaped circle in a square object world. Upon falling onto the ground you’ll notice the colors are somewhat saturated and not vibrate like you’d expect, little odd but it’s still in development.  You can run around find animals to ride, & randomly dropped vehicles are placed, and you can interact with per-determined pieces or else punch them for coins to purchase prebuilt items. That’s basically part of the survival aspect.
The build aspect is where I really have the issue. You can’t build vehicles. I hope this is changed. I don’t want a pre-built car purchased with coins or randomly dropped throughout the world. I want to make my own crazy design. On top of it I want to be able to assign assets to each vehicle. For example A helicopter engine would make your vehicle behave like a helicopter and you can assign multiple aspects to it as well like water floats so it can land on water. This is a must. I also want the vehicle to break apart if it crashes and you have to repair it.  I can see having the coin aspect to buy pre-built buildings and vehicles for kids, however kids are creative and that’s why Minecraft is so popular.
So far the direction I see Lego Worlds going is dumbing down the youth, and has zero adult appeal. Kids using Minecraft showed us that they had no issue building their own creations in Minecraft. It was challenging and rewarding, and educational.  They’re already master builders treat them like it Lego.
This game needs the following in order for it to succeed, or it will fall short of Minecraft.
- First Person mode (you can switch back to 3rd person)
- Infinite worlds (it can be done)
- Vehicle designer with engine and featured assets that effect the vehicles behavior.
- Multiplayer (this was in the very early stages of Minecraft, do it.)
- remove pre-built buildings/vehicles (kids are more creative than you think!)
- The ability to buy your vehicle or small buildings and build them with real Lego’s.
- Survival mode: Pick up pieces and place them in an inventory for building. Not coins
- Creative mode option is okay but separate game like Minecraft.
- Ability to make flowing water
Overlooking controls, graphics, and a polished interfaces and just basing this review only on the gameplay which it’s trying to mimic.  I can’t recommend this yet.

Downwell is  a deceptively simple game. All you do is fall, well... down a well. At its heart, this game is a platformer. You can jump and shoot a limited amount of bullets out of your boots. You can kill enemies with these or by landing on top of them. If you can manage to land from one enemy to the next, you chain combos that award you gems; the more enemies you chain, the larger the bounty. Also sctatered through the levels are shops where you can spend your gems in items that give you a largar life pool or more charge from your boots.
And that's about it. You go from level to level trying to chain as many enemies as you can and trying to stay alive. Every 3 levels or so you enter a new area with different twists; some have spiky floors, others are underwater, etc... Things get pretty insane past area number 3, I'd say.
Maintining a rythm and chaining enemies together is satisfying as all hell, but hard to pull off.
If you want a challenging platformer you can play casually, give this a go, you won't regret it.

For the most part, Fallout 3 lives up to the hype.  I had a great deal of fun with this game for the first thirty hours of play or so.  The RPG character development is strong, the FPS aspect is great considering it's an RPG, and the VATS system which is a combination of both is unique and adds a certain cinematic appeal to combat.  And of course, the perk system adds a certain excitement to leveling up that wasn't standardized for RPG gaming yet at the point of this game's release.
The open world is exciting to explore as you seem to run across all kinds of events and quests that (as far as I could tell) you weren't handheld and led to from any other place in the game.  The main storyline and the enjoyable DLCs lead you to the far corners of the map, though additional quests are plentiful.  Multiple quests also seem to offer something entirely unique, especially those related to the DLC, where you'll unlock special perks and otherwise unobtainable weaponry - weaponry which often has its own mechanics that differentiate it from other gear in the game.
My only complaint with the game, and this may be self-inflicted, is that as I neared the end and started playing the different DLCs it seemed to begin to drag.  I ended up having to push myself to start the game up, even though I, generally, enjoyed my time playing the game even then.  This could be related to your character becoming drastically overpowered if you allow them to in the higher levels.
All in all, a great game and one that I highly recommend to RPG and Post-Apocalyptic fans.  I secondarily recommend this game to FPS, as the gunplay is fun, but it won't blow your mind if that's solely what you're hopping into the game for.

Don't let the short play time on my account fool you. I've been playing this game a lot in its testing phase and got to know it quite well. It's come a long way and it's become almost intimidating - there are lots of interfaces, skills, features and some fairly unusual mechanics to get used to at first. Give it some time to grow on you, and once you get the hang of it, you might find you really enjoy this game.
Pros:
* Ultimate freedom. Do what you want; no safe zones, no questions asked. Combine items, skills etc. to your liking.
* Some inventive game design concepts (once you understand them).
* Cool soundtrack.
* Nice visuals. There are lots of biomes and beautiful, imaginative assets.
* Fair and square monetization concept for an MMO.
Cons:
* Vague combat controls. Ranges and areas of effect don't really match the animations.
* Despite the tutorial it's a bit hard to get into. Some larger concepts are not explained properly (but hey, explore them!).
* Occasional rubberbanding.
Since the problems the game has now are mostly things that concern optimization and/or require larger amounts of player feedback to be optimized, I'm sure they will be fixed by the time this game leaves Early Access. It'd be a shame to see this game die down before it really has a chance, so be sure to get on board soon and give the devs and ourselves a change of making it the best it can be. Without going into great detail (which other reviews will cover) the game does have a rather large difficulty spike as the missions go on. And the game is much more fun with some friends in co-op. The cover-shooting mechanic is a large part of the gameplay since you'll be ravaged horribly by high-tier bullet-sponge enemies if you don't hide behind something. It's a pretty ambitious game, and while it doesn't nail everything it sets out to, the sheer amount of exploration and fun with friends makes it a game i can recommend to people looking for a casual single-player/cooperative experience.

Let me state up front, this game is brilliant on so many levels, one of the best fighting games not just of this era, but of all time.  That said, there are five issues this game has that any would be buyer needs to know up front.
1) The community is pretty awful.  Exceptionally so if you're a casual player.  Don't get me wrong, there are some good people in it too, but its not uncommon for people to treat you poorly in game, and even more common for them to treat you poorly on forums... and then instead of other people in the community chastining the poor behavior, they will actually LIKE the hateful or bully post directed at your person.  I'm talking posts where they verbally abuse you, curse at you, and tell you to quit the game.  These terrible people have likely lead to the community remaining small, so you need to have thick skin, especially if you just want to enjoy the game as a game and not a second job.
2) The art, while beautiful beyond words and easily as good as if not superior to any other fighting game on the market, is very fan service heavy, with a largely female cast, many of which wear the sort of clothes you'd expect to see in a strip club, over bodies that could almost go toe to toe with Dragon's Crown.  Frankly, all that doesn't bother me, but it does bother some people so it bares mentioning.
3) This is a combo fighter.  If you like combo fighters, great, personally I hate combo fighters.  Yet everything else about this game is so good that I can look past the combos and enjoy the game.  Some people can't.  Its worth noting that unlike some combo fighters, the combos in this game are VERY beginner friendly, most characters having at least one solid combo that can be done by average human beings with out spending months in training, but as a combo fighter this still means that a good portion of every match consists of one player playing solitaire.  Also, being a combo fighter means this game has a pretty large gap between beginners and intermediates, which wouldn't be that big a deal if not for the next issue.
4) The game has no skill based match making.  The game once had skill based match making, but my understanding is it was removed because the community was so small that finding matches took forever.  In my opinion this decision only made a bad situation worse as beginners are routinely matched with experts and usually no fun is had by either player in those situations.  It should be noted that the game does have a good lobby format and good netcode, so there are ways to have fun against players of your skill online, but its much more difficult to set up then it shoudl be.
5)The roster is small.  This again, doesn't bother me, as the roster is also extremely varied and better balanced then many other fighters out there, so I'd argue that the number of viable options is actually on par with or actually higher then most other fighting games, but I know some people really want to see a huge screen of characters to choose from, even if half of them are useless or clones of the other half.
So in conclusion, what's good?  The music!  The story!  The characters!  The graphics!  The gameplay!  The netcode!  The training mode!  The tutorials!  The frequent updates!  So if those 5 bad things didn't scare you off, you owe it to yourself to give this game a chance.  It's that good.  But I feel its vital a potential new player be aware of the issues the game has upfront, especially those with the community, or the community really will always remain small and dominated by the same intolerrant bullies it is currently.

Lego Worlds is a fantastic adventure game and a decent building game. THAT SAID the game is 2 days old, in early access, but is still more functional, fun, and mechanically sound than 90% of other Early Access titles I've played. Lego Worlds keeps it's own ideas from previous Lego themed games such as collecting studs as currency, but also takes inspiration from Minecraft and Landmark.
The exploration and adventure is a lot of fun - roaming mountains, fighting wizards and dragons, finding Drill Machines and going straight through that mountain, under the ocean, and dig up to find yourself on a snowy island full of cute huskie puppies, polar bears, and snowmen. Not to mention that you can interact with just about anything you see. Along your adventures you can find giant chests which is incredibly exciting and just makes me excited to explore.
Now for the building aspect of the game. Being a Lego game, remember that these started out as physical building blocks you bought in a box and dumped out on the floor then find the missing piece like a landmine hours later, it seems like the building mechanics and contraptions should have been some of the most refined parts of the game, but unfortunately this is where the game got frustrating for me.
Laying brick by brick, easy - fun to do - little issues. Building pre-made stuff - pretty awesome! Look at my suddenly Old West town in the swamp lands! But when it comes down to making your own mansion like you dreamed of having digging through you Legos as a child - you might as well pull out your old Legos. Getting these parts of the game to cooperate are frustrating as a competent adult that has played Minecraft and Landmark for several several days worth of game time. I can't imagine how a child would fair in these conditions. Again, the pre-made stuff is great and is an adventure all it's own plopping down a cottage next to your obsidian volcanic structure. But right now the Undo is completely broken and when you make a mistake - you better know how to bend your hammer at a 90 degree angle to bang that back into shape or just select it all, delete and start from scratch.
The Select Tool itself was amazing at first. I'm so glad to see it implemented because it's a genius tool that Landmark made work incredibly well. But it got stale and frustrating and deflated as a clown's party tricks for 3 year olds  in an outdoor party in the Artic. Copy and paste? Forget it. The pasting is based off of where your cursor is and not where the objects would interact with each other once pasted. I was building a set of stairs in my mansion and wanted to have a classic big stairway that splits in two toward the second level and so I thinks to myself "Self, I'll just copy that side and paste it here." Nope. You can't mirror, only rotate, and when I pasted the bricks were either a few studs off or a mile away with no in between in my control - and no undo. Select, delete, start again.
THAT VERY CRITICAL THING SAID I go back to my first point of view, this game still functions better than any other Early Access game I've played - save a few. And even then they operate on the same high quality level that you would expect from a big production from someone like Lego. Although the UI is a little bulky and cumbersome and the building tools need work I still played this game for close to 6 hours straight and had a blast the whole time. It's so much fun to ride a horse then find a boat, ride the boat, then find an eagle, then ride the eagle, scale a mountain, find a dragon, and then fly around spitting fireballs at the fully destructable world. I didn't go into detail on the world manipulation tools and UI here because they fell in between for me - worked, but obviously were early versions of the amazing tools they will be some day.

Hella hard, but the story is so incredible, you can't not finish it once you start.  I wept at every cutscene.  The level of polish is incredible, just everything is spot on; beautiful art and sound, smooth quick movement (you feel like a little grasshopper), interesting and varied environments that are remarkably fun to re-explore after getting new abilities.  And speaking of which, crazy game-changing abilities.  You won't be playing the same game at the end that you were at the beginning.
The biggest reason to not play this game is the difficulty - particularly of the "chase sequences", of which there are 3 major ones, each at the end of a major chapter of the game.  It's been noted that the first one is especially difficult, and it is - and I think this is mostly just because it's so long.  I felt a little bit like a woman being rescued from a deserted island when I finally beat it.  On the other hand, I suck at platformers, so if I can do it, you can do it!
Other than that, I only have minor complaints.  One such is the ability point tree, which lets you unlock upgrades to abilities that you haven't gotten yet.  This confused me a lot at the beginning of the game.  For example, there is water in the game that kills you.  I saw far up on the ability tree that there was an ability that allowed you to breathe in "clean" water.  I rushed for that ability, but when I got it I still couldn't go in any of the water.  Well, I found out later that finishing the first chapter "cleans" all the water, so after I finished that I could finally use this ability I bought.  And many of the abilities on this tree are like this; you can buy them right away, but they do nothing until you get to a certain part in the story (but not knowing what's going to happen, their descriptions are very confusing).
But that's just a quibble.  I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  Highly recommended

I played in open alpha for a month, and let me just say the majority of the people giving this game negative reviews haven't given this game a fair shot. The game is intended to be quick to get into with a playing field resembling most MOBAs, with PVP and objective-control based gameplay.
PROS:
*Lots of customization on weapons and armor. Better armor has larger stat variance, so you can push stats to higher levels.
*Anti-zerg: All abilities can friendly fire. Very few damaging abilities occur instantly at a point. They are all either delayed or shot as a projectile. This means that when a ton of people gather together, they are as much at risk of hurting themselves as you are at risk of them hitting you. Good strategy can help smaller forces outmaneuver larger ones.
*Huge ability customization: Some abilities are great as they are. Some abilities need to be leveled (Aether Form). Some abilities suck when you grind, but are amazing in PVP (Energy Drain). Some are amazing when you grind, but underpowered in PVP (Toxic Spray, Gravity Well). Some are better in groups and some are better solo.
*Skill-based: All combat involves skillshots or hit confirmation of some kind. You can outmaneuver and kick the hell out of someone as long as you are remotely decently leveled (You can unlock all your skill slots in 2-3 days of 2-3 hours each).
*World sustainability system: Servers are kept alive by their players. Every day, a certain amount of resources need to be contributed to the 'war effort', or the server dies, and all progress (gates being opened, bases, resources not in player inventories or stashes) is lost. This ensures two things: One, people can't just be killing other people all the time, because resource need to be collected. Also, since players can transfer off a server, bullying players on your server is a good way to A. have an empty server and as a result B. Lose all your progress that your clan's fought so hard to gain. The amount of contribution needed rises every day. This encourages some level of cooperation and discourages spam killing someone.
*Exciting abilities: Abilities don't just 'do damage'. They have unique properties, like one of the bow's auto attacks increasing damage with distance from the target, or Droplets, a Totem skill, doing more damage with successive hits on the same target. They reward and encourage good positioning (alongside the friendly fire system) and keep combat fresh since you're never just auto attacking; you're looking for opportunities.
*Communicative developer base: Report a bug? Expect a response in 2-3 days, and maybe a little reward on top. I got a 7 day extension on my free account just for reporting a bug. They do look and listen for feedback. The reporting interface is pretty nice, too (F3 to report, automatically takes a screenshot of the area, and then gives you a fair bit of text to report an issue).
*Good visual aids: A lot of MMOs nowadays suffer from screen clutter and general confusion in larger fights, which just leads to reliance on very specific cues or 'throw damage into the center until one side dies'. This game more frequently operates on 'clashes', where parties fight together, break away, and then re-engage. Effects have distinct sound effects and graphics, so when you get hit by something, or see/hear a friend get hit by something, you'll know, and you can act. This makes combat very structured and allows you to be reactive without having to read minute cues.
CONS:
*Lag: There are some latency issues given the large amount of people playing the game now compared to open alpha. They are addressing these issues, and have fixed a lot of them from open alpha
*Skill inconsistencies: This mainly has to do with similar effects and their stacking. Poison damage and other damage over time always stacks 'highest source first'. You can't stack multiple instances of Poison or multiple Toxic Sprays. I hope this is fixed in a future patch.
*Ganking: Although the mentality of the developer is that they want to leave PVP to the players, they did advise against repeat-ganking people because it drives them off the game. Still, inevitably you see newbies getting ganked, and the systems to protect them are rather inadequate. Again, if you're crafty, you can escape those players even with lower level skills, though.
*Lack of directional voice chat: There is area voice chat, but you can't tell who is talking. This is infuriating.

I'll recommend this game with some noted exceptions.
The servers are bad, lots of lag/rubberbanding which gets really disruptive when you are trying to stand there and setup your skills for instance.  Not to mention the obvious issues for combat.
It is 100% open PvP there is no safe areas, putting stuff in a bank or setting up skills?  Yeah you can get ganked.  With that said its the culture of these games to be absolutely horrible to new players and dumpster them repeatedly.  Except to be mistreated, abused, and otherwise harassed by the rest of the players in the game.
There are TWO(2) "US-Serenity" servers, this made it stupidly difficult for my friends and I to end up on the same server and required some trial and error.
Information inside the game and the official wiki as far as what to do, whats going on, etc.  Is pretty lacking and much of the official wiki is not up to date from what I noticed with many section using an older name for the game, referencing UI elements that have been seemingly drastically changed, and so on.
All of that said though this is a game with potential.  Its grinding is minimal and within a few hours of gameplay once I figured out the systems I was able to get most of my abilities, fill out my skill bars, and unlock all the ability slots. I think the level cap might be 20, and I got to 16-17 range within about 3-4 hours knowing nothing about the game before setting for in it. That really shows just how easily/freely you can level up in this game.
This is a game for groups, a solo player can survive but you can't really thrive as a solo player.  Getting materials for items requires guarding points you activate for 5 minutes, any group that rolls up on that point can and will kill you and take your stuff.  A solo player with the right skills can probably escape/runaway but thats about the best they can hope for assuming player skill is otherwise even in an uneven numbers fight.
The population of the game right now seems pretty low.  While playing I noticed a small group of 2-4 players here or there, and by the time midnight rolled around the server was mostly dead except a random person here or there.  Due to the nature of the current 7 day free trial I think a lot of people showed up, tried the game, ran into the lag/server issues and likely never looked back after their trial as people were talking in game like it was previously more populated.  Perhaps as the game gets more updated, servers get sorted out, etc things can change but as it stands I wouldn't expect huge populations right now.
So I'd recommend giving this game a shot, its decently unique, the 7day trial system is nice, grinding is minimal and there is a clear focus on PvP.   There is no P2W to be seen here besides "buying the game" once your trial is over.  It has a lot of good points, but the server issues and population, combined with its niche gaming nature as a 100% open PvP game is certainly not for everyone.

Fell in love with TWWH1, grabbed this immediately, so glad I did.  Fantastic strategy game that I might describe as Civilization with more war.    That is, more emphasis on war and battle, where you conquer the planet and all the cities on it, but you actually command your units in battle as well, and the intent is to violently CONQUER the planet.   Diplomacy exists, but it is almost entirely based simply on who is stronger, and who are you enemies with?  Its simple stuff.  The units are wonderfully detailed, and to back it all up there is the well known, deep and expansive lore of the Warhammer fantasy universe.
Being part 2 of 3 in the series that Creative Assembly announced, it integrates TWWH1 into a huuuuge map, if you own it.   Any DLC you have for TWWH1 can be played in TWWH2, such as any factions you purchased, and you do not need to re-purchase them.   TWWH2 introduced a new campaign for the 4 new factions though, and it deviates from the old 'conquer cities' objective from before.  It gives you a goal, a race of sorts, which is a great break from simply becoming a massive wrecking ball and flattening the map.
With the addition of the Mortal Empires update, this game remains the absolute best dollar to time value on steam. Completely unlimited replayability.
