I've heard some good and a whole lot of bad about this game, but seeing that the game has gone through changes over the year and coupled with the fact of it being free for the weekend, I decided to give this game a go.
As a fan of RPG-like loot-based/farming shooters such as Warframe and Borderlands, seeing The Division become free for the weekend naturally caught my attention.
Thirteen hours of gameplay later... I can say that the overall experience is a mixed bag at best, especially as someone who usually plays solo in games. What I'm going to say are the highlights that stuck out to me the most: the good, the "meh," and the bad.
Most of what I'm going to mention is coming from purely solo play, so take that as you will.
 
I wouldn't have stuck to this game for long if the loot and rewards I got didn't feel meaningful. Finding a new weapon that had increased stats and/or an attached unique Talent really does feel satisfying, as it's another toy for you to use on your local mobs.
The same goes for finding clothes, vests, backpacks, knee pads, etc. and seeing what you get affects your three primary attributes: Firepower, Toughness, and Skill Power. Whatever you equip on your character can have significant effects on what weapon Talents you can use, how much Armor you equip, the bonus stats that may or may not come with it, etc.
In short, each piece of clothing, armor piece, mask, and weapons you equip can heavily affect how you perform in combat, and The Division does a very good job in emphasizing that.
This was touched upon in the previous point, but there are many ways to build your character's stats via the equipment and Mods you use. Although I haven't gotten around to use this yet, stats on equipment can further be edited using the Recalibration Station in the Tech Wing, another thing that I'm looking forward to explore.
Appearance is a big thing too, as I wasn't expecting the game to have as many clothing options as it does... not that I'm complaining, of course. This is welcome in my eyes.
Coming from games like Warframe and Borderlands, I'm used to being able to move around and attack enemies from different angles at a fast pace. With regenerating shields and health gating (Borderlands 2), I could move around in combat in the open as long as I didn't leave myself exposed too long, and using my Abilities usually gave me free reign over the battlefield.
However, in The Division... you don't get those luxuries.
Compared to the aforementioned games, movement is more restricted, and you'll notice this even more if you're coming from the same or similar background as I do. Going in guns blazing out in the open even for a few seconds is spelling out your death sentence. Popping in-and-out of cover and positioning yourself in the safest firing conditions is the main way to survive and keep yourself from taking damage, and in this game this is a play style that you
get used to.
I don't mind bullet sponges that much as I've gotten used to playing against them in other games, but boy do they get incredibly spongy quickly. For the first 10 levels when leveling up the health and armor scaling of mobs isn't so bad... however reaching around level 15, it's like running into a brick wall.
Even with even or close-to-even leveled weapons and gear, mobs can chew up entire SMG/assault rifle clips and still fire a few potshots at you. Fortunately, the game does compensate for this by allowing you to carry metric-tons of ammo for your bullet spraying pleasure and using your Abilities becomes more important than ever.
Sniper rifles are extremely helpful, as most of the sniper rifles do come with a +100% headshot damage multiplier, allowing you to take down mobs easily from a distance... if you can aim, of course.
 
This might be more of a nitpick than anything, but the game could've done more to get you acclimated to the volatile environment of the DZ. In my experience, all the game did was give me a mission telling me to discover the DZ, which meant me just throwing myself in there knowing little to nothing about it. The DZ was mentioned in the story's narrative beforehand, but as a new player there's little to no way for me to gauge how dangerous it actually is seeing as how until that point I had spent all my time being in the Light Zone.
It can be argued that there's really no way to know better other than experiencing it yourself, which I do agree. To clarify, my complaint
that you shouldn't go into the DZ to learn about it, rather my complaint is that there should've been more of an effort to help new players
to the environment due to how radically difficult and more unpredictable it is compared to the LZ, perhaps some sort of mission or tutorial, opposed to just straight up telling them to go in there and figure out everything.
In my case it wasn't until a semblance of a tutorial popped up on my screen after I died the first time in the DZ... it would've been better if that popped up before I went into the DZ for the first time.
If you like playing solo like I do, you
to consider grouping up with other players. Not only is this preferable in the DZ, but in the LZ as well. The amount of bullet-spongy mobs that the game throws at you from multiple angles can make you feel like it's a little bit too much for one player to handle alone... even more so when multiple purple-bar and yellow-bar enemies are on the field.
It's still manageable in solo play if you play smart and carefully, but the experience can be enhanced if you have multiple people or friends playing with you.
Overall, The Division isn't a bad game. It does an okay job to get new players started. It mainly depends on the players to learn the mechanics, figure out which weapons can suppress or operate most efficiently, learning how stat bonuses can affect your character's combat performance, etc. And all of that can only be learned by playing the game.
If you like playing solo, expect to run into problems as you go through the story missions and do expect yourself to die a couple of times as a learning experience.
If you're a fan of loot-based shooters, upgrading your character in many different ways, shredding up bullet sponges, and can adapt to the cover-emphasized mechanics of the game, you should consider trying this game out... either for free or when it goes on sale.
Also, ♥♥♥♥ enemy snipers. :D

I have mixed feelings about this title. Note that I played only SP campagin.
the hook:
On each level you have to fight through a linear map i.e. get from point A to B with only one possible route with boss at the end. Inbetween some maps you will have something to break the monotony (minigames), like shooting down planes, etc.
gameplay:
Overall, the gameplay is fun, splashing orks head, or fixing his teeth with a chansword was much more fun than I expected. That being said, there are some things I didnt like.
- The moves are ridiculouslly simple to perform. This trivialized button combinations are a slap to the face of classic walking-fighting games you could encounter in the 90's.
- As a fan of the WH40k lore, I have to say that the arcade'y gamestyle ruined the atmosphere for me. the game lacks the heavy, dark atmosphere that the books/short stories have, so you might reconsider, If that's what you're expecting (example: automatic healing, 'immortal' AI teammates).
summary:
The game is OK, the story is a little clichee (but I enjoyed it), so are the characters, gameplay is fun, but simple, it does not have much replay value to me. Some people might find this game awesome, but I cannot recommend this game to any random bloke without a word of warning.
recommendation:
This game deserves a third kind of rating, 'MEH', but since there is none, I give thumbs down, replayability being the main factor.

Sword & Sworcery's atmosphere is heavily built on the use of sound and music. It uses it to create tension during combat as well as a sense of calm and mystery during the more exploratory parts of the game.
The story is structured from short sentences describing your surroundings, the thoughts of various characters, and the presence of reoccuring characters. Most of the time it builds a light mythology for itself, though some of the phrasing used is designed to replicate a more modern speech pattern, a sort of meta-narrative.
Difficulty is created by reducing the player's health as they progress, and while this may sound trivial, it is cleverly tied into the story and allows for simple combat that doesn't need to throw additional mechanics at the player.
Don't let pixels scare you off, this game is beatifully looking, incredibly sounding and irresistably involving.

What a great game. This is a lovely ipad conversion of a short, amusing, yet subtly bleak fantasy tale. You play a girl who turns up in a forest, accidentally causes a bad thing to come about, and then must fix things, all the while getting to know the few people you're stuck in the forest with and your destiny. It's divided into four parts and carefully narrated by a mysterious archetype figure. He even suggests when you might have had enough by punctuating the end of each chapter with a sort of summary of events and a kind of 'until next time...' attitude. Even though the game is quite short, it's broken up into four of these easily digestible chapters. Having EP in the title, the music is obviously one of the centrepoints and Guthrie does a great job of stimulating an apt mood for the moment with some unusual synth tracks. There are things that might put people off - it's pixel-art, it's fairly slow going, sometimes the way to do some of the puzzles is a little obtuse, but the pace is important to setting the mood, the weird puzzles further fit with the unique nature of the game, and the humour is great, with regular comments from "you" and others that tend to look at situations sideways and often break the fourth wall. It's a lovely tale to see, hear and play and more people should experience the whole of this.

Let me state up front, this game is brilliant on so many levels, one of the best fighting games not just of this era, but of all time.  That said, there are five issues this game has that any would be buyer needs to know up front.
1) The community is pretty awful.  Exceptionally so if you're a casual player.  Don't get me wrong, there are some good people in it too, but its not uncommon for people to treat you poorly in game, and even more common for them to treat you poorly on forums... and then instead of other people in the community chastining the poor behavior, they will actually LIKE the hateful or bully post directed at your person.  I'm talking posts where they verbally abuse you, curse at you, and tell you to quit the game.  These terrible people have likely lead to the community remaining small, so you need to have thick skin, especially if you just want to enjoy the game as a game and not a second job.
2) The art, while beautiful beyond words and easily as good as if not superior to any other fighting game on the market, is very fan service heavy, with a largely female cast, many of which wear the sort of clothes you'd expect to see in a strip club, over bodies that could almost go toe to toe with Dragon's Crown.  Frankly, all that doesn't bother me, but it does bother some people so it bares mentioning.
3) This is a combo fighter.  If you like combo fighters, great, personally I hate combo fighters.  Yet everything else about this game is so good that I can look past the combos and enjoy the game.  Some people can't.  Its worth noting that unlike some combo fighters, the combos in this game are VERY beginner friendly, most characters having at least one solid combo that can be done by average human beings with out spending months in training, but as a combo fighter this still means that a good portion of every match consists of one player playing solitaire.  Also, being a combo fighter means this game has a pretty large gap between beginners and intermediates, which wouldn't be that big a deal if not for the next issue.
4) The game has no skill based match making.  The game once had skill based match making, but my understanding is it was removed because the community was so small that finding matches took forever.  In my opinion this decision only made a bad situation worse as beginners are routinely matched with experts and usually no fun is had by either player in those situations.  It should be noted that the game does have a good lobby format and good netcode, so there are ways to have fun against players of your skill online, but its much more difficult to set up then it shoudl be.
5)The roster is small.  This again, doesn't bother me, as the roster is also extremely varied and better balanced then many other fighters out there, so I'd argue that the number of viable options is actually on par with or actually higher then most other fighting games, but I know some people really want to see a huge screen of characters to choose from, even if half of them are useless or clones of the other half.
So in conclusion, what's good?  The music!  The story!  The characters!  The graphics!  The gameplay!  The netcode!  The training mode!  The tutorials!  The frequent updates!  So if those 5 bad things didn't scare you off, you owe it to yourself to give this game a chance.  It's that good.  But I feel its vital a potential new player be aware of the issues the game has upfront, especially those with the community, or the community really will always remain small and dominated by the same intolerrant bullies it is currently.

**Note this review was written for the first beta prior to the launch and some things may have or may not have changed. I have not played the game since beta and will do a edit on the changes at a later date.** The game is really good but it does have it's flaw. I got this game for free for signing up to the beta and learning about it after buying the forced complete collection for $24 about a month ago (Oct/Nov 2016). The game is similar to the mobile phone game Clash Royale so if you are into those type of games then this game you should check out.
Now the break down of the game:
Pros:
+ The concept of having special abilities as you level up during the match (Passives+Abilities differs based on who you play as)
+ The role to have an objective of keeping both bridges rather than just 1 lane play as in other games makes it more enduring to choose your strategy
+ The visual concept is good considering it is from forced
+ The solo content is a plus with rewards to help you understand the game
+ No need to recollect to level up cards once you get them (this made me hate clash royale and eventually became a grind and pure cash grab with future legendaries taking over with only a few obtaining due to rng)
Cons:
- Needs a filter during deck building (Spells, units, buildings etc)
- Add multiple deck building layouts so you can switch between them
- Limited characters to play as with only 6 (Hoping to see alot more at launch with alot of bosses being playable)
- Land visuals applies nothing but cosmetics (would love for this apply some small buffs or something to help customize gameplay that you can earn through the ingame currency, i.e something like your units gain x% movespeed or health regen while on your side etc which will make it more vital in terms of defending and not getting steamrolled)
- No side towers means getting steamrolled is a bit easier and harder to defend once your falling behind + with the exp and hero passives makes it even harder if you are far behind.
- Some of the spells seem underused due to cost or value being too high in cost as it seems better to just steamrole and spam units to win.
Overall this game is surprisingly good. Its similar to clash royale in a way but without the hassle of having to spend your entire wallet to level up units. The variety in units itself is pretty spot on and if your familiar with clash royale then you will notice that some of the units play similar to those you have seen there henced I used some of my knowledge from that game when i played this one.
Would I recommend you try it? Yes, this game is good and will keep you occupied for awhile. The quick matches help to be one of those quick play games you go to when you just want to play something to remove some stress or to play if your limited on time. At the moment I rate this game a 6 out of 10. My hopes is that it does not turn pay to win or force you to pay heavily just to unlock something that may be OP.
What I would like to see implemented or improved:
1. Since your straying away from having side towers, I would like to see innovation like maybe have some random enviromental events throughout the match kinda like how it is in forced showdown. (Ex: like random fireballs that dmg any units, forst blizzards that slow and freeze all units on the field)
2. One problem I see is that if your far behind, it is usually GG considering your hero isnt too strong depending on who you play as and also because there is no side towers to help protect the waves. Also the exp+bonus for controlling the bridge makes it even more of a GG to someone who is far behind. Maybe consider adding like a loser's card bonus that you draw once you take X amount of dmg to your hero (some cards like maybe a windborne gust that pushes all units to your opponents side or maybe a hail freeze to freeze all units for x seconds or a free mana boost card that adds x amount of mana to help you formulate a small comback.
3. The concept of leveling up is good but I would like maybe more customizable characters. In forced showdown you have alot of class cards that influenced class skills. Maybe add in a skill tree where whatever character you choose, you are able to choose the attack it has, other effect, and passive effect. This way not every character plays the same and plays differently. (Wishing they do that in forced showdown as I would love to change alot of the melee play to have a different ability)
4. Add more defensive buildings (Since there are no side towers) as there seems to be like 2 or 3 that i have seen that are actual defense structures with the rest being a spawner building. (Possibly you can use this to customize the characters like idk maybe have side towers be based around the character of your choice, Like if you play as volvo then your side towers can be like fire golems that stand there and erupt a volcanic eruption from the floor that does aoe on the lane)
5. Here is an idea for innovation, Have a co-op play where you have 2 people playing together to fight either npcs or other 2 players. It would work like normal like it is now where there is 2 lanes but there would be 1 hero for each player allocated on separate lane on your side (each teammate protects one lane) and you both coordinate to protect your lane or your team mates lane by allowing the players to summon on either side of their field. If your hero goes down, then whatever lane you were protecting, those enemy minions will start to shift over from your lane once they reach your hero's corpse to your partner's lane till your both destroyed. (kinda like you have an attack from the front which is normal but because your teammate is dead, you will now have assaults from the back as well or technically in this case the side)

I'm really surprised by how much I've come to hate this game. It is such a load of closed minded, sexist, anti-scientific, moralising rubbish.
Many of the restrictions are merely reflections of the rating system in place for games so the devs aren't really to blame but when you put it in this context they become so incredibly infuriating. So for example, it is perfectly fine to spawn a flame-thrower and burning everyone alive. One the other hand woe betide you if you try to spawn anything relating to sex, drugs or alcohol because none of those words are in Scribbenauts' vocabulary. I get that this is a children's game but then why can we spawn flame throwers? Why is violence so often featured in the puzzles, often unavoidably? Why does one level feature torture? Why can we spawn iron-maidens if we feel like it? It is garbage. Moralising garbage that shoves a twisted morality down the player's throat where torture and violence are a-okay and sex and alcohol are the works of the devil.
Other things are clearly in place just to reduce controversy so you can spawn old religious figures that not many people take seriously any more like Thor and Zeus but not Jesus, and Mohammed is right out. Mind you so are most of the historical figures I've wanted to spawn so far. Someone was clearly in the grip of internalised capitalist oppression so I tried to spawn Marx to talk some sense into them, I didn't seriously expect this to work but I did expect to be able to spawn Marx but no. I gave up and spawned a Lemon when that was the suggestion when I tried Lenin.
On another occasion a scientist wanted someone to talk to so I tried to spawn Aristotle, this worked but it seems the game doesn't consider Aristotle to be a scientist so the scientist refused to talk to him. Einstein of course worked but it felt like such a hollow victory to resort to the bloody obvious. And the game forces you to resort to the bloody obvious so often. Thinking outside the box is so often met with no reaction at all from the game. Sometimes the box you're meant to be thinking inside is bloody stupidly defined as well. One of the hints was to solve the problem of needing to melt a block of ice to thaw out a prehistoric man "with science". I tried heating the ice in various ways. The ice melted but level was failed. I tried ordering the ice to melt with adjectives. The ice melted but level was failed. I tried spawning salt and using that on the ice. The ice melted but level was failed. Eventually I resorted to Google. It seems "with science" in the Scribblenauts world means "don't try to solve this yourself, spawn a scientist to do it for you". Good god, such a stupid anti-scientific attitude to science.
Finally there is Lilly, poor, poor Lilly. First off she is a Ms. Male by which I mean she is a female version of Maxwell with no other distinguishing personality or features except for being pink. Then she gets damseled in the opening cut-scene. Then you find that each level you can unlock one more of her siblings as a new playable character if you don't want to play as Maxwell, how many of these are sisters? None. Seemingly the other god knows how many playable characters are brothers. *sigh* Maybe Lilly becomes playable after the end of the story missions and she is released from her predicament but if so it is too little and far too late.
No. Enough. There is joy in the heart of this game but after you're over the initial rush of apparent power the limitations and all the rubbish that come with it suck all the joy of it. I dare say some might say that as a grown man I shouldn't be surprised that I can't enjoy this since I'm hardly the target audience but honestly given the amount of twisted crap that is wrapped up with this game there is no way I'd let a child play it.

I'm quite disappointed with this game. When buying this I expected an rpg-like roguelike with advanced tactics, simplistic but nice graphics and tons of loot.
The art style is quite nice, I admit that, however, the game lacks depth drastically.
At first it may seem fun, but as soon as you unlock few other classes it turns out that there's not much more to see, as every class feels the same apart from the few skills you might use. One might say that every class has probably some over 20 items, however, the items are exactly the same for every class so it's really just 20 items in the whole game (not counting usables and few accessories I found).
The game is tagged as "roguelike", "strategy" and "RPG", but in my opinion is neither of them.
- As for being a roguelike, it does not have permanent death, the loot is scarce and the game itself is rather easy.
- As for strategy, there is not much of strategic thinking in waiting a turn for your enemy to come closer to avoid him attacking you,
- As for RPG, there are so-called quests in this game, however, each one requires you to clear a small dungeon and that's basically it. The story is probably not too bad, however, I found myself skipping the dialogues as they resolved about the same things all the time (another civilization -> blablabla -> message of peace -> blablabla).
The game also feels like it was made having mobiles in mind, so it couldn't have been too complicated in terms of strategy and controls. The whole experience is a bit bland, there's no sense of achieving anything when completing a dungeon after you clear first few, it's just pretty much the same over and over again (apart from few new enemies).
I believe some people might actually get hooked on this game, however, I really can't see more play value than 5-10 hours. Personally, it took me 2, to get fed up. I believe this game could be much better, if creators added more different items for each class, maybe work on the village a bit more and implemented more INTERESTING quests.
All in all, I don't recommend the game. Do not buy it for it's full price, it's not worth it. I've paid 5€ and I think that it still was too much for this game...

I'm scrounging for "story-rich" with playable graphics, large time investment, and action/fighting along the way.  And by "story-rich" I don't mean the let's read an interactive picture book indie dime-a-dozen thingy that's peppered all over Steam these days.  I'd beg someone to shoot me now, in the forehead, before going there.  By "story rich", I mean complex with different endings and snappy dialogue and voice acting (see Dragon Age.  Or Neverwinter nights 2.  Or even Mass Effect).  Yes, the higher budget stuff.
Fallout 3 had a "story-rich" tag so I gave it a shot.  It's not "story rich."  Ok, so child seeking parent via various foiled quests and vice-versa is a time-honored plot device to be sure, but this is not in the scale of epic adventure of the parenthetically named games above.  I never considered Skyrim to be "story rich" either.
The detail here was good.  The plausibility of some of the human crazy made it less pretty than Skyrim (same makers, very familiar engine and first person perspective) but so much better.  Strange religions?  Dog eat dog world? Clean water as a prime motivator?  Sure.  Hell, skirmishes and even wars were fought over water throughout history.
The voice acting was terrible.  Not quite on the bad side of good like the original Resident Evil cheeseball writing, just plain bad.  With 2 men and women voicing the entire thing and a silent protag (always bad) it's hard not to slide down that side of the bell curve.
Dialogue option win.  I really do like getting the option of saying "F you", twice, to someone.  It can be cathartic in some cases, especially this game given main plot events.  After all, there are times when an F bomb is the only right answer.
The radio bit was a great immersive detail.  Travelling in and out of range of various radio towers, different channels giving different style news.  Radio static.  Old timey music as a soundtrack......."Set the world on fire" in a post nuclear wasteland?  Nice.
And the humorous commentary on the food that would somehow survive 200 years.  Frozen salisbury steak, spam, and bottled Coke.  Sure. Why not? I just want to know where all the twinkies got off to ala Homer Simpson.
Three words: giant naked molerats.
I only explored about a 3rd of the map.  I find sandboxes tiresome, boring, and repetitive (and lacking in plot motivators).  As much as I wanted to be completionist about it, I could not.  So I jumped to the end and won.  Yay me for saving the day.  Main plot done, I'm done because the prime motivator is gone, but you can go off and explore and complete as many side quests as you like after.  Though why you'd want to...
Even so, recommended overall.  As ugly as a post nuclear landscape is I found this one much more compelling than elder scrolls and I fully intend to purchase the Fallout 4 after they issue the first patch.

The short answer is yes, Warhammer II is pretty good, and it will only get better with time. Much like Warhammer I, Warhammer II is getting a long line of free-lc, on top of that it will be patched until Warhammer III comes out, at which time that game will consist, at least for those that own all three games, of all of the content that this game holds. Warhammer II by itself is still a good game however, it has a base of four races that each feel different whether you base that on the looks of each race or their playstyle. There is a endlessly replayable campaign mode, and with the introduction of the vortex mechanic this game has more of a direction than the other games, if you don't like that, it's fine you can skip the vortex altogether.
The game will get some dlc content that will flesh out the game a bit more, adding new races with their own special mechanics and goals, as well as new lords for existing races that will alter the way you play the game, whether that be what settlements you try to take, what races you come into conflict with, how many agents you  hire and how they act, or what units you put into your army composition and what they are capable of. For example in game 1 they added Skarsnik the Warlord, he allowed for a new composition of goblin centric armies as he was added along side squigs, squig-hoppers, and nasty skulkers that served as a new form of strong goblin cavalry and armor peircin damage dealers, this type of variation in army comp can allow for some fun themed armies that make one races roster feel like mulitiple different races in one, goblins, orcs, and savage orcs for example.
The other big thing to consider in your purchase of this game is whether or not you own the first game, and can therefore play mortal empires, this is a combination of the campaigns of Warhammer I and Warhammer II that makes the game feel much more complete and vibrant, with a host of lords and races. However, the mortal empires campaing currently is a tad lackluster because of the exclusion of Norsca, bugs, and absence of 30th anniversary RoR units. This does not mean that the campaing is unplayable, and it will eventaully include those changes and a host of others which will expand it even more, so if you are only after that sweet sweet combined map full Warhammer world experience then you might want to wait for the next sale.
That all being said, the team at CA have done a wonderful job at creating this game, and listening calmly to the overbearing complaining on the subreddit that goes in all different directions. They interact with the community, listen to feedback, and just generally do a good job. If you want to support a dev team like that, give this game a try. For all the complaints about this game it is undoubtedly the best Warhammer experience on the market, and it will only get better with time as it shores up any gaps in content. The flip side to the great dev team is the incredible modding seen for this game, with the limited tools currently at their disposal they have made some amazing content in a small space of time, and it never really stops going. If you want a more table top gaming experince its there, if you want a more cinematic experience its there, if you want to mod the graphics to incredible heights browse some community screenshots, or check out the subreddit, which for its complaints, is still a great community always waiting to give feedback, share stories, gameplay, or talk about lore and expectations for the series, Warhammer or not.
Overall I recommend this game, and the community that comes with it, I plan to play many, many more hours of this game. It is accesible, deep, and fun.

This is an old game, with elements of classic arcade in level design and game play features. This translates into linear corridor style gameplay with fixed/scripted encounters that have to be overcome via the only means possible before the area is unlocked and player can progress forwards with the level. The levels blend seamlessly into one another with cutscenes dialogues and animations delivering characterbackground and plot elements between major events and chapter ends. The single player campaign relies on an autosave checkpoint system but once played the different chapters become available for replay directly from the menu.
SP levels include static defense against waves, i'll drive u shoot mobile defense, advance and clear (vast majority) and boss style arenas, and jumppack sections. There are 16 sections split across 6 chapters, which i completed within 12 hours as a casual gamer.
The game controls are simple and fairly responsive albeit a little clunky in design. Gun play is as expected 1 button to shoot another to zoom another to reload and some guns have an additional quirk or feature like charge up/overheat or delayed activation. The play carries 1 pistol, 1 bolter and upto 2 specialist weapons at any point with limited ammo and pickups through the levels on all but the pistol. Periodically through the mission one will find weapon caches where they can reconfigure their gear and resupply on ammo and grenades.
Melee combat is more complex 1 button to attack another to stun each weapon has its own combo animations and lastly a recharge health mechanic called execute which locks the player into a sychronised slow motion animation of varying lengths that recharges ones health a certain degree upon its completion (all enemies remain active during this time leaving the player incredibly vunerable). There are 4 melee weapons in single player, 1 of wich prevents the use of specialist weapons firing.
The game feels like a console port at times, levels have invisible walls or ancle hieght impassable terrain giving one the impression of more freedom and better visuals. Certain points of the game have additional mechainics requiring one to spam a certain key or active the keys in sequence as prompted on screen. There is no jump feature as such but the inclusion of the jumppack as a mechanic means some levels/sections are more 3 dimensional by design.
The graphics are functional, the faces of the characters being decent, while the armour texture and details is lacking when close up, namely dialogue scens. The levels convey the atmosphere, but won't have you stopping to take in the scenery much like some games do.
The music score and sound effects are all decent, or atleast not immediately irritating after hearing the same thing ad infinitum. The voice acting and audio logs one finds are also note worthy, and while the script isn't all that it is atleast consistently delivered with the characters remaining true to themselves throughout. For those that know 40K they'll understand when i say the Titus would have been more plausable as a Spacewolf than an Ultramarine.
The multiplayer is split into 2 aspects, PvP and PvE. They are however, somewhat empty at this time and requires using the autofinder so jumping on a pug game isn't easy but Steam intergration allows friend invites. Both modes can however, be launched without being filled meaning they can be self hosted as SP if one so desires. The gameplay and handling of weapons is slightly different in MP for balance reasons, as one might expect.
The multiplayer also has a cosmetic customisation and skills rewards system based on various unlocks through online gamplay. This adds incentive and rewards failure in addition to success helping new players find their feet against the better equipped and more experienced community. Alas these don't work in Sp, which is to relaint upon fixed animations to allow for customisation.
Played on I7, win10 64bit, GTX970, Keyboard n Mouse.

I'll just say before I start, I've been a member of Steam for 5 years and I've never written a review because...well, most times it didn't feel warranted. Most games, are covered by a huge amount of media and I am but a humble gamer...one whose opinion usually falls in line with the rest of the crowd. I haven't written a review before, because, most times it didn't feel like the ends would justify the means and...well...
This game changes that.
Ori and the Blind Forest, developed by Moon Studios, produced by Microsoft Studios take a softer turn in the realm of Metroidvania stylized games by invoking lush, elaborate set pieces and smooth mechanics. The story feels familiar to something of the likes of a Studio Ghibli film and has the gentle, polished look of a lifelike watercolor painting. It has the general scenario you'd expect: An orphaned object falls from the sky only to be retrieved by a mother like figure who then raises the creature. From there, the world becomes a dark place and light has fallen from the world. Your job, pretty simple: Restore the light to the forest.
But realistically, part of me doesn't really care about the story. It's all about the mellow nature of the game and the beautiful score that accompanies it. It sucks you in and you don't want to leave because, aside from the astonishing amount of times you'll respawn...it is a very peaceful way to spend your time.
Do take the time to remember to save. (Cuz, I didn't....a lot)
Now, I can't say you can play the game in a multitude of ways. It's a fairly straight path to leveling up: You explore the map, you find hidden spots, you gain new power-ups and you collect energy, life, or ability orbs to enhance those power-ups. The orbs are vital in order to die less. There's just no getting around that.
But to sum it all up: The game offers an amazing, breathtaking wonderland full of waterfalls, lava pits, the greenest of forests and comes with a pleasant story-line. The soundtrack is amazing and I'd highly recommend this to anyone who loves the old school platformer format with a modern, alluring aesthetic.

General rundown-You start out by picking one of 8 nations. British, America, Spain, Dutch, Danish, Sweden, French, or Pirates(Pirates are #1). You start out in a little cutter and work your way up from there. The more you level the more crew you can have under your command. You can get into any ship, but until you can fully crew it you are at a disadvatage. To start off...
Fallout is the game that you'll spend a lot of time playing while doing nothing but walk, talk, shoot and bash them with something or even punch it out with your own hands. For player who are similar to open world RPG (Skyrim, GTA) this is the game for you.
The story set in the world after the nuclear war in the future and the protagonist was born and living safely underground after the war has ended. The father set out on a journey to recover the land and it is our job to find and help make it a better (or worse) place.
The perk of playing this game is like any other open world series is that you can do anything and by 'anything' I mean everything. You can be the Good, the Bad or you can balance it out in your journey into the wasteland. There will be choices along the way which will make you say "Seriously? Do I really have to pick?" and then save at that point before making a decision and watch where your choices lead you.
The outcome of the game is pretty much influent by how you play the game from the start to finish. There will be a lot of side quests which you can totally ignore them and still getting to the ending. (but they are worth it!)
The combat system are not too chabby but not that great either. Since the game consists on the story more than the gameplay. Also, the difficulty of this game depends your your skills choice and how you manage it when when you level up. There will be many status like poison and radiation (it was a nuclear post-apocalyptic and all) .
The AI or the enemies on this game are pretty easy to read (since they are only coming straight at you), but most of them are the hardhitters (mostly the non-human enemies) and they could totally whoop your butt into your last save in just a couple of hits (remember to save often!).
The most important thing in this game is the soundtrack. It somehow became the best thing you can hear in the game while slaughter some radiated monsters. Also, the graphic might not be that great compare to these days' standard but there is nothing you can't fix with a little modding which can be found in many other reviews or community discussions.
There are some downside of this game that many people are talking about like, can't play with windows 7 or higher but there are solutions. All you need to do is open up a browser (or two if you want) and type for "fallout 3 fix" or something similar to "Fallout 3 window 7/8 fix" and your problem will be gone in just a few mins.
Other than OS problem the game doesn't have a cloud save which will be a problem because you will play this game for a long long time and you don't want to start over if your PC/Laptop just broken or you're changing them to a better one. But on the bright side, the game have save files for everytime you save during the game in your documents folder. I recommend you to make a backup once in a while or you will be just like me who have start all over again for 3 times already and it's pretty frustrating.
All in all, Just buy it when it's on sales and play and I promise you won't regret it.

Decided to re-do my review as it's the end of season 5.
It is exactly what it claims to be : A open world MOBA of sorts with a customized character based on weapon/armor choice, sieges, full PVP, full loot (with some conditions), and events which can be contested by anyone regardless of who starts it.
If you are expecting "amazing" PVE or "dungeons", this is not the place. The focus is PVP and it provides it to the best of it's ability, but it lacks population currently due to "7 day trail" periods.
The major downfall of this game is it "needs" population to actually function as well as "resets" every "season" which currently is in 1 month intervals where you must restart completely. You will need to level, gear up, farm, unlock the map, and claim your settlements all over again each "Season".
On the plus side to these seasons, it doesn't allow someone to stay in power constantly on the best settlements. But this does not mean they cannot claim them on the next Season, it simply means they will lose their stockpile of resources so they can't just throw bodies/equipment out constantly.
Another major flaw with seasons/trails is that when a season ends, you must wait an entire day which means those with a trail will lose an entire day of play without any access.
~Example~
Season End : July 12th 4:30AM EST
New Season : July13th 4:30AM EST (Unless there's delay on it's restart...)
Anything else should be covered below.
Most lag/errors seem to be resolved besides a bit of rubberbanding and getting stuck in objects. Error 418 does not seem to happen anymore to my knowledge.
A party system was added for those who wish to team with others without being in the same clan.
Cloth armor was added which honestly feels broken in group play between sheltering link, protective link, and CC/debuff AoE cleanses. For solo play tho, this armor is not recommended.
Splint Mail is the hardest armor to use still, mostly due to lack of self-sustain. It does have it's uses tho.
Leather has high self-sustain and decent mobility while Robe has heavy mobility, possible 100% crowd control immunity, and solid CC. It is recommended that you go one of these two armors.
Most weapons are balanced to some degree but I have released videos to explain what each ability does as well as base stats.
This game is strictly for people looking for harsh PVP as truthfully all other areas are lacking.
- Friendly Fire : You can hit allies with damage and enemies with heals, be mindful of where you aim as well as where you are positioned.
- Full Looot : Truthfully is only the inventory but there is a mechanic in place to drop equipment.
- Equipment Drop Rate : When you die the chance to drop your equipment is raised, press "C" to find out the current chance to drop. Higher grades of weapons/armor are more likely to drop without any deaths.
- PVE Events : Aren't exactly "fun" after awhile but are required if you wish to quickly claim a settlement, advance farther up the map if it has not already been unlocked, and can be stolen by passing players.
- "This is mine" : Just because you start an event doesn't mean it stays yours, you can be killed or kept out of the "capture" zone until someone else claims ownership. If you want to secure loot, secure the objective and do not allow others outside of clan/party to stand within the black ring.
- Contestable Territory : Settlements have a lengthy siege process, which does not mean it's 100% safe. Even if it is not under siege, players can pass through gates when you open them even without access, once inside however they can open it for others wanting to come in.
- Alliances : There is an alliance and enemy system as well as options to allow clans or individuals access to all buildings but must be added by those with access to do show.

Based on a popular Nintendo DS game, Scribblenauts is an action puzzler where the player assumes the rooster-headed roll of Max, the protangonist. Lily, Max's sister, must be saved from a curse caused by abuse of a magic notebook. The notebook is the core mechanic of the game - the ability to describe an object and have that object appear in the world to be used by Max or the game itself. It's a simple premise, but one where the huge open ended variety of the dictonary used by the game really makes the puzzles (which get progressively vague or specific, including required actions with items) stand out as both endearing and enjoyable.
The game itself has a decent length, with a solid ending that wraps up the PG storyline in a neat package worthy of Aesop. The quality graphics, catchy and unobtrusive sound track, and genuinely creative player-centered gameplay should delight pretty much anyone of any age and ability. Probably the only gripes I have are the removal of particles (no "bag of salt", you have to make a bag and salt separately then put the salt in the bag) and that it's very easy to destroy required parts of the level, necessitating lengthy replaying of certain challenges.

It's the reason such games are the grindiest of most games around: to try and tempt players into spending real money as a "convenience" to get what they want in the game. This is low. Just because something's legal, doesn't make it genuinely ethical. If a developer sees that the grind it too painful for so many people, the right thing to do would be to simply make there be less of a grind, but that won't line the developer's pockets with money, so instead, they go to the trouble of setting up an in-game store with real-world monetary purchases and different currencies.
The game is only $19.99 at its normal retail price, though, so it
to be a better deal than even a really good $59.99 "AAA" title, right?  Let's add up the costs of the in-game stuff you can unlock, shall we? Cost of permanently unlocking all 5 current heroes (instead of getting certain ones on lone different weeks): 3150 rubies. Cost of unlocking all 8 arenas (they're the same arena with different skins, sound effects, etc): 6450 rubies. Alright, so 3150 + 6450 = 9600 rubies to permanently unlock the heroes (masters) and arenas. The cheapest way to buy rubies is in packs of 3350 for $18.99. So, we would need 3 sets of those, which is 3 x $18.99, which is $56.97 in real money, with 450 rubies left over from that purchase.
Getting more cards costs 750 rubies per attempt, and the other currencies you can use take quite a while to build up. I'm not even including additional card purchases. Just permanently getting all the masters and arenas, which is far too simplistic to be argued as something that would be DLC in a legitimate game, costs $56.97...on top of the $19.99 price tag the game will have any time it's not on sale, and that will run players a total of $76.96 before any purchases of additional cards (or should I say
at getting cards. You could just get 25 or so units of one of the other currencies since that 750 ruby purchase just gets you a random chance at cards, currencies, etc.
Instead of spending $76.96 (and probably more if you want to hasten your acquisition of cards and such), to have access to content in the game that would be available in any game not designed to rip you off, I would actually recommend purchasing a $59.99 game. One might argue "but DLC! You're forgetting DLC!" No, I'm not. With rare exception, not having the DLC in a full game does not make the base game less enjoyable. However, not spending real money in a fee to play game almost always makes the base game less enjoyable, since the "fix" for the un-fun part of the game is for you to mash your dollars against your screen until your problems go away, instead of the developer programming their game to be so enjoyable that no one would be that desperate as to spend real money to save time in the game.
TL;DR: This is a fee to play game. Avoid it because there's not much to do in the game, and unlocking things is such a boring process that the developers would prefer you spend real money to bypass that boring process, and they would insult your intelligence by claiming it's to benefit you, the consumer, by continuing to update the game with the money they rake in. Fee to play is anti-consumer; always has been, and always will be, and this is simply unacceptable.

Total War: Warhammer 2 performs horribly on machine, and it shouldn't.
I have a Radeon R9 380x with 4 gigs of RAM - I realize that's not exactly ideal, but it's not an ancient video card - it's 2 years old :/ My cpu is a 4.2ghz i7 - it has 4 cores and hyperthreading. I'm running on a samsung ssd that reads about 600mb/sec. I not only meet the minimum specs, but I am above the recommended specs too.
At the "Recommended" settings - which is "high" in my case - I am getting 37 fps at 1080p for the battle benchmark and 37 fps at 1080p for the campaign benchmark - worse obviously during the vortex scenes.
Warhammer 2 looks so bad without SSAO turned on, and if I turn it on, my fps plummets to unplayable levels at 1080p. Why is this such an fps hog? Games on my ps4 locked at 30fps actually look smoother. Honestly, they look a lot smoother. Warhammer 2 has stuttering, and I'm not believing the fps. And before you comment, my drivers are up to date - using Radeon drivers version 17.11.2!
I realize that 37fps (without SSAO) is considered "playable", but it still feels choppy and it looks so much worse than Warhammer I, where I have SSAO and 100% ultra settings and I achieve 47fps @ 1080p. Warhammer 1 is so smooth, I cannot even see the frame transitions!
Why is Warhammer 1 a better looking game than Warhammer 2 for a 2-year old graphics card? Could the optimizations and graphical fidelity not have had a bit more finesse? I really am not interested in spending $1000 to upgrade my video card just to play this game. Every other modern game in 2017 looks beautiful and runs smooth and at much better framerates with my current hardware :/
My specs are above the recommended specs for the game. So are the recommended specs just trying to achieve 20fps or something? I don't see how a 3.2ghz processor with a r9 280 would achieve even 30fps given my results. I am forced to go below 900p to get a little better fps with SSAO turned on. I can get 35fps with SSAO this way. To get a steady 55-60fps, I had to turn everything down or off, but then the game looks like it came out 10 years ago :/ Honestly, even with the "high" settings, it looks like a game that came out 10 years ago.
There's also a problem with the lightning and saturation - it makes everything look like it has a blurry yellow-ish white applied to it. It's like someone's boosting the contrast or saturation way too much, and it looks terrible.
The task manager says the game is only using 30-35% cpu utilization. That is a serious bummer that it cannot use more to help it out. All cores are checked in the affinity section.
I just think games released in 2017 should look good and run well at 1080p with a 2 year old computer. It should be optimized that these computers get 45-60fps out of the box for a given hardware profile. I get the impression that this game was built to only look good on Ultra settings and at 4k, but you need a 1080 Ti to see it. It just doesn't look as good as Warhammer 1. The difference is pretty massive. The game looks like crap at 1080p or lower.
As a test, I did a blind test with a friend so he could tell me which game was the better looking game, and he picked Total War: Warhammer 1 instantly. He thought Warhammer 2 was the older game. I am not joking.
I am one seriously frustrated girl trying to play Warhammer 2 in the same way I used to play Warhammer 1 graphically and fps-wise, but I can't. What else can I do? I am disappointed and I have no idea what to do. The game just isn't enjoyable with all the stuttering on the campaign map. The vortex is the worst. It's really bothering me, and I just don't want to play it anymore.
A lot of my time spent in the game hasn't been playing it, but it's been messing with the settings and running benchmarks constantly, and being alt-tabbed as I research ways to fix it.
CA really needs to stop releasing games so quickly and get to work on optimizating their engines, and rewriting them to take advantage of modern hardware. You should not need bleeding-edge clockspeeds just to brute force away the performance problems. I have 3 other cores to use! I do not recommend this game if you don't have a 1080-series card.

This was the roguelike experience I was looking for: each class plays differently, every enemy has different behavior, changing equipment requires tradeoffs, and most decisions are tricky. Unfortunately, it feels like the first chapter of something, not a full $10+ game. I beat it in five hours. I will probably revisit it with the different characters, but the gorgeous art and forced story can't make up for lack of content -- not at that price.

At first glance, it seems like a nice, pretty rogue-like game and you will probably be addicted to it for several hours, until you realize that there really isn't that much content in the game. The only "quests" that you receive are basically just "go to the next level and defeat the boss", nothing more. The villagers that you 'rescue' or acquire from clearing the levels have absolutely no impact on the game. They are just trophies who wander aimlessly in your village, walking on water and spouting nonsense. There's a moderate amount of classes to choose from, which is nice, but some are clearly outshined by others. For example, the vampire is a pretty weak class compared to the wizard who is extremely powerful compared to the rest. Each class has the exact same equipment, which I can only chalk up to laziness.
I was fascinated by the game at first until I realized all of these points mentioned above. I like rogue-like games, but this game honestly needs some polishing. As far as I know, there's not even a Hard difficulty setting, only Easy and Normal. I don't hate the game, but I probably won't be clearing all stages with all classes after beating the game, since it has gotten redundant by now.
Here are my suggestions as to how the game could be improved:
- Make class equipment more unique. Seriously, it's pretty lame to have every character with a weapon that shoots fire or freezes enemies. It shouldn't take much creativity to come up with something less generic.
- More difficulty settings. I'm a sucker for unfair challenge, and I can never understand when game developers don't implement a brutal, hard difficulty option in their games. It shouldn't be a difficult task and it will surely please hardcore gamers.
- REDO THE VILLAGE. I don't even want to look at it, it's hideous. Aside from the villagers being pointless drones walking around (on water I might add, for some inexplicable reason), the quest system serves no purpose either. If you're gonna have a quest system in your game, MAKE ACTUAL QUESTS and not just a pointer saying that I have to kill the evil mushrooms in the next level, which is the only thing I can do anyway!
This could be a good game if it was more polished and had more content and effort put into it, but as it stands now, I wouldn't recommend it, especially not for 15€.

I first need to state that this game was one of my early childhood games so it could be that my review is not entirely unbiased but I will try to keep it as objectively as possible.
Emergency 4 or 911: First Responders is - as you will now hopefully know - a real time strategy game in which you take complete control over the fire brigade, the police, the ambulance and technical services. That means that you cannot simply pause, give commands and then let it all work out. Though there is a pause button, you can only move around and do nothing else when it is activated. Before getting into more details, I have to say that buying this game on Steam has the following disadvantage that the Deluxe Edition is not included. Therefore, you will not have a second map to choose from in freeplay and three deluxe missions will not be playable. Furthermore, this is the american version of the game so the cars themselves won't have the original German names on them but rather big, not as fitting English general ones. (That is just a minor detail and I don't think anyone will be bothered that)
The Campaign in Emergency 4 consists of 20 missions that follow this vague pattern: There will be a little animation followed by an information text about what has happened and what you will need to do. Then you will try to master the tasks at hand while mostly at some point one or more surprising events occur that make the mission even more difficult. After completing one you will be taken to a freeplay-like map in which you have to take care of random day to day missions in that city until you can buy some special vehicle, equipment or training so you can go on to the next mission.
Whilst every mission is fairly manageable, completing all of them with 90-100% (i.e. noone died, personnel and property damage have been mostly avoided, budget and time are okay) is going to be extremely difficult. You will have to do way more stuff on all fronts at once than you can handle but thus the reward was for me even more satisfying when I scored a relatively high percentage.

When you've decided to play freeplay you are presented with two options: Endless Game and Challenge Mode. On both you will be thrown into a city where random events will occur that you will have to deal with by controlling again all 4 services at hand. The difference between these modes being that on the first, events will be completely random whilst on the second, things will start off relatively easy and will get harder the longer you play.
This mode has been for me quite a nice option to waste time on when I am bored or when I want to do something trivial when watching something else but after 40-60 minutes things will mostly get repetitive.
Therefore, I highly recommend the usage of mods (which there are plenty of) and as a newcomer I'd start with the easiest to use and the most famous one: The Los Angeles Mod.
The Gameplay definitely isn't for everyone. You will need to control every single unit individually, they will not put out fires, treat patients or follow criminals themselves no matter how close they are (except the doctor who will run towards the next injured person when he is out of the vehicle). To give an example of this: There have been reports of a fire nearby and you naturally sent a fire truck. Once you've sent it there, you will need to tell the firemen to get out of the vehicle, then make them equip i.e. a hose, connect it to the truck (or a hydrant) and then tell each of them which fire to put out. To be fair, they are going to put out fires around them once they have connected their hozes but only to a certaint degree.
So you can imagine that dealing with everyone individually will be extremely hard and chaotic when you have events everywhere which all need your attention but that is the core of the game. You will be stressed alot, trying to maintain control at all fronts.
Overall, if you are searching for a game like this choose Emergency 4. I haven't tested all of the other ones but based on their review rate compared to this one it is fair to say that the 4th part of this series is definitely the best one with a huge modding community so it shall never get bored.

VODKA is what happens when you make a joke game but put actual effort in and don't just hide behind the idea of it being "satire".
This developer understands that a proper satirical, joke game should still offer gameplay value and a degree of fun for the player. Otherwise you simply release trash that is a huge waste of time.
VODKA is a rogue-lite bullet hell game where you control a ship that fires vodka at a variety of space ships, which I guess were sent from the USA for some reason. Cool, this actually sounds like a real game.
The gameplay is fairly simple, you shoot things, collect coins and sometimes upgrades. At the end of each level you can use your coins to refill health, ammo or upgrade your ship.
Every few levels there is a boss battle which turns you into another character for some reason. The boss battles are the most difficult part of the game and are what caused my runs to end. The other levels seem much easier, but they are still mildly enjoyable.
The artstyle is done very well in VODKA. The game has a great retro effect, not only in the pixel art, but also with some nice color overlays on the screen to simulate playing on an old T.V or arcade monitor. The game looks good in general.
The music is also pretty good. Nothing incredibly special but it's got a proper theme and didn't get annoying while looping.
My biggest issue with the game is that it's not very clear what items do in most circumstances. For instance, pickles will increase your health, but there is no indicator so you need to figure it out for yourself. There are also pickle enemies in the game so it made it more confusing. It's not a game-breaker by any means but it could be much more clear.
Overall, VODKA is pretty solid for what it is and should be seen as a standard for joke-oriented games.

The short version is that this game is better than I expected, but far worse than it could be.
The Division is decently optimised, I rarely get frame drops on my 1080ti except in very specific areas. I also get a 1-2 second freeze every 30 minutes or so for no apparent reason. The world is beautiful too, you can tell it has been crafted delicately. The story is surprisingly interesting too for an MMO and really feels like a singleplayer story. Whilst the game obviously has some great features going for it, there are some inherent issues with the game I'd like to address.
Honestly, after hearing people talk crap about this game over the past 2 years I am genuinely amazed at how well made this is. The thing is, whilst the actual 'game' is good, the gameplay is not. The end game content is sorely lacking. I reached max level and max item level in 2 days. Now the only things left to do is nitpick over which piece of gear isn't perfectly optimal and run the horribly unbalanced PvP modes that can take 20+ minutes to queue for. Once you hit item level 256 every upgrade you get is miniscule. There is extremely rare classified gear but those are too and far between. One thing I don't understand is why they didn't make it harder to get to 256 ilevel so that players with better gear actually appear to have a higher item level rather than everyone at max level being the same.
Don't get me wrong, as I said the game has many things going for it, but longevity is not one of them unless you really force yourself to nitpick over your gear. This is the type of game where a casual player can make a character, get to level 30 in 10 hours then max out their gear over the next 10 hours. For a game, 20 hours isn't bad, for an MMO, 20 hours is god awful. It really depends on how you look at it. You can indeed get more than that out of it, but the average player wont.
Oh and you may think, "Hey I'll get this game and once I get to the point this guy is talking about I'll just do PvP." Well maybe it's just the games I got into, but PvP simply wasn't fun. Everyone in the PvP modes are the people I mentioned earlier who have spent the last 6+ months nitpicking over each piece of gear and can shred you before you can even react. I don't hate the PvP in Division, but I in no way consider it fun enough to be worth recommending, especially considering the other flaws in the game.
One of the game's other main issues is that a lot of the end game content is just balanced poorly and honestly feels like it was made by someone who has never played the game. All of the end game raids (incursions) feel like they were created by some interns for a school project. Whilst playing each of them I genuinely started to dislike the game more and more which is a shame. Some content is insanely difficult to solo, but the second you have a team with you, it becomes an absolute pushover. Others are just insanely hard no matter what and require specific cheesy strategies to complete which completely removes your ability to play the way you want. Multiple people on your team will be forced into using skills they don't want to use.
As far as non-raid level content went, there didn't appear to be any scaling at all and there were no buffs for playing solo. In a group the enemies damage is essentially quartered (if not more due to abilities) and if you go down a teammate will instantly get you back up. I constantly felt myself getting bored due to lack of enemies to kill. We'd all kill 1-3 enemies each then we'd move on to the next area. In the other side of the spectrum, if you try to solo the same content, the enemies will rush you very quickly and killing them all in time is often impossible before they are on top of you. Put it like this, the content in this game is either so easy that you can solo it mindlessly or so difficult that you don't even want to do it because it will take so many attempts and you can get screwed over by the smallest, uncontrollable factors.
Conclusion: Only play this are happy with a beautiful singleplayer game with a shallow multiplayer endgame. Do not go into this expecting something you can no-life for weeks unless you're the type of person who enjoys obsessing over tiny details to perfect a build. This is the type of game that a casual player would enjoy for a week or two before moving on to something else. I did have fun with it but once the flaws started to show themselves I found myself losing interest. I do still play the game but like I said, most people will not enjoy the end game grind for miniscule improvements to gear.

Game is nice to look at and the enviroment looks great but like with many Ubisoft titles the gameplay portion is basically phoned in. Very few of the great looking environments are actually great places to have gunfights in, many devolving into simple cover-studded pipes with no flanks to cover or take.
The basic gameplay is also creatively bankrupt, having you collect guns and gear with bigger numbers so you can shoot bigger numbers at a variety of human opponents who take ever increasing amounts of numbers directly to the face to go down. There are some interesting mechanics in play to make combat slightly varied and at rare times there's almost a glint of brilliance, but that is often dispelled as you get back to emptying magfulls of ammo into the next opponent's head to kill them.
Probably the worst of all is how the game handles multiplayer, something the game was supposedly built around yet comes off as a complete afterthought. The more people you have on your team, the more mags must be emptied into heads to knock them off. Technically this should just mean that 4 people shoot and kill the thing together instead of alone, but in practice this means 4 people are shooting at various things which now take literally hundreds of bullets to kill. The most damning thing I can really say about The Division is that it's a multiplayer game where the best game experience you'll ever get is playing strictly solo.
This game isn't completely without merit though so if it's current price point is low enough to be pocket change for you, you might want to check it out. Otherwise, save your money for something better.

If difficult video games with retro aesthetics are your jam, then Downwell is an instant pick. If either of these things are turn-offs to you, maybe not. At just over a dollar, Downwell was worth the price for me, even if I can't beat the third area for the life of me.

I consider games "great" when they leave nothing to be desired, Downwell is one of those cases.  The game moves at such a breakneck pace, I love how I can pick it up, play it for 15 minutes, and still get a complete and fulfilling experience.
In the vein of roguelikes, there are multiple, randomly-generated gunboots (with either a Health or Charge bonus) that you can find littering in caves, which constantly alters your playstyle and keep you on your toes.  There are also upgrades that give you various buffs, and while there are only a few of them compared to other roguelikes, I at least see it as being unlikely for me to get screwed by a bad streak, in fact nothing in the game made me think I had horrible luck.
As for replay value, there are multiple palettes to collect and a Hard Mode.
Again, I really had nothing to complain about, it's great for short sessions and to unwind.

Fast paced and easy to learn. It's great for short sessions though not too sure of it's payment method at the moment. For some context, I got this game from the Humble Monthly Bundle like what I assume a good few others.
In short it's a tower defense game with cards as your attackers. You can choose a hero to play which give certain abilities or buff as the round progresses. You send out troops that take control of the bridge between you and the opponent to gain exp for your hero. Your goal is to manage to break though your opponents defenses and have your troops attack the enemy's hero. The stronger the card, the more the cost to use them. From what I can tell from my a bit over a hour play, it's kinda balanced. They set you up with a few challenging solo enemies at the start which after defeating a few, gives you a reward of having a chance to get better monsters. My time in online play was pleasing as well. I lost but the reasoning why I lost was easy to understand. You see, the hero he got is able to to revive monsters after he gets enough exp to do so. He's monsters were mostly low in cost and they eventually out numbered me and soon enough out powered me. I was able to put up a fight for a while but in the end, my lack of realization for his plan cost me and I lost the game. Yes, I lost... by getting Zerg rushed. It was interesting to see what other strategies can come about with similar monsters but a different hero. All in all, a fun game.
So where does the RNG fall in? Well mostly in the card you can draw in. As far as I can tell, they don't seem too unbalanced since the stronger monsters are harder to bring out anyway. I guess an issue you can face is that if you need a type of monster (ranged, melee, or building) it's up to RNG to decide it for you. There are some RNG in the rounds themselves though but only a minor one. Most the monsters you summon. Like mentioned before, there is the use of card. A bad hand can give you a bad day but it's also how you utilize your monsters and how you set up your deck.
So like I mentioned before, I got this on a bundle. So you view on it price-wise is a little biased. That said, for a game you pay for it, seems to rely a bit on micro-payments. As of writing this, the game is on early access so I don't know if it will stay this way or the game will become a free to play later on but at least if you got it around the time I wrote this review, you get a free DLC which gives you a lot of the paid currency and some boost in exp and such. The amount given is quite a lot and you can easily purchase a hero you like, a map/arena you like and even some chances to get some new monsters. I haven't the need to use any of the paid currency at this time and the card and the heroes on rotation seem to do me alright. So as of now, the payment method is particularly unfair but it is something you should consider when buying this game.
The game is fun. Nothing about it is too offensive, it seems balanced and the strategies you can utilize make it a challenge in higher levels. It's pretty cheap as well though depending on how the developers go through the game (making f2p or keep their current model) it might be fair to consider a price drop before making any rash decisions. All in all, not bad.

I am a fan of Warhammer and of Turn Based Strategy games... So for me this is just Beautiful!
Pros:
Fantastic visuals, unit management, attention to detail, packed full of lore, very accurate to the brand, very true to the Total War series, great battle maps with impressive landscapes, overall extremely enjoyable and engrossing.
Pros:

I must say, since the trend of terribly released Total War games like Attila and Rome II, CA has brought this franchise back to life with the Warhammer Fantasy series.
First off, don't be ignorant and not play the game at all since its not a historically based Total War. I feel the same way about the first game and when I got it I absolutely hated it, but as time grew and I played more and more of the campaign the game began to grow on me. Please give this game a try or the first one a try.
Let's get into specfics now, I will first talk about bigger stuff like the campaign, multiplayer and factions. Then at the end I'll focus on stuff like UI, graphics and performace.
First let's talk about campaign the bread and butter for every total war game. So what's different from the first game? Well the map, it's huge, and with mortal empires it's even bigger. The Campaign alone can be up to 1000 hours in gameplay. New campaign mechanics? Let's start off with rituals. They are another way of playing the campaign. You can choose to either weaken the vortex (the giant spinning hurricane that protects the realm) or protect it. Its a nicely added victory game mechanic, that helps progress any stalemates. There also rites, now don't get them confused with rituals, these "rites" give you global buffs like public order, troop replenishment, and experience. These seem to be the only new campaign features that seem new and fresh others are just improved from the first game, which is alright. Though one con to this game is that the map is mostly water, and sea battles are all auto resolve. Note this game does not have playable sea battles. Thats my only con towards the campaign.
Next the factions. With the first game we had several different unique factions, and here we have four new and unique factions. The question is are they worth they worth the sixty dollars, the anwser is yes. The Dark Elves, High Elves, Lizardmen and Skaven. Let's start with the skaven, the skaven to me are a bit reminiscent to the factions in Medieval 2 where units can route rather quickly if you are outflanked or charged by cavalry. They are also a rather fast factions (like the units are actually really fast) they maybe very vulnerable to flanks, but yet ironically it can be their greatest weapon. In campaign they are a fast expending faction with a unique food based system that allows you to build higher tier settlements, also in addition to that all their settlements are hidden, as in they appear on the campaign map as razed settlements. Next come the Lizardmen a very strong factions with high morale, great monsterous units, and generals. This faction focuses mostly on flanking and using its cheaper spear units with high health pools as meat shields. In campaign they are slightly less slower than the skaven, but can field really powerful units rather quickly in campaign which can make them into a powerhouse early on. In addition, they receive more powerful "blessed units" in campaign which is a nice touch also. Next come the High Elves, a factions that focuses on elite units and powerful heroes to win battles. The High Elves have a rather slow and sluggish style of play, since their best units are rather expensive, and come later in the campaign than most other factions. They also have unique campaign mechanic known as influence which can be used to recruit amazing generals or improve relations with other factions. Lastly, we have the Dark Elves who are really built around their unique ability "murderous prowess" which makes any of their units just as good as the next with that ability active. Their unique campaign abilities involve summoning a massive ship known as a black ark very good in the early phases of the campaign.
In terms of multiplayer, yes multiplayer is fun, Free for all battles are way better in this than Medieval II, since they implemented scores of each player based on damage and kills. Factions are all equally balanced as each have counters to each other. One main complaint this game gets from people is that this game has zero strategic value. In my opinion that's just people being ignorant. In my opinion this game has probably the most strategic value than its predecessors. There are many strategies one can employ on this game compared to other Total War titles. For instance in Rome II, when I played online nine times out of ten if someone played barbs they would sword rush or in Medieval 2 multiplayer which was just cavalry spam since people would always love to fill up their slots with the eight cavalry of their choosing. Nonetheless, Warhammer II is game in which strategy varies game to game. And there is Magic! Yes Magic! One thing traditional Total War players like myself hate, but as time went by, I began to like magic. Since Magic prevented blobing and helped prevent flanks or stop stalemates. Magic in my opinion added a lot more of this "strategic value" people talk about. If you want to play this game competitively online please play a campaign first or even play a few skrimishes before hoping into ranked multiplayer, since the game can be very hard to learn.
In conclusion, the UI is new and freshly polished perhaps the best UI I've seen so far in any Total War game to date. Graphics are very good, the game is absolutely beautiful on Ultra. Lastly, in terms performance this game is not very good. YOU NEED HIGH SPECS TO PLAY THIS GAME. More recent Total War games usually need high specs, it is no different from this one this game is very graphically demanding if you want to play on the highest of qualities.
Please give this game a try and you won't regret it. To veteran Total War players who prefer the more historic titles, please also try this game out and try to approach it with an open mind, this game is a very great Total War title and is worthy of praise. Thank you for reading.
