They call it a roguelike but it didn't necessarily feel like one to me.  Here's why:
1) If you die you're right back on your feet and you simply just 'failed' your mission.
2) Death has little or nothing to do with the progress you've currently obtained in terms of unlocks.  You keep all of your upgrades you have purchased, all of your gold, all of your unlocked characters and all of your unlocked inventory.
That said, I really enjoy the game.  I like that it's nice to me.
The enemies don't move unless you move which is similar to something like Crypt of the Necromancer so long as you're on the beat (However, there is no "beat" in Sproggiwood.  It's your own pacing).  Enemies have different attack patterns and some enemies even leave hazards that need to be avoided.
You unlock different classes which all feel different to play in terms of everything beyond the melee combat.  The thief can swap spots with enemies or leave traps down whereas the farmer just flat out places a bomb or throws his melee weapon along with a heal.  The knight has a circular swipe, a charge, and a move to tank damage.
If you find a weapon in the dungeon it'll be available for purchase (in-game cash, no microtransactions) back in your town.
I haven't put a ton of time into it yet so I haven't seen everything but I've seen enough to recommend it.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I’ll break this review down by Environment, Story, and Gameplay.
Environment: I don’t know anything about Warhammer 40,000, but the world and character design in this game really give you a sense of what this universe is like. I found myself several times just looking around at how cool the backdrops are and how massive everything is. The graphics are very solid and I found little glitching, leading to a rich aura as you slaughter everything evil. Super polished and immersive. 9/10
Story: The story seemed to be divided into two halves; the first slow half and the second intriguing half. The story in the first half of the game seemed to be dragging, but once it hits a certain point it defiantly makes you want to keep playing to see how it all concludes. The characters seemed to be really cool and gave you insight into the whole attitude of the ultra-marines. The villains and Orcs are done well enough and the story seem to have a solid twist. 7/10
Gameplay: This was by far the game’s biggest blight. I loved the violence and gore that you are able to achieve threw hack and slash play, but they entire first half of the game is simply that. There is little variation from this model which makes the game get very tiresome after the first 30 minutes. Coupled with a dry first half of the storyline, the game is kind of challenging to keep playing. I was defiantly board after the first hour. The game also seems to have a very limited number of enemies. Later in the game, you can defiantly tell you’re fighting reskinned versions of early sprites with maybe a tweak. With the addition of more weapons, the game does get some variety in tactical gameplay, but I kind of felt like it was too little too late. 4/10
Overall, I’d give the game a solid B-. The story is ok, environment is beautiful, but play is boring a repetitive. If you’re a 40k fan, Id say you’ll love it, but for a normal gamer I’d only pick this up if you like just slaughtering everything in melee combat.

If you are attracted to the historical period known as "the Age of Sail," this game is for you.  The art work of the game is excellent.  The sailing conditions are realistic and challenging.  For newcomers, there exists a wealth of material to help one get started in the game.  Everyone begins with a basic ship which is free and the fastest ship in the game.  Money is important and hard to comeby early in the game so don't be too much in a hurry to buy better ships.  Save your money until you can afford to purchase a Snow which is the first good ship you to which you will have access.  The game is absorbing and challenging.  Thinking through alternatives and making good decisions in light of long term consequences are both rewarded by this game.  Investing in in-port resouces which can be used to build your own ships or ship parts is another way of increasing your income.  Fighting ship to ship battles is important in successful game advance but picking the proper battles to fight is even more important.  In short, this is a game that rewards critical thinking, good decision making, and long range planning but allows players to recover from mistakes made.  The game can be adapted to a number of game-playing styles.  The developers listen to and respond to suggestions by the game membership and are continuously adding to the game on a monthly basis.  If my review sounds interesting to you, I strongly recommend you give this game a try.

First it should be pointed out that this game is not for everyone. In my opinion that is one of it's strong points, because it is anything but a standard MMO. Many have listed as a flaw the slow pace of the game but if you have knowledge of the time period then you know that it would take upwards of 30 minutes to tack a large sailing ship, and their top speed was nearly 20 miles per hour! Battles would not be won in a few short minutes but would take hours to conclude. Historical accuracy is a vanguard of this beautifully rendered game, and the screen shots you see posted are not cut scenes but actual game play shots. As a ship modeler I am continually amazed by the ships this game offers, and it reads like a list from a Model Expo catalog: Fair American, Alert, Onterio, Rattlesnake, Constitution, Victory. To see these majestic ships in three dimensions spreading their sails and heeling to a stiff breeze is a source of endless enjoyment for me.
It is not an easy game to play; the cannons are as inaccurate as they would be historically, the ships must be sailed in combat and not mearly turned about by the rudder and the risk of getting caught in irons, where you cannot move or turn while the enemy is mercilessly raking your stern is a real concern. 2 game modes cater to the casual gamer and the hard core alike, with PVE for the former and PVP for the later. A system for trade and ship crafting adds another dimension for those not content with fighting.
"Aye, tear her tatteren ensign down, long has it waved on high, and many an eye has danced to see that banner in the sky..." If you reccognize this as the opening lines of the poem 'Old Ironsides' by Oliver Wendell Holmes then then you must, no you need to buy this game.

At time of writing Naval Action is still in its early access alpha phase. So if you start to play this you have to come in with the right mind set. It's not finished and things are are changed around and tweaked by the developers all the time. New stuff is also being added, for example national diplomacy just went in.
Ok so assuming you are happy to run with the alpha state of the game what are you getting? Well it is what it says on the tin. 18th Century sailing ships ( plus or minus a few decades ) sailing round the carribean doing their thing. You pick a nation when you initially load up and that is locked ( you used to be able to become a pirate inside the game but im not sure if thats still the case after the last patch). The various nations have been perpetually at war taking and retaking each others ports for the last few months, unofficial alliances created by the larger of the games clans held or didnt, we'll have to see how the new diplomacy meta game changes things.
The game itself is beautiful, you wont be disapointed with how it looks. My rig is pretty awesome at the moment top end and under 6 months old but my last machine was a few years old and still ran things at a good frame rate and with quality settings. The ship models are nicely crafted and you can tell the artist/s have howned their techniques over the years as the newer ones are looking decidedly nicer than the first ships that came out. This is mostly in the texture work though and I'm 100% sure upgrade work is on the backlog.
Ship to Ship combat is handled on an instanced basis. You sail along in the Open World, tag your target and head into an instance to fight. I was initially quite disappointed with this approach but got used to it it. There are pro's and con's to it but it is what it is. The combat itself is the most involved and worked on part of the game, once you get your head round the initial mechanics it one of those easy to learn hard to master things. Same goes for sailing ( in the instances ). You need to use both rudder and sail direction to aid your turning through the wind.
In fact everything Naval Action does it does very well. You may not like a particual direction the developers have decided to take something but they will have done a good job of it. Problem with Naval Action ( if it is indeed a problem ) is the stuff they haven't done. If you came at this game after playing something like Assassins Creed Black Flag ( like I did ) then you will be disappointed with no avatars. Theres no walking around your ships, or getting out and exploring islands, boarding is handled in a very simplistic UI manner. To be honest i can't see this sort of thing ever changing. They are too small a team and the cost implications of doing full on character art/animation/traversable enviroments are so unbelievably massive that they will never be able to do these things. It's a shame but it doesnt spoil the game they have made, it would just have made it more utterly amazing!
But if you set your expectations to the right level, read around the reviews, check out the official forums. If you have an interest in the period and sailing then i think you will enjoy this game. Make sure you ask questions in the various chat channels, people are usually very helpful and willing to show new players the ropes.

Imagine any of the recent Lego video games, then imagine it was solely open world and you just sort of did your own thing.    That's basically Lego World in a nutshell.   You explore, and as you touch certain objects/characters/animals/whatever, you then learn them and can later re-create them out of thin air.  Sort of like creative mode in Minecraft with about a thousand times more ease and speed.
A lot of people here are lamenting the lack of multiplayer and saying that this will make or break the game for them, but I have to say...it's is EXTREMELY doubtful there will be any form of multiplayer simply because of the issue of controlling what content kids will see.  Lego shut down Lego Universe because the costs of moderating it were growing beyond control and I seriously doubt they will put their seal on anything they cannot fully control.  All it takes is a few kids' parents getting upset their children saw a giant lego dong in someone's world, and you have a "controversy" and PR disaster on your hands.   If I'm wrong, then great...but I suspect there will never be any meaningful multiplayer.
That said, as a single player game eve, this is a lot of goofy fun and very much in the spirit of the other Traveller's Tale games out there right now.   This will be great on console.

'Minion Masters' developed and published by 'BetaDwarf', is a fun and fast-paced strategy game. The game requires you to think on your feet, while still being quite casual, which is something I particularly enjoy, being someone who mostly plays games for fun and not competitively overall.
When I first took a look at the game, I thought based on the screenshots it would play out a lot like Hearthstone or Clash Royale, however after playing it, I can say that the game is very different from what I originally had in mind, and the experience was much more wholesome than what I thought it would provide.
The game feels well-balanced, and even after playing against players who had the premium DLC, I didn't feel like I was at a major disadvantage. I see many people who got the game for free complaining about that, which I think is a bit silly otherwise the developers wouldn't be able to capitalize off the product at all, which would mean less time put into the game, which would mean a less wholesome expereince, which isn't what anybody wants.
I think that the price-tag is slightly steep, but chances are if you don't like the game you'll realize it soon enough to refund it, because the rounds played are quite fast, and usually only take around 15-20 minutes, but that also may come off a bit bias since I did receive the product for free. Other than that, I don't have any major problems with the game, it's fun, and my only real complaint is that I wish I would've had more time to play during the beta stages, the servers weren't up very often, but I don't see that really being a problem in the future unless maitnence checks become prevalent.

Sproggiwood Review
PS: 10/10

Ah, a new day, a new roguelike. This time I’m reviewing FreeHold Games’ Sproggiwood. The title suggests we’re dealing with a more mildly roguelike here, but is that really true ? After all, looks can be deceiving. Continue reading and you’ll find my conclusion right here, in just a few minutes time:
Sproggiwood is a story-driven roguelike with turn-based gameplay. It has a bright presentation, unlike many other games in this genre, which is a bit surprising, but not unique.
You begin the game as a simple farmer and within minutes after starting the game you step through a portal that transports you to the land of Sproggiwood. Here begins your quest to thwart the spirit Sproggi’s plans by joining a rival civilization, or… you can choose to keep Sproggiwood all to yourself.
Sproggi will give you quests that you have to complete in order to be able to make progress. Each level has a quest and it speaks for itself that all of these levels are randomized, like what we’ve come to expect from the roguelikes of the last couple of years.
Each level lets you travel through several floors. The last floor usually has a boss fight. Getting there requires both skill and luck. Thankfully, you can improve your luck by purchasing better gear or upgrades. You see, killing enemies will earn your both experience and gold, and smashing pots and opening chests will also earn you money (and let’s not forget the random items).
After each game you can go to town to buy new gear or to upgrade your stats, like gaining more experience for killing enemies. These items usually come at a hefty price and you usually have to play a couple of times before you’re even able to purchase something worthwhile. But after that the game becomes a bit easier, if only for a little while, because the next quest will be even harder, take it from me. Weapons and other items like scrolls and potions are unlocked by smashing pots, by the way. Note that you won’t be able to purchase anything in the town before you’ve unlocked/found it during a game. After that it’s being added to the town inventory for you to purchase.
As I already mentioned killing enemies will also earn you experience that allows you to level up. There are four skills to unlock and each one has several stages. For example, there’s a skill to throw a pitchfork in front of you. The second stage allows you to throw it both backward and forward and the third stage lets you throw it in all directions. Because each stage gives you a better opportunity at killing your foes you can’t unlock them right after each other. I’m not sure but I think you have to level up two or three times before you’re able to select the next stage. This makes sense because it pushes you forward, always looking for more enemies that you can kill.
If you’re able to successfully finish a quest you’ll be able to buy a town upgrade. In this case it’s usually a building that unlocks a new class you can play with. The town itself has no real function but you can design it yourself by placing buildings, trees and roads. Completing quests will also add villagers to your town. They can say random (useless) stuff, but they can also tell you more about the (back)story. Overall, this is a fun addition that isn’t really needed in a game like this, but I can appreciate it nevertheless.
All in all, the game can be pretty unforgiving, despite its looks. Don’t think you’re dealing with an easier game here because it might be a tad easier; it’s still bloody difficult at times.
The game has a very cartoony and charming look. Above all, it’s beautiful, colorful and sharp and looks just magnificent in motion.
The interface isn’t all that intuitive and it takes some getting used to, but once you get the hang of it it works perfectly fine. Still, it could use a little work.
There isn’t any real music except for a track that plays whenever you enter a dungeon. It’s limited, but what’s there is good enough. The sounds play a bigger part here and they do the job just fine. They all supplement the game nicely.
The game can last quite a while. I haven’t been able to finish it, but let’s say you could spend 10-15 hours here and still not be done with it. It also depends on your luck and skills, so it’s a hard thing to say, but as you can see you get plenty of bang for your buck.
Sproggiwood is a great roguelike that tries to add some new stuff to the formula. It only partially succeeds in doing this, however. But let it be clear that it definitely has its heart in the right place. It was clearly made with passion, you can tell by the fact that it tried something new.
The final product has become a polished and fun game. Newcomers to the genre will definitely have a blast with this and even veteran roguelike players will have a very good time with it, guaranteed.

This is a fantastic game that is well worth the money (during one of Relic's annual sales). A must-have for any Warhammer 40k fan, as it continues Relic's tradition of trying to be as accurate as possible to the feel and spirit of the 40k universe.
The gameplay is a good balance between third-person shooting and melee combat. It is challenging while still making you feel like the superhuman killing machine you are. It has a good variety of weapons, including bolters, plasma guns, lascannons, and melta weapons for ranged, and chainswords, power axes, and even thunderhammers for melee. My favorite combo is a jump pack with a thunderhammer, which allows you to smash the God-Emperor's enemies with the necessary amount of righteous fury.
The music and sound design was surprisingly good, with very good sound quality and an appropriately epic tone. It has some fantastic setpieces for the levels, like giant cathedrals and bridges decked out by the Adeptus Mechanicus. In general, it has very high production values and stays true to the lore.
It had me truly awestruck at times, as I am a huge fan of the 40k universe and have read tons of the books, but even people new to the franchise should appreciate the grand scale of it all.
Get it as soon as it goes on sale.

I don't really know anything about Warhammer, so I can't comment on whether or not Space Marine is faithful to the source material. What I can say is that Space Marine is a good game, and I enjoyed playing it. Even though its a few years old, it still compares favourably to newer games in some ways.
Gameplay is really fun. Its a fast paced third person shooter where you're constantly fighting dozens of enemies at a time. There's a decent mix of short and long range weapons, and a few different enemy types. In some sections you fight alongside two other space marines, and their AI is surprisingly helpful. I tended to hang back and use the two variations of sniper rifle, and my allies actually did a good job of keeping melee enemies out of my face.
After about an hour you unlock a "fury" meter, which is filled by damaging enemies, and when activated will increase your damage output while regenerating your health, which is really useful in tough fights. There are also a couple of sections where you get a jetpack and a massive, powerful warhammer, which allows you to jump high in the air to avoid enemies, then smash down on them for an AOE attack that will either kill or stun a group of enemies.
Level design is entirely linear, and this means the game is also quite short. I finished it in just under 6.5 hours, on normal difficulty. It would have benefited from having a few side paths containing optional objectives.
The story is okay, but fairly basic. The Orcs are attacking a Human world, and Captain Titus of the Ultramarines (that's you) is trying to stop them. It gets a bit more interesting about halfway through when something happens that I don't want to spoil. But it never really gets any deeper than "the enemy is over there, go shoot them". However, it does have a fun, ridiculous, over the top but not too serious atmosphere. And it really feels like you're caught up in the middle of a massive war, with other battles in progress around you.
As a player who is new to the Warhammer universe, I would have liked a bit more detail so I could properly understand the story. There's lots of jargon, technical terms and faction names such as "codex astartes", "inquisitor" and "psyker" and it seems like the developers just assume that the player is already familiar with the lore. (One of the reasons that I decided to play this game is that there seems to be alot of Warhammer games coming out these days, so I want to try to learn what its all about).
The voice acting is pretty good, and features an experienced TV/film actor Mark Strong as Captain Titus. Controls are fully rebindable and I didn't encounter any bugs.
I definitely recommend picking up Warhammer 40K Space Marine, and you should be able to grab it on a 75% off deal during one of Steam's many sales.

I highly recommend this game as it has amazing co-op. Be warned however, this game does not hold your hand. It can be very unforgiving especially if you do not save often. There is no tutorial which makes the learning curve quite steep. Divinity's challenge comes in part from its robust combat system. One example is lightning magic, and how it reacts to weather effects and standing "water" such as puddles or the pooling blood of your foes and allies. Having the "wet" status effect also makes you more vulnerable to frost magic. The use of frost magic contributes to altering the battlefield which allows for enemies and friendlies to be knocked down. The game's numerous environmental factors force the player to always be on their toes; to change and adapt to suit the situation. A player can also have a great deal of fun with repeated run-throughs, trying different builds to attempt to exploit different mechanics of the combat system. You can potentially load the game if something goes wrong. Be aware the A.I. is not obliged to follow their previous pattern and your co-op partner may not have the patience having the perfect outcome. Keep in mind though the consequence of that is a much longer playthrough.

Throughout the game you are referred to as the Lone Wanderer, why... The Vault Overseer believes you had a part to play in the escape of your father from a fallout shelter known as Vault 101, which reportedly had been sealed for 200 years protecting those who lived there from the aftermath of the Great War.
At game start after your birth you get to pick what you will look like within the game. It then goes through your early years up to age 16 spent inside Vault 101.
As I have said the Overseer believes you helped your father to open the huge Vault door to the outside world and make good his escape. The only thing wrong about that is you are not guilty. However, The Overseer is not going to believe you, guilty or not, and sent his security force to arrest you. Faced with no other option and the help of the Overseers daughter you escape the vault and go in-search of James (your father).
This is where the game really begins. The Great War has left Washington, D.C. area in ruins. Among those ruins are the Capitol Building, the Jefferson Memorial, the battered remains of the Washington Monument and various museums all referred to as the Capital Wasteland.
Large settlements can be found throughout the area known as the Wastelands: Rivet City has been formed from the shell of an aircraft carrier carried and dumped far inland by high waters, now long gone. Other large settlements include the towns of Megaton, Arefu, Big Town, Canterbury Commons, Tenpenny Tower, The Republic of Dave and Paradise Falls and many others.
In the early stages of the game you get to these places on foot however, once you have found a place you can teleport back and forth between towns and any-where else you may uncover on what can be only called a Hugh map of places to visit.
Many of the places you visit in and around the Capitol Wasteland is in ruins with collapsed building barring you way to other parts of the same area, not to worry... to get round this use the DC Metro tunnels and be prepared to battle every step of the way. Ghoules and Feral Ghoules are humans turned psychotic from radiation. The Super Mutants are your main enemy along with the Enclave ruled by President John Henry Eden and his ruthless second-in-command Colonel Augustus Autumn.
There are others but, that would be what I would call a spoiler. On the good side (sort of) is the Brotherhood of Steel who have set-up shop in the ruins of the pre-War Pentagon known as the Citadel.
Your use of various weapons throughout the game degrade with use. Weapons of the same kind can be used to repair degraded weapons. Your stat's skill influences how much you can restore broken weaponry.
Real time combat can be stopped by the use of The Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System, or V.A.T.S. Some reviews say the game can not be completed without using V.A.T.S. hand on heart I played the game second time around in real time combat mode only.
There is so much more to this game than going around shooting monsters. The story line is excellent, the graphics are as real as they come (my opinion), quests to keep you busy for some time, and the nasties you meet along the way are just that... nasty...
The one in-game thing I thought was an excellent touch the use of Three Dog (Erik Todd Dellums) relaying your finished Quests over his radio station Galaxy Radio (most colorful) and not forgetting the chance to take to outer space and do battle there...
For me this game is top of my tree for realistic entertainment at its best, along with the Elder scrolls, Skyrim, Bioshock.
More Fallout would keep me happy and maybe the chance of a bigger quest around Oasis Spreading to the wasteland.

This is a message for the devs;
If you want this game to be successful, consider doing following:
+ Make towns guarded and implement a PK system as in Ultima Online. After a certain amount of innocent kills, players should be flagged as Player Killers and should not be allowed in guarded towns. Instead, they need to handle their stuff in unguarded towns.
This will alter the mentality behind playstyle and will make players think before taking action therefore giving a more realistic and tense experience which is essential for openworld pvp games. (First, put some towns to the game. Not 2x2 zones with 2 buildings where there's a complete zergfest). Also replace "stash" with "banks"
+ Remove all of the events and camps. Put dungeons where players can enter freely and farm stuff inside. (This will boost open world pvp both in front of  dungeon entrances and inside dungeons as well)
+ Fix the spike issue. You instantly go backwards from time to time. If this occurs when you try to pass through obstacles, polish it a little bit so we don't feel like we are pushed back from nowhere.
+ Add sound effects. Bow and spear should not sound the same.
+ Customizing and upgrading your character/build feels completely dumb. Make it more detailed and non-linear. Current system should  be completely removed.
+ Implement proper housing instead of donating resources to pre-built bases. Allow players and guilds to place houses anywhere in the world.
+ Produce new content after maintaining a proper and healthy infrastructure.
+ Full loot means looting items first, THEN resources and skills. Characters should equip more than 2 pieces of items and stat/skill balance should be re-arranged around that. Otherwise looting 20 pelts or 30 leather or 20+ skills from a player does not really feel rewarding even though it might be when current mechanics are considered.
I wont bother mentioning bugs in the ui when it comes to tracking events and stuff because I believe this game will perish in shorter than estimated without altering basic mechanics. Besides, there's a really nice concept with full loot, openworld pvp. I will give a thumbs up since the game's built by an indie company and I believe they're reasonable enough to consider what's best for their game.

I downloaded the game for the free weekend, have had lots of fun in both PVE and PVP, so was happy to spend £15 to own the game and keep playing.
I think i would prefer if I could give this an impartial review score rather than just thumbs up or thumbs down, as I completely understand the perspective of the negative reviews and agree with much of what they say.
For example, head shots should be one shot kills but they are not, which makes combat a mix bag between tactical realism (in the fictional computer game sense) and arcade. Most mobs are complete bullet soaks and you will often empty a whole clip into them before they go down and the mini bosses are even worse - they wear very little armour but are impervious to all weapons until you have expanded all ammo. This is a shame because the actual flow of combat and the control you have over your avatar is really good and overall I really enjoy the combat but a touch more realism and smarter AI (they will just stand there on occassion and let you shoot them) would vastly improve this.
Similarly there is the play area. New York is rendered in wonderful detail astehtically and is lovely to traverse through but you soon feel like you are on a film set as all the scenery is essentially painted on and is only interactive in small scripted doses. It is still a lovely set piece and with the in-game weather effects it looks great, it's just rather hollow. There are a smattering of NPC's wandering about (i still dont really understand why, the story is a bit foggy in my opinion)
Player progression works well mostly because of the changes you can make to your characters appearance. There are micro transactions for this (for a paid game!) but so far I have found enough asthetic items from drops that I have been able to give my character a unique look. The guns and items all look great and the weapons have weight and are punchy.
There are various skills and perks that open as you level up your character and your main base of operations (instanced per player). This area at least feels more alive than the rest of New York.
Missions so far seem a little samey and many dont make much sense. There are a plethora of hostage situations but no real motive behind it (this is, after all, a derilict city with no authority in control so who are the bad guys expecting to demand ransom from??) and many other generic, go there, grab this/kill them, missions that we've seen a million times in other games.
This all sounds quite negatve i know, but bare with me.
Where the game shines is in its overall polish and delivery of whats on offer. The environments are great, with good atmosphere (albeit rather linear), and running around in the snow always feels tense and exciting. The combat is loads of fun and in solo or group there is benefits to using tactics and skill. Multiplay is great, it is easy to find groups and all missions feel much more exciting when you are part of a group. Dodging between cover, rolling out of the way of a grenade at the last minute, managing to first aid your buddy before he succumbs to his wounds, and landing a kill shot all feel satisfying and fire fights are tense affairs.
Drop rates are pretty good and as with most loot games the harder modes you play the better the rewards.
As a tactical mulitplayer FPS with RPG elements this game is pretty awesome but the shallowness of the environments and generic, bullet soak bad guys will probably wear thin for most overtime.
Great for short bursts. A partial thimbs up overall.

This game is classic naval battles. Rolling seas, winds, sails, cannon aiming and your skill at managing these will go into each shot or broadside you send to the enemy. Aim for their sails with chain to try to demast their ship or shred as much of their sails as possible to slow them down. Or, aim for their water line with ball or double ball to open up some holes and let some water in. Aim for their crew with grapeshot to widdle their numbers prior to boarding. Your choices, your skill, your guile, your ship make the difference between success in battle and a wattery grave.
You start out on a small ship, with a few crew. The world is open, your oyster to pluck pearls from. You can trade with other ports, set up proffitable routes and make your money as a trader. Or, you can fight battles for your nation, earning money and skill in naval combat. You can hunt down pirates and smugglers, taking their cargo for your own. Or, you can be a Pirate! Hunt down enemy ships, fight, board and steal their cargo, commandier their cargo ship and bring it back into harbor to sell or use as you see fit.
Dedicated PvP and PvE servers allow you to play with as much (or as little) player interaction as you desire.
I started out on a PvE server, playing with a buddy. We learned to sail, shoot, fight, craft on the PvE and eventually, we longed for a battle against other players. The fights with AI are fun and definitly worth the practice of battle, but the fight against another human controlled ship, who can make mistakes, fool you with their guile, surprise you with their speedy ship, or just beg you to spare their ship and cargo from your plunderous ways, make the game exciting and very playable.
This game is in early access, and as such, is constantly being developed. Each week or so are updates that improve, expand or occasionally break things. But that is to be expected in an early access game.
I have played several early access games and this is one of the better ones because you can instanly file bug reports from within the game and the developers actually listen.
I cant wait to see what this game will eventually become, but at this point, I do recommend it to friends.

Sproggiwood, developed by FreeHold Games, puts you in the role of a Cloghead individual who has been pulled from another dimension to give this world another shot. Apparently someone has enough pull for a redo. This is a rouge-like adventure game in which you will have to take on many dungeons to see if you can make this world thrive instead of waste away. The problem is that you are not the only being running around, it turns out that a race of Mushrooms is also taking up residence in this world, and it would appear no matter how many times you interact with them you are always going to cause more damage than good.
Graphically this game is a 3/4 view 3Dish game in which you will thrive, or die, in a square grid world. The thing about this game is that since it is rogue-like, you are going to deal with randomized dungeons. That's not to say that the game length with change dramatically between playthroughs, but the levels will always look different, and might contain different enemies that you will have to deal with. Speaking of enemies, I have to say that I like the simple, yet strong design. Yes there are a lot of gelatinous cubes moving around, but the subtle differences in color (yellow, pink, black, blue, etc) can mean a ton of different effects that might make your adventure a bit more perilous. The color scheme is definitely light-hearted, you are not going to get nightmares from playing through the game. Well at least not the look of the game, you might end up having nightmares of being surrounded by enemies that tear you to shreds because you were not careful enough.
To stop you from being torn to shreds you will have the ability of collecting items in your journey. Now the one thing that you have to watch out for is that since this is a rogue-like game, when you enter a new dungeon it is essentially a new you, you are going to start back at level 1. The thing is that the items (potions, armor, weapons, scrolls, etc) they can be purchased so that you can start at a slight advantage in the next dungeon you find yourself in. Since we are talking about items and weapons, and whatnot one of the BIGGEST things for me when I think of changing equipment, is I want to see an actual change in the character, and this game delivers. Are you wearing different armor, well then you are going to look different. Are you using a new weapon, well your weapon will look different. The little things, like this, usually make the game that much more solid.
Now lets get into the one thing that was a bit of a letdown for me, and fortunately or unfortunately it is not a bug. I'm talking about the music in the game. I liked it, in every level, I thought it was subtle, blended well with the game, and wasn't abrasive to hear in a loop. The thing is that design-wise the music is set to drop out and come back after a certain amount of time, which will leave you playing your game, in which all the rest of the sounds work, in silence.
The controls of the game are REALLY easy to pick up, you are going to move left, right, up, and down. You are going to use the 1-5 button for skills, and any choices that require other button presses will be clearly labeled for you so that there is no confusion. Oh and the space bar is your friend if you want to wait a turn and have the enemy move that one extra spot so you don't have to take damage first.
So I don't know what I was expecting out of this game, but what I got was something that I couldn't put down. I decided to test this game out as one of the games I would play during my Extra-Life, 24 hour game-a-thon. The thing is that I kept coming back to this game. It wasn't that it was too easy, in fact there are still many levels that I'm not able to defeat with specific characters, but it was the fact that I knew what I was getting into, I saw the challenge, and it was an easy one to accept over and over again. You see the ease in the ability to pick up the game, understand the game, and play it, made it so that I just had to keep coming back to see if the little bit of time I took off would be enough for the gaming gods to look down upon me and guide me through another level so that I could unlock more of the game.
Now it is possible to play the game all the way through with just one character, but where's the fun in that. You start of as the farmer class, and although it does have some fun special attacks, it is not my favorite class to play as. You also have the warrior, archer, thief, vampire, and wizard. Personally I'm all about the warrior with his attack that will attack every square around him, this has saved my bacon more times than I can count. It also helps to have the shield ability which can absorb a couple of rounds of damage when your life is on the line. I do want to point out, however, that all the other classes are excellent, and well balanced. I do enjoy playing as the thief, and the rest of the gang. If you play this game, you should too, especially since for each class you get through a level you get a bonus of gold, which in turn can greatly help you.
So lets talk about the gold, the gold is the magical substance that will allow you to level up your buildings which in turn will help your character level up faster, have more hit points, interact with more unique items, etc. You also can use the gold towards unlocking items, weapons, armor, and more so that you can choose to start off with it at the beginning of a level.

Worth the price.  Lots of fun.  The gameplay mechanics are well thought out where you have to plan each move based on what types of enemies are around you, where exactly they are and how many.  It pays as well to choose wisely where you place skill points and which items you equip.  Different classes definitely require different strategies as well.  Many rougue-likes do not shine as well in this area.
And yet the gameplay remains fast paced.  At least as much as you want it to.
Story and dialogue are humorous and interesting.  And overall not overdone, no eternal clicking to get past the waves of text and back to playing.
Graphics are good, colorful and engaging.
Downsides are minimal but here they are.  There is no "end game" or more accurately, nothing to do after winning.  Which is kind of disappointing since it's a fairly short play through and you'll be wanting more.  You end up with way more awesome classes than you started with, and a ton of gold - but nothing to do with them.
Only other word of caution is that if at any time you so much as click "new game" from the title screen your current save will vanish forever.

I've been playing this game for a few hours now, since getting my Steam Controller & Steam Link.  It is easily 100 times better with a controller than with the keyboard.
Pros:
1.  Mushroom Men franchise is awesome!  I would really love to see some more interesting games with this IP!  Can we have a Mushroom Men MMO please?
2.  Impressively crisp graphics and VERY refined game play.  I'm not sure I've ever seen a PC game that is so well polished.
3.  Interesting and engaging gameplay, though gets repetitive after a while.
Cons:
1. The constant chase of the Truffle Princess makes the game too challenging for me to get passed the 8th level.  It also left me feeling stressed out.  So I set it to easy, which removes her, and just enjoyed solving the puzzles at my own pace.  Much better game that way!
2. This game isn't really distinctly Mushroom Men, other than that it has Pax as the avatar and the Truffle Princess chasing you.  All of the levels have clever names with puns on fungi related things, or puns relating to the area you're in...but those things never really come into play.  Would be cool to see some differing mechanics as the game progresses.
3.  Ultimately this game was fun, but left me wanting more Mushroom Men content, and less of the puzzle solving content.
SHOULD YOU BUY?: Yes.  It's only $2.99 and it may encourage the studio to make more games with this IP.  It's also pretty fun to play, and an amazingly polished game.

Sproggiwood is really interesting and addicting. The cute graphics are paired up with fitting music for a really good gaming experience. It's a story-driven, roguelike, entry-level-turn-based-rpg with procedurally generated dungeons.
As you progress through the story, more and more characters unlock for you to play through the dungeons. I have unlocked 4 of 6 at the moment and they really do offer very different playstyle:
We have our farmer, the character you start with. Hes more of a tank in my eyes - can stand his ground, heal himself to full, drop pumpkin bombs or fear the enemies.
Then we have the warrior - a classic "in your face" character, charging into enemies to cleave them down or whirlwind 'em to dust.
The archer is as expected a squishy one, "leave me alone" kinda guy, that avoids direct fights and pew-pews from a safe distance.
And the last, that I have unlocked, is the Thief - a stealthy one, jukes enemies around and uses stealth to avoid fights.
As you can see, fairly different gameplay is offered by those 4 classes and you get incentive to complete each dungeon with each character to earn that dosh, that you so desperately need.
Money is the only thing that persists trough death, character swap and dungeon entrance/exit. Every time you enter a dungeon - you start as level 1 character with the gear/consumable you brought with you from the village. In the village there is a shop, where you buy different character upgrades (faster leveling, more starting hp), gear and consumables. The gear and consumables in the shop are only those, that you have previously seen drop/picked up in the dungeons for you - so I guess there is some luck involved for the best drops, at least initially(as there are not that many weapons and eventually you'll discover them all).
On the other hand, totally game irrelevant, as far as I can tell, you can customize your village to your heart's content - you can build bridges, mansions,plant trees and modify the grass around - I think I've spent an hour just messing around with it to make it as cute as possible ;)
The humor in the game,and the game in general is fairly amusing and can wholeheartedly recommend it, although I think the price tag is just a bit steep, but you should definitely get it, when it comes on sale.
TL:DR you can check my first impressions video, where I struggle with different characters to complete the 4th dungeon

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP
Superbrothers is an odd little adventure game. It's not out-and-out good, but it's definitely stylish and unique.
The gameplay suffers a bit because it was born for tablet gaming. I own this game on my iPad, too, and it definitely plays better there than it does on my PC.
The game is funny, and very self-referential, but the story is a zilch.
The story and gameplay combine to give you a "go here, do this. Now go there, do that" sort of experience. You don't do much puzzling out of anything for yourself. Just... go to the special place, and do the special thing. Now go to that other special place, and do another special thing. Rinse and repeat until the game tells you that it's over.
But the art is pretty, and the game has a sense of humor about itself. It's weird, and oddly hypnotic. The music is immersive. It's not a great soundtrack that stands on its own, but the music and sound improve the gameplay.
I cautiously recommend this game for people who enjoy weird, indirect, self-referential media (you know who you are.) But not enthusiastically. More importantly, if you're considering a choice between buying on Steam or on tablet, definitely play Superbrothers on your tablet. It's better there.

Endorsement: “A Gears of War-clone that should have replaced the original’s series”
I love Gears of War as much as the next guy, it’s awesome and fun. But 40K Space Marines really gives Gears a run for its money in terms of quality of gameplay, and if fully realized, could have easily replaced Microsoft’s exclusive as king of 3rd Person Shooters.
Pro:
01)	 An action-style, Warhammer 40K game
02)	 A genuine twist on the “Gears of War” formula that makes it a personal and engaging-style of play
03)	 Visceral game that is hugely satisfying
04)	 Uniquely-written characters that go against the “Vanilla, Angry-marine” cliché
Cons:
X1) Gameplay can get too hectic for its unique-style, resulting in unfair deaths
X2) Online modes are pretty barren
X3) The story is “porn” for Warhammer fans who want a Space Marine action-game, so you may be indifferent or constitute a contagious case of “eye rolling”
Verdict:
In a “What If” multiverse scenario, I’d rather see 40K Space Marine’s grow as a mainstay series than Gears. The game is extremely fun and has more gameplay potential than Gears of War could ever have. Get it if you’re looking for a unique-spin on the Gears formula

I'm recommending the game under the premice of this being an early-access that will undergo lots of improvement. I definitely wouldn't suggest going into purchasing this game expecting a strong and extensive experience at this moment in time.
Overall Positives:
+ Looks like Lego, feels like Lego, it's defintely Lego.
+ World truly feels entirely moldable (especially with the in-built tools
+ Game has huge potential
+ Feels charming
+ Discovery (however quick it currently can be) encourages world exploration.
+ Actually has some quite comprehensive systems in place already.
Current Negatives:
- Camera - It needs a lot of work. Currently it can make you feel out of control and in many situations it just doesn't feel that it's in the right place. For example, I personally feel that the camera is way too close to the player when in vehicles (some more than others). On another note, I don't see why this game should be locked into the standard lego game third-person mode, I found it to be uncomfortable in this kind of game, for me it just leaves a lot to be desired and a lot of the time just doesn't feel right.
- Environments - However much they can look nice, many times they are very visually cluttered and noisy. In my opinion, too many micro-sized bricks are used, it's rare to find a flat area of any kind and this leads to it being hard to find an area that feels right to build on without substantial terrain alteration.
- Interface - Visually it feels clunky and really needs to be scaled down (or least have the option for it to be)
- Gameplay Pt 1 - Exploration, discovery and other non-building gameplay feels weak, no goals, only slight interations with world, there needs to be something added to give a sense of progression other than just finding things. Also, discovery of something new can be very overpowering at the moment, more so than it needs to be. The game currently very "creative mode" orientated. I'm not saying this is a bad feature but it feels much less rewarding than a resource gathering and building experience.
- Gameplay Pt 2 - Building feels seperate to the actual player journey, feels more of a map editor than general gameplay, it can be quite disconnecting from your character. I've also found it to feel stressful at times due to the unatural feeling camera movements and hard to pick up controls.
- NPCs - Animals are pretty much what you'd expect but humanoids feel lifeless, they don't seem to really be doing anything other than walking around.
- Scale - The scale of the world is hard to understand (no map or refrence points). It's easy to get lost and because of this, anything you build is easy to lose, you can build it somewhere, wander off and have no idea where it was you came from. As terrain isn't particually unique (two of the same biome more or less looks the same) this doesn't help the "where did I build that again?" situation.
- Character - There is no character development of any kind and customisation is limited.
I really do think the game shows a lot of promise but has a long way to go before it feels "right" and considered worth the buy. I'm interested to see where the development proccess takes it.

Perhaps they should add the ability to hold down shift while pressing a movement key to simulate pressing that key once every half second or so. Also another minor annoyance is the way the text scrolls when characters speak. It is a fun game, but here is my list of pros/cons (So far):
Pros:
- Cute and fun, doesn't have the "pixel art" graphics a lot of the newer indie games have (I do like the pixel art style, but this graphic style works too)
- You can re-arrange things you earn in your town so that is looks more unique to what you want, and there is no cost to "buy" new "decorations," though some must be unlocked (understandably).
- Fun, useful (if a little overpowered at times) items to find and equip.
Cons (This list may seem longer, but honestly, the Pros are still better):
- You have to unlock every other class in the game (besides the initial farmer). While not bad, can be annoying picking between who to unlock. Negated upon playing though, so not horrible.
- Can't rotate buildings you place in your "town."
- Items (Weapons/Armor) found in dungeons cannot be kept; you must buy them in town first then you have perma-use of them.
- (Edit, added) After playing a while longer, seems you don't keep your level(s) between dungeon, so every dungeon you start at level 1, *again* - This is actually a little frustrating, but is also part of the game play I suppose.
- I would like to be able to name my little adventurer(s). I love customizations. Plus, the skills are limited in selection for my taste - especially for a $14.99 game.
- Dungeons can be rather short
- The initial story is some what annoyingly confusing. I don't want to spoil things, but it changes 3 times before you hit the first dungeon (not the tutorial "walk in a straight line"). It makes me almost not want to see what the story line does next, since it does change so much suddenly, in a "ok, I lied, this is what is really up now."
It is a fun game, and worth a try, but maybe at a discounted price. More of a $4.99 indie game in my opinion.

It's a lot of fun to see Mushroom Men again. The original game on Wii was so much fun. This game is much different, it's a platformer with small puzzles sprinkled in by having to place crates and trampolines in the right places to progress through the level. This game is crazy hard tho! You're being chased by the Truffle Princess which basically times you to get these puzzles in place to platform ahead before she catches you, otherwise you die. You can change the difficulty of the game to "easy" and she won't be present tho so the game basically becomes a more casual puzzle-solving game. Personally, right now I prefer this mode which makes it nice to platform along and enjoy things without feeling rushed as you figure out the puzzles.
Art is amazing. There's a rendered cinematic movie at the start of Level 1 that looks like something from Blur or Pixar. And the cutscenes between worlds are great as well. The environment is nice and still has that great charm from the original Mushroom Men. The main character is great, enemies are great, Truffle Princess is hideously great, and the music is great.
Overall I think this game is a lot of fun, pretty original and it's refreshing to have a challenge these days with so many watered down games out there that dumb down the difficulty to the point that you are sick of them too quickly. I won't be sick of Mushroom Men: Truffle Trouble anytime soon.

Were to start?  Well the beginning is the best place but it is only after several play's at this monster that you really start to see all that it has to offer.
There are plenty of character choices, from fighter to warlock and back again and each type of character offers different play styles.  It does not stop there either - the side kicks you get to choose or on your own if you are really good.  Various endings and helper plots to grant other story changes.  From a cursed wizard with demon troubles, to a failed source hunter.  It is all here waiting to be discovered.
Then there are the difficulity levels - these alone call for their own tactics.
There is alot of depth to the game but to say it is without fault would be misleading.  Often puzzles are hard to beat because there is little or no help available to solve them - in game that is.  Thank goodness for youtube.  Some of this is down to game design but the game does make you think.  This is no diablo clone with endless clicking.
You may find some quests harder to solve because you have characters with too low perception or you have no one who has excelled in nasty deeds.  This does make each play unique as the choice of characters and skills play a high role.  This could make the game seem tiresome but there are simply too many things happening to ever make it feel stale.
Enemy encounters are turn based but the rest of the game happens in real time - classic crpg style and it rates up there with the best.
The story maynot be the most original but what is there is compelling enough to make you want to reach the end.  The enhanced edition does feature some changes in areas and encounters so if you have played the original release there is still some new content to be found.
It also feratures a full editor but there seems to be very little on the workshop.  The 4 player mod however is worth checking out.
In conclusion the game is good, not perfect but enjoyable just the same.  It will take approx 100 hours to complete the main quest and all sub-quests.

Singleplayer is fun, in a mindless kind of way, but satisfiying because of the accuracy in the portrayal of Space Marines from the 40k universe in that they are pretty much walking tanks with shield generators. The sad thing is, multiplayer is pure cancer. Singleplayer creates this notion of near invincibilty of your character through a healing mechanism to regenerate either by sitting around waiting, or by the stomping of greenskins. Well, in multiplayer, all you do is the former.
Each engagement feels like you will die, and in most cases you do. Which isn't too bad, but being that many of the modes ask you to be in the thick of combat to win, waiting over ten seconds to spawn or spawn at your base that could be quite a far walk from said thick, becomes very, very annoying. Yes, there is a perk that will bring this down to a couple of seconds, but sometimes that slot could be used for something more useful. Like protection for Tazmanian Devils with Jumppacks and chainsaw swords...
The couple of issues I have with this game online stems from the fact that no proper balancing was ever done. As you rank up winning rounds and killing Heretics, (or non-believers), weapons, armor cosmetics, and class perks become available. Challenges were also included to add some reward for doing such things as kills, kill-streaks, or multikills. But this isn't only restricted to exp toward your level, this also includes weapons perks. The things is, when host has advantage, as well as the many others that have near-perfect connection with them, the game becomes unbearable to play. Killing a single enemy is like perdicting the future in milliseconds. Each action must be made thinking that someone will move into celestial alignment with your sights, granting you access to the heavens and their many gifts thinking once you earn that weapon's perk for completing a specific challenge, you could finally start competing on an equal footing.
Not so much.
Unfortunatly, the god's were unforgiving. THQ was striken down before any balancing could be made. Oh, yeah and hacks are there. Go figure. Just giving you fair warning. Don't expect a lot out of this game multiplayer-wise.

While the gameplay isn't really anything special, this game does an incredible job of capturing the feel of Warhammer 40,000.  The art design is just wonderfully faithful to the source material, and the soundtrack compliments it perfectly.

Almost five years after launch, the multiplayer community is pretty much dead.  I don't consider that to be too much of an issue, though, as the single-player campaign is where the game really shines.
It's aged pretty well.  I recommend it for anyone who enjoys WH40k.

The lore in this game shapes up pretty well to the original lore except for a few places one place being the implamentation of the melta gun which instead of the constant stream it acts more like the shot gun of this game. The single player has a decent story with good gun play and fun if simple melee combat with some exceutions which are reasonably entertaining. The pvp multiplayer is a bit janky with some weapon changes from the single player but is overall solid. The exterminius multipler coop survival is fun and will provide some entertenment even if it gets repetitive. Overall a fun solid if repetitive game which is a worthy entry to a very small list of good warhammer 40k games.

I'm recommending the game under the premice of this being an early-access that will undergo lots of improvement. I definitely wouldn't suggest going into purchasing this game expecting a strong and extensive experience at this moment in time.
Overall Positives:
+ Looks like Lego, feels like Lego, it's defintely Lego.
+ World truly feels entirely moldable (especially with the in-built tools
+ Game has huge potential
+ Feels charming
+ Discovery (however quick it currently can be) encourages world exploration.
+ Actually has some quite comprehensive systems in place already.
Current Negatives:
- Camera - It needs a lot of work. Currently it can make you feel out of control and in many situations it just doesn't feel that it's in the right place. For example, I personally feel that the camera is way too close to the player when in vehicles (some more than others). On another note, I don't see why this game should be locked into the standard lego game third-person mode, I found it to be uncomfortable in this kind of game, for me it just leaves a lot to be desired and a lot of the time just doesn't feel right.
- Environments - However much they can look nice, many times they are very visually cluttered and noisy. In my opinion, too many micro-sized bricks are used, it's rare to find a flat area of any kind and this leads to it being hard to find an area that feels right to build on without substantial terrain alteration.
- Interface - Visually it feels clunky and really needs to be scaled down (or least have the option for it to be)
- Gameplay Pt 1 - Exploration, discovery and other non-building gameplay feels weak, no goals, only slight interations with world, there needs to be something added to give a sense of progression other than just finding things. Also, discovery of something new can be very overpowering at the moment, more so than it needs to be. The game currently very "creative mode" orientated. I'm not saying this is a bad feature but it feels much less rewarding than a resource gathering and building experience.
- Gameplay Pt 2 - Building feels seperate to the actual player journey, feels more of a map editor than general gameplay, it can be quite disconnecting from your character. I've also found it to feel stressful at times due to the unatural feeling camera movements and hard to pick up controls.
- NPCs - Animals are pretty much what you'd expect but humanoids feel lifeless, they don't seem to really be doing anything other than walking around.
- Scale - The scale of the world is hard to understand (no map or refrence points). It's easy to get lost and because of this, anything you build is easy to lose, you can build it somewhere, wander off and have no idea where it was you came from. As terrain isn't particually unique (two of the same biome more or less looks the same) this doesn't help the "where did I build that again?" situation.
- Character - There is no character development of any kind and customisation is limited.
I really do think the game shows a lot of promise but has a long way to go before it feels "right" and considered worth the buy. I'm interested to see where the development proccess takes it.

Ori and the Blind Forest is the best action platformer I have ever played, as well as one of the best games ever made. The world of the forest of Nibel is portrayed extremely well; the environment is simply beautiful and very detailed. The soundtracks are amazingly well done and complement the game perfectly. Each of the playable regions has a unique feel to it and never gets boring, not even when you keep dying and are forced to see the same part again and again for a while. The game is actually very well balanced and you will probably be slowed down more by the tricky terrain rather than the enemies. There is a good number of challenging situations that bring a sense of accomplishment when you finally overcome them. The game lets you spend energy points (which are very common) to create save points virtually anywhere you want, a system that feels incredibly right and useful in this game. There are of course several regular save locations as well as auto-saves after important events.
The story itself is told mostly through exploration and cutscenes with little dialogue, but having completed the game I can't say I ever felt the need for more words. It is a very emotional, dramatic story that quickly unfolds before you and sneaks tears into your eyes before you know it. The ending is fitting and satisfying. The only thing that I miss is no New Game+ or at least a way to revisit every area to collect things you might have missed before finishing the game. Sadly there are a couple areas that are blocked after being beaten and you can never return there so it keeps you from achieving 100% clear game if you missed anything. At least this was so at the time this review was written. If they fix it meanwhile, then this game has become flawless :)
It took me 8 hours to beat the game and that was with 98% completion (due to the couple areas I couldn't re-enter). I would say there is replay value here despite the story and exploration being quite linear, simply because it is such a fun, exciting, beautiful and rewarding game. I know I will definitely keep coming back to it. It is absolutely worth the full price of 20 EUR I paid for it.
+ Beautiful, detailed graphics
+ Amazing soundtracks
+ Fun and exciting gameplay
+ Highly emotional and dramatic story
+ A good balance of difficulty with some challenging but rewarding parts
+ Still enjoying the game after 20+ hours
+ Replayability despite being linear, due to all the other pros
- No New Game+ or way to continue playing after beating the game
- Some areas are blocked after clearing and cannot be revisited to collect missed items/discovery
- Some achievements might not be properly recognized at times

I was fortunate enough to grab Sproggiwood in a giveaway.  I didn't stop playing until I had defeated every dungeon with every class.  Me likey.  A lot.
The game leans toward the casual side, but that suits me. Earning new starting equipment, boosts and classes provides long term goals. However, levels have to be earned again in each dungeon so the game doesn't become too easy.  Meanwhile, the starting equipment is optional so those who desire more challenge can ignore it.
As someone who loathes inventory management, I particularly like that it is kept to a minimum with players only holding one item in each slot at a time.  In a nice touch for hoarders like myself, found consumable items can be used immediately without replacing the held item and there is no such thing as leaving an item on the ground.  Overall, this kept my focus on tactical positioning and strategic leveling of my class skills.  When I worried that I was relying on certain starting items too much, I'd enter a dungeon that revealed their quirks, realize the other items still had a purpose and choose my gear accordingly.
I didn't do much decorating in the town sandbox, but I enjoyed the unlock system it's tied to.  Buildings which grant classes are placed (along with NPCs) by defeating certain dungeons.  Finding new items in a dungeon makes them available in the town store.  Purchasing items in the store makes them available as starting equipment.  Together with the overworld's record of which dungeons were defeated by each class, there was always something new to do for one more round.

Full review at:
But in short, Sproggiwood is a gateway game into the roguelike genre. If you've been afraid of how punishing other roguelikes have been, but you're intrigued by the mechanics of roguelikes, Sproggiwood is the game for you. It's a great way to introduce you to the genre and its mechanics in a meaningful and fun way - and the game is a lot of fun once you discover the layers of depth and strategy involved. Six classes in total, lots of loot to be found, all set in a charming and visually pleasing world.

The Good:
- adorable, beautiful art style in every map, dungeon, village, and loading screen
- multiple classes to choose from means replayability
- items have specific effects without complicating things by adding to your 'stats'
- story interwoven between the dungeons (something you don't see often in roguelikes)
- buying back items in the village adds another layer of progression to the game
The Bad:
- I'm addicted to this game

Let me start this off by saying this game is a Roguelike, and that I've always liked Roguelikes but they are very hit or miss with me, I can't get into Stone Soup but loved Shiren the Wanderer for example, if this sounds like you, who likes them but finds that Dwarf Fortress is to 'hardcore' for you, then seriously consider this one.
Sproggiwood may be on the casual side of the spectrum of Roguelikes, but don't let that make you think that this one is any less of a Roguelike or that it will be an easy one, you'll definitely need to plan your attacks and with proper movement if you plan to beat this, less you be overrun but duplicating slimes.
I'm not gonna lie, I have no idea what the story's about, some Sprite, some God, Mushrooms, whatever. I look at the screen during the cutscenes and go OMGoud sooooo cute, then before I know it all the talking is over and I'm in a dungeon killing things and getting loot.
Gameplay there's not to much to say, it's a Roguelike.... is simple but still hard to master, you have 6 classes to choose from, but 5 of them are locked and need to be unlock first, they each have 4 very distinct skills and play very differently from one another, this is all great for the replay value BTW! Dungeons are short, which is a good thing! they take about 5 to 10 minutes to beat. By beating dungeons (or even dying in them) earns you gold, and with that you can buy upgrades and better equipment that makes your little guy better for even easier dungeoning, shopping is all done from your little Village or Home Base of sorts, that can be customized to your liking, but customizing things around in your Village like adding sidewalks or making a garden are all purely a cosmetic thing, they have no impact on anything unfortunately.
That's probably the only negative thing I can say about Sproggiwood, is that the 'Village' part seems empty and pointless,  they could have made it into something fun, something to do in between dungeon runs, like by having a garden in your Village would let you harvest ingredients on a timer, then those could be made into powerful one time potions, or having the forge/blacksmith building craft powerful equipment from materials you would find in dungeons or maybe from rare drops from the end bosses, I dunno seems like a missed opportunity here.
Anyway let's wrap this up, if you like Roguelikes, Casual Roguelikes, Coffee break Roguelikes, Cute things, Steam Cards, Achievements, then get this game, it's a very polished gem, I highly recommend it.

Creative Assembly has been making total war games since I was a wee lad.  Looking at WTW2 compared to Rome is night and day.  The interface is slick, the graphics are gorgeous, there has been a massive improvement.  But, and this is one of those buts that sticks out more than the butts on the character models in Overwatch, the AI is still terrible.  There are numerous instances where the tactical AI just breaks, this is most obvious on siege maps with melee units sitting on walls eating ranged fire indefinitely.  On the strategic layer the AI has perfect knowledge of your settlements, a huge resource advantage over you, and depending on the difficulty level will either ignore you or target you specifically.
I really want this game to succeed.  CA's plan to combine all the WTW games and have a massive campaign with all the races is an amazing idea.  But, it doesn't matter how awesome the Skaven look or how impressive it is to see a line of dinosaurs smash through a line of zombies if the AI powering it all isn't up to the task.

Now this game was an unique experience. Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP offers you rather straightforward, but surprisingly moving story. As in any point & click game, you have to solve puzzles (varing in difficulty and nature) to move forward - and, well, it took some time for me to get used to SS&S EP mindset.
Music is beatiful - even if you're not interested in game, soundtrack is worth listening to. If you like pixel art, you will also love graphics. The world is detailed and alive, and holds much potential in my opinion; given how little we get to know about its mythology and geography, I feel kind of disappointed that SS&S EP offers only a small figment of its world. I would certainly like to see more.
I recommend Superbrothers Sword & Sworcery EP to anyone curious enough to try rather meditative atmosphere. Do give this game a chance, you might love it :)

I was initially really interest in playing this game, especially because of how they managed to troll people who pirated it. Once I had gone through a few careers, however, the novelty wore off, but I still kept trying to like it. The novelty seems to have worn off for the developer as well, because the interface feels very sloppy, years after release.
While the early game is fairly intuitive, it becomes increasingly less so, with little to no guidance along the way. The training of employees, for instance, becomes a tedious balancing act, but completely necessary as later games demand increased development points, and the salary increases as employees level up makes it untenable to keep employees at their base levels. Installing a mod to allow for some level of improvement from the hands-on process of making games corrects this to a degree, but why would someone else have to come up with that element? You will also want to pick up mods to allow you to speed up events like the game conference and the like. Things like this all compound to make it feel like Greenheart Games hasn't perfect their own slider mechanic either.
It is also an extremely buggy game, with the mouse clicking straight through buttons on one window and hitting elements behind it regularly. The movement between the main screen and the others (R&D and the Hardware Lab) is also inconsistent and annoying.
Because of all of these issues I wouldn't recommend this game unless they made a solid update for it, but after almost 3 years on the market I think it's safe to say that they will not be correcting anything at all.

And soon, you'll start using quotes when writing about other games' "stories", implying that To the Moon has such a unique story that it will make all other "stories" seem like poorly written junk.
So, do I recommend To the Moon?
Obviously.
Am I mad at myself for waiting too long to play To the Moon?
Absolutely.
