I had some bad experiences with this game in its beta, but I decided to give it another go with friends.
The game launched in windowed mode, defaulting to low for all of the graphics settings. I have an R9 390, even my 660 TI back in the beta worked with the auto-optimization.
We all experienced multiple crashes. Trying to run the game in DX12 in fullscreen (or borderless fullscreen) mode also immediately crashes. A friend running on low settings had bizzare issues in cutscenes, like a major character model being duplicated, another have no eyelids, etc. Another friend running on higher settings had some similar issues (like the duplicate character models) in cutscenes, though not as severely. Audio completely cut out for me about an hour in during a mission and required a restart.
Running on a mixture of high and ultra settings, the game looks... okay. The benchmark ran alright, but had severe amounts of non-LOD-based pop-in; many objects simply loaded higher detail versions after being on-screen for a moment. The bridge shown near the beginning reliably loads a higher detail version when it zooms *out*.
Achieving 60 FPS on a pre-Ryzen AMD CPU (even Piledriver OC'd to 4.5 GHz) also seems just not feasible. Combat dropped below 30 FPS even at multiple points. CPU usage sat at ~75% in open areas with no visible enemies and only a handful of friendly NPC's standing still.
And I have no idea what it's used for, because the enemy AI clearly isn't running some advanced behavior algorithms. They frequently just walk out in the open with little sense of self-preservation. Team AI too; many times, I saw one stand in the middle of a firefight and eat my shots.
Which brings me into the combat. I heard they really improved the time to kill, and god what a nightmare it must have been if this was an improvement. They really took solid tactical, cover-based shooter mechanics and ruined it by throwing enemies at us that take inordinate amounts of damage to kill, even with multiple people. I understand it's hard to merge an FPS with an RPG like this, but it's hard to suspend my disbelief when combat consists of guys in hoodies slowly walking at me with baseball bats and pistols, and eating 10+ bullets to the head each from automatic weapons that are designed to punish extended automatic fire. This game makes some of Destiny's worst enemies look like glass cannons.
The instability of the game, the poor performance, the cliche story, the muddy visuals even on high settings, the dull shooting mechanics all come together to form a really mediocre impression. Maybe there's a fun game buried somewhere in here, but there's just way too much jank to justify spending the time to get there.

Before I played this game I had no initiation into the Warhammer 40K universe.
I need to make it clear that I judge this game purely on its own merits, absent of any ideological bias due to a long-standing love of Warhammer.
That said, because of this game, I'm now very interested and learning more of the 40K universe.
As a rule my favorite games are big-budget third-person action games, the Arkham series, Asassins Creed, God of War, Etc...  I also have an affinity for first person shooters...  borderlands, bioshock.
Generally, I Don't Stray too far off the beaten path for my entertainment.
I would have to insist that this game is the most Grievous example of the public just completely missing it...  my Affinity for video games is a recent affectation, so I freely admit that I missed many mainstream titles during what could be termed the "PS3 era".  I am sure that if I were better informed I would understand that certain aspects of this title may possibly be derivative.  But I'm going to attempt to give you my honest assessment of what I considered to be one of the most enjoyable game experiences I've ever had.
For starters, as I write this I am 38 years old.  I've been through many public entertainment consumption stages in my life, the wide-eyed gullibility of the late seventies and eighties.  The emerging consumerism of the 1990s, and the sad cynicism that came after.
The title of this game immediately captured my imagination.  "SPACE MARINE"...  two words that when combined were able to instantly encapsulate multiple Fascinations into a single idea.  Reading the blurb on the store Page I saw words like "chainsword" and "ork".
The game was on sale...  I HAD to know.
The game play was fast and satisfying combining an accessible melee combat system with polished shooter mechanics.  As the game progressed there were various upgraded capabilities and better weapons, though the game doesn't have a true RPG ethic.  You ARE a space marine.
Knowing nothing of the Warhammer lore, I still found the story to be exciting and intriguing...  I didn't feel lost, if anything it has me motivated to learn more.
The levels are fairly linear but the combat can be handled based on personal preference.  There are altered combat action sequences such as using the jump pack or fighting from a vehicle with a turret.  If you die, the penalties are not egregious, I never found even repeated death to be too frustrating.
Most importantly there were a good dozen moments in the game when I found myself saying "Oh hell yeah", out loud.
Part military shooter, part Space Opera, this game came through when many others have failed.  I think that it's better than the video game community at large has given it credit for.  When so many very popular games are boring cut and paste, formulaic things, rife which cliches and microtransactions. This game took me to a place I've never been.  And I will be going back..
Addendum - 09/30/2016
Finishing the game for the second time...  I enjoyed it even more this time.  Like watching my favorite movie...  however I'm much more skilled at the combat system.
A part of me is bitterly angry that this title will never get the sequel it deserves.  According to the former director of Relic Studios they had a Trilogy of games planned for Captain Titus.  And without too many spoilers this game definitely leaves you on an unfinished note, like the end of a Brandon Sanderson Story You're just dying to know more.
If the game gods are out there reading this know that I and hopefully many like me would pre-order any prospective sequel to this game.  I know the gaming industry is addicted to multiplayer and Co-op because of microtransactions and the amount of time spent in multiplayer games, but this single player campaign was one for the ages.
Only takes 5ish hours to finish, left me with to much time for myself after to go outside and interact with real people, and no one wants that

The combat has it's quirks, but is generally tight and responsive.  It was billed at the time as the "anti-Gears of War" - it's a 3rd person shooter but not intended to require abuse of cover mechanics.  Unfortunately, the last quarter punishes the player for playing it that way; ditching melee and focusing on ranged firepower is the only way I was able to beat this very difficult part of the game.
This is also nice and short, clipping in at 8 hours, so it doesn't overstay it's welcome.  If you like W40K, or 3rd person action games, you can't go wrong picking this one up.  Recommended.

The greatest aspects of this game though, are it's soundtrack and the gameplay mechanics.
The soundtrack is the best soundtrack I've ever heard from a video game. I call it the best for this reason: at no point during the game did I get sick of the sountrack, at no point did the soundtrack detract from the feeling of the game and every time the soundtrack makes an effort to make you feel more involved it succeeds. Also, the soundtrack is absolutely beautiful. There's a certain element of peace, or joy, or happiness, or even sadness in all of the music that is always present. And most importantly regarding the soundtrack: it is blended into the game in way that makes it feel more like part of the game than just the soundtrack. It's immersive to the fullest extent.
The gameplay mechanics are amazing as well, or more accurately, the progression of mechanics. As you gain new abilities the game's puzzle elements and challenges change and progress in complexity in a way that builds upon itself. Take just a generic jumping puzzle as an example. The first form is almost always very easy and very simple. Most games continue to use that generic model at several points throughout the game as an easy challenge that becomes more or less a side task that you don't even really notice after a while. In Ori and the Blind Forest, that challenge evolves to meet new abilties, new settings, and new gameplay mechanics until almost every aspect of gameplay is involved in any given task. The closest thing to this I've ever seen in any other game is the way that Portal 2's puzzles progress (Have not played the first one so no comment on it). The progression of your abilities and the way the game's puzzles adapt to them and incorporate them is among the absolute most satisfying feelings I've ever had while playing a game.
Overall the game is simply amazing, however a word of warning to anyone who is considering buying it - this game can be unforgivably hard at points. Personally I enjoy this, but not all people will enjoy it quite as much as me. In particular, there are 3 "run" sequences that, while amazing, literally do not let you make a mistake under pain of death. Now, you immediately start at the beginning of the run sequences when you die, which makes them feel much more tolerable in their difficulty, but many people will have a problem with them I imagine. I personally don't hold it against a game when the game is difficult but not unfair in the sense that it doesn't prepare you for the task or just simply cheats you. This game is fair, it is just very difficult. I would advise against letting the difficulty turn you off to it, the satisfaction from playing this game far outweighs the difficulty; it is well worth the effort. I recommend this game 100%.

You may remember this game from its brief demo at E3 last year (2014) where a white squirrel thing was shown jumping through beautiful scenery. It was one of the most visually memorable trailers I saw at E3 last year. And I'm happy to report the game is just as strikingly beautiful as its trailer. Ori and the Blind forest is a Metroidvania style platformer and is the first game from indie developer Moon Studios. I suspect Moon Studios is comprised of at least a couple industry veterans as this game is beautiful, very well designed and oozes quality.
Before being published by Microsoft, Ori and the Blind Forest was developed in the Unity engine over the course of four years. Moon Studios cited the Rayman and Metroid franchises as influences for these games, and that's immediately obvious in both the high quality artwork (Rayman) and gameplay (Metroid). I'm personally a big fan of Metroidvania style gameplay, but since the Metroid series is somewhat MIA right now and Castlevania seems to be content making God of War clones, I've had to turn to other games like Ori to get my Metroidvania fix
If you've never played a Metoidvania style game before, the game is usually set in a large, non-linear game world with an emphasis on exploration and finding secrets. They often feature some sort of blend of platforming and combat, and often have light RPG elements where you can progress and improve your player character. Ori chooses to go somewhat light on the combat aspect (most enemies can be defeated by simply mashing the attack button), but instead focus most of the difficulty in the game around platforming. I didn't find the combat in this game that engaging or challenging at all, but there were a few segments that demanded perfect execution of precision platforming in a limited amount of time and messing up required repeating the entire platforming segment. It never felt TOO frustrating, but it was close.
Aside from this game's striking visuals, the first unique thing I noticed about it is that Ori will let you save nearly anywhere you like and at any time you like, provided there are no enemies nearby and you also have enough "spirit energy", which this game uses as currency for saving. Since the player can save anywhere and anytime they wish, Ori is free to ramp up the difficulty of the platforming to a pretty high level and also introduce enemies and hazards that can kill you in one hit. But it never feels unfair because you only lose as much progress since you last saved. I found I had enough spirit energy to comfortably save about every 30 seconds. It's kind of the Super Meat Boy effect. The game is quite difficult and you'll die often, but it never becomes too frustrating or feels too unfair because you only lose about 5-10 seconds of progress and then the game immediately brings you right back to try again.
Summary
If you like Metroid or Castlevania styled games, or games like Guacamelee!, for instance, you may want to give Ori a try. Or if you dig really artsy and visually striking games, Ori also applies. I really enjoyed my time with Ori and the Blind Forest and am looking forward to see what's next from Moon Studios

The Exiled is an Early Access, social, open PvP, partial loot, sandbox MMORPG. It’s in active development, and has been on Steam Early Access for a little over 1 month, with 2 updates so far. There are EU, US and Brazilian servers. I recommend you give it a try yourself if you're interested, since it’s only a 500 MB download. Note that most of the events with high rewards occurs at 7pm-11pm server time, so that is when the people log on and fight over things with each other.
In terms of actual gameplay as it exists now, the combat is quite fun (WASD movement + mouse aiming for skills). It has full friendly fire, everything is a skill shot, in isometric combat (like League of Legends without any auto-targetting or auto-attacks). There are multiple social tools such as clans, parties etc. to aid you in coordinating groups or doing some active diplomacy.
You can establish bases, lay siege to settled bases, and in general do whatever you feel like. All equipment is player crafted, which includes weapons and armour. The weapon type and armour type define what sort of skills your character can use, which can be changed at any time. There are 5 weapons and 4 armour types at the moment, with more to come. Skills can be leveled, with the max level of skills defined by character level.
Character level has a catch up mode which gives you a bonus to get closer towards the max level on the server faster. Grinding levels has significant diminishing returns, so that people always have a chance to compete without having to always grind levels. The diminishing returns on XP is reset every day, so that the max character levels on the server gradually increase as the season progresses. Seasons at the moment last 28 days, but the devs say that there are plans for all kinds of different game modes and rules in the future. There are no safe zones so they can’t be exploited, even in the beginner zones. People compete over high score related to how well they control resources and convert their surplus to score.
At the moment, the main conflicts occur during peak time (7-11pm local time) over resource control points, which give a lot of resources if you control them. The game doesn’t force you directly to group, so if you want to go at it solo you’ll have to deal with the consequences of that, good and bad. You could act as a mercenary, for example. I started the game without knowing anyone, and made friends and enemies through shifting alliances in the game, sometimes there are agreements on terms of battle, sometimes not. I’ve been playing for over a month now, and there are monthly resets of the game world to keep it fresh and for the developers to try different experiments.
They have recently (April 20) done a third update after 2 months of release, which adds more tools to join clans, and various bug fixes. They look like they will do monthly updates which coincide with the monthly reset.

Let me start this off by saying this game is a Roguelike, and that I've always liked Roguelikes but they are very hit or miss with me, I can't get into Stone Soup but loved Shiren the Wanderer for example, if this sounds like you, who likes them but finds that Dwarf Fortress is to 'hardcore' for you, then seriously consider this one.
Sproggiwood may be on the casual side of the spectrum of Roguelikes, but don't let that make you think that this one is any less of a Roguelike or that it will be an easy one, you'll definitely need to plan your attacks and with proper movement if you plan to beat this, less you be overrun but duplicating slimes.
I'm not gonna lie, I have no idea what the story's about, some Sprite, some God, Mushrooms, whatever. I look at the screen during the cutscenes and go OMGoud sooooo cute, then before I know it all the talking is over and I'm in a dungeon killing things and getting loot.
Gameplay there's not to much to say, it's a Roguelike.... is simple but still hard to master, you have 6 classes to choose from, but 5 of them are locked and need to be unlock first, they each have 4 very distinct skills and play very differently from one another, this is all great for the replay value BTW! Dungeons are short, which is a good thing! they take about 5 to 10 minutes to beat. By beating dungeons (or even dying in them) earns you gold, and with that you can buy upgrades and better equipment that makes your little guy better for even easier dungeoning, shopping is all done from your little Village or Home Base of sorts, that can be customized to your liking, but customizing things around in your Village like adding sidewalks or making a garden are all purely a cosmetic thing, they have no impact on anything unfortunately.
That's probably the only negative thing I can say about Sproggiwood, is that the 'Village' part seems empty and pointless,  they could have made it into something fun, something to do in between dungeon runs, like by having a garden in your Village would let you harvest ingredients on a timer, then those could be made into powerful one time potions, or having the forge/blacksmith building craft powerful equipment from materials you would find in dungeons or maybe from rare drops from the end bosses, I dunno seems like a missed opportunity here.
Anyway let's wrap this up, if you like Roguelikes, Casual Roguelikes, Coffee break Roguelikes, Cute things, Steam Cards, Achievements, then get this game, it's a very polished gem, I highly recommend it.

Tl;Dr: You can shoot magic missiles that explode into a giant wheels of fire, decimating whole groups of adorablly hand painted mushroom people and sheep, all for the twisted desires of a probably evil forest spirit. It's great.
If you've never played a roguelike before, Sproggiwood is probably the best entry level one on the market. Its easy to learn, not overwhelmingly punishing, and is a pretty good game to relax with. They're also working on porting it to mobile if that's more your thing.
It has a passive progression system with unlockable gear, perks, and character classes. The weapons/armor tend to have similar effects, but with slight variation as well as higher damage and the like. That said, for the length/simplicity of the game, this really isn't an issue. The perks passively increase your hp/xp gain/reduce the cost of items, which doesn't have a huge effect on dungeon crawling, but does speed things along as you go.
There are 6 character classes: The farmer, warrior, archer, thief, mage, and vampire. The farmer uses throwing pitchforks and exploding mushrooms for hit & run tactics. The warrior has a spin move, charge, fortify, and hit everybody in a 5 square radius move. The thief has traps, stealth, and backstabs. The mage is an absolute powerhouse with magic missiles, fireball, teleport, and yeti summoning. And the vampire... drains health or turns into a bat. Many of these special attacks can be augmented with weapon effects for greater destruction. My favorite is to use the Mage's magic missile, combined with a type of fire staff, to shoot multiple magic missiles that explode with an AoE fire effect. As long as you kill one enemy with this attack- you can cast it over and over. It's pretty fun.
The game especially shines in the writing department, as the characters (despite their short screentime) are fairly unique and amusing- and there's a lot of twisted morality that gets thrown around as well. It's rare that you get to play as a truly evil character, and I think they designed the main character perfectly for the role.
The game itself is replayable up until you've cleared everything/finished the story. There are some unlockable cosmetic characters for your town, but not much more than that. That said, with random generation and a fair number of dungeons to clear, it's worth the price, especially on sale.
The UI is fairly mobile-y, but you can adjust it to fit your preferences, which is really nice.

This game is different a great way. Every level you advance in has something new to offer, different strategies to come up with, and it really makes you think. The game's cute but deadly qualities really make it stand out from other rogue-likes. I've enjoyed a great deal of the game and I plan to enjoy even more.

Sproggiwood is a beautiful, fun, and challenging rogue-like game that definitely deserves a play. The classes are all varied, require different strategies, and are each genuinely fun to play.
While I didn't spend a lot of time in the town decoration mode, it isn't a requirement and can be a nice distraction in between dungeon runs.
Overall I highly recommend this game to any roguelike veteran looking for something with a quicker pace and more modern flare and also anyone new to the genre that might be turned off by the more traditional roguelike game that can be intimidating to start with.

I’m always looking for a short burst, drop-in drop-out toilet game on my mobile. And when I first saw Downwell I was sure I found a great companion for deuces to come.
I think Devolver digital has been publishing games for me. They seem to be on a role with Titan souls, Olli Olli, Ronin and of course Hotline Miami. Most of the game they publish seem to have similar attributes; unique presentation and creative balls-in-your face gameplay. Also guns...lots of guns.
The art in Downhill shines through its simplicity, the developer (Moppin) used 8-bit style graphics with great effect that suit the idea of where the game takes place, Downwell. From the name Downwell, the game starts by simply jumping down a well. The game is constructed in a level based progression, and you have a number of hit-points if depleted you have to start from the top. Simply put, it’s a roguelike.
The gameplay mechanics are all in the boots. Touch the the direction button and the character will jump towards where you pressed, press the shoot button and his boots will shoot downwards. Along the drop, you will find upgrades in caves or shops that will either give you more HP, more bullets or  different kind of Gunboots. There are a number of excellent Gunboots to play with, ranging from Shotgunboots, Lasergunboots, Blastgunboots...etc.
There is mostly two ways to kill enemies; obviously the first is by shooting them with your Gunboots, the other is simply by jumping on their heads. And with each kill the enemies drop red gems for bartering in the shops. Kill enemies in succession and your kills will generate even more gems.
At first the game may seem, or at least to me, to be impossible to get through, but the mechanics are well-made to make you learn something new with each death.
Each level in the game is made with it’s own unique theme and enemies. And each level is divided into four parts. It also keeps each run fresh as it’s randomly generated. In the end of each part of each level, you will have the option to choose from a number of upgrades; refill HP, shop items cost 10% less, shooting enemy carcass will cause them to explode...etc. What’s great about these abilities is that they stack up as you progress, but of course, being a roguelike, die and you lose it all.
In the end, if you want a mobile game good enough to make your legs go numb on the toilet, I highly recommend Downwell. The game also available on Steam if you prefer it on the big screen with a controller.

I'm going to go ahead and say this is probably going to be one of the nicest and prettiest games we'll see in the year of 2015.
And that's the thing that stands out the most to me about this game: It's pretty. From the characters to the world to its story, everything about it is pretty, not even counting the fact that Ori is probably the most adorable main character I've played as in a very long time.
But recommending the game out of how pretty it is alone would be somewhat shallow of me so I'm going to talk about its gameplay aspect for a bit.
It's a nice metroidvania-style game with a series of skills to explore its world and the ability to upgrade them as you keep playing, and the best thing about this is that said series of skills allow you to tackle some areas and puzzles in more than one way in a fashion that makes it depend on how creatively (and boldly) you put them to use. One thing to point out, however, is that this doesn't make the game easy; There's plenty of challenge and more than one part had me stuck for a bit trying to get through, but this challenge is rarely, if ever, taken to a level where you'd say things were unfair. More often than not, dying is going to be your mistake and not something the game pulled on you.
All-in-all, this is a nice-looking and nicely-challenging game that I really recommend to fans of platforming and metroidvania-style games, and I'd say the world and lenght of the game are worth the price.

(yes, I'm salty...)
I usually talk a lot about the story in my reviews, but for this one, I kind of don't want to tell too much.
It's not a huge story and it's perhaps not quite as "perfect" as some people say it is, but it is very emotional and deserves to be experienced unspoiled.
At its core, Ori is a MetroidVania game, but with a heavy emphasis on precision platforming.
The controls are tight and precise and traversing the environment feels really fun.
The difficulty is hard enough to really give you that sense of accomplishment that many gamers crave, without being frustrating.
It can get really intense at some points though.
You set your own checkpoints, which is interesting and helpful, but can be a bit disheartening when you die and realize that you forgot to set one for half an hour ^^"
You start off with just a jump and a basic attack, but as you go through the game you'll get a lot of different abilities, some of them very unique to the genre.
One for example allows you to bounce yourself off an enemy projectile, in any direction while sending it the opposite direction.
You also have an upgrade system where you can spend points to enhance your abilities and gain new ones.
There's a ton of secrets to find, like health and energy upgrades, or more points to upgrade.
They are often not easy to get to and there's a real satisfaction to finally reaching some of them.
Of course, there will be a lot of backtracking if you're planning to get all of them, as is typical for the genre.
But it doesn't really feel that way, since after gaining new abilities, the way you traverse the previously done sectors will have changed completely.
The level design is close to perfection.
There's a real flow to traversing the environments if you do it well and there's a lot of secrets and hidden passages to discover.
The main path usually leaves some room for errors, so it won't be frustrating, while the secrets and shortcuts often require perfect timing and control to reach, giving the people that want it the ultimate difficulty, without putting up roadblocks for lesser skilled players.
Many of the secrets that require abilities that you'll learn later on are kept just slightly out of reach, giving you that desire to come back later when you can finally get them.
Despite how perfectly planned out all the sections are, it still feels very natural, like that's just how this world is, which does a lot to help the atmosphere.
The soundtrack is a beautiful mix of orchestral music and choral vocals that carries a lot of emotion.
Whether calm, cheery, haunting or intense, it always fits the current situation perfectly.
It's rare for me to buy game soundtracks, but this one I bought and loaded onto my Mp3 player, so I can listen to it wherever I go.
The aesthetic in this game is wonderful. Honestly, it's perhaps the most beautiful looking 2D game I've ever played in my entire life.
The environments are varied and interesting, the characters are adorable, the lighting is intense and colorful, the background paintings are stunning and the animations just make everything feel a lot more alive.
I played through this game in just 2 sittings and I can't wait to play through it again.
Even tough I usually dislike MetroidVania game and I'm not too fond of platformers, this has easily become one of my top 10 favorite games of all time.
Despite the fact that I usually don't give a damn about achievements, I want them all.
Despite the fact that I have no interest in Steam playing cards, I will collect them, because I want the badges and backgrounds.
If you didn't buy it because it didn't seem like your thing, give it a try anyway.
I think you won't regret it :)

It was not an easy decision to flag this game as NOT recommended.
I'm a big fan of Platform and after I've seen the screens, videos and reviews, I had no doubt this will be a Platform I will remember and love for a very long time.
I finished the game and I enjoyed it. But. But something was definitely missing.
The beginning of the game was really outstanding, anticipating a very deep story and tears guarantee. But the story during the whole game just appears in a superficial way. It's a shame because the concept itself is great, but it needs a deeper development to caught yourself in the story.
The controls and the graphic are amazing - absolutely nothing to complain about it (maybe a bit too sparkling during fights, but this is only personal taste). The landscapes are also great. The musics..I don't know, they are good indeed, but somewhat repetitive. It's like they don't "bound" with the level you are playing sometimes.
What it was kinda disappointing for me, is the LACK of boss fighting. Sure, there are parts that can be considered "boss" levels when you need to escape, but it's not the same thing. And about the mobs - so few types of mobs for the whole game? In every zone you encounter the same type, maybe just stronger, but with the same attack and you can  use the same strategy to defeat them over and over. There are too many level up perks and not enough mobs.
The custom saving point is something not convincing me completely. The game (other than metrovania exploration alike, that is good), looks like a very-lite version of super meat boy. Most of the time you will just die and restart at your last custom check point, train a few until you beat it, and create the next check point. I found this system removed the "challenge" and was just giving me nerves - playing not so focused (and loosing more) because I know I can save just after a few again.
The levels were you need to escape - water and wind -  were great levels. Adrenaline kick and no save in between. My favorite part indeed. And I'm not saying I want an hardcore platform, some parts were very difficult, it's just with this system you don't feel rewarded for your efforts. Game focus too much on this mechanic.
Again, this is absolutely a well crafted game, but I recommend it only to Platform gamers who are more oriented to exploration/100% complete or like the try-die-learn-repeat mechanics. If you are looking for a deep-involving story Platform or something with more "biodiversity" (other than landscapes), you should check somewhere else.

This game is an excellent blend of ranged and melee combat that manages to encapsulates the Warhammer 40,000 universe and it is a shame that it never got any follow-ups.
Combat is smooth flowing, allowing for precise strikes and brutal finishing moves as the main form of healing... there is no hiding behind cover when it comes to your health and encourages you to go toe-to-toe with your opponents in true "They Shall Not Know Fear" Space Marine fashion.

not a masterpiece, not by a long shot with (at times) repetitive combat and linear pacing.
however, this is a case of a game painting by the numbers in all the right way; combat is satisfying, exploration yields interesting data logs, and the game's pacing and difficulty is spot on (and never feels cheap). if you like the 40k universe by all means jump in, relic (who made the dawn of war series) knows this universe inside and out and hasn't failed in bringing it to life.
if you're on the fence jump in when it's on sale you probably won't be disappointed.

Multiplayer overall
Pro's
-Exterminatus and Seize ground are somewhat active

-Armor customization objectives and acheivements add some pretty dank armor and something to play for
-Dlc isnt overbearing given that most people play classic anyways

Cons

To the Moon is a game released by Freebird Game. Previously, To the Moon was sold on Freebirds Games' website before made its way to Steam. The game is designed by using RPG Maker XP which is responsible for its "retro" looks and simple gameplay.
When we are talking about playing video game in general, we are expecting stuff that would engage us to play the game. Generally, gameplay is the one that keeps us to play the game and that what makes video game fun. To the Moon, however, does not offer any gameplay; you spend most of the game walking and reading, and that's all. Therefore It's safe to say that To the Moon offers only cinematic experience than an actual engaging gameplay. Fortunately, the story and the soundtrack of To the Moon are really well crafted that it makes up for the lack of the gameplay.
To the Moon as a game may not offer an incredible gameplay experience. However, it compensates the lack of gameplay with a wonderful journey of unraveling the repressed emotions and desires of a dying person that would leave you captivated even after you finish the game.

I've been a fan of top down skill shot PvP games for years. I've played with the very best and have a great insight into this genre. I cannot recommend Exiled.
1) It's clunky. Movement doesn't feel good, characters seem buggy and are constantly rubberbanding. This may be server related.
2) Random objects placed around the map that you're constantly getting stuck on; even mobs get stuck on them.
3) Very limited outplay potential. As soon as you commit to fighting, you're slowed to a crawl allowing your opponent(s) to burst you down with little to no aim required, and obviously you're unable to dodge due to being practically rooted in place.
4) There is way too much empty space.
5) Grind, grind and grind some more. You'll grind forever without knowing what the purpose is for. You're grinding for XP, abilities, and random materials. But more often then not, you'll get 1v5 ganked before you can even spend them. Think the towns are safe? HAH!
6) It's just bad.

I played about three hours over a free weekend, and I find almost nothing to recommend about the game.  I could go into a lot of detail, but two things really killed it for me:
1) In the initial parts of the game that I played, the enemies were all looters who were trying to survive on the streets of NYC in the midst of a complete societal breakdown.  In most games, you would play as one of these desperate survivors.  In this game, you play the government agent who is summarily executing scavengers for trying to steal food and medical supplies.  Especially when they start to freak out and panic when you gun down their buddies, this just struck me as all kinds of f--ked up, especially the cheerful comments like, "Wow, nice grouping!" from the NPC cops after you gun down a crowd of people with baseball bats.  The premise of this game is basically every right-wing paranoid nightmare about jackbooted government thugs with you as the villain, except that the game clearly thinks you are a hero.
2) You have to remain in cover to survive more than a few seconds in a gun fight, and a few bullets will drop you.  This kind of realism is fine (or even awesome), except that there are Boss enemies you will soak up 100+ bullets before going down, and have laser-like precision to headshot you as soon as you pull the left trigger to pop up and aim over cover.  Blind fire is an option, but it's incredibly inaccurate, and the aforementioned Boss will charge around your cover pretty quickly to hose you down with his AK-47, killing you in less than two seconds, even as you pour full auto-fire into his head at point-blank range.  Maybe there's a trick to killing him, maybe you have to be playing with other people, but either way I quit and uninstalled the game after he cheese-killed me this way 5-6 times.  This is the Boss at the end of the first non-tutorial mission, BTW.
Bottom line, the game has a truly f--ked up premise, and the mechanics are awful.  If it goes FTP at some point, maybe give it a whirl, but I heartily recommend that you play pretty much anything else.

This game is a real-time strategy game in which the player must command emergency services during a wide variety of situations.
It is also the digital embodiment of stress and panic.
Now the game does have a story-line but I haven't played it, I just play free mode in which you can play an endless game as emergencies occur across the city and you must command all your resources.
At first it is deceptively relaxing. The occasional stroke, small fire, or pickpocket to deal with. Then situations get more and more severe and more and more frequent Not gradually, it just spikes and spikes up.
Before you know it your fingers are moving across your keyboard at lightning speed as your rapidly clicking the minimap to bring you all over the city to deal with 10 situations at once. Those situations can also create more situations.
Example:
- I receive word that there is an unauthorized demonstration going on in the north part of town. I look over there and it's just some guy with a sign shouting "Resist!". So I send a police car over and pay the man no mind.
- Then there is a traffic accident on the other side of town and one of the vehicles involved is now in the river along with the driver. So I'm sending ambulances, some firefighters, a divert, some tow trucks and a crane.
- While this is happening a rabid dog is on the loose. I send some armed police to go deal with it.
- I have now forgotten about the Unauthorized demonstration.
- Now I'm micromanaging the traffic accident. Having the firefighters pry open one of the cars to rescue the injured driver and shoving them in an ambulance. The diver is slow as a turtle but ends up attaching a buoy to the submerged vehicle so the crane can pull it out of the water.
- I check back on the rabid dog and instruct the officers to put it down. A civilian was injured so I deploy an ambulance and bring the officers back to HQ.
- The other car in the accident is out of the water and the firefighters pry it open, Sadly the driver is already deceased. I have the towtrucks recover the vehicles and send it all back to HQ.
- The ambulance aiding the injured civilian (that may have rabies now) is on the scene and I micromanage the process and then bring it back to HQ.
- I have now noticed that there is a fire on the minimap. Though since I wasn't notified it wasn't part of the Endless modes generated emergencies.
- Turns out that Unauthorized demonstration has grown from one man to a full blown mob on a rampage that has started a large fire and killed the officer that I sent.
- I kick into high gear. I deploy all of my officers and ambulances to the scene along with a hydro-pup equipped armored vehicle. I decide not to risk any fire fighters and just pay a bunch of in-game money to have an airplane drop a load of water onto the building.
- I ignore the medical and criminal emergencies that pop up while I organize my forces to put down the riot. Though I do divert attention to any fires.
-So my police forces arrive and attempt to put down the riot non-lethally. While the officers are over-whelmed the hydro tank is able to repel the rioters just fine. Sadly the water plane hasn't arrived yet so the fire is still going. Since I am monitoring 5 places at once I am too late to notice that the hydro tank caught fire and exploded. Killing multiple officers.
- Many rioters are injured, but whenever any civilians walk by and see the riot they join in, so their numbers keep growing while I keep losing my officers.
- Eventually matters grow grave. So I lure the rioters into a parking lot and let them attack the remaining police cruisers. The area is now on fire. I make sure to contain the fire and the rioters inside with my remaining forces.
- I should note that during this another traffic accident, a bank robbery, more fires, and a bomb threat have occurred.
- Eventually all the rioters are dead or dying. I save as many as I can and deliver the rest to the morgue and breath a sigh of relief.
- Then mere seconds later there is an earthquake which causes fires and injuries across the city.
- I quit the game so I do not have a heart attack.
***********************************************************************************************************************

Fallout 3. Immersive, intriguing, and badass. The story is one of the best stories in gaming. I find it to be just as good a story as BioShock. You may hear,"Oh it's just you tryna find your dad. It's really not that interesting." To HELL with that. You need to actually expirience this game in order to truly and fully appreciate Fallout 3's story. Three issues I have with the game. Number one, the game will not work properly on Windows 7 or above. Now this CAN BE FIXED. If you cannot figure it out, message me because I want you to enjoy this game. Number two, the visuals are not impressive. This was to be expected with a huge open world RPG such as this. Like most other games, you can modify this game.  Taking the visuals to a whole 'nother level. It rivals SKYRIM and BIOSHOCK INFINITE. That said, you need a beefy graphics card to handle the visual mods. With advanced shaders, blue skies and better looking textures, this game looks phenomenal. I don't enjoy the fact that you have to modify the game to make it prettier, but what has to be done must be done. Having siad that, the game isn't unbearable vanilla. I said the visuals are not impressive, not that they are bad. Number three, Fallout has a reputation for being one of the BUGGIEST PIECES OF LOVELY♥♥♥♥♥♥ It isn't as bad as DayZ but the fact that the two can even be compared is saddening to me. Fortunately, most common and random bugs disappear when playing on pc. They occasionally occur and most are easy fixes. Most. Crashing is eliminated with a 4gb patch and stuttering is solved with a simple mod. At long last you can enjoy your childhood once more at 60fps (good graphics card) and no crashing as it did on console. I rate 10/10 vanilla on PC, 9/10 on console and with mods 11/10. I would recommend this game a million times if I could.

It was not an easy decision to flag this game as NOT recommended.
I'm a big fan of Platform and after I've seen the screens, videos and reviews, I had no doubt this will be a Platform I will remember and love for a very long time.
I finished the game and I enjoyed it. But. But something was definitely missing.
The beginning of the game was really outstanding, anticipating a very deep story and tears guarantee. But the story during the whole game just appears in a superficial way. It's a shame because the concept itself is great, but it needs a deeper development to caught yourself in the story.
The controls and the graphic are amazing - absolutely nothing to complain about it (maybe a bit too sparkling during fights, but this is only personal taste). The landscapes are also great. The musics..I don't know, they are good indeed, but somewhat repetitive. It's like they don't "bound" with the level you are playing sometimes.
What it was kinda disappointing for me, is the LACK of boss fighting. Sure, there are parts that can be considered "boss" levels when you need to escape, but it's not the same thing. And about the mobs - so few types of mobs for the whole game? In every zone you encounter the same type, maybe just stronger, but with the same attack and you can  use the same strategy to defeat them over and over. There are too many level up perks and not enough mobs.
The custom saving point is something not convincing me completely. The game (other than metrovania exploration alike, that is good), looks like a very-lite version of super meat boy. Most of the time you will just die and restart at your last custom check point, train a few until you beat it, and create the next check point. I found this system removed the "challenge" and was just giving me nerves - playing not so focused (and loosing more) because I know I can save just after a few again.
The levels were you need to escape - water and wind -  were great levels. Adrenaline kick and no save in between. My favorite part indeed. And I'm not saying I want an hardcore platform, some parts were very difficult, it's just with this system you don't feel rewarded for your efforts. Game focus too much on this mechanic.
Again, this is absolutely a well crafted game, but I recommend it only to Platform gamers who are more oriented to exploration/100% complete or like the try-die-learn-repeat mechanics. If you are looking for a deep-involving story Platform or something with more "biodiversity" (other than landscapes), you should check somewhere else.

This is one of the most enjoyable Total War titles to date. Especially when you have Mortal Empires installed. Diverse and unique factions is my favorite aspect of this game -something other titles in this franchise can't even come close to comparing to.
The battles are quick and stategic, giving you satisfying army clashes without lingering for too long. This keeps things from getting too stale. However, at times, battles do seem a little TOO short. Most of the time it's to my personal liking, though.
The campaign is an interesting direction for Total War. It prioritizes a sort of narrative to give better context to why these factions are at each other's throats. It's not perfect, but it's a nice change of pace. If you prefer more sandbox-like campaigns, then the free Mortal Empires DLC is the way to go. You'll need Total War: Warhammer 1 to access it, though. Keep that in mind.
Overall there isn't much else to say that others haven't. The game's minor shortcomings can be frustrating at times, but for the most part Total War: Warhammer II is a great experience to sink many hours into.
As a Total War game: 8/10
As a Warhammer game: 10/10
As a game in general: 8/10

On its own, this is a fantastic game that has managed to address many of the issues from its predecessor. However, with the addition of the Mortal Empires expansion, both the replayability and variety found within Warhammer 2 have been built upon significantly.

- invisible walls which prevent you from traversing maps as you like
- the camera which is way too close to the character
- the very shallow melee combat system
- fun sections with the jetpack are few and far between and yet they are sooo fun ! Why not more ?
- wave base shooter that doesn't give you enough guns and/or ammo. Either make it a survival type game to conserve ammo or go all out with guns and ammo and throw waves after waves of enemies at the player (ala Serious Sam)
It also has some strong points:
- The feel of the ultra marine feels weighty - that's good
- Good voice acting
- Nice, juicy gun sounds
- Sections with the jetpack are really fun
Should you buy it ? My answer would be - depends. If you are a big fan of the 40K universe, go right ahead. If you don't really care about the universe, I'd pass and go for other, better 3 person shooters out there.

At it's core this is a great adventure game. The point and click move system doesn't require you to excessively micromanage your moves. The puzzels are interesting and feel part of the worlds mistique. The combat is appropriately challenging with the exception of the boss battles which are disproportianately punishing, and have you sitting through long animations between each failure. The worlds not going to blow you away with it's originality but it's certainly a solid execution of the classic fantasy setting.
Unfortunately this is all for nothing. Rather than let me sink into this worlds story and characters, the game repeatedly pulls the camera back for some 4th wall exposition. These don't actually add much information to the plot they just interrupt immersion for the sake of some snarky self referential, self congratulatory, ironic commentary. It feels like there were 4 writers and one of them was too cool to be a team player. After the second of these scenes you get this feeling you're just going through the motions to see the next lifeless monologue from "the smoking man". A lot of good work seems to have gone in this game, but an adventure game that can't hold your interest in it's story can't really accomplish anything.

Is the game fun? It depends.
The game is a "sandbox pvp mmo with MOBA combat".
The idea is that a game world does not last forever, after some time (weeks/months) some world events happen and the world could die. So you start again in a new world.
Imagine LoL or Dota in a larger map, with a match lasting for weeks instead of 45 min, with "events" similar to Guild Wars 2 Hearts, where the objective is just to survive and, perhaps, build your own community/clan/settlement.
In this map everyone can kill anyone, but in the end all players "should" cooperate to keep the game world alive (by giving donations), otherwise the world will die.
The overall feeling of this game is, oddly enough, that of a Survival Game, like Rust or DayZ.
So we can say that this is a LeagueOfLegends/GuildWars2/Rust mash-up

I have been following The Exiled for some time now, and I was really excited to play it at launch. After about two hours of gameplay, it's clear to see that the devs put a lot of hard work in this game. The world is beautiful, with many different biomes/areas to explore. The tutorial is straight-forward and informative.
Unfortunately the game does fall short in some places. After completing the tutorial, you are left to do your own thing - no hand-holding whatsoever. And there isn't much else to do other than to grind the same events over and over, or kill other players. Also, the combat is weird and clunky, with plenty of lag.
The devs say there is "no grinding" but actually, there's plenty of it. You need to kill monsters/participate in events to obtain items to level up your equipment/to craft new equipment, which seems kind of pointless (unless you're leveling up to kill other players and steal their loot, I don't see why you'd want to grind for countless hours just to level up your equipment a bit).
Finally, the community has been quite toxic so far. Since it's PvP
, almost everyone is trying to kill you
. I found a ton of loot at one stage, and two of these guys came up to me and rekt me and I lost everything 5 minutes later.
This is just unfair, especially since I had just spent the last 5 minutes doing an event for [a little bit of] loot. I did however find an awesome guy that I had helped to finish an event and he shared half the loot with me. That was pretty cool.
Another thing is that all the events are practically the same. In my experience, all you do in an event is defend a site from a bunch of attacking monsters that look the exact same pretty much every time. Fun, right? Wrong.
All in all, I'd say this game is good to an extent, but it definitely does need to be improved in some areas. It's also only free for 7 days, and thereafter we have to pay $20. If you want to support the devs, then you should definitely buy it, but otherwise I don't think the game is worth $20 in it's current state.
Give it a try though, I mean it's free - won't hurt to try! I'm giving it a thumbs up for now, but it is subject to change.
Also if you enjoy trolling people, then this is definitely the game for you.
Thanks for reading and hope you have a great day!

I played about 5 hours during the free weekend. Some people would probably say that 5 hrs isn't enough to judge an MMO style game like this but I think that's enough time to judge what the game is like.
The first thing you'll notice about this game is that it's absolutely gorgeous. This is one of the most detailed, atmospheric open world games ever made. You'll want to explore just to see the different parts of the city. And if you have a thing for post-apocalyptic modern environments, you'll definitely enjoy that aspect of the game.
The combat is good but not great. It's heavily cover based - being out in the open will lead to a very quick death. And almost anything in the environment can be used for cover. If it looks like you can get behind it, you can. This led to my first frustration with the game: Too many times, I died because I was glued to a cover spot and couldn't get out quick enough. Or in the middle of a firefight I tried to get behind an obstacle to take cover only to have my character snap to the side of it and get shot. You sort of get the hang of the controls after a while but getting *out* of cover is never very efficient.
Which brings me to the difficulty. In short, this is NOT a solo experience. Sure, you can attempt the missions solo. But wave after wave of bullet sponge enemies will keep pouring in. And by level 8 or so, they can take you down in a 1-2 shots. Worse, you may find that the nearest spawn point is half a mile away, meaning that you have to run back to the mission area just to repeat the process all over. Teaming up with other players is a necessity and even then, expect to die and restart missions over and over. And over.
That is, if you can even find people to play with. Again, I played during the free weekend, a time when you would expect there to be tons of people playing but that really wasn't the case. Matchmaking would take forever and since you can't select which mission you're matchmaking for, you probably won't make any progress that way. Setting your group privacy to Open so that anyone can join means that, just maybe, you'll get a second person to join you when you're 5 seconds away from finishing the mission on your own.
I don't mind grinding. In fact, I'd say I rather enjoy it most of the time. But this is just repeating the same bland missions of "go here and kill all the bad guys" over and over. I want to like this game, I really do, but it's like the devs did everything possible to make sure I didn't. Maybe The Division 2 will fix the balance issues and actually be, you know, fun.

1. When in combat the enemy will ignore anybody else in the squad and focus on you. They will even go so far as to run/walk directly past any one else in your squad to get at you. Yeah, that makes total sense.
2. I can shoot someone in the head twice that doesn't have any sort of helmet or ohter protection on their head and they keep on going like nothing happened.
3. Can not save the game after a checkpoint in a mission. The game semi auto saves after a check point (you start over at a checkpoint if you die during a mission), but if you leave the game for any reason after a check point the game starts you over at the beginning of the mission. Once a mission is over you can leave the game just fine, but if something happens and you need to leave before a mission is over then be ready to play it all over again.
If I had other people I played with the game might be very enjoyable, but as a SP game it falls short IMO.

Just don't buy it expecting a challenging puzzle game.

Naval Action is an open world age of sail game with fantastic combat, but requires long sessions for maximum enjoyment.
The current 'mixed' reviews are largely due to frustration with the development process in recent months, the lack of a recent patch, and several mechanics problems that are difficult to solve - (the community is split on how to solve several of these problems).  However, the game is, in my opinion, hugely more enjoyable than the recent reviews suggest.
You can sail a wide range of ships from the tiny and nimble gunboat, to large and lumbering 1st rate ships of the line. The sailing characteristics and gunnery in the battle instances feels excellent. The ships are 'relatively' balanced in the current state (although not perfect). For example, a skilled frigate captain could capture a ship of the line, but an experienced captain would still be able to defend themselves.
The core of the RVR part of the game is the 25 v 25 port battles (which is really the end-game content).  These involve trying to make it into the port past the enemy screening fleet,  and then obtaining 1000 points inside the battle. The is done by capturing circles and sinking enemy ships.  These battles are, for me, the highlight of Naval Action and are extremely exciting.
The open world map is very large, perhaps too large for the current playerbase.  New players start in the cutter, and will typically begin by finding missions in the open world to fight against small numbers of NPCs.  Despite contradictory comments in some other reviews, experienced players are generally eager to help new players learn the game.  There is no tutorial, as this would have to be continuosly updated as the mechanics change during development, but there are numerous youtube videos explaining the mechanics, and questions in the help chat are generally answered well.
In summary; the combat mechanics are second to none and hugely enjoyable, but the game in it's current form is not really for the casual player due to the long sessions required to fully enjoy the game.

First, this game is not for everyone. Its a niche game. You will not be given a story, you must make your own. This is a sandbox PvP game (also PvE but I don't reccomend that). There may be a huge enemy player fleet around that island even in your home waters waiting to sink you, or there may be nothing. Some people complain about the "grind" but honestly within a week you can fully crew some excellent ships that are very important and effective in PvP (like the Rattlesnake).
This is a slow paced game where you can easily take on a group of more ships in bigger ships if you have the skill. There are upgrades etc.. that help, but at the end of the day one missed broadside, or a badly timed maneuver negates the positive effect of most of them. The combat mechanis are very detailed, with tons of room to micro manage all the while you must manually aim every shot. Sometimes this means a whole broadside into a wave, sometimes it means enough hits below the waterline (leaks) to sink a ship with otherwise full HP.
I'll add to this review later, but long story short if you are into this sort of game there is nothing else like it, but again its not for everyone.... which is where the best games come from. The learning curve is steel, but the reward is great. Just get into your nations TS or group up with a clan and more then likely they will be very supporting (at least thats what its like in Sweden).

I've seen the board game.  I didn't like it.  I thought the characters looked cartoonish and even in this video game they were odd looking.  I didn't have high hopes for this game but I thought I would try it out anyway.
Playing it...it was like the game walked up to me, looked me in the eye, slapped me and told me to shut my big fat face.
The game is good!
This isn't the typical 3rd person shooter.  In many scenarios you need to think of where you need to move to, stand at, take cover behind...what type of weapon would work best...  You just cannot take the approach of "charge in and kill everything".  You actually need to think.  By the second half of the game you will get used to switching weapons in battle to match the conditions.  You will also be using grenades regularly.  Unlike in a alot of games where I never had to use them at all to finish the game.  BTW, for those who are asking on the myriad of boards....  The Vengeance launcher.  When you fire you can detonate the bomb by pressing "R".  If you fire five, the sixth will detonate the oldest bomb in play.  If you shoot and hit the bomb with a firearm, that too will set it off.  But really, pressing "R" is the easiest.
Also, there are no "health items" in this game.  At the end/start of certain scenarios you are healed.  But in every other part of the game you have to excecute someone to heal or use the rage and hit/shoot people to heal.  At first, I thought this was strange.  But the game mechanic of it is actually quite appealing.  It makes you work to stay alive and not just gobble up potions or etc...
The first thing you will notice about the game is that there is no jumping.  Pressing the spacebar only makes you combat roll.  At first this ticked me off.  But, after playing for a bit, it made sense in the game universe.  They are wearing advanced versions of big, heavy and bulky medieval armor.  So of course they can't jump.  That is why they have the jet packs.
The second thing you will notice is that there isn't the fake, ultra fast reloads you see in most games.  Reloading takes a bit of time.  It really makes you pay attention to your weapon and switch or use your melee weapon.  With your melee weapon you can have various combos depending on which one you pick up.  This was kind of a fun thing for me to try out to emulate fighting games.
The third thing...thankfully...is skippable cutscenes.  If you've seen it once why watch it again?  Unlike in some games I've played here on Steam where you cannot skip the cutscenes...being able to is always a plus and always something I will mention in order to get game makers in the habit of doing so.
Fourth...I had no in game crashes, stutters, drop in FPS or bugs.  Insert a choir of angels singing "Hellelujah!"
Fifth, this is not open world and it will pretty much funnel you from point "A" to point "B".  This wasn't so bad as the battles you would envariably encounter didn't feel repetative.  The game designers did a FANTASTIC job of varying the opponents and creating different environments in order to get you to do things differently otherwise you would die.
Lastly...  I will leave the finer points of the game to the other, better, reviewers on here.  But to wrap it up.  This game was GOOD.  Maybe not great.  But definitely worth the money even if it isn't on sale.  Will I replay it?  Probably not.  But the first run through was good so I would very much consider it.  Even if not, I will leave this game with good memories of it and a feeling of satisfaction in playing it.

I can understand that players seeking a much more conventional gaming experience are disappointed very early on into S&S. However, if you're willing to try something that deviates from the conventional and provides a rich and enjoyable story with compelling sound and visuals, play this game.

S: S&S EP is a rare game in the current generation of titles, both mainstream and Indie.
Less about action and more oriented towards exploration and actual puzzle solving, the pacing and advancement tied to the real-world lunar cycle and muscial pieces / problem solving. This along with obtuse hinting at your advancement means a lot of trial-error to progress. The main mechanics of advancement in the game is by performing 'Songs of Sworcery' which are great mix of music and visual for physical interaction with the game environment.
The game might look staid with its 2D side-scrolling 8-bit graphics but with Jim Guthrie's sound scapes and appropriate colour pallet's the crux points of the game become EPIC, SETPIECE moments in their own right.
All in all, if you have the time, the patience and are willing to use a little bit of logic you will find a solid narrative and game-play experience in S&S EP.

This game is incredible!
The first thing you'll notice is the stunning visuals, and I don't think it would be hyperbole to say that this one of the best-looking games that's ever been made. Just peep one of the preview videos to get an idea. It has a relatively timeless, color-drenched style that I think will hold up very well over time.
Broadly the game falls into the so-called "Metroidvania" genre where you explore an ever-growing game world while constantly finding upgrades and steadily growing your arsenal and mobility. It's as fine an example as any game in the genre. The world is large and fun to explore, but not too big to lose track of.
The music, gameplay design, cutscenes, and pacing of the game are all admirably consistent and it's very clear that it's the product of a strong creative vision executed flawlessly. I finished it in 9 or 10 hours and it's a treat the entire way - no half-baked portions or dull plods. It lasts as long as it needs to and finishes great. Every ounce of it is pulled off perfectly without any seams showing.
The only thing I would caution you about before you buy it is that it's more challenging than it appears at first glance. There aren't any difficulty levels so there's no way to put it on easy and stroll through the game to see the content if that's what you're used to. It's never patently unfair but you'll need decent twitch skills and some persistence to get through some of the trickier portions. If you die, respawning is super quick, and in the process of dying the game teaches you how to get good at it. Stick with it a little bit (and use a good controller) and I think you'll be surprised at what you can pull off.
I'm deliberately avoiding talking about the plot or gameplay specifics because I think those are best experienced with as little foreknowledge as possible, but I can't recommend this game enough. Check it out!

Alright so I'm only an hour and a bit into this but
I have to write a review on this because the game needs them and first impressions are always important for getting a game.
Splinter Zone is almost what happens if you have Vlambeer remake Megaman 1-3.
Here's what I mean by that:
If you have played Megaman's 1 to 3, some of the level segments will feel VERY familiar. .So will some of the enemy behaviours. This is not a bad thing. It's charmingly familiar.
The Vlambeer part comes in with this RIDICULOUSLY MEATY GUN NOISES and the OBLIGATORY SCREENSHAKE (which you can tone down if you wish in the settings). I cannot tell you how delicious the explosions are too, you have to see them for yourself.
Importantly you wanna know how the game looks and plays and sounds though, right?
Sounds:
The music is very 90s dos platformer or amiga protrakker. Think Jazz Jackrabbit sort of music. There are certianly some very familiar sounding samples. It's enjoyable for me, and it works great. I've not gotten terribly far but having listened to the soundtrack on bandcamp, it's great stuff :D Super listenable without being grating or distracting.
The sound effects are HUGE. Seriously those explosions and gun sounds are loud enough that they make my speakers freak out slightly if the volume is too loud. I considered turning the volume of them down to be honest, you might wish to do the same, but oh man they sound good. Properly meaty, the gun SOUNDS like it has a huge kick and is powerful. It's amazing :D
Graphics:
Again, very early 90s DOS platformer (Commander Keen, Duke Nukem 1 and 2, that sort of thing). The sprite work though is very competent and has some great detailing on it. It's timed well with the movements, the enemy designs are fun and a little on the silly side at times, but in a charming, fun way. The main character looks cool and unique, and did I mention the gun being meaty and big and powerful? Yeah. check out those bullet sprites :D delicious. Also there's some segments with rain and the character has rain dripping off them when they are out in it AND for a while after they get under shelter. Utterly unnecessary, but still great detailing and I love it.
The HUD is nice and tidy and not in the way too much but is still immediately visible and understandable. It's simple, but it works great with the overall aesthetic of the game.
Gameplay:
Rock solid. It's proc-gen in that whilst each of the level segments is hand crafted, they are stitched together in a pseudorandom fashion to make each level different. Some segments are harder than others, some are a cakewalk, it's a nice mixed bag. It keeps things interesting and stops it becoming samey.
Momement feels slick and responsive, you never feel like it's clunky or you're suffering from the character not quite moving fast or slow enough, your jump height is great, response is immediate.
Your gun has six charges which replenish on their own when you don't fire, and it doesn't take that long to replenish, but button mashing will end up costing you time on that reload, so time your shots, don't get panicky or greedy. Killing foes drops XP orbs which as you go up level grants you more firepower. Taking damage drops a fair chunk off that XP gauge, potentially lowering your level as well, giving a bit more of a challenge and rewarding cautious and skillful gameplay. Learn those enemy patterns and room types! :D Also your score multipler is dictated by the level you've reached through gaining XP. Soooo, keep that in mind too :3
You ALSO have a Hyper Mode option, which consumes your built up XP to give you infinite ammo, full power shots, and rapid fire as well as a heal of some damage you took, giving a great Risk/Reward element to gameplay. Do you expend your XP now, mid stage, to get past a particularly tough segment and heal some damage you took? Do you keep it to get full power hopefully before the boss? or do you just take what you've got and expend it on a boss to finish it off as fast as possible before it inevitably kills you or eats up all the power you gained anyway? Or do you have full confidence in your skills to keep that power for the next level too and maybe reach even higher levels and score multipliers?
Downsides:
(because it would be unfair to just list all the best parts and not mention some of the downsides.)
The early 90s DOS platformer aesthetic is not gonna be for everyone. It can seem a bit "dated" and rudimentary but it's not dull, and it's really charming in my opinion. A lot of love has gone into it, and the backgrounds are nicely animated and detailed too.
Randomised level layout means that it's a mixed bag and some segments are just a little on the cruel side, so it can be difficult at times NOT to lose a bunch of XP and life on a segment.
Remember I said about the megaman influence being worn on its sleeve? Yeah. Remember those invincible roomba bots from MM1 and 2 that speed up when you are on the same vertical level as them?....yyyyeeah. They're in this game too :/ Fair's fair though, they are somewhat on the rare side and only show up in a small minority of level segments so far. (I'd mention the vanishing block platform puzzle thing that everyone hates from classic megaman, but that's not done the same as in megaman here, and the platforms are bigger. so that gets a well deserved pass :) )
Sometimes there's some slowdown due to explosions D: It can get a bit confusing at times as to what's happening. The game is responsive enough to input though that it's not really a huge issue. I've never taken damage or gotten killed as a result of the slowdown even when it crops up unexpectedly.
Other little oddities:
This game has a fantastic Cracktro style start screen before the menu, evocative again of 90s games. It's fantastic. I love it! It also lets you activate cheats if you're having a hard time on a segment, including playing in "Tourist Mode" if you just wanna do platforming without enemies.
There's a segment that is very clearly inspired by Canabalt. I love it ^^
There's APPARENTLY secrets to find too :o
Every time you finish a boss, you get a brief flash of some text, and there is a story of sorts to the game. One of those "All There in the Manual" type things. Despite the slightly goofy nature of some of the enemies, it's a surprisingly grim and dark story :3 Check out the Trading Card descriptions sometime too.
Overall, I'd say this game is a REALLY solid game, and at its price point you'd be making a terrible mistake not trying it out. Support an indie dev, support a game that deserves some love, and support some good, low priced fun :D

Splinter Zone features - uhm... a bunch of -  levels in six different settings with all their own platforming challenges, like ice, buildings that breack down, or platforms that activate/deactivate alternately as the player jumps, presented in mostly random order in sequences of 4 levels (firstly an easy one, then medium, then hard, and then medium again) and one of the six bosses (you guessed it, every setting has one boss).
Furthermore, as one may need to get the real high scores, for (at least nearly) every killed enemy, the player gets xp, which both levels up their weapon aswell as their multiplier up to level four. As they get hit though, they loose some (currently 50%) of their xp and with that both level and multiplier, but also is the score that might have been multiplied added to the overall score just as it is. So, to get the real high score, the player has to activate Hyper Mode, which gives them rapid fire and heals them for a limited time, after which they are back on level one and have their stored score multiplied by the level they were on.
Now, the game would kind of get easy after learning the levels a bit, wouldn't it? So, ok, it still does get somewhat easy as I can tell, but the damage the player takes is increased every 10 min in a run, which makes the game become far less forgiving the longer the player survives. The most interesting part about this game seems to be, that when you're on a certain skill-level, you can pretty much go on forever. But I think, there's more to it, than to just beat your own highscore over and over again. The story seems to be, that you can decide for yourself, if you wanna stay in this sourrounding of shoot, kill, die, repeat or if there's a way out of it. On the surface, Splinter Zone looks like a lo-fi take on the old Megaman formula. And indeed, you'll immediately feel at home with its jumping and shooting if you've ever played a game starring the Blue Bomber. It emulates the classic's basics just right and even improves on them in some ways. The controls in particular feel a lot more responsive and precise, which is no mean feat.
It also has one of the juiciest screenshake effects in ages, coupled with some wonderfully intense controller rumbling. It is apparent that a lot of thought went into how the game actually feels to play. (Needless to say, you can tone these effects down or even remove them altogether - but why would you?)
In short: plays good, feels good. Cool game, recommended!

"Write anything, solve everything." This has been the mantra for Scribblenauts since its creation in 2009, and each new installment comes closer and closer to realising this goal. Scribblenauts Unlimited on Steam has taken the "write anything" part to heart, but falters a bit of the "solve everything" side of the equation.
The Steam Workshop support for this game is quite huge. If you can think of an object that the game doesn't recognise (mostly copyrighted content), then it's possible that someone has either created it for you, or some toying around with the game's impressive object editor will make your dreams a reality. Even better, you can upload your creations for all Steam users to enjoy.
As awesome as this is, the gameplay is a tad disappointing. At least, we finally have an explanation for Maxwell's endless search for Starites (the game's MacGuffin). The story acts as a prequel to the series, as Maxwell struggles to retrieve the errant Starites to rescue his sister, Lilly (one of literally dozens of his relatives, all of whom are playable characters), from being turned into stone. This story is quickly forgotten once you start summoning vuvuzuela-playing pink jaguars to fight a winged preposterous black knight riding atop a cowardly telekinetic cybernetic T-rex, with only the occasional interlude reminding you of your main objective.
To retrieve the Starites, Maxwell must help people around the game's expansive world with various problems, from helping an up-and-coming rock band gain a fanbase, to helping patients in a hospital with their various ailments. While its nice to have a large amount of different areas to explore, many of which feel alive with various characters mulling about, I couldn't shake the feeling that I was just playing nicer-looking versions of the DS games' title screens. Worse yet, many of the main challenges don't encourage your imagination as often as you think they would.
Despite these problems, I would still highly recommend this game to anyone who hasn't played the series before. The visuals are crisp, the sheer amount of objects that can be generated is mind boggling (not counting the extensive Workshop creations), and it's still fun to see how each object and adjective interacts with each object in the world.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ Graphics look amazing, even on low-powered laptops
+ Amazing object editor
+ "Write anything": only limited to your imagination
+ Always fun to see object/adjective interactions
+ Nice origin story for Maxwell...
- ...but is quickly forgotten while goofing off
- Worlds feel like glorified title screens from the DS games
- Many challenges limit/stifle creativity
You will kill time.

I don't generally write reviews but I see almost no one bring this up and it bothers me deeply: If you got recommendations on playing To The Moon for including neuroatypical characters, be very afraid.  They (the wife and her friend) are the most interesting part of the game and I found their relationships well-depicted and affecting, but the game's 'twist' and how it is resolved turns the wife into a mere prop for making the dying male character's life more tragic and profound. On top of that, the playable characters act in an irrational way for the sake of forcing more drama (in an Inception-esque scene that's really obnoxious to play through), and in doing so infer that it's worth writing the wife out of existence for the benefit of (other male characters). The concept would be interesting to explore but the way it was handled came across as over-the-top nonsense, not to mention problematic.
The very end pulls it together, but the experience was already soured for me. In a way, it was even more annoying than playing a game with Generic Japanese RPG Plot Featuring Spiky Hair, because it was SO GOOD up until that nonsense. I'll play the mini games that came out to see if the writing has improved any, but I'll probably never play To The Moon again or recommend it to anybody.
