To the Moon is a very special game for so many reasons.
The most important one for me is the following: While some of the Telltale Games managed to evoke strong emotions like anger, frustration and helplessness; To the moon is the only game I ever played that made me so very sad.
But let’s first get the basic data out of the way.
The game was developed in 2011 by a small indie dev called Freebird Games using the RPG maker engine.
It is basically a point and klick adventure but it looks like a Square game on the SNES.
When I reached the ending credits I realized that one person called Kan Gao more or less made this game on his own. It’s his concept and writing and he worked - with a few others - on every aspect of the game, even the musik is mostly composed by him.
This segment is gonna be short: You control the main characters with your mouse and on very little occasions use the directional keys and space to mix it up.
The game controls clunky and sluggish but that is not at all an indicator of quality because it simply doesn’t matter in this game.
There is no combat, there is only exploration, some puzzles and the great interactive story.
The tropes and graphics in the style of 16Bit Era JRPGs put players like me who grew up with the NES and SNES games in a fuzzy nostalgic high that is only affected negatively by 640x480 resolution.
You can play in fullscreen with huge black borders or - by pressing alt+ENTER - in windowed mode.
When I first started the game I was put off by the resolution and the fact that you cannot change itn but I can only urge you to keep playing!
There are a few workarounds, I believe, but what worked best for me is entering windowed mode and using Windows’ native magnifying tool, which is triggered by pressing the windows- and pluskey and then centering on the games’ window.
The pixel art is nice, the character sprites and environments all have a distinctive and interesting character and some places in the world, namely the ones where important parts of the story take place are very beautiful.
Laura Shigihara and - as mentioned earlier - Kan Gao are responsible for the soundtrack, you probably know Shigihara’s work from other game music, the Plants vs Zombies OST for example.
To the Moons music consits mainly of classical arrangements with some synthesizers sprinkled in here and there but most of it is piano centric. The songs are memorable, emotional and really well written and perfectly fit the atmosphere of the game.
Now, if you haven’t played To the Moon yet and are thinking about it: Stop reading now and just play it.
Going into it with as little knowledge as possible is the best thing you can do to thoroughly enjoy it!
At the heart of it all is it’s unique story, it is hard to really talk about this game without spoilers but let me introduce you to the situation our heroes find themselves in.
Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts work as a team for Sigmund Corp., using technology to alter the memories of dying people who wish their life would have taken a different turn or two.
The protagonists new objective is to alter Johnny Wiles memories to fullfill his dream of travelling to the moon.
Rosalene and Watts enter at his last memory and travel backwards through his life to his earliest memories, where they try to implement the urge to become an astronaut to change his complete memories from there on and therefore, his perception of his own life.
But as it turns out, things aren’t as easy as they seemed in the beginning.
Wiles’ dead wife River plays a big role for example and Watts and Rosalene have to figure out how everything is connected and what they need to do complete their job.
Now, this story is in equal parts Sci-Fi and Romance, maybe with a little Mystery here and there and it has a lot of unexpected twists and turns to offer and had my full attention from start to finish.
Kan Gao forged a detailed world with very strong and likeable characters and I quickly became emotionally invested in all of them and it really got to me to see the harsh reality of life as we all know it burn it’s marks into their lives.
I spent roughly 3 to 4h completing the game and enjoyed it immensely.
The premise is philosophically thought provoking and the story arc well thought-out and executed and presented in the perfect length and good pacing.
Dr. Watts’ referantial nerd humor is a welcome counterpoint to the emotional rollercoaster story and gives it all some self-awareness when the cheese starts to drip almost to hard to bear.
If at any point in time, neuroscience could change the memories of a life that has already been lived fundamentally, it’s basically time travel! For that person, there would be no difference, and what a great idea that is to me as a Sci Fi fan!
I guess Kan Gaos main motives in coming up with the story had to be of a philosophical nature though: Existenitialistic ideas permeate the whole game and the hedonistic paradox came to mind when I thought about the fact that wishes and goals very often lose their appeal as soon as you have achieved them.
It’s the same with the Sigmund Corp., their efforts are futile in the end, because fullfilling someones wish doesn’t necessary mean he will find more happiness than he had in his actual life.
And then there is the question of sacrifice: In order to forge new memories, old ones have to go. What is it that actually makes a life worth living and happy and who is able to decide that?
Sometimes happiness can only be achieved by unforeseen measures and through secondary circumstances.
And after all “the ending isn’t more important than any of the points leading up to it” , to quote the game itself.
So, Mr. Kan Gao, I can see a TV series in the near future, Rosalene and Watts played by Kandyse McClure and Joseph Gordon-Levitt or maybe even Michael Cera, just for the Lulz.
I can even provide you with a name: “Billions of lighthouses stuck at the end of the sky”.
I would watch the living hell out of that.

I've seen the board game.  I didn't like it.  I thought the characters looked cartoonish and even in this video game they were odd looking.  I didn't have high hopes for this game but I thought I would try it out anyway.
Playing it...it was like the game walked up to me, looked me in the eye, slapped me and told me to shut my big fat face.
The game is good!
This isn't the typical 3rd person shooter.  In many scenarios you need to think of where you need to move to, stand at, take cover behind...what type of weapon would work best...  You just cannot take the approach of "charge in and kill everything".  You actually need to think.  By the second half of the game you will get used to switching weapons in battle to match the conditions.  You will also be using grenades regularly.  Unlike in a alot of games where I never had to use them at all to finish the game.  BTW, for those who are asking on the myriad of boards....  The Vengeance launcher.  When you fire you can detonate the bomb by pressing "R".  If you fire five, the sixth will detonate the oldest bomb in play.  If you shoot and hit the bomb with a firearm, that too will set it off.  But really, pressing "R" is the easiest.
Also, there are no "health items" in this game.  At the end/start of certain scenarios you are healed.  But in every other part of the game you have to excecute someone to heal or use the rage and hit/shoot people to heal.  At first, I thought this was strange.  But the game mechanic of it is actually quite appealing.  It makes you work to stay alive and not just gobble up potions or etc...
The first thing you will notice about the game is that there is no jumping.  Pressing the spacebar only makes you combat roll.  At first this ticked me off.  But, after playing for a bit, it made sense in the game universe.  They are wearing advanced versions of big, heavy and bulky medieval armor.  So of course they can't jump.  That is why they have the jet packs.
The second thing you will notice is that there isn't the fake, ultra fast reloads you see in most games.  Reloading takes a bit of time.  It really makes you pay attention to your weapon and switch or use your melee weapon.  With your melee weapon you can have various combos depending on which one you pick up.  This was kind of a fun thing for me to try out to emulate fighting games.
The third thing...thankfully...is skippable cutscenes.  If you've seen it once why watch it again?  Unlike in some games I've played here on Steam where you cannot skip the cutscenes...being able to is always a plus and always something I will mention in order to get game makers in the habit of doing so.
Fourth...I had no in game crashes, stutters, drop in FPS or bugs.  Insert a choir of angels singing "Hellelujah!"
Fifth, this is not open world and it will pretty much funnel you from point "A" to point "B".  This wasn't so bad as the battles you would envariably encounter didn't feel repetative.  The game designers did a FANTASTIC job of varying the opponents and creating different environments in order to get you to do things differently otherwise you would die.
Lastly...  I will leave the finer points of the game to the other, better, reviewers on here.  But to wrap it up.  This game was GOOD.  Maybe not great.  But definitely worth the money even if it isn't on sale.  Will I replay it?  Probably not.  But the first run through was good so I would very much consider it.  Even if not, I will leave this game with good memories of it and a feeling of satisfaction in playing it.

It's important to understand what you're buying when you're getting this game.
This is one of the earlier hidden object games in the genre, which has since evolved into more intricate games with plot, inventory, and variety.  It's very important to know that this is almost EXCLUSIVELY hidden object scenes, and very detailed ones (in that these scenes are packed edge to edge with objects), with only a small matching minigame in between levels and one minigame at the end.
If the hidden object aspect of more recent (and more complex) games appeals to you a lot, you may enjoy this game.  If you're actually looking for plot, puzzles, inventory management, and a cast of characters, you probably want to avoid it.
It is an older game and graphically it didn't age well; some objects can be blurry or pixelly and hard to make out.  For the most part, however, the game is perfectly playable and the hint button can be used for anything that's hiding too successfully.  The scenes can get repetitive and it's not really a "play it all through in one sitting" sort of game; I usually would play a level, or a few scenes from a level, at a time as a time-killer.
This is a timed game.  However, on each level I had ample time to find all of the objects in all of the locations and usually ended the level with at least 20 minutes left on the timer (and usually more).  The timed aspect didn't seem to be much of a challenge.
All things considered, despite the sometimes-unclear objects and the repetition of scenes, this is a reasonably-priced time killer that is worth the money for six hours of total gameplay.

This review was first published elsewhere in 2010. I've edited it.
Grandma Rose is a lucky and unlucky woman. She won the big lottery which means she's now very rich but before touching her money, she needs her ticket... And she thinks she lost it. So you're sent by your agency to find it within 12 hours... You're not an ordinary P.I., you're the Mysterious P.I..
Basically, there is nothing extraordinary in the storyline and it's just a background for the game: you're never interacting with the town citizen, you're just visiting places. So, you can't really say if the game is parody, comedy, drama, thriller, etc.. And I can really say that the end is providing a total different answer I've imagined. Was it a good surprise? Yes and no. Yes because of my imagination and no because it's not really an end I love generally.
Mysterious P.I. was a good title but behind, there is no real story and no real ID on who he or she is and even if it's bothering me at some levels, in the end, you're the Mysterious P.I.. It's up to you to give him/her a name, to decide if his badge will show a fingerprint, a male or a female.
Mystery P.I. is nothing else than an HoG with minigames at the end of each level. However, you have two modes: Normal and Unlimited Search.
The Normal Mode is self-explanatory: it's the story mentioned above. Each level is divided in different scenes. The much you advance, the more scenes you'll get to visit. Your goal is to find a list of given items. When you clear a level (in other words, when you have cleared all scenes), a minigame is appearing. It will be always variants of "find the pair", for example, find a pair of the same object but one is depicted in an ancient state and the other in his actual state. You receive a piece of puzzle that would be useful at the end of the game. Each level is timed, which means that all scenes must be visited before the clock shows 00.00.
You should know about the score because it's tied to your rank. I explain: you can climb up a ladder of ranks by scoring points. Each object found is worth of 5000 points. If you're being fast to find them in row, you have a bonus (first is 2500, second is 3500, etc..). An hidden key is also worth of 10 000 points. And if you're clearing the level of all objects (instead of choosing to solve the puzzle when you have between two and four items still in the scenes), you can score a 25 000 bonus points for a perfect investigation. If the numbers are different (without key and perfect investigation), this schema is applying also to the ending puzzle.
And what about the Unlimited Search? Every location visited during the normal story is open and you have still to clear them but here, it's about all the objects.
Graphics are correct: the map itself is clear, the HUD is in my favorite color (blue) and the scenes are well-drawn. Perhaps some scenes are invaded by a lot of objects, like in the Firemen Station, where some objects are difficult to spot because you're viewing a sort of blur but the graphics are at least representing the level you're playing.
The soundtrack is fitting to the game but unfortunately, it's always the same track which is played. As it's not something weird, you're not really paying attention to it.
Also, for some of you, as it's not really an adventure game, you will probably be bored rapidly.
Regarding all these elements, Mystery P.I. can be a little deceiving at the end: a classic gameplay, only one track as soundtrack, no real story behind (no cutscene for example) and perhaps a little too long. But the game is redeeming itself with an unlimited mode, with the fact that you really want to find the lottery ticket because you're curious to know where it is and the fact that the game is at a medium difficulty (you don't have very small objects at least).
I recommend to play it for the afficionados, just because after that, Vegas Heist will improve, in terms of minigames mainly.

Alright, this is the second of the Mystery P.I. games I completely finished, and the third game of this kind I played through. Contrary to the "Lost in Los Angeles" game, "The Lottery Ticket" offers a slightly faster, and more difficult gameplay. While there are no instances when the object to look for is described instead of directly named, there is no option for relaxed gameplay, forcing the player to properly manage time they spend on each site.
Adding to that, I found that compared to "Lost in Los Angeles", some objects blended much more into the background, making it hard to find them, and required me to use the "hint" option more often.
Since "The Lottery Ticket" was made earlier than "Lost in Los Angeles", I suppose that "The Lottery Ticket" still lacked some of the options given by the later games. I think it's quite good that the game gives you limited time only to find everything.
Overall, I still wouldn't recommend this game really. While it did take me more time than "Lost in Los Angeles", it still suffers from the same problems as "Lost in Los Angeles" and "Escape Rosecliff Island", with extremely repetitive gameplay and a requirement to be patient and tenacious to complete the game.
However, since I acquired it in a bundle, it was quite worth it. I'd recommend buying in a bundle and/or when the price is reduced.
I still have two more Mystery P.I. games to complete from the bundle, and will do so in the next weeks. As for the previous two, I will write reviews upon completion.

This review is intended for those who are somewhat familiar with the game but unsure of purchasing/coming back to it. I hope something here will help you decide.
Negative Reviews -
I have played since closed beta. Ever since then, the game has changed and been experimented on a lot. Many players write a negative review when the devs try a feature that is perceived to ruin the game (Myself included). Those people tend to leave the game and their review stays even after the devs correct their mistake. Reviews would improve if those players (Such as me) tried the game again.
Developers -
I and others have criticized the devs for being partial to certain nations or scummy in their ways of dealing with the community. While I believe some of this criticism to be valid, I do not personally hold it against them considering who they are: A tiny indie team working closely with an opinionated and often split community. They cannot possibly satisfy all of us when everyone is asking for something different. I think most players would agree that they do a great job churning out new content and trimming bad mechanics to a very experimental game.
Grind -
A common issue new players have is the amount of time it takes to do anything. It can be daunting at first because it takes hours to sail across the giant map and hours of PVP/PVE to reach bigger, more powerful ships. But is it really so bad? Consider other MMO's and the time that must be invested before you are relevant to your nation/team/guild. In Naval Action, you are relevant and useful from the very beginning. Even as the highest rank, I will very often sail "beginner" ships for their handling and speed characteristics so that I can scout, trade precious small items, or privateer others doing the same thing while possesing the ability to avoid those in larger ships with inferior sailing profiles. This is why many players have alternate accounts. Fresh accounts can own just as many assets as accounts with the highest rank. Skill and ability is really what determines a player's value in Naval Action.
Additionally, the grind as of the recent patch (9/11/17) is very soft. For example, you can easily earn 100k gold from a single 5th rate level mission that is accomplished in ~25 minutes from the moment of leaving port to returning. With 100k gold, you could establish a new outpost, purchase a player-built trade ship, and start a production buildings with gold to spare. XP rewards and the time it takes to rank-up is also much decreased from what it was a year ago. If the grind is what kept you from playing the game, then now would be the time to give it go.
Solo vs Clan -
Players often say you have to join a clan to have fun. In my opinion, this is not true. There are many players who are filthy rich trading, PVPing, and crafting solo. Some of the most fun I have had playing Naval Action has been solo patrolling hostile waters in a Surprise frigate, looking for balanced fights and enemy traders.
Ganking -
It is the nature of Naval Action that you are risking your hard-earned ship or cargo to an unbalanced fight. There are ways to prevent this from happening, such as using fleet ships, paying a player escort, using safe trade routes, or sailing within protected zones, but the reality is that you may at some point find yourself in an unwinnable situation. Personally, I would never wish to see this game become so casual as to fully alleviate ganking. To me, it is an open and free world, where the fun and excitement is derived from the risk of losing and the joy of winning. (Also, I think I have only been actually "ganked" once or twice in all my 800+ hours, so NBD really)
Overall, I believe the game was fun when it first came out Feb. 2016, became bad, and then is better now than it ever was. If you do decide to purchase or return to Naval Action, I look forward to seeing you on PVP Global!

Like other reviews, I want to give this game a thumbs up but I feel it would be disingenuous for me to do so.
Is it a bad game overall? No. It's an early access title being worked on by devs who have taken up the bad habit of trying to use a sledgehammer to balance the game, when they should be using something with a lighter touch.
They're also doing their best to make the game into a ludicrous time sink where players who don't have 10 hours a day to devote to the game will be left behind by those who do. Furthermore, the dev team also seems to be stuck on the creation of "rare" and "exclusive" ships which has no place in an Open World sandbox MMO. That kind of stuff needs to be left to grind-fest theme park games a la Everquest, World of Warcraft, and *insert dime a dozen game title here*
They release a patch with mechanics changes and then in less than a week of testing by the early access players, a completely new overhaul is announced. Really guys? If you were just going to scrap what you just patched in, you shouldn't have wasted the time to deploy it. We understand this is an "in development game" and as such would have been fine with certain changes not being patched in.
Developer attitude regarding the plummeting player numbers is "We're getting closer to the release wipe". While to some degree that may be true, it's not the whole fact of the matter.
Player decline has been more due to the following:
PvP servers turning into carebear PvE servers. Players don't want to PvP because right now good ships are so time consuming/expensive to get that nobody wants to lose them. This is part of why "rare" or "exclusive" ships are a stupid idea in a game like this. PvP needs to be ENCOURAGED and REWARDED. Not DISCOURAGED and PUNISHED.
Rules of Engagement changes that make it very hard to support/defend friendly players.
Excessive amounts of NPC fleets that also exacerbate the ROE changes. Nobody wants to suck in an AI fleet when they're just trying to get in some PvP.
Totally unrealistic number of AI fortifications along coast lines. Again, nobody wants to deal with being shot up by OP forts/towers when they're trying to PvP. I'm sorry but no coastline in the era this game represents was bristling with cannon towers.
Conquest mechanics that actually encourage PvE over PvP. It's faster/more efficient to grind up hostility points to trigger a port battle than it is to do so via PvP.
If this game is going to survive beyond the "release wipe", these problems need to be addressed.
PvP is a (not mandatory)  HUGE aspect of the entire design of the game. In its current state PvP is hamstrung by poor decision making on the devs part.
In one patch my clan went from having 20 active people on during prime time, to 5-10. I know we're not the only ones who've reduced our play time and/or support of the game over the past month.
So, if you're on the fence about this game. Wait until it leaves Early Access and enters "Release". Then, wait a little more and see if it goes on sale. So that way, when the dev team hasn't fixed the problems you won't feel completely violated when you log into ghost town game servers.

Despite still being in early access, it is already one of the most beautiful games I ve ever played.
It is an unforgiving game, a mistake during a battle can turn the tides completely, and a course badly plotted, without considering wind shifts or dangerous zones, could make a 30 min voyage last an hour. But Naval Action doesn´t rush you like other multiplayer games and gives you the freedom to play it at your own time. It´s not hard to recover your losses, and you learn very quickly from the mistakes you make.
While playing I also haven´t felt a lot of pressure to level up. It´s as fun to play with a Privateer or with a Small Trader, as with the huge ships that require higher experience. Small ships are fast and can escape easily from those monstrous floating fortresses, while making fast attacks on vulnerable slow traders. Big ships are more challenging but really powerful and fun to play.
One time I was hunting for Brtish traders. When an enemy player with a frigate appeared in my line of sight, he immediately started to chase me. I was several miles of the coast, but south of my position was an island with a huge area of shallow waters surrounding it. So I, sailing on a Brig and with a huge disadvantage of firepower, and with the enemy controlling the wind, decided to run to this waters where the frigate couldn´t enter. My plan worked perfectly, the frigate once near this waters had to desist the chase.
But then, I realized several other enemy players were expecting me near the island, tired of running I let them engage me, 8v1, I manage to give them a big punch, but they were smart, destroyed my masts and sank me. Totally worth it.
Naval Action is a game that requires patience and planning. But at the same time gives you accelerating and fun moments.
Before you buy, is important that you realize it is still early access, so a there are plenty of things that aren´t finished or polished. But the developers are extremely aware of the players comments and ideas, wich is fantastic.

This review is a bit mixed. While I do recommend this game (Despite early access), I will tell you why and why not you should buy this game.
For starts, the game is beautiful, but can hog a lot of power from your computer. The game needs to be better optimized.
The next issue is the resetting of graphic settings/effect settings. Occassionally, when the game starts, my graphics will default to the highest. A minor issue, but something that so far hasn't been addressed in the reviews.
Another issue is with the current "world generation" as it stands. Right now, everything is beautifully done, and you will enjoy visiting many islands with scenic views. However, there are a few "Biome types" currently, meaning you will run into : lava land, candy land, ice land, tropic land, horror land, desert land, rock land, and china land. (If I missed one, please forgive me. :c)
The other issue with world gen is how it handles certain things. For example, lava will spawn and conflict with water that has spawned. Meaning lava will still be underneath the water. It won't be too hard to miss if you play the game a bit, and if you swim over the water that is over the lava, you will die. (Not that death is currently even a "punishment", but this error in generation does need to be addressed.) Another bug is the issue with some sides of bricks not showing, or being transparent. This means that one side of a brick will be opaque and then the other side you can see the entire underworld skybox through it.
The camera is wonky, but it isn't extremely abhorrent to the point of unplayable. Some notable issues are as follows:
-The camera freaks out in tightspaces. (EX: Using the bulldozer to dig into a mountain will create a space too tight for the camera, and it will spazz out.)
-The camera occassionally gets its own free will and moves of its own accord, specifically noted while terrain/brick editing.
There are many denizens in the game, however only skeletons are aggressive. Others have mentioned this, but for the sake of sanity, they are the only enemies who attack, and they take two hits to kill. I am almost 100% certain more enemies will arrive with updates. But if they don't then... :-\ IDK. Engage sad face.
So to sum up the issues of the game: Sketchy world gen (As expected from early access), and sketchy camera controls, and extremely limited enemy fighting.
Now I haven't played for an extensive period of time, but I do find the game enjoyable as a current time killer, and a long time investment in something different.
The good things this game has going for it, especially for early access, is the extensive amount of props, characters, and editing tools. However, some of these will get stale, especially characters and customizing them. You sadly have only one sect of brix to build with and that is it. And there are a good number of them. However, in the future, there should be more that are acquirable. However, despite this, building is fun and enjoyable, but that and exploration are all there is to the game currently.
THERE IS NO MULTIPLAYER YET. However, there are plans for multiplayer, so says certain websites.
Now onto control bugs.
-Pressing Z (undo in building mode) will not always undo the last thing you did. Fix this bug please.
-Pressing Z (undo in building mode) will occassionally do absolutely nothing but make a sound. Fix this please.
-While in building mode, your floating character will occassionally decide to noclip through things and move around awkwardly. Assume you are a building a castle in a lava biome. There is a high chance your character will go into that lava, and you will hear the painful death sound that is over and over until you move him out of harms way. Also, when you finish editing, your character will fall, no matter where he is. FIX THIS PLEASE. Either make building First person or something. Also the camera can get a bit wonky, but this is rare during my time of playing.
Other note-worthy mentions : Why have brick generation for things underwater, or even let the player see underwater if the submarine doesn't GO UNDERWATER WHAT WHY PLEASE. For this reason alone, I turned texture quality down so the water would be opaque.
The game is early access. This means you are paying, upfront, for an incomplete, almost alpha-esque build of a game. I have heard word on the winds say that the devs are planning for more builds to come out.
This game is currently for people who enjoy walking around, have tolerance/patience for building (This isn't like real life legos, and getting used to the controls can be irritating at times.) and enjoy finding things. Remember, this is a 15 USD price tag on something without a whole lot of anything other than running and jumping around, unless you like to build, and even then that requires the utmost patience and dedication.

To the Moon from Freebird games is quite simply a work of art! In the game you play as Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts as they try to make a dying man’s wish to go to the moon come true.
I simply fell in love with this game, from the start to the end I was going straight from laughing until my belly hurt to sobbing like a giant mess on the floor. The characters all seem very real, they all have unique personalities and flaws which are essential in a story-driven game like this one.
The story itself was very well written, every scene and action added to the story which is probably the reason it only had 3-5 hours of gameplay; depending how quickly you went through the game. There was however very little actual gameplay, mostly you walked around finding objects with memories attached to them so you could go further back into Johnny’s life. However these objects never felt random and always told you more about the characters.
The soundtrack for this game is absolutely breath-taking, it really adds to the emotion of the story and River’s Song will get stuck in your head (I was humming it for weeks). I would definably recommend buying the soundtrack bundle on Steam.
My one flaw is that I feel it is overpriced for £7, for this kind of game I would usually spend £3-£5 so I would recommend waiting for a sale. However Freebird have released two ‘minisodes’ for free as a holiday special.
Overall I would proudly give this game a 9.5 out of 10
If you want gameplay, I’d stay away. But if you want to experience a truly heart-wrenching story, you must pick this up!

To the moon, is an indie game that will take you on an emotional roller coaster. This game with it's story, and execution will make the biggest of gaming men choke up with this beautifully story. Are you ready to ride this roller coaster of feels?
Game play: 5
While this game is a very story driven, it kinda of lacks in any real game play. You run around as one of the two main characters either in the dying old man johnny's memorys or around his house and outside of it.While inside the his memorys you are task to find key pieces to his memorys after each scene that plays out to unlock earlier memorys. Pretty simple, you look for the “shines” that shows up. After each memory chapter you are given a small puzzle of flipping tiles of a picuture to complete the memory. Overall the game play isn't the main focus here.
Story 10
The story takes place with an the old man named, johnny, who is on his death bed with only one wish. To go to the moon.  The two main characters you follow are, Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts who are from the Sigmund Corp. who has technology that altar the memory’s of people. They usely use the technology on people who are dying to grant them one last wish. It is the job of Rosalene, and Watts to altar johnny's memory to send him to the moon. While digging deep into the memory’s of Johnny you find out about his wife who passed away years ago. Who has had mental problems who befriends a light house.  You also find out more about his pass on why he wants to go the moon even though he doesn't know himself. You'll end up meeting other characters from his, from his childhood to his aduit life who plays a big role in his life. With some dark twist.
This game proves that sometimes isn't not always about having the best game play or graphics to have a compelling story to get you immersed in whats going on.
Graphics: 9
This game goes with a 16-bit graphic style, with mostly bright and colorful graphics mix with some dark looking graphics to set up each scene nicely. Ir's like playing a classic Super Nintendo game. They paid attention to details to make sure they where fitting for the story thats unfolding in front of your eyes.
Music: 9
The music is well placed and helps to set the mood for each scene. The music goes hand and hand with the story. They did a great job in matching the music to how they wanted you to feel at that current moment. They also did a great job on the music overall. Having a great story and music can mean all the difference on how well a game like this could do, over all the music mixes well with the story and adds a unique experience that you wont find in many other games.
Final Though:
I found this game one of the best story driven indie games that I have ever played. The story gets really deep and it will touch most peoples hearts, While giving you a lot of overwhelming feelings that you though you didn't have. The story is a sad story, and can make almost anyone cry or at least choke up. I can safely say that I can compare this to the aeris death scene in final fantasy VII when it comes to emotional feelings.
As soon as I started playing. I was immersed in the story with in the first 15 minutes or so. I didn't even want to get up for anything. I only got up one time to use the bathroom, even then I was holding it in for at least an hour before hand. I beat this game in one sitting from start to end. I won't lie to you. I was crying by the end. I remember walking out of my room and my roommates asking why are my eyes so red and I said back to them “im just really tired I didn't get much sleep last night”.
If you are wanting a heavy story driven game, then this game WILL be for you.
There isn't any real amazing game play here but the story makes up for it ten fold. So for the people who are more about action style games, don't bother in picking up this game you'll most likely find it boring and not to your liking.
This game is just overall amazing plain and simple! It's a MUST buy for any story driven game fans out there.
Final Score: 10

Downwell is one of the more frustrating titles I have picked up this year. It gets repetitive quickly, with its limited range of enemies to fight, environments to traverse, and upgrades to unlock. I am also bewildered as to why this game's performance can dip so dramatically at times on my better-than-average PC. I can run GTA V at 60fps consistently, but Downwell chokes and studders when too much is going on on-screen. Totally unacceptable for a 2D pixel game. The enemy hitboxes leave something to be desired too, as my character will often take damage from jumping on enemies from skewed angles. The shopkeeper only stocks four unique items, by the way. Devolver had a flawless record of publishing unique and intellegent games until now.

The first time I saw my cannon balls bounce off an opponent's hull, I knew I was hooked on Naval Action.
Naval Action is an Age of Sail naval combat simulator wrapped in an open world MMO. The game is really centered around, and shines as, a combat simulator that requires true skill, strategic thinking, and sound tactics to be successful. Combat is not a twitch fest and really only a small to moderate amount of manual dexterity and precision is required. However with wind, ship, and munition physics well modeled it's a thinking man's game where patience, planning, and a solid understanding of what works and doesn't work is super helpful.
The devs have done a brilliant job of laying out a long career path for captains in the game as you start with the smallest Cutter and work your way up. Each successive upgrade helps you develop your skills and become more proficient as a captain without dumping you off the deep end. PvP is amazing and a variety of scenarios are available from dueling, attacking traders, port battles, fleet missions, and individual missions. For those who are adverse to PvP a PvE only server is available that offers a solid player experience without the stress and unpredictability of the PvP environment.
On top of all this, the game has a solid economy, trading, crafting, ship building, and most recently inter-nation alliances. The devs are continually improving the game, adding perks, features and new twists while striking a really good balance between being responsive to their player base and keeping the game playable and accessible to all.
Another selling point for Naval Action is the community. The community within Naval Action is one of the most welcoming and helpful I have encountered. Most everyone is willing to answer questions from new players and help them out. Many more senior players will keep a low level ship or two in their inventory just so they can sail on missions with newer players, help them learn, and level up.
Overall Naval Action is an excellent game that continues to improve over time and is well worth your time if you are interested in the genre.

ZHUST- THE ILLUSION SOUL will most appeal to fans of the Devil May Cry / Chaos Legion / El Shaddai games as its enemy, world, and character designs resemble some of the gothic influence of those games, while depicting a strange, dream-like, sci-fi realm unique to itself. This game is VERY rough around the edges, however. From its graphics to its animations to the layout of the worlds, the game isn't the "best-looking" but it all works together into a cohesive whole which fits the game's unique identity.
I personally really like the graphical style, its somewhat sketchy feeling figures have a unique aesthetic. The character faces up close, however, appear for lack of a better word "ugly" at times, especially when they inexplicably seem to contort their face or wink with one eye for no reason. It's unfortunate that some of the animations (most notably your character's running) look a bit wonky. (the developer addressed this in an earlier patch to make it appear less so, but when moving from left to right while running straight ahead your character still kind of jumps from facing forward to facing a 45 degree angle kind of abruptly) the character's default jump animation looks pretty bad as well, but once you unlock the double jump it appears to be more natural.
In combat the game moves smoothly, and the actions you input are pulled off reliably. The game features logical controller support (on Xbox One USB) which makes using your abilities, such as pulling enemies toward you (or yourself toward enemies ala DMC) fluid as you rack up combos similar to DMC's "style" system. You are rewarded with a currency in the game to purchase a variety of upgrades from better combos to a double jump to items to assist you as you navigate the areas.
The levels seem varied and the story is well-presented, including full cutscenes with a variety of characters and frequent, large boss fights that shake up the action.
The level design, while looking quite nice and colorful at certain moments can look pretty bad in others. A pet peeve of mine in games is when there are invisible walls restricting your movement through an area and this game has many of those in its city sections, you just "cant go that way" a lot of the time and while there is some exploration and hidden areas to discover, other areas are simply cordoned off and unexplorable due to these invisible walls, which is unfortunate and breaks some of your immersion in the interesting world being presented.
Despite this game's low price, quite a bit of content is present including the broad storyline, numerous levels, player upgrades, and enemy variety. While at times the game can look a bit "cheap", it's obvious the developer(s) want their product to be received well and are very receptive to feedback and addressing bug issues encountered with the game.
This game was a nice surprise to find! Its world and design are unique, which make its shortcomings in other areas (animation / some low-budget looking sections) less noticable. I would recommend looking up some raw gameplay footage to get a better idea of how it looks in motion (and to perhaps temper your expectations a bit) before pulling the trigger, but I'm glad I did and I hope this game can find its audience.

To be fair I was thinking for a quite long time how to review this game. Over the course of years, major publishers seemingly convinced us that story should be simple so that even 5 year old can understand it, action should start instantly and quality of 3d modelling is a thing that really defines good game. This game is not like that. It's opposite.
Forget about instant action like in Modern Warfare. In here story is the game, you need to explore, examine, talk, read and learn about characters and locations. This takes time. While at the beginning it's taxing to switch from action packed titles into slower narrative, once you pass tipping point you start to realize how flat and uninteresting other games are nowadays.
As you progress through game, you will be surprised not only by U-turns of plot, but also sudden shifts of flavours, from humorous to dark, from sentimental love story to story of personal trauma. And even sudden change in a plot will surprise you and it won't be Dishonoured type, where you knew it's coming, you weren't just sure when it will happen.
Perphaps the most amazing part I realized, is that this game has no violence and yet it's very cruel.
If I compare to in my opinion the best story in game so far Grim Fandango, To the Moon is not there yet. But is very close. While Grim Fandango is close to comedy, this one is more to psychological drama.
I recommend this game for everyone that looks for something new and interesting in gaming or for those that are sick with games that uses story as a justification why you should kill every other character on the map. If you one of them, you won't be disappointed, despite the facts that there a bits and pieces that are not polished to perfection.

I never got around to playing the classic version, but the EE was immense fun both solo and in co-op with a buddy. The art style and music are excellent, and the fights and all the skills at your disposal for controlling the battlefield are very satisfying. They also encourage novel approaches to some of the tougher fights, and definitely reward players who are willing to put a bit of thought into placement and pre-gaming the battlefield in their favor.
The story was a bit nonsensical, but generally in a charming, self-aware D&D adventure kind of way, and the interaction between the two main characters was an amusing (albeit shallow) way to differentiate encounters and dialogue choices. The named companions and their evolving quests were also satsifying, and helped to flesh them out as characters and traveling compations beyond their martial contributions.
This is another example of crowdsourcing done right, and I'm ecstatic that we've entered a new golden age of old-school turn-based SPRPGs. Also, kudos to the devs for releasing the EE for free to prior owners of the original.
But on to the negatives, which will hopefully be addressed in D:OS2:
Some of the puzzles are fun and require creativity on the part of the player, but most are just tedious slogs to find specific objects in the environment, avoid mines and other traps, and boost your perception high enough to "see" hidden doors and the like (sometimes for extra loot, but often to advance quests). I'm sure plenty of other players are more observant or intuitive than me when it comes to this stuff, but creeping around levels mine-sweeping and scoping out potential hiding places is not very fun and takes away from the game's greatest strength: combat.
Also, inventory management, crafting, and bartering prices are a total mess. I'm sure it's been beaten to death in the reviews here, but all its nicities (e.g., easy transfer between characters, bags and pouches for storing things that can also be mounted on your quick bars, arrow crafting, etc.) are overshadowed by just how ridiculously tedious and messy the inventory system is. No shared party-level gold, the need to sell everything from the character with the highest charisma and bartering, the lack of adequate item stacking for many things, an impossible overabundance of junk crafting materials, and a frustatingly tedious crafting system without any batch conversation or other UI changes to streamline the making of stuff.
I crafted things because I felt like I needed to for survival -- not just arrows and grenades, but also weapons and armor due to the lower quality of a lot of the stuff I was finding -- but would have happily done without if I felt like that was an option. I would welcome intelligent simplification of the crafting system, and also a huge reduction in the amount of raw materials that go into making things in the first place.
I would love to see crafting and repairing undergo a shift in D:OS2, where they exist in a parallel, party-wide pool of skills and are always accessible to every character, so long as you also have other required elements (not just the raw materials, but a furnace, whetstone, anvil, etc.). Bartering could be in here too, so that repairing and crafting doesn't become such a tedious time-sink that both forces you to dedicate one of your unused NPC companions the task and leaves you dreading your crafting runs back to the End of Time.
And finally, the AI is both dumb and predictable. The early game was a bit toughter on Tactician difficulty because of how fragile everyone is, but it's not too hard to steamroll most baddies from level 12-15+ as you gain access to better adept and, eventually, master-level skills and spells. I hope that the sequel toughens up the enemy AI, since the game's many skills and spells are a blast to use but so rarely used correctly by the enemy.
In any case, don't let the cons dissuade you here. This was the most fun I've had with a SPRPG in a long time, even with all its rought edges, and I eagerly await both D:OS2 and new properties from these folks in the future.

This game is fantastic. It has an awesome randomly generated world made entirely  out of individual legos that is INCREDIBLY beautiful.
This game has no major flaws (assuming that you like open world exploration games that allow you to collect things to build or generally mess with). However, it has its fair share of minor annoyances.
The first problem you will notice with this game are its menus. They are clunky. Very clunky. There are slight delays, the mouse is huge (And no option in-game to disable it), and things are organized a little nonsensically. When you open the settings page, you can adjust the volume, disable and enable vibration, and change the terrain quality. Then you also have the options of going in further to video settings, and effects settings. Under video settings you have brightness, resolution, vsync, and then texture quality. Under the effects menu you have fsaa, motion blur, shadow quality, bloom, and a few other settings. This splits the settings you are going to be adjusting for performance across 3 different screens. However, note that if you change the terrain quality, it instantly sets all the effects settings to their defaults.
The next problem with this game is its camera. It too is very clunky. navigating the small, narrow hallways of a pyramid is next to impossible as you need to enter the next corridor before the camera properly adjusts, making you walk blindly into anything there. You can't disable the automatic control of this camera, so you leave the game in control of zoom level and various other aspects. You can however manually adjust the camera, but it immediately returns to directly behind your character if you let go of the camera controls for more than half a second (I would love to get a nice view of my character on horseback galloping across the desert, but maybe that is just me). There are also no sensitivity options in the game, which isn't the worst if you use mouse and keyboard, but it is very noticable on the xbox 360 controller.
(Side note: I'd kill to play this game in first person)
Also, this game has some issues with its controls. They are a bit odd (Jump on spacebar, and right mouse tap, but if you hold right mouse it moves camera. But then attacking is f and left mouse tap, but if you hold left mouse you walk to the place). It would be nice if we could rebind them, and it would be fantastic if we could still bind things to tapping and holding the mosue buttons seperately.
Additionally: Often in order to collect studs (The in-game currency) you end up needing to walk around an area to collect everything that an object drops. It can get pretty annoying after a while. It would be nice if the player had a bit of magnetism when it comes to picking them up.
Issues aside, this game has a wonderful world to explore, and the collecting aspect is fairly addicting. The animations are great for building, although I would like to see more variation for the attacks. It is far from the worst game in early access.

A game ahead of its time, Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery EP is a point-and-click (and drag, and listen, and what-have-you) adventure game. It's very slow to start, but the game becomes very suspenseful towards the end and you'll be glad you've stuck with it if you make it that far.
Perhaps this revitalization of the Adventure Game genre is ahead of its time and not easily understood by the more impatient gamers, but I found it to be a magical story. I went in curious as to what this game was (I received it with Humble Indie Bundle 5), and came out with a heavy heart. The emotion at the end really struck me. Is it ?MURDER? possibly, a mystery maybe, but an adventure is a bit much to award this game.  Incredibly slow room transitions make the experience play out much longer than it deserves.  The mini-games do change up the flow but are awkward at best.
Tasked with solving a mystery but exchanging single lines of dialog and never seeing the crime scene is an additional amount of difficulty, especially since determining the murder weapon would be a heck of a lot easier if one could see the wounds on the body.

Despite the game's terribly generic name, I was honestly excited when I first saw this title. I am a fan of murder mysteries and point-and-click adventure games. Murder Mystery Adventure was a disappointment on both counts. While stills make the game look inviting and lush, the pre-rendered 3D graphics are static with a panoramic effect allowing you to rotate in place up to 360 degrees. The very first room of the game, the main foyer, prevents players from turning all the way around, limiting you to 270 degrees. Clicking on anything noteworthy yields either a random PowerPoint transition effect and zoom-in or dizzying animated cinematic through a sometimes incomprehensible labyrinth of hallways and staircases. While the goals of the game are clearly stated in the opening animatic and available for review in the player's notebook, information is not something the developer provided freely. There is one required mini-game that involves a card game of, I think, the game designer's own creation. Even if this is an existing game, no rules are given in-game and the player is  either assumed to be familiar with it already or able to figure it out on their own. This particular mini-game is a point of contention for me because there were many glitches even after the recent update said to resolve gameplay problems. It was painfully tedious to struggle through the required 3 out of 5 full games to get the necessary lockpicks in order to progress. I spent more time here than in any other part of the game, but it was not fun gameplay. Other mini-games included a crossed telephone wire puzzle that hidden behind a non-descript hidden passage, a variation of the marble solitaire puzzle obscure enough to make locating a walkthrough solution quite difficult for those players frustrated and stuck, and a safe cracking game that required background music to be activated in order to play. Speaking of music, I would like to point out that ambient sound effects are not removed when music is deactivated. There is no feature to turn these off. Oddly, one such "sound effect" was a very loud victrola playing a record: not the white noise needle on record sound, but a full volume song with vocals! Other sound effects include creepy laughter and disembodied voices more fitting in a horror game than a murder mystery grounded in reality. There was a living doll, a maniacally laughing jack in the box, a book flipping its own pages, moving utensils in the kitchen... all to add atmosphere to a game premise without a supernatural element. The characters have names reminiscent of a short story from a freshman creative writing class. the layout of the mansion is impractical. Every room is plastered with prints of famous paintings and portraits except the bathroom. Speaking of the bathroom, I had to reach out on the discussion forum to learn from the developer that one key item for the completition of the game was hidden in the bathroom. Although I had clicked on everything in it, going back and spamming the mouse button on the toilet allowed me to "use" the facilities and, from that vantage point, discover a stethoscope that had - naturally - fallen behind the bathtub. This is needed for the safe cracking puzzle. I should note that none of the game's characters are medical professionals. A drinking glass might have been more fitting for a hearing aid. There were several on the table in the dining room. What's especially infuriating about this to me is the fact that similar games discourage players from juvenile humor. Growing up with adventure games, I distinctly remember Laura Bow admonishing me for interacting with the toilet with a reference to the Leisure Suit Larry series. I would never have imagined that a murder mystery game would require that I use the toilet to progress. I investigated the room thoroughly before requiring this helpful hint. Once you've spoken with everyone (including two who will not speak with you until you complete mini-games), found all eight of the remaining weasons in the house (including one locked in a trunk in the kitchen, which you only get the key to by completing a mini-game), discovered the blood stain hidden in one of the eight main rooms of the house, and repaired the telephone line, you may call the police to report the murder. Using process of elimination, you name the culprit whose alibi was not confirmed by any other guest. After all of the frustration, the jerky crawling movement from room to room, and the forced mini-games, you are finally treated to a box of text that reads: "Congratulations! You have correctly solved the crime." It reiterates the solution to this particular game and you return to the main menu to click, no joke, "Sadly, I want to leave this beautiful game." If this game had been made in the hayday of adventure games in the late '80s and early '90s with these graphics, it would have been a masterpiece. Neither gameplay nor graphics are compelling enough for a game that was published in 2016. I bought it as part of a 28 game bundle for $1 and should not expect much for my pennies, but this sells for $7.99 full retail by itself. It is not worth that. Had it been a free to play game, I might have been able to praise it some. It had potential, but this is not something the developers should have ever charged people money for. Please do not waste your money. There are better games out there. Instead, try the retro Gabriel Knight or Laura Bow titles if you like adventure games. Play the Whodunnit? or Clue board games if you like mysteries that require strategy. Ask your toddler to hide your keys and spend the afternoon searching for them if you just want to waste some time. You'd have a more satisfying mystery to solve in the end.

It's a testament to this game that they could have made it look terrible and it would still be a terrific platformer. But instead they also made Ori one of the best looking games I've played on Steam. The only minor draw back is that areas get blocked off if you progress too far without being careful. Pro's
+ five dollars isn't asking too much for what it delivers

+the weapon customization is pretty nice

+tiles for the map are pretty cool
+Strange coin rolling somehow pleasing to the eye

Con's
-besides the norman warrior, not enough weapon customization options.
-enemies can damage you while still rising out of the ground, and for the most part lack indication of attack altogether
-bow ocassionally stops working altogether for the roman archer.
-Animation quality in general is lacking, with the teutonic knight's animation being particularily awful
-not enough enemy variation
-strange bugs in wall texture, and in the case of red pots, gravity.
-Coins despawn almost as soon as they spawn on occassion
-Characters poorly balanced, combat in general seems broken.
-not enough tiles for the only currently available tileset, leading to large amounts of repeating to dungeons
-ocassionally the exit spawns about a room away from the dungeon entrance.
-hits both to and against enemies (warrior,archer,knight) feel unresponsive.
-not enough noise, silent weapon swings, arrows, impacts and the like make for a rather quiet game.
- oh god, the heads of the other people in the tavern

One thing I noticed in the beginning of the campaign was the lack of ammo. Luckily, as you keep playing, you get more weapons, and you'll find more ammo crates too (one crate will reload every weapon in your inventory). In the end, you'll even have trouble emptying your weapons.
Pros :
- You get to be a Space Marine for once, rather than being the inexistant guy that command them
- Variety of melee and ranged weapons
- A nice campaign story
- The servo skulls you find sometime hidden in the map give some extra stories to follow, and some of them were... quite immersive
- There's a Coop multiplayer mode called Exterminatus, in which you fight through a wave of enemies to survive with your mates, or alone
Cons :
- The story is quite short. Despite being good, there's nothing special : it's just okay
- Despite being a Space Marine, you die quite quickly. The only moment you could survive getting surrounded by enemies without any trouble at all is when you're surrounded by grotz.
- I always spend hours and days playing games without problem, but this game seems to be quite aggressive with our eyes. If you intend to play this game, you'll either have to take a break to protect your eyes/prevent seizures, or be really tough.

As an Alpha Minecraft player, I have played my fair share of so-called 'Minecraft clones', so first off let me be clear;
This is NOT a Minecraft clone.
For starters, there is no 'crafting' per se. Merely the opportunity to build nearly anything your imagination can... well... imagine! Whilst being in Early Access, I have been stunned and surprised by the amount of content in this game already. Dozens of vehicles and animals to ride, characters to discover, blocks to find and hidden items and treasure chests to unlock. There feels like there is so much to do and discover already! My wife was sat beside me as I played and we were both thoroughly amused by the animation and humor in the game; it is very charming and adorable. I suffered no performance issues on my mid-spec gaming PC, no lag, no crashes, a few graphical glitches, but nothing game breaking.
There are one or two downsides but, I believe all of them will be resolved by release. For one, the control system is very unrefined. It seems to have been designed with a controller in mind, but even then, it is inaccurate and clumsy. I stuck it out with mouse and keyboard and found that 10 minutes later I was merrily running, driving, swimming and flying myself around the blocky landscapes with ease. The interaction system is a little awkward and will occasionally put you where you do not want to be, but this is usually no more than a minor inconvenience.
Since Minecraft, I've always been on the lookout for a procedurally generated exploration/sandbox game that gives me the same feeling Minecraft did for the thousands of hours I played it...
That 'What could be on the other side of that mountain, or down that cave?'
That drive, the need to explore is what kept me coming back to MC for all those hours, and I feel that drive in this game. It's barebones at the moment, but I think this is the beginning of something wonderful! This is the Lego game I have dreamed about since the early days of Lego Creator. It's finally here!
P.S. I rode a dragon as a yeti and threw apples at a king. If that doesn't make you want this game, then you have issues.

Ok this is my first review and given that I'm taking the time to write one highlights just how good this game is. This game has beautiful graphics and soundtrack with a story so emotional and heartfelt I cried at the end (as in bawling throughout the credits, nevertheless the ending was just famtastic and this game will leave you satisfied) and was close to tears throughout. Sein's voice actor really got across his/her emotions and as a result I was getting teary more than normal! Gameplay is smooth and great and the save system a bit unique - definitly adding a challenge. Particularly early on in the game! Some of the abilities you learn are fairly unique/have never really been used in this kind of game before.
This game does get challenging fairly quickly after the first section, but in terms of frustration it was not. And no game has ever succeeded in that before - normally I'd be swearing! But repeating sections was actually fun, even the section where the tree floods, it's all about practice and knowing the technique. I already love platformers and this has set the bar truely high!
OK, yes, I did get slightly annoyed with some sections as they were quite hard. But honestly, you should not be complaining - try Swordigo, another platformer. Now that is a hundred times harder than this game!
One feature I really liked was the lack of boss battles. There are 2-3 mini-bosses that are fairly easy to beat. But for the final section you have a running sequence/obestecale(?) course which I found far more fun and way less frustrating.
I really have no complaints, the hard sections just take practice and a bit of strategy.
A minor note is that if you notice the sound is acting up, so you are getting crackling, and your computer/laptop is very new. Then your system has probably overheated, as this game is very graphically demanding. So just close the game for about an hour and you should be OK!
Overall a huge well-done to Moon Studios and I look forward to your next project!

One of my favourite games of the past year, Ori is a real stand out.
It manages to be both a beautiful looking game, with each screen looking like concept art. Has a story that is engaging and very touching and completes the set with fantastic gameplay.
For those that don't know, Ori is a very challenging platformer with extremely tight controls (think Super Meat Boy for a close example).
The art design is phenominal, Each screen moves like you are watching an animation, from little details in the foreground to character animations and distant backgrounds, They are all polished to such an extent that each screenshot I took looked like concept art.
To support this incredibly detailed art and animation is a stellar soundtrack. Sweeping orchestral tracks accentuate the scenes and emotionally tinged choral tracks bring together some touching moments in the story.
It is a fantastic package, with some great surprises and new gameplay round every corner. I can see this being on many GOTY lists for 2015.
The short? You really owe it to yourself to play this masterpiece of modern platforming.

This review has gone from initially good, to previously bad, to now good again, here's why.
The new 10.0 wipe/update has breathed new life into this game. Its much more MMO like instead of MMOlite. The reason I say this is that before 10.0 its was EXTREMELY easy to get gold/ships. People were sailing first rates like nothing. Gold wasn't an issue.
Now the game is much more challenging and player driven. Just like in EVE it takes time to get a new ship, in NA it takes time to get a new ship aswell. As how it should be with MMOs.
Many people we're spoiled with the pre 10.0 version of NA. It was much easier as a lone wolf to get anything you wanted. Now it requires a clan, and teamwork, to amass gold and loot. And IMO is a lot more fun and diverse.
Some of the negative reviews  bring up good points, such as heavy initial grind. But a lot of them are just people who wanted a more layed back, casual NA that they had pre 10.0. They will get that when Naval Action Legends comes out this summer (Free for all NA buyers)
That being said, yes getting out of the first ship will take the most time. But after that gold is much easier to aquire. If you enjoy games like E.V.E, Arch age, POTBs, or just enjoy the age of sail setting, then I reccomend you pick this up. Its a fun game that has a lot to offer, and from here will only improve.

Downwell is the definition of videogame design. Everything in it has reason to exist, and it all intertwines to create an incredibly fun and addicting experience.
It only requires 3 buttons to play, and the single focus of the game is to reach the end of the well. While that might seem way too simplistic, it is the reason why the game is so well designed and grabs you from the very beginning.
Shooting and bouncing on enemies is extremely fun and the beautiful genius of the game is that it rewards players who go for the "fun" way of playing the game, while also being more challenging if you do so. It creates a perfect balance between being cautious and wreckless, with the health system being the constant that ties those two together. Health is incredibly vital and every mistake you make will be felt.
The way the game gives you different weapons is also brilliant, because even if you get attached to  certain one, you may feel inclined to swap it for another one who also comes with a health point. This dynamic is what keeps the game tense and engaging, and keeps the game from becoming boring and predictable.
Beating each stage earns you a new power up from a handful of choices, and they all have their uses and advantages.
The presentation of the game is great, with a very retro style 8-bit aesthetic that manages to give alot of charm to the enemies and environment, and the color is used to great effect to make the objects of interest stand out and pop up.
I came into this game with the mindset that it was just a mobile game, with every kind of pejorative aspect people seem to atribute to that name, but I was surprisingly glad to find out it was one of the best games I played in a while.
Really the one thing I can think of that might be a negative is that there doesnt seem to be any kind of narrative incentive to make you finish the game? Was my time spent here really worth it? *watches the post credit scene*. No, that was definitely totally worth it for sure.

911: First Responders is one of those little gems you pick up in the “dollar bin” not realizing what you’ve found, let it sit on your shelf for a few months, and when you finally get around to playing it you almost feel like you owe it an apology.
While this isn’t the best emergency response game I’ve ever played it is one of the most well rounded.  In a 911 title you’d expect to have units from the Police, Fire, and Medical fields but this game goes further.  It also brings in services like clean-up wreckers and specialty vehicles.  In addition, all of your vehicles have their specific roles to play in combating the events that occur in your city.
If I had one thing to nitpick about this game it would be that it’s too busy, specifically in the “nonstop” mode.  This mode is almost like a sandbox where you are given event after event to deal with.  The problem here is that occasionally an event is so complicated, like a bush fire, that it takes you a while to deal with it.  While combating that bush fire you may end up getting assigned another fire, or a police action.  This leaves you either losing ground in your complicated task while you deal with the others, or ignoring the others and completing your complicated task.  The limit on how many vehicles you can have active at once also hinders the ability to deal with multiple emergencies
Things get a little better in multiplayer mode, but not much.  Yes, there is a multiplayer mode.  In this mode you and a friend can tackle emergencies in the same city.  The only downside here is that the ability to dispatch new vehicles is turn-based.  Players have to have good communication and use excellent team work in “passing the torch” so their partner can help dispatch vehicles to emergencies without delay.  Once the vehicles are on the map, however, you don’t need control of dispatch in order to maneuver them around.  You do, however, need to return them to headquarters so vehicles are available for other emergencies.  I found it was advantageous to have one player act as the dispatcher and collecting up vehicles that were finished their tasks, while the other focused on the on-scene rescues.  As stated earlier though, communication is paramount to success!
Graphically this game is pretty good.  The game plays out in a somewhat 3D map view of the entire city.  You can easily use the mini-map to jump around the city, or scroll off the side with your mouse.  The level of detail is pretty good, as you’ll find yourself needing to access everything from equipment in the vehicles to fire hydrants.  Doors have to be broken down.  Hostages have to be rescued.  Fire victims have to be rescued from buildings.  Injured have to be extricated from vehicles and treated by medics.  It’s a fairly involved game for the graphics being so “zoomed out”.  I never really found myself fighting the camera, it was fairly easy to control and rotate around structures.
Sound in the game got somewhat repetitive after a while.  There is one announcement for each type of emergency, and it’s repeated every time the specific emergency happens.  Music is fast paced but also gets a little repetitive at times.  Still, it suits the theme of the game and brings in a little bit of excitement.
All in all… I have to refer to my opening statement.  When I got this game I wasn’t expecting much, but I was pleasantly surprised.

SB:S&S EP is a fine example of a game that-is-so-good-yet-hard-to-describe-why, because it just IS.  The premise is simple enough, you are a female Scythian warrior on a woeful quest to rid the world of an ancient evil that lurks below. Yet there is so much more to this title. The music is some of the greatest I have heard in an indie game. It fills the surroundings and oozes with life. Sound effects play a key-role in puzzle solving and give ample combat hints to dodge an enemy attack. The puzzles are also cleverly constructed and are not hard to solve, yet leave you with a pleasant feeling after doing so. 'The graphics are 8bit and we are fine with that.' If you want to have an immersive experience that will stick with you for a long time, this one is worth picking up.

In a sea of indie games ranging from bad to mediocre to amazing, some titles have really stood out to me. This is one of the games that left a lasting impression in the best of ways. This game does a great job of creating a stylistic experience that is always entertaining, despite being designed for touch devices and having a gameplay difficulty aimed at the most casual of audiences. The game excels mostly in its audio and visuals. The game looks fantasic. The stylized sprites look great and really look smooth in their animations, not to mention the beautiful environments that are augmented by some great lighting. The audio is even better. This game features a soundtrack that is beyond great. The music fits perfectly with each scene and transitions are seemless making the soundtrack is worth listening as a stand alone experience. Even the voice acting and dialog are great. The dialog is witty and the VA adds a little extra spice when it is rarely used.
This game is a great experience for the price and time.

Downwell is a simple game, and this simplicity makes it a highly addictive arcade-shooter-style game.
In this game you decend down a well, using your gun-boots to shoot enemies below you on your way down. The goal is to see how far you can get and/or how high a score you can get. The simplicity of the controls makes it easy to get into, but the ways you can interact using said controls can get a bit complicated. Your gun-boots have a limited number of bullets, and you reload automatically when you land. However, there are certain enemies which can be jumped on (this is made clear by the colors - red is dangerous, white is safe), and in addition to killing them, jumping on an enemy will also reload your gun. This way, you can juggle back and forth between shooting enemies that can't be jumped on and reloading your gun by landing on safe enemy's heads. How many enemies can you kill before having to land on the ground? The game will reward you for combos with exp/gems, which adds an addictive layer of complexity to the gameplay.
In addition to the core gameplay machanics, there are are also gems to colelct which can be used to buy stuff at stores, which sell extra health and extra ammo slots. There are different weapon types to pick up, Contra-style (some of which are bundled with health, which can create some fun choices - this gun I know I don't like, but should I take it anyway to get the extra heatlth?). At the end of each section, you get to pick from one of three random free upgrades. You'll never know which three you'll get to choose from, but you do get to take your pick from the three presented to you. Lots of fun power-ups and upgrades to keep things interesting.
At the begining of each round you have your choice of "style" which are slightly differing playstyles to pick from (for example, one might give you more health to start with but fewer upgrade options after each section). These will need to be unlocked using exp, which get after each round, based on how far you got, how many combos you made, etc. They add a little variety to the game, letting players choose a prefered play style.
Another thing you'll unlock with exp is color pallete swaps, which are super fun. The game is by default only three colors - white, black and red. Black is background, white is platforms/safe parts of enemies to touch, and red is gems/unsafe parts of enemies to touch. The pallete swaps just change what these colors are, which is a fun little aesthetic touch. Be warned, though - some of the color palletes actually make the game harder. You'll know what I mean when you try them out.
Overall, this is an excellent little game and a steal for the price. I highly recomend it to anyone in search for a high-action, highly-addictive distraction with an elegant balance of simple controls and deep gameplay.

+ Fun fast-paced addictive gameplay.  The goal is to make it as far down the well as you can without dying. There are many enemies that you must dodge or defeat by landing on or shooting them with your Gunboots.
+ Many roguelike elements which add a great deal to replayability such as being able to select a perk at the end of each stage which will make every run different from the previous.
+ A good selection of weapons that add a nice sense of variety to each run. These will change your default gunboots to things like a downward laser, shotgun, machine gun, and so fourth.
+ Enemies drop gems which can be used at the shop to buy health or additional energy (ammo). This adds a nice strategic element to the game. Do you slow down to kill all the enemies to collect gems, or do you avoid them completely to avoid being hit?
+ Very challenging. This is the type of game were you will constantly improve overtime as your reflexes, knowledge, and skill grow.
+ Surprisingly enjoyable visual style. The game has a very minimalistic retro style mainly consisting of only 3 colors (you can unlock additional color pallets)  At first I thought I'd be turned off by this, but red mixes with the black & white environments quite well and the developer did a great job creating a variety of enemies and obstacles.
- I was a bit annoyed that many enemies can fly from above down toward you (bats, ghosts, etc.) and you do not have the ability to shoot up or sideways.
- No real end-game goal or story objective. I feel like there should be a reason for jumping down the well.
