To the Moon is a good game. It's a good game because the release trailer marketed it as this epic, intricate, dramatically sad & vastly musically infused game. Whereas... it really wasn't. The game has some great “oh” moments in it. None of which I'd mention because the way in which you are introduced to them is part of the experience. To the Moon is a hard game to review without giving away too much.
Simply put; it's what I consider to be at the helm of RPG Makers capabilities. There's some unique features, good (although repetitive and short lived) music, and a nice addition of custom textures. There's also a decent story at heart, but not what the trailer was hinting at.
My only major problem with the game was the volume of Animorph references. There were just to. Damn. Many. At least for my taste. As well as a fair share of another book (not spoiling this one) but it sort of applies to the game.
Excluding the story, TTM had some pretty good dialogue. It's a bit topical, so 5 years from now we might have to think about the sayings and phrasing, but otherwise it was solid and funny. I can't recall finding any typos throughout the game so that's just another plus.
All in all TTM was good. Its wanting to be something more than what it is makes me feel like the developers should have enlisted a more suitable game engine. Imagine playing Heavy Rain, or Beyond: Two Souls on RPGM- just doesn't do it justice. That being said, for the price I paid (I think $4) I got my monies worth and am pretty happy. I won't be playing it through again anytime soon but it's a game I'll be letting friends take a whack at!

Pick this game up if you like these types of games and especially if you have a friend to play them with.

I've been playing Total War games ever since I stumbled upon the first Rome in an internet cafe more than a decade ago. And I've had an interest in Warhammer ever since a friend showed me the first Dawn of War (okay, it was 40K, but it was an entry into the IP) at around the same time. So, it shouldn't come as a surprise that the two combined sparked my interest.
What was surprising was just how much the first Total Warhammer outdid my expectations. Every faction had a brand new feel to it, every DLC felt like it added something significant, and mod support meant lots and lots of replayability thanks to all the fun tweaks the modding community brought to the table. It wasn't perfect, the sieges in particular could stand to improve, but it still was good enough for me to sink 800ish hours into it.
So, when the sequel was coming out, I had high expectations. And when I finally got to play it, all the hype I'd accumulated felt vindicated. It was everything I'd enjoyed in the first game, but more. The campaign mechanics and faction playstyles felt more unique and added their own challenges, battles felt more epic, the Vortex campaign itself added the kind of urgency that forced me out of my comfort zone and into adventure, the climate system finally meant I could form an enormous empire without needing mods. My only real disappointment was that occupied settlements now didn't get changed to fit the occupying force, which made painting the map somewhat less satisfying, which was a shame, because I liked the new settlement skins better than the old ones (they look more like towns/cities and less like Monopoly houses).
Then the Mortal Empires came, and it was the same way, but more. Simultaneosly more impressive and more disappointing than the base game. The New World and the Southlands had pieces cut off, the parts that did remain admittedly expanded (a fairly decent compromise, considering just how awkward a shrunk New World would look on the map, and how absurdly huge a full-sized Southlands would be when compared to the Old World, but still disappointing if only due to high expectations); the Old World factions felt like they were lagging behind the new, with Norsca and the foundation update not yet implemented. But, everything excluding these caveats still managed to exceed expectations.
Overall, very much recommended.

My review was really different when this game was in early-access, so I thought that maybe I should update it.
PROS:
*Character Costumization - at first you dont have many choices.... but once you find that hat, pants, shirt, you wanted, things can get really interesting -
*Fully LEGO Open World - the game is totally done in LEGO Bricks, from the clouds to the caves, enabling possibilities to build what you want to, in the way you want to -
*Brick-By-Brick Building - somethimes it really sucks building stuff brick-by-brick (in the case of large builds), the Copy/Paste tool helps a lot in this sense, but not everything can be copies because of the low precision it has to paste the copied bricks... still, it can be really fun to build what you want to -
*Game Animations are awesome - in the terms of character animations, the game fells really natural -
*Textures - bricks textures really feel like they were made of plastic, which makes the game closer to reality (HIGH Graphics Setting) -
*Infinite Worlds - you can just keep creating more and more worlds
*Multiplayer - go ahead, play with your friends, get crazy :P -
CONS:
*Collision Bugs - yes, there are lots of collision bugs, an example, would be you falling throught bricks while inside caves -
*Movement Bugs - somethimes after getting out of a vehicle that is not perfectly aligned with the ground, you might end up walking upside down... -
*Floating Chests? - somethimes I find some floating chests in caves... not much of a problem, but you will have to use the terrain tool to get to the chest -
*Not fair Quest Rewards - quest rewards are really basic, some coins, coins, coins, and item here, or a gold brick -
*Really Small Story - the game doesnt have much of a story, just a basic "collect gold bricks until 100" and a narrator that explains how much gold bricks you need to get the next tool or world size -
What it still needs:
*Bigger story mode - somethimes a game that is just sandbox all the time really sucks -
*Better quests - do I have to explain this one? -
*SPAAAAACEEEEEE Building - really, you have a spaceship and you can't build a starbase? -
The game is really good and you can have a really fun time if you ignore the bugs (which some times really sucks) and the small story mode. ( Dont forget to play with your friends )

Do you enjoy a nice neon-paletted future where corporations rule and humanity is kept down by an oppressive government? Well then you'll like this, provided you don't want the neon palette. This is the vision of a future where humanity is past its' prime and is trying to fend off the slow decay of time; all while fending off hordes of aliens and daemons. The grimness of this universe is a refreshing twist, even after several decades as a series.
Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine puts you in the boots and bulky armour of one of the Imperiums' chapters of Space Marines. If you like sitting behind a wall and occasionally firing over the wall, then just stop there. In this game, there ARE no walls (metaphorically speaking of course)! YOU are the wall. You are a shield for the weak and a sword to be swung by the powers that be. As much as the game preaches that life is the Emperors' currency; you are a sturdy block of gold, in a world populated by pennies and pound coins. So what makes you so valuable, apart from the shiny aspect of your nature?
You are a block of Gold. Let's do a comparison. I want you to drop a penny onto your fingers while they are on a desk. Didn't hurt, did it? Now; drop a big block of Gold. If you actually did, I applaud your delusion of invulnerability, but I'm not going to kiss your boo-boo better. If you didn't; you're smarter than the person asking me to kiss the boo-boo. You see, logical thought dictates that there is a big difference in the damage a penny and a Gold Brick can do. You play the heavier of the two objects; that most delightful bringer of death. You are a big stompy thundering cannon comprised of flesh and muscle, located securely behind an energy shield and a hell of alot of metal. You don't fire a little 9mm pistol as you do in so many other titles. With your bulkier stature, you should be able to wield more mighty weapons and this game will allow you. Ever wondered what happens when a rocket propelled explosive shell (with a diameter of nearly an inch) comes into contact with the face of a 6 foot Ork, armed with naught but a club and a suicidal disregard for the laws of physics and mortality? If you answered "red?" then the klaxons in your room, set to ring with the sounds of victory when you are correct (at least if you're as egocentric as I) should be deafening you in reward for your foresight.
In a world full of games with lots of brown or orange; this game decides that red is still a viable colour. VERY viable. In fact, so viable that often times you will encounter pools of red where once a green enemy stood. If you are discouraged by blood, this game isn't for you. If you like blood, this game delivers it in such vast amounts that even the least sadomasochistic of us would still require the unbuttoning of the jeans to alleviate the tightness the combat produces. While I recommend this game to women as well, this game has an undeniable reek of man about it. I would be surprised if the word "testosterone" was not included once in every five lines of code written for the engine. While there is a brilliant plot behind the title, it isn't one that I'd recommend you buy the game for. The plot isn't what you want in a game, is it? Plot is a nice addition but gameplay is what differentiates a game from a movie or book and this is a shining example of that ideology. You fire rocket propelled shells from a fully automatic death-cannon; when you aren't lobbing balls of corrosive plasma into the faces of a tiny little green fellow. But range is only a part of the game. To regenerate health, you are not allowed to cower. Your health is tied to your efficiency in combat, as it drops when your shield is depleted and raises when you execute an enemy in close combat. To replenish your red goo, you need to turn your foes into red goo, and presumably the splat perks your character up enough to make him healthy again. Still makes more sense than being eaten by a dog in an open world game and healing up by pulling a bullet out of your left arm. It sounds better too. There is a definite booming sound behind your guns and your mighty melee weapons sound vastly different when they smash into metal in comparison to tearing through flesh. Your chainsword revs pleasurably as you swing it and your heavy bolters sound exactly as the name makes you believe. They sound heavy, as if they were firing bolts.
Now let us discuss multiplayer. Six big stompy fellows clash against six big stompy fellows and there are three types of big stompy fellow you can be. You can be a tactical marine, who lumbers across the battlefield with some medium power ranged weapons. The assault marines jet around the battlefield with jump packs, slamming with a mighty force into the ground before spinning their melee weapons viciously to rend the flesh of all who oppose them. If you are more of a heavy fellow, the Devastators will fit you perfectly. Armed with the biggest weapons of all three, they stomp and wield death at range. They are so heavily equipped that instead of shoulder charging an enemy to interrupt the swing of their sword; they kick them. Even as you walk, the camera shakes to give you the true sense that you are heavy, gifted the power of a ton of metal and muscle. The ground never seems to sit still when you introduce twelve armoured Goliaths upon a map.
This is a game of David versus Goliath; except this time, you play Goliath and logic wins over storybook morality. Big stompy fellows don't get stopped by a stone, they club the sling wielder into the ground with fist and foot.

I've been searching for quite a long time for an Age of Sail game with a realistic touch, for those of you that rather skip the details, I found that in Naval Action.
An open world, pvp and rvr oriented Age of Sail game. You’ll ruffly be able to captain all kind of ships from late 1600 to early 1800. Everything from shooners and cutters to first rates ship of the line will be craftable.

Open world is centered on the carabians. Ports are distributed between 8 Nations : Danemark-Norge, France, Great Britain, Pirates, Spain, Sverige (Sweeden), United States, Verenigde Provinciën (Netherland). By default, all theses nations wage war among one another, but diplomatic pacts gathers them into « blocks ». Theorically, they are infinite ways of playing the game :
Trading, port battles, « Guerre de course » (trade-hunting), boat building, smuggling, governing (Most nation partly unite around a player-made « council ») etc.
Sailing in the open world is basic : You will need to handle the wind, but not your sails. But once you are in battle, using sails, wind, inertia etc… is part of the game. Outmaneuvering your opponent will often mean victory against a better armed and armoured opponent.
It all depends what you take out of it. The game itself offers a lot of time consuming things, sailing from one point to the other is time consuming in fact ! If you want to go into politics, port battles, trading all together, then yes, you will need time.
But game, in my opinion, also sutes players with small to medium playing times. To illustrate this, I will quote a answer I made to someone complaining about the « sailing times » on the official forum :
One last thought that made me, without a doubt, like this game : The developpement Team behind it. A 8 men small Ukrainian development team working there♥♥♥♥♥off to make this game with us. They answer forum posts and suggestions on an everyday basis, help the comunity organise major events, add content every month etc.
This is still an early acces, and you’ll most likely find a few bugs from time to time. Yes, the game may not be perfect, but what game is anyway ? I’ve enjoyed and played this on Alpha and Early acces for more time then most full-out AAA game.

To the Moon is a good game. It's a good game because the release trailer marketed it as this epic, intricate, dramatically sad & vastly musically infused game. Whereas... it really wasn't. The game has some great “oh” moments in it. None of which I'd mention because the way in which you are introduced to them is part of the experience. To the Moon is a hard game to review without giving away too much.
Simply put; it's what I consider to be at the helm of RPG Makers capabilities. There's some unique features, good (although repetitive and short lived) music, and a nice addition of custom textures. There's also a decent story at heart, but not what the trailer was hinting at.
My only major problem with the game was the volume of Animorph references. There were just to. Damn. Many. At least for my taste. As well as a fair share of another book (not spoiling this one) but it sort of applies to the game.
Excluding the story, TTM had some pretty good dialogue. It's a bit topical, so 5 years from now we might have to think about the sayings and phrasing, but otherwise it was solid and funny. I can't recall finding any typos throughout the game so that's just another plus.
All in all TTM was good. Its wanting to be something more than what it is makes me feel like the developers should have enlisted a more suitable game engine. Imagine playing Heavy Rain, or Beyond: Two Souls on RPGM- just doesn't do it justice. That being said, for the price I paid (I think $4) I got my monies worth and am pretty happy. I won't be playing it through again anytime soon but it's a game I'll be letting friends take a whack at!

This is one of the best examples of a game with VERY simple mechanics, but uses them to their fullest.  The game is deceptively simple, and will suprise you with its difficulty.  The controls are tight and focused, and the visuals are clear and unambiguous.  This straight-forward design provides a clarity that forces you to own every mistake you make.  When you do die (and you will die), it'll always be because you messed up many times.  You will then learn from those mistakes, and improve.  The rush of speeding downward as you blast your way through hordes of enemies is incredible, and getting huge combos brings an immense feeling of satisfaction.  That combo system makes playing through earlier levels an absolute joy as you build huge combos that'll give you the resources to tackle later levels.  The various Styles mix up gameplay in unique ways, and due to how quickly you unlock them all, it never feels like the game is holding any of its mechanics hostage.  Every unlock after that is entirely comsetic palette swaps, which gives the game an old-school charm.  The music is fantastic, and the way it syncs up to your first contact at the start of every level provides not only simple satisfaction, but also serves as feedback when attempting the "Ground Allergy" acheivement.  The game is just full of these clever little desgn decisions.  In conclusion, this game is incredibly well designed and inexpensive, you really don't have any reason not to buy it.

Having played this a bit, I can say that this game really needs a continue mode. Some choices are a bit too rigid and final, and it is not fun to replay just because you didn't realize how draconian the game can be.
There needs to be more games like this of course, and the execution can be better. Ultimately this is a game about the psychology of "what is normal," with a little "awareness of how life is tough" thrown in. However, it could go further in allowing greater variation in life stories. Some choices seem to lead to the same result every time, where they would serve better as likelihoods. This limits playthrough value.
Without giving spoilers, there are some options that will always lead to get-rich-now situations if taken. Life isn't like that, and this damages repeat playthrough value. Most choices are therefore not really different for different protagonists. The game becomes routine and mundane very quickly.

Im a very fast paced kind of gamer. I like big action shooters like the Battlefield or Overwatch and i like fast baced skill based games like Battlerite and Dota. Yes i do love my RPGs aswell but only if the gameplay is exciting enough to get me hooked onto everything else.
Its my love of action packed gameplay that kept me clear of Divinity Origional Sin for such a long time. The word turn based, and the term "dense with interesting dialog options and discussion" put me off even attempting to try the game even after multiple sales. I went far away and instead stuck to my usual, Skyrim, Borderlands others like this.
One day though a massive sale went on the entire series including the Enchanced Edition of Origional Sin which boasted full camera rotation, new content and full voice acting. With all the gear complexity i loved about RPGs and a setting a could defintely get myself immersed into i thought "why not".
Ill admit the first few hours bored me. Theres a slow early period as the game brings forth the new setting and teaches the game to you. This early period is also surprisingly punishing as there is no handholding in this game. At all. This was something that, being a young gamer, i was not used to. It was intimidating and confusing being thrown into a world with no guidance and having to rely on "turns" to keep me alive.
However looking back now 70 hours in, im so glad there wasnt any. This game taught me the virtues of patience and it allowed for the most rewarding exploration i have ever experienced in an RPG. There was a need for me to explore and this constant drive to discover the next piece of the puzzle soon kept me hooked. Even with this amazing exploration i thought the slow pace of the game with a unfamiliar classic style of RPG leveling and gear, and a turn based system would completely turn me off. However quite the opposite. I now see why people of the era love to see these types of systems return. I now understand why everyone gets so hyped about a gameplay formula that is so old and classic. Because its amazing. The turn based combat was, in a lot of ways, more action packed in this game than in games like Skyrim. The leveling system had depth and importance and the gear was well designed, balanced and exciting to come accross.
For a game like this to engage me so much was a surprising and eye opening experience and a true testiment to incredible game design. If you are like me and find yourself intimidated or bored during classic turn based RPGs, unable to take the small step needed to immerse and invest yourself in this genre. This is definetely the game to start with.

First thing's first. See that title? Sword & Sworcery is an EP, not a game proper. It is music foremost and a storytelling experience second.
Despite what you may think and hear, this game is far from pretentious, and one of few examples where people will point to when they say that games can be art. Here is one so accutely self-aware that it nearly transcends it.
At its base, Sword & Sworcery is a wacky adventure tied onto a pretty nifty soundtrack. It is an experiment in modern storytelling and game design. A fruitful experiment, infusing music with puzzles and battles and decidedly not vice versa. The visuals, as you can already tell, are beyond stunning.
S&S is a game that tells its story almost in a sarcastic, tongue-in-cheek manner. At risk small of ruining the surprise, I will say this: it is exactly this silliness that both allows you to come even close to taking it seriously, and the cleverness that makes you appreciate it all the more.
If the plot were presented in a serious manner, few would take it seriously and it would just seem as pretentious and obfuscated as Braid. It is the humour and quirkiness of the title that makes the story penetrable at all. Despite the jests, the story is even more compelling if you take it as being honest.
Now here's the sad bits: this is not meant for the PC at all. Find yourself a touch screen copy of this game. It is not meant to be completed in one or two sittings. You are meant to pace yourself and take it in chunks, and you'll be more likely to finish the game that way.
Missing the ending is something you do not want to do. That is when everything sinks in.

My review was really different when this game was in early-access, so I thought that maybe I should update it.
PROS:
*Character Costumization - at first you dont have many choices.... but once you find that hat, pants, shirt, you wanted, things can get really interesting -
*Fully LEGO Open World - the game is totally done in LEGO Bricks, from the clouds to the caves, enabling possibilities to build what you want to, in the way you want to -
*Brick-By-Brick Building - somethimes it really sucks building stuff brick-by-brick (in the case of large builds), the Copy/Paste tool helps a lot in this sense, but not everything can be copies because of the low precision it has to paste the copied bricks... still, it can be really fun to build what you want to -
*Game Animations are awesome - in the terms of character animations, the game fells really natural -
*Textures - bricks textures really feel like they were made of plastic, which makes the game closer to reality (HIGH Graphics Setting) -
*Infinite Worlds - you can just keep creating more and more worlds
*Multiplayer - go ahead, play with your friends, get crazy :P -
CONS:
*Collision Bugs - yes, there are lots of collision bugs, an example, would be you falling throught bricks while inside caves -
*Movement Bugs - somethimes after getting out of a vehicle that is not perfectly aligned with the ground, you might end up walking upside down... -
*Floating Chests? - somethimes I find some floating chests in caves... not much of a problem, but you will have to use the terrain tool to get to the chest -
*Not fair Quest Rewards - quest rewards are really basic, some coins, coins, coins, and item here, or a gold brick -
*Really Small Story - the game doesnt have much of a story, just a basic "collect gold bricks until 100" and a narrator that explains how much gold bricks you need to get the next tool or world size -
What it still needs:
*Bigger story mode - somethimes a game that is just sandbox all the time really sucks -
*Better quests - do I have to explain this one? -
*SPAAAAACEEEEEE Building - really, you have a spaceship and you can't build a starbase? -
The game is really good and you can have a really fun time if you ignore the bugs (which some times really sucks) and the small story mode. ( Dont forget to play with your friends )

This game is friggin awesome! It is the lego game everyone has waited for. Because now! FOR the FIRST time, EVERYTHING, IS,  literally LEGO!!! WHOOOOOOOOOOOOooooOOOOoo
Seriously though this game is really fun. And looks incredible.
There are 2 main "modes" you could say to this game.
MODE 1. Adventure.
This mode plays out a lot like any normal lego game. This includes movement and interacting with your environment. Just like any lego game you can bash various structures in the world to get coins. These coins are used to unlock more characters and virtually anything you find in the game.
The more you wonder around the more you discover. Basically any person, animal. vehicle, and small structures in the world can be be unlocked and placed back down again anywhere you want. At least once you have discovered them.
There are several different biomes which all have unique things that spawn in them.
MODE 2. Building.
Since every little cube in the world is rendered as an individual lego brick it allows you to customize EVERYTHING! There are some very helpful tools to change large chunks of the world very rapidly. Which means you can make mountains out of hills in a mater of seconds. Of course you can also build block by block to make anything you can think of. Whats even better is that anything you build can be saved into a library of sorts and put down anywhere else in the world.

Visuals and Sound:
Very nice atmosphere, amazing art and great soundtrack.
Controls:
Smooth and very responsive. A controller is necessary in my opinion.
Difficulty:
The overall difficulty was good, some challenges but after a few tries I usually made it through. The chase scenes are very unforgiving though, pretty much any mistake leads to death, it's not always clear where to go (especially the last one) and the time limit makes it somewhat frustrating.
Length:
It took me about 7 hours to complete the game (not 100%, missed a few things) and I spent a decent amount of that time backtracking to get some upgrades. Without that it's probably about 4-6 hours of playtime, depending on how often you have to repeat stuff after dying.
Story:
Original and creative ideas, while the story is good it's not very deep.
Puzzles:
There are puzzle elements in the game. not the 'pull this lever than that one than put something on the pressure plate' kind, but a lot of rooms have some objective (especially in the last area) which isn't always obvious at first sight. there are no hard puzzles, but you will have to think a bit about how to get through somewhere quite often.
Upgrades:
Lots of useful little upgrades for your powers. I don't particularly like the upgrade system, as I needed to take traits I had no interest to get to the ones after. I only missed 2 upgrades at the end, so it's not too restrictive.
Replayability:
For achievement hunters there's tons of stuff to explore.
Overall impression:
Very enjoyable game, the challenging parts take either some stubborness to try time and time again or great reflexes to get them on the first few tries. if you enjoy or at least don't mind having to try stuff out and retrying the game is definitely worth playing. It is rather fast paced and needs some reflexes, so it's not exactly a relaxing game.

Ori and the lind forest is a truly amazing game.
This platformer made me skip much needed sleep until i cleared it and watched the ending with an very relieved "Awww!". Only few other titles bring tragedy, encouragement, intuitive and challenging gameplay and such adorable creatures into one great game. Great storytelling, beautiful handdrawn graphics, intruiging physics and riddles, inviting to explore the world and challenging the player to find all the secrets are only a few points in this game that made me pull all-nighters over and over again.
The really cute and well animated protagonist Ori starts its story in a seemingly doomed world with only a spark of hope(literally!). Soon the way becomes more visible and so is the gameplay. Not bombarding the player with crazy combos for their controlling skills, but introducing more and more movement options and features over the whole game make this an excellent title for newcomers.
The gameplay is fluent and only a few parts at each end of the story arcs made me swear and curse my controller (I had to buy a new one during the first clearing run... ;) ). The reason for that was at the end of every arc are sections where the player has to move the figure in a race against the clock for approximately 2 minutes in a perfect manner because the slightest mistake causes a tidal wave or lava outburst (or other adversary events) to swallow him up and the segment starts anew. Fortunately these segments are quite rare and with great maneuvering skills, tons of calmative agent or just pure luck the story continues without delay. After clearing the game I had to start a second run on the spot.
Another negative point is the lack of replay value as there is nothing more to do if you found all the secrets in your first run other than spending more time with this game's adorable creatures.
All in all it is an amazing game. Adn now you have to excuse me. Ori is waiting... ;)

But mostly, in these beginner lobbies, you won't find many beginners. I will admit I'm not very good at fighting games, but I practise and try hard to become better, and it doesn't help when I think I'm going to practise with others at my level, and they only use neverending combos and obviously are better than beginner status. Overall this is a very good game if you want to get into fighting games and don't know where to start, but stay away from multiplayer unless you are fully confident in your abilities.

The game plays like EVE online for the sea, but with combat that feels so much more visceral. Wood splinters fly, sails become tattered messes, and your crew cheers when they get a good broadside on an enemy. Paying attention to wind direction and your sails matters, but once you get the hang of it becomes as much a part of the game as aiming your cannons. The port battles and captures add a nice Realm vs. Realm element, and while it's still very much an alpha in terms of the UI, the game already has less bugs and more features than a lot of triple-A titles. The devs put out new content on a monthly basis...
Let me put it this way: at the very LEAST, you'll get your money's worth. Do yourself a favor though, and create a character on the PvP1 EU server rather than the others--it has the largest community, and they're extremely welcoming.

For me, To the Moon was one of those rare instances in life where I related so strongly with an experience on an emotional level that it has become a waystone in my life. Something that doesn't define who I am, but forms a part of me that I will not forget. When I was younger, these instances were much more frequent, but as I get older, they only come along once in a while. Star Wars, Fight Club, Everquest, Lord of the Rings...I can clearly remember how I felt the first time I engaged with them. I can remember how old I was, where I was living, and what was important to me at the time. While they themselves remain mere movies, books, and video games, for me they have taken on a greater meaning. The memories I formed, and the emotions I felt, added to who I am as a person. I suspect that the same will prove true of To the Moon.
To the Moon is a story-driven role playing experience that follows two doctors from the near future. Their job is to fulfill the dying wish of near-terminal patients. To do this, they enter the patient's memories with the assistance of technology. While there, they create a plausible chain of events which the client's brain will not reject, and which will lead to the fulfillment of their wish. To accomplish ths, the doctors must manipulate emotions and memories, creating a falsehood. This also comes at a physical cost. The tampering is fatal, and the fulfillment of their wish is the last thing the patient will ever experience.
These ideas and themes are deep and thought-provoking. The story is engaging. The characters are believable and relatable. They drive the story, and you can easily empatize with all of them. You understand why they make the choices they do, and you see their consequences. There is no contrived plot, no bad guys, and no good guys. There is just life. As a detached observer, you get to see all of it.
The main story takes place in the mind of Johnny, who is dying, and wishes to go to the moon. He has hired two doctors from the Sigmund Corporation to fulfill this final wish. The catch is, he doesn't understand why he wants to go to the moon. Eva and Neil, a team of doctors employed by the Sigmund Corporation, must discover where the origin of this ambition lies. As they delve deeper, they learn just how fallible what we think we know really is, and how often we don't really know what we want, or why we might want it.
The story unfolds like a mystery, as you work backwards from Johnny's most recent memories until you reach his earliest. You identify the reocurring themes, people, and items in his life, and it's up to Eva and Neil to piece together their importance. Many are imbued with the deep meaning and emotion that only time and memory can impart, and the story is driven by exploring the lives of the people who valued them. I still feel a twinge of sadness when I think of a certain object which explains as much about two of the main characters as Rosebud did for Charles Foster Kane.
I heard in an interview with the creator, Kan Gao, that his inspiration was in wondering whether he would have any regrets when he reached the end of his life. This is an idea that resonates with me, and I find it especially poigniant because, while the character of Johnny is an old man, he's the same age as me. It's easy for me to project onto him, and so examine myself through him. When I'm on my death bed, will I have regrets? What will they be? Is it inevitable for people to drift apart? How many beautiful or painful memories have I already lost, or will lose? The game didn't shove these questions in my face, but instead provoked me to look inward and examine them for myself.
The only criticism I can level at To The Moon is that it rarely leverages it's identity as a game. It does require a visual medium to be told as it was, but it could just as easily have been an animated or live action series or movie. You do have minor control over the characters, and you do investigate the game's environments, but rarely does this feel like anything other than filler. Occasionally the gameplay serves the story, but it's very rare. The aforementioned object is one of these appropriate uses, as  both the gameplay and story emphasize its importance. On the other hand, there's a sequence that attempts to evoke a feeling of dread and a struggle against time, but is largely just frustrating. But on the whole, there just isn't very much there.
I wish that more thought had been put into how to integrate gameplay and story to make something that could not have been told any other way, but I realize that is asking for a lot. I don't fault the creator for not being able to pull off what takes an immense amount of time, energy, and creativity, when he's clearly focused on telling the best story he can. As I've already said, I absolutely believe he succeeded. The pixellated graphics are actually conducive to this. They give enough information, but not too much. Like a book, you still have to utilize your magination to fill in the gaps, and thus the interpretation is unique to you. As a child, imagination is what made video games so important to me, and it's nice to be able to experience it again.
Even after factoring in my minor criticisms and accounting for my biases, I still cannot do anything other than recommend this game to anyone and everyone. Like great theatre it will make you laugh, it will make you cry, and it will especially make you think. So set aside four hours, grab a blanket, grab a snack, and just immerse yourself in the story. You won't be disappointed.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is an extraordinary, exploratory action adventure with an emphasis on audiovisual style.
This is a game of little gameplay, as there are at best six battles that need to be fought and none of these can really be called challenging. But that's not the point of Superbrothers. The game is about exploring if anything. With the help of the minimalistic but mesmerizing and authentic visuals and the truly fascinating soundtrack you get sucked into the unique world of Superbrothers.
Superbrothers uses a unique feature, where the position of the moon defines your ability to progress in the game. This is a fun feature, but you can always avoid it by changing the date on your computer should you be in a rush. I did run into an issue with this, as you can be blocked out of a certain part of the game (and achievement) when you play at a 'no moon' part of the cycle.
Its story is one for the personal interpretation, so I dare not giving any details. However, if you are going to play this, take the time to chat with NPCs as well as reading your journal. The devil is in the details.
The true beauty of Superbrother is in the complete package. The graphics, the music, the sounds... allow yourself to get sucked into the dream... it'll be a good one.
One final tip, go for the #moar achievement.
+ Masterful audiovisuals that complement each other
+ Compelling storyline
+ Original and unique
+ Interesting moon-mechanics

Very good racing game, especially when played in local multiplayer. The presence of items makes it possible to lesser-skilled and/or newer players to compete against more experienced ones (not to mention the system that allows you to fire missiles at another player when you're out of the race), which is a very good point for me, because any of my guest might have fun with it. Of course, if you are looking for a LAN tournament-worthy game I guess you might want to look for something else.
The single player mode is actually interesting, it offers a good challenge and game modes that go beyond the classic races and time trials. The presence of online leaderboards also gives it some replayability, although I suspect some people of cheating (or at least exploit unintended shortcuts) given the scores that are displayed but it's still nice to replay a level to try to beat a friend. This single player mode also seems mandatory to unlock new vehicles, unless I missed something, but it took me only three hours to complete and having several vehicles is really not needed to have fun in multiplayer.
Don't expect to be able to join strangers in online games though, it seems like no one is playing this online. Again, it's really meant for local multiplayer and making fun at other players next to you anyway.
I love the artistic direction, the "tabletop" style is really well exploited, with environments full of details and the cute toy vehicles make the whole thing feel like a toy race.
The camera angles are not ideal, which I think is actually fine in multiplayer because I only expect fun mayhem from this game in this case, but when playing solo I had the weird feeling that learning the track wasn't enough, I had to remember the camera's movements as well.
I think one of the weaknesses of the game might be to feel too "Micromachines-esque", most people I played with or saw me play did the same remark: "Oh, it's Micromachines!". They seemed to recognize the usual environments of the series. I suppose it's also one of its strengths, but given that I didn't play any Micromachines game I didn't take this into account too much.
I also wished this would be playable by more than four players.

Cons - Getting the correct lane draws during boss fights/races makes a huge difference in outcomes and AI is very scewed against player, making boss fight quite difficult and tedious, especialy in later stages. You are stuck to class vehicles and class tournaments only, not allowed to race owned cars in other class tournament races, even once that race is completed. Who thinks it is a good idea to have a camera that swings around willy-nilly and completely independent of payer control?
You can't play a racing game where the camera swings around like crazy, because it changes how you steer the car.
That's what you get here, where you start racing and the camera immediately swings to a 3/4 top down view of your car at 57.7 degree angle and then keeps moving randomly at every turn.
Who the EFF could possibly control a car under these circumstances?  Putting the camera setting to "top down" or "top down retro" cuts off critical parts of the upcoming track so you really can't play with those settings and you need to use the game default... which is unacceptable.
I continually marvel at how companies can spend YEARS developing games like this and not see how OBVIOUS the clear deficiencies are.  Seriously... every single race game I've ever played has a camera setting to "follow behind car" or something similar.  Not here.
Unreal.

I had not played a MicroMachines-like game since the original MM back in the 90's (if my memory does not betray me). While the concept is the same here and the gameplay feels the same at first, something seems to be missing. Is it because of the 3D? The zoom being a bit too close to the cars? Not sure...
The single player part is composed of different maps/types of events that you need to perfect to 3 stars in order to amass money and be able to buy slightly better/different cars. It's quite easy to unlock them all. At some point you will have to replay some events in order to get more money, but you will have to do it anyway later on in order to perfect them as you most likely won't manage it the first time.
Cars look different and their handling seems to match their characteristics, however this is all relative to a rather strange physics engine. Everything seems like rubber... You get used to it fast but still...
Perfecting all events, unlocking all cars and winning more than 1000000 cash (achievement related) took me a little bit more than 3 hours. After that, you are left with local and online multiplayer... And nobody is playing online.
While my review may sound negative I would still recommend it. All in all, it's cartoon-pretty, has 0 bugs, single player difficulty progression is well done and is fun while it lasts, rather easy, and worth a few bucks (got it for 1USD as part of a bundle). If you have someone to play with on the couch, it's even better.

Ori and the Blind Forest is definitely a touching game, it invokes strong emotions with a good degree of finesse and overall the product is of incredibly high quality.
Pros:
•	Excellent 2D platforming reminiscent of the Metroid and the Castlevania series.
•	Beautiful art assets that demonstrate a good deal of love being put into this game.
•	An interesting plot that relies very little on words to convey meaning, instead relying on music and art assets.
•	Challenging gameplay that manages to not descend into platform hell.
Cons:
•	Many of the ‘Escape’ based platforming sections rely on luck to a degree due to the firing patterns of enemies and the sway of certain jump points.
•	Some of the game (The escape sections specifically) rely on trial-and-error gameplay.
•	The game experiences an unusual difficulty spike in the ‘Water Temple’ almost as if it were homage to the Ocarina of Time.
•	The game ends seemingly abruptly after the ‘Fire Temple’ and will not let you reload a previous save, so if you didn’t create a secondary save you will not be able to aim for 100% completion without restarting the game.
•	The game is unfortunately quite short, possessing about 3-12 hours of gameplay depending on competence and need to collect all the things.
•	The 'Ice/Wind Temple' possesses a weird gravity switching mechanic, but fails to tilt the screen to orient with the character’s view.  Leading to a disorientating feeling much like what some people experienced with Mario Galaxy.
Overall I highly recommend this product for those seeking a AAA quality platformer without the AAA price tag. I sincerely hope these is a sequel to this series and will be waiting in anticipation for it.

I had pretty high expectations for this game and it mostly delivered.  The gameplay itself is pretty basic: movement is done by double clicking a place on the screen and combat has only two buttons (attack or block).   Most of the odd controls are due to the game being an iOS port, but beyond the odd phrasing of the tutorial the controls are pretty decent.  The game gets better when it starts giving you puzzles: early on you unlock the power to "sing" and can interact with the environment to progress.  Mostly this boils down to clicking on the screen like a maniac until you figure out the order of things to press but there are few times where the game actually surprises you beyond the cookie-cutter puzzles that are introduced at the start of the game.
However, the story more than makes up for the decent gameplay.  The game presents you with a fairly original fantasy universe where most of the lore is told in the background.  Once you finish the first act, you gain access to a device that allows you to see what other characters think about the events going on; this gives more lore and occasionally hints about how to progress.  Our universe's lingo mixes in occasionally: words like "upload" find their way into the dialogue and help create a mix of fantasy and contemporary.  The game surprised me with its unique sense of humor as well; the game is narrated in first person and this often leads to humorous self-revelations.  The game is a visual treat with its stylized and elongated pixel characters and rich backgrounds.  Of course the music is also incredible: the game was made with the music in mind and it shows.
The game took me around 4.5 hours, which is decently long for a cheap indie game.  It doesn’t lend itself to be replayed, although there are a few easter eggs you may miss on your first run through.  The game splits itself into 4 parts; the third part notably takes a whole lunar month to complete (unless you are a cheater).  I suggest you follow the game’s recommendation to take a break between acts; it helps break the sometimes repetitive gameplay.  Overall, it’s worth the asking price and is for sure a buy if it goes on sale for $5 or less.

I find this game far more enjoyable than Wh:TW1 for many reasons. (Keep in mind I'n going to be talking base game, no DLC)
Firstly, the races have vastly different and varied play styles from one another and don't really force you to stick with one strategy over another. Why bludgeon with masses of infantry when you can go bowling with bigferocious monsters? I'm not stuck with a horribly unbalanced force like bretonnia where my infantry is useless and my cavalry gives rise to the other guys spamming halberds and spears.
Plus the campaign is more than simple expansion, and each stage brings a sense of (I forget the word) movement, as all factions can invest in interfering with their rivals, including you. It's actually interesting when enemy funded doom stacks poof in and force you to react rather than just watching your lvl.30 lord streamroll your neighbors.
And that's another thing, you can actually conquer all the regions. And while there are climate penalties (after all lizards in the snowy north, nu-uh) you aren't prevented from conquering even the worst of regions.
But wait, there's more! An actual plot! Okay fine I've kinda touched on that already but there's more to look forward to than suddenly "CHOAS!" after X number of turns of sitting around and expanding. It's almost like you've got a bigger steak in the world than conquering simply because campaign demands it. And being able to throw down for an intervention force to screw around with the guys across the map.
AI has been improved some and is more proactive on the battlefield. And the new Rites mechanic (and Influence for HE) adds to the uniqueness of the underlying playstyles.
I've loved every moment so far, from that nail-biting moment a doom stack of elves appears on your door step to the grand sight of a stegadon smashing down the gates to let in the rest of your army. Totally Warth it!
Plus I think this is the only TW game since Medieval II that I've actually felt the need and interest to complete a campaign.

Toybox is just another run of the mill top down racer.
And considering it doesn't excel at anything, in fact it's undeniably inferior to Micro Machines v4, in size and gameplay. I would have appreciated something new. Instead, its all we came to expect from  tabletop MicroMachines clones, except less of it.
A Small track amount, repeated over different modes. All tracks are short in length and  incredibly similar to one another.
On top of that, they are all rather uncreative.  With no secret routes but rather, painfully obvious and easy to access side roads.
Little interaction with the environment and at most you will come across simple obstacles like objects in the road, or projectiles.
A small variety, and to an extent unbalanced.
So in reality there is an even smaller choice of vehicles, and that along with very easy to memorize track design, does not make it the ideal game for MP.
Cars are divided into categories, which leaves you with maybe 5 choices, and within those choices you will find 2 of them similar, and the rest just leaning over a negative aspect. It being, size, oversteering, understeering, lightness, heaviness.
And of course, the customization is just the option to change colors.
Once again a very small variety of unbalanced weaponry. I find that some deal little to no damage, or have a small field of effectiveness.
for instance,  the Hammer is a closed ranged weapon that only works with a car directly in front and practically touching your vehicle. while weapons like the machine gun or the hook, have a lock-in and don't need to be aimed.
So really, i end up having less choice than supposed to, because only 3 of the power ups are useful.
The camera rotates as it follows, and it cant quite keep up at a similar speed on tight curves, it tends to snap too fast while reorienting.
For whatever reason slower cars cant catch much air (game assumes you left the track and respawn the vehicle) It makes, To keep with tradition,  cars like the Moon Buggy worthless.
Well, it feels like a Codemasters game, unlike World Tour.
Responsive controls
Smooth 60fps
well optimized
Simple UI
A good portion of the cars are visually different
And most importantly, its a low budget game that can be purchased for a low price
Get Micro Machines instead.

Ori and the Blind Forest is definitely a touching game, it invokes strong emotions with a good degree of finesse and overall the product is of incredibly high quality.
Pros:
•	Excellent 2D platforming reminiscent of the Metroid and the Castlevania series.
•	Beautiful art assets that demonstrate a good deal of love being put into this game.
•	An interesting plot that relies very little on words to convey meaning, instead relying on music and art assets.
•	Challenging gameplay that manages to not descend into platform hell.
Cons:
•	Many of the ‘Escape’ based platforming sections rely on luck to a degree due to the firing patterns of enemies and the sway of certain jump points.
•	Some of the game (The escape sections specifically) rely on trial-and-error gameplay.
•	The game experiences an unusual difficulty spike in the ‘Water Temple’ almost as if it were homage to the Ocarina of Time.
•	The game ends seemingly abruptly after the ‘Fire Temple’ and will not let you reload a previous save, so if you didn’t create a secondary save you will not be able to aim for 100% completion without restarting the game.
•	The game is unfortunately quite short, possessing about 3-12 hours of gameplay depending on competence and need to collect all the things.
•	The 'Ice/Wind Temple' possesses a weird gravity switching mechanic, but fails to tilt the screen to orient with the character’s view.  Leading to a disorientating feeling much like what some people experienced with Mario Galaxy.
Overall I highly recommend this product for those seeking a AAA quality platformer without the AAA price tag. I sincerely hope these is a sequel to this series and will be waiting in anticipation for it.

Overall though, Ori and the Blind Forest is a very beautiful and enjoyable game, and I highly recommend it.

This game takes gives you the experience of traversing a small land.

You watch as she slowly fades.
This girl who wants the same goal as you. Watch as you lead her through fight after fight, leading her closer to your mutual goal. And she fades. Her health is but a secondary note as you fight to your ultimate goal.
But is it really worth it? Is it really worth sacrificing the life of this girl to seal what could be this eternal monster that haunts her forever? Do you wan't to watch her through every moment of her everlasting agony, as she's injured, diseased, and physically destroyed from your escapades to rid her of her problem?
Well, I guess that's really your decision. Isn't it?

Divinity: Original Sin is an RPG where you control a party of 4 adventurers as you travel through the land of Rivellon completing large and small interconnected quests. It plays a lot like a pen and paper RPG (think DnD). This means you are able to move your party independently of one another, create arguments and strife between your party members or work together toward a common goal.
One of the things I liked best about DOS was how involved, but clear character customization (in terms of stats) was. There have been several times where I've felt completely overwhelmed playing an RPG because there are stats all over the place and I end up not understanding which stats do what, which ends up being quite frustrating. I found DOS hit just the right balance of having enough different stat options to allow for several different builds across my party while being simple enough that I wasn't overwhelmed or confused by what any of the different stats, traits and abilities did. I look forward to playing through the game again in the future, so I have the opportunity to experiment and customize a new party of adventures.
Another thing I really liked about DOS was how there were several paths to complete the majority of the game's quests. When I received a quest sometimes a way to complete it would be immediately present, but I often spent time exploring the game world and eventually found an alternative route to complete the quest. This is easily one of the game's strongest points and one of the reasons the game remained so interesting to me well beyond the point when I become bored with most games.
I can't think of any immediate glaring flaw I found while playing the game. There was a few times that the dialogue being said by the characters didn't match up with the sequence of actions I had taken. This may have been a result of the somewhat open way quests can be completed. This only happened twice in 100 hours of playing the game.
If you aren't a fan of RPGs this game won't change your mind, but if you are a fan of RPGs I highly recommend this game. I had a boat load of fun playing it and it is one of the better RPG experiences I've played and my favourite game played this year.

Wimp: Who Stole My Pants is a puzzle platformer where you control a blob and take part in his quest to recover his stolen underwear from a giant fly. It is a strange plot guided along with a few comic book style pages after each world. There is really nothing to say about the plot other than you want your panties back and will do whatever it takes to get them back. Your adventure will take you through four themed worlds and the first one is by far the least interesting taking place in a sewer. It gives you the impression that this is a 'gross out' type of game though in reality the other three worlds are pretty charming and happy. Before you start the game you are given the choice of Hardcore that gives you a single life per level, Time Travel that adds a timer and Adventure which gives you infinite lives, no time limit, just you and puzzles to solve. That's not to say Adventure is a walk in the park, you will be set back to a nearby respawn point and you still have a single life during boss fights.
Platforming definitely takes a backseat here as jumps are pretty easy and liberally scattered about. Your main challenge will come from the three collectible toilet rolls in each level that are always place in a hard to get position. They usually have some intricate puzzle in place to keep them from you and these require a decent amount of thought as most can be messed up to the point of being unsolvable without a level restart. Toilets rolls are required to fight the boss though they are not too demanding with the amount that you need. Aside from jumping you can also stick to things which lets you swing over locations too wide to jump over or navigating underwater by sticking to a surface and pushing yourself downwards. All levels are pretty small and can be beaten rather quickly, even more so if you are competent at puzzle games unlike myself. The entire set of levels for each world also shares a single song to fit that certain theme making the music feel a bit repetitive. Never to the point of being annoying but some more variation certainly wouldn't hurt.
In later worlds you will get new powers that replace your sticky ability, like teleporting and becoming a chunk of ice. Teleporting allows you to set a bubble on an area and teleport back to it on the press of a button while becoming a hunk of ice allows you to sink down in water as well as freezing any enemies you touch which is your only real form of defending yourself. I am not particularly sure what the enemies are though they look like square shaped pig creatures and will kill you if touched. There is another worm like enemy that pops out of a hole in the wall though none of the enemies pose that much of a threat to you as they are immobile. The things most likely to kill you are the sharp objects littered around like saws, spikes, acid and the occasional boulders. It gets pretty darn difficult by the third world and I found myself dying over a dozen times on a level so it may be a bit much to try to play the game on Hardcore for your first playthrough. All environments are filled with detail and color making it a pleasure to look at. It has tons of nice little details like your blob having various different animations while you are idling and pigs letting out of puff of smoke in the snow.
Controls are solid and all the deaths felt like they were my fault instead of being able to blame wonky physics or loose controls. The only thing that felt wonky was the overworld menu while using a controller as it makes you click through the levels until you reach an arrow to go to the next world. Boss fights are fast paced and intense though they are all against the same enemy with the same method of attacking every time. He will hover over you and pelt you with objects until you solve all three of the puzzles required to take him down. Die once and it's back to the beginning of the boss fight though you shouldn't have much trouble getting back to the point you died as you already know how to solve the puzzle and the boss doesn't get any faster after being damaged, he just slowly flies toward you. I did experience a glitch the second time I faced him that caused him to stop moving and required me to kill myself or restart the level to get him moving again so I could solve that puzzle.
One of the strangest things about this game is that it doesn't have an ending. It just kicks you back to the overworld rather abruptly causing me to think I pressed something and skipped through the ending. I played the last boss fight again and had the same outcome. Most other games would at least have a poorly spelled ending scene like “conragtulations” or a simple “Thanks for playing!”. It's not game breaking by any means as there is barely a plot but it is rather curious as to why they choose to end it like that. In any case Wimp: Who Stole My Pants is a fun little puzzle/platformer in a nicely made and charming setting. It is a laid back and forgiving title if you play on Adventure mode that has a nice difficulty to the puzzles you will face. There is nothing that will have you stuck for too long and the puzzles aren't usually so easy as to knowing exactly what to do with a single glimpse. With all the fun abilities that change the way you approach things and so many levels it is a great game to pick up if you are searching for a quirky little brain teaser.

Things that need fixing;
-bugs do too much to ruin your games, if you make a great game with only one bug you won't even make back a fraction of your money. They say that there is beauty in simplicity, and that couldn't be more true than with Downwell. It's simple, arcade-style fun that's
hard to put down. If you like retro games and games that are easy to pick up and play, this is the game for you.
Trust me, this game is well worth the small price tag, and I
recommend you buy it if you have some cash leftover.
This game is the kind of game that makes you want to rip your lungs out, but, despite the pain, you must keep going.

Right, if you want a game where you can just relax, take your time and gradually eat your way into a dark abyss, this is for you. Similarly, if you're interested in tearing everything to shreds under your ammo-filled gunboots in a flurry of gems and distressed pixels, the same applies.

Sometimes the simplest concepts are the best. This is especially true in the case of Downwell, which at first glance seems like a game with little depth but is actually one of the deepest and most fun experiences I’ve had all year.
The goal of Downwell is pretty simple: you’re a boy falling down a well and you have to reach the bottom. Sounds easy right? But standing in your way are all manner of enemies and obstacles. Each ‘floor’ of the well is divided into 3 sections, and when you reach a new floor a new challenge awaits you. Thankfully you’re not helpless: your character is equipped with special bullet-firing boots which you use to vanquish your enemies and remove obstacles blocking your path. The boots have several different modes that you can switch between by collecting power-ups hidden in side caves, from the powerful shotgun that cuts through enemies likes butter but uses up your ammo just as fast to the rapid-fire machine gun. It adds greatly to the strategy of the game. You can replenish your ammo at any time by landing on the ground, although the more enemies you can kill before that happens, the greater the reward. These rewards can range from gems (that you use to buy items in shops) to extra hit points.
And you’ll need all the hit points you can get, because this game gets difficult in a hurry. On the game’s default settings you can only take four hits & then it’s game over. You can get health refills from shops, by picking up new weapon modules or exceeding a certain amount of kills before you hit solid ground, but that can only take you so far. Make no mistake; when you first start playing Downwell you’ll die, and you’ll die a lot, but never in a way that feels particularly unfair. If you failed, it’s because you weren’t ready or you just aren’t good enough yet. Fortunately you’ll pick up the basics pretty quicker and from there you’ll get better and better until you actually win. Practice makes perfect.
But perhaps the biggest appeal of Downwell is that it’s so easy to pick up and play. In spite of the simplistic pixel art graphics I couldn’t stop myself coming back to it again and again. The game rewards you more the more time you put into it. At the end of every game you’ll receive XP depending on how well you played and how far you got. The more XP you have, the more rewards you can unlock, from new colour palettes that can completely change the way the game looks to new gameplay styles, such as making your character’s physics more floaty or having more HP at the start of the game, at a cost. You can also unlock
by beating the game once, although this feels unfair at times and honestly, isn’t as fun in my opinion.
Ultimately Downwell is a rip-roaring experience that packs so much content into its tiny package. No two games ever feel quite the same. With a price tag of just $2, this is one title I’d recommend for any gamer’s collection

Disclaimer: This review is based on the Desura version I played a couple years back.  So far I've only farmed the cards of the Steam version.
Wimp: Who Stole My Pants is a very well made puzzle platformer on the easier side of the genre.  On each level, the goal is to collect your stolen underpants and unlock the exit.   One interesting puzzle mechanic is altering the properties of the "bubble" that the "wimp" uses to explore the levels - it's actually a bit similar to Gish, except that instead of transforming at the press of a button you have to use special stations in the level. There are the usual hazards and enemies in your way to puzzle and platform through.  Optionally you can attempt to gather all the collectable toilet rolls, which is not all that hard - I was able to do it on all levels, and I'm not the best at this genre.
The boss fights are pretty cool too - each boss level has several traps that you must lure the boss into.  Each trap can only deal damage once, but if it misses, it can be used again.
All in all, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to any fan of the genre who does not require their puzzle platformers to have brain-melting puzzles or keyboard/controller-destroying platforming.  I'm not playing the Steam version because I feel no need to replay puzzles I solved once already, and I'm not into leaderboard chasing.  I understand that a new set of levels is coming, and when it does I'll try to get a hold of a save state that will allow me to play just those.

This is a bit like Ultima 7: The Black Gate.  In that it is made out of pixels.  But not too many pixels, that would be bad.

Note: I played this on Android, and so a lot of what I say here is specific to playing on a mobile device. I would definitely recommend playing on mobile as opposed to PC, as it was clearly built with that form factor in mind.
As the name suggests, Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a bit of a musical experiment wrapped up in a video game. Records (or Big Black CDs as I used to call them) show up with some frequency in the game as little reminders to pay attention to the awesome sounds being gently pushed into your ear canals. I enjoyed the music so much that I went and bought the soundtrack.
Most of the visuals are very simple, very 16-bit. But every once in a while there is something that is nice and smooth. These objects usually don't belong with the rest of their surroundings, and the difference in visual style helps to emphasize that sense of alienation.
Despite the fact that the visual style is very pixelated, there were quite a few moments that just took my breath away. The best part about them is that I didn't see them coming, so the awe factor was even greater.
Most of the game is spent with the device in landscape, and you walk around by either holding down on the spot you want your character to walk to, or you double-tap there.
However, when you rotate the device into portrait, she will unsheathe her sword and prepare for battle. Obviously whenever there is an enemy nearby this is what you want to do.
The combat always follows the pattern of "tap the shield when your enemy is going to attack" until "your enemy is vulnerable, tap the sword." Each enemy has different patterns to them (usually the music gives you a hint at what that pattern is) so you have to stay on your toes. The boss battles are really intense, especially if you make a couple of mistakes at the beginning and can't afford to get hit when it gets really crazy. I'm pretty sure that I got more than a few weird looks while I was sitting in the TV lounge yelling at my tablet that it wouldn't defeat me.
In between the battles there are quite a few puzzles. The hints are often very cryptic, but they are always enough to get you going in the right direction and once you have started the rest just kind of follows.
The tone of the game is hard to describe, as it has several parts that almost conflict. The game is very meta, and makes references to the fact that you are outside of the game world affecting the events inside the game world. It also has a great sense of humor, and is often very frank with its jokes. At the same time it is very serious, and you are always aware that the events that are taking place cannot lead to a happy ending.
The game, while being very story-driven, is also very easy to digest in small chunks. This is very important in  a mobile game. The chapters are not too long, and they make sure to remind you what is going on at the beginning of each one.

When I decide on games to buy for the Wii, I had one rule that prevent bowing money on bad games: Never buy a game from a third company except Okami.  World of Zoo is a good reason for the rule, even though I payed for this game dirt cheap on Steam instead of buying it for my Wii.  I do praise the game for being gentle on PC parts, temperature wise; I also praise it for including animal customization, believable animal sounds, a fun art style, and the attempt to be educational.  However, the game play is very poor from the controls, mechanics, and a lack of challenge.
I will start with the controls.  I understand that this game is on the Nintendo Wii and the controls were meant for the Wii-Mote pointing at the screen.  The transition from Wii-Mote to mouse and keyboard went well, but I am very concerned about the left-handed people who want to play this.  Unless they go through the control panel, there is no way to play this on left handed mode.  In game, the clicking commands do not work 100% of the time.
There is another in game issue and those are the mechanics, or how the game works.  The first thing that irks me is the fact that you are a camera stick in one position with the only movement being pivoting from the spot.  This causes some of the clicking command issues I have mentioned earlier.  For example, there was a treasure that was behind a play set structure.  Most of the clicks landed on the structure instead of the treasure spot.  If I had the ability to move my camera around more freely, stuff like that could have been prevented.  The animals also have response issues, especially since there is no ability to pick a specific one for separate commanding.  The last complaint in this department is the use of an annoying video game trope.  I don't know what it is called, but here's how it functions: You keep playing the game to unlock a needed thing, but it is useless because there is no more game play value (Pokemon Mystery Dungeon Explorers of Time/Darkness is guilty for this, but I can't explain why because it will contain spoilers).  Going back to World of Zoo, the game made me play one enclosure for a long time with 2 animals just to unlock certain parts to create my ideal 3rd creature.  This is indeed optional, but nobody should have to deal with the struggle of staying awake in boredom for a creature that will barely be played with once the player leaves the exhibit.
Speaking of struggling with wakefulness, the game lacks a good challenge.  Having a "needs" bars like hunger and sleepiness would be a good fix to this issue.  The challenges the game provides are too easy and they are not leveled according to animal count.  I know that this game is meant for kids, but that does not excuse it from this issue.  The Super Mario series are for kids, but they provide fair challenges that even stump some adults.
Overall, this is not a good game to buy because of controls, mechanics, and a lack of challenge.  If you are a parent looking for educational material covering animals for your kids, I would pass this game and have them watch Zaboomafoo instead.

LEGO Worlds is all about exploration and discovery. There are so many cool characters, animals, vehicles, buildings, etc in the game that you'll spend hours upon hours flying from island to island unlocking new things to later build those islands up with. That's essentially what the game boils down to:
Part 1: Explore and unlock things by simply just finding them.
Part 2: Build up your world with all the cool things you find.
There's no survival aspect, other than don't be killed by skeletons or animals. It's the sandbox LEGO game experience so many of us have wanted for all these years. I'm not going to list pros, because there are way too many small things that you should discover on your own, but I will list some cons.
CONS
-Some of the islands are just too small and spaced out. Sometimes you'll have to fly around for minutes looking for another spot of land.
-The view depth is shallow, blurring a lot of your surroundings a bit.
-Best played with a controller. Controls can be very wonky either way, but playing with a mouse and keyboard was nearly unbearable for me.
-There's no real challenge to the game, although that could also be a pro. Having all this stuff to build with might get frustrating if someone's constantly tearing it apart. (Just like with real-life LEGOS).
-The cars controls are pretty bad and made me sick more times than not.
-Can't locate any map of the world. Maybe it's an unlockable item?
-The game is repetitive and doesn't really have much of a point to it outside of exploration and building. Again, that's not a problem for myself, but it may be for others.
All in all, LEGO Worlds is an incredible game that will hopefully only get better as time goes by. I've had a smile on my face nearly the whole time I've played it. WELL worth the $15 price!
