I bought this game last February, my friends who played PotbS got into it hot and heavy, we started a clan, and enjoyed the naval combat for many hours.
I have over 580 hours in this game, all prior to the major Port/land update.  Since then I've had zero desire to play.
Here's why:
Firstly, some of the bugs were annoying, it was an Alpha build, so no biggie, I knew the updates were coming to fix those things, so I took time off to wait.
Since then I have seen all the updates and patches and fixes. I can say that I really like this Dev team. They know what they are doing as far as code and art, and all other facets of software development. What I don't like is where they are going with the game.  They're adding perks and skills to the game, thus making it go the way of Pirates of the burning Sea. That is an excercise in failure. Skills, changes, and Nerfs destroyed that game, also the fail econ and the Pay to Win implementation.  This game is gorgeous! However, they're taking it down an ugly road in it's development.
When we first started the game it was slow combat, as all Tall Ship combat was. Adding skills and Perks is going to take away the nature of the combat and make it a Button Skill game.  Not OK.
Other reasons I left this game:  Each player is forced into a Faction. - You can not simply roam the high seas as you wish.
No Pirate Heavens.
Port Battles - Turning out to be exactly like PotbS. The game devolves into having to fight for ports.  Which REALLY sucks if you're Pirate, because all the nations just gang up on you until they need your help, then they backstab you anyway.
Ship Speeds: These were previously broken. Where an SOL would go over 8kts. Then players can add fittings, rigging etc. to increase this speed even more.  This is game breaking, they fixed it at some point, but ships the size of the Constitution were too fast and could chase down smaller, faster ships. (Not sure if they will attempt to reign in the insane speeds of the larger ships at some point, but it's not OK that ships of great size would go over 13kts for the time period, regardless of fittings and such.
Pirates can't enter "Neutral" ports labeled as such, but Nationals can. - HUH? Seems quite dumb to me.
There's no Reputation system.  - At the time I played Pirates could only enter Nation's ports if they had a Letter of Marque. Otherwise, you were simply denied the ability by the game mechanics. The problem with that was you had to go INTO the port to get the Letter...  Have they fixed this? Or implemented those mechanics all the way?
They allow fittings on ships that improve performance in some way, some of them have drawbacks, which is fine. However, players can not fully customize their ships. Players, (especially painful for Pirates) can not change what their cannon load outs are. EVERY single Cannon in the game has a Class assigned to it, and every ship is allowed a specific range of allowed Gun Classes.  There needs to be more customization. At the time I stopped playing it felt like people desperately wanted to fit a Square Peg into a Round Hole. We asked for the ability to more customize our ships. I don't think they're going to bother with that at this point.
Port Water depth: I understand that with Physics being a factor in game design, players need to be able to enter ports. Period.
I don't care what port it is.  Obviously HUGE ships like SOLs couldn't enter shallow water ports, but other ships could. In the game, even now, most ships have a problem with collision with the bottom.  IT'S ANNOYING AF!! You can get ganked because the bottom stopped you dead in the water inches from the port, or you can't enter the port at all.  The problem with this mechanic is that it's like this for EVERY SHIP. Not just ships of great size.  Even if you can outrun potential gankers, you should still be able to enter a port.
No In-Game map tools. OK, this was cool at first, but when grouping up with others, it's a PITA. "Hey, where are you?" Is the question of the day if you're not in the same port as others.
The game does NOT mark you on the map, not even a crude approximation based on your navigation. Nope. Nothing.
It's cool, but not practical.  At some point they need to implement tools to do this, make it a "Crew Perk" or Officer talent or something. Otherwise, you'll spend 3 hours sailing from Cuba to the South Eastern part of the map. Don't get lost!
People would log out because they would get frustrated at sitting in front of their computer for 3 hours... DOING NOTHING.
(You couldn't set your ship to sail by itself because the server would log you out after 30 minutes bcause you're AFK. - which is dumb, because your ship is moving.) Not sure if they fixed this.
I would recommend this game over every other Naval combat game on the market, because right now, it's the best of what we've got on the market.   (Still hoping that if they're going to add real physics to the game, they won't keep adding skills based on buttons to press on your keyboard, true ship customization, and Pirate Havens. Because that's what I'd do.)

captains.

One of the biggest things to note is the beautiful art with fluid character animations that are just a treat to the eye and really nice backgrounds and presentation along with a really great soundtrack by Castlevania: Symphony of the Night composer Michiru Yamane. The only thing that may turn some away from the game is the fact that some of the characters may come off a bit too sexualized, but what else could you expect from a fighting game? When you first fire up Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP, you are greeted by a mysterious cigar smoking figure with the following introduction:
"We are profoundly grateful that you have chosen to participate in this experimental treatment for acute soul-sickness."
That's as good an indication as any that this isn't your average run of the mill entertainment. While the core gameplay matches that of a classic 2D point and click adventure, the distinct elements that feed the whole are original and uniquely charming and the sum of their parts makes for an experience that is quite unlike anything else.
You will be presented with the option to tweet the messages that pop up throughout your quest, and as hinted at earlier, I guess this is meant to function as an experiment in social networking and provide real-time feedback and meta-commentary while you play. It's a novel way of integrating real-world social networks and to my knowledge hasn't been attempted before in this medium in such fashion. This is a game that isn't afraid to be self-conscious and sometimes poke fun at itself and at what it is trying to achieve. The ironic tone of the dialogue makes this clear from the onset, and although I enjoyed the wry wit and humour on display, there were times when I couldn't help but think what might have been if the developers hadn't felt the need to abruptly break the fourth wall so often and had taken this wonderful thing they had created at face value and just ran with it. Because there is real magic to be found here.
While playing Sword & Sworcery, I'm reminded once again that aiming for fidelity in computer generated graphics can be something of a double-edged, well, sword. While there's something to be said for games that push polygons to their limits and dazzle and awe with their polished "cinematic realism", what the developers of S&S EP have achieved with simple 2D sprites and pixelated lo-fi is nothing short of... magical. Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is, without a doubt, one of the most beautifully designed and evocatively atmospheric games I have ever witnessed. The beauty and artistry of the visual landscape never cease to fascinate.
It can't be stated often enough that a huge part of what gives the game its one-of-a-kind otherworldly feel is the stellar work of musical genius Jim Guthrie. The hauntingly atmospheric music and brilliantly minimalist sound design make this wonderful mystical world come to life. Sometimes, while wandering around, I would just stop and not do anything at all and just look and listen and just try to soak it all in.
But of course there's more to this whole strange and fantastic adventure, there's a mystery to be solved, secrets to be uncovered, moon phases to be observed, hidden things to be clicked on, places to be discovered, monsters to be fought, and a story to be told and experienced and remembered and cherished. I can't but recommend Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP in the strongest terms. It's a wonderful thing to behold.

Players also later have the option to add more of the same family of an animal to an exhibit, such as multiple monkies in the "Small Monkies" exihibit or Zebras and wild horses in the "Horses" exihibt. There an online portion too whihc allows for sharing soem content and mutiplayer care-taking with freinds or family, though we have nto really explored that option. I reccomend this game if you have children, or you yourself like to spend some time with a funny warm-hearted virtual animal care-taking environment.

Skip to "Will I like this game?" at the bottom if you want the summary!
Pro's:
Campaign - Fun smashing orks with brutal and varied finishing moves. Combat employs  both melee and ranged attacks seamlessly. Ripping off a mounted heavy bolter and mowing down Ork grass is always 400 bullets of pure joy. The voice acting is good and a decent story line. The audio books you find along the way add a nice touch.
Exterminatus - Co Op survival vs hordes is also fun with a group of guys, gets very challenging at the end!
Con's:
Campaign - This is really the best part of the game. The only con is the levels seem pretty plain as far as design, variety, and fine details. Much of a halo 1 type feel.
Exterminatus - The 2nd best part of the game. Pretty good, but really disappointing you don't get the very useful finishing moves and some of the melee combos you get in the campaign. There are also only a couple of maps so variety isn't there.
PvP - This is where the review starts to take a big negative. I'm not sure if the game originally had dedicated servers, but it sure doesn't now. It uses peer to peer connections. Since the game is a little old, the player base is pretty small and scattered worldwide. Playing peer to peer across continents in an FPS game is a nightmare.
The worst offender to game experience is assault marines warping all over the place. It looks like you've dodge rolled out of the way and they aren't swinging even close to you but your guy just falls over dead. The fall speed from jump packs is way to slow. Once an assault marine jumps they can just float in the clouds for 2 min until you show up and slam down with their laggy swings to lock you in. While the jump pack is on its few second cool down they get very boosted "mini" jumps. If the game didn't suffer from horrible lag every single match I could work with it.
Plasma Cannons are annoying with grenade launcher like shots all over the map. But I guess I can't blame people for using them. You need to cover a lot of ground to hit a warping assault marine.
Another problem is every time someone joins a match the games slows to a crawl while they connect to all other players(another benefit of P2P). It's incredibly disrupting to game play.
Yet another constant disruption during matches is "host migration". I'm not sure if it only changes when the host leaves or starts to have poor performance, but it happens many times during matches and you guessed it, the match comes to a complete stop until the new host is in place then resumes. The game usually waits until you are in an important fight to screw you.
Achievement Hunters - Stay away!!! The campaign achievements are fun. It's when you get to multiplayer where you will get killed. There are 3 really bad achievements here.
1. Completing all 90+ weapon challenges . It takes a very, very long time to get and will make you depressed if you want 100%. They aren't all just based on getting x amount of kills with x weapon. They include things like kill streaks, multi-kills, and head shot only kills(not terrible but keep in mind the lag).
2. Getting 40k kills(combined all game types). The best way is playing exterminatus where you fight waves, but the game will get boring way before that.
3. The 3rd is having a 10 KD on annihilation. That's a problem because either no one plays it or the match is too short to get in the 10 kills in time. You could boost in a private match to get, up to your standards.
Will I like this game?
Achievement Hunters: No!! Do not buy. You will suffer greatly.
Single Player: You will love it! Wait for a sale though.
DLC: Do not buy, no one plays it.
Co Op: Limited amounts of replay ability since only one mode and a couple of maps, worth it on sale only.
PvP: Although has potential to be fast paced, brutal, and constant action; it's just drowned out by aweful P2P lag. Do not buy at any price.

I rate the game Warhammer 40k: Space Marine 4/5. Good.
Generally, I don't particularly like 3rd-person perspective games. The perspective continually interrupts any feeling of immersion I would otherwise have. Seeing my character on the screen merely serves as a continual reminder that this is all just a computer game and is nothing to get tense or worked up about. As a result I often find myself doing silly stuff with my character which I otherwise wouldn't do quite so much (like throwing him off of ledges or jumping around for no apparent reason, mostly just to see if the game would let me). I did this a little bit in Space Marine, but not so much as I usually would. Space Marine is THAT good. This game does a great job at getting you into the spirit of things.
It is solidly built with few bugs, has a good, serious plot and an interesting ending which adequately wraps things up for your character while leaving space for a potential sequel to answer the plot's one remaining loose thread. The action is excellent, the sound and music are okay. The level design is very linear though and this single (and very common) downfall severely hampers replayability. This game has only one ending. I haven't yet played any multiplayer matches so I don't really know about that aspect of the game.
The Good:
+Solid gameplay with good action throughout. Both the gunplay and the melee action are done very well and work very well when each is used to complement the other. The Elder Scrolls games might be able to learn a few things from this game so far as melee fighting is concerned.
+The graphics are not amazing or particularly flashy by today's standards but they accurately depict the world of Warhammer 40k in terms of the scale of the battles, their inherent chaos and how all the participating units should fight. In fact I don't think I've ever seen any other game do a better job of accurately depicting the world of Warhammer 40k.
+The controls are good. You really will feel like you are playing as a big, power-armored clunky space marine who moves like a walking tank (but who has MUCH faster reaction time).
+The opening of the game sets the right tone and is truly excellent. The final boss fight is pretty good too. The ending leaves room for a sequel but didn't feel like it was too much of a cliff-hanger.
+Everything felt very, very true to Warhammer 40k. Indeed, this game might be a great introduction to that world for anyone who's not yet very familiar with it (including the unsaid silly ludicrousness of the power armor designs (Does this armor make my head look small?))
The Mediocre:
+/-The game is a third-person perspective game and this hampers any sense of immersion I would otherwise have had but I know first person perspective games aren't for everyone. A third person perspective probably makes the game most accessible to the widest possible audience I guess. Still I wish I had a choice. Also, I can't turn off the irritating Heads up display. I would particularly like to be able to turn off the warning that I should reload. I'm a Space Marine captain and I will reload when I want to! Plus, all my guns are clip-fed anyhow!
+/-The sound is mediocre at best. They tell the story adequately and let you know what's going on but the gunshot sounds could have had even more 'oomph.' The sounds of artillery are good though and this game can get very, very noisy.
+/-The music is merely adequate. The music in the opening sequence/prologue is pretty good but after that it's unremarkable (except for some nifty drums throughout but a true melody or theme never fully develops).
+/- The gore is fairly well done but relies too heavily on fluid, Mortal Kombat style splotches which vanish almost as suddenly as they appear. To its credit this game does have corpses which litter the battlefields and they do not immediately disappear but even more realistic gore could have increased the sense of tension in the game even further.
+/-The AI gets the job done but isn't amazing. But then the enemy characters you are fighting aren't supposed to be that bright anyhow so this makes perfect sense.
The Ugly:
-The absence of any Adeptus mechanicus personnel is a glaring omission. You hear them get referred to and hear that they are all dead but what happened to their corpses? They look strange and you would definitely notice them. You see statues of them but aside from their monuments and engravings you don't see enough evidence of them or of their Skitarii war cohorts either. They could have been present to add some sort of perfectly cannonical comic relief from time to time.
-This game is extremely linear. Most of the time you just have to run and gun and fight your way to a place that lies roughly in front of wherever you are. There are few puzzles to solve or tests of your logic abilities. Mostly you just fight and fight and fight (like a true space marine should and this is very accurate for Warhammer 40k space marines) But this fact limits replayability severely. There won't be any situations where you might think 'what else could I have done instead and if I had done that, what else would have happened?' The game does have 3 difficulty levels though.
-The game is fairly short and it is fun enough that you will probably wish it were much longer despite how linear the gameplay is. Indeed, the gameplay is so linear I would have expected the game designers to have been capable of making a much longer game as a result (I would have thought a linear game would need less programming work and so would give developers more time to add more levels and more environments and more weapons and such).

A lack of any kind of initial in game guide compounds the difficulty of the game, but that can be fixed by watching/reading online guides.  It looks like a good game, but I can't recommend it due to the amount of time doing anything takes.

It's a very surreal game that really makes you want to keep exploring it; and while the setting and retro graphics seem simple on the surface, the wonder and mystery of the world is not something you will have encountered before. I can see this game not being for everyone, as at times it can be a little slow and the 'next step' can be a little vague and require lots of wandering to figure out. I see this as a normal part of an adventure game and wasn't put off by it, but would understand if anyone had issues with it. If you have this game in your library, pop it on some evening where you just want a relaxed game night :)

Skullgirls is a great love letter to fans of fighting games. All the characters are unique in appearance and play style, and the ability to have one powerful character or a team of two-to-three makes for a wide selection of battle strategies and tactics. Another thing Skullgirls does right is in teaching new players through one of the best tutorials in a fighting game ever, in which you will be able to learn all the basics in a really simple way such as character specials and advanced combos. One of the biggest things to note is the beautiful art with fluid character animations that are just a treat to the eye and really nice backgrounds and presentation along with a really great soundtrack by Castlevania: Symphony of the Night composer Michiru Yamane. The only thing that may turn some away from the game is the fact that some of the characters may come off a bit too sexualized, but what else could you expect from a fighting game? Overall if you're looking for a fighting game that controls great, has interesting and fun characters, and can teach you fast, then Skullgirls should be right up your alley.

Description:
-Inspired by the old 2d fighting games. Skullgirls is one of the best out there. It follows the path of currently 9 girls on their quest for the infamous Skullheart. The skullheart will fill them with their darkest and deepest desires. Having to fight their way to get it. You can fight in a match consisting of a player party of 1,2, or 3 people. Each varying assist moves and balanced strength depending on how many people you choose to fight with.
Controls:
-Standard arcade format, closely similar to street fighter, with low,mid, and high punches and kicks.
-Compatability with keyboard, console controler, or arcade joystick.
-Easy to learn, even for casual gamers not used to fighters. As most characters share the same combinations for   blockbusters and special moves.
Pros:
-Fast pace
-Fun for high skill and low skill players
-Unique artstyle and music
-Unique and original characters with their own personality
Cons:
-Not many players online to find a match with. If you're looking for a match it's easier to go into ranked matches, but this isn't reccomended for low skill/casual players.
-Servy laggy at times
-Not a huge character selection as compared to Mortal Kombat or Street Fighter or Marvel Vs. Capcom
-There isn't a reliable combo breaker, you can literally be infinite combo'd after someone hits you once.
-Fighting games aren't for everyone, it is a dying breed of games and the player-base will always be low. So find/make friends who own this game to always have someone to play with.

Fighting games have never been an easy genre to get into for anyone other than the truly devoted. Most games require massive amounts of meta knowledge regarding frames, hitboxes, and matchup knowledge. Skullgirls is a unique game to me in that, it has all these requirements but, unlike most other games, is willing to offer you a hand in getting started. The game wins a massive number of points for having a well designed and implemented tutorial that explains everything from basic mechanics to specific character playstyles, allowing for players new to the genre or the game itself, to easily pick up the fundamentals easily.
Character design is vibrant and beautifully illustrated making the game just much fun to look at as it is to play. It also deserves points for being the first game to have a cast of mostly women, with the inital playable characters being exclusively female.
Another thing I appreciate is that the game is constantly being patched and evaluated in this PC port. Patching on consoles was a rare occurance and often lead to massive exploits becoming simple facts of the game that would alter the way the game was played for long stretches. With the PC port, I feel like the game is constantly evolving with the meta, allowing for the game to stay consistently fresh.

I'm going to start this review with how impressed I am at this game's optimization. I have a crappy PC with a dual core processor, and this game is frequently hitting 60 fps with some infrequent stuttering here and there when the particle effects and environments get a little thick. Even at the lowest graphical settings, this game still looks good, so props to Relic on making this run like a dream on PC.
Now, to the review proper. A lot of 3rd person shooters focus far too much on stale cover-based shooting, ever since Gears of War did it relatively okay. Space Marine says to hell with cover and lets you tromp around and stomp the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of xenos and heretics while using movement to keep yourself alive.
It uses a system where you have regenerating shields, but your actual health has to be recovered by getting into the thick of things and execute enemies when they're stunned. You need to make intelligent use of your dodges and know when to stun certain enemies and keep them out of combat while you work on the other guys in melee. While the combos themselves aren't particularly complex or challenging, they provide a surprising depth in your approach to close combat.
As for the shooting, Space Marine gets it right. If you're going to commit yourself to mid or long-range combat, you need to be constantly mindful of what pillars or walls you can use to peek around and use to run through, breaking up the enemy's fire. You can't just sit in once place forever, since the AI will know what you're trying to pull, and will make use of grenades to get you in their line of fire. They will also attempt to flank you and surround you all of the time.
This, combined with the melee combat system, makes for an actually challenging game that has you constantly scanning your surroundings and flushing out your enemies. There's hardly ever a dull moment, and each encounter tests you on what you've been learning throughout the game. While newbies are going to be frantically hunting for a spot to rest and be on edge in every battle, more experienced players can make it look hilariously easy.
Sound Design
The bolters are so damn punchy in this game. Everything is punchy. Even the steps taken by you and your fellow space marines sound massive and thud like you'd expect. Every aspect of this game sounds authentic, and never leaves you dissatisfied. This is also part of what keeps the shooting aspect of the game so fun, as the bolter makes thunderous noise and your enemies blow apart in juicy blood splatters.
When it comes to the narrative, it is standard 40k fare, but the characters themselves are, for me, the most memorable thing in the story. Mark Strong does a great job voicing Captain Titus, and the captain himself is a pretty badass dude. The Ultramarines are often mocked as ponces and an obnoxious, uptight chapter. While this does hold true in many cases, Titus shows the best attributes of the chapter, and embodies the ideals of his primarch. Hell, I'd say the guy is the spitting image of Guilliman.
Sidonus is a cool guy, Leandros is a whipped little ♥♥♥♥♥, the Blood Ravens make an appearance along with the Black Templars, the IG is as manly as ever, and the the chaos lord is actually kind of cool; while he doesn't match up to the likes of Eliphas, he's still leagues better than other chaos lords we've seen in the past. The ork warboss, Grimskull, is probably one of my favorite orks ever, right behind Gorgutz 'Ead 'Unter.
Overall, I'd say that this is a game that certainly does 40k justice, and is a great starting point for anyone who wants to get more into the lore side of the setting. As a game, it's pretty damn good, and keeps me coming back constantly with its campaign and multiplayer. I would love to see Relic revisit Space Marine sometime in the near future, and finish it off proper, since the cliffhanger at the end is downright criminal. So, yes, I do recommend Space Marine.

Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP is a pretty cool experience. It's mainly a point-and-click, adventure game with a few mild puzzles and a smidgen of combat thrown in. It relies heavily on a strong narrative and kinda, sorta delivers. I had fun, I guess.
Basically, Sword & Sworcery is a retro, sidescrolling version of Dear Esther, except it has combat and stuff. You're an adventurer set out on an adventure to carry out an adventure. You generally succeed. There's a bunch of peculiar characters you meet along the way.
There's a few easter eggs and hidden locations in S&S if you're into that kind of thing. The music is pretty cool. The pixel art is also quite nice, the environments are fairly eccentric, mostly.
Oh yeah, S&S also incorporates Twitter into the game experience for some reason, but it's not necessary to further your enjoyment. I have no idea why it's an option, all it does is let you tweet certain phrases.
Whilst Sword & Sworcery is mainly text-based there are a few spoken lines for some reason. Kinda caught me off guard at first but it was interesting. Yeah. That's all I have to say about that.
The general tone of the game is quite whimsical and sort of reads like this recommendation. It's slightly odd. Sort of a typical fantasy setting but with modern forms of speech, slang, "cool, hipster" vernacular, et cetera. It's like being told a story by a pretty chill, arty-farty, pretentious twenty-something year old who kinda mumbles a bit. I'm not sure if it adds or subtracts from the experience but it wasn't at all grating, it just sort of worked.

This is one of the most refined fighters that I have played so far! This game is the definition of "easy to learn but hard to master". The basics of the games are very simple while the advanced stuff cater to the most hardcore fighting game players. The tutorial in this game is also very good at teaching not only the game but also the fundamentals of all fighting games. Also, this game has the best training mode in any fighting game in my opinion. There are many tools in there for you to level up your game with.
On the gameplay side, it's similar to Marvel but it's also a bit different. The ratio system and the custom assists (More games should have this! I'm looking at you, Capcom!)  makes it so that you can customize your own playstyle. On top of that, the game is backed by GGPO for online which makes your online experience much better.
Overall, this is a great fighter however, the learning curve is a bit steep. I also think that the number of characters is a bit lacking but this will be remedied in the future with 5 DLC characters (with Squigly already being out). In the end, it's definitely worth checking out.

While this may not look like a mechanics fighter on the front, Skullgirls has a combat system worthy of (and has been in!) tournament play. This game can be quite the learning curve if you are new to fighter games (like myself), but once you learn the way combos and super moves work, it is an amazing experience. Most fights boil down to fraction-of-a-second button and stick combination, but once you get a feel for it, you can be devastating. Of course, this game is just as fun playing with friends casually on a lazy afternoon alongside Smash Bros, or placing bets and fighting it out! I totally recommend you use a controller, I use a USB xbox 360 controller, but Skullgirls also supports those 6-button USB fighter pads, which some of my friends have.
With it's unique gameplay mechanics, art style, character stories, and a development team dedicated to listening to the community, Skullgirls is a game I recommend any hardcore or casual gamer to pick up.

The inclusion of adjectives, and perhaps better framed puzzles (with more useful clues) makes for a more encouraging game than the original, and I've blitzed through the main game in a few hours. I may not be using the most creative ways to complete puzzles, but I feel happy completing them regardless; books, teachers, and mirrors get used a lot! Only on certain puzzles did I get stuck, such as what item needed to be placed in a toy barrel (hint: its not toys). There's a lot of "extra" content I've not got to after meeting the requirements for end credits and map completion, and I'm looking forward to picking up the achievements for completion.
I love a bit of literary humour and Scribblenauts has plenty. There's a tonne of game, movie, and internet meme references too. The art style is cute and the soundtrack is both appropriate and richer than you'd expect. Unlimited is a great go-to game, and if I had kids, I'd want them playing this (and them letting me join in).

Here's the thing.
I quite like this game. I like the setting, I like the shooty shoots and the hit hits, I like how the story is nonexistent, how the plot is as cliche 40k as they come, how the Thunder Hammer absolutely destroys once you get it, and how your big meaty boots shake the ground when you run. I like a lot about this game. There are two fundamental design flaws that ruin the experience, though, and I cannot recommend this game to anyone unless you are willing to put up with incredible frustration. They are:
--In melee: enemies will stun you, but you do not stunlock enemies (during normal attacks)
--Your dodge roll and execution animations do not have any invincibility frames.
These pretty much ruin the actual gameplay experience. Add to that your surprisingly low health and shield bar and the propensity for the game to load encounters with RocketBoyz past the 6th chapter or so, and pretty soon the game becomes a frustrating slog that never quite feels fair.
Fighting bigger enemies is frustrating because you can't stunlock them and do damage at the same time, but they can stun you through your attack animation. Eventually you'll learn the only way to beat them is by stunning them over and over for a minute or so (as stuns do little damage) and waiting for the little "execution" prompt to appear; during this time you may be getting wrecked my melee Orks or RocketBoyz. Eventually you may decide to  just hang back and bullet-sponge them into oblivion--considering your weapons are inherently innacurate and shooting isn't the focus, this is a real drag.
If the Dodge Roll actually worked, this might not be a problem. It doesn't. Unlike plenty of other slash-em-ups (God of War, DMC, etc., Dark Souls), there are no i-frames (that I can tell) in a roll. As a result, there's no point in dodging: you'll still be hit during the dodge, and more often that not it will just propel into further danger. Enemies have long-range melee attacks, and most arenas are so small you'll end up getting caught on the claustrophobic level design. Add to that the fact you're probably being peppered by impossibly accurate ranged Orks and a limited health bar and you may just give up entirely.
Finally, the execution system. The only way to regain health in this game is by "executing" enemies with a stylish animation. This is awesome in theory and brutal and fun in practice. During the actual animation, though, you'll still take damage; and, considering you're effectively standing still during this time, you'll be taking a LOT of damage. It defeats the purpose of a melee system entirely: it's better to just stay back and let Orks soak up an astonishing amount of bullets rather than risk getting killed trying to regain health after you've had your chainsword fun. And when checkpoints start getting wonky and put you behind not one but two enemy encounters every time your die, you'll really start to resent the unfair deaths.
So there it is. There are other problems with the game (they could have removed RocketBoyz entirely and the game would have been better for it), but I still enjoyed myself while the fun lasted. At least play until you get the Thunder Hammer, because that's a blast. And maybe try playing on Easy your first time (I wasn't able to tell the difference between Easy and Normal, but at least Easy may get rid of more frustrating deaths). Oh, and that first Ork Boss? Probably the worst boss design I've encountered in a long time. It doesn't really telegraph what you're supposed to you, how you're supposed to do it, floods the arena with enemies, and gives the boss an almost one-hit kill that's hard to dodge. Yup.
But then again Jim Sterling thought it wasn't bad, so maybe give it a shot. Jim is pretty good at gauging when games are too frustrating to play. Maybe I just sucked at this one. PS: Nvidia cards are known to have problems. I have a 750 Ti and it had graphical glitches from time to time that required a force restart. YMMV.
UPDATE: Playing the game through on Easy is way better, and that boss is a cakewalk if you happen to bring along a Melta-Gun. I didn't my first time, and the checkpoint is after you have the opportunity to pick one up so there's no way to go back and change your mind. In general, any time you're presented with weapons in the game you'll never know which ones to pick, and certain encounters are CLEARLY designed for specific weapons. This, I think, contributed to the game being very easy fro some people and very hard for others. The review stands.

OOOH BOY ! Do I recommend this game ? I couldn't give it enough thumbs up!
This game filled a specific void for me that was a turn based rpg with the option to explore a huge and live world. I've checked out a few other games, but none did it as good as Divinity: Original Sin.
My first playthrough was a solo one and it grabbed me so hard that I didn't sleep that night. In the morning I wondered when the time flew by, but didn't regret a thing! The atmosphere in the game was astounding, the world felt live and vivid and the combat was the cherry on top. The multitude of ways you could approach each combat scenario and the fact that you could get creative with it in so many ways simply amazes me.
I though that it might lose its charm on the second playthrough, that I did with a friend, but boy was I wrong. Obviously the rock, paper, scissors mechanic worked better with a co-op partner and at the time we didn't care how each decision affected our character. We were playing it for fun. We made so many wrong/bad choices and still came out laughing in the end. After that we started a new game on Honour Mode (which is the game's "one shot and if you die you lose" mode) and we took it a little more seriously. One thing I could remark as an inherent flaw (not too bad though) was that the more you level up, the easier the game gets and by the end it's all a cake walk. You're just so powrful ! However that's fine if you like the feeling of crushing all your foes with a single spell or whirlwind attack.
So, overall I recommend this game wholeheartedly, but I recommend it even more if you have a friend to play it with, as that experience is even more precious. This game is truly a gem!

This game is just so charming. Most race games seem to go either for ultra realism or for an infinite runner style (including tricks). This one is off on its own, and not just because of the setting. Toybox turbos not only looks as if you're playing with miniature cars, it plays like it as well: cars are flipped over instantly, it's easy to tip over if you take a turn too sharp (but not as much as that it makes it too hard) and there's a fast standstill->full speed ratio. The tracks are littered with objects (pencils, paperclips, text books, ...) that serve to hinder the racers as well as mark the tracks.
And it's these details that are just everywhere. This isn't a race for championship of the world, but more to be the best kid in school (which is in the end equally rewarding).It's about having fun while racing, which is implemented in the weapons: they can hinder you a bit, but are overall more that piece of nuisance that can JUST mean the difference between winning and losing.
I could nitpick a bit on things (money is so abundant you can pretty much buy every car from the get go, camera angle isn't optimal when ahead in boss fights and a few other things, the game isn't that long), but in the end there's no contest: this game gives you exactly what the screenshots and videos promise: simple yet enjoyable fun.

This is one of the most refined fighters that I have played so far! This game is the definition of "easy to learn but hard to master". The basics of the games are very simple while the advanced stuff cater to the most hardcore fighting game players. The tutorial in this game is also very good at teaching not only the game but also the fundamentals of all fighting games. Also, this game has the best training mode in any fighting game in my opinion. There are many tools in there for you to level up your game with.
On the gameplay side, it's similar to Marvel but it's also a bit different. The ratio system and the custom assists (More games should have this! I'm looking at you, Capcom!)  makes it so that you can customize your own playstyle. On top of that, the game is backed by GGPO for online which makes your online experience much better.
Overall, this is a great fighter however, the learning curve is a bit steep. I also think that the number of characters is a bit lacking but this will be remedied in the future with 5 DLC characters (with Squigly already being out). In the end, it's definitely worth checking out.

While this may not look like a mechanics fighter on the front, Skullgirls has a combat system worthy of (and has been in!) tournament play. This game can be quite the learning curve if you are new to fighter games (like myself), but once you learn the way combos and super moves work, it is an amazing experience. Most fights boil down to fraction-of-a-second button and stick combination, but once you get a feel for it, you can be devastating. Of course, this game is just as fun playing with friends casually on a lazy afternoon alongside Smash Bros, or placing bets and fighting it out! I totally recommend you use a controller, I use a USB xbox 360 controller, but Skullgirls also supports those 6-button USB fighter pads, which some of my friends have.
With it's unique gameplay mechanics, art style, character stories, and a development team dedicated to listening to the community, Skullgirls is a game I recommend any hardcore or casual gamer to pick up.

Sometimes a game comes along that just hits it on every level for you, and Skullgirls is one of those games for me. I've been looking to get into Fighting games for a while, a genre that can be very intimidating to start, and I knew from the moment I saw it Skullgirls would be the place to start. The game looks great, plays great, has a very down to Earth community (probably due to its small size at the moment. Hopefully it will grow with time and get the love it deserves), and a great tutorial system that teaches someone who knows very little about the genre quite a bit. More than teach, however, it shows you how deep the knowledge pool can go. It makes you want to learn more, and that's something most games with such a high skill ceiling fail to do well.
If you're offended by busty girls and panty shots, you may want to give this one a pass, as it has more than its fill of fanservice. If, however, that doesn't bother you (or it's your thing) then you'll love the style. The art is beyond amazing, with each movement drawn to give things a great flow and feel.
Whether you're looking to get into the genre or you're a fighting game fan in general, you'll probably enjoy skullgirls. It's worth every penny, and is often on sale. So check it out if you're in the market for a fun and sexy fighting game that won't empty your wallet.

So, the good, the bad, and the ugly.
Good:
- Let's you be creative, it has hundreds of different bricks and pre-build items which is great.
-Random worlds are great and I'm sure there will be lists of seeds that come out for specialty worlds (no land, all flat, etc.)
-Exploration and a little bit of action give a slight feeling of minecraft. (but not as good, see "bad"

Bad:
-Enemies seem like they were thrown in last minute, they don't really affect the gameplay at all.

-Worlds are pretty small.
-No map of the world.
-No mechanical builds (there are mechanical items but you can't build any yourself)
-The female characters sound like males.
Ugly:
*These are just things that I'm personally worried about, they may or may not actually happen*
-Set's and certain items may become costly DLC.
-Improvements and bug fixes may not be made, making for a game that will only be fun for a few hours.
On a side note, I'm not sure why people are having issues with it being slow and lagging. I only have a mid range setup and it works fine for me.

This game's early release is bittersweet for me.  I am excited that it will be played by many.  I am excited that it wants to encourage building, creating, and exploring.  Unfortunately, it wants you to do that in the laziest way possible.  I love going to the Lego store, excitedly buying kits, and then asking the employees to assemble it for me...said no one ever.  Lego Worlds captures all the excitement of exploring that Minecraft has and distills all to bumping into things and "building" prefabricated kits.  You can still build piece-by-piece, but with the camera and character controls in their current state, you're better off using the prefabs.
Positives...
- You can build piece-by-piece (but it will take forever)
- Visually appealing
- Retains the most of the charm of a Lego game
Negatives...
- Poor camera control
- Poor character controls
- Poor UI for those without a controller
- Childish theme could be toned down to make more universal for creators, not just children who want to play a Minecraft version of the Lego games
- You cannot design a vehicle
- Framerate issues
- Camera loses control for some random event from time to time
- Tunneling felt like it only went downward due to poor vehicle controls
- Needs more of a tutorial to help players feel competent in what they are doing
I want this to be better than it is.  This should not be about Minecraft vs. Lego Worlds.  Their goals are different, but they are about different venues for creation.
Minecraft succeeds because you are exploring the world to find your components for your creation.  I get Lego's need for the prefabs, but not every kid is going to want everything built for them.  Ultimately, I wished this game felt more like the Lego Movie and less like the Lego games.  As an adult in his 30s who works with 3D software, I cannot say with much confidence that the average user will find this easy to build in.  Children will enjoy throwing Lego pieces down, but Lego is about creativity and building.  Lego Worlds has dumbed that down, making exploration more of a primary than a complimentary action for the creating/building.

Other reviews I see people saying it's a boring world and you spend most of your time going from A-B doing nothing and blah blah blah. Do you even know what game you bought? Helloooo, it's a 1800's naval game that takes place in a huge ocean and you sail old wooden vessels at 2-18 knots depending on the weather gauge; obviously it's going to take some time getting around. Some things I've found amazing they've added to the game just off the top of my head are: ship armor thickness, weather systems, seagulls (with sounds), different nations ports have different looks, fishing, they average adding about 2-3 new ships each month, and plenty more.
All in all this game is everything and more that I can ask for. Just a few experiences from my voyages in the Caribbean, the other day I stumbled upon Captain Kidd's hideout (not on the map), currently I'm sailing to the Santa Cecilia ship wreck (the location of which I discovered in a sealed bottle), all the while having my crew fish from the sea. Last week I went and visited the American Colonies just to say I had been there. Before taking off to find the lost ship wreck I intercepted a French Essex and also a 3rd Rate Pirate vessel with the help of my brother. It's a great game to play with friends, the community is excellent, and there is more than enough things to do with more and more being added each time a patch comes out every week or so. Don't let the negative reviews fool you, this game is absolutely amazing and I absolutely recommend it to everyone who loves the seas!

Skullgirls is an interesting fighting game that seems to remix the best aspects of the genre into one cohesive and fun game.
If you are familiar with fighting games, Skullgirls will play as you expect. As with any good fighting game, characters control as an extention of the player. Fighting game fans will also not have to spend any time learning any special dpad motions as Skullgirls works on the everpopular system of dragon punch and fireball motions. Skullgirls is a game that seems to cater to a more hardcore audience, but that is not to say it doesn't welcome complete newbies as well. Skullgirls  boasts one of the most complete and informative tutorial systems for any fighting game I've ever seen. The game includes gameplay tutorials teaching a new player everything he or she would need to know from basic blocking, to cross-ups and combos. Skullgirls also includes a fairly indepth tutorial for each and every character that divulges the character's special moves as well as some basic gameplay stratigies.
Skullgirls features some of the most beautiful hand drawn sprites I have seen in almost any game period, think animated feature film quality. The character movements are silky smooth and give the characters some real personality. This coupled with the artfully drawn backgrounds create an overall visually inspired experience throughout the game. The characters themselves are also quite interesting and likable. While other games may have a catgirl character, Skullgirls takes it a step farther and has a catgirl that also happens to be an undead zombie. While other games may have a ninja character, Skullgirls has a ninja with a medical degree that uses syringes and scalpels as weapons instead of shurikens. While some players may consider these tropes cliché Skullgirls pulls it off well and makes the characters genuinely fun to play as. Although, at the time of this writing, the roster may seem small, the cast is varied enough that everyone will find at least one favorite amongst the line-up.
As far as gameplay modes, the game has everything you could expect. A single player story mode, a single player arcade mode, local competitive play, online competitive play (with a leaderboard), and online lobby play. The game works with most any game pad and controller set-up is a breeze. Skullgirls also enjoys continued support for the developers and with new updates coming almost every week and new characters on the way this year, it seems support won't be dropped anytime soon which is a huge plus for any game, but fighting games in particular. The only somewhat negative thing I can say about Skullgirls is that while it does bring quite a lot of new mechanics to the fighting genre, (Fortune's detachable head, Squigly's interesting charge mechanic, Valentine's poison needle thing, among others) it also relies heavily on precidents already established in the genre. While not a downside entirley, (if it ain't broke etc...) this may leave core players desiring more.
At the end of the day Skullgirls is a terrific fighter as well as a wonderful game. The few downsides are easily drowned out by the fun and fast gameplay, beautiful art direction, fitting music, and exciting characters. In my opinion it is a "must have" for any fighting game fan, a good place to start for those interested in fighting games, and it is different enough from other fighters to warrant a try from those who thought they disliked the genre. As far as fighting games for pc go, Skullgirls easily deserves to be mentioned in the same breath as greats such as Street Fighter and BlazBlue.

In the fast-paced world of the fighting game tournament scene, there is one thing that matters above all else: balance. If a game has severely unbalanced fighters, then it may as well be thrown straight out the window. Another problem is cloning, to make it seem like a game has plenty of characters to go around, the devs may simply take one characters mechanics and re-apply it to another. We constantly see examples of games that just try too hard to shoehorn everything in to one crowded roster, and with games like Ultimate Marvel Vs Capcom 3 shoving 48 playable characters into the spotlight there is just no hope of a fair and balanced fight.
Thankfully, we have Skullgirls on pc now. When it comes to the lofty ambition of being the perfect tournament fighter, it manages to deliver on all levels! Lab Zero has made an already smashingly impressive console brawler shine even brigter on the PC. By bringing together a team of fighting game industry experts to craft Skullgirls into a pulse-pounding pandemoniac plethora of pugilistic perfection, Lab Zero has once again saved the day for fighting fans. What we have here is a set of 8 well-tuned femme fatales who are ready to kick♥♥♥♥♥and take names. You have the option of choosing either one full-powered character, a halved-strength duo, or a tag team trio of weaker fighters. No matter your choice you can rest assured that the game is ready to balance itself out, so choose the playing style that suits your tastes.
The graphical merits of Skullgirls are quite astounding, with each character fluidly hand animated in 1080p. The graphical quality is quite in it's own class, even upstaging recent fighters such as Blazblue. The stages themselves are no less detailed, with throngs of fully animated background characters, and a gorgeously parallaxed art style that almost feels three-dimensional. The eye-catching visuals are underlined by an impressive score by none other than Michiru Yamane, famous for her long running contribution to the aural tapestry of the Castlevania series. All of these elements perfectly meld together into a wonderfully film-noire/art deco aesthetic.
One last point I'd like to touch on is the excellent online gameplay, provided by the GGPO (Good Game Peace Out) netcode. It allows for a virtually lag-free online experience, regardless of the player's real-world proximity to one another. In my online experiences with Skullgirls I found no lag or dropped frames at all. In my humble opinion Reverge labs has crafted the finest tournament fighting experience possible, and for that I salute them. Skullgirls is well worth the price, so get out there and buy it today!

In general I don't get geeked for fighting games, but Skullgirls has earned all of my hype and love. The combat is probably THE most fluid of any game I've played. The handdrawn graphics are gorgeous and the cast of playable characters are quirky and cute, each with their own story and playstyle that have me hooked.
The game is definitely tuned for quick paced gameplay but Lab Zero has made the game accessible to the beginner like myself through a comprehensive tutorial section. It goes over everything from the most basic ideas of fighters, to focused lessons in specific characters. All in all it keeps the game balanced for everyone before shipping them off to the versus lobbies.
What I enjoy most about skullgirls, however, is that it's not the conventional fighter. Each playstyle per character is vastly different from the others, from the more standard playstyle of Filia to the split control mechanic of Ms. Fortune, there's always something new to uncover and master in the game. The console releases for this game were amazing, but the PC version has won me over entirely, with hours invested and many more to come I can honestly give this game my glowing recommendation.

Look, if you're reading this review, I think you're in one of three camps: The first camp, you've played the game before and are combing for funny reviews as a walk down memory lane. Second camp, you've played before, but not the PC version, and want to make sure the experience is the same. Third camp, you have never played this before, and, after some hype from Fallout 4, decided to see if you should brush up on the franchise. Let me just stop you right here and say that you really don't need to read much further. Yes, you should get Fallout 3: GOTY, and YES it will be glorious.
You should know this by now, but just in case...
The year is 2277 (or something like that). You exist in a world where the transistor was never invented, and so nuclear power took precedence, powering everything from cars to robots. Two hundred years prior to where our story begins, a nuclear war had broken out over the Earth. In an instant, the world as it had been known was no more, and was torn apart by the rain of bombs. Many American people were sheparded into nearby underground Vaults, created by Vault Tec. The Vaults were designed to withstand the blasts from the inevitable nuclear war, and hold a few people for when the fallout had died down.
You play as a young man from Vault 101, born 200 years after the war. You escape your vault one day to find that the world above has been torn apart. Structures have been leveled, and rubble coats the barren, empty wasteland. Create a character that plays exactly how you want to, putting points into Stealth, Lockpicking, Science, Speech, Barter, etc. and travel the wasteland in search of your father. The biggest boast the Fallout franchise claims is that you have complete freedom in the world, meaning that everyone you run into can be interacted with differently, and everything that isn't tied down (or hard-coded) can be stolen, traded, sold, or blown up. Get it. It's awesome.

Chapter I. Bourgeois and Proletarians(1)
[German Original]
The history of all hitherto existing society(2) is the history of class struggles.
Freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guild-master(3) and journeyman, in a word, oppressor and oppressed, stood in constant opposition to one another, carried on an uninterrupted, now hidden, now open fight, a fight that each time ended, either in a revolutionary reconstitution of society at large, or in the common ruin of the contending classes.
In the earlier epochs of history, we find almost everywhere a complicated arrangement of society into various orders, a manifold gradation of social rank. In ancient Rome we have patricians, knights, plebeians, slaves; in the Middle Ages, feudal lords, vassals, guild-masters, journeymen, apprentices, serfs; in almost all of these classes, again, subordinate gradations.
The modern bourgeois society that has sprouted from the ruins of feudal society has not done away with class antagonisms. It has but established new classes, new conditions of oppression, new forms of struggle in place of the old ones.
Our epoch, the epoch of the bourgeoisie, possesses, however, this distinct feature: it has simplified class antagonisms. Society as a whole is more and more splitting up into two great hostile camps, into two great classes directly facing each other — Bourgeoisie and Proletariat.
From the serfs of the Middle Ages sprang the chartered burghers of the earliest towns. From these burgesses the first elements of the bourgeoisie were developed.
The discovery of America, the rounding of the Cape, opened up fresh ground for the rising bourgeoisie. The East-Indian and Chinese markets, the colonisation of America, trade with the colonies, the increase in the means of exchange and in commodities generally, gave to commerce, to navigation, to industry, an impulse never before known, and thereby, to the revolutionary element in the tottering feudal society, a rapid development.
The feudal system of industry, in which industrial production was monopolised by closed guilds, now no longer sufficed for the growing wants of the new markets. The manufacturing system took its place. The guild-masters were pushed on one side by the manufacturing middle class; division of labour between the different corporate guilds vanished in the face of division of labour in each single workshop.
Meantime the markets kept ever growing, the demand ever rising. Even manufacturer no longer sufficed. Thereupon, steam and machinery revolutionised industrial production. The place of manufacture was taken by the giant, Modern Industry; the place of the industrial middle class by industrial millionaires, the leaders of the whole industrial armies, the modern bourgeois.
Modern industry has established the world market, for which the discovery of America paved the way. This market has given an immense development to commerce, to navigation, to communication by land. This development has, in its turn, reacted on the extension of industry; and in proportion as industry, commerce, navigation, railways extended, in the same proportion the bourgeoisie developed, increased its capital, and pushed into the background every class handed down from the Middle Ages.
We see, therefore, how the modern bourgeoisie is itself the product of a long course of development, of a series of revolutions in the modes of production and of exchange.
Each step in the development of the bourgeoisie was accompanied by a corresponding political advance of that class. An oppressed class under the sway of the feudal nobility, an armed and self-governing association in the medieval commune(4): here independent urban republic (as in Italy and Germany); there taxable “third estate” of the monarchy (as in France); afterwards, in the period of manufacturing proper, serving either the semi-feudal or the absolute monarchy as a counterpoise against the nobility, and, in fact, cornerstone of the great monarchies in general, the bourgeoisie has at last, since the establishment of Modern Industry and of the world market, conquered for itself, in the modern representative State, exclusive political sway. The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.
The bourgeoisie, historically, has played a most revolutionary part.
The bourgeoisie, wherever it has got the upper hand, has put an end to all feudal, patriarchal, idyllic relations. It has pitilessly torn asunder the motley feudal ties that bound man to his “natural superiors”, and has left remaining no other nexus between man and man than naked self-interest, than callous “cash payment”. It has drowned the most heavenly ecstasies of religious fervour, of chivalrous enthusiasm, of philistine sentimentalism, in the icy water of egotistical calculation. It has resolved personal worth into exchange value, and in place of the numberless indefeasible chartered freedoms, has set up that single, unconscionable freedom — Free Trade. In one word, for exploitation, veiled by religious and political illusions, it has substituted naked, shameless, direct, brutal exploitation.
The bourgeoisie has stripped of its halo every occupation hitherto honoured and looked up to with reverent awe. It has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, the man of science, into its paid wage labourers.
The bourgeoisie has torn away from the family its sentimental veil, and has reduced the family relation to a mere money relation.
The bourgeoisie has disclosed how it came to pass that the brutal display of vigour in the Middle Ages, which reactionaries so much admire, found its fitting complement in the most slothful indolence. It has been the first to show what man’s activity can bring about. It has accomplished wonders far surpassing Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, and Gothic cathedrals; it has conducted expeditions that put in the shade all former Exoduses of nations and crusades.
The bourgeoisie cannot exist without constantly revolutionising the instruments of production, and thereby the relations of production, and with them the whole relations of society. Conservation of the old modes of production in unaltered form, was, on the contrary, the first condition of existence for all earlier industrial classes. Constant revolutionising of production, uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions, everlasting uncertainty and agitation distinguish the bourgeois epoch from all earlier ones. All fixed, fast-frozen relations, with their train of ancient and venerable prejudices and opinions, are swept away, all new-formed ones become antiquated before they can ossify. All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind.
The need of a constantly expanding market for its products chases the bourgeoisie over the entire surface of the globe. It must nestle everywhere, settle everywhere, establish connexions everywhere.
The bourgeoisie has through its exploitation of the world market given a cosmopolitan character to production and consumption in every country. To the great chagrin of Reactionists, it has drawn from under the feet of industry the national ground on which it stood. All old-established national industries have been destroyed or are daily being destroyed. They are dislodged by new industries, whose introduction becomes a life and death question for all civilised nations, by industries that no longer work up indigenous raw material, but raw material drawn from the remotest zones; industries whose products are consumed, not only at home, but in every quarter of the globe. In place of the old wants, satisfied by the production of the country, we find new wants, requiring for their satisfaction the products of distant lands and climes.

You ask: Is this another Minecraft-like block-building game or is there something different here?   My answer is Yes and Yes.  This is obviously a block building game in the Minecraft style, has many of the same gameplay elements of Minecraft, but given the many layers of polish and shine that only a much bigger budget can provide.
I'll start with the graphics.  While Minecraft's deferred shadows both made the game look stunning (especially in bigger builds) as well becoming an important part of gameplay (torches to light your caves/fortresses/etc), Lego Worlds actually looks darn photorealistic.  I spent the entire time in awe of how despite being a blocky, cartoonish world, it looked like a real physical place.  Animals in the world are not 'blocky' but have continuous non-jaggy surfaces that move very fluidly.
The 'blocks' are not simple squares but actual Lego pieces of different shapes including angled edges so there is a considerable greater level of detail in every scene.  The worlds appear to be procedural generated, but the algorithm chooses out of various Lego pieces, sometimes creating some really gorgeous looking patterns in the landscape.  You can paint bricks, which is rather awesome - I just hope they don't remove this feature for eventual multiplayer mode.
I haven't gotten into manual building yet but there are two prebuild sets you can drop in and watching them appear is a bit like watching a very fast 3D printer, cutting out a flat area then spraying the shapes into the scene.  One scene contains a lot of objects that your character can interact with like a BBQ, swimming pool and a house - I suspect there will be many many more of these.  One very cool aspect is that animals and vehicles are rideable and *extremely fun* - especially the car racing over hills.  I don't know if building custom vehicles is in the plans but that by itself would make this game worth 3x it's early release price.

The Lego game we always wanted.
The game plays like your standard TT Lego game, combat and stud collecting. The Differance comes as this is a sandbox Lego game, and everything ingame is made from Legos (destructabled, and digable, unlike the standard stagnet Lego game background). The worlds are randomly generated using a seed, with a "micro" build showing you a general idea of what the world is going to be like.
Combat. This is done is done like standard TT Lego games. You have a heart health bar, and basic character attacks. Skeletons are the main type of monster you'll currently face, and you have to beat villian characters to unlock.  Upon being defeated the player, enemy, or vehicle breaks apart. You do have weapons unlocks ingame (The bazooka can level anything), some being powerful, some being a banana. Aiming tends to be a little harder as the character doesn't attack the nearest, instead attacking the end of the mouse pointer. Also, you can climb or crawl about any surface.
Unlocks. Currently the game has only a few of the planned items ingame (Still quite alot). I have yet to see or hear anything about "special" bricks (typical for TT's Lego games, red block can give you bonus studs or abilities). You find weapons and item in chests (ability items like Binoculars don't currently work), after you have collected all currently ingame, the chests start giving lots of studs. Studs are used to unlock the things you have found, just like other TT Lego games. In game there are characters to unlock, not many right now, but they are from the "Minifigures" line giving great customizing option for both male and female. Unlocks include; Items, Vehicles, Animals (yes you can ulock and ride a dragon), Sets (actual lego sets), Brick Builds (basic structures), and props (plants, fences, ect.).
Open World. This is the big differance between the standard TT games, and makes the title worth the EA price alone. I have yet to find any limit in world except digging down, I have heard of people flying quite a distance in all other direction with no wall. The world isn't a stagnet background, its there in front of you, and built with legos (even the water). I haven't found anything that can't be destroyed. Its like having free reign over a lego world. The world feels like with a little work you could make a world that would rival one in the Lego Movie.
Building. Free building is the most difficult part of the game, while really not hard, it can be very overwhelming at times with its power. You can manipulate the train with some terrain tools, and you also have a free build mode with ALOT of lego elements, colors, and designs. I have't gotten to far into building just yet, but what I have played with are amazing. It would be nice if they added Lego IPs to the game; Ninjago, Ultra Agents, Monster Fighters, ect....
Multiplayer. None yet, it has been discussed. In my opinion, that would be the best thing they could add to this game for future features. Looking forward to it.
Lego Digital Designer Software & Steam Workshop. For those of us that use it, its compatable with Lego Worlds, you can bring /Some/ models into the game. With future implementation, this could be the greatest feature the game can have. LDD is software used to make digital Lego models inside a modeling program that's easy to use. That will mean lots of custom models being downloaded from steam, and brought ingame.
Goals. Currently none, no quests, nothing. But plans to have goals implemented are in the works
Cons. You will get game stutter after traveling alot and seeing the open wold, but for me it was never a constent thing, happening maybe once an hour. Camera, you view is indepentant of your character and does not follow behind, and has to be moved indepentant of movment, and while diving or flying while in motion alows very little movement to the camera. Opions, not too many mostly just basic grafics settings right now. Opimazation and a few camera options are the biggest need for the game.
Lego games have always held your had and walked you through a story, now they are alowing you to build your own world. With more tools, this has the promise to be one of the best sandbox building games ever. Even at the current price of $15 this game is more than worth it in its current EA state. Price for features this game rocks AAA titles, and would give it 4.5 stars out of 5.

I have always been a huge fan of Metroidvania games since the days of the original Metroid on the NES. It's hard not to compare a Metroidvania game to the likes of Super Metroid and Symphony of the NIght but I am here to tell you that Ori and the Blind Forest jumped into my top ten favorite games and I strongly feel it is a game of the year contender.
The first thing you will notice about the game is the beautiful, hand drawn visuals. Immediately following that you will hear the INCREDIBLE soundtrack. These two alone drew me into the world that the new comer Moon Studios has brought to the table.
The first ten minutes of the game. Many reviews on Steam claim that the first ten minutes of the game is one of the most heartfelt things to watch in gaming. This is not an exaggeration. I was crying by the end of the opening. I played through it again so I could show my wife. My wife was crying at the end of the first ten minutes.
The story is told though a disembodied voice that speaks in an unknown language. As you progress to different areas or come up to story points, this voice will narrate what is happening. The story has a very folk tale/fable like quality to it. Is there a lot of complexity? Not really. There are a few MINOR twists and turns but overall you will find the story satisfying if you walk in understanding that there are a lot of heartfelt, tried and true tropes.
The gameplay is classic Metroidvania. Open world concept, where you collect power ups for your health and energy, as well as collect various abilities that increase your options in combat and allow you access to newer, previously hard/impossible to reach areas. In addition, there are RPG elements: you collect spirit light, which turn into ability points when you collect enough. At save points (the game calls them soul links, which you can create almost anywhere you want) you can access three trees of abilities that you can level up.
The game can be quite challenging but the save system is so fluid that any death immediately respawns you with no load time to give you another shot. I found myself laughing when I died and not discouraged. It was trial and error: that didn't work, I'll get it this time. Or die again. And try again. And nothing feels better than finally clearing those escape scenes, which are absolutely thrilling.
The game averages about 8-12 hours, depending on your desire to explore (which should be strong since you never get tired of the beautifully drawn world or the soundtrack). That can be considered pretty short, but the top player on the leaderboards has beaten it in 27 minutes with 0 deaths. I beat it in 9 hours with 450 something deaths. Because spikes hurt (but not as bad as in a Megaman game).
I encourage everyone to try this game. It deserves the acclaim it has received and I hope more people get the chance to experience the world of Ori and the Blind Forest. It's $20. Do it.

This is a very mechanically solid Metroidvania platformer, elevated above its many peers by beautiful art and above-average sound design and writing. While there are no big gameplay innovations, Ori is one of the most well-rounded and polished platformers in recent memory.

Ori has become one of my all time favorites games.  It is incredible how much love Moon Studios has put into this title. What makes Ori really shine is how flawlessly every aspect of  the game is executed. The artwork, mechanics, map, puzzles, narrative, soundtrack, everything has so much attention to detail and thought put into it.
My background: I came into this game excited to play, but at the same time this is not my typical genre of gaming. From my very little experience with platformers I found them to be repetitive, require too much trial and error, and muscle memory. Despite these platformer aspects, Ori still managed to win my heart. There is so much variety in the different map areas that it does not get repetitive. There is a good balance between puzzle areas and skill-focused areas.
Coming in with very little platform experience I sucked. 25% of the way in, the Ginso Tree water esape stage took me about 4 hours to complete, which I'm sure the devs would not expect. I was very frusterated, and when I finally beat it, it was more of a "ugh, finally" than a feeling of satisfaction. Fortunately, after that, I learned a lot more quickly and did not have too much difficultly with the rest of the areas, even the final escape only took me about 30 minutes.
Besides that one moment of complete suckage, I felt the pacing for the game was very well done. The first 25% is pretty normal platform stuff, which I felt was the right amount of time needed to get a good grasp of the controls and core skills. After the first 25%, the game starts to pick up speed with skills being learned more frequently and areas getting much more crazy. Skills sets are reiterated throughout the game so you never forget what you previously learned. Ignore my time - it took me about 20 hours to complete, I did not rush, and I almost 100% the game..maybe like 96%.
Story: I loved the story and how it was interwoven into the game. It is a simple story, not the most original but still very well done. It is very disneyesque, a bit predicable, so if you're looking for some complicated deep story, this is not that kind of story. But very emotional, beautifully done, endearing, and yes. I criez every teim. (No really, I've watched the opening several times, and I cried almost every time.)
Critisism: I would no doubt give Ori a 11/10 rating, but ofcourse I have some thoughts I want to share. First of all, the controls. Please use a controller if you can. I played the first 25% with mouse and keyboard, ofcourse it is do-able, but controller is sooo much better. And this is coming from someone who has never owned a console (I borrowed a controller from a friend). Once I switched to controller the controls were so much more fluid, responsive and natural. I think I would be stuck on the water escape for a long time if I did not switch to controller after failing for 2 hours with mouse and keyboard. Second. I think the escape areas need an option for an easier mode, with more time before you die. Because not everyone is good at platformers, and not everyone wants to spend their time redoing the escapes over and over. Third, I wish the ending was a bit longer, since the beginning was about 10 minutes. Fourth, encountered two minor bugs, walking through a floor and walking through a rock, also getting stuck on spikes sometimes, but nothing that really impacted my gameplay. Fifth, the ability unlocks for life cells and energy cells showing up on the map are not very useful, because by the time you have enough point to unlock those, you have pretty much already found all the cells, if you are trying to collect. I would group those abilities and move them down on the ability tree.
Overall, 11/10. Simply an amazing experience that I will always cherish. I hope this game gets a lot more recognition.
